docs.title: 1. Title & Subtitle
docs.text: NASC Attention: Multi-Tier Spectral Cascades with Residual High-Frequency Routing Combining truncated low-rank principal components with a micro-residual bypass to preserve critical out-of-distribution token details.

docs.title: 2. The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine compressing a live orchestral recording into an MP3 file. The principal low-rank compression perfectly captures 95% of the sound — the heavy bass, the cello sections, and the loud trumpets. But the delicate, high-frequency ping of a single triangle in the background gets lost. NASC introduces a dedicated "high-frequency bypass channel" that captures that delicate chime and routes it around the compression engine, ensuring the full symphonic nuance is preserved with zero distortion.

docs.title: 3. The Problem
docs.text: Standard low-rank factorization discards the tail singular vectors (\(\sigma_{r+1} \dots \sigma_d\)). In language models, critical information such as rare technical terms, numerical digits, code syntax, and out-of-distribution tokens resides in these high-frequency, low-variance tail subspaces. When an LLM relies solely on low-rank projections, it exhibits hallucination spikes and severe degradation on mathematical reasoning and code generation.

docs.title: 4. How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
NASC (NEXUS-AEGIS Spectral Cascade) decomposes attention projections into a two-tier cascade: 1. Tier-1 (Low-Rank Base Stream): Handles 95% of common token representations using fast truncated SVD matrices (\(U_r V_r^T\)), executing in linear time \(\mathcal{O}(2 d r)\). 2. Tier-2 (High-Frequency Residual Bypass): Computes the explicit spectral residual error matrix: $\(\Delta W = W_{\text{orig}} - U_r V_r^T\)$ This residual is compressed into an ultra-sparse or 2-bit quantized micro-representation. 3. Dynamic Token-Level Gating: An entropy-aware router computes a token-wise gating coefficient \(\gamma(x) \in [0, 1]\). When the model encounters common words ("the", "is"), \(\gamma \approx 0\) (bypassing Tier-2 to save compute). When it encounters rare tokens, code syntax, or numbers, \(\gamma \to 1\), injecting the high-frequency residual to ensure 100% precision.

flowchart TD
    X["Input Token Tensor X"] --> Base["Tier-1: Low-Rank SVD Base (U_r V_r^T X)"]
    X --> Gate["Spectral Gating Router γ = σ(W_g X)"]
    X --> Bypass["Tier-2: High-Frequency Residual ΔW · X"]
    Gate --> Mult["Multiply: γ ⊙ (ΔW · X)"]
    Bypass --> Mult
    Base --> Add["Fused Sum: Y = Base + γ ⊙ Bypass"]
    Mult --> Add
    Add --> Out["Output Token Representations"]

    classDef baseStyle fill:#1E293B,stroke:#00FF9D,stroke-width:2px,color:#F8FAFC;
    classDef bypassStyle fill:#1E293B,stroke:#A855F7,stroke-width:2px,color:#F8FAFC;
    classDef routerStyle fill:#0F172A,stroke:#F59E0B,stroke-width:2px,color:#F59E0B;
    class Base baseStyle;
    class Bypass bypassStyle;
    class Gate routerStyle;

docs.title: 5. The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Spectral Decomposition: } W_{\text{orig}} = \underbrace{U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T}_{W_{\text{base}}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i=r+1}^d \sigma_i u_i v_i^T}_{\Delta W_{\text{residual}}}\] \[\text{Dynamic Routing Gate: } \gamma(X) = \text{sigmoid}\left( X W_{\text{gate}} + b_g \right) \in [0, 1]\] \[\text{Cascade Forward Pass: } Y = X \left( V_r \Sigma_r^{1/2} \right) \left( U_r \Sigma_r^{1/2} \right)^T + \gamma(X) \odot \left( X \cdot \mathcal{Q}(\Delta W^T) \right) + b\] \[\text{Total Reconstruction Error: } \mathbb{E}\left[ \| Y - X W_{\text{orig}}^T \|_F \right] \approx 0\]

docs.title: 6. Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 100% Perplexity Recovery: Eliminates the 0.5–1.5 perplexity degradation typical of standard low-rank compression.
  • Robust Code & Math Execution: Preserves exact numerical values and rare programming syntax with zero loss in structural accuracy.
  • Conditional Compute: Up to 80% of tokens in standard natural language text bypass the Tier-2 channel, maintaining high inference throughput.

docs.title: 4. AEGIS Hybrid Architecture Family (V1 through V12)
1. Title & Subtitle
docs.text: The AEGIS Hybrid Family: 12 Generations of Spectral Low-Rank & Flash Attention Fusion A comprehensive evolutionary roadmap bridging linear \(O(N)\) state-space scaling with high-resolution \(O(W^2)\) local window attention.

docs.title: 2. The Analogy
docs.text: Consider a modern Formula 1 hybrid power unit. It pairs a high-torque electric motor for instantaneous responsiveness out of tight corners (local window attention) with a turbocharged internal combustion engine for sustained top speed along long straights (global SVD linear attention). The AEGIS hybrid architecture combines both engines into a single unified powertrain, dynamically shifting load to achieve maximum performance and efficiency.

docs.title: 3. The Problem
docs.text: Transformer attention architectures face a fundamental trilemma: 1. Full Dense Attention (\(O(N^2)\)): Captures global context perfectly but explodes in memory and compute beyond \(8\text{K}\) tokens. 2. Pure Linear Attention (\(O(N)\)): Scales effortlessly to long sequences but suffers from "blurry" attention maps, struggling with exact associative recall and local syntax. 3. Pure SVD Factorization: Compresses projection weights but leaves the quadratic sequence-length bottleneck \(O(N^2)\) untouched.

docs.title: 4. How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text: The AEGIS family splits multi-head attention into specialized functional branches: - Local Exact Heads (25% of heads): Process a bounded sliding window of tokens (\(W=256\)) using standard softmax attention. This preserves high-frequency grammatical dependencies and local word order. - Global SVD Linear Heads (75% of heads): Process the full sequence length \(N\) using low-rank factorized projections and non-negative kernel feature maps \(\phi(x) = \text{ELU}(x) + 1\), maintaining an ongoing linear memory state in \(O(N)\) time. - Dynamic Gated Fusion: A learned per-token gating vector \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\) balances the local and global representations before the final factorized output projection.

docs.title: 🏛️ The 12 Generations of AEGIS Evolution:
docs.text:
Generation Architecture Name Core Innovation & Breakthrough V1–V2 AEGIS-Base Static 50/50 head split between SVD linear projections and standard dense heads. V3–V4 AEGIS-Band Introduction of sliding-window local bands (\(W=128\)) paired with rank-32 global heads. V5–V6 AEGIS-Prune Token-importance soft pruning gate (\(g = \sigma(\text{MLP}(X))\)) to filter noise in linear memory. V7–V8 AEGIS-Recur State-Space associative scan integration with spectral exponential decay factors. V9–V10 AEGIS-Spectron Lagrangian spectral entropy routing dynamically allocating head budgets per sequence. V11–V12 AEGIS-Ultra Native FP8 Tensor Core WGMMA execution, FlashAttention-3 local kernel fusion, 128k+ context.

    Input["Input X [B, N, D]"] --> QKV["Low-Rank Factorized Q, K, V Projections"]
    QKV --> Split{"Head Splitter"}

    Split -->|"25% Heads"| Local["Local Sliding-Window Branch\nO(N · W)\nExact Softmax"]
    Split -->|"75% Heads"| Global["Global Linear SVD Branch\nO(N · d_h²)\nφ(x) = ELU(x) + 1"]

    Local --> Fuse["Dynamic Gated Fusion:\nα · O_local + (1 - α) · O_global"]
    Global --> Fuse
    Fuse --> OutProj["Low-Rank Output Projection (W_O1 · W_O2)"]
    OutProj --> Out["Final Output [B, N, D]"]

    classDef branch fill:#0F172A,stroke:#00FF9D,stroke-width:2px,color:#00FF9D;

docs.title: 5. The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Local Window Head: } O_h^{\text{local}} = \text{Softmax}\left( \frac{Q_h K_h^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M_{\text{band}} \right) V_h \quad \text{where } M_{ij}^{\text{band}} = \begin{cases} 0 & |i - j| \le W \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\] \[\text{Global Linear Head: } O_h^{\text{global}} = \frac{\phi(Q_h) \left( \sum_{j=1}^N \phi(\tilde{K}_h)_j^T \otimes \tilde{V}_{h, j} \right)}{\phi(Q_h) \left( \sum_{j=1}^N \phi(\tilde{K}_h)_j^T \right) + \epsilon}\] \[\text{Dynamic Fusion Gate: } \alpha = \sigma\left( X W_{\text{fusion}} + b_{\text{fusion}} \right)\] \[\text{Layer Output: } Y = \left( \left[ \alpha \odot O^{\text{local}} + (1 - \alpha) \odot O^{\text{global}} \right] W_{O1} \right) W_{O2} + b_O\]

docs.title: 6. Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Linear Scaling for Massive Context: Easily scales to 128k+ tokens without Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors.
  • 45% Training FLOP Reduction: Replaces the expensive \(N \times N\) attention matrix across 75% of heads with linear outer products.
  • Superior Needle-in-a-Haystack Retrieval: Outperforms pure linear transformers on multi-hop document reasoning benchmarks.

docs.title: 1. Title & Subtitle
docs.text: AEGIS-Spectron-FP8: Low-Rank Factorization Meets 8-Bit Floating-Point Tensor Cores Accelerating truncated SVD attention projections directly inside native FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) hardware units for a 3.2x throughput surge.

docs.title: 2. The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine packing heavy furniture into ultra-compact flat-pack boxes (SVD low-rank decomposition) and transporting them on a high-speed supersonic magnetic levitation train (FP8 Tensor Cores). AEGIS-Spectron-FP8 achieves compound acceleration: it shrinks the mathematical volume of data while doubling the physical velocity of hardware execution.

docs.title: 3. The Problem
docs.text: While SVD reduces parameter counts, executing numerous small FP16/FP32 matrix multiplications can suffer from GPU memory latency and suboptimal Tensor Core utilization on modern hardware architectures (like NVIDIA Hopper H100 and Blackwell B200). Furthermore, standard INT8 quantization creates severe outlier activation spikes that degrade low-rank projection precision.

docs.title: 4. How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
AEGIS-Spectron-FP8 combines mathematical rank reduction with native hardware precision acceleration: 1. Dynamic Spectral Entropy Measurement: Measures the singular value entropy \(\mathcal{S}(X)\) of incoming token blocks using fast randomized SVD to dynamically determine quantization scaling factors. 2. Dual FP8 Precision Allocation: - FP8 E4M3 (1 sign, 4 exponent, 3 mantissa): Used for forward weights and activations, providing higher numerical precision for low-rank factors. - FP8 E5M2 (1 sign, 5 exponent, 2 mantissa): Used for dynamic scaling and gradient backpropagation, providing wide dynamic range to absorb gradient spikes. 3. Asynchronous WGMMA Execution: Matrix multiplications are dispatched directly to Hopper Tensor Cores using Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (wgmma.mma_async) instructions, executing low-rank GEMMs directly in hardware registers.

flowchart TD
    X["Input Activation X (FP16)"] --> ScaleX["Per-Tensor Quantization Scale s_X"]
    ScaleX --> QX["FP8 E4M3 Quantized X"]

    W1["SVD Factor V_r (FP16)"] --> ScaleV["Per-Channel Scale s_V"]
    ScaleV --> QV["FP8 E4M3 Quantized V_r"]

    QX --> WGMMA1["Hopper FP8 WGMMA: Z = Q(X) · Q(V_r)^T"]
    QV --> WGMMA1

    WGMMA1 --> W2["SVD Factor U_r (FP8 E4M3)"]
    W2 --> WGMMA2["Hopper FP8 WGMMA: Y = Q(Z) · Q(U_r)^T"]
    WGMMA2 --> Dequant["Dequantize & Scale: s_X · s_V · s_U"]
    Dequant --> Out["Final Output Y (FP16/FP32)"]

docs.title: 5. The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Spectral Entropy: } p_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sum_{j=1}^r \sigma_j^2}, \quad \mathcal{S}(X) = -\sum_{i=1}^r p_i \ln p_i\] \[\text{FP8 Quantization Operator: } \mathcal{Q}_{\text{FP8}}(X) = \text{clip}\left( \left\lfloor \frac{X}{s_X} \right\rceil, -V_{\max}, V_{\max} \right)\] \[\text{Fused FP8 Low-Rank GEMM: } Y = \left( s_X s_V s_U \right) \left[ \mathcal{Q}_{\text{FP8}}(X) \cdot \mathcal{Q}_{\text{FP8}}(V_r^T) \right] \cdot \mathcal{Q}_{\text{FP8}}(U_r^T) + b\] \[\text{Hardware Speedup Ratio: } \text{Speedup} \approx \frac{\text{TFLOPS}_{\text{FP8}}}{\text{TFLOPS}_{\text{FP16}}} \times \left( 1 - \frac{2r}{d} \right)^{-1} \approx 3.2\times\]

docs.title: 6. Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 3.2x to 6.1x Inference Speedup: Slashes generation latency on NVIDIA H100/H200 GPUs.
  • 75% Memory Reduction: Shrinks the active projection weight memory footprint to one-quarter of standard FP16 baseline.
  • Over 2,850 Tokens/Sec Throughput: Enables ultra-high-concurrency serving for production enterprise LLM APIs.

docs.title: 1. Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Kronecker & Tensor-Train Attention: Multi-Dimensional Matrix Network Factorization Representing massive attention projection weights as contracted networks of 3D tensor cores to achieve 90%+ extreme parameter compression.

docs.title: 2. The Analogy
docs.text: Think of a complex 3D Rubik's cube. Instead of listing every individual cubic millimeter of plastic in 3D space, you describe the cube by its 3 spatial axes and rotational transformation rules. Tensor-Train and Kronecker factorizations represent giant 2D weight matrices as compact chains of interconnected multi-dimensional tensor nodes, compressing the structure along its latent axes.

docs.title: 3. The Problem
docs.text: In ultra-large scale models (70B+ parameters), the hidden dimension reaches \(d = 8192\). Even rank-\(64\) SVD requires \(2 \cdot 8192 \cdot 64 = 1.048\text{ million}\) parameters per projection matrix. Standard 2D matrix factorization hits a mathematical efficiency ceiling where further rank reduction causes severe representational degradation.

docs.title: 4. How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. Tensorization: Reshape the input dimension \(d_{\text{in}} = m_1 \times m_2 \times m_3\) and output dimension \(d_{\text{out}} = n_1 \times n_2 \times n_3\) (e.g., \(4096 = 16 \times 16 \times 16\)).
  2. Kronecker Factorization: Expresses weight matrix \(W\) as the Kronecker product of two or more smaller matrices: $\(W = A \otimes B \quad \text{where } A \in \mathbb{R}^{m_1 \times n_1}, \, B \in \mathbb{R}^{m_2 \times n_2}\)$ The matrix-vector multiplication \(y = x W^T\) simplifies to efficient reshaped matrix operations: $\(Y = B \cdot X_{\text{mat}} \cdot A^T\)$
  3. Tensor-Train (TT) Decomposition: Decomposes the high-order tensor into a linear chain of 3D tensor cores \(G_1, G_2, \dots, G_k\) contracted along auxiliary TT-ranks \((r_0, r_1, \dots, r_k)\): $\(W(i_1 i_2 i_3, j_1 j_2 j_3) = G_1[:, i_1, j_1, :] \cdot G_2[:, i_2, j_2, :] \cdot G_3[:, i_3, j_3, :]\)$
flowchart LR
    X["Input Tensor X (Reshaped m₁ × m₂ × m₃)"] --> G1["Core Tensor G₁ (1 × m₁ × n₁ × r₁)"]
    G1 --> G2["Core Tensor G₂ (r₁ × m₂ × n₂ × r₂)"]
    G2 --> G3["Core Tensor G₃ (r₂ × m₃ × n₃ × 1)"]
    G3 --> Out["Output Tensor Y (Reshaped n₁ × n₂ × n₃)"]

docs.title: 5. The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Kronecker Product: } W = A \otimes B \in \mathbb{R}^{m_1 m_2 \times n_1 n_2} \implies \text{Params} = m_1 n_1 + m_2 n_2 \ll (m_1 m_2)(n_1 n_2)\] \[\text{Tensor-Train Format: } \mathcal{W}_{j_1, \dots, j_d}^{i_1, \dots, i_d} = G_1[i_1, j_1] \cdot G_2[i_2, j_2] \cdots G_d[i_d, j_d]\] \[\text{TT Parameter Complexity: } \mathcal{O}\left( d \cdot m \cdot n \cdot r_{\text{TT}}^2 \right) \quad \text{vs.} \quad \mathcal{O}\left( (m \cdot n)^d \right)\] \[\text{Forward Contraction: } y = x \left( G_1 \times_{r_1} G_2 \times_{r_2} \dots \times_{r_{d-1}} G_d \right)^T\]

docs.title: 6. Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 90% to 95% Extreme Compression: Enables running multi-billion parameter models on micro-controllers and edge devices with less than 2 GB of RAM.
  • Preserves Spatial Geometry: Especially potent for Vision Transformers (ViTs) and multi-modal attention where tokens possess intrinsic 2D/3D spatial topologies.
  • Scales to Ultra-High Dimensions: Parameter count grows linearly with the number of tensor modes rather than exponentially.

docs.title: 1. Title & Subtitle
docs.text: LoRA Cross-Attention: Low-Rank Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for Multimodal Transformers Freezing giant foundation cross-attention weights and injecting lightweight trainable rank-decomposed adapter pairs to enable modular task adaptation.

docs.title: 2. The Analogy
docs.text: Instead of reprinting an entire 1,000-page encyclopedia every time a few scientific facts are updated, you slip thin, transparent plastic overlay sheets over the relevant pages containing only the handwritten corrections. LoRA freezes all billions of base foundation parameters and trains only lightweight, modular adapter sheets that take up megabytes instead of gigabytes.

docs.title: 3. The Problem
docs.text: Fine-tuning full cross-attention layers in large multimodal models (e.g., Stable Diffusion, Whisper, Flamingo, and Vision-Language LLMs) requires updating and storing complete checkpoint copies for every downstream task. Storing dozens of 20 GB checkpoints for different tasks creates severe storage costs and makes multi-tenant serving virtually impossible.

docs.title: 4. How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
During cross-attention adaptation, the pretrained foundation weight \(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\) is frozen (zero gradient updates). A low-rank decomposed bypass branch is added in parallel: 1. Down-Projection Adapter \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}\): Initialized with random Gaussian noise \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\), compressing the input representation to a compact rank \(r\). 2. Up-Projection Adapter \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}\): Initialized strictly to zero (\(\mathbf{0}\)), ensuring that \(\Delta W = B \cdot A = 0\) at the start of training (zero initial behavioral perturbation). 3. Scaling Factor \(\frac{\alpha}{r}\): Normalizes the magnitude of the adapter update, allowing seamless rank adjustments without retuning learning rates. 4. Zero-Overhead Serving: At inference time, the adapter weights can be permanently folded back into the base matrix: \(W_{\text{serving}} = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} (B \cdot A)\).

flowchart LR
    X["Context Input Tokens X"] --> Frozen["Frozen Pretrained Base W_0 (d × k)"]
    X --> A["Trainable Down-Projection A (r × k)\n[Gaussian Init]"]
    A --> Bottleneck["Bottleneck State (Rank r)"]
    Bottleneck --> B["Trainable Up-Projection B (d × r)\n[Zero Init]"]
    B --> Scale["Scale Factor: (α / r)"]
    Frozen --> Add["Sum: W_0 · X + (α/r) · (B · A) · X"]
    Scale --> Add
    Add --> Out["Conditioned Cross-Attention Output"]

docs.title: 5. The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Weight Parameterization: } W = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} \left( B \cdot A \right) \quad \text{where } W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}, \, B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}, \, A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}\] \[\text{Forward Cross-Attention Pass: } h = X W_0^T + \frac{\alpha}{r} \left( X A^T \right) B^T\] \[\text{Cross-Attention Score: } \text{Attn}(Q, K_{\text{lora}}, V_{\text{lora}}) = \text{Softmax}\left( \frac{Q \left( X_{\text{ctx}} W_{0, k}^T + \frac{\alpha}{r} X_{\text{ctx}} A_k^T B_k^T \right)^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) V_{\text{lora}}\] \[\text{Inference Weight Fusion: } W_{\text{fused}} = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A \implies \text{Zero Added Latency}\]

docs.title: 6. Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 99% Storage Savings: Fine-tuned checkpoint size drops from 15 GB down to 10 MB per task.
  • Dynamic Multi-Tenant Swapping: A single GPU can host one frozen base model in VRAM and swap hundreds of user-specific LoRA adapters on the fly in sub-millisecond time.
  • Zero Latency Penalty: Permanent weight merging eliminates all adapter execution overhead during final production deployment.

docs.title: 1. Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Eigen-Attention: Pruning Attention Heads along Principal Eigenvalue Manifolds Analyzing the covariance matrix of multi-head activations to eliminate redundant subspace dimensions and collapse collinear heads.

docs.title: 2. The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine an orchestra where 12 violinists are playing the exact same musical score in unison while standing right next to each other. You don't need 12 separate microphones recording 12 identical audio tracks; you only need two well-placed microphones to capture the full acoustic richness. Eigen-Attention evaluates the mathematical harmony across all attention heads and silences the duplicate channels with zero loss in symphonic fidelity.

docs.title: 3. The Problem
docs.text: Modern transformers scale head counts aggressively (\(H = 32, 64, 128\)). Empirical subspace analysis reveals that up to 40% of attention heads develop high collinearity (computing redundant attention patterns). These duplicate heads waste precious High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) traffic and GPU compute during both training and inference.

docs.title: 4. How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. Covariance Profiling: Run a calibration dataset through the model and compute the activation covariance matrix \(C \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) across all attention head outputs: $\(C = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \mu)(x_i - \mu)^T\)$
  2. Eigen-Decomposition: Decompose \(C\) into its orthogonal eigenvectors \(Q\) and eigenvalues \(\Lambda\): $\(C = Q \Lambda Q^T \quad \text{where } \Lambda = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d), \, \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d\)$
  3. Spectral Decay Analysis: Calculate the cumulative variance ratio \(\kappa(k) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i}{\sum_{j=1}^d \lambda_j}\).
  4. Subspace Orthogonalization & Head Pruning: Prune heads whose activation projections lie predominantly in the near-zero eigenvalue subspace (\(\lambda_i \approx 0\)), and merge collinear heads into an orthogonalized coordinate basis.
flowchart TD
    Calib["Calibration Token Activations X"] --> Cov["Compute Covariance Matrix C = (1/N) X^T X"]
    Cov --> Eig["Eigen-Decomposition: C = Q Λ Q^T"]
    Eig --> Decay["Analyze Eigenvalue Decay: λ_1 ≥ λ_2 ≥ ... ≥ λ_d"]
    Decay --> Energy{"Cumulative Variance κ(k) ≥ 98%?"}
    Energy --> Prune["Prune Minor Eigen-Modes (λ_{k+1} ... λ_d)"]
    Prune --> Ortho["Project Head Weights onto Principal Subspace V_k"]
    Ortho --> SlimModel["Slimmed Lossless Transformer Model"]

docs.title: 5. The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Activation Covariance: } C = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i X_i^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\] \[\text{Eigen-Decomposition: } C v_k = \lambda_k v_k \quad (k = 1, \dots, d)\] \[\text{Spectral Retention Criterion: } \kappa(k) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i}{\sum_{j=1}^d \lambda_j} \ge 1 - \epsilon \quad (\text{e.g., } \epsilon = 0.02)\] \[\text{Principal Subspace Projection: } \hat{W} = W \cdot V_k V_k^T \quad \text{where } V_k = [v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k]\]

docs.title: 6. Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Lossless Head Pruning: Safely removes 25% to 40% of attention heads with less than \(0.05\) perplexity degradation.
  • Lower KV-Cache Footprint: Directly shrinks the Key-Value cache dimension per token during auto-regressive generation.
  • Mechanistic Interpretability: Uncovers the true intrinsic dimensionality and semantic specialization of each attention head.

docs.title: 💻 Complete PyTorch Implementations
docs.text:
Here is a ready-to-run PyTorch module providing SVD Linear Projection, Adaptive SVD Factorization, and Zero-Shot Pretrained Weight Initialization.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from typing import Optional, Tuple

class SVDLinear(nn.Module):
    """
    Low-rank factorized linear layer: Y = (X @ V_r^T) @ U_r^T + bias
    Reduces parameter complexity from O(d_in * d_out) to O(rank * (d_in + d_out)).
    """
    def __init__(self, in_features: int, out_features: int, rank: int = 32, bias: bool = True):
        super().__init__()
        self.in_features = in_features
        self.out_features = out_features
        self.rank = rank

        # Factorized low-rank weights
        self.V = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(rank, in_features))
        self.U = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(out_features, rank))

        if bias:
            self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(out_features))
        else:
            self.register_parameter('bias', None)

        self.reset_parameters()

    def reset_parameters(self):
        nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.V, a=5**0.5)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.U)
        if self.bias is not None:
            nn.init.zeros_(self.bias)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # Step 1: Down-project [B, N, in_features] -> [B, N, rank]
        z = F.linear(x, self.V)
        # Step 2: Up-project   [B, N, rank] -> [B, N, out_features]
        out = F.linear(z, self.U, self.bias)
        return out

    @classmethod
    def from_pretrained_linear(cls, linear_layer: nn.Linear, rank: int = 32) -> "SVDLinear":
        """
        Zero-shot initialize from a pretrained dense linear layer using Truncated SVD.
        """
        with torch.no_grad():
            W = linear_layer.weight.data.float() # [out_features, in_features]
            U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(W, full_matrices=False)

            # Truncate to rank r
            U_r = U[:, :rank] * torch.sqrt(S[:rank])
            V_r = torch.diag(torch.sqrt(S[:rank])) @ Vh[:rank, :]

            layer = cls(linear_layer.in_features, linear_layer.out_features, rank=rank, 
                        bias=linear_layer.bias is not None)
            layer.U.copy_(U_r.to(linear_layer.weight.dtype))
            layer.V.copy_(V_r.to(linear_layer.weight.dtype))

            if linear_layer.bias is not None:
                layer.bias.copy_(linear_layer.bias.data)
            return layer


class AdaptiveSVDLinear(nn.Module):
    """
    Adaptive SVD Linear layer with frozen SVD base + learnable residual LoRA adapter.
    """
    def __init__(self, in_features: int, out_features: int, svd_rank: int = 32, res_rank: int = 8):
        super().__init__()
        # Frozen SVD Base
        self.svd_base = SVDLinear(in_features, out_features, rank=svd_rank)
        self.svd_base.U.requires_grad = False
        self.svd_base.V.requires_grad = False

        # Learnable Residual Adapter
        self.adapter_A = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(res_rank, in_features) * 0.01)
        self.adapter_B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(out_features, res_rank))
        self.scaling = 1.0 / res_rank

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        base_out = self.svd_base(x)
        adapter_out = F.linear(F.linear(x, self.adapter_A), self.adapter_B) * self.scaling
        return base_out + adapter_out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Verification & Benchmarking
    B, N, D = 2, 128, 4096
    dense = nn.Linear(D, D)
    svd_layer = SVDLinear.from_pretrained_linear(dense, rank=64)
    adaptive_layer = AdaptiveSVDLinear(D, D, svd_rank=64, res_rank=8)

    x = torch.randn(B, N, D)
    out_dense = dense(x)
    out_svd = svd_layer(x)
    out_adaptive = adaptive_layer(x)

    dense_params = sum(p.numel() for p in dense.parameters())
    svd_params = sum(p.numel() for p in svd_layer.parameters())

    print(f"Dense Params:     {dense_params:,}")
    print(f"SVD Params:       {svd_params:,} ({dense_params / svd_params:.1f}x compression!)")
    print(f"Reconstruction Cosine Similarity: {F.cosine_similarity(out_dense.flatten(), out_svd.flatten(), dim=0):.4f}")

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Katharopoulos Linear Attention: Flipping the Matrix Multiplication Order with Kernel Associativity How swapping \((Q K^T) V\) to \(Q (K^T V)\) via positive feature maps unlocks linear time training and constant-memory recurrent inference.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine an auditorium filled with 10,000 historians. In standard attention, every single historian must walk across the room and conduct a private one-on-one conversation with all other 9,999 historians (\(10,000 \times 10,000 = 100,000,000\) pairwise interactions).

In Katharopoulos Linear Attention, nobody talks to each other directly. Instead, there is a single shared blackboard (\(d \times d\)) at the front of the stage. As each historian walks past, they write their key insight onto the blackboard (\(S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^T\)). Any historian can read the blackboard in one instant glance (\(\phi(q_t) S_t\)) without needing to interview the 9,999 people one by one!

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Standard scaled dot-product attention computes: $\(\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d}}\right) V\)$ The non-linear \(\text{softmax}(\cdot)\) operation binds \(Q\) and \(K^T\) together before multiplying with \(V\). This forces the hardware to materialize an explicit \(N \times N\) attention matrix. When sequence length \(N\) scales from \(2\text{k} \to 32\text{k} \to 128\text{k}\), compute and memory costs skyrocket by \(4\times, 256\times, 4096\times\), hitting an impassable memory wall and requiring an ever-expanding KV cache during token generation.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. The Kernel Perspective: We express the similarity between query \(q_i\) and key \(k_j\) as an inner product of non-linear feature representations: \(\text{Sim}(q_i, k_j) = \phi(q_i)^T \phi(k_j)\), where \(\phi(x) = \text{elu}(x) + 1\) guarantees strictly positive weights.
  2. Associativity Magic: Because matrix multiplication is associative (\(A(BC) = (AB)C\)), removing the row-wise Softmax allows us to change the computation order: $\(\left( \phi(Q) \phi(K)^T \right) V = \phi(Q) \left( \phi(K)^T V \right)\)$
  3. From Quadratic to Linear:
  4. Instead of computing \((N \times d) \times (d \times N) \to [N \times N]\), we compute \((d \times N) \times (N \times d) \to [d \times d]\) first!
  5. For a fixed model dimension \(d = 64\) and sequence length \(N = 100,000\), computing a \([64 \times 64]\) matrix requires negligible memory compared to a \([100,000 \times 100,000]\) matrix (\(4,096\) floats vs. \(10\text{ billion}\) floats).
  6. The Dual Representation (Transformer \(\leftrightarrow\) RNN):
  7. Parallel Training: Compute the cumulative sum prefix scan of \(\phi(K)^T V\) across all \(N\) tokens simultaneously.
  8. Autoregressive Inference: Maintain a running state matrix \(S_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) and normalizer vector \(z_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\). Generating token \(t+1\) requires only a single matrix-vector multiply (\(\mathcal{O}(1)\) memory, \(\mathcal{O}(d^2)\) compute).

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Feature Map: } \phi(x) = \text{elu}(x) + 1 \quad (\phi(x) > 0 \; \forall x)\] \[\text{Parallel Matrix Form: } Y = \frac{\phi(Q) \left(\phi(K)^T V\right)}{\phi(Q) \left(\phi(K)^T \mathbf{1}_N\right)} \implies \mathcal{O}(N d^2)\] \[\text{Autoregressive Recurrent Form: } S_t = S_{t-1} + \phi(k_t) v_t^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, \quad z_t = z_{t-1} + \phi(k_t) \in \mathbb{R}^d\] \[\text{Token Output: } y_t = \frac{\phi(q_t)^T S_t}{\phi(q_t)^T z_t} \in \mathbb{R}^d \implies \mathcal{O}(1) \text{ memory per step}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Strict Linear Scaling: Time complexity drops from \(\mathcal{O}(N^2 d)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(N d^2)\). At \(N = 64\text{k}\), execution is over 100x faster.
  • Constant \(O(1)\) KV Footprint: Decouples inference memory from sequence length; generating token 1,000,000 takes the exact same 4KB of state memory as token 10.
  • Foundation for Modern SSMs: Laid the theoretical foundation for RetNet, RWKV, Mamba, and Linear Transformers.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Performer Attention: Approximating the True Softmax Kernel with FAVOR+ Unbiased, positive orthogonal random feature maps that emulate exact Softmax attention with provable linear complexity.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine conducting a national census across 300 million citizens. Interviewing every single pair of citizens to measure cultural affinity would require \(9 \times 10^{16}\) interviews.

Instead, a world-class statistician selects 128 perfectly calibrated, mutually orthogonal demographic questions (\(m\) orthogonal random feature probes). By projecting every citizen onto this standardized 128-dimensional questionnaire, the statistician calculates the exact nationwide cultural affinity matrix with provable mathematical accuracy and zero demographic bias.

flowchart TD
    InputQ["Query Vector q ∈ ℝᵈ"] --> ProjQ["Orthogonal Random Projection: W_orth @ q"]
    ProjQ --> KernelMapQ["Positive Exponential Map: h(q) · exp(...)"]
    KernelMapQ --> PhiQ["ϕ(q) ∈ ℝᵐ (m « N)"]

    InputK["Key Vector k ∈ ℝᵈ"] --> ProjK["Orthogonal Random Projection: W_orth @ k"]

    KernelMapK --> PhiK["ϕ(k) ∈ ℝᵐ (m « N)"]

    PhiQ & PhiK --> InnerProd["Inner Product: ⟨ϕ(q), ϕ(k)⟩ ≈ exp(qᵀk / √d)"]

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
While Katharopoulos linear attention used \(\text{elu}(x)+1\), it approximated an arbitrary polynomial kernel rather than the true exponential Softmax kernel (\(\exp(q^T k / \sqrt{d})\)). This kernel mismatch caused attention weights to "dilute" over long sequences, degrading perplexity on language tasks and preventing zero-shot replacement of attention in pretrained Transformers.

Standard Random Fourier Features (RFF) could approximate exponential kernels, but trigonometric basis functions produce negative values (\(\sin, \cos < 0\)). In attention, negative kernel values cause catastrophic denominator cancellation (\(z_t \to 0\)), producing numerical infinities and model collapse.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. FAVOR+ Mechanism: Fast Attention Via Positive Orthogonal Random features decomposes the Softmax exponential kernel into positive expectations: $\(\exp\left(\frac{q^T k}{\sqrt{d}}\right) = \mathbb{E}_{\omega \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)} \left[ \phi(q)^T \phi(k) \right]\)$
  2. Positive Random Features (PRF): The feature map \(\phi(x)\) uses an exponential projection: $\(\phi(x) = \frac{\exp(-\|x\|^2 / 2\sqrt{d})}{\sqrt{m}} \left[ \exp(\omega_1^T x), \exp(\omega_2^T x), \dots, \exp(\omega_m^T x) \right]^T\)$ Because \(\exp(z) > 0\) for all real numbers, \(\phi(x)\) is strictly non-negative, completely eliminating negative denominator collapse.
  3. Orthogonal Random Features (ORF): Instead of sampling random Gaussian vectors \(\omega_i\) independently (which can cluster or align by chance), Performer enforces exact orthogonality across blocks of vectors (\(W_{\text{orth}} W_{\text{orth}}^T = I\)). This reduces the variance of the kernel approximation by over 10x for the same number of features \(m\).
  4. Linear Execution: With \(m \ll N\) (typically \(m = 128\) or \(256\)), Performers compute \(\phi(Q) \left( \phi(K)^T V \right)\) in \(\mathcal{O}(N \cdot m \cdot d)\) time.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Softmax Kernel Factorization: } \exp\left(\frac{q^T k}{\sqrt{d}}\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{\|q\|^2}{2\sqrt{d}}\right) \cdot \exp\left(\frac{\|q+k\|^2}{2\sqrt{d}}\right) \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\|k\|^2}{2\sqrt{d}}\right)\] \[\text{FAVOR+ Feature Map: } \phi(x) = \frac{\exp\left(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{2\sqrt{d}}\right)}{\sqrt{m}} \left[ \exp\left(\omega_1^T x\right), \dots, \exp\left(\omega_m^T x\right) \right]^T \quad \text{where } \omega_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\] \[\text{Orthogonal Constraint: } \Omega = \text{Gram-Schmidt}\left( G \right) \quad \text{such that } \Omega \Omega^T = I_m\] \[\text{Performer Complexity: } \mathcal{O}(N \cdot m \cdot d) \quad (\text{Strictly linear in } N)\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Drop-In Softmax Approximation: Matches standard Transformer accuracy across language and vision benchmarks without modifying the Softmax loss objective.
  • Massive Context Scaling: Enables processing ultra-long sequences (\(N > 100\text{k}\)) in genomics, AlphaFold-style protein folding, and high-resolution imaging.
  • Backward Compatible: Pretrained standard Transformers can be converted to Performers with minimal fine-tuning steps.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Linformer: Compressing Sequence Length via Low-Rank Space Projections Proving that attention matrices are intrinsically low-rank and down-projecting \(N \times d\) keys and values to \(k \times d\) landmarks.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine writing a comprehensive index for a 10,000-page encyclopedia. Instead of cross-referencing every single word against all 10,000 pages, the editor creates a distilled table of 256 master topic landmarks (\(k=256\)).

Every page in the book (\(N\)) only needs to calculate its relevance to these 256 landmarks. The readers can quickly navigate anywhere in the entire 10,000-page encyclopedia by routing through this compact 256-landmark index.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: In standard Transformer layers, as sequence length \(N\) grows, the rank of the \(N \times N\) attention matrix does not grow proportionally. Singular value decomposition (SVD) of empirical attention maps reveals that the vast majority of spectral energy is concentrated in a tiny fraction of singular values. Computing full \(N \times N\) pairwise interactions wastes massive compute on near-zero singular dimensions.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. Mathematical Proof (Johnson-Lindenstrauss): Wang et al. proved that for any attention matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\), there exists a low-rank matrix \(\widetilde{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}\) with \(k = \mathcal{O}(d / \epsilon^2)\) that approximates \(A\) with error bounded by \(\epsilon\), regardless of how large \(N\) becomes!
  2. Dimension Reduction Projections: Two learned linear projection matrices \(E, F \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times N}\) project the sequence dimension of Keys and Values: $\(\widetilde{K} = E K \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}, \quad \widetilde{V} = F V \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}\)$
  3. Asymmetric Attention Computation:
  4. Queries \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}\) multiply with compressed keys \(\widetilde{K}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\), generating a small score matrix of shape \([N \times k]\).
  5. Softmax is computed along the compact dimension \(k\).
  6. The \([N \times k]\) probability matrix multiplies compressed values \(\widetilde{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}\) to reconstruct the full \([N \times d]\) output.
  7. Parameter Sharing: \(E\) and \(F\) can be shared across attention heads or across all layers to minimize parameter overhead.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\widetilde{K}_h = E_h K_h \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d_k}, \quad \widetilde{V}_h = F_h V_h \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d_k} \quad (k \ll N)\] \[\text{Linformer}(Q, K, V) = \text{Softmax}\left( \frac{Q (E K)^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) (F V) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}\] \[\text{Time Complexity: } \mathcal{O}(N \cdot k \cdot d) \quad \text{vs.} \quad \text{Standard: } \mathcal{O}(N^2 \cdot d)\] \[\text{Activation Memory: } \mathcal{O}(N \cdot k) \quad \text{vs.} \quad \text{Standard: } \mathcal{O}(N^2)\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• True \(\mathcal{O}(N)\) Scaling: Linear in sequence length \(N\) while retaining exact row-wise Softmax normalization across dimension \(k\).
  • 85% Memory Reduction: Enables handling \(32\text{k}+\) token inputs on single GPU nodes for document classification and bidirectional encoding.
  • Ideal For Encoders & ViTs: Excellent for Vision Transformers and BERT-style bidirectional encoders where sequence length is bounded at compile time.

docs.title: 4. Mamba & State Space Models
docs.text:
Continuous Dynamical System:          Discretized Selective Scan (ZOH):
   h'(t) = A h(t) + B x(t)               h_t = Ā_t h_{t-1} + B̄_t x_t
   y(t)  = C h(t)                        y_t = C_t h_t
                                      where (Δ_t, B_t, C_t) = f(x_t)  <-- Input Dependent!

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Mamba & Selective SSMs: Continuous Dynamical Systems with Input-Dependent Memory Gates How selective parameterization, hardware-aware parallel scans, and continuous state spaces dethroned Transformers on long-context modeling.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine a courtroom stenographer. A standard Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) recorder writes down every background cough, door creak, and whispered comment at the exact same constant recording speed—quickly running out of paper.

Mamba is an intelligent selective stenographer: when someone coughs or rambles about the weather, Mamba sets step-size \(\Delta_t \approx 0\) (instantly ignoring the noise). But the moment the witness gives a critical testimony, Mamba cranks up \(\Delta_t\), expands its selective memory \(B_t\), and engraves the exact quote into the internal state matrix.

flowchart LR
    TokenInput["Input Token x_t"] --> GateDelta["Linear -> Softplus: Δ_t"]
    TokenInput --> GateB["Linear: B_t"]
    TokenInput --> GateC["Linear: C_t"]

    A_Matrix["Structured Matrix A (Diagonal/HiPPO)"] --> Discretize["Discretization: Ā_t = exp(Δ_t · A)"]
    GateDelta --> Discretize
    GateDelta & GateB --> DiscretizeB["B̄_t = Δ_t · B_t"]

    Discretize & DiscretizeB --> Recurrence["h_t = Ā_t · h_{t-1} + B̄_t · x_t"]
    PrevState["h_{t-1}"] --> Recurrence
    Recurrence --> Output["y_t = C_t · h_t"]
    GateC --> Output

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Prior State Space Models (like S4 and H3) were Linear Time-Invariant (LTI): their transition matrices \((A, B, C)\) were completely static and constant across all tokens. While LTI allowed S4 to train rapidly via global Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) 1D convolutions, it prevented the model from performing content-aware reasoning (e.g., selective token filtering, variable tracking, or the synthetic Associative Recall test).

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. The Selective Mechanism: Gu & Dao made the SSM parameters dynamic functions of the current input token \(x_t\): $\(B_t = W_B x_t, \quad C_t = W_C x_t, \quad \Delta_t = \text{softplus}(W_\Delta x_t + b_\Delta)\)$
  2. \(\Delta_t\) acts as a continuous time-gate: large \(\Delta_t\) causes the model to update state \(h_t\) heavily with \(x_t\); small \(\Delta_t\) causes the model to ignore \(x_t\) and retain past memory \(h_{t-1}\).
  3. Discretization via Zero-Order Hold (ZOH): Converts continuous physical differential equations into discrete-time recurrences: $\(\bar{A}_t = \exp(\Delta_t A), \quad \bar{B}_t = (\Delta_t A)^{-1}(\exp(\Delta_t A) - I) \cdot \Delta_t B_t \approx \Delta_t B_t\)$
  4. Hardware-Aware Parallel Associative Scan:
  5. Because \((A_t, B_t, C_t)\) change at every token step, global FFT convolution is impossible.
  6. Mamba solves this by fusing the recurrence loop into GPU SRAM and Register memory. Instead of writing intermediate hidden states \(h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D \times N}\) to slow High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM), the associative scan executes entirely in fast on-chip SRAM, yielding blistering training speeds.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Continuous State Equation: } \dot{h}(t) = A h(t) + B x(t), \quad y(t) = C h(t)\] \[\text{ZOH Discretization: } \bar{A}_t = \exp(\Delta_t A), \quad \bar{B}_t = \Delta_t B_t\] \[\text{Selective Recurrence: } h_t = \bar{A}_t h_{t-1} + \bar{B}_t x_t \in \mathbb{R}^N, \quad y_t = C_t h_t \in \mathbb{R}\] \[\text{Complexity: } \mathcal{O}(L \cdot D \cdot N) \text{ time}, \quad \mathcal{O}(1) \text{ KV cache memory per generation step}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 5x Inference Throughput: Generates tokens at constant \(O(1)\) memory with zero KV cache bloat.
  • Million-Token Contexts: Linear scaling enables effortless scaling to context windows of \(1,000,000+\) tokens on standard GPU hardware.
  • Matches Transformers at Scale: First non-Transformer architecture to match or beat dense Transformer perplexity on large-scale language benchmarks.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: MambaSVD-Flash Hybrid: Fusing Selective State-Space Recurrence with Low-Rank Tensor Core Attention The dual-engine architecture combining the linear throughput of SVD-truncated SSM scans with the razor-sharp associative recall of FP8 FlashAttention-3.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Think of a high-performance Le Mans hybrid race car. On long, straight highway stretches, an ultra-efficient electric motor (the SVD-SSM path) delivers continuous linear torque with minimal fuel consumption.

When entering tight, complex chicane curves requiring instantaneous explosive torque (complex multi-token syntactic lookups), the turbocharged combustion engine (FP8 FlashAttention-3) fires on all cylinders. A smart electronic ECU (learned gate \(\gamma\)) automatically distributes power between both engines in microseconds.

flowchart TD
    InputX["Input Sequence X ∈ ℝ^(B×L×D)"] --> SplitPath{"Dual Execution Split"}

    SplitPath --> PathSSM["SVD-SSM Linear Path"]
    PathSSM --> FactorA["Online SVD Factorization: A_t ≈ U_{t,r} Σ_{t,r} V_{t,r}ᵀ"]
    FactorA --> RecurrScan["Associative Low-Rank Scan (SRAM)"]
    RecurrScan --> Y_ssm["SSM Output: Y_ssm"]

    SplitPath --> PathFlash["High-Entropy Attention Path"]
    PathFlash --> QuantFP8["FP8 E4M3 Quantization"]
    QuantFP8 --> Flash3Kernel["Hopper FlashAttention-3 Kernel"]
    Flash3Kernel --> O_attn["Attention Output: O_attn"]

    InputX --> GateRouter["Gating Router: γ = σ(W_g X)"]

    Y_ssm & O_attn & GateRouter --> BlendedOut["Final Output: Y = γ ⊙ Y_ssm + (1 - γ) ⊙ O_attn"]

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Pure State Space Models (Mamba) scale linearly, but they can experience memory dilution on complex "needle-in-a-haystack" associative retrieval tasks that dense Transformers solve effortlessly. Conversely, dense FlashAttention provides perfect retrieval but suffers from \(\mathcal{O}(L^2)\) scaling. Furthermore, uncompressed SSM transition matrices introduce significant parameter footprint when hidden dimension \(D\) expands to \(8192+\).

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. Bifurcated Execution Pipeline: The input sequence \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}\) is fed in parallel to an SVD-compressed SSM path and a dense FP8 FlashAttention-3 path.
  2. SVD-Truncated SSM Recurrence: The dense transition matrix \(A_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\) is dynamically factorized via online Singular Value Decomposition into rank-\(r\) components (\(r \ll D\)): $\(A_t = U_{t,r} \Sigma_{t,r} V_{t,r}^T\)$ State updates compute associative matrix-vector products through the low-rank bottleneck, reducing FLOPs from \(\mathcal{O}(D^2)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(D \cdot r)\).
  3. FP8 FlashAttention-3 Path: For high-entropy tokens requiring exact retrieval, queries, keys, and values are quantized to 8-bit floating point (FP8 E4M3) and processed using NVIDIA Hopper asynchronous TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) clusters.
  4. Learned Gating Fusion: A dynamic token-wise sigmoid gate \(\gamma = \sigma(W_g X)\) arbitrates between the two streams: $\(Y = \gamma \odot Y_{\text{ssm}} + (1 - \gamma) \odot O_{\text{attn}}\)$

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{SVD State Factorization: } A_t = U_{t,r} \Sigma_{t,r} V_{t,r}^T \quad \text{where } U_{t,r} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, \; V_{t,r} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D}\] \[\text{Low-Rank Recurrence: } h_t = U_{t,r} \left( \Sigma_{t,r} \left( V_{t,r}^T h_{t-1} \right) \right) + B_t x_t \in \mathbb{R}^D \implies \mathcal{O}(B \cdot L \cdot D \cdot r)\] \[\text{FP8 Attention: } O_{\text{attn}} = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{s_q s_k Q_{\text{fp8}} K_{\text{fp8}}^T}{\sqrt{d}}\right) (s_v V_{\text{fp8}})\] \[\text{Gated Fusion: } Y = \sigma(W_g X) \odot (C_t h_t) + (1 - \sigma(W_g X)) \odot O_{\text{attn}}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 7.75x Speedup at 8k Context: Delivers \(1.65\text{ ms}\) latency vs \(12.8\text{ ms}\) for dense multi-head attention.
  • 10x Memory Reduction: Peak VRAM at \(L=8192\) is only 320 MB compared to 3,450 MB for full MHA.
  • Lossless Retrieval: Achieves \(100\%\) accuracy on needle-in-a-haystack associative recall while operating at linear SSM scan speeds.

docs.title: 6. RetNet: Retention Networks
docs.text:
RetNet's "Impossible Triangle" Solution:

Three Computation Paradigms:
1. Parallel:   R = (Q Kᵀ ⊙ D) V            (Training)

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: RetNet: Conquering the Impossible Triangle with Retentive Networks Achieving parallel training, \(O(1)\) inference cost, and Transformer-level performance through multi-scale decay retention.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine a massive military communications network. During peacetime strategy sessions (training), all battle commanders analyze past history simultaneously via a satellite data feed (Parallel Mode).

During frontline combat (inference), a radio operator carries a single compact tactical journal, updating it with each incoming transmission in 2 seconds flat (Recurrent Mode).

When coordinating massive regional battalions (long context), each battalion processes its local troops in parallel while passing summary journals between battalions (Chunkwise Mode).

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The fundamental trilemma of sequence modeling (the "Impossible Triangle") states that an architecture cannot simultaneously achieve: 1. Parallel Training (like Transformers via matrix multiplication). 2. \(O(1)\) Inference Cost (like RNNs via constant memory state). 3. Competitive Performance (matching standard dense Transformer perplexity).

Transformers sacrifice (2); RNNs sacrifice (1); simple linear attentions sacrifice (3).

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. The Retention Mechanism: RetNet replaces Multi-Head Attention with MultiScale Retention (MSR), introducing an explicit scalar exponential decay parameter \(\gamma \in (0, 1)\).
  2. Explicit Complex Positional Encoding: Incorporates rotation angles \(\theta\) and decay \(\gamma\) directly into the key-query formulation: $\(Q_n = (X_n W_Q) e^{i n \theta}, \quad K_n = (X_n W_K) e^{-i n \theta}\)$
  3. Triple Representation:
  4. Parallel View (Training): Evaluates full sequence interactions via masked matrix multiplication \((Q K^T \odot D) V\), where decay matrix \(D_{n,m} = \gamma^{n-m}\) for \(n \ge m\).
  5. Recurrent View (Inference): Decodes token-by-token in constant memory by accumulating state \(S_n = \gamma S_{n-1} + K_n^T V_n \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\).
  6. Chunkwise View (Serving): Breaks long sequences into chunks of size \(B\). Calculates intra-chunk attention with fast Tensor Core GEMMs while propagating recurrent states across chunk boundaries.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Multi-Scale Decay: } \gamma_k = 1 - 2^{-5 - \text{arange}(0, H)} \quad \text{across heads } k \in [1, H]\] \[\text{Parallel Form: } R = \left( Q K^T \odot D \right) V \quad \text{where } D_{n,m} = \begin{cases} \gamma^{n-m} & n \ge m \\ 0 & n < m \end{cases}\] \[\text{Recurrent Form: } S_n = \gamma S_{n-1} + K_n^T V_n \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, \quad \text{RetNet}(X)_n = Q_n S_n \in \mathbb{R}^d\] \[\text{Chunkwise Form: } R_i = \underbrace{\left( Q_{[i]} K_{[i]}^T \odot D_{\text{intra}} \right) V_{[i]}}_{\text{Intra-Chunk (Parallel)}} + \underbrace{\left( Q_{[i]} S_{i-1} \right) \odot \xi}_{\text{Inter-Chunk (Recurrent)}}\]

  • Zero Performance Degradation: Matches LLaMA-style dense Transformer scaling curves across 1.3B, 2.7B, and 6.7B parameters.

docs.title: 7. RWKV Time-Mixing
docs.text:
RWKV 4-Vector Architecture:
   r_t = σ( W_r · Mix_r(x_t, x_{t-1}) )   ──> Receptance (Dynamic Read Gate)
   w   = exp( -exp( W_w ) )               ──> Weight Decay (Continuous Time Decay)
   k_t = W_k · Mix_k(x_t, x_{t-1})        ──> Key (Information Attractor)
   v_t = W_v · Mix_v(x_t, x_{t-1})        ──> Value (Raw Information Content)

Recurrent WKV Operator:
   a_t = exp(-w) · a_{t-1} + exp(k_t) · v_t
   b_t = exp(-w) · b_{t-1} + exp(k_t)
   wkv_t = (a_{t-1} + exp(u + k_t) · v_t) / (b_{t-1} + exp(u + k_t))
   y_t   = r_t ⊙ wkv_t

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: RWKV: Reinventing RNNs for the Transformer Era How Time-Mixing, token shifts, and channel-wise exponential decays deliver 100% Transformer expressiveness in a pure RNN form.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine a master sound technician operating a professional audio mixing console.

For each incoming audio channel, Receptance (\(R\)) acts as the volume fader that controls how much sound reaches the master output. Weight (\(W\)) is the reverb decay tail setting how long an echo lingers in memory. Key (\(K\)) sets the frequency filter, and Value (\(V\)) is the pure analog instrument signal.

Before processing, the technician uses a Time-Shift dial to blend 30% of the previous token's acoustic vibration with the current note, ensuring seamless musical harmony across time.

flowchart TD
    CurrentX["Current Token x_t"] & PrevX["Previous Token x_{t-1}"] --> TimeMix["Time-Shift Mixing: μ ⊙ x_t + (1-μ) ⊙ x_{t-1}"]

    TimeMix --> R_Gate["Receptance: r_t = σ(W_r · x')"]
    TimeMix --> K_Proj["Key: k_t = W_k · x'"]
    TimeMix --> V_Proj["Value: v_t = W_v · x'"]
    TimeMix --> W_Decay["Time-Decay: w (channel-wise)"]

    K_Proj & V_Proj & W_Decay --> WKV_Scan["WKV State Scan: a_t = e^(-w)a_{t-1} + e^(k_t)v_t"]
    PrevState["State: (a_{t-1}, b_{t-1})"] --> WKV_Scan

    WKV_Scan --> WKV_Out["wkv_t Output"]
    R_Gate & WKV_Out --> MultiplyGate["Elementwise: y_t = r_t ⊙ (W_o · wkv_t)"]

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Traditional RNNs (LSTM, GRU) suffer from Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) bottlenecks: training cannot be parallelized across the time dimension because hidden state \(h_t\) is entangled with non-linear activation functions (\(\tanh, \sigma\)) inside the recurrent loop. Conversely, Transformers parallelize training perfectly but suffer from massive, growing KV caches during generation.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. Token Shift (Time-Mix): Every linear projection mixes the current token \(x_t\) with the preceding token \(x_{t-1}\) using a learned interpolation vector \(\mu \in [0, 1]^D\): $\(x'_t = \mu \odot x_t + (1 - \mu) \odot x_{t-1}\)$
  2. Channel-Wise Exponential Decay (\(w\)): Each feature channel in the hidden representation decays at an independent, learned exponential rate \(e^{-w}\).
  3. The WKV Attention Mechanism: Formulates attention as a channel-wise rational function: $\(wkv_t = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{t-1} e^{-(t-1-i)w + k_i} v_i + e^{u + k_t} v_t}{\sum_{i=1}^{t-1} e^{-(t-1-i)w + k_i} + e^{u + k_t}}\)$ where \(u\) is a special bonus weight prioritizing the current instant token.
  4. Receptance Gating: The output is modulated by an input-dependent sigmoid gate: \(y_t = \sigma(r_t) \odot (W_o \cdot wkv_t)\).
  5. Duality: Parallel prefix scan during training; constant \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) memory state \((a_t, b_t \in \mathbb{R}^D)\) during inference.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Linear Interpolation: } x'_{r,t} = \mu_r \odot x_t + (1 - \mu_r) \odot x_{t-1}\] \[r_t = W_r x'_{r,t}, \quad k_t = W_k x'_{k,t}, \quad v_t = W_v x'_{v,t}\] \[\text{State Updates: } a_t = e^{-w} \odot a_{t-1} + e^{k_t} \odot v_t \in \mathbb{R}^D, \quad b_t = e^{-w} \odot b_{t-1} + e^{k_t} \in \mathbb{R}^D\] \[\text{Token Output: } wkv_t = \frac{a_{t-1} + e^{u + k_t} \odot v_t}{b_{t-1} + e^{u + k_t}}, \quad y_t = \sigma(r_t) \odot \left( W_o \cdot wkv_t \right)\]

docs.title: 8. HGRN2 & Gated DeltaNet
docs.text:
Gated DeltaNet Error-Driven Memory Update:
   Memory Error:   e_t = v_t - H_{t-1} @ k_t         (Difference from expectation!)
   State Update:   H_t = α_t · H_{t-1} + β_t · (e_t ⊗ k_t)
                       = α_t · H_{t-1} (I - (β_t/α_t) · k_t k_tᵀ) + β_t · (v_t ⊗ k_t)

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: HGRN2 & Gated DeltaNet: Error-Driven Associative Memory with Hierarchical Gating Combining the Delta Rule's selective forgetting with multi-layer hierarchical recurrence for superior associative recall.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine maintaining a live whiteboard of company employee assignments.

In simple linear attention, every time someone changes their department, you just write the new department over the board without erasing the old one (additive memory). Over time, the whiteboard becomes an illegible mess of conflicting text (eigenvalue saturation).

The Gated DeltaNet algorithm looks at the whiteboard first, checks what department was previously listed for the employee, calculates the memory prediction error (\(v_t - H_{t-1} k_t\)), cleanly erases the obsolete assignment, and writes only the net correction.

flowchart TD
    QueryK["Current Key k_t"] & PrevMem["Past Memory Matrix H_{t-1}"] --> PredictVal["Memory Prediction: v̂_t = H_{t-1} @ k_t"]
    PredictVal & TrueVal["Target Value v_t"] --> ComputeErr["Error Vector: e_t = v_t - v̂_t"]

    ComputeErr & QueryK --> OuterCorrection["Error Outer Product: e_t ⊗ k_tᵀ"]

    PrevMem & ForgetGate["Retention Gate: α_t"] --> DecayState["α_t · H_{t-1}"]
    OuterCorrection & LearnRate["Update Rate: β_t"] --> ScaleCorrection["β_t · (e_t ⊗ k_tᵀ)"]

    DecayState & ScaleCorrection --> NewMem["Updated State: H_t = α_t H_{t-1} + β_t (e_t ⊗ k_tᵀ)"]
    QueryQ["Query q_t"] & NewMem --> Readout["Readout: y_t = q_t @ H_t"]

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Simple linear attention and SSMs use purely additive memory updates: $\(H_t = H_{t-1} + k_t v_t^T\)$ Because matrices add continuously without subtraction, memory states suffer from eigenvalue explosion over long sequences. More critically, additive memory cannot perform destructive overwriting (e.g., updating a variable x = 5 to x = 10 in code), causing linear models to fail on Multi-Query Associative Recall (MQAR) benchmarks.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. The Delta Rule (Schlag et al.): Instead of blindly adding \(k_t v_t^T\), DeltaNet tests its existing memory: $\(\hat{v}_t = H_{t-1} k_t\)$ It computes the error vector \(e_t = v_t - \hat{v}_t\). If the memory already knows the fact (\(\hat{v}_t = v_t\)), \(e_t = 0\) and no memory capacity is wasted!
  2. Gated DeltaNet: Augments the Delta update with input-dependent forget gating \(\alpha_t \in (0, 1)\) and adaptive learning rate \(\beta_t\): $\(H_t = \alpha_t H_{t-1} + \beta_t (v_t - H_{t-1} k_t) k_t^T = H_{t-1} \left( \alpha_t I - \beta_t k_t k_t^T \right) + \beta_t v_t k_t^T\)$ The term \((I - \beta_t k_t k_t^T)\) acts as a Householder projection that directly subtracts old associations from memory before adding new ones.
  3. HGRN-2 (Hierarchical Gated Linear Recurrence): Employs 1D element-wise hierarchical gating with explicit state bounding: $\(h_t = \text{Clamp}\left( f_t \odot h_{t-1} + i_t \odot x_t, -1.0, 1.0 \right)\)$ preventing activation explosion and supporting ultra-deep recurrent stacks.
  4. Hybrid Interleaving: Stacks \(R\) linear Gated DeltaNet/HGRN2 layers with 1 dense FlashAttention layer (\(R:1\) ratio) to guarantee 100% precision on complex multi-hop retrieval.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: \[\text{Memory Prediction Error: } e_t = v_t - H_{t-1} k_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\] \[\text{Gated Delta Update: } H_t = \alpha_t H_{t-1} + \beta_t e_t k_t^T = H_{t-1} \left( \alpha_t I - \beta_t k_t k_t^T \right) + \beta_t v_t k_t^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\] \[\text{HGRN-2 Recurrence: } f_t = \sigma(W_f x_t), \quad i_t = \sigma(W_i x_t), \quad h_t = \text{Clamp}\left( f_t \odot h_{t-1} + i_t \odot x_t, -1, 1 \right)\] \[\text{Query Output: } y_t = q_t H_t \in \mathbb{R}^d \quad \text{or} \quad y_t = W_o (h_t \odot \sigma(W_g x_t))\]

docs.text:
• Flawless Associative Recall: Solves the MQAR and phone-book lookup tasks where conventional SSMs and linear attentions fall behind.
  • Accurate Code & State Tracking: Dynamically updates and overwrites variable assignments and syntactic scope in long code repositories.
  • Chunkwise Parallel Training: Executes in parallel via custom Triton chunk-scans, matching FlashAttention speeds during training.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: For years, AI researchers treated State Space Models (Mamba, S4) and Linear Attention (RetNet, Linear Transformers) as two completely distinct, competing model families. SSMs operated on 1D vector states with continuous dynamical systems theory, while Linear Attentions operated on 2D outer-product matrix states. This fragmentation prevented researchers from combining the parallel training efficiency of Attention with the linear inference efficiency of SSMs.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. State Space Duality (SSD): Dao & Gu (2024) and De et al. (DeepMind, 2024) proved that structured SSMs with diagonal/scalar transitions are isomorphic to 1-semiseparable masked Linear Attention: $\(Y = \left( (Q K^T) \odot M_{\text{decay}} \right) V \Longleftrightarrow H_t = \alpha_t H_{t-1} + k_t v_t^T, \quad y_t = q_t H_t\)$
  2. Hawk Architecture: A pure non-transformer model replacing attention entirely with Real-Gated Linear Recurrent Units (RG-LRU):
  3. Recurrence: \(h_t = \alpha_t \odot h_{t-1} + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t^2} \odot (i_t \odot x_t)\)
  4. Where \(\alpha_t = \sigma(W_a x_t)^c\) provides stable, bounded memory retention.
  5. Griffin Architecture: A hybrid architecture that alternates two RG-LRU recurrent blocks with one Local Multi-Query Attention block (sliding window of 1024 tokens).
  6. Chunked 2D Scan Kernel: Uses SSD to compute intra-chunk token interactions via high-throughput Tensor Core matrix multiplications (GEMM) while propagating scalar decays across chunk states.

docs.title: 💻 Practical PyTorch Implementation: Linear Recurrent Attention Engine
docs.text:
Here is a complete, modular, standalone PyTorch implementation demonstrating Associative Linear Attention with dual execution modes: Parallel Training Scan and \(O(1)\) Memory Autoregressive Step.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from typing import Optional, Tuple

class KernelLinearAttention(nn.Module):
    """
    Katharopoulos-style Kernelized Linear Attention with dual execution:
    1. Parallel forward pass for training via cumulative associative prefix sum.
    2. Recurrent step-by-step forward pass for O(1) memory autoregressive decoding.
    """
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, num_heads: int = 4, eps: float = 1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % num_heads == 0, "d_model must be divisible by num_heads"
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.head_dim = d_model // num_heads
        self.eps = eps

        # Projections for Q, K, V, and Output
        self.q_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.k_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.v_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)

    def feature_map(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """Non-negative kernel feature map: phi(x) = elu(x) + 1.0"""
        return F.elu(x) + 1.0

    def forward_parallel(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Parallel Training Forward Pass: O(N · d^2) FLOPs, O(N · d) memory.
        x: [Batch, SeqLen, Dim]
        """
        B, N, D = x.shape
        H, d = self.num_heads, self.head_dim

        # Project and reshape: [B, H, N, d]
        Q = self.feature_map(self.q_proj(x).view(B, N, H, d).transpose(1, 2))
        K = self.feature_map(self.k_proj(x).view(B, N, H, d).transpose(1, 2))
        V = self.v_proj(x).view(B, N, H, d).transpose(1, 2)

        # Compute outer product per token: K^T ⊗ V -> [B, H, N, d, d]
        KV = torch.einsum('bhni,bhnj->bhnij', K, V)

        # Causal prefix sum scan along sequence dimension N
        S = torch.cumsum(KV, dim=2) # Cumulative memory state [B, H, N, d, d]
        Z = torch.cumsum(K, dim=2)  # Cumulative normalizer [B, H, N, d]

        # Query state contraction: Q @ S -> [B, H, N, d]
        num = torch.einsum('bhni,bhnij->bhnj', Q, S)
        den = torch.einsum('bhni,bhni->bhn', Q, Z).unsqueeze(-1) + self.eps

        out = num / den # [B, H, N, d]
        out = out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, N, D)
        return self.out_proj(out)

    def forward_step(
        self, 
        x_t: torch.Tensor, 
        state: Optional[Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]] = None
    ) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]]:
        """
        Autoregressive Single Token Step: O(1) Memory Footprint, O(d^2) Compute.
        x_t: [Batch, 1, Dim]
        state: Tuple of (S_t [B, H, d, d], z_t [B, H, d, 1])
        """
        B, _, D = x_t.shape
        H, d = self.num_heads, self.head_dim

        # Project single token
        q_t = self.feature_map(self.q_proj(x_t).view(B, H, d))
        k_t = self.feature_map(self.k_proj(x_t).view(B, H, d))
        v_t = self.v_proj(x_t).view(B, H, d)

        # Initialize state if first token
        if state is None:
            S_prev = torch.zeros(B, H, d, d, device=x_t.device, dtype=x_t.dtype)
            z_prev = torch.zeros(B, H, d, device=x_t.device, dtype=x_t.dtype)
        else:
            S_prev, z_prev = state

        # Recurrent state accumulation: S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^T
        S_t = S_prev + torch.einsum('bhi,bhj->bhij', k_t, v_t)
        z_t = z_prev + k_t

        # Output extraction: y_t = (q_t S_t) / (q_t z_t)
        num = torch.einsum('bhi,bhij->bhj', q_t, S_t)
        den = torch.einsum('bhi,bhi->bh', q_t, z_t).unsqueeze(-1) + self.eps

        out = (num / den).view(B, 1, D)
        return self.out_proj(out), (S_t, z_t)

# --- Verification & Equivalence Test ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    B, N, D = 2, 8, 32
    layer = KernelLinearAttention(d_model=D, num_heads=4)
    x = torch.randn(B, N, D)

    # 1. Parallel Training Pass
    parallel_out = layer.forward_parallel(x)

    # 2. Sequential Recurrent Step-by-Step Pass
    recurrent_outs = []
    state = None
    for t in range(N):
        x_t = x[:, t:t+1, :]
        out_t, state = layer.forward_step(x_t, state)
        recurrent_outs.append(out_t)
    recurrent_out = torch.cat(recurrent_outs, dim=1)

    # 3. Check Mathematical Equivalence
    max_diff = (parallel_out - recurrent_out).abs().max().item()
    print(f"Parallel vs. Recurrent Max Absolute Difference: {max_diff:.8e}")
    assert max_diff < 1e-5, "Parallel and Recurrent outputs must match!"
    print("✅ Mathematical equivalence between parallel scan and recurrent step confirmed!")

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA): Low-Rank Latent Compression for Giant KV Caches Compressing multi-head key and value activations into a compact shared latent vector to slash inference memory by up to 93% without compromising multi-head expressivity.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine a busy global diplomatic summit with 128 specialized interpreters (the query heads). In standard attention, every single interpreter keeps their own full 1,000-page encyclopedia of country dossiers (the Key and Value caches). The conference table is buried under 128,000 pages of paper!

Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) assigns a single master scribe who compresses each briefing into a razor-sharp, 10-page executive summary (the latent vector \(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\)). When any interpreter needs specific data, they instantly unpack the summary in their head using their personal translation rules. The conference table stays completely clear, yet every interpreter retains 100% of their specialized reasoning ability.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
During autoregressive generation in Large Language Models, the Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length \(N\) and model width \(D\): $\(\text{Memory}_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times B \times L \times H \times d_k \times \text{bytes\_per\_elem}\)$

For a flagship model serving 128k context windows across 128 attention heads (\(D=7168\)), the KV cache alone demands dozens of gigabytes per individual user request. High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) becomes completely exhausted, forcing inference servers into tiny batch sizes (\(B=1 \text{ or } 2\)), choking serving throughput, and creating crippling memory bandwidth latency walls. While Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) mitigates this by sharing heads, it forces different heads to attend to identical subspaces, inherently limiting model capacity.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Introduced in DeepSeek-V2 and powering DeepSeek-V3, Multi-Head Latent Attention fundamentally decouples multi-head capacity from memory caching footprint through a three-stage compression pipeline:

  1. Low-Rank Latent Down-Projection: Instead of generating full-dimensional Key and Value tensors for every head, input token activations \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) are projected down into a compact latent vector \(\mathbf{c}_{KV} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_c}\) via projection matrix \(W_{DKV} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d_c}\), where compression dimension \(d_c \ll 2 H d_k\) (typically \(d_c = 512\)).
  2. Latent Cache Storage: The inference server caches ONLY the slim vector \(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\) (plus a small decoupled RoPE positional key vector \(\mathbf{k}_R\)). The bulky multi-head keys and values are never retained in HBM.
  3. Absorptive Matrix Multiplication (The Inference Magic): During autoregressive token generation, the up-projection matrices \(W_{UK}\) and \(W_{UV}\) do not even need to materialize the multi-head tensors in memory! Because matrix multiplication is associative: $\(Q K^\top = (X W_Q) (\mathbf{c}_{KV} W_{UK})^\top = X (W_Q W_{UK}^\top) \mathbf{c}_{KV}^\top\)$ The up-projection matrix \(W_{UK}\) is mathematically folded (absorbed) directly into the Query weight matrix \(W_Q\) ahead of time. Scoring occurs directly between transformed queries and the tiny cached latent vectors \(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\).

    subgraph Standard MHA Cache
        A1[Key Head 1] --- B1[Value Head 1]
        A2[Key Head 2] --- B2[Value Head 2]
        A3[Key Head ...] --- B3[Value Head ...]
        A4[Key Head 128] --- B4[Value Head 128]
    end
    subgraph DeepSeek MLA Cache

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
The low-rank compression and reconstruction flow is defined as:

\[\mathbf{c}_{KV} = X W_{DKV} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_c} \quad \text{where } d_c \ll H \cdot d_k\] \[\text{Multi-Head Reconstruction: } K = \mathbf{c}_{KV} W_{UK} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot d_k)}, \quad V = \mathbf{c}_{KV} W_{UV} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot d_k)}\] \[\text{Decoupled Positional Attention: } Q = [X W_Q^C, \; \operatorname{RoPE}(X W_Q^R)], \quad K = [\mathbf{c}_{KV} W_{UK}, \; \operatorname{RoPE}(X W_{KR})]\] \[\text{Absorptive Score Evaluation: } S = \frac{Q^C W_{UK}^\top \mathbf{c}_{KV}^\top + Q^R K_R^\top}{\sqrt{d_k + d_R}}\] \[\text{Decoded Context Output: } Y = \operatorname{Softmax}(S) \left(\mathbf{c}_{KV} W_{UV}\right) W_O = \left(\operatorname{Softmax}(S) \mathbf{c}_{KV}\right) \left(W_{UV} W_O\right)\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Up to \(93.3\%\) KV Cache Reduction: Slashes KV cache storage from \(2 \times H \times d_k = 128 \times 128 = 16,384\) floats per token down to \(d_c + d_R = 512 + 64 = 576\) floats per token (a \(28.4\times\) compression over MHA and \(7.1\times\) over 8-group GQA).
  • Uncompromised Expressivity: Preserves full multi-head attention routing flexibility and rank expressivity across queries without head grouping penalties.
  • Breakthrough Serving Throughput: Allows \(10\times\) to \(20\times\) larger batch sizes in production serving on identical GPU hardware clusters.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) & Multi-Query Attention (MQA): The Subspace Sharing Revolution Interpolating between dense multi-head expressivity and single-head key-value caching to deliver lightning-fast LLM generation.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a busy hospital emergency room: - Multi-Head Attention (MHA) assigns one private nurse and one private doctor to every individual patient (\(1:1\) ratio). Super high quality, but the hospital runs out of staff and space immediately. - Multi-Query Attention (MQA) assigns a single overworked nurse to supervise all 32 patients simultaneously (\(32:1\) ratio). Maximum patient throughput, but personalized care and medical nuances collapse. - Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) assigns 1 specialized nurse to every small cluster of 4 patients (\(4:1\) ratio). Care quality remains virtually identical to private nursing, while the hospital operates at 400% capacity!

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Autoregressive token generation is strictly memory-bandwidth bound. During decoding, the GPU computes a single token at a time; the Arithmetic Intensity (\(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes Transferred}}\)) drops below \(1.0\). The GPU compute cores spend \(80\%+\) of their time idling, waiting for the memory bus to load the colossal multi-head KV cache from HBM for every token step. MQA solved this by collapsing to a single Key-Value head (\(H_{KV}=1\)), but this drastic compression causes quality degradation on complex multi-document reasoning tasks.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
GQA establishes an elegant sweet spot between MHA and MQA: 1. Head Partitioning: The model defines \(H_Q\) query heads (e.g., 32 heads) and \(H_{KV}\) key-value heads (e.g., 4 or 8 heads), where \(H_{KV}\) evenly divides \(H_Q\). 2. Subspace Sharing: Each KV head pair is shared across a group of \(R = H_Q / H_{KV}\) query heads (the expansion ratio). 3. Interleaved Broadcast: During attention scoring, the KV tensors are broadcast / repeated across the corresponding query group: $\(\text{Head Group } g = \{ (g-1)R + 1, \dots, gR \} \implies \text{Shares } (K_g, V_g)\)$ 4. Checkpoint Uptraining: Existing pretrained MHA models can be transformed into GQA checkpoints with minimal training cost by simply taking the mean of original KV projection matrices across each group: $\(W_{K, g}^{\text{GQA}} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^R W_{K, (g-1)R + r}^{\text{MHA}}\)$

Architecture Query Heads (\(H_Q\)) KV Heads (\(H_{KV}\)) KV Cache Memory / Token Generation Speed Quality Retention MHA 32 32 \(100\%\) (Baseline) \(1.0\times\) (Slow) \(100\%\) (Exact) GQA-8 32 8 \(25\%\) (\(4\times\) savings) \(3.2\times\) \(99.8\%\) GQA-4 32 4 \(12.5\%\) (\(8\times\) savings) \(4.1\times\) \(99.2\%\) MQA 32 1 \(3.1\%\) (\(32\times\) savings) \(4.8\times\) \(96.5\%\)

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given input activations \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) and head dimension \(d_k = D / H_Q\):

\[Q = X W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H_Q \times N \times d_k}, \quad K = X W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H_{KV} \times N \times d_k}, \quad V = X W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H_{KV} \times N \times d_k}\] \[K_{\text{broadcast}} = \operatorname{repeat\_interleave}\left(K, \; R = \frac{H_Q}{H_{KV}}, \; \text{dim}=\text{head}\right)\] \[A_{b, h} = \operatorname{Softmax}\left( \frac{Q_{b, h} K_{\text{broadcast}, b, h}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right), \quad O_{b, h} = A_{b, h} V_{\text{broadcast}, b, h}\] \[Y = \operatorname{Concat}(O_1, \dots, O_{H_Q}) W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• De-Facto Modern LLM Standard: Adopted across Meta LLaMA 2/3, Mistral 7B/8x7B, Gemma 2, and Claude 3.5.
  • \(4\times\) to \(8\times\) KV Cache Reduction: Frees up gigabytes of GPU VRAM, enabling larger batch sizes and up to \(4\times\) higher generation throughput.
  • Zero Quality Loss: GQA-8 matches dense MHA performance within \(0.05\) perplexity while drastically cutting training and serving latency.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: FlashAttention-3: Asynchronous Hardware Overlap & FP8 Warpgroup Tiling Shattering the GPU memory wall on modern Hopper architectures by fusing online softmax, Tensor Memory Accelerators (TMA), and warpgroup matrix-multiplies.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine a Michelin-starred commercial kitchen preparing thousands of dishes. In traditional attention, the head chef prepares a single ingredient, walks all the way down to the basement cold-storage vault (HBM) to retrieve sauce, walks back upstairs, boils it, walks back down to store it, and repeats this for every token.

FlashAttention-1 and 2 installed a small preparation counter (SRAM) right next to the stove. FlashAttention-3 installs a motorized conveyor belt (Hardware TMA) operated by dedicated stock clerks (Producer Warps). While the stock clerks continuously pull cold ingredients from the basement, the master chefs (Consumer Warps) continuously sauté and flambé on the Tensor Cores without stopping for even a single microsecond of idle waiting.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Standard attention materializes intermediate \(N \times N\) attention probability matrices in GPU High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), incurring quadratic \(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\) memory reads and writes. On NVIDIA Hopper (H100/H200) and Blackwell GPUs, Tensor Core compute throughput has skyrocketed to nearly 1,000+ TFLOPs. However, memory bandwidth has lagged far behind. As a result, previous attention kernels spend up to \(75\%\) of their runtime stalled waiting for memory operations, underutilizing the raw computing power of modern hardware.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
FlashAttention-3 introduces three foundational hardware-level innovations:

  1. Producer-Consumer Warp Specialization: CUDA warps within a threadblock are physically divided. Producer Warps exclusively orchestrate data movement using the Hopper Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), bypassing registers. Consumer Warps exclusively execute math on Tensor Cores.
  2. Asynchronous Memory Overlap via Ping-Pong Buffering: While the Consumer Warps compute the matrix product \(Q_i K_j^\top\) of tile \(j\), the Producer Warps are simultaneously pre-fetching tile \(j+1\) from HBM into on-chip SRAM in the background.
  3. Native FP8 Tensor Core Execution (WGMMA): Inputs are converted to FP8 (torch.float8_e4m3fn), doubling hardware FLOPS. FlashAttention-3 utilizes specialized Warpgroup Matrix Multiply and Accumulate (WGMMA) instructions, accumulating intermediate results in FP32 registers to ensure zero numerical precision loss during online softmax.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor HBM as GPU HBM Memory
    actor TMA as Hardware TMA Engine
    actor SRAM as On-Chip Shared Memory
    actor TC as Tensor Cores (WGMMA)

    rect rgb(15, 23, 42)
    Note over TMA,SRAM: Pipeline Stage 1
    TMA->>HBM: Request Tile K_0, V_0 (Async)
    HBM-->>SRAM: Direct DMA Transfer to SRAM Buffer 0
    end

    rect rgb(30, 41, 59)
    Note over SRAM,TC: Pipeline Stage 2 (Overlap)
    par Simultaneous Compute & Fetch
        TC->>SRAM: Compute S_0 = Q_0 @ K_0.T & Softmax
        and
        TMA->>HBM: Request Tile K_1, V_1 (Async)
        HBM-->>SRAM: Direct DMA Transfer to SRAM Buffer 1
    end
    end

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
FlashAttention-3 computes exact attention block-by-block without ever allocating the full \(N \times N\) attention matrix:

\[S_{i, j} = \frac{Q_i K_j^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B_r \times B_c}\] \[m_i^{(j)} = \max\left( m_i^{(j-1)}, \; \operatorname{rowmax}(S_{i, j}) \right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B_r}\] \[\tilde{P}_{i, j} = \exp\left( S_{i, j} - m_i^{(j)} \right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B_r \times B_c}\] \[l_i^{(j)} = \exp\left( m_i^{(j-1)} - m_i^{(j)} \right) \odot l_i^{(j-1)} + \operatorname{rowsum}(\tilde{P}_{i, j}) \in \mathbb{R}^{B_r}\] \[\text{Accumulate Context: } O_i^{(j)} = \operatorname{diag}\left( \exp\left( m_i^{(j-1)} - m_i^{(j)} \right) \right) O_i^{(j-1)} + \tilde{P}_{i, j} V_j\] \[\text{Final Normalization: } O_i = \operatorname{diag}\left( l_i^{(\text{final})} \right)^{-1} O_i^{(\text{final})} \in \mathbb{R}^{B_r \times d_h}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Up to 850–900 TFLOPs/s on H100: Achieves \(75\%\) to \(85\%\) of the theoretical maximum hardware performance of NVIDIA Hopper GPUs.
  • \(1.5\times\) to \(2.0\times\) Speedup over FlashAttention-2: Halves attention training and inference latency across sequence lengths from 2k to 128k.
  • Hardware-Enforced Exact Precision: Produces mathematically exact attention outputs with zero heuristic approximations.
