docs.title: 4. PagedAttention & Block Virtual Memory (vLLM KV Paging)
Title & Subtitle
docs.text: PagedAttention: Virtual Memory Paging for Large Language Model Serving Eliminating 60%–80% memory waste from GPU memory fragmentation through operating-system style non-contiguous block tables.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine booking hotel rooms for tour groups of unpredictable sizes. Traditional serving engines operate like an inflexible hotel manager who insists that every tour group must be assigned rooms in a single continuous hallway. If a group might stay for 10 days and expand, the hotel reserves 50 adjacent rooms immediately. If the group leaves early, those 40 empty rooms sit locked and wasted—preventing other guests from checking in!

PagedAttention acts like a modern hotel keycard system: guests are assigned any available room anywhere in the hotel across different floors and wings. A central computer database (the block table) links their room keys seamlessly. When a new guest arrives, the hotel allocates exactly one room from the global pool on demand. Zero empty rooms are wasted!

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
In production LLM serving, the total number of tokens generated by an autoregressive request cannot be known in advance. To prevent catastrophic Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes, traditional frameworks pre-allocated large contiguous GPU memory buffers sized to the model's maximum context length (\(L_{\max}=2048 \text{ or } 8192\)). This caused three devastating forms of memory waste: 1. Internal Fragmentation: Reserved slots waiting for future tokens that are never generated. 2. External Fragmentation: Free memory scattered in tiny chunks too small to accommodate a new contiguous allocation. 3. Reservation Waste: Serving systems idling \(60\% \text{ to } 80\%\) of their precious VRAM, artificially capping serving concurrency to tiny batch sizes.

pie title Traditional Serving vs PagedAttention Memory Utilization
    "Active Token Data" : 28
    "Internal Fragmentation" : 42
    "External Fragmentation" : 22
    "Virtual Buffer Waste" : 8

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Developed by Kwon et al. and forming the core architecture of vLLM, PagedAttention adapts the classic concept of Virtual Memory Operating System Paging directly to transformer Key-Value caches:

  1. Logical Token Blocks: A sequence’s dynamic KV cache is split into fixed-size logical blocks of tokens (typically \(B_{\text{size}} = 16 \text{ or } 32\) tokens).
  2. Physical Memory Pages: GPU High Bandwidth Memory is partitioned into an array of fixed-size physical memory pages.
  3. Dynamic Block Table Lookup: A lightweight Page Table maps logical block indices to physical HBM memory pages on the fly: $\(\text{Physical Address}(t) = \text{BlockTable}[i, \; \lfloor t / B_{\text{size}} \rfloor] \times B_{\text{size}} + (t \bmod B_{\text{size}})\)$
  4. Copy-on-Write (CoW) Prefix Sharing: When serving parallel sampling, beam search, or multi-turn dialogues with identical prompt prefixes, multiple requests point to the exact same physical memory pages. Only when a request writes a unique token does the engine allocate a new physical block!

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Let \(B_{\text{size}}\) be the block size, \(K_j, V_j\) the key and value vectors of the \(j\)-th token. The physical key tensor for block \(b = \text{BlockTable}[i]\) is stored in memory as:

\[K_{\text{block}}(b) = \begin{bmatrix} K_{b \cdot B_{\text{size}}} \\ K_{b \cdot B_{\text{size}} + 1} \\ \vdots \\ K_{(b+1) \cdot B_{\text{size}} - 1} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{B_{\text{size}} \times d_k}\]

The PagedAttention kernel computes the attention score vector for query \(q_t\) by gathering non-contiguous physical pages:

\[A_{t, j} = \frac{\exp\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} q_t \cdot K_{\text{block}}(\text{BlockTable}[\lfloor j / B_{\text{size}} \rfloor])_{j \bmod B_{\text{size}}}^\top \right)}{\sum_{l=1}^t \exp\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} q_t \cdot K_{\text{block}}(\text{BlockTable}[\lfloor l / B_{\text{size}} \rfloor])_{l \bmod B_{\text{size}}}^\top \right)}\] \[O_t = \sum_{j=1}^t A_{t, j} V_{\text{block}}(\text{BlockTable}[\lfloor j / B_{\text{size}} \rfloor])_{j \bmod B_{\text{size}}}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Near-Zero Memory Waste (\(<4\%\)): Reduces KV cache memory fragmentation from over \(70\%\) down to under \(4\%\), approaching physical hardware limits.
  • \(2\times\) to \(4\times\) Serving Concurrency: Allows \(2\times\) to \(4\times\) more parallel user requests to be batched concurrently on the exact same GPU cluster.
  • Zero-Cost Prefix Caching: Eliminates redundant compute and storage for system prompts, few-shot examples, and complex agent reasoning chains.

docs.title: 5. Ring Attention & Blockwise Parallel Context Scaling
Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Ring Attention: Infinite Context Scaling via Distributed Circular KV Shuffling Breaking the single-GPU memory boundary by overlapping blockwise attention computation with peer-to-peer ring communication across clusters.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine 8 research scholars sitting in a circle around a round table, tasked with cross-referencing a massive 8-volume historical encyclopedia. The encyclopedia is so gigantic that each scholar can only fit 1 volume on their desk at a time.

Instead of trying to photocopy the entire encyclopedia for everyone (which would collapse the desks under the weight), each scholar opens their personal notebook containing their specific questions. Scholar 0 cross-references Volume 0. Then, on a synchronized timer, every scholar passes their physical book to the neighbor on their right and receives a new volume from their left. They cross-reference the new volume, update their notes, and pass again. After 8 circular passes, all 8 scholars have cross-referenced their questions across all 8 volumes without any scholar ever holding more than 1 volume at a time!

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Processing millions of tokens in a standard transformer causes single-GPU memory to explode due to \(O(L^2)\) intermediate activations and linear \(O(L)\) KV cache scaling. For example, a 1-million-token context requires hundreds of gigabytes of KV storage for a single prompt—far exceeding the 80GB capacity of an NVIDIA H100. Existing distributed methods like Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-LM) require massive All-Reduce collective communications at every layer, which quickly saturate inter-GPU interconnect bandwidth.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Developed by Hao Liu, Matei Zaharia, and Pieter Abbeel (UC Berkeley), Ring Attention breaks through the single-device memory wall by distributing the sequence dimension across a ring of GPUs:

  1. Spatial Sequence Partitioning: The input sequence of length \(L\) is sliced into \(D\) chunks of length \(L/D\). GPU \(i\) holds query block \(Q_i\), key block \(K_i\), and value block \(V_i\).
  2. Local Block Computation: At step \(0\), each GPU computes local attention between its query \(Q_i\) and its local key/value pair \((K_i, V_i)\), initializing running online softmax statistics (\(m_i, l_i, O_i\)).
  3. Non-Blocking P2P Ring Exchange: GPU \(i\) initiates an asynchronous peer-to-peer send (ncclSend) to pass its current key-value block to GPU \((i+1) \bmod D\), while simultaneously receiving the key-value block from GPU \((i-1) \bmod D\) via (ncclRecv).
  4. Compute-Communication Overlap: While the high-speed NVLink network transfers the next KV block in the background, the Tensor Cores are computing attention on the current block.
  5. Exact Mathematical Equivalence: After \(D\) circular steps, every query has attended to every key-value block in the sequence, producing mathematically exact global attention.
graph TD
    subgraph Step 0: Local Compute
        A0[GPU 0: Q0 @ K0] --- B0[GPU 1: Q1 @ K1] --- C0[GPU 2: Q2 @ K2]
    end
    subgraph Step 1: P2P Ring Shift
        A1[GPU 0: Q0 @ K2] --- B1[GPU 1: Q1 @ K0] --- C1[GPU 2: Q2 @ K1]
    end
    subgraph Step 2: P2P Ring Shift
        A2[GPU 0: Q0 @ K1] --- B2[GPU 1: Q1 @ K2] --- C2[GPU 2: Q2 @ K0]
    end

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Let \(D\) be the number of devices in the ring. For device \(i \in \{0, \dots, D-1\}\) at ring iteration step \(s \in \{0, \dots, D-1\}\), the active key-value block index is \(j = (i - s) \bmod D\):

\[S_{i, j} = \frac{Q_i K_j^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \quad (\text{with causal masking enforced if } i \ge j)\] \[m_i^{(s)} = \max\left( m_i^{(s-1)}, \; \operatorname{rowmax}(S_{i, j}) \right)\] \[l_i^{(s)} = \exp\left( m_i^{(s-1)} - m_i^{(s)} \right) \odot l_i^{(s-1)} + \operatorname{rowsum}\left( \exp\left( S_{i, j} - m_i^{(s)} \right) \right)\] \[O_i^{(s)} = \operatorname{diag}\left( \exp\left( m_i^{(s-1)} - m_i^{(s)} \right) \right) O_i^{(s-1)} + \exp\left( S_{i, j} - m_i^{(s)} \right) V_j\]

The communication latency is fully hidden as long as the block compute time exceeds the P2P transfer time: $\(T_{\text{compute}}\left( \frac{L}{D} \times \frac{L}{D} \right) \ge T_{\text{NVLink}}\left( 2 \cdot \frac{L}{D} \cdot D \right)\)$

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Near-Infinite Sequence Scaling: Scales context length linearly with the number of GPUs: 8 GPUs \(\to\) 512k tokens, 64 GPUs \(\to\) 4M tokens, 512 GPUs \(\to\) 32M+ tokens.
  • 100% Exact Mathematical Precision: Incurs zero loss in accuracy or perplexity because it computes exact dense global attention.
  • Zero Communication Overhead: With block sizes \(B \ge 512\), computation completely hides NVLink transfer time, achieving near-perfect linear scaling efficiency (\(>95\%\)).

docs.title: 6. BigBird & Longformer (Sparse Window + Random + Global Tokens)
Title & Subtitle
docs.text: BigBird & Longformer: The Tri-Partite Sparse Attention Blueprint Taming quadratic complexity down to linear \(O(N)\) through a strategic trifecta of sliding local windows, random routing, and global anchor tokens.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine how information spreads across a metropolis of 10 million citizens: 1. Local Connections: You talk daily to your immediate neighbors on your street (the local sliding window). 2. Random Acquaintances: You strike up spontaneous conversations with strangers on the subway, in coffee shops, or at airports (random expander graph connections). 3. Global News Anchors: Everyone in the city listens to the mayor's morning broadcast and reads the city newspaper (global anchor tokens).

Thanks to this three-way combination, any important news or idea spreads to every single person in the city in just 2 or 3 degrees of separation—without requiring all 10 million people to hold individual phone calls with everyone else!

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Full self-attention constructs an all-to-all dense connectivity graph where every token attends to all \(N\) tokens, creating an \(N \times N\) matrix. When sequences grow from 512 to 16,384 tokens, memory and compute increase by \(1,024\times\). Conversely, naively restricting attention to a narrow local window severely harms performance: information can only propagate \(W\) tokens per layer, making long-range reasoning across distant chapters or long legal contracts completely impossible.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Pioneered by Google Research (BigBird, Zaheer et al.) and Allen Institute for AI (Longformer, Beltagy et al.), these architectures replace the dense \(N \times N\) matrix with a sparse graph formed by three complementary routing mechanisms:

  1. Sliding Local Window (\(W\)): Every token attends to \(w\) neighbors to its left and right. This handles local syntactic patterns, word conjugations, and nearby punctuation with high resolution.
  2. Global Anchor Tokens (\(G\)): A small set of designated tokens (e.g., [CLS], question tokens, or summary tokens) attend to ALL tokens in the document, and all tokens attend back to them. This acts as a centralized information exchange highway.
  3. Random Expander Graph Connections (\(R\)) (BigBird): Each token attends to \(r\) randomly chosen distant tokens. Based on Expander Graph Theory, adding random edges reduces the graph diameter from \(\mathcal{O}(N)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(\log N)\), guaranteeing that any two tokens can exchange information within 2 layers.
graph TD
    A[Dense Attention: O N^2] --> B[Tri-Partite Sparse Graph: O N]
    B --> C[Local Window: High-Res Syntax]
    B --> D[Global Anchors: Cross-Doc Context]
    B --> E[Random Nodes: Log-Diameter Expander]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
The BigBird sparse attention mask \(\mathcal{M} \in \{0, 1\}^{N \times N}\) is the boolean union of three index sets:

\[\mathcal{M}_{i, j} = 1 \iff j \in \mathcal{N}_{\text{window}}(i) \cup \mathcal{N}_{\text{global}} \cup \mathcal{N}_{\text{random}}(i)\]

where: $\(\mathcal{N}_{\text{window}}(i) = \{j \mid |i - j| \le w\}\)$ $\(\mathcal{N}_{\text{global}} = \{1, 2, \dots, g\} \cup \{N - g + 1, \dots, N\}\)$ $\(\mathcal{N}_{\text{random}}(i) = \text{RandomUniformSubset}(\{1, \dots, N\}, \; r)\)$

The total number of non-zero attention computations per query token is bounded by: $\(d_{\text{sparse}} = 2w + g + r \implies \text{Total FLOPs} = \mathcal{O}\left( N \cdot (2w + g + r) \cdot d_k \right) = \mathcal{O}(N)\)$

Theoretical Guarantee: BigBird is mathematically proven to be a Universal Approximator of Sequence-to-Sequence Functions and Turing Complete, preserving all theoretical expressivity of full dense transformers!

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Linear Scaling \(\mathcal{O}(N)\): Slashes computational and memory requirements from quadratic to linear, enabling processing of 8k–32k token documents on older generation GPUs.
  • Small-World Graph Topology: Bridges distant sequence sections in \(\mathcal{O}(\log N)\) hops via expander graph shortcuts.
  • Pioneered Structural Sparsity: Established the foundational graph sparsity patterns that modern long-context models and sparse attention kernels build upon today.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: MoE-DeltaKV: Mixture-of-Block-Attention with Dynamic Delta-Compressed KV Caching Unifying top-k expert block routing with low-rank temporal difference compression to cut KV cache memory by 8x.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Think of digital video compression (like MPEG-4 / H.264). A movie streaming service doesn't store 60 uncompressed, high-definition photographs for every single second of video. Instead, it stores one full master keyframe (an I-frame) every few seconds, and for all intermediate frames, it only records the tiny pixel changes (motion deltas / P-frames).

MoE-DeltaKV applies this exact video compression principle to transformer memory: instead of storing massive dense Key-Value vectors for thousands of tokens, it only stores compressed differences (\(\Delta\)) between adjacent tokens, factorizes those differences via truncated SVD and 4-bit quantization, and routes queries only to the most relevant memory pages!

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: As context length scales to 128k+, transformer inference faces two simultaneous roadblocks: 1. Compute Bottleneck: Evaluating attention across hundreds of thousands of historical tokens wastes massive compute on irrelevant background text. 2. Memory Footprint Bottleneck: Even if attention is sparse, traditional sparse models still force the GPU to store the full, uncompressed 16-bit Key and Value representations for every single token in HBM, causing memory exhaustion.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
MoE-DeltaKV couples a top-\(k\) Mixture-of-Block-Attention (MoBA) router with temporal low-rank delta compression in a unified two-tier architecture:

  1. Paged Memory Structure: The sequence history is partitioned into discrete physical pages of size \(S_{\text{page}} = 64\) tokens.
  2. MoE-Block Gating Router: A lightweight router compares incoming query block centroids \(\bar{Q}_i\) against historical key page centroids \(\bar{K}_j\), computing gating probabilities and activating only the top-\(k\) expert pages (typically \(k=4 \text{ or } 8\)).
  3. Temporal Delta Factorization: Because adjacent tokens within a document share high semantic correlation, the module computes temporal differences: $\(\Delta K_t = K_t - \hat{K}_{t-1}, \quad \Delta V_t = V_t - \hat{V}_{t-1}\)$ These deltas are aggressively compressed via Truncated SVD (rank \(r=16\)) and non-uniform 4-bit quantization.
  4. Ephemeral SRAM Reconstruction: Uncompressed states exist only ephemerally inside GPU registers/SRAM during the fused block-sparse attention kernel, then are immediately discarded—keeping the HBM footprint ultra-compact.
graph LR
    A[Input Tokens] --> B[Delta-KV Engine]
    B --> C[Compute ΔK = K_t - K_t-1]
    C --> D[Rank-16 SVD + INT4 Quant]
    D --> E[Store in Paged Delta Cache: 8x Smaller]
    E --> F[Top-K MoE Router Selects Active Pages]
    F --> G[Ephemeral SRAM Unpack & Attention]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given query block \(\bar{Q}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and page centroids \(\bar{K}_j\), the top-\(k\) page routing probabilities are:

\[g_j = \operatorname{Softmax}\left( \operatorname{TopK}\left( \frac{\bar{Q}_i W_{rg} \bar{K}_j^\top}{\sqrt{d}}, \; k_{\text{experts}} \right) \right)\]

For each token \(t\) in an active page \(j \in \mathcal{P}_{\text{active}}\), the compressed delta is stored as:

\[\hat{\Delta K}_t = \mathbf{U}_{k, r} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{k, r} \mathbf{V}_{k, r}^\top \cdot \operatorname{Quantize}_4\left( K_t - \hat{K}_{t-1} \right)\]

The ephemeral state is reconstructed in registers:

\[\hat{K}_t = \hat{K}_{t-1} + \hat{\Delta K}_t, \quad \hat{V}_t = \hat{V}_{t-1} + \hat{\Delta V}_t\]

The block-sparse paged attention evaluates as:

\[O_i = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_{\text{active}}} g_j \cdot \operatorname{Softmax}\left( \frac{\bar{Q}_i \hat{K}_j^\top}{\sqrt{d}} \right) \hat{V}_j\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• \(8\times\) KV Cache Memory Reduction: Reduces KV cache memory from \(2.0 \cdot d_{\text{model}}\) bytes/token (FP16) down to just \(\approx 0.25 \cdot d_{\text{model}}\) bytes/token.
  • Linear Computational Scaling: Lowers time complexity from \(\mathcal{O}(L^2 d)\) down to \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot k \cdot S_{\text{page}} \cdot d)\).
  • \(5.68\times\) Inference Speedup at 8k Context: Delivers massive decoding acceleration while maintaining full accuracy on WikiText-2 and C4 perplexity benchmarks (\(\Delta \text{PPL} < 0.2\)).

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Infini-Attention: Bounded Memory for Infinite Sequences via Segment Recurrence Combining local sliding-window attention with an associative recurrent memory matrix to process million-token streams in constant GPU memory.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
When you read a 1,000-page historical book, you utilize two distinct cognitive memory systems: 1. Working Memory (Local Attention): You pay close, word-for-word attention to the specific sentence and paragraph you are reading right now. 2. Episodic Long-Term Memory (Compressive Memory): You don't remember every single exact word from Chapter 1 that you read three days ago. Instead, your brain maintains a consolidated, high-level mental summary matrix of key characters, major plot points, and historical relationships.

Infini-Attention pairs these two systems in transformers: an exact local window handles immediate sentence context, while a fixed-size associative memory matrix continuously absorbs and updates historical context across infinite sequence lengths!

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Standard transformers must store an ever-expanding KV cache whose memory grows linearly \(\mathcal{O}(N)\) without bound. For real-time streaming agents, continuous audio/video feeds, and 1-million-token enterprise documents, caching millions of key-value vectors exhausts all GPU High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)—causing Out-Of-Memory crashes regardless of how many GPUs are in the cluster.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Developed by Google Research (Munkhdalai et al., 2024), Infini-Attention drops into standard Multi-Head Attention layers with minimal modification:

  1. Segmented Stream Processing: The input sequence is sliced into streaming segments of length \(N\) (e.g., \(N=2048\)).
  2. Local Attention Branch: Within the current segment, standard masked sliding-window attention computes exact dot-product interactions to produce high-resolution local context \(O_{\text{local}}\).
  3. Associative Compressive Memory Retrieval: Simultaneously, queries are projected through a non-linear feature kernel \(\phi(Q) = \text{ELU}(Q) + 1.0\) to retrieve global historical context \(O_{\text{mem}}\) from a persistent memory tensor \(M \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_k \times d_v}\).
  4. Learnable Gated Fusion: A learned gating parameter \(\beta\) blends the local context and the retrieved long-range compressive memory: $\(O_{\text{fused}} = \sigma(\beta) \odot O_{\text{local}} + (1 - \sigma(\beta)) \odot O_{\text{mem}}\)$
  5. Constant-Memory Recurrent State Update: After processing the segment, the memory matrix is updated by adding the outer product of the transformed keys and values: \(M \leftarrow M + \phi(K)^\top V\). The memory matrix size never grows, maintaining bounded \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) memory!
graph TD
    A[Input Segment: X] --> B[Linear Projections Q, K, V]
    B --> C[Local Sliding Softmax: O_local]
    B --> D[Compressive Memory Retrieval: phi Q @ M / norm]
    C --> E[Learned Gated Fusion: sigmoid beta]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Segment Output: Y]
    B --> G[Update Recurrent Matrix: M_new = M + phi K .T @ V]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
For query, key, and value representations \(Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k}\):

\[\text{Local Context: } O_{\text{local}} = \operatorname{Softmax}\left( \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M_{\text{window}} \right) V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k}\] \[\text{Feature Map: } \phi(x) = \operatorname{ELU}(x) + 1.0 > 0\] \[\text{Memory Retrieval: } O_{\text{mem}} = \frac{\phi(Q) M}{\phi(Q) z + \epsilon} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k}\] \[\text{Fused Output: } O_{\text{fused}} = \sigma(\beta) \odot O_{\text{local}} + (1 - \sigma(\beta)) \odot O_{\text{mem}}\] \[\text{Recurrent State Update: } M_{t} = M_{t-1} + \phi(K_t)^\top V_t \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_k \times d_k}\] \[z_t = z_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^N \phi(K_{t, i})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_k \times 1}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Constant Memory Footprint \(\mathcal{O}(1)\): The memory tensor \(M\) is fixed at \(H \times d_k \times d_k\) floats regardless of whether the context is 10k tokens or 100 million tokens.
  • \(114\times\) Memory Compression: Compared to dense 500k-token LLM baselines, Infini-Attention slashes memory consumption by over \(100\times\).
  • Seamless Continual Pretraining: Can be plugged directly into existing pretrained LLM weights (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma) and fine-tuned on long sequences with minimal compute overhead.

                                                                                                 │

  Query Q_i ───► MatMul(Q_i, K_coarse^T) ───► Select Top-k Blocks: Blocks {3, 14, 182}          │
                                                      │                                          │
  Stage 3: Fine-Grained Token Gathering               ▼                                          │
  Gather Full-Resolution Keys/Values from Blocks {3, 14, 182}                                    │

  Combine Dynamic Top-K Blocks with Mandatory Local Sliding Window: (|i - j| <= W) ──────────────┘

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Native Sparse Attention (NSA): Multi-Scale Coarse-to-Fine Dynamic Routing Combining local sliding windows with content-aware coarse-grained block selection and fine-grained token gathering for ultra-long context LLMs.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine a master detective searching for a specific clue inside an enormous 50,000-page city archive: 1. First, they read the immediate 5 pages on their desk line-by-line (the local sliding window). 2. For the remaining 49,995 pages, they don't read every single word. Instead, they skim the 1-paragraph summary at the start of each chapter (the coarse-grained block pooling). 3. The summaries immediately point them to Chapter 4 (financial records) and Chapter 89 (customs logs). 4. The detective pulls down those exact two folders and reads every word on those pages with full focus (the fine-grained token gathering).

The detective finds the exact needle in the haystack in 10 minutes instead of spending 3 months reading all 50,000 pages!

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Purely localized sliding windows miss global dependencies, while static sparse patterns (like fixed strides or dilated convolutions) are content-blind—often skipping the exact needle-in-a-haystack sentence needed to answer a query. On the other hand, evaluating full dynamic token-level top-\(k\) attention still requires calculating the full dense \(N \times N\) similarity matrix first, completely defeating the computational and memory purpose of sparsity on modern GPUs!

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Introduced in modern frontier models (including DeepSeek-V3), Native Sparse Attention (NSA) implements a hardware-aligned, multi-scale hierarchical routing pipeline:

  1. Coarse-Grained Key/Value Compression: Key and Value tokens are downsampled into coarse block representations (e.g. block size \(B_{\text{block}} = 32 \text{ or } 64\)) using average pooling or strided sampling: $\(K_{\text{coarse}} = \operatorname{AvgPool}(K, \; \text{stride}=B_{\text{block}})\)$
  2. Fast Coarse Selection: Query tokens compute dot products against the small coarse keys \(K_{\text{coarse}}\), selecting only the top-\(k_{\text{blocks}}\) most relevant blocks (e.g. \(k=4\) blocks).
  3. Fine-Grained Token Gathering: Inside only the selected active blocks, full-precision token-level Keys and Values are gathered into fast SRAM.
  4. Unified Boolean Mask Union: The active fine-grained tokens are merged with the mandatory local sliding window tokens (\(|i - j| \le W\)) through a boolean OR operation.
  5. Fused Hardware Kernel Execution: A custom Triton block-sparse kernel executes scaled dot-product attention exclusively over the combined sparse token set, skipping all inactive memory regions.
graph TD
    A[Sequence Tokens L=64k] --> B[Coarse Block Pooling: Stride 32]
    B --> C[Coarse Dot-Product Routing: Q @ K_coarse.T]
    C --> D[Select Top-k Relevant Blocks]
    D --> E[Gather Fine-Grained Tokens in Selected Blocks]
    A --> F[Local Sliding Window: |i - j| <= W]
    E --> G[Boolean Union Mask]
    F --> G
    G --> H[Fused Block-Sparse Triton SDPA Kernel]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given Query \(\mathbf{Q}\), Key \(\mathbf{K}\), and Value \(\mathbf{V}\) tensors in \(\mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times d_h}\):

\[\mathbf{K}_{\text{coarse}} = \operatorname{AvgPool}(\mathbf{K}, \; \text{kernel}=B_{\text{block}}, \; \text{stride}=B_{\text{block}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times \lceil L/B_{\text{block}} \rceil \times d_h}\] \[\mathcal{B}_{\text{selected}}(i) = \operatorname{TopK}\left( \frac{\mathbf{Q}_i \mathbf{K}_{\text{coarse}}^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}}, \; k_{\text{blocks}} \right) \subset \left\{ 1, \dots, \lceil L/B_{\text{block}} \rceil \right\}\]

The total unified active attention index set \(\Omega(i)\) for query token \(i\) is:

\[\Omega(i) = \underbrace{\{ j \mid |i - j| \le W \}}_{\text{Local Sliding Window}} \; \cup \; \underbrace{\bigcup_{b \in \mathcal{B}_{\text{selected}}(i)} \left\{ (b-1) B_{\text{block}} + 1, \dots, b B_{\text{block}} \right\}}_{\text{Dynamically Routed Top-}k \text{ Fine Blocks}}\]

The context vector is computed strictly over the sparse active set:

\[\mathbf{O}_i = \sum_{j \in \Omega(i)} \operatorname{Softmax}_{j \in \Omega(i)}\left( \frac{\mathbf{Q}_i \mathbf{K}_j^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}} \right) \mathbf{V}_j \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_h}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• \(4\times\) to \(8\times\) Compute and Memory Acceleration: Drops active token interactions from \(L\) down to \(2W + (k_{\text{blocks}} \cdot B_{\text{block}})\), speeding up training and decoding by up to \(8\times\) on 64k–1M context windows.
  • 100% Needle-in-a-Haystack Retrieval: Dynamic content-aware routing guarantees that critical distant tokens are never missed, matching dense transformer retrieval accuracy.
  • Hardware-Aligned Block Sparsity: Aligns perfectly with GPU Tensor Core memory tiles (\(32 \times 32\) or \(64 \times 64\)), maximizing hardware compute occupancy without sparse memory stalls.

docs.title: 🎯 Summary & Key Takeaways
docs.text:
The evolution of modern transformer attention is defined by a relentless push to dismantle the quadratic \(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\) compute and linear \(\mathcal{O}(N)\) memory bandwidth barriers:

  1. Latent & Subspace Factorization (MLA, GQA) proves that we do not need to store massive independent key-value tensors for every query head. Compressing key-value representations into low-rank latent bottlenecks (\(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\)) or shared groups reduces serving memory by up to \(93\%\) with virtually zero quality loss.
  2. Hardware-Aware IO Optimization (FlashAttention-3, PagedAttention) shows that understanding GPU hardware—from on-chip SRAM tiling and Hopper TMA asynchronous pipelines to OS-inspired virtual memory block tables—delivers massive real-world throughput leaps without modifying model math.
  3. Multi-Scale & Distributed Scaling (Ring Attention, MoE-DeltaKV, Infini-Attention, NSA) unlocks processing across millions of tokens by dynamically routing to active memory pages, compressing temporal deltas, distributing circular context across GPU rings, and bridging local windows with recurrent associative memory matrices.

Together, these nine architectures form the foundation of next-generation large language models, multimodal agents, and infinite-context reasoning engines.

docs.title: 🧭 The Compression Engine Ecosystem
docs.text:
Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) with tens or hundreds of billions of parameters are constrained not by raw compute capacity, but by memory bandwidth limits (the Von Neumann bottleneck) and GPU VRAM capacity. Standard dense linear layers require \(d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}}\) parameters per weight matrix. In a 70B parameter model, fetching these billions of floating-point numbers from High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) into SRAM at every decoding token step creates an immense latency ceiling.

The compression engines detailed in this guide approach this fundamental challenge from the perspective of linear algebra, spectral theory, and tensor networks. Rather than naively discarding weights or quantizing numbers blindly, these engines decompose high-dimensional operators into compact, geometrically aligned, low-rank manifolds.

docs.title: 1. AASVD: Anchored Activation-Aware Singular Value Decomposition
Title & Subtitle
docs.text: AASVD: Anchoring Low-Rank Factorization to the Empirical Activation Manifold Projecting weight matrices onto dynamic token activation subspaces before singular value truncation to eliminate zero-shot perplexity collapse.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine tailoring a bespoke astronaut flight suit. An amateur tailor fits the suit to a motionless plastic mannequin in an empty room (standard static SVD on weight matrix \(W\)). When the astronaut actually climbs into the cockpit and bends their knees, elbows, and shoulders, the rigid seams burst.

AASVD (Anchored Adaptive SVD) attaches motion sensors to the astronaut in high-gravity simulation (dynamic input token activations \(X\)) to discover the exact axes of movement. It then cuts and anchors the suit’s fabric specifically along those high-strain stress lines. The suit uses 60% less material, yet provides complete, unrestricted movement where it matters most.

       Standard SVD (Weight Only)                   AASVD (Activation-Anchored)
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  Treats all input directions as      │     │  Measures dynamic activation data X  │
 │  equally probable in R^d.            │     │  Builds Anchor Projector P = A A^T   │
 │  Cuts weights blind to real tokens!  │     │  Decomposes W_anchored = W P         │
 └──────────────────┬───────────────────┘     └──────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                    ▼                                            ▼
        [Catastrophic Perplexity]                    [Zero Perplexity Explosion]

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Traditional truncated Singular Value Decomposition finds the mathematically optimal rank-\(r\) approximation \(\hat{W}\) minimizing the Frobenius norm error \(\|W - \hat{W}\|_F^2\) under the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem. However, the Eckart-Young theorem assumes that all input directions in \(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\) are uniformly distributed on a unit hypersphere.

In real transformer architectures, input activations \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{in}}}\) are drastically non-uniform: 1. LayerNorm and RMSNorm channel outputs into sharp, low-dimensional coordinate valleys. 2. Attention routing and residual streams produce high-magnitude outlier channels where less than 1% of feature dimensions carry over 80% of dynamic token variance. 3. If standard SVD discards a singular vector that has a small singular value \(\sigma_i\) in \(W\), but that singular vector happens to align with a massive activation outlier in \(X\), the layer's output error \(\|X W^T - X \hat{W}^T\|_F^2\) explodes, causing total model hallucination.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
AASVD resolves this misalignment by anchoring weight factorization directly to the empirical token activation subspace extracted from a small calibration dataset (e.g., 32 to 128 sequences of text):

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Calib as Calibration Data
    participant Hook as Forward Hooks
    participant ActSVD as Activation SVD
    participant Anchor as Anchor Subspace P
    participant Fact as Anchored SVD (W @ P)
    participant Layer as Factorized Linear Layer

    Calib->>Hook: Pass calibration tokens through model
    Hook->>ActSVD: Intercept activation matrix X (Tokens x d_in)
    ActSVD->>Anchor: Compute SVD(X) -> Extract top-r basis A_anchor = V_X[:, :r]
    Anchor->>Fact: Construct P = A_anchor @ A_anchor^T & Project W_anchored = W @ P
    Fact->>Layer: Truncated SVD(W_anchored) -> U_r, Sigma_r, V_r^T
  1. Activation Capture: Forward hooks record the input activations \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d_{\text{in}}}\) flowing into a linear layer across \(K = B \cdot N\) tokens.
  2. Subspace Basis Extraction: AASVD performs SVD on the centered activation matrix \(\bar{X} = U_X \Sigma_X V_X^T\). The right-singular matrix \(V_X \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) represents the principal variance directions of the activation distribution.
  3. Anchor Projection Matrix: Extracting the top \(r\) columns of \(V_X\) yields the anchor basis \(A_{\text{anchor}} = V_X[:, :r] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times r}\). The orthogonal projector is \(P_{\text{anchor}} = A_{\text{anchor}} A_{\text{anchor}}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\).
  4. Anchored Factorization: AASVD projects the static weight matrix onto the anchor space: \(W_{\text{anchored}} = W P_{\text{anchor}}\). Performing SVD on \(W_{\text{anchored}}\) produces factors whose left and right singular vectors are intrinsically weighted by activation importance.
  5. Two-Stage Low-Rank Linear Execution: The compressed layer decomposes \(Y = X W^T\) into an inward bottleneck projection followed by an outward expansion: $\(\hat{W} = U_{\text{anc}}[:, :r] \operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_{\text{anc}}[:r]) V_{\text{anc}}[:r, :]^T\)$

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given flattened calibration activations \(\bar{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d_{\text{in}}}\) and weight matrix \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\):

\[\text{Activation Covariance Basis: } \bar{X} = U_X \Sigma_X V_X^T \implies A_{\text{anchor}} = V_X[:, :r] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times r}\] \[\text{Subspace Projection Operator: } P_{\text{anchor}} = A_{\text{anchor}} A_{\text{anchor}}^T \quad (P_{\text{anchor}}^2 = P_{\text{anchor}})\] \[\text{Anchored Weight Tensor: } W_{\text{anchored}} = W P_{\text{anchor}} = W A_{\text{anchor}} A_{\text{anchor}}^T\] \[\text{Anchored SVD Decomposition: } W_{\text{anchored}} = U_{\text{anc}} \Sigma_{\text{anc}} V_{\text{anc}}^T\] \[\text{Low-Rank Factorized Forward Pass: } Y = \underbrace{\left( X V_{\text{anc}}[:, :r] \right)}_{\text{Down-project to } r} \operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_{\text{anc}}[:r]) \cdot U_{\text{anc}}[:, :r]^T + b\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Zero-Shot Accuracy Preservation: Retains up to 98% of original uncompressed model perplexity at 50% parameter reduction without requiring expensive backpropagation or fine-tuning.
  • Outlier Immunity: Prevents critical activation channels (such as token delimiter spikes) from being clipped by weight-only truncation.
  • Target Applications: Zero-shot post-training compression of 7B–70B parameter models for edge devices, instant mobile deployment, and embedded robotics.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: AdaSVD: Dynamic Nuclear-Norm Rank Allocation with Alternating Least-Squares Refinement Allocating variable rank budgets across transformer layers based on spectral energy distribution and polishing factors via iterative matrix refinement.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Think of packing emergency expedition supplies across a convoy of cargo trucks. A naive convoy manager puts exactly 500 kg of cargo into every truck (rigid uniform rank \(r=32\) across all layers). But the medical truck and water purification truck need 1,200 kg of equipment, while the sleeping tent truck only needs 200 kg.

AdaSVD acts as the intelligent logistics coordinator: it weighs the structural complexity of every layer using its Nuclear Norm (total spectral energy). It assigns massive rank capacity (\(r=96\)) to the critical token-routing attention layers and strips redundant deeper MLP layers down to ultra-compact ranks (\(r=12\)), all while keeping the total convoy weight beneath a strict target.

 Uniform SVD: Rigid & Suboptimal
 [Layer 1: r=32] ── [Layer 2: r=32] ── [Layer 3: r=32] ── [Layer 4: r=32]
  (Under-parameterized!)                                 (Over-parameterized!)

 AdaSVD: Information-Weighted Dynamic Rank Allocation
 [Layer 1: r=72] ── [Layer 2: r=48] ── [Layer 3: r=24] ── [Layer 4: r=12]
  (High Capacity)    (Balanced)         (Compact)          (Ultra-Sparse)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Standard SVD compression compresses every linear layer to a uniform rank \(r\). However, empirical spectral analysis reveals that deep neural networks possess highly heterogeneous layer rank profiles: 1. Early self-attention projections (\(W_q, W_k\)) and MLP gate projections exhibit slow singular value decay (heavy spectral tails), meaning they carry dense, non-redundant syntactic mappings. 2. Deep feed-forward layers exhibit steep exponential singular value decay, where 90% of singular values are near zero. 3. Forcing a uniform rank across all layers wastes scarce parameter budget on redundant layers while starving information-dense layers, leading to severe accuracy degradation.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Uncompressed Model: L Linear Layers"] --> B["Compute Layer Nuclear Norms: ||W_l||_*"]
    B --> C["Calculate Global Importance Fractions alpha_l"]
    C --> D["Dynamic Rank Allocation: r_l = clamp(R_max * (1-rho) * alpha_l * L)"]
    D --> E["Initial Truncated SVD per Layer"]
    E --> F["Alternating Least-Squares Iterative Refinement: ALS"]
    F --> G1["Solve U_l with V_l fixed"]
    G1 --> G2["Solve V_l with U_l fixed"]
    G2 --> G3["Re-project Diagonal Singular Values S_l"]
    G3 --> H["Optimized Low-Rank Compressed Model"]
  1. Spectral Energy Profiling: For every layer \(l \in \{1, \dots, L\}\), AdaSVD computes the exact singular values \(\Sigma^{(l)}\) and calculates the Nuclear Norm \(\mathcal{I}_l = \|W^{(l)}\|_* = \sum \sigma_i^{(l)}\).
  2. Normalized Importance Metric: The engine calculates the layer's global importance share \(\alpha_l = \mathcal{I}_l / \sum_{j=1}^L \mathcal{I}_j\).
  3. Adaptive Rank Assignment: Given a global parameter removal target \(\rho \in (0, 1)\), AdaSVD assigns rank \(r_l\) proportional to \(\alpha_l\): $\(r_l = \min\left( \max\left( 1, \left\lfloor R_{\max}^{(l)} \cdot (1 - \rho) \cdot \alpha_l \cdot L \right\rfloor \right), R_{\max}^{(l)} \right)\)$
  4. Initial Truncated Factorization: Extracts initial factors \(U_{r_l}, S_{r_l}, V_{r_l}^T\).
  5. Alternating Least-Squares (ALS) Refinement: To compensate for cross-layer rank truncation errors, AdaSVD performs \(T\) iterations of alternating ridge-regularized updates, holding \(V\) fixed to update \(U\), then holding \(U\) fixed to update \(V\), driving reconstruction error to the theoretical minimum.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Let \(W^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{M_l \times N_l}\) be the weight tensor of layer \(l\).

\[\text{Nuclear Norm Importance: } \mathcal{I}_l = \|W^{(l)}\|_* = \sum_{i=1}^{\min(M_l, N_l)} \sigma_i^{(l)}\] \[\text{Normalized Importance Ratio: } \alpha_l = \frac{\|W^{(l)}\|_*}{\sum_{j=1}^L \|W^{(j)}\|_*}\] \[\text{Allocated Dynamic Rank: } r_l = \operatorname{clamp}\left( \left\lfloor R_{\max}^{(l)} \cdot (1 - \rho) \cdot \alpha_l \cdot L \right\rfloor, \, 1, \, R_{\max}^{(l)} \right)\] \[\text{ALS Update Step 1 (Left Factor): } U_{r_l}^{(t+1)} = W^{(l)} V_{r_l}^{(t)} \left( \operatorname{diag}(S_{r_l}^{(t)}) + \epsilon I \right)^{-1}\] \[\text{ALS Update Step 2 (Right Factor): } (V_{r_l}^{(t+1)})^T = \left( (U_{r_l}^{(t+1)})^T U_{r_l}^{(t+1)} + \epsilon I \right)^{-1} (U_{r_l}^{(t+1)})^T W^{(l)}\] \[\text{Singular Value Re-Projection: } S_{r_l}^{(t+1)} = \operatorname{diag}\left( (U_{r_l}^{(t+1)})^T W^{(l)} V_{r_l}^{(t+1)} \right)\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Optimal Pareto Efficiency: Outperforms uniform SVD by 3.2–5.8 perplexity points at identical 50% parameter budgets.
  • Automated Rank Discovery: Eliminates manual grid-searching of per-layer rank hyperparameters.
  • Convergence Guarantees: ALS iterative refinement guarantees monotonic reduction of Frobenius reconstruction error.

docs.title: 3. ASVD: Activation-Weighted SVD with Gradient-Free Calibration
Title & Subtitle
docs.text: ASVD: Activation-Weighted SVD with Explicit Singular Scaling Decoupling singular value vectors from orthogonal frames for rapid, gradient-free calibration on downstream domain distributions.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Consider a state-of-the-art multi-speaker acoustic sound system. The wooden speaker cabinets and driver cones represent the fixed physical framework (orthogonal singular bases \(U\) and \(V\)). When you move the sound system from a small carpeted bedroom to a giant echoey cathedral, you don't rebuild the wooden cabinets from scratch.

You simply adjust the equalizer gain dials (the explicit singular scale vector \(S \in \mathbb{R}^r\)). ASVD factors linear layers such that the heavy matrix frames remain fixed, while a lightweight vector of singular scales \(S\) can be instantly tuned with a few calibration samples to adapt the model to new domains.

 Standard Low-Rank Layer: W = A @ B  (Updating requires tuning full matrices A and B)
 ┌──────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────┐
 │ Matrix A: d_out x r      │   @   │ Matrix B: r x d_in       │
 └──────────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────┘

 ASVD Layer: Y = ((X @ V^T) ⊙ S) @ U^T + b  (Tuning requires adjusting ONLY vector S!)
 ┌───────────────┐     ┌───────────────┐     ┌───────────────┐
 │ V^T: r x d_in │ ──► │ Vector S: r   │ ──► │ U^T: d_out x r│
 │ (Orthogonal)  │     │ (Scale Dials!)│     │ (Orthogonal)  │
 └───────────────┘     └───────────────┘     └───────────────┘

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: When compressing foundation models for specialized downstream tasks (medical QA, legal analysis, financial forecasting), standard low-rank adaptation requires fine-tuning all entries of the factorized projection matrices \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}\) and \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}\). 1. Updating full low-rank matrices during post-training calibration requires substantial GPU memory for activation caching and backpropagation gradients. 2. If the calibration dataset is tiny (e.g., 50 medical documents), fine-tuning millions of weights in \(A\) and \(B\) risks severe catastrophic forgetting and weight overfitting.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
graph LR
    subgraph Calibration Phase
        X["Input Activations X"] --> Var["Channel Variance Scale s_x = diag(std(X))"]
        W["Dense Weight W"] --> ScaledW["W_scaled = W @ diag(s_x)"]
        ScaledW --> SVD["SVD: U, Sigma, V^T"]
        SVD --> Descale["V_bar^T = V^T @ diag(s_x)^-1"]
    end

    subgraph Fast Inference / Calibration Tuning
        Input["Token Input X"] --> Down["X @ V_bar"]
        Down --> Scale["⊙ Explicit Scale Vector S"]
        Scale --> Up["@ U^T + Bias"]
        Up --> Output["Layer Output Y"]
    end
  1. Activation Variance Weighting: Measure the standard deviation of input token activations across feature channels: \(s_x = \text{std}(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\).
  2. Feature-Scaled Factorization: Scale the weight matrix columns by activation variance before SVD: \(\tilde{W} = W \cdot \operatorname{diag}(s_x)\). Perform truncated SVD on \(\tilde{W}\) to obtain \(U_r, \Sigma_r, V_r^T\).
  3. De-Scaled Orthonormal Decomposition: Invert the variance scaling on the right factor: \(\bar{V}_r^T = V_r^T \cdot \operatorname{diag}(s_x)^{-1}\).
  4. Explicit Parameterization: The layer is implemented as: $\(Y = \left( (X \bar{V}_r) \odot S \right) U_r^T + b\)$ where \(S = \Sigma_r \in \mathbb{R}^r\) is maintained as an independent 1D learnable scaling vector.
  5. Gradient-Free Calibration: During post-training adaptation, \(U_r\) and \(\bar{V}_r\) remain completely frozen. Only the \(r\)-dimensional vector \(S\) is tuned using lightweight linear regression or coordinate descent.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given input activation distribution \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d_{\text{in}}}\) with per-channel scaling \(s_x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\):

\[\text{Activation-Scaled Weight: } \tilde{W} = W \cdot \operatorname{diag}(s_x) \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\] \[\text{Truncated SVD: } \tilde{W} \approx U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T \quad \text{where } U_r^T U_r = I_r, \; V_r^T V_r = I_r\] \[\text{De-Scaled Right Factor: } \bar{V}_r = \operatorname{diag}(s_x)^{-1} V_r \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times r}\] \[\text{ASVD Linear Forward Operator: } Y = \underbrace{\left[ \left( X \bar{V}_r \right) \odot S \right]}_{\text{Bottleneck Projection with Gain } S} U_r^T + b\] \[\text{Gradient-Free Update Objective: } \min_{S \in \mathbb{R}^r} \frac{1}{2K} \left\| Y_{\text{target}} - \left( (X \bar{V}_r) \odot S \right) U_r^T \right\|_F^2\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Microscopic Calibration Overhead: Only \(r\) parameters per layer (e.g., 32 floating-point values instead of 262,144 weights) are updated during domain transfer.
  • Zero Catastrophic Forgetting: The frozen orthogonal frames preserve global language comprehension while the scale vector adapts to new vocabulary distributions.
  • Fast Edge On-Device Tuning: Enables on-device fine-tuning directly on edge microcontrollers without storing gradient graphs for large matrices.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: FastSVD & Randomized SVD: Sub-Cubic Matrix Factorization at Scale Harnessing Gaussian random projections and power iterations to factorize multi-billion parameter LLMs in minutes instead of hours.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine taking a census of a 50-million-person nation to determine the primary occupational demographics. Conducting a full door-to-door survey takes two years and billions of dollars (exact full SVD \(\mathcal{O}(M N^2)\)).

Instead, a top statistical bureau surveys 1,000 randomly selected citizens across diverse zip codes with mathematical oversampling (Randomized SVD with Gaussian test matrix \(\Omega\)). Within 48 hours, they reconstruct the nation's dominant occupational breakdown with 99.9% statistical confidence at 1/10,000th the cost.

 Full Deterministic SVD: O(M * N^2) FLOPs
 [Compute Full Gram Matrix W W^T] ──► [Full Spectral QR / Divide-and-Conquer]
 (Extremely slow, high VRAM, cubic scaling!)

 Fast Randomized SVD: O(M * N * log(r) + (M + N) * r^2) FLOPs
 [Gaussian Matrix Omega] ──► [Sample Range Y = W @ Omega] ──► [Fast QR] ──► [Tiny SVD]
 (Blazing fast, constant working memory, mathematically bounded error!)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Computing exact SVD for massive weight matrices using deterministic algorithms (such as Golub-Kahan bidiagonalization or Jacobi rotations) has cubic time complexity \(\mathcal{O}(\min(M N^2, M^2 N))\). - In a modern 70B parameter LLM with \(d = 8192\) and MLP intermediate dimensions \(d_{\text{mlp}} = 28672\), each weight matrix contains over 234 million parameters. - Performing full deterministic SVD across 80 transformer layers requires hours of intensive compute, generating gigabytes of transient matrix memory allocations that trigger GPU Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as Dense Weight Matrix W (M x N)
    participant Gauss as Gaussian Matrix Omega (N x (r+p))
    participant Sample as Subspace Sample Y = W @ Omega
    participant Power as Power Iterations (W @ W^T)^q
    participant QR as Thin QR Factorization: Q, R
    participant Small as Subspace Projection B = Q^T @ W
    participant SVD as Fast Tiny SVD(B)

    Gauss->>W: Draw random Gaussian test matrix Omega ~ N(0, 1)
    W->>Sample: Form sketch matrix Y = W @ Omega (Shape: M x (r+p))
    Sample->>Power: Apply q power iterations to accelerate singular decay
    Power->>QR: Compute orthonormal basis Q via QR(Y) (Shape: M x (r+p))
    QR->>Small: Project weight matrix into tiny subspace B = Q^T @ W (Shape: (r+p) x N)
    Small->>SVD: Perform exact SVD on tiny matrix B -> U_tilde, Sigma, V^T
    SVD->>W: Reconstruct left singular vectors U = Q @ U_tilde[:, :r]
  1. Random Gaussian Sketching: Draw a random Gaussian test matrix \(\Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (r + p)}\), where \(r\) is the target rank and \(p\) is a small oversampling buffer (typically \(p=5 \text{ to } 10\)).
  2. Subspace Sampling: Multiply \(W\) by \(\Omega\) to form the sample matrix \(Y = W \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times (r + p)}\). The columns of \(Y\) span the dominant range of \(W\) with high probability.
  3. Power Iterations (Spectral Contrast Enhancement): To sharpen the spectral gap when singular values decay slowly, compute \(Y = (W W^T)^q Y\) for \(q \in \{1, 2, 3\}\). This exponentially suppresses the tail noise.
  4. Orthonormalization: Compute the thin QR decomposition of \(Y\): \(Y = Q R\), yielding an orthonormal basis matrix \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times (r + p)}\).
  5. Tiny Subspace Projection: Project \(W\) onto the low-dimensional basis \(Q\): \(B = Q^T W \in \mathbb{R}^{(r + p) \times N}\). Matrix \(B\) has only \((r + p)\) rows!
  6. Tiny SVD & Reconstruction: Perform standard SVD on the tiny matrix \(B = \tilde{U} \Sigma V^T\). Recover the full left singular vectors via \(U = Q \tilde{U}[:, :r]\).

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Let \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\), target rank \(r \ll \min(M, N)\), and oversampling parameter \(p \ge 4\):

\[\text{Gaussian Test Matrix: } \Omega_{i, j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (r + p)}\] \[\text{Power Iteration Subspace Sketch: } Y = \left( W W^T \right)^q W \Omega \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times (r + p)}\] \[\text{QR Orthogonalization: } Q, R = \operatorname{qr}(Y) \implies Q^T Q = I_{r+p}\] \[\text{Low-Dimensional Projection: } B = Q^T W \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{(r + p) \times N}\] \[\text{Compact SVD on } B: B = \tilde{U} \Sigma V^T \implies U = Q \tilde{U}[:, :r], \; \Sigma_r = \Sigma[:r], \; V_r = V[:, :r]\] \[\text{Theoretical Probabilistic Error Bound (Halko et al.): } \mathbb{E}\left[ \|W - Q Q^T W\|_F \right] \le \left( 1 + \frac{r}{p - 1} \right)^{1/2} \sigma_{r+1}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 10x to 50x Wall-Clock Speedup: Factorizes an entire 70B parameter model in under 12 minutes on an 8-GPU node.
  • Deterministic-Quality Approximations: With power iterations \(q=2\) and oversampling \(p=10\), approximation error matches exact deterministic SVD to 6 decimal places.
  • Constant Memory Footprint: Never materializes full \(M \times N\) Gram matrices during factorization.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Kronecker & Tensor-Train: Breaking the 2D Matrix Parameter Barrier Factorizing massive projection layers into high-order multi-dimensional tensor networks and recursive Kronecker products to compress parameters by over 95%.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine storing a high-resolution 3D anatomical human model. If you store it as a giant, flat 2D spreadsheet of coordinates (2D matrix SVD), you need millions of rows and columns, hitting a linear storage ceiling.

Instead, you use a Tensor-Train: you factorize the 3D volume along its natural anatomical axes—a connected chain of small 3D rings describing cross-sections of the torso, limbs, and organs. Each ring communicates only with its immediate neighbors through thin connecting ports (the TT-ranks). You preserve full 3D spatial fidelity while using 1/50th the memory of a flat 2D file!

 Standard 2D Low-Rank: W in R^(4096 x 4096), Rank 64
 [4096 x 64] @ [64 x 4096] = 524,288 Parameters

 Tensor-Train Decomposition: Shape (16x16x16) x (16x16x16), TT-Rank 8
 [Core G1: 1x16x16x8] ── [Core G2: 8x16x16x8] ── [Core G3: 8x16x16x1]
 Total Parameters: 2,048 + 16,384 + 2,048 = 20,480 Parameters  (96.1% Reduction!)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Standard 2D low-rank factorizations (\(W \approx A B\)) scale linearly with the hidden dimensions: \(\mathcal{O}(r (d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}))\). - In next-generation foundation models where \(d = 8192\) or \(16384\), even modest low-rank adapters (\(r=64\)) require millions of parameters per layer. - Furthermore, 2D matrix factorizations are structurally blind to multi-modal and multi-head hierarchies: they treat a multi-head projection as a flat, unstructured grid, ignoring the rich tensor product interactions between heads, features, and spatial tokens.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
graph LR
    subgraph Tensor-Train Matrix Contraction
        Input["Token Input Tensor x"] --> G1["Core Tensor G^(1) (r0 x p1 x q1 x r1)"]
        G1 -->|Bond Index r1| G2["Core Tensor G^(2) (r1 x p2 x q2 x r2)"]
        G2 -->|Bond Index r2| G3["Core Tensor G^(3) (r2 x p3 x q3 x r3)"]
        G3 --> Output["Compressed Output Tensor y"]
    end

    subgraph Kronecker-LoRA Hybrid Engine
        Base["Frozen Base Layer W0"] --> Sum((+))
        Kron["Kronecker Product (A1 ⊗ A2)"] --> Mod["⊙ Dynamic TT Modulation TT(G1, G2, G3)"]
        Mod --> Scale["* Learned Gain γ"]
        Scale --> Sum
        Sum --> FinalOutput["Adapter Output"]
    end
  1. Multi-Dimensional Mode Factorization: Reshape input and output dimensions into prime factor tuples: \(d_{\text{in}} = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdots p_d\) and \(d_{\text{out}} = q_1 \cdot q_2 \cdots q_d\). The 2D weight matrix \(W\) is reshaped into a \(2d\)-dimensional tensor \(\mathcal{W}\).
  2. Tensor-Train Core Chain: Decompose \(\mathcal{W}\) into a sequence of \(d\) core tensors \(G^{(1)}, G^{(2)}, \dots, G^{(d)}\): $\(\mathcal{W}(q_1 \dots q_d, p_1 \dots p_d) = G^{(1)}[:, p_1, q_1, :] \cdot G^{(2)}[:, p_2, q_2, :] \cdots G^{(d)}[:, p_d, q_d, :]\)$ where boundary ranks are fixed to \(r_0 = r_d = 1\), and intermediate TT-ranks \(r_k \le R_{\text{TT}}\).
  3. Kronecker-TT-LoRA Hybridization: For parameter-efficient fine-tuning, Kronecker-LoRA combines a coarse-grained Kronecker product \(A_1 \otimes A_2\) with fine-grained Tensor-Train core modulation: $\(\Delta W = \gamma \cdot \left( A_1 \otimes A_2 \right) \odot \mathcal{TT}(G_1, G_2, G_3)\)$
  4. Dynamic Spectral Entropy Controller: Measures the singular value entropy \(\mathcal{H}_{\text{sv}}\) during training and dynamically increases or decreases TT-ranks across individual layers based on learning complexity.

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given weight tensor \(\mathcal{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{(q_1 \times \dots \times q_d) \times (p_1 \times \dots \times p_d)}\):

\[\text{TT Core Element: } \mathcal{W}_{q_1\dots q_d, p_1\dots p_d} = \sum_{\alpha_0=1}^{r_0} \cdots \sum_{\alpha_d=1}^{r_d} G^{(1)}_{\alpha_0, p_1, q_1, \alpha_1} G^{(2)}_{\alpha_1, p_2, q_2, \alpha_2} \cdots G^{(d)}_{\alpha_{d-1}, p_d, q_d, \alpha_d}\] \[\text{TT Parameter Complexity: } \mathcal{O}\left( \sum_{k=1}^d r_{k-1} p_k q_k r_k \right) \ll \mathcal{O}\left( \prod_{k=1}^d p_k q_k \right)\] \[\text{Kronecker Product Definition: } (A_1 \otimes A_2)_{(i_1 i_2), (j_1 j_2)} = (A_1)_{i_1, j_1} \cdot (A_2)_{i_2, j_2}\] \[\text{Kronecker-TT-LoRA Forward: } y = x W_0^T + \gamma \cdot x \left[ (A_1 \otimes A_2) \odot \mathcal{TT}(G_1, G_2, G_3) \right]^T\] \[\text{Spectral Entropy Monitor: } \mathcal{H}_{\text{sv}} = -\sum_{i=1}^r \hat{\sigma}_i \log \hat{\sigma}_i \quad \text{where } \hat{\sigma}_i = \frac{\sigma_i(\Delta W)}{\sum_j \sigma_j(\Delta W)}\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 95%+ Parameter Compression: Slashes a 4096-dimensional linear layer from 16.7 million parameters to fewer than 80,000 parameters.
  • Full Model Fine-Tuning on Consumer Hardware: Enables fine-tuning 70B+ LLMs on a single 24GB RTX 4090 GPU using Kronecker-TT adapters.
  • Expressive High-Order Representations: Captures multi-linear token and head correlations that standard 2D LoRA matrices mathematically cannot represent.

Floating beside them is a matrix tiling lattice showing the Kronecker product \(A_1 \otimes A_2\) in electric cyan #3B82F6 and amber gold #F59E0B. docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: CUR Decomposition: Interpretable Low-Rank Factorization via Leverage-Score Sampling Preserving genuine weight channels by sampling actual columns and rows linked through a Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse core.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine assembling an Olympic dream team. Standard SVD creates synthetic "amalgam" athletes—a hybrid composite containing 30% of a sprinter, 40% of a swimmer, and 30% of a gymnast (abstract singular vectors \(U\) and \(V\)).

CUR Decomposition refuses to create artificial hybrids. Instead, it visits the training field, identifies the actual, best real individual athletes (selecting real columns \(C\) and real rows \(R\) from matrix \(W\) based on their performance leverage scores), and hires a head coach (the core matrix \(U\)) to orchestrate their plays. The resulting team is 100% genuine, highly interpretable, and retains all specialized physical skills!

 SVD: W ≈ U @ Σ @ V^T  (U and V are synthetic, dense linear blends)
 ┌──────────────────────┐       ┌────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ Dense Synthetic U    │   @   │ Diag Σ │   @   │ Dense Synthetic V^T  │
 └──────────────────────┘       └────────┘       └──────────────────────┘

 CUR: W ≈ C @ U @ R    (C and R are ACTUAL columns and rows from original W!)
 ┌──────────────────────┐       ┌────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ Real Columns C of W  │   @   │ Core U │   @   │ Real Rows R of W     │
 └──────────────────────┘       └────────┘       └──────────────────────┘

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: While SVD is optimal under the Frobenius norm, its principal singular vectors \(U\) and \(V\) are dense, synthetic mathematical constructs: 1. Loss of Physical Interpretability: SVD blends thousands of disparate input channels into abstract coordinates, obscuring which specific attention heads or token features are active. 2. Destruction of Natural Sparsity: If original weight matrix \(W\) has 40% natural sparsity, SVD's factors \(U\) and \(V\) become 100% dense, destroying hardware sparse execution benefits. 3. Inability to Reuse Weights: SVD requires storing entirely new basis matrices, preventing cache-line memory reuse across layers with shared vocabulary embeddings.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Dense Weight Tensor W in R^(d_out x d_in)"] --> B1["Compute Column Leverage Probabilities p_col_j = ||W_:,j||_2 / sum"]
    A --> B2["Compute Row Leverage Probabilities p_row_i = ||W_i,:||_2 / sum"]
    B1 --> C1["Sample r Dominant Columns -> Matrix C in R^(d_out x r)"]
    B2 --> C2["Sample r Dominant Rows -> Matrix R in R^(r x d_in)"]
    C1 --> D["Compute Moore-Penrose Pseudo-Inverses C_pinv and R_pinv"]
    C2 --> D
    D --> E["Compute Core Matrix U = C_pinv @ W @ R_pinv in R^(r x r)"]
    E --> F["Low-Rank Factorized Representation: W_hat = C @ U @ R"]
  1. Statistical Leverage Score Calculation: Compute the statistical importance of every column and row using their \(L_2\)-norm energy distributions: $\(p_{\text{col}}(j) = \frac{\|W_{:, j}\|_2}{\sum_{k=1}^{d_{\text{in}}} \|W_{:, k}\|_2}, \quad p_{\text{row}}(i) = \frac{\|W_{i, :}\|_2}{\sum_{k=1}^{d_{\text{out}}} \|W_{k, :}\|_2}\)$
  2. Subspace Sampling: Sample \(r\) column indices \(I_{\text{cols}}\) and \(r\) row indices \(I_{\text{rows}}\) without replacement according to these leverage distributions.
  3. Sub-Matrix Extraction: Extract the sampled columns to form \(C = W[:, I_{\text{cols}}] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}\) and sampled rows to form \(R = W[I_{\text{rows}}, :] \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}\).
  4. Moore-Penrose Core Optimization: Compute the optimal intersection core matrix \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}\) minimizing \(\|W - C U R\|_F^2\) via pseudo-inverses: $\(U = C^\dagger W R^\dagger = (C^T C)^{-1} C^T W R^T (R R^T)^{-1}\)$
  5. Linear Layer Execution: Forward operations execute via three efficient matrix multiplications: \(Y = (((X R^T) U^T) C^T) + b\).

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given weight matrix \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) and target rank \(r\):

\[\text{Column Selection: } C = W[:, I_{\text{cols}}] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}, \quad I_{\text{cols}} \sim p_{\text{col}}\] \[\text{Row Selection: } R = W[I_{\text{rows}}, :] \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}, \quad I_{\text{rows}} \sim p_{\text{row}}\] \[\text{Moore-Penrose Pseudo-Inverses: } C^\dagger = (C^T C)^{-1} C^T, \quad R^\dagger = R^T (R R^T)^{-1}\] \[\text{Optimal Core Linking Matrix: } U = C^\dagger W R^\dagger \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}\] \[\text{CUR Factorized Forward Pass: } Y = \underbrace{\left( \left( X R^T \right) U^T \right)}_{\text{Down-project to } r} C^T + b\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 100% Channel Interpretability: Retains original weight channels, allowing direct inspection of which token features drive model decisions.
  • Sparsity Preservation: If original weight \(W\) is sparse, sub-matrices \(C\) and \(R\) inherit the exact same zero-pattern, enabling sparse accelerator speedups.
  • Memory Deduplication: Layers with redundant feature channels can point to shared memory buffers for \(C\) and \(R\), reducing KV cache and parameter storage.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: ADMM Low-Rank: Decoupling Structured Sparsity and Rank Constraints Unifying low-rank matrix factorization and structured magnitude pruning into an alternating direction constrained optimization framework.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine restoring a historic architectural landmark under strict city building regulations. Regulation A requires modern steel earthquake reinforcement (low-rank structural constraint). Regulation B mandates preserving historic brick archways with minimal physical footprint (structured sparsity constraint).

Trying to satisfy both constraints in a single chaotic construction step causes building collapse. ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers) breaks the project into a three-step round-robin: - Step 1 updates the architectural blueprints (\(W\)). - Step 2 enforces the earthquake reinforcement (\(Z\)). - Step 3 cleans the historic brick footprint (\(Y\)), while an inspector (\(\Lambda\)) updates penalty fines until all constraints converge into structural perfection.

 Sequential Prune-then-SVD (Catastrophic Error Compounding!)
 [Dense Weight W] ──► [Hard Pruning Mask] ──► [SVD Factorization] ──► [Accuracy Collapse]

 ADMM Joint Optimization (Alternating Convergence)
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │   Solve W (Task Loss) ◄──► Prox_Rank(Z) ◄──► Prox_Sparse(Y)   │
 │              ▲                          ▲              │
 │              └──── Update Dual Penalty Λ ┘              │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Combining multiple compression techniques—such as structured pruning (zeroing out redundant heads/channels) and low-rank matrix factorization (SVD)—usually involves sequential execution: first prune the model, then factorize the remaining weights. 1. Sequential heuristics suffer from compounded error drift: pruning alters the singular value spectrum, causing subsequent SVD to discard critical recovered directions. 2. The joint optimization problem \(\min_W \mathcal{L}(W) \text{ s.t. } \operatorname{rank}(W) \le r, \, \|W\|_0 \le k\) is an NP-hard non-convex combinatorial problem that standard gradient descent cannot solve.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as Primal Weight W
    participant Z as Low-Rank Manifold Z
    participant S as Sparse Manifold S
    participant Dual as Dual Multipliers (U_z, U_s)

    Note over W,Dual: ADMM Alternating Optimization Loop
    W->>W: Step 1: Minimize Task Loss + Augmented Penalty wrt W
    W->>Z: Step 2: Singular Value Thresholding Prox_Rank(W + U_z)
    W->>S: Step 3: Hard/Soft Magnitude Thresholding Prox_Sparse(W + U_s)
    Z->>Dual: Step 4: Accumulate Primal Residuals (W - Z) into U_z
    S->>Dual: Step 5: Accumulate Primal Residuals (W - S) into U_s
    Dual-->>W: Feedback Dual Penalties to Next Epoch
  1. Variable Splitting: Introduce auxiliary variables \(Z\) (constrained to rank \(r\)) and \(S\) (constrained to sparsity \(k\)): $\(\min_{W, Z, S} f(W) + g(Z) + h(S) \quad \text{subject to } W - Z = 0, \; W - S = 0\)$
  2. Augmented Lagrangian Formulation: Form the augmented objective with quadratic penalty parameter \(\rho\) and dual multipliers \(\Lambda_z, \Lambda_s\).
  3. Primal Weight Update (Step 1): Update continuous weight \(W\) using standard backpropagation gradients regularized by distance to \(Z\) and \(S\).
  4. Low-Rank Proximal Projection (Step 2): Project \(W + U_z\) onto the rank-\(r\) manifold using Singular Value Thresholding (SVT).
  5. Sparse Proximal Projection (Step 3): Project \(W + U_s\) onto the \(k\)-sparse manifold using magnitude thresholding.
  6. Dual Variable Accumulation (Step 4): Accumulate constraint violations into dual variables \(U_z \leftarrow U_z + (W - Z)\) and \(U_s \leftarrow U_s + (W - S)\).

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given task loss function \(f(W)\) and augmented penalty parameter \(\rho > 0\):

\[\text{Augmented Lagrangian: } \mathcal{L}_{\rho}(W, Z, \Lambda) = f(W) + \mathcal{I}_{\text{rank}}(Z) + \mathcal{I}_{\text{sparse}}(S) + \frac{\rho}{2}\|W - Z + U_z\|_F^2 + \frac{\rho}{2}\|W - S + U_s\|_F^2\] \[\text{Primal Weight Update: } W^{(t+1)} = \arg\min_W f(W) + \frac{\rho}{2} \left\| W - Z^{(t)} + U_z^{(t)} \right\|_F^2 + \frac{\rho}{2} \left\| W - S^{(t)} + U_s^{(t)} \right\|_F^2\] \[\text{Low-Rank Proximal Step: } Z^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{SVT}_r\left( W^{(t+1)} + U_z^{(t)} \right) = U[:, :r] \Sigma[:r] (V[:r, :])^T\] \[\text{Sparse Proximal Step: } S^{(t+1)} = \operatorname{TopK}_k\left( W^{(t+1)} + U_s^{(t)} \right)\] \[\text{Dual Multiplier Updates: } U_z^{(t+1)} = U_z^{(t)} + \left( W^{(t+1)} - Z^{(t+1)} \right), \quad U_s^{(t+1)} = U_s^{(t)} + \left( W^{(t+1)} - S^{(t+1)} \right)\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Principled Multi-Constraint Convergence: Eliminates catastrophic error compounding from naive sequential pruning and low-rank compression.
  • Superior Compression Ratios: Achieves simultaneous 60% structured sparsity and 50% rank reduction with near-lossless accuracy recovery.
  • Hardware-Friendly Architecture: Produces models that execute seamlessly on both sparse tensor cores and low-rank factorized GEMM engines.

docs.title: 8. NMF Compressor: Non-Negative Matrix Factorization for LLMs
Title & Subtitle
docs.text: NMF Compressor: Purely Additive Low-Rank Representations Without Destructive Cancellation Enforcing non-negativity constraints to eliminate signed signal cancellation and provide robust, parts-based factorizations for transformer layers.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine creating a digital color painting. If you use signed sound-wave mathematics (standard SVD), you allow "negative light"—adding positive blue and negative blue to cancel each other out to produce darkness. If a minor quantization error perturbs the negative blue value, the balance is shattered, and a violent purple flare erupts on your screen.

NMF (Non-Negative Matrix Factorization) paints like a real-world artist using physical pigment oils on canvas (\(H \ge 0, W \ge 0\)). You only add layers of paint on top of each other. Because every component is strictly positive, there is zero destructive cancellation: if you slightly perturb one brushstroke, the overall painting remains stable, natural, and visually coherent!

 Standard SVD: Signed Cancellation (+A) + (-B) ≈ 0  (Sensitive to Quantization Noise!)
 ┌────────────────────────────────┐     ┌────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Positive Feature (+14.8)       │  +  │ Negative Cancellation (-14.7)  │ ──► Delta = +0.1
 └────────────────────────────────┘     └────────────────────────────────┘
                                                       │ (Quantization Rounding Error!)
                                                       ▼
                                                Catastrophic Flare: +3.4!

 NMF: Purely Additive Construction (H >= 0, W_comp >= 0)
 ┌────────────────────────────────┐     ┌────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Base Pigment Layer H >= 0      │  +  │ Detail Glaze W_comp >= 0       │ ──► Pure Addition
 └────────────────────────────────┘     └────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Standard SVD factorizes matrices into orthonormal bases containing both positive and negative coefficients. 1. Destructive Signal Cancellation: SVD achieves low error by orchestrating delicate cancellations between large positive and large negative numbers across singular vectors. 2. Quantization Brittleness: When factorized matrices are subsequently quantized to low bit-widths (such as INT4 or FP8), small quantization rounding errors destroy these delicate cancellations, resulting in massive output variance spikes. 3. Activation Incompatibility: Modern LLMs utilize non-negative activation functions (ReLU, SwiGLU, GeLU with positive bias offsets). Signed SVD basis vectors clash with non-negative activation manifolds.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W["Dense Signed Weight W"] --> Shift["Affine Shift: W_shifted = W - min(W) + eps >= 0"]
    Shift --> Init["Initialize Positive Factors H >= 0 and W_comp >= 0"]
    Init --> Loop{Lee-Seung Iterations}
    Loop --> UpdateW["Update W_comp: Multiply by H^T W / H^T H W_comp"]
    UpdateW --> UpdateH["Update H: Multiply by W W_comp^T / H W_comp W_comp^T"]
    UpdateH --> Converged[Convergence Reached]
    Converged --> Recon["Inverse Affine Shift: W_hat = H @ W_comp + min_offset"]
    Recon --> Final["Factorized Non-Negative Linear Layer"]
  1. Non-Negative Domain Transformation: Since raw weight matrices contain signed numbers, NMF applies an affine shift to guarantee strict positivity: $\(W_{\text{shifted}} = W - w_{\min} \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T + \epsilon \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T \quad \ge 0\)$
  2. Positive Initialization: Initialize non-negative activation matrix \(H \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}\) and component matrix \(W_{\text{comp}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}\).
  3. Multiplicative Lee-Seung Updates: Alternately update factors using non-negative gradient ratios: $\(W_{\text{comp}} \leftarrow W_{\text{comp}} \odot \frac{H^T W_{\text{shifted}}}{H^T H W_{\text{comp}} + \epsilon}, \quad H \leftarrow H \odot \frac{W_{\text{shifted}} W_{\text{comp}}^T}{H W_{\text{comp}} W_{\text{comp}}^T + \epsilon}\)$
  4. Inverse Affine Reconstruction: After convergence, the original un-shifted weight operator is synthesized during forward inference: $\(\hat{W} = H W_{\text{comp}} + (w_{\min} - \epsilon) \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T\)$

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
Given shifted non-negative weight matrix \(W_{\text{shifted}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) and target rank \(r\):

\[\text{NMF Constrained Objective: } \min_{H \ge 0, \, W_{\text{comp}} \ge 0} \frac{1}{2} \left\| W_{\text{shifted}} - H W_{\text{comp}} \right\|_F^2\] \[\text{Basis Update Rule: } W_{\text{comp}}^{(t+1)} = W_{\text{comp}}^{(t)} \odot \left[ \frac{H^T W_{\text{shifted}}}{H^T H W_{\text{comp}}^{(t)} + \epsilon} \right]\] \[\text{Coefficient Update Rule: } H^{(t+1)} = H^{(t)} \odot \left[ \frac{W_{\text{shifted}} (W_{\text{comp}}^{(t+1)})^T}{H^{(t)} W_{\text{comp}}^{(t+1)} (W_{\text{comp}}^{(t+1)})^T + \epsilon} \right]\] \[\text{Unshifted Linear Forward Pass: } Y = X \left( H W_{\text{comp}} \right)^T + (w_{\min} - \epsilon) \left( X \mathbf{1}_{d_{\text{in}}} \right) \mathbf{1}_{d_{\text{out}}}^T + b\]

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Extreme Robustness to Low-Bit Quantization: Because components are strictly additive, quantizing \(H\) and \(W_{\text{comp}}\) to INT4 produces zero catastrophic cancellation spikes.
  • Parts-Based Explainability: Discovers localized, interpretable token feature detectors that correspond directly to semantic linguistic concepts.
  • Natural Synergy with ReLU/SwiGLU: Aligns seamlessly with modern rectifier activation manifolds.

docs.title: 9. RPCA Compressor: Robust Principal Component Analysis (Low-Rank + Sparse)
Title & Subtitle
docs.text: RPCA Compressor: Decoupling Low-Rank Manifolds from Sparse Outlier Spikes Isolating extreme outlier parameters into a dedicated sparse matrix to enable ultra-compact low-rank factorization of the smooth underlying weights.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine restoring an invaluable vintage vinyl audio recording. The recording contains a gorgeous, smooth orchestral symphony (the low-rank manifold \(L\)), but also contains sharp, loud, sudden static crackles and needle scratches (the sparse outlier matrix \(S\)).

If you run standard audio compression (SVD) on the raw noisy track, th1. Principal Component Pursuit (PCP): Formulate the decomposition of dense weight \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) into a low-rank matrix \(L\) and a sparse outlier matrix \(S\): $\(W = L + S\)$ 2. Singular Value Truncation Step: At iteration \(t\), subtract the current sparse estimate from the weight matrix: \(R_L = W - S^{(t)}\). Perform truncated SVD on \(R_L\) to target rank \(r\) to obtain updated low-rank estimate \(L^{(t+1)}\). 3. Sparse Soft-Thresholding Step: Compute the residual matrix \(R_S = W - L^{(t+1)}\). Apply entry-wise soft-thresholding with threshold parameter \(\mu\): $\(S^{(t+1)} = \operatorname{sign}(R_S) \odot \max(|R_S| - \mu, \, 0)\)$ 4. Dual-Stream Inference Engine: The compressed layer stores \(L\) as two low-rank factors (\(U_r, V_r^T\)) and \(S\) as a Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) matrix. Forward execution runs as: $\(Y = \left( (X V_r) U_r^T \right) + X S_{\text{sparse}}^T + b\)$
