docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Rotational SliceGPT-INT4: Orthogonal Basis Transformation Meets Structured Weight Slicing Rotating activation coordinate systems via orthogonal transformation matrices to concentrate signal energy, physically slicing away redundant channels, and quantizing the dense core to INT4.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine packing an oddly shaped, sprawling collection of luggage into a tight cargo trunk. If you throw the items in at random angles, they bump into each other, creating dead space and sticking out of the edges. But if you first rotate every suitcase to align perfectly with a geometric grid (orthogonal rotation), all the heavy mass settles tightly into the first 75% of the trunk. You can then slice off the empty remaining 25% of the trunk compartment entirely, and vacuum-pack the rest (INT4 quantization) without crushing a single fragile item.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Traditional pruning algorithms fall into two extremes, both of which struggle on modern hardware: 1. Unstructured Sparsity: Zeroes out arbitrary individual weights. While this retains model accuracy, modern GPU Tensor Cores cannot execute irregular sparse patterns efficiently without specialized sparse libraries that introduce severe latency overhead. 2. Standard Structured Pruning: Drops entire weight columns or attention heads to produce smaller, dense matrices. However, large language models develop complex inter-channel dependencies and extreme activation outliers. Naively dropping channels destroys critical representations, causing catastrophic perplexity degradation unless recovered by expensive full-scale retraining.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Rotational SliceGPT solves this dilemma through a two-phase mathematical transformation: 1. Orthogonal Basis Rotation: Using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) or Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on calibration activations, we compute an orthogonal transformation matrix \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) (where \(Q^T Q = I\)). Because \(Q\) is strictly orthogonal, inserting \(Q Q^T\) between linear layers and normalization layers does not alter the mathematical output of the network. 2. Energy Concentration: The rotation rotates the coordinate system of the activations such that signal variance is sorted in descending order. The first \(k\) dimensions (e.g., \(k = 3072\) out of \(d = 4096\)) retain over \(98\%\) of the total activation variance, while the trailing \(d - k\) dimensions decay close to zero. 3. Structured Slicing: The model physically truncates the weight matrices from \(d \times d\) down to \(k \times k\). The unneeded channels are deleted from VRAM permanently, reducing the physical dimensions of all linear layers. 4. INT4 Quantization: The remaining compact \(k \times k\) dense core is quantized to 4-bit integers using group-wise symmetric uniform quantization.

flowchart LR
    A["Input Tokens X"] --> B["Orthogonal Rotation Q"]
    B --> C["Rotated Space XQ"]
    C --> D["Variance Slicing: Keep top-k"]
    D --> E["INT4 Quantization W_sliced"]
    E --> F["Ultra-Fast Dense INT4 Tensor Core"]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: Given an activation matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}\) and linear weight \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_{\text{out}}}\), we insert the identity \(I = Q Q^T\): $\(Y = X W = (X Q) (Q^T W) = \tilde{X} \tilde{W}\)$ We compute \(Q\) from the eigenvalue decomposition of the activation covariance matrix \(C = \frac{1}{T} X^T X = Q \Lambda Q^T\). By selecting the top-\(k\) principal components, we slice the rotated weight: $\(\tilde{W}_{\text{sliced}} = (Q^T W)_{[:k, :]} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d_{\text{out}}}\)$ We then quantize \(\tilde{W}_{\text{sliced}}\) into 4-bit signed integers with scaling factor \(S\): $\(W_{\text{INT4}} = \text{clamp}\left( \left\lfloor \frac{\tilde{W}_{\text{sliced}}}{S} \right\rceil, -8, 7 \right), \quad S = \frac{\max(|\tilde{W}_{\text{sliced}}|)}{7}\)$

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Physical Tensor Shrinkage: Slicing 25% of hidden dimensions cuts parameter count and FLOPs by \((1 - 0.75^2) \approx 43.7\%\) before quantization.
  • Hardware-Native Dense Execution: The pruned model runs on standard cuBLAS and CUTLASS dense GEMM kernels with zero sparse indexing penalties.
  • 5.3x Total Compression: Combining a 25% slice with INT4 quantization reduces a 70B parameter model footprint from 140 GB (FP16) down to ~26 GB, fitting on a single 32 GB workstation GPU with negligible perplexity loss.

docs.title: 2. DeltaKV & CacheNotes
docs.text:
Token Stream:     [t_0: Anchor]  ───>  [t_1: Delta]  ───>  [t_2: Delta]  ───>  [t_3: Delta]
  KV Storage:       [Full FP16/FP8]     [2-bit Resid]       [2-bit Resid]       [2-bit Resid]
                     └─────────────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                                               ▼
                              [CacheNotes: Distilled Semantic Note]

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: DeltaKV & CacheNotes: Dynamic Key-Value Differential Compression Exploiting cross-token contextual redundancy in generative decoding by storing anchor keyframes, ultra-low-bit delta residuals, and hierarchical semantic notes.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Consider modern video streaming formats like H.265 (HEVC). The video player does not store a full, uncompressed 4K image for every single 60-fps frame (I-frames). Instead, it stores one high-fidelity reference frame every few seconds, followed by tiny differential motion vectors (P-frames and B-frames) that describe only what changed. DeltaKV applies video codec delta-compression to the Key-Value cache of large language models: it keeps rare anchor tokens in high precision and stores the subsequent 90% of tokens as micro-precision residual deltas.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: During autoregressive text generation, the Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly with context length (\(O(B \cdot L \cdot H \cdot D)\)). For a 70B model operating at a 128k context window: - The KV cache demands >160 GB of VRAM, far exceeding the memory required by the model weights themselves! - Memory bandwidth saturation from reading this massive KV cache during every single decoding step throttles generation speed down to single-digit tokens per second.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. Anchor Token Identification: When a new prompt or sequence is processed, tokens with high semantic saliency or periodic interval tokens (every \(N\) tokens) are designated as Anchor Keys and Values (\(K_{\text{base}}, V_{\text{base}}\)) and kept in FP8/FP16.
  2. Differential Residual Formulation: For intermediate tokens \(t\), the attention key and value vectors are highly correlated with the local anchor. DeltaKV computes the difference vector: $\(\Delta K_t = K_t - K_{\text{base}}, \quad \Delta V_t = V_t - V_{\text{base}}\)$
  3. 2-Bit / 3-Bit Residual Quantization: Because \(\Delta K_t\) and \(\Delta V_t\) are tightly clustered around zero with minimal variance, they can be aggressively quantized to 2-bit or 3-bit non-linear integer grids without loss of fidelity.
  4. CacheNotes Hierarchical Summarization: As context recedes into the distant past (\(>4096\) tokens back), DeltaKV merges clusters of delta tokens into a single compact low-rank "CacheNote" centroid vector, freeing up cache lines while retaining long-range associative recall.
sequenceDiagram
    participant LLM as Decoder Layer
    participant Anchor as Anchor Buffer (FP16/FP8)
    participant Delta as Delta Storage (2-bit INT)
    participant Notes as CacheNotes Engine

    LLM->>Anchor: Write Keyframe Token (t=0)
    LLM->>Delta: Compute & Quantize Delta ΔK, ΔV (t=1..7)
    Note over Delta: 2-bit Non-linear Quantization
    LLM->>Notes: Background: Compress Past Blocks into Semantic Centroid
    LLM->>LLM: Fast Reconstructed Dequant Decode: K = K_anchor + dequant(ΔK)

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: Let \(K_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}\) be the key vector at time \(t\) and \(K_{\text{anchor}}\) be its assigned reference key. The quantized residual representation is: $\(\mathbf{q}_t = \mathcal{Q}_{b\text{-bit}}\left( K_t - K_{\text{anchor}} \right) = \left\lfloor \frac{K_t - K_{\text{anchor}}}{s_t} \right\rceil\)$ During the attention score calculation between query \(Q_{\tau}\) and cached key \(K_t\), the dot product expands linearly: $\(\text{AttnScore}(\tau, t) = \frac{Q_{\tau} K_t^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} = \frac{Q_{\tau} K_{\text{anchor}}^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \frac{Q_{\tau} \left( s_t \cdot \mathbf{q}_t \right)^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\)$ Because \(Q_{\tau} K_{\text{anchor}}^T\) can be pre-computed or shared across clustered tokens, the inner loop computes low-precision integer dot products against \(\mathbf{q}_t\).

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 4x to 6x KV Cache Reduction: Reduces 128k context KV memory footprint from 160 GB down to ~32 GB.
  • 3.2x Decoding Throughput: Massive reduction in memory bandwidth traffic allows GPU compute engines to run closer to peak FLOPS.
  • Zero Hallucination on Needle-In-A-Haystack: Unlike naive token dropping, DeltaKV preserves every single token's position and gradient direction in residual space.

│                                                                             │

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: ZeroKV-Neo: Zero-Footprint Persistent Memory with Dynamic Eviction & State Recurrence Achieving constant O(1) KV cache memory bounds during infinite-horizon generation by combining attention-sink preservation, dynamic mass eviction, and recurrent summary compression.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a courtroom stenographer working on a 6-month trial. If they tried to keep every single open sheet of paper spread out across the courtroom floor, they would run out of physical space within days. Instead, a master stenographer keeps: 1. The original charge sheet pinned to the front podium (Attention Sinks), 2. The active testimony from the current witness (Local Sliding Window), 3. Key exhibits that are frequently referenced (Heavy Hitters), and 4. Summarizes all resolved daily arguments into an ongoing master case ledger (Recurrent Summary State), recycling the scratch paper.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Autoregressive transformers suffer from the Infinite Context Memory Wall. If a model generates text continuously (such as in autonomous agent loops, continuous streaming chat, or real-time sensor processing), the KV cache will eventually exhaust GPU VRAM, leading to out-of-memory (OOM) crashes. Simple sliding-window cache strategies fail catastrophically: when early tokens (especially the first 4 tokens) are evicted, the model exhibits sudden, complete perplexity collapse due to the loss of "attention sinks."

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
ZeroKV-Neo establishes a bounded, constant-size memory architecture: 1. Permanent Attention Sinks: The initial 4 tokens (\(t \in [0, 3]\)) are permanently locked in high-precision cache. They absorb surplus softmax attention scores and prevent numerical instability. 2. Cumulative Attribution Scoring: For all intermediate tokens, ZeroKV-Neo tracks an exponential moving average (EMA) of attention scores received from recent queries: $\(S_i^{(t)} = \beta S_i^{(t-1)} + (1 - \beta) \sum_{h=1}^H A_{h, t, i}\)$ 3. Dynamic Heavy-Hitter Retention: Tokens with high cumulative attribution scores are retained in the active cache pool. 4. Recurrent Summary Eviction: When a token's attribution score drops below an eviction threshold, it is not simply deleted. Instead, its Value vector is projected and blended into a fixed-size recurrent state vector \(h_{\text{neo}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\), preserving background semantic context in \(O(1)\) memory.

flowchart TD
    In["New Token Query Q_t"] --> Attn["Compute Attention Over Cache"]
    Attn --> UpScore["Update Attribution Score S_i for all tokens"]
    UpScore --> Check{"Memory Limit Exceeded?"}
    Check -- No --> Store["Append to Cache"]
    Check -- Yes --> Split["Partition Cache"]
    Split --> Sinks["Keep Pinned Initial Sinks (0..3)"]
    Split --> Local["Keep Recent Window (t-W .. t)"]
    Split --> TopK["Select Top-K Highest S_i"]
    Split --> Evict["Evict Low-Scoring Tail"]
    Evict --> Compress["Blend into Recurrent Summary Vector h_neo"]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: The active key-value cache indices \(\mathcal{M}_t\) at step \(t\) are dynamically maintained under a strict budget \(B\): $\(\mathcal{M}_t = \underbrace{\{0, 1, 2, 3\}}_{\text{Attention Sinks}} \;\cup\; \underbrace{\{t-W, \dots, t\}}_{\text{Recent Sliding Window}} \;\cup\; \text{TopK}_{B - W - 4}\left( \left\{ S_i^{(t)} \;\middle|\; i \in [4, t-W-1] \right\} \right)\)$ For evicted token indices \(\mathcal{E}_t\), the recurrent summary vector \(h_{\text{neo}}\) is updated via gated recurrent absorption: $\(h_{\text{neo}}^{(t)} = \alpha_t h_{\text{neo}}^{(t-1)} + (1 - \alpha_t) \sum_{j \in \mathcal{E}_t} \left( \frac{S_j^{(t)}}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{E}_t} S_k^{(t)}} \right) V_j\)$ During attention, \(h_{\text{neo}}\) is appended as a single virtual token at position 4.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• True \(O(1)\) Memory Consumption: Guarantees fixed VRAM usage whether generating 1,000 tokens or 10,000,000 tokens.
  • Infinite Streaming on Edge Devices: Allows running a 7B/13B parameter chatbot continuously on an 8 GB VRAM laptop or mobile chip without memory leaks or degradation.
  • Zero Softmax Collapse: Retains baseline perplexity across multi-day streaming sessions.

docs.title: 4. FLAP: Fluctuation-Aware Structured Pruning
docs.text:
Channel Feature Maps X_i across Calibration Tokens:
  Channel A (Static / Bias-dominated):  [ 5.01, 5.00, 5.02, 4.99, 5.01 ]  ──> Low Variance σ_A  ──> PRUNE (Fuse μ to Bias)
  Channel B (Dynamic / Informative):    [-3.20, 8.40, 0.10, -5.60, 4.20 ]  ──> High Variance σ_B ──> RETAIN

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: FLAP: Fluctuation-Aware Structured Pruning without Retraining Eliminating entire transformer channels and heads by evaluating output variance fluctuations and absorbing static baseline biases into downstream layers.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a control panel with 100 indicator dials monitoring a chemical plant. If 30 of those dials constantly point to "5.0" regardless of whether the plant is running at idle, full blast, or in an emergency, those 30 dials are not providing dynamic information—they are just reporting a static baseline. You can safely remove those 30 dials, wire their constant "+5.0" signal directly into the alarm logic (bias compensation), and focus the control room's attention entirely on the 70 dials that actively fluctuate with real-world changes.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Traditional structured pruning relies on weight magnitude heuristics (e.g., pruning weight rows with the smallest \(L_1\) or \(L_2\) norm). In modern LLMs with RMSNorm and residual connections, this fails for two major reasons: 1. Large weight values often serve merely to cancel out constant baseline offsets, producing zero dynamic variance. 2. Channels with small weight norms often carry critical, high-frequency signals that govern fine-grained logical reasoning. Pruning based on weight magnitude alone rips out sensitive dynamic channels, destroying the model's reasoning capabilities unless repaired by expensive multi-epoch retraining.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. Sampling Dynamic Fluctuations: Pass a small calibration dataset (e.g., 128 sequences from C4) through the model and record post-activation feature maps \(X_{:, i}\) for each channel \(i\).
  2. Variance vs. Bias Decomposition: Decompose each channel into its static mean component \(\mu_i = \mathbb{E}[X_{:, i}]\) and its dynamic fluctuation \(\sigma_i^2 = \text{Var}(X_{:, i})\).
  3. Bias Compensation Fusion: For channels with near-zero fluctuation \(\sigma_i \approx 0\), their static contribution is completely predictable. When channel \(i\) is removed from weight matrix \(W\), its mean contribution \(\mu_i W_{i, :}\) is added directly into the downstream layer's bias vector: $\(b_{\text{new}} = b_{\text{old}} + \sum_{i \in \text{Pruned}} \mu_i W_{i, :}\)$
  4. Structured Dimension Truncation: Channels, heads, or MLP intermediate widths are ranked by their dynamic impact score \(I_i = \sigma_i \cdot \|W_{i, :}\|_2\), and the lowest-scoring dimensions are physically sliced out.
flowchart LR
    A["Calibration Data"] --> B["Compute Feature Mean μ & Variance σ²"]
    B --> C{"Is Variance σ² Significant?"}
    C -- "High Fluctuation" --> D["Retain Dynamic Channel in Dense Matrix"]
    C -- "Low Fluctuation" --> E["Prune Channel from Weight Tensor"]
    E --> F["Fuse Static Bias Contribution (μ * W) into Layer Bias"]
    D & F --> G["Compensated Pruned Model (Zero Retraining Required)"]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: Given a linear projection \(Y = X W + b\), where \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d_{\text{in}}}\) and \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}}}\), the contribution of channel \(i\) is \(X_{:, i} W_{i, :}\). We express \(X_{:, i}\) in terms of its mean and deviation: \(X_{:, i} = \mu_i + \Delta X_{:, i}\), where \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_{:, i}] = 0\) and \(\text{Var}(\Delta X_{:, i}) = \sigma_i^2\). The layer output becomes: $\(Y = \sum_{i \in \text{Retained}} X_{:, i} W_{i, :} + \underbrace{\sum_{j \in \text{Pruned}} \mu_j W_{j, :} + b}_{\text{Updated Bias } b^*} + \underbrace{\sum_{j \in \text{Pruned}} \Delta X_{:, j} W_{j, :}}_{\text{Reconstruction Error } \mathcal{E}}\)$ The Fluctuation-Aware Metric minimizes the error \(\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{E}\|_2^2]\) by selecting channels to maximize: $\(I_i = \sigma_i \cdot \|W_{i, :}\|_2\)$

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• True Zero-Retraining Structured Pruning: Reduces model size by 20% to 30% in minutes on a single GPU without requiring fine-tuning datasets or gradient updates.
  • Hardware Agnostic Acceleration: Produces standard, smaller dense matrices that immediately accelerate inference on any backend (PyTorch, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Apple Silicon).
  • Exact DC Bias Preservation: Prevents distribution shift in deep residual networks.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: ARMOR & Wanda: Pruning by Weights and Activations without Optimization Evaluating weight importance through the element-wise product of static weight magnitudes and dynamic input activation norms for rapid, one-shot sparsification.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine judging the productivity of a bridge's structural cables. If you only look at the thickness of a cable (weight magnitude \(|W|\)), you might cut a thin cable. But if that thin cable happens to carry a high-voltage power line delivering electricity to an entire city (input activation norm \(\|X\|_2\)), cutting it causes an instant blackout! Wanda ensures you never cut a wire without checking how much current is actively flowing through it.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Historically, pruning large language models required either: - Magnitude Pruning (\(|W|\)): Fast, but causes catastrophic perplexity spikes at \(>30\%\) sparsity because it ignores activation outliers (isolated channels that have activation values up to 100x larger than normal). - Hessian / Second-Order Methods (SparseGPT / OBS): Highly accurate, but computationally expensive because they require computing, storing, and inverting giant Hessian matrices (\(H = X X^T\)) for every layer, which can encounter numerical instability on massive models.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Wanda (Weights and Activations) and its robust adaptive counterpart ARMOR recognize that the output impact of any weight \(W_{ij}\) is directly proportional to both its own absolute magnitude and the \(L_2\) norm of the input feature channel \(j\) feeding into it: 1. Pass Calibration Data: Run a forward pass of 128 sequences through the model and compute the aggregate \(L_2\) norm for each input feature dimension \(j\): $\(s_j = \|X_{:, j}\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T X_{t, j}^2}\)$ 2. Compute Joint Importance: For every weight entry \(W_{ij}\) (row \(i\), column \(j\)), compute the joint importance metric: $\(S_{ij} = |W_{ij}| \cdot s_j\)$ 3. Per-Output Pruning: Compare scores locally across each row \(i\). For 50% unstructured pruning or 2:4 semi-structured sparsity, zero out the lowest-scoring weights within each row or 4-element window. 4. ARMOR Robustness: ARMOR introduces adaptive outlier shielding and local gradient-free residual compensation across surviving adjacent weights to prevent cumulative layer-to-layer drift.

flowchart LR
    A["Input Activation Tensor X"] --> B["Compute Column-wise L2 Norm: ||X_j||_2"]
    C["Weight Matrix W"] --> D["Compute Absolute Magnitude: |W_ij|"]
    B & D --> E["Wanda Saliency Matrix: S_ij = |W_ij| * ||X_j||_2"]
    E --> F["Apply 2:4 or Unstructured Mask per Row"]
    F --> G["ARMOR Residual Local Compensation"]
    G --> H["Deployable Sparse Model"]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: The output component \(Y_i\) generated by row \(i\) of weight matrix \(W\) is: $\(Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^{d_{\text{in}}} W_{ij} X_j\)$ By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the maximum error \(\Delta Y_i\) induced by setting \(W_{ij} = 0\) is bounded by: $\(|\Delta Y_i| \le |W_{ij}| \cdot \|X_j\|_2\)$ Thus, the Wanda importance score is defined as: $\(S_{ij} = |W_{ij}| \cdot \|X_{:, j}\|_2 = |W_{ij}| \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T X_{t, j}^2}\)$ The pruning mask \(M \in \{0, 1\}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) is obtained by: $\(M_{ij} = \mathbf{1}\left( S_{ij} \ge \text{Quantile}_p\left( S_{i, :} \right) \right)\)$

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 100x Faster than Second-Order Methods: Prunes a 65B/70B model in under 10 seconds on a single GPU with zero matrix inversions.
  • Outlier Protection: Naturally protects all weights connected to activation outlier channels, preventing the reasoning collapse that plagues magnitude pruning.
  • Seamless 2:4 Sparsity Generation: Directly produces 2:4 sparsity patterns ready for hardware acceleration on NVIDIA Tensor Cores.

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: SparseGPT: One-Shot Inversion for 2:4 Hardware-Accelerated Sparsity Solving the layer-wise Optimal Brain Surgeon problem at scale using block Cholesky decomposition to achieve 2x Tensor Core throughput with zero retraining.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a delicate game of giant Jenga. If you walk up to the tower and randomly kick out 50% of the wooden blocks, the entire tower will crash to the ground. However, if a structural engineer uses a precision laser to measure the exact load stress across every beam, carefully slides out 2 blocks from every row of 4, and instantly micro-adjusts the remaining 2 blocks by a fraction of a millimeter to redistribute the load, the tower remains standing at 100% stability while weighing half as much.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: While unstructured 50% sparsity saves theoretical operations, modern GPU architectures (NVIDIA Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, Blackwell) cannot accelerate arbitrary sparse matrices—they require dense, coalesced memory access. To bridge this gap, modern GPUs introduced 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse Tensor Cores, which double math throughput if and only if exactly 2 out of every 4 consecutive values in a weight row are zero. However, finding the optimal 2:4 pattern naively creates severe cumulative error, destroying complex LLM benchmark performance across deep layers.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
SparseGPT frames structured 2:4 pruning as a constrained quadratic optimization problem: $\(\min_{\hat{W}} \| W X - \hat{W} X \|_2^2 \quad \text{s.t. } \hat{W} \text{ satisfies 2:4 sparsity}\)$ 1. Inverse Hessian Computation: The algorithm computes the activation correlation matrix \(H = 2 X X^T + \lambda I\) and its inverse \(H^{-1}\) using stable Cholesky decomposition. 2. Block-Wise Column Updates: Rather than updating weights one by one (which would require millions of matrix updates), SparseGPT processes columns in blocks (e.g., \(B = 128\) columns at a time). 3. Optimal 2:4 Selection: For each 4-element window, SparseGPT evaluates all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) possible pruning combinations and selects the pair that minimizes reconstruction loss weighted by \([H^{-1}]_{pp}\). 4. Surviving Weight Compensation: The moment 2 weights are pruned, SparseGPT immediately updates all remaining unpruned weights in the row using the closed-form Optimal Brain Surgeon formula, canceling out the mathematical error before moving to the next block.

flowchart TD
    A["Compute Hessian Matrix H = 2 X X^T + λI"] --> B["Cholesky Factorization of H^-1"]
    B --> C["Iterate over Column Blocks (B=128)"]
    C --> D["For every 4 weights: Pick optimal 2 to prune via (W_p)^2 / [H^-1]_pp"]
    D --> E["OBS Weight Compensation: Update unpruned weights via Error Vector"]
    E --> F{"More Blocks?"}
    F -- Yes --> C
    F -- No --> G["Export Native 2:4 Sparse Weights + Metadata to Tensor Cores"]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: Let \(H = 2 X X^T\) be the Hessian of the layer loss. When weight \(w_q\) at index \(q\) is pruned (\(w_q \to 0\)), the optimal compensation update \(\delta W\) for all surviving weights in the layer is given by: $\(\delta W = - \frac{w_q}{\left[ H^{-1} \right]_{qq}} \cdot \left( H^{-1} \right)_{:, q}\)$ The resulting increase in reconstruction error is: $\(\Delta E = \frac{1}{2} \frac{w_q^2}{\left[ H^{-1} \right]_{qq}}\)$ For 2:4 sparsity, SparseGPT groups columns into sets of 4, computes \(\Delta E\) for all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) masks, selects the minimum-error mask, and applies the vectorized OBS update across the remaining dense block.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• True 2x GEMM Speedup: Directly unlocks the hardware 2:4 Sparse Tensor Cores in NVIDIA RTX 3090/4090, A100, and H100 GPUs.
  • 50% Memory Footprint: Compresses FP16 weight tensors into half their original byte size by storing only non-zero values and 2-bit index metadata.
  • Negligible Perplexity Impact: Retains \(>99\%\) of baseline zero-shot accuracy on massive 70B models (LLaMA-3, Mistral) without a single step of gradient backpropagation.

docs.text:
Standard Quantization Problem:

  Weights W (Smooth Distribution):   [ 0.4, -0.3,   0.2, -0.5 ]  ──> Easy to quantize

  Smoothed Activations X_hat:       [ 0.3,  0.6,   3.8,  0.9 ]  ──> Uniform INT8 Quantization
  Scaled Weights W_hat:             [ 0.13, -0.10, 6.06, -0.16] ──> Uniform INT8 Quantization

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: SmoothQuant & AWQ: Outlier Migration and Activation-Aware Weight Quantization Taming activation outliers by mathematically shifting dynamic range from activations to weights, and shielding salient weight channels for zero-degradation 4-bit inference.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine trying to pack two items into identical rigid boxes: a soft foam pillow (smooth weights) and an iron sculpture with one sharp 3-foot spike sticking out (activation outliers). Trying to force the spiky sculpture into the small box crushes the spike and breaks the box (clipping error). SmoothQuant takes a file and gently files down the iron spike, using the iron filings to reinforce the soft pillow. Both items end up smooth, moderately sized, and fit into standard boxes (INT8/INT4) without breaking anything.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Post-training quantization of LLMs encounters a massive roadblock: Activation Outliers. - While weight tensors have smooth, Gaussian-like distributions that are easy to quantize to INT8 or INT4, activation tensors develop persistent outlier channels with magnitudes up to 100x larger than normal values. - In per-tensor or per-token activation quantization, these rare outlier spikes force the quantization scale factor \(S\) to be very large, effectively rounding all normal tokens to 0 or 1 and destroying model reasoning.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
1. SmoothQuant (Activation-to-Weight Migration): SmoothQuant observes that a linear layer \(Y = X W\) can be scaled by an arbitrary diagonal matrix \(s \in \mathbb{R}^d\) without changing the output: $\(Y = (X \cdot \text{diag}(s)^{-1}) \cdot (\text{diag}(s) \cdot W) = \hat{X} \hat{W}\)$ By setting \(s_j = \frac{\max(|X_j|)^\alpha}{\max(|W_j|)^{1-\alpha}}\) (with migration strength \(\alpha \approx 0.5\)), SmoothQuant divides the spiky activation channel by \(s_j\) while multiplying the corresponding weight column by \(s_j\). This balances the dynamic ranges so both activations and weights can be cleanly quantized to INT8 (W8A8).
  2. AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization): AWQ observes that not all weights are equally important: only the top \(1\%\) of weight channels that interact with large activation magnitudes dictate perplexity. Instead of keeping those salient channels in FP16 (which ruins GPU memory alignment), AWQ searches for an optimal per-channel protection scale \(s^*\) that minimizes the reconstruction error of the output feature map under INT4 weight quantization: $\(W' = W \cdot \text{diag}(s), \quad X' = \text{diag}(s)^{-1} \cdot X\)$
flowchart LR
    A["Raw Activations X (Has Outliers)"] --> B["Calculate Per-Channel Outlier Saliency s_j"]
    C["Raw Weights W"] --> D["Scale Weights: W_hat = diag(s) * W"]
    B --> E["Scale Activations: X_hat = X * diag(s)^-1"]
    D --> F["INT4/INT8 Quantized Weight Matrix"]
    E --> G["INT8 Quantized Activation Stream"]
    F & G --> H["Fast W8A8 / W4A16 Tensor Core GEMM Engine"]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text:
The SmoothQuant per-channel migration scale \(s \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\) is defined as: $\(s_j = \frac{\left( \max_{t} |X_{t, j}| \right)^\alpha}{\left( \max_{i} |W_{i, j}| \right)^{1-\alpha}}, \quad \alpha \in [0, 1]\)$ - \(\alpha = 1\): Pushes all quantization difficulty to weights. - \(\alpha = 0\): Pushes all quantization difficulty to activations. - \(\alpha = 0.5\): Optimal geometric balance between activation and weight dynamic ranges.

For AWQ, the optimal scaling vector \(s^*\) is found by minimizing the Frobenius norm: $\(s^* = \arg\min_{s} \left\| W X - \mathcal{Q}\left( W \cdot \text{diag}(s) \right) \cdot \text{diag}(s)^{-1} X \right\|_F^2\)$ where \(\mathcal{Q}(W) = \text{clamp}\left( \left\lfloor \frac{W}{S} \right\rceil, -2^{b-1}, 2^{b-1}-1 \right) \cdot S\).

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• SmoothQuant: Enables full W8A8 (INT8 weights + INT8 activations) integer matrix multiplication on GPU Tensor Cores, doubling throughput and cutting memory in half with zero loss in accuracy.
  • AWQ: The industry-standard foundation for W4A16 (INT4 weights + FP16 activations) inference (used across vLLM, HuggingFace TGI, AutoAWQ), delivering 3.5x faster generation on memory-bound workloads.

docs.text:
Teacher Multi-Head Layer (32 Heads)            Student Multi-Head Layer (8 Squeezed Heads)

│ H0  H1  H2  H3  H4  H5  H6  H7  ... H31 │ ===>│ S0 (H0-H3)  S1 (H4-H7)  ...  S7        │
│ (High redundancy, identical patterns)   │     │ (Distilled representation, 4x KV cut)   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘     └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                     │                                               ▲
                     └──────── Cross-Layer Attention & Feature ──────┘
                                    Distillation Loss L_distill

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: Squeezing Heads Distillation: Structured Head Pruning with Cross-Layer Distillation Pruning redundant multi-head attention mechanisms and compressing deep multi-head layers into compact student models via attention-map and hidden-state transfer.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a corporate advisory board with 32 consultants. During meetings, 20 of them simply repeat or rephrase what the top 8 consultants have already stated, creating immense noise, scheduling delays, and high payroll costs. Squeezing Heads Distillation identifies the 8 master thinkers, trains them through intensive mentoring (cross-layer distillation) to absorb all subtle secondary perspectives of the entire original 32-person board, and dissolves the redundant seats, allowing decisions to be made 4x faster with zero loss in strategic depth.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Modern Large Language Models allocate 32 to 64 attention heads per layer. Empirical research reveals that: - Many heads exhibit identical attention patterns (e.g., simple previous-token lookups or uniform broadcast). - Each attention head requires dedicated projection weights (\(W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o\)) and allocates an independent Key-Value cache line. - Naively deleting heads causes catastrophic degradation on reasoning tasks, while training a smaller model from scratch costs hundreds of thousands of dollars in compute.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
Squeezing Heads Distillation combines Taylor-expansion head ranking with a multi-objective distillation pipeline: 1. First-Order Head Importance Estimation: Measure how sensitive the validation loss is to the removal of head \(h\): $\(I_h = \sum_{t=1}^T \left| \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \text{Head}_h(t)} \cdot \text{Head}_h(t) \right|\)$ 2. Head Squeezing & Grouping: The least important heads are progressively pruned, collapsing the architecture (e.g., from 32 heads down to 8 heads, or converting Multi-Head Attention into compact Grouped-Query Attention). 3. Multi-Tier Distillation Objective: - Attention Map Distillation: Student attention matrices \(A^S\) are trained to match the attention distribution of the teacher \(A^T\) via Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. - Hidden State Alignment: Student layer outputs are projected and aligned with teacher representations using Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss. - Logit Matching: Soft target probabilities are matched using temperature-scaled cross-entropy.

flowchart TD
    Teacher["Teacher Layer (32 Heads)"] --> Imp["Compute Head Importance Attribution I_h"]
    Imp --> Prune["Prune Bottom 75% Heads (32 -> 8)"]
    Prune --> Student["Student Layer (8 Squeezed Heads)"]
    Teacher -- "Teacher Attention Maps A^T" --> L_attn["KL Divergence Loss"]
    Student -- "Student Attention Maps A^S" --> L_attn
    Teacher -- "Teacher Hidden States H^T" --> L_mse["Projected MSE Loss"]
    Student -- "Student Hidden States H^S" --> L_mse
    L_attn & L_mse --> L_tot["Total Distillation Loss: Train Student Weights"]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: The composite distillation objective function \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}\) is formulated as: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(y, \hat{y}_S) + \lambda T^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}\left( \sigma\left(\frac{z_T}{T}\right) \;\middle\|\; \sigma\left(\frac{z_S}{T}\right) \right) + \gamma \mathcal{L}_{\text{Attn}} + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\text{Hidden}}\)$ Where the Attention Map Distillation Loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Attn}}\) across selected layer pairs \((l_T, l_S)\) is: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Attn}} = \sum_{i=1}^{H_S} D_{\text{KL}}\left( A_{l_T, \phi(i)}^T \;\middle\|\; A_{l_S, i}^S \right)\)$ And the Hidden State Alignment Loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Hidden}}\) using learned projection matrix \(W_{\text{proj}}\) is: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Hidden}} = \left\| H_{l_T}^T - W_{\text{proj}} H_{l_S}^S \right\|_F^2\)$

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• 4x Reduction in KV Cache Size: Pruning from 32 heads to 8 heads directly quarters the runtime KV memory requirement.
  • 2.5x Decode Latency Acceleration: Smaller projections and reduced memory traffic dramatically speed up autoregressive decoding.
  • Sample-Efficient Recovery: Recovers 99%+ of original teacher benchmark accuracy with only 1% to 2% of original pre-training tokens.

docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          CoOpQ Unified Execution Engine                     │
│                                                                             │
│  [Attention Projections W_q,k,v,o]  ───>  INT4-Symmetric (Dense MAC Arrays) │
│  [MLP SwiGLU Gating W_gate,up]      ───>  FP4-E2M1 (High Dynamic Range)    │

docs.title: Title & Subtitle
docs.text: CoOpQ: Coordinated Heterogeneous Quantization with Mixed-Format INT4/FP4 Matrix Engines Co-optimizing distinct numerical data types across transformer sub-modules to achieve optimal dynamic range retention, maximum integer compute density, and sub-4-bit effective precision.

docs.title: The Analogy
docs.text: Think of a Formula 1 racing car powertrain. It does not use only an electric battery or only an internal combustion engine. It uses a hybrid cooperative powertrain: the high-torque electric motor delivers instant zero-RPM acceleration (uniform INT4 for massive attention matrix multiplication), while the high-RPM turbocharged engine delivers top-end power across a wide dynamic rev range (floating-point FP4/FP8 for non-linear MLP expansion). The central computer coordinates both engines seamlessly in real time.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: One-size-fits-all quantization enforces the same numerical format across every layer in a transformer: - Pure INT4 Quantization excels at linear projection layers with bounded values, but severely clips the heavy-tailed, non-linear activations inside MLP SwiGLU layers. - Pure FP4 (E2M1) Quantization handles wide dynamic ranges and outliers in MLP layers, but suffers from lower signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on uniform attention weights due to having only 1 mantissa bit. Forcing an entire model into one format leads to unnecessary perplexity loss or under-utilizes hardware compute capabilities.

docs.title: How It Works (The Intuition)
docs.text:
CoOpQ (Cooperative Optimized Quantization) assigns mathematically specialized numerical representations to each distinct transformer sub-module based on empirical loss sensitivity: 1. Attention Projections (\(W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o\)) \(\to\) INT4-Symmetric: Attention weights exhibit uniform, zero-centered distributions. CoOpQ maps them to INT4 with fine-grained group scaling (\(G=64\)), maximizing raw arithmetic throughput on integer ALUs. 2. MLP SwiGLU Blocks (\(W_{\text{gate}}, W_{\text{up}}, W_{\text{down}}\)) \(\to\) FP4 (E2M1): Gated feed-forward layers generate wide dynamic activation ranges. CoOpQ assigns them FP4 (1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits, 1 mantissa bit), providing exponential representation spacing that preserves tail features. 3. Cross-Module Co-Optimization: Instead of quantizing layers in isolation, CoOpQ solves a joint optimization objective where the scaling factors of the attention block and MLP block are co-tuned against a shared reconstruction loss. 4. Fused Mixed-Precision Kernels: A single fused CUTLASS kernel manages dual-format execution without host-to-device memory round-trips.

flowchart TD
    In["Transformer Layer Input"] --> AttnBlock["Attention Sub-Module"]
    In --> MLPBlock["MLP SwiGLU Sub-Module"]
    AttnBlock --> INT4["INT4 Symmetric Uniform Engine (Max MAC Density)"]
    MLPBlock --> FP4["FP4-E2M1 Non-Linear Engine (Wide Dynamic Range)"]
    INT4 & FP4 --> Fuse["Coordinated Scale Normalizer & Fused Kernel"]
    Fuse --> Out["High-Fidelity Output at 3.5 Effective Bits"]

docs.title: The Math (Light)
docs.text: The representation sets for the cooperative engines are: $\(\mathcal{S}_{\text{INT4}} = \left\{ -8, -7, -6, \dots, 6, 7 \right\} \cdot S_{\text{int}}\)$ $\(\mathcal{S}_{\text{FP4 (E2M1)}} = \left\{ 0, \pm 0.5, \pm 1.0, \pm 1.5, \pm 2.0, \pm 3.0, \pm 4.0, \pm 6.0 \right\} \cdot S_{\text{fp}}\)$ The cooperative optimization problem over all network parameters \(\Theta = \{W_{\text{attn}}, W_{\text{mlp}}\}\) is: $\(\min_{S_{\text{int}}, S_{\text{fp}}} \sum_{l=1}^L \mathbb{E}_{X}\left[ \left\| \mathcal{F}_l\left(X; W_{\text{attn}}, W_{\text{mlp}}\right) - \mathcal{F}_l\left(X; \mathcal{Q}_{\text{INT4}}(W_{\text{attn}}, S_{\text{int}}), \mathcal{Q}_{\text{FP4}}(W_{\text{mlp}}, S_{\text{fp}})\right) \right\|_F^2 \right]\)$ Where \(\mathcal{F}_l\) denotes the full composite forward function of transformer layer \(l\).

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Sub-4-Bit Effective Footprint: Delivers an average model precision of 3.5 bits per parameter while outperforming uniform 4-bit baselines.
  • Hardware Synergy: Leverages native FP4 and INT4 Tensor Cores on next-generation architectures (NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper, Qualcomm Oryon).
  • Zero Saliency Degradation: Solves the long-standing accuracy drop in multi-step reasoning, mathematical proofing, and code generation.

docs.text: Assigned Subagent: Agent 01: Registry Architect & Discovery Specialist Target Codebase Paths: - neuralops/core/registry.py - neuralops/__init__.py - neuralops/attentions/__init__.py - neuralops/layers/__init__.py - neuralops/compression/__init__.py - neuralops/_lazy_family.py - neuralops/core/legacy_aliases.py

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
In high-performance deep learning systems supporting dozens of neural attention variants and compression algorithms, eager importing of all modules at startup introduces catastrophic latency and memory bloat. In early revisions of NeuralOps, importing neuralops triggered immediate eager imports of PyTorch CUDA C++ extensions, Hugging Face transformers, SciPy, Triton JIT compilers, and 203 distinct operator implementations. This ballooned startup latency to 3420 ms and incurred high resident memory overhead even for simple CLI inquiries (neuralops --version or neuralops list).

Part 01 details the architectural overhaul centered on PEP 562 lazy module discovery, unified dynamic registries (ATTENTION_REGISTRY with 131 operators and COMPRESSOR_REGISTRY with 72 operators), meta-path import finders (_ModuleAliasFinder, _LegacyAttnFinder), zero-overhead AST family scanners (neuralops/_lazy_family.py), and universal parameter synchronization wrappers (_make_universal_attention_class). This architecture collapsed startup time from 3420 ms down to 22 ms (a 155x acceleration) while maintaining 100% type safety and backward-compatible import syntax (from neuralops.attentions import FlashAttention2, from neuralops import create_attention).

docs.title: 4.1 Meta-Path Interception (_ModuleAliasFinder & _LegacyAttnFinder)
docs.text:
To guarantee backward compatibility with legacy research codebases and scripts without paying import costs, NeuralOps registers custom importlib.abc.MetaPathFinder implementations at position 0 of sys.meta_path:

class _ModuleAliasFinder(MetaPathFinder):
    def find_spec(self, fullname: str, path: Any, target: Any = None) -> Any | None:
        if fullname.startswith("neuralops.kernels.cuda."):
            sub = fullname[len("neuralops.kernels.cuda.") :]
            canonical = f"neuralops.core.cuda_kernels.{sub}"
            mod = importlib.import_module(canonical)
            sys.modules[fullname] = mod
            return getattr(mod, "__spec__", None)
        if fullname in self._ALIASES:
            canonical = self._ALIASES[fullname]
            mod = importlib.import_module(canonical)
            sys.modules[fullname] = mod
            return getattr(mod, "__spec__", None)
        return None

docs.title: 4.2 AST-Driven Family Discovery (neuralops/_lazy_family.py)
docs.text:
Rather than eagerly importing dozens of files in each subpackage's __init__.py, install_lazy_family(namespace) statically parses source files on disk via Python's ast module:

def _scan_family(namespace: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[dict[str, tuple[str, str]], tuple[str, ...]]:
    package_name = namespace["__name__"]
    package_dir = Path(namespace["__file__"]).parent
    exports: dict[str, tuple[str, str]] = {}
    module_names: list[str] = []

    for source_path in sorted(package_dir.glob("*.py")):
        module_name = source_path.stem
        if module_name == "__init__" or module_name.startswith("_"):
            continue
        module_names.append(module_name)
        tree = ast.parse(source_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        module_path = f"{package_name}.{module_name}"
        for node in tree.body:
            if isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef) and not node.name.startswith("_"):
                exports[node.name] = (module_path, node.name)
    return exports, tuple(module_names)
This builds _LAZY_EXPORTS and _FAMILY_MODULES mappings in under 1.2 ms without executing a single line of PyTorch or Triton code.

docs.title: 4.3 PEP 562 __getattr__ and __dir__ Protocol
docs.text: When a symbol is requested (e.g. neuralops.attentions.FlashAttention3 or neuralops.load_model): 1. __getattr__(name) checks if the symbol exists in _LAZY_EXPORTS or _API_EXPORTS. 2. It calls importlib.import_module(target_path). 3. It stores the resolved object in globals()[name]. 4. Subsequent lookups bypass __getattr__ completely, achieving near-zero overhead dictionary access. 5. __dir__() merges globals().keys(), _LAZY_EXPORTS, and __all__ to ensure full REPL tab-completion.

docs.title: 4.4 Universal Parameter Synchronization (_make_universal_attention_class)
docs.text: Attention constructors across research literature use widely conflicting parameter conventions (d_model, embed_dim, hidden_size, dim, num_heads, n_head, num_attention_heads, config). _make_universal_attention_class wraps any registered attention class dynamically: - Intercepts __new__ and __init__. - Normalizes dimension and head counts across all keyword variations. - Synthesizes a valid Hugging Face BertConfig if the module requires a config object. - Executes an ordered sequence of signature attempts (config-based, keyword-based, positional-based), raising descriptive errors only if all fail.

docs.text: Assigned Subagent: Agent 02: Kernel Dispatch & Fallback Specialist Target Codebase Paths: - neuralops/ops/cuda/_fallback.py (Core 3-level fallback dispatcher & telemetry engine) - neuralops/core/cuda_kernels/_fallback.py (Compatibility re-export shim) - neuralops/core/backend/dispatch.py (High-level operator & device backend selection) - neuralops/core/hardware.py (Memoized hardware topology probing & capability discovery) - neuralops/ops/triton/_common.py & neuralops/ops/triton/_types.py (Triton dispatch & fallback reasons) - neuralops/ops/triton/op_registry.py (TorchDynamo custom ops registration) - neuralops/ops/ (Tier 1 operator hierarchy: cuda, triton, pytorch)

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Deep learning operators face extreme execution diversity across production environments: from dedicated data centers with NVIDIA Hopper (SM 90) or Ada Lovelace (SM 8.9), to consumer workstations with partial driver setups, to CPU-only CI/CD runner nodes.

Part 02 details the 3-Level Kernel Dispatch Hierarchy in NeuralOps: - Level 1 (Native CUDA C++ / HIP): Compiled C++/CUDA extensions in neuralops.ops.cuda.* achieving maximum throughput via hardware-level primitives (warp shuffles, tensor cores, shared memory double-buffering). - Level 2 (Triton JIT): Autotuned JIT kernels in neuralops.ops.triton.* compiled directly to PTX for FP16/BF16/FP32. - Level 3 (Vectorized PyTorch Reference): Universal pure-PyTorch mathematical references in neuralops.ops.pytorch.* and *_pytorch_ref ensuring 100% correct execution on any CPU or MPS environment.

Crucially, this system enforces the Zero Silent Fallback Law: a system failure in Level 1 or 2 must NEVER silently degrade to Level 3 without emitting structured warnings, failure reasons, and telemetry records.

docs.title: 3.2 Mathematical Tolerance Contract
docs.text:
For any tensor input \(\mathbf{X}\) and parameter set \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\): $\(\max \left| \mathcal{O}_{\text{CUDA}}(\mathbf{X}) - \mathcal{O}_{\text{PyTorch}}(\mathbf{X}) \right| \le 10^{-3} + 10^{-3} \cdot |\mathcal{O}_{\text{PyTorch}}(\mathbf{X})|\)$ $\(\max \left| \mathcal{O}_{\text{Triton}}(\mathbf{X}) - \mathcal{O}_{\text{PyTorch}}(\mathbf{X}) \right| \le 10^{-3} + 10^{-3} \cdot |\mathcal{O}_{\text{PyTorch}}(\mathbf{X})|\)$

Finite-difference autograd gradient checks must pass with \(\text{atol} = 10^{-3}, \text{eps} = 10^{-5}\).

docs.title: 4.1 Dispatch Routing (neuralops/ops/cuda/_fallback.py)
docs.text: The canonical dispatch() function handles: 1. CPU Fast-Path: _is_first_tensor_cpu(*args, **kwargs) immediately executes pytorch_fn when tensors are on CPU, avoiding accelerator driver roundtrips and JIT overhead (\(< 0.5\,\mu\text{s}\) dispatch latency). 2. Backend Forcing: Under force_kernel_backend("cuda") or force_kernel_backend("triton"), missing implementations or runtime errors raise RuntimeError immediately rather than silently falling through. 3. Autograd Bridging (_AutogradBridge): When has_grad = True, wraps native C++ or Triton execution inside torch.autograd.Function, detaches forward tensors, and computes exact VJPs using the PyTorch reference during backward pass. 4. Strict CUDA Control: In forward evaluation, catches CUDA C++ failures, records _LAST_DISPATCH_ERROR[kernel_name] = str(e), and re-raises immediately if os.environ.get("NEURALOPS_STRICT_CUDA") == "1".

docs.title: 4.2 Telemetry Tracking & Counter Invariants
docs.text:
The global _DISPATCH_STATS dictionary records: 

_DISPATCH_STATS = {
    "cuda": 0,              # Successful Level 1 CUDA executions
    "triton": 0,            # Successful Level 2 Triton executions
    "pytorch": 0,           # Level 3 PyTorch fallback executions
    "cuda_failures": 0,     # Level 1 CUDA failure count
    "triton_failures": 0,   # Level 2 Triton failure count
}
Telemetry is accessed via get_dispatch_stats() and reset via reset_dispatch_stats(). Per-kernel backend resolution is tracked via get_last_dispatch_backend(kernel_name).

• NEURALOPS_STRICT_CUDA=1: Disables fallback on CUDA failure; raises immediately.
  • FORCE_PYTORCH_FALLBACK=1: Globally forces Level 3 execution. Evaluated in neuralops.ops.triton._types.check_triton_suitability and _fallback.FORCE_PYTORCH_FALLBACK.
  • NEURALOPS_DEBUG_DISPATCH=1: Streams real-time dispatch decisions and stack traces to sys.stderr.

• Hardware Topology: neuralops.core.hardware.probe_hardware is decorated with @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=32).

docs.text:
1. Logging Level Alignment:
  2. Current State: neuralops/ops/cuda/_fallback.py logs fallback failures using logger.debug(...) (and sys.stderr when NEURALOPS_DEBUG_DISPATCH=1).
  3. Standard Requirement: AGENTS.md §7 requires that fallback from Level 1 or Level 2 emit a logger.warning with the failing level and reason to prevent silent performance degradation.

  5. Autograd Path Strict CUDA Check:

  8. Recommendation: Add if os.environ.get("NEURALOPS_STRICT_CUDA") == "1": raise to the autograd CUDA exception handler.

  9. Environment Variable Parsing in _fallback.py:

docs.title: Native CUDA C++ Kernel Architecture: 112 Packages & 114 Operators
docs.text: Assigned Subagent: Agent 03: CUDA C++ HPC Kernel Engineer Target Codebase Paths: - neuralops/ops/cuda/ (Canonical implementation: 112 packages, 114 native implementations) - neuralops/core/cuda_kernels/ (Backward-compatibility shim redirecting to ops/cuda/) - neuralops/kernels/cuda/ (Public API facade with dynamic symbol resolution)

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
For memory-bound and communication-intensive deep learning primitives, standard high-level frameworks introduce significant overhead: repetitive DRAM memory roundtrips, excessive kernel launch latency, and non-fused intermediate allocations.

Part 03 documents the 112 native CUDA C++ kernel packages (housing 114 native implementations) in neuralops/ops/cuda/. These kernels are engineered using low-level CUDA idioms: - Intra-Warp Communication: Zero-shared-memory reduction and sorting via __shfl_xor_sync, __shfl_down_sync, and __shfl_sync. - Register Pressure Budgeting: Enforcing \(\le 48\) registers per thread via explicit __launch_bounds__ directives to achieve high theoretical warp occupancy on NVIDIA Ada Lovelace (SM 8.9) and Hopper (SM 90). - Shared Memory Tiling & Tensor Core MMA: Explicit shared memory tiles (__shared__) with bank-conflict padding and WMMA matrix fragments. - 128-bit Vectorized Memory Transactions: Utilizing 128-bit vector types (int4, uint4, float4) to maximize DRAM memory bandwidth saturation. - Micro-Fused Math: Fusing normalization, rotary positional embeddings, and activation gating directly into single-pass execution.

This achieves speeds up to 1340.6x faster than native PyTorch (e.g. moe_routing accelerating from \(29.596\,\text{ms}\) down to \(0.022\,\text{ms}\)).

docs.text:
NeuralOps does not require pre-compiled static .so binaries to be shipped with the repository. Instead, native CUDA kernels leverage an inline JIT compilation engine in neuralops/ops/cuda/_bindings.py:

[Caller Request]

      ▼
_get_module() in <pkg>_autograd.py

load_cuda_module(name, cpp_sources, cuda_sources, functions, ...)

      ├─► Check filesystem build cache: ~/.cache/torch_extensions/

docs.title: 4.1 moe_routing (1340.6x Speedup)
docs.text:
• Problem: PyTorch top-k gating requires sorting across experts, followed by non-coalesced indexing and token gather/scatter operations.
  • CUDA Solution:
  • Each warp handles gating for a token. Lane values load gate logits directly.
  • A bitonic sort network executes entirely within warp registers using __shfl_xor_sync across 32 lanes (stride \(16, 8, 4, 2, 1\)).
  • Softmax over top-k is reduced across lanes using unrolled __shfl_down_sync.
  • Dispatched tokens are copied via 128-bit vector stores (using vec_t = int4;).

docs.title: 4.2 selective_scan (99.1x Speedup)
docs.text:
• Problem: Recurrent SSM state updates (\(h_t = \bar{A}_t h_{t-1} + \bar{B}_t u_t\)) cause high DRAM roundtrips when executed sequentially in Python.
  • CUDA Solution:
  • The hidden state array float h[D_STATE] is templated and unrolled (template<int D_STATE>) into GPU register files.
  • Discretized transitions \(\bar{A} = \exp(\Delta A)\) and \(\bar{B} = \Delta B\) are evaluated in FP32 with numerical stability bounds fmaxf(-20.0f, fminf(20.0f, ...)).
  • Full analytical gradient kernels (selective_scan_bwd_kernel) compute gradients in a single backward sweep.

docs.title: 4.3 fused_rotary_emb & unified_rope_offset (3.4x Speedup)
docs.text:
• Problem: Rotary embedding applies complex rotation \([x_1 \cos \theta - x_2 \sin \theta, x_2 \cos \theta + x_1 \sin \theta]\). Separate slice, trig, and mul-add kernels cause redundant memory bandwidth consumption.
  • CUDA Solution:
  • Vectorized float4 loads retrieve 4 consecutive elements of \(x_0\) and \(x_1\) simultaneously.
  • Single-cycle hardware fused multiply-add (fmaf(x0, c, -(x1 * s)) and fmaf(x0, s, x1 * c)) rotates elements in-place.
  • Supports arbitrary token offsets directly for KV cache inference.

docs.title: 4.4 block_sparse_attn (5.0x Speedup)
docs.text:
• Problem: Evaluating full dense attention on long sequences is \(O(N^2)\). Standard PyTorch masks still evaluate inactive blocks.
  • CUDA Solution:
  • A bitmask index (block_mask) is pre-filtered by thread 0 of each block into shared memory array s_active_kv.
  • Warps completely skip zero blocks, avoiding memory transactions for unallocated attention regions.
  • Shared memory allocations use padded strides STRIDE = HEAD_DIM + 8 to completely eliminate 32-way shared memory bank conflicts.

docs.title: 5.1 Ada Lovelace (SM 8.9) & Hopper (SM 90) Launch Budget
docs.text: \[\text{Block Size} = 128 \text{ or } 256 \text{ threads}$$ $$\text{Shared Memory per Block} \le 48\,\text{KB (allowing } \ge 2 \text{ active blocks per SM)}$$ $$\text{Registers per Thread} \le 48 \quad (\text{Occupancy} \ge 66.7\%)\]

docs.title: 5.2 Warp Reduction Idiom (_common.cuh)
docs.text:
__device__ __forceinline__ float warp_reduce_sum(float val) {
    #pragma unroll
    for (int mask = 16; mask > 0; mask >>= 1) {
        val += __shfl_xor_sync(0xffffffff, val, mask);
    }
    return val;
}

docs.title: 5.3 Memory Coalescing & 128-Bit Vectorization
docs.text: Consecutive threads within a warp (lanes \(0 \dots 31\)) must access contiguous memory addresses. Where dimensions permit (\(D \pmod 4 == 0\) or \(D \pmod 8 == 0\)), loads and stores are cast to float4 or uint4 (16 bytes per transaction), saturating the 128-byte cache line interface in two warp instructions.

  6. Double-precision finite difference checks pass torch.autograd.gradcheck(cuda_fn, inputs, eps=1e-5, atol=1e-3).
  7. Three-Level Fallback Continuity:
  8. Every CUDA operator gracefully degrades to Level 2 (Triton JIT) and Level 3 (Vectorized PyTorch reference) when CUDA hardware is unavailable.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
While native CUDA C++ delivers unmatched throughput, it requires lengthy ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation cycles and platform-specific tuning. The Triton JIT Kernel Suite in neuralops/core/triton_kernels/ comprises exactly 26 canonical modules housing 62 unified operators spanning all 4 architectural tiers.

Triton provides compiler-driven optimization at Python execution time: - Automatic shared memory buffer allocation and synchronization (tl.syncthreads() automation). - Hardware-adaptive autotuning across block sizes (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), warp counts (num_warps), and pipeline stages (num_stages). - Universal multi-architecture support across NVIDIA GPUs and Huawei Ascend NPUs (with specialized dialect configurations).

Crucially, in the mainline NeuralOps Triton codebase, block pointers (tl.make_block_ptr / tl.advance) are strictly prohibited to ensure portable JIT stability across all compiler backends (with an explicit exemption only for the Huawei Ascend NPU backend).

docs.title: 2. Assigned Subagent Responsibilities (Agent 04)
docs.text: Agent 04 is responsible for: 1. Module Invariant: Verifying that neuralops/core/triton_kernels/ contains exactly 26 canonical modules. 2. Autotuning Grid Integrity: Ensuring @triton.autotune configurations specify clean power-of-two block sizes without causing compiler timeouts. 3. Numerical Budget Enforcement: Mandating that all intermediate accumulations for FP16 and BF16 inputs are performed in FP32 (tl.float32) to prevent catastrophic cancellation or overflow. 4. Ascend & CUDA Portability: Ensuring code avoids backend-specific intrinsics unless properly guarded by target device conditionals.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Upgrading pretrained large language models from quadratic attention (\(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\)) to linear, state-space, or hybrid attention traditionally required retraining foundation models from scratch at immense computational expense.

Part 05 details the Model Surgery Engine in neuralops/surgery/. This subsystem performs zero-cost, in-place attention transplantation on arbitrary pretrained PyTorch/HuggingFace transformer architectures: - Recursive AST Traversal: Automatically detects and isolates transformer attention blocks (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, or combined qkv_proj). - In-Place Module Grafting: Replaces target attention layers with efficient equivalents from ATTENTION_REGISTRY via replace_attention(). - Weight Reconciliation: Splits or tiles projection weights, aligns head dimensions, and ensures exact preservation of positional embeddings (RoPE, ALiBi) and causal attention masking contracts.

docs.title: 2. Assigned Subagent Responsibilities (Agent 05)
docs.text: Agent 05 is responsible for: 1. Zero-Copy Parameter Grafting: Guaranteeing that parameter grafting maintains existing memory pointers where possible or allocates aligned contiguous blocks without memory leaks. 2. Projection Alignment: Handling fused-QKV projections (qkv_proj \(\in \mathbb{R}^{3D \times D}\)) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) head expansions seamlessly. 3. Shape Invariant Preservation: Enforcing the strict tensor contract: $\(\text{Input Shape } (B, T, D) \equiv \text{Output Shape } (B, T, D)\)$ 4. Manifest Generation: Ensuring every surgical operation produces a deterministic SurgeryManifest detailing parameter changes, rank reductions, and modified tensor keys.

docs.title: 5.1 Fused QKV Slicing Protocol
docs.text:
When grafting an architecture where Q, K, and V are stored in a single combined projection \(\mathbf{W}_{\text{qkv}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(d_q + d_k + d_v) \times D}\): 

def reconcile_qkv_weights(orig_layer, target_attn):
    if hasattr(orig_layer, "qkv_proj"):
        qkv = orig_layer.qkv_proj.weight.data
        dq, dk, dv = target_attn.q_dim, target_attn.k_dim, target_attn.v_dim
        target_attn.q_proj.weight.data.copy_(qkv[:dq, :])
        target_attn.k_proj.weight.data.copy_(qkv[dq:dq+dk, :])
        target_attn.v_proj.weight.data.copy_(qkv[dq+dk:, :])
    elif hasattr(orig_layer, "q_proj"):
        target_attn.q_proj.weight.data.copy_(orig_layer.q_proj.weight.data)
        target_attn.k_proj.weight.data.copy_(orig_layer.k_proj.weight.data)
        target_attn.v_proj.weight.data.copy_(orig_layer.v_proj.weight.data)

docs.title: HNC-SVD: Streaming Whitening & Fisher-Ridge Calibration
docs.text: Assigned Subagent: Agent 06: SVD & Whitening Compression Specialist Target Codebase Paths: - neuralops/compression/svd/hnc_svd_continuation.py - neuralops/compression/svd/direct_svd.py - neuralops/compression/svd/adaptive_ranks.py - neuralops/compression/low_rank/svd_llm_compressor.py - neuralops/core/low_rank/svd_linear.py - neuralops/core/low_rank/factorized.py - neuralops/surgery/universal_calibrator.py - neuralops/surgery/calibration.py - neuralops/core/_attention_surgery.py - neuralops/ops/triton/low_rank.py

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Direct post-training truncation of weight matrices using naive Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) degrades model representations because standard SVD implicitly assumes isotropic, white input activations. In actual deep transformer networks, activations exhibit extreme channel-wise anisotropy (feature kurtosis, outlier dimensions with magnitudes up to \(100\times\) baseline, and heavy-tailed spectral distributions).

Part 06 details the HNC-SVD (Hessian Null Space Continuation SVD) and Streaming Whitening Calibration Subsystem. This architecture achieves high-fidelity compression without fine-tuning by combining four core mathematical principles: 1. OOM-Free Streaming Activation Covariance: Accumulating empirical second-moment statistics \(\mathbf{S} = \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbf{X}_k^\top \mathbf{X}_k\) on the fly without storing activation trajectories in GPU memory. 2. Cholesky Preconditioned Whitening: Factorizing regularized covariance \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top\) to project weights into an orthonormal isotropic coordinate frame before SVD truncation. 3. Closed-Form Fisher-Ridge Output Alignment: Re-aligning the surrogate output projection \(\mathbf{W}_O^*\) in closed form in \(< 100\,\text{ms}\), neutralizing \(> 60\%\) of post-transplant representation loss at Step 0. 4. Householder-Newton Spectral Correction & Energy Thresholding: Guiding singular vectors along the layer Hessian null space while maintaining singular energy preservation \(\tau \ge 0.90\).

docs.title: 3.1 Streaming Activation Covariance Accumulation (Zero-OOM Guarantee)
docs.text:
To avoid storing full activation histories \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \cdot T \times d_{\text{in}}}\) across calibration batches, activation covariances are accumulated incrementally via forward pre-hooks:

\[\mathbf{S}_K = \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbf{X}_k^\top \mathbf{X}_k, \quad N_K = \sum_{k=1}^K n_k, \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}} = \frac{1}{N_K} \mathbf{S}_K\]

Implementation Verification (neuralops/surgery/universal_calibrator.py): 

x_mat = x.detach().reshape(-1, x.shape[-1]).float()
num_samples = x_mat.shape[0]
gram = torch.matmul(x_mat.t(), x_mat)
if mod_name not in self.hessian_dict:
    self.hessian_dict[mod_name] = gram
    self.sample_count_dict[mod_name] = num_samples
else:
    self.hessian_dict[mod_name] += gram
    self.sample_count_dict[mod_name] += num_samples
- Memory Complexity: \(\mathcal{O}(d_{\text{in}}^2)\) persistent GPU memory buffer, completely independent of the sequence length \(T\) or calibration dataset size \(K\). - Tensor Dtype: Computation and accumulation run strictly in FP32 to prevent catastrophic cancellation or numerical overflow on long sequence tokens.

docs.title: 3.2 Regularized Cholesky Whitening & Numerical Conditioning
docs.text: Given input activation covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\): 1. Tikhonov Damped Regularization: $\(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{X}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}} + \lambda \mathbf{I}, \quad \text{where } \lambda = \epsilon \cdot \frac{\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{X}})}{d_{\text{in}}} + 10^{-6}\)$ 2. Cholesky Factorization: $\(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{L}^\top\)$ When ill-conditioned or rank-deficient tokens occur, an adaptive regularisation loop (\(\epsilon \in [10^{-6}, 1]\)) or eigenvalue clipping fallback is invoked: $\(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{V} \operatorname{diag}(\max(\mu_i, 10^{-6})) \mathbf{V}^\top \implies \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{V} \operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\mu_i})\)$ 3. Whitened SVD Truncation: $\(\widetilde{\mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{L} \approx \mathbf{U}_r \mathbf{S}_r \mathbf{V}_r^\top\)$ 4. De-whitened Low-Rank Factor Recovery: $\(\mathbf{A}_r = \mathbf{U}_r \mathbf{S}_r^{1/2}, \quad \mathbf{B}_r = \mathbf{S}_r^{1/2} (\mathbf{V}_r^\top \mathbf{L}^{-1})\)$ computed via triangular solve \(\mathbf{L}^\top \mathbf{B}_r^\top = (\mathbf{S}_r^{1/2} \mathbf{V}_r)^\top\) without forming explicit matrix inverses.

docs.title: 3.3 Closed-Form Fisher-Ridge Output Alignment for \(\mathbf{W}_O\)
docs.text:
During attention surgery, replacing quadratic attention with a surrogate linear/SSM attention causes Step-0 feature drift. The output projection \(\mathbf{W}_O\) is immediately re-aligned by solving the closed-form Ridge regression problem over captured intermediate outputs:

\[\mathbf{W}_{\text{align}} = \left( \mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}}^\top \mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}} + \lambda \mathbf{I} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}}^\top \mathbf{Y}_{\text{c}}, \quad \mathbf{b}_{\text{align}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_Y - \boldsymbol{\mu}_Z \mathbf{W}_{\text{align}}\]

where \(\mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\) is the transplanted operator output and \(\mathbf{Y}_{\text{orig}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\) is the teacher attention output.

Execution Contract (neuralops/core/_attention_surgery.py): 

reg = ridge_lambda * torch.eye(D, device=Z_flat.device, dtype=torch.float32)
ZT_Z = torch.matmul(Z_c.t(), Z_c) + reg
ZT_Y = torch.matmul(Z_c.t(), Y_c)
W_align = torch.linalg.solve(ZT_Z, ZT_Y)
b_align = (mu_Y - torch.matmul(mu_Z, W_align)).squeeze(0)

# In-place parameter blending with convex anchor:
W_new = (1.0 - blend_alpha) * W_cur + blend_alpha * torch.matmul(W_align.t(), W_cur)
out_proj.weight.data.copy_(W_new.to(dtype=out_proj.weight.dtype))
- Throughput: Solved via torch.linalg.solve in \(< 100\,\text{ms}\) on NVIDIA SM 8.9 / SM 90 GPUs. - Degradation Neutralization: Recovers \(> 60\%\) of initial accuracy degradation at Step 0 prior to any gradient distillation.

docs.title: 3.4 Householder-Newton Iterative Correction & Energy Preservation
docs.text:
1. Newton-Schulz Quintic Orthogonalization (neuralops/trainer/optimizers/muon.py): Iteratively projects 2D matrix gradients onto the Stiefel manifold: $\(\mathbf{X}_{k+1} = a \mathbf{X}_k + b (\mathbf{X}_k \mathbf{X}_k^\top) \mathbf{X}_k + c (\mathbf{X}_k \mathbf{X}_k^\top)^2 \mathbf{X}_k\)$ with coefficients \((a, b, c) = (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315)\), achieving machine precision \(\|\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{I}\|_F \le 10^{-6}\) within \(\le 5\) iterations.
  2. Gauss-Newton Matrix-Free Pearlmutter HVP (hvp_gauss_newton): Computes \(\mathbf{G} \mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{J}^\top (\mathbf{J} \mathbf{v})\) in \(\mathcal{O}(P)\) time and memory without materializing the parameter Jacobian \(\mathbf{J}\).
  3. Singular Energy Threshold Invariant: Enforces cumulative energy retention \(\tau \ge 0.90\) across all layers: $\(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{j=1}^d \sigma_j^2} \ge \tau \quad (\tau \in [0.90, 0.98])\)$
  4. AdaptiveRanksCompressor: default \(\tau = 0.92\), dynamically computing \(r = \min \{ i \mid \sum_{j=1}^i \sigma_j^2 / \sum \sigma^2 \ge \tau \}\).
  5. FactorizedLinear: default \(\tau = 0.95\).
  6. tt_compressor: default \(\tau = 0.995\).

docs.title: 4. Triton Kernel Acceleration: Fused HNC Null-Space Step
docs.text:
The inner loop of Hessian Null-Space continuation requires computing the layerwise soft null-space update: $\(\mathbf{D}_W = \nabla \phi(W) \cdot \left(\mathbf{I} + \frac{1}{\mu_X} \mathbf{H}_X \right)^{-1}, \quad W \leftarrow W + \eta \|W\|_F \frac{\mathbf{D}_W}{\|\mathbf{D}_W\|_F} - \alpha \nabla \mathcal{L}_{\text{restore}}\)$

In neuralops/ops/triton/low_rank.py, _fused_hnc_nullspace_spectral_step_fwd_kernel fuses this matrix multiplication and parameter update directly inside GPU SRAM: - Block Configuration: BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=64. - Memory Bandwidth: Eliminates global memory roundtrips between the resolvent projection and parameter addition. - Architectural Fallback: Transparently falls back to fused_hnc_nullspace_step_pytorch on architectures below SM 7.0 or on CPU/MPS hosts.

docs.title: 5. Audit & Verification Standards
docs.text: Exhaustive verification is codified in tests/test_hnc_svd_exhaustive.py across 16 invariant groups: - Group 1: Anchor exact zero loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{func}}(\theta_0) = 0\) and zero first-order gradient across MLP, Conv1D, RNN, SVDLinearAttention, and Transformer blocks. - Group 2: Gauss-Newton positive semidefiniteness \(\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{G} \mathbf{v} \ge 0\) over arbitrary seeds. - Group 3: Matrix-free Pearlmutter HVP parity vs dense Jacobian Gram matrix \(\mathbf{G}_{\text{dense}} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{J}^\top \mathbf{J}\) (\(atol=10^{-4}\)). - Group 4: Matrix-free LOBPCG flat subspace finder and Rayleigh quotient verification. - Group 5: Analytical SVD spectral tail potential \(\phi_{\text{SVD}}(W)\) and closed-form gradient \(\nabla_W \phi\) without autograd differentiation through repeated singular values. - Group 6: Conjugate Gradient (CG) soft null-space projection and warm-start acceleration. - Group 7: Fast layerwise Kronecker null-space step with bounded relative drift. - Group 8 & 9: Function-restoring steps ablation (\(m \in \{0, 2, 6, 12\}\)) and damping factor sweep (\(\mu_{\text{rel}} \in [10^{-8}, 10^{-3}]\)). - Group 10: Loss ceiling \(\tau\) rejection, parameter rollback, and step-size halving. - Group 11 & 12: HNC vs naive penalized optimization and full-logit preservation (\(N \times C\)). - Group 13: SGD/Adam numerical stability of HNC-steered low-rank endpoints. - Group 14: Triton fused kernel parity vs PyTorch reference and automated SM 6.1 fallback. - Group 15: DirectSVDCompressor and SVDLinearAttention end-to-end surgery parity vs naive SVD (\(err_{\text{HNC}} < 0.75 \cdot err_{\text{naive}}\)). - Group 16: SmoothMaxOverLayersCKASteeringLoss, HNCContinuationTrainer, and registry count invariants (131 attentions, 72 compressors).

docs.title: The 6-Pillar Knowledge Distillation & Post-Surgery Healing Pipeline
docs.text: Assigned Subagent: Agent 07: Distillation & Post-Surgery Healing Scientist Target Codebase Paths: - neuralops/trainer/distillation/ - neuralops/trainer/peft_recovery/ - neuralops/core/peft/ - neuralops/trainer/optimizers/

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Post-surgical models retain general feature extractors but suffer from slight representational misalignment between the surrogate attention operator and the downstream feed-forward networks. Traditional fine-tuning requires thousands of optimization steps and risks catastrophic forgetting.

Part 07 details the 6-Pillar Knowledge Distillation Engine and Spectral PiSSA Recovery Suite in neuralops/trainer/. This subsystem restores \(> 99\%\) of baseline accuracy within 50 to 250 micro-tuning steps by optimizing a synergistic multi-objective loss across six representational pillars: 1. Logit Divergence (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}}\) via KL-divergence). 2. Representational Similarity (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{CKA}}\) via Centered Kernel Alignment). 3. Attention Distribution Parity (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Attn}}\)). 4. Angular Directional Alignment (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Cos}}\)). 5. Grassmannian / Stiefel Manifold Orthogonality (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Stiefel}}\)). 6. Latent Space Entropy Stability (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Entropy}}\)).

docs.title: 2. Assigned Subagent Responsibilities (Agent 07)
docs.text: Agent 07 is responsible for: 1. Multi-Pillar Loss Composition: Auditing the composite objective function to ensure stable gradient backpropagation without numerical underflow or exploding loss weights. 2. Spectral PiSSA Initialization: Verifying that low-rank adapters are initialized from the principal singular vectors rather than Gaussian noise, cutting required training steps by \(4\times\). 3. Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) Scheduling: Ensuring learning rate schedulers implement the standard WSD schedule required by high-throughput compression sweeps. 4. Frozen Backbone Guard: Guaranteeing that all non-adapter parameters remain frozen (requires_grad=False) during the healing phase to avoid memory explosion.

docs.title: 3. Mathematical Formulation of the 6 Pillars
docs.text: The composite training loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Total}}\) is defined as: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Total}} = \alpha_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} + \alpha_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{CKA}} + \alpha_3 \mathcal{L}_{\text{Attn}} + \alpha_4 \mathcal{L}_{\text{Cos}} + \alpha_5 \mathcal{L}_{\text{Stiefel}} + \alpha_6 \mathcal{L}_{\text{Entropy}}\)$

docs.title: 3.1 Pillar Formulations
docs.text:
• Pillar 1 (Logit KD): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} = T^2 \cdot D_{\text{KL}}\left(\softmax\left(\frac{\mathbf{z}_s}{T}\right) \,\Big\|\, \softmax\left(\frac{\mathbf{z}_t}{T}\right)\right)\)$
  • Pillar 2 (Linear CKA Similarity): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{CKA}} = 1 - \frac{\|\mathbf{X}_s^\top \mathbf{X}_t\|_F^2}{\|\mathbf{X}_s^\top \mathbf{X}_s\|_F \cdot \|\mathbf{X}_t^\top \mathbf{X}_t\|_F}\)$
  • Pillar 3 (Attention Map Parity): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Attn}} = \frac{1}{H} \sum_{h=1}^H \|\mathbf{A}_s^{(h)} - \mathbf{A}_t^{(h)}\|_F^2\)$
  • Pillar 4 (Cosine Representation Alignment): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Cos}} = 1 - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\mathbf{h}_{s,i}^\top \mathbf{h}_{t,i}}{\|\mathbf{h}_{s,i}\|_2 \|\mathbf{h}_{t,i}\|_2}\)$
  • Pillar 5 (Stiefel Manifold Orthogonality): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Stiefel}} = \|\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{I}\|_F^2 + \|\mathbf{B} \mathbf{B}^\top - \mathbf{I}\|_F^2\)$
  • Pillar 6 (Entropy Regularization): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Entropy}} = \left| \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{p}_s) - \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{p}_t) \right|\)$

docs.title: 4. Implementation Blueprint: PiSSA & Trajectory Healing
docs.text:
# In neuralops/trainer/distillation/engine.py
class SixPillarDistillationTrainer:
    def __init__(self, student_model, teacher_model, loss_weights=None):
        self.student = student_model
        self.teacher = teacher_model.eval()
        for p in self.teacher.parameters():
            p.requires_grad = False

        self.weights = loss_weights or {
            "kd": 1.0, "cka": 0.5, "attn": 0.2,
            "cos": 0.5, "stiefel": 0.05, "entropy": 0.1
        }

    def compute_step_loss(self, batch):
        with torch.no_grad():
            t_out = self.teacher(**batch, output_hidden_states=True)
        s_out = self.student(**batch, output_hidden_states=True)

        l_kd = compute_kd_loss(s_out.logits, t_out.logits, temperature=2.0)
        l_cka = compute_linear_cka(s_out.hidden_states[-1], t_out.hidden_states[-1])
        l_cos = compute_cosine_loss(s_out.hidden_states[-1], t_out.hidden_states[-1])
        l_stiefel = compute_stiefel_penalty(self.student)

        total = (self.weights["kd"] * l_kd +
                 self.weights["cka"] * l_cka +
                 self.weights["cos"] * l_cos +
                 self.weights["stiefel"] * l_stiefel)
        return total
