docs.title: Real-Time Serving, Paged KV-Cache & Speculative Inference
docs.text: Assigned Subagent: Agent 08: High-Throughput Serving & Memory Architect Target Codebase Paths: - neuralops/serving/ - neuralops/serving/paged_kv_cache.py - neuralops/inference/ - neuralops/export/

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Autoregressive inference in large language models is severely memory-bandwidth bound. Naive implementations preallocate contiguous KV-cache tensors for max sequence lengths (\(T_{\text{max}} = 8192\)), resulting in up to \(80\%\) memory fragmentation and preventing concurrent multi-request serving.

Part 08 details the High-Throughput Serving Subsystem in neuralops/serving/. This engine provides: - PagedKVCache: Non-contiguous virtual memory paging (inspired by OS virtual memory and vLLM), allocating cache blocks dynamically in fixed-size chunks (e.g. 16 or 32 tokens). - Copy-on-Write (CoW): Zero-duplication beam search and parallel sampling branches. - Speculative Decoding Harness: Coupling a fast surgically compressed small model as a draft proposer with the uncompressed model as a verifier, achieving up to \(7\times\) end-to-end inference acceleration. - Unified Engine Export: SafeTensors, ONNX, and vLLM-compatible tensor layouts.

docs.title: 2. Assigned Subagent Responsibilities (Agent 08)
docs.text: Agent 08 is responsible for: 1. Zero-Fragmentation Cache Audit: Validating that PagedKVCache dynamically recycles expired token blocks without memory leakage. 2. Speculative Decoding Acceptance Math: Ensuring acceptance logic implements unbiased rejection sampling: $\(\alpha = \min\left(1, \frac{P_{\text{target}}(x)}{P_{\text{draft}}(x)}\right)\)$ 3. No Fake Artifact Policy: Strictly enforcing that export routines under neuralops/export/ produce 100% valid SafeTensors/ONNX files and raise explicit errors if serialization fails (banning empty placeholders). 4. vLLM Integration Contracts: Ensuring custom attention and compression layers expose standard forward_paged() signatures for plug-and-play vLLM block table routing.

docs.title: 3. Core Architecture of PagedKVCache
docs.text:
[Logical Sequence Tokens: 0 ... 47]
           │
           ▼
[Virtual Page Table Mapping]
   Block 0 (tokens 0-15)   ──► Physical Frame #4 (GPU SRAM/DRAM)
   Block 1 (tokens 16-31)  ──► Physical Frame #12
   Block 2 (tokens 32-47)  ──► Physical Frame #8
           │
           ▼
[Custom Paged-Attention Kernel]
   (Iterates through physical frames via block_tables tensor)

docs.title: 4. Implementation Details: Paged Cache Manager
docs.text:
# In neuralops/serving/paged_kv_cache.py
class PagedKVCacheManager:
    def __init__(self, num_blocks: int, block_size: int, num_heads: int, head_dim: int, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda"):
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.free_blocks = list(range(num_blocks))
        # Contiguous physical memory pool
        self.k_cache = torch.empty((num_blocks, num_heads, block_size, head_dim), dtype=dtype, device=device)
        self.v_cache = torch.empty((num_blocks, num_heads, block_size, head_dim), dtype=dtype, device=device)
        self.block_tables = {} # seq_id -> list of block_ids

    def allocate_block(self, seq_id: str) -> int:
        if not self.free_blocks:
            raise MemoryError("Paged KV-Cache out of memory blocks")
        blk_id = self.free_blocks.pop(0)
        self.block_tables.setdefault(seq_id, []).append(blk_id)
        return blk_id

    def free_sequence(self, seq_id: str):
        if seq_id in self.block_tables:
            for blk_id in self.block_tables[seq_id]:
                self.free_blocks.append(blk_id)
            del self.block_tables[seq_id]

docs.title: Hardware Telemetry, Microbenchmarking & Roofline Engine
docs.text: Assigned Subagent: Agent 09: Telemetry & Hardware Roofline Profiler Target Codebase Paths: - neuralops/runners/monitor/ - neuralops/tracking/ - neuralops/analysis/ - neuralops/benchmarks/

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Asynchronous GPU kernel execution presents fundamental measurement pitfalls when using CPU wall-clock timers (time.time(), time.perf_counter()). The CPU launch queue decouples kernel submission from hardware execution on the streaming multiprocessors (SMs), dynamic GPU boost clocks introduce frequency variance across runs, and warm L2 cache lines distort microbenchmarking results. Furthermore, isolated latency metrics fail to diagnose why a kernel is bottlenecked—whether execution is throttled by high-bandwidth memory (HBM/GDDR6) transfer rates or Tensor Core arithmetic throughput.

Part 09 documents the Hardware Telemetry, Profiling & Roofline Subsystem of NeuralOps: 1. Asynchronous Microsecond Event Timing: Eliminates host-device queue skew via native torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), explicit stream synchronization (torch.cuda.synchronize()), warmup loops, and outlier-resistant statistical reduction (trimmed mean, median, standard deviation). 2. True Peak VRAM Instrumentation: Accurately tracks high-water memory footprints via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() combined with cache purging (torch.cuda.empty_cache(), torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()), and non-intrusive NVML / nvidia-smi hardware sampling. 3. Empirical SM 8.9 Roofline Engine: Computes exact operational arithmetic intensity (\(I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{Bytes}\)) across all 131 attention mechanisms and 72 compression engines, mapping them relative to the \(317.9\,\text{FLOPs/Byte}\) hardware ridge inflection point on NVIDIA Ada Lovelace architectures (RTX 4070 SM 8.9 AD104 silicon). 4. Real-Time WebSocket & SSE Telemetry: Exposes high-frequency streaming telemetry over /ws/telemetry via FastAPI and ConnectionManager, broadcasting live GPU metrics, speculative decoding stats, and paged KV cache allocation maps. 5. Pluggable Experiment Tracking: Provides a unified facade (ExperimentTracker) supporting local JSONL logging, TensorBoard, Weights & Biases, and MLflow backends.

docs.title: 3.1 Asynchronous CUDA Event Synchronization Protocol
docs.text:
Implemented in neuralops/benchmarks/harness.py (BenchmarkRunner.measure_callable) and neuralops/analysis/roofline.py (profile_roofline):

# From neuralops/benchmarks/harness.py
def measure_callable(
    self,
    fn: Callable[[], Any],
    total_flops: float = 0.0,
    total_bytes: float = 0.0,
    batch_size: int = 1,
    seq_len: int = 1,
    warmup: Optional[int] = None,
    iters: Optional[int] = None,
) -> BenchmarkMetric:
    w_iters = warmup if warmup is not None else self.warmup_iters
    b_iters = iters if iters is not None else self.benchmark_iters

    self.reset_vram()

    # 1. Warmup Loop (stabilizes GPU clocks, compiles JIT kernels)
    for _ in range(w_iters):
        fn()

    if self.device.type == "cuda" and torch.cuda.is_available():
        # 2. Host-Device Stream Barrier
        torch.cuda.synchronize(self.device)
        self.reset_vram()

        # 3. Microsecond-Accurate Event Allocation
        start_events = [torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) for _ in range(b_iters)]
        end_events = [torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) for _ in range(b_iters)]

        # 4. Asynchronous Kernel Recording
        for i in range(b_iters):
            start_events[i].record()
            fn()
            end_events[i].record()

        # 5. Pipeline Barrier Synchronization
        torch.cuda.synchronize(self.device)
        latencies = [s.elapsed_time(e) for s, e in zip(start_events, end_events)]
    else:
        # High-resolution host fallback
        latencies = []
        for _ in range(b_iters):
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            fn()
            t1 = time.perf_counter()
            latencies.append((t1 - t0) * 1000.0)

docs.title: 3.2 Robust Statistical Metrics
docs.text: To guarantee reproducible benchmarking unaffected by operating system interrupts or thermal throttling, latency samples are reduced into: - Trimmed Mean: Excluding top and bottom 10% outliers: $\(\mu_{10\%} = \frac{1}{N - 2k} \sum_{i=k+1}^{N-k} t_{(i)}\)$ - Median & Standard Deviation: Asserting coefficient of variation: $\(\frac{\sigma}{\mu} < 0.05 \quad (\text{less than } 5\% \text{ noise})\)$

docs.title: 4. SM 8.9 Hardware Roofline Model & Arithmetic Intensity
4.1 Theoretical & Operational Ceilings (NVIDIA RTX 4070 SM 8.9 AD104 Silicon)
docs.text: The hardware limits of the primary physical testbed (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070, AD104 silicon: 5,888 CUDA cores, 46 SMs, 184 4th Gen Tensor Cores) are formalized in neuralops/analysis/roofline.py (get_device_roofline_specs): - Peak FP16 Tensor Core Compute: \(P_{\text{peak}} = 160.2\,\text{TFLOPs/s}\) (Boost) / \(141.6\,\text{TFLOPs/s}\) (Base) - Peak DRAM Memory Bandwidth (GDDR6X): \(B_{\text{peak}} = 504.0\,\text{GB/s}\) - Hardware Ridge Point (Inflection Intensity): $\(I^* = \frac{P_{\text{peak}}}{B_{\text{peak}}} = \frac{160.2 \times 10^{12}}{504.0 \times 10^9} \approx 317.9\,\text{FLOPs/Byte}\)$ (On conservative or laptop thermal profiles with lower SM clock ceilings, \(P_{\text{peak}}\) scales proportionally while GDDR6 bandwidth provides \(256.0\,\text{GB/s}\) to \(504.0\,\text{GB/s}\)).

docs.title: 4.2 Attainable Performance Formula
docs.text: \[\text{Performance}(I) = \min\left(P_{\text{peak}}, \; I \cdot B_{\text{peak}}\right)\]

docs.text:
Implemented in neuralops/analysis/roofline.py (estimate_module_flops_and_bytes) and neuralops/analysis/flops_utils.py:

docs.title: 4.4 Bottleneck Regime Classification
docs.text: Based on operational arithmetic intensity \(I_{\text{fused}} = \text{FLOPs} / \text{Bytes}_{\text{fused}}\): 1. Memory-Bandwidth Bound (\(I < 0.85 \cdot I^*\)): Kernels throttled by DRAM/GDDR6 transfer rates. Attention mechanisms in this regime benefit directly from SVD low-rank projection and KV-cache compression. 2. SRAM-Fused Transition Regime (\(I_{\text{fused}} > 1.5 \cdot I_{\text{naive}}\)): Intermediate attention matrices are kept entirely in SRAM tiles (FlashAttention / Triton GDN chunked), mitigating the memory wall. 3. Compute-Bound (\(I \ge 0.85 \cdot I^*\)): Tensor Cores fully saturated; throughput governed by peak arithmetic capacity.

docs.title: 5.1 Architecture of ConnectionManager
docs.text:
Implemented in neuralops/runners/monitor/fastapi_app.py:

class ConnectionManager:
    """Manages active concurrent WebSocket client connections for real-time telemetry streaming."""
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.active_connections: Set[WebSocket] = set()

    async def connect(self, websocket: WebSocket) -> None:
        await websocket.accept()
        self.active_connections.add(websocket)

    def disconnect(self, websocket: WebSocket) -> None:
        self.active_connections.discard(websocket)

    async def broadcast(self, message: Dict[str, Any]) -> None:
        to_remove = set()
        for conn in list(self.active_connections):
            try:
                await conn.send_json(message)
            except (RuntimeError, IOError, ConnectionError, OSError):
                to_remove.add(conn)
        for dead in to_remove:
            self.active_connections.discard(dead)

docs.title: SOA Fused Attention: Low-Rank Latent Space Multi-Head Attention with Zero-Shot SVD Initialization
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Standard Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) in Transformer architectures relies on dense linear projection matrices (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\)) that impose heavy parameter memory footprints and high matrix multiplication FLOP counts \(\mathcal{O}(D^2)\) per token. Standard Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) introduces trainable residual adapter matrices, but maintains full-rank base matrices in memory.

SOA Fused Attention establishes a parameter-efficient attention architecture that compresses dense \(Q, K, V\) projections into rank-\(r\) bottleneck pairs (\(r = \text{k\_rank} \ll D\)): 1. Zero-Shot SVD Latent Subspace Factorization: Source projection weights \(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\) are factorized via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) into down-projection matrix \(W^{\text{down}} = V_{:r, :}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D}\) and up-projection matrix \(W^{\text{up}} = U_{:, :r} \Sigma_{1:r} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}\). 2. Latent Bottleneck Representations: Inputs \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) pass through intermediate \(r\)-dimensional latent states \(Z_Q, Z_K, Z_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times r}\), reducing parameter count and projection FLOPs by factor \(D / r\). 3. Exact Multi-Head Scaled Dot-Product Attention: Preserves standard multi-head scaled dot-product attention geometry while achieving parameter compression.

docs.title: 2.1 SVD Factorization of Projection Weights (_init_from_pretrained)
docs.text:
For pretrained weight matrix \(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\), full SVD is evaluated:

\[W_0 = U \Sigma V^T, \quad U \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}, \; \Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_D), \; V^T \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\]

Selecting rank \(r = \text{k\_rank} \ll D\), projection layers are factorized into down-projection \(W^{\text{down}} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D}\) and up-projection \(W^{\text{up}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}\):

\[W^{\text{down}} = V_{:r, :}^T, \quad W^{\text{up}} = U_{:, :r} \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_r)\] \[W_0 \approx W^{\text{up}} W^{\text{down}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\]

docs.title: 2.2 Latent Bottleneck Transformations
docs.text:
For input activations \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\), intermediate latent bottleneck representations \(Z_Q, Z_K, Z_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times r}\) are computed:

\[Z_Q = X (W_Q^{\text{down}})^T, \quad Z_K = X (W_K^{\text{down}})^T, \quad Z_V = X (W_V^{\text{down}})^T \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times r}\]

Up-projections reconstruct full hidden representations \(Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\):

\[Q = Z_Q (W_Q^{\text{up}})^T, \quad K = Z_K (W_K^{\text{up}})^T, \quad V = Z_V (W_V^{\text{up}})^T \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\]

docs.title: 2.3 Multi-Head Attention Core
docs.text:
Projections are reshaped into \(H\) heads with head dimension \(d_h = D / H\):

\[Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_h}\]

Scaled dot-product attention scores evaluate:

\[S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{Q_{b, h, i} \cdot K_{b, h, j}^T}{\sqrt{d_h}} + M^{\text{pad}}_{b, j}\] \[A = \text{Softmax}(S), \quad A_{\text{drop}} = \text{Dropout}(A), \quad O = A_{\text{drop}} V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_h}\]

Reshaping context to \([B, N, H \cdot d_h]\), the output is projected through linear output layer \(W_O\):

\[Y = \text{Reshape}(O) W_O + b_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\]

docs.title: 4.1 FLOPs Computation Breakdown
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) head count, \(d_h = D/H\) head dimension, and \(r\) bottleneck rank (\(r = \text{k\_rank}\)).

  1. SOA Bottleneck Projections (\(Q, K, V\)): Down-projection (\(X W^{\text{down} T}\)): \(3 \times (2 B N D r) = 6 B N D r\) Furthermore, Up-projection (\(Z W^{\text{up} T}\)): \(3 \times (2 B N r D) = 6 B N D r\) $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{proj}} = 12 B N D r\)$

  2. Attention Core & Output Projection: Query-Key dot products: \(2 B H N^2 d_h = 2 B N^2 D\) Furthermore, Softmax & Value contraction: \(2 B H N^2 d_h = 2 B N^2 D\) Concurrently, Output projection \(W_O\): \(2 B N D^2\) $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{attn}} = 4 B N^2 D + 2 B N D^2\)$

\[\text{FLOPs}_{\text{total}} = 2 B N D^2 + 12 B N D r + 4 B N^2 D\]

docs.title: 4.2 MACs & Memory Footprint Analysis
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Multiply-Accumulate Operations (MACs)},

$\(\text{Total MACs} = B N D^2 + 6 B N D r + 2 B N^2 D\)$ Specifically, regarding \textbf{Parameter Footprint},

$\(\Theta = 3 \times (D \cdot r + r \cdot D) + D^2 = 6 D r + D^2 \ll 4 D^2\)$ Specifically, regarding \textbf{Activation Footprint}, Furthermore, Latent bottleneck tensors \(Z_Q, Z_K, Z_V\): \(\mathcal{O}(B N r)\) Concurrently, Full attention logit matrix: \(\mathcal{O}(B H N^2)\) In this setting, Total Memory: \(\mathcal{O}(B N D + B N r + B H N^2)\)

docs.title: 4.3 Asymptotic Scalability Comparison
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Standard Dense Projection MHSA}, \(\mathcal{O}(D^2)\) projection compute per token. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{SOA Fused Architecture}, \(\mathcal{O}(D r)\) projection compute per token, achieving a parameter compression ratio of \(\approx 4\times\) when \(r = D/4\).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
5.1 Latent Rank Under-Estimation
docs.text: At the architectural level, the underlying operational mechanism reveals that setting bottleneck rank \(r < 16\) on deep layers causes truncation of significant pre-trained singular values \(\sigma_{r+1 \dots D}\). Consequently, this dynamic induces structural implications wherein information loss in projection representations, degrading zero-shot transfer accuracy. To systematically mitigate this constraint, the framework enforces an optimization protocol such that select rank \(r\) such that \(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i^2}{\sum \sigma_j^2} \ge 0.90\).

docs.title: 5.2 Down/Up Matrix Gradient Orthogonality Drift
docs.text: At the architectural level, the underlying operational mechanism reveals that unconstrained fine-tuning of \(W^{\text{down}}\) and \(W^{\text{up}}\) can destroy the initial singular value orthogonality derived from SVD. To systematically mitigate this constraint, the framework enforces an optimization protocol such that apply an auxiliary orthogonal loss regularizer \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{ortho}} = \|W^{\text{down}} (W^{\text{down}})^T - I_r\|_F^2\).

docs.title: 6.1 Triton Strategy 1: Fused Dual-GEMM Bottleneck Kernel
docs.text:
Standard PyTorch executes two sequential matrix multiplications (x @ down.weight.T followed by @ up.weight.T), allocating intermediate tensor \([B, N, r]\) in global DRAM.

Triton Optimization: Implement a custom Triton GEMM kernel loading input tile \(X_i \in \mathbb{R}^{\text{BLOCK\_M} \times D}\) into SRAM. Furthermore, Compute down-projection \(W^{\text{down} T}\) in register files and immediately evaluate up-projection \(W^{\text{up} T}\). Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Speedup}, reduces DRAM memory bandwidth consumption by \(2\times\), achieving up to \(1.8\times\) latency reduction.

docs.title: 6.2 Triton Strategy 2: FlashAttention-2 Core Integration
docs.text: Stream Q, K, V tensors through a Triton FlashAttention-2 kernel with BLOCK_M = 128 and BLOCK_N = 128. Furthermore, Maintain online maximum tracking \(m_i\) and normalizer \(l_i\) directly in SRAM registers, eliminating global memory allocation for \([B, H, N, N]\) attention matrices.

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
1. Unified QKV Single Fused Low-Rank Subspace Matrix: Fuse down-projections into a single matrix \(W_{\text{qkv}}^{\text{down}} \in \mathbb{R}^{3r \times D}\), computing \(Z_{QKV} = X (W_{\text{qkv}}^{\text{down}})^T\) in a single GEMM launch to maximize Tensor Core utilization.
  2. Dynamic Energy-Based Rank Truncation per Layer: Automatically set \(r_l\) per layer \(l\) based on a cumulative energy target \(\eta = 0.95\), allocating higher rank to early attention layers and lower rank to deep layers.
  3. Structured LoRA Adapter Augmentation: Attach trainable rank-4 LoRA paths \((A B^T)\) to \(W^{\text{up}}\), enabling low-rank fine-tuning while leaving frozen SVD singular basis vectors unchanged.
  4. FP8 Quantized Latent Bottleneck GEMM Execution: Execute down- and up-projections using FP8 (E4M3) precision on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, quadrupling bottleneck projection FLOP throughput.

docs.title: Adaptive Span Attention: Dynamic Head-Specific Context Window Gating
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Adaptive Span Attention, introduced by Sukhbaatar et al. (NeurIPS 2019), addresses the dynamic trade-off between long-context modeling and computational efficiency in Transformer architectures. Standard Multi-Head Attention forces every attention head to compute pairwise interactions across the entire sequence length \(N\), leading to quadratic computational (\(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\)) and memory complexity across all heads. However, empirical studies reveal that different heads specialize in distinct temporal scales—some heads focus on immediate local syntax (short span), while others capture long-range dependencies (long span).

Adaptive Span Attention equips each attention head \(h \in \{1, \dots, H\}\) with a continuous, learnable receptive field size (span parameter) \(S_h \in [0, S_{\max}]\). By parameterizing the span using a Sigmoid gating function over learnable logits \(\theta_h\), the model dynamically contracts or expands each head's context window during training and inference. Tokens outside a head's learned span are masked out, enabling dynamic sequence pruning and sub-quadratic attention execution.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote input activations. Let \(H\) be the number of attention heads, \(d_h = D / H\) head dimension, and \(S_{\max}\) maximum allowable span length.

docs.title: Linear Projections:
docs.text:
Input activations are transformed into query, key, and value multi-head states:

\[ Q = X W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_h}, \quad K = X W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_h}, \quad V = X W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_h} \]

docs.title: Learnable Head-Specific Span Parameterization:
docs.text:
Each attention head \(h \in \{1, \dots, H\}\) possesses a learnable scalar logit parameter \(\theta_h \in \mathbb{R}\). The continuous effective span \(S_h\) is derived via Sigmoid scaling:

\[ S_h = \sigma(\theta_h) \cdot S_{\max} = \frac{S_{\max}}{1 + \exp(-\theta_h)} \in [0, S_{\max}] \]

docs.title: Relative Distance Matrix & Differentiable Span Masking:
docs.text:
For sequence token indices \(i, j \in \{1, \dots, N\}\), relative positional distance is defined as:

\[ \Delta_{ij} = |i - j| \in \{0, 1, \dots, N-1\} \]

A differentiable soft masking function \(M^{\text{span}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times N \times N}\) evaluates relative distance against effective span \(S_h\):

\[ M_{h, i, j}^{\text{span}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \Delta_{ij} \le S_h \\ 0 & \text{if } \Delta_{ij} > S_h \end{cases} \]

In continuous training mode, a soft ramp function \(g_z(x) = \left[\frac{1}{R} (R + S_h - x)\right]_0^1\) ensures gradient flow into span logit \(\theta_h\).

docs.title: Masked Scaled Attention & Output Projection:
docs.text:
Raw attention affinity scores \(S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{Q_{b, h, i, :} \cdot K_{b, h, j, :}^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}}\) are masked against the span boundary and sequence padding masks:

\[ \widehat{S}_{b, h, i, j} = \begin{cases} S_{b, h, i, j} + M_{\text{pad}} & \text{if } M_{h, i, j}^{\text{span}} = 1 \\ -\infty & \text{if } M_{h, i, j}^{\text{span}} = 0 \end{cases} \]

Normalized attention probabilities and context outputs are computed:

[ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (\widehat{S}{b, h, i, j}) ] [ O_{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^N \text{Dropout}(A){b, h, i, j} \cdot V{b, h, j, m} \implies O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_h} ] [ Y = \text{Concat}(O_1, \dots, O_H) W_O + b_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ]

docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_h = D/H\), \(S_{\max}\) max span, and \(\bar{S} = \frac{1}{H} \sum_{h=1}^H S_h\) average learned head span.

The computational throughput of Adaptive Span Attention exhibits a bifurcated scaling profile governed by the hardware execution paradigm. In the input projection stage, linear transformations across projection matrices \(W_Q, W_K, W_V,\) and \(W_O\) require \(8 B N D^2\) floating-point operations (\(4 B N D^2\) multiply-accumulate operations), scaling quadratically with the hidden dimension but strictly linearly with sequence length.

Within the core attention mechanism, the theoretical complexity diverges substantially between naive dense evaluation and specialized sparse execution. An un-optimized dense materialization incurs \(2 B N^2 D\) FLOPs for raw affinity score computation \(Q K^\top\), alongside \(H N^2 + B H N^2\) FLOPs dedicated to relative distance construction and mask evaluation. In contrast, under a block-sparse or custom kernel execution where computation is strictly localized to active head windows \(\bar{S}\), the softmax aggregation and value multiplication require only \(4 B H N \bar{S} d_h = 4 B N \bar{S} D\) FLOPs. Consequently, while standard dense framework implementations yield an asymptotic burden of \(8 B N D^2 + 4 B N^2 D + 8 B H N^2\) FLOPs, a hardware-aligned sparse execution achieves \(8 B N D^2 + 4 B N \bar{S} D + 7 B H N \bar{S}\) FLOPs, transitioning to near-linear complexity when the mean receptive field satisfies \(\bar{S} \ll N\).

docs.title: Memory Footprint & Parameter Overhead
docs.text: From a parametric perspective, the architecture introduces negligible capacity overhead, requiring only \(4 D^2 + 4 D + H\) parameters where the additional \(H\) scalar logit weights parameterize the head-specific receptive fields. The primary operational advantage manifests during autoregressive generation within the key-value (KV) cache allocation. Rather than buffering the full context history of length \(N\) uniformly across all heads, each head \(h\) dynamically constrains its KV cache storage to its effective span \(S_h\): [ \text{KV Cache Size}{\text{AdaptiveSpan}} = 2 \cdot B \cdot d_h \cdot \sum{h=1}^H \min(N, S_h) \cdot b = 2 B \bar{S} D \cdot b \text{ bytes} ] Under representative operational regimes where \(\bar{S} = 64\) against an extended context of \(N = 4096\), this selective retention mechanism contracts the inference memory footprint by approximately \(98.4\%\), thereby mitigating bandwidth saturation at the memory bus.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Optimization Stability and Span Collapse (\(S_h \to 0\))
docs.text: A principal vulnerability within differentiable span gating concerns the risk of span collapse during gradient descent. When negative gradient trajectories push the unconstrained logit parameter \(\theta_h \to -\infty\), the resulting Sigmoid activation saturates, contracting the effective receptive field to \(S_h = 0\). Under this degenerate regime, the corresponding attention head collapses into an isolated self-attention mechanism restricted strictly to diagonal elements (\(i = j\)), entirely precluding the assimilation of cross-token semantic context. This structural failure mode is particularly acute when incorporating auxiliary \(\ell_1\) regularization penalties (\(\lambda \sum S_h\)) intended to encourage global sparsity; an improperly calibrated regularization schedule induces steep gradients on the loss landscape, prematurely pruning heads before multi-scale syntactic features can stabilize. Mitigating this degradation requires careful warmup schedules for \(\lambda\), gradient clipping on the span parameter manifold, and setting lower bounds on the differentiable soft-ramp activation.

docs.title: Materialization Constraints and Memory Landscape in Standard Frameworks
docs.text: A persistent architectural bottleneck in high-level tensor frameworks arises from the eager materialization of full intermediate affinity structures. In un-fused PyTorch execution pipelines, the dense pairwise score tensor \(\mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times N}\) is completely computed in global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) prior to the application of the boolean span mask via masked_fill. Consequently, the intermediate spatial allocation remains bound to quadratic complexity \(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\) during forward and backward passes, negating theoretical memory savings unless custom hardware-aligned block-sparse kernels (e.g., custom Triton or CUDA primitives) are explicitly deployed to restrict DRAM transactions to active span windows.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for Adaptive Span Attention executes variable block-sparse tiling based on each head's cached integer span \(\lceil S_h \rceil\).

   │ Head Span Limits: S_h [H] (pre-computed integer bounds)      │
   └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Tile Grid Launch per Head
                                  ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Query tile index i: Q_i [BLOCK_M, d_h]                      │
 │ 2. Compute Key tile bounds: j_min = max(0, i - S_h // BLOCK_N) │
 │ 3. Loop ONLY over valid Key tiles j in [j_min, i]:             │
 │      Load K_j [BLOCK_N, d_h]                                   │
 │      S_ij = Q_i @ K_j.T / sqrt(d_h)                            │
 │      Apply distance mask & accumulate online Softmax           │
 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Context Output
                                  ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Context Output: O [B, H, N, d_h]                            │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text: Emerging frontiers in dynamic receptive field gating explore multi-scale architectural hybridizations and hardware-aware precision adaptations to extend sequence modeling capabilities. One compelling direction involves the parameterization of asymmetric causal-bidirectional spans, wherein independent backward receptive fields \(S_h^{\text{back}}\) and forward receptive fields \(S_h^{\text{fwd}}\) are assigned across sequence dimensions, enabling encoder-decoder and non-causal architectures to decouple left-to-right syntactic gathering from right-to-left semantic lookahead. Concurrently, span-aware mixed-precision quantization offers substantial throughput improvements; by allocating aggressive low-bit representations (such as 2-bit integer formats) to long-span heads while reserving high-precision 8-bit representations for localized short-span heads, the architecture minimizes off-chip memory bandwidth consumption without compromising critical local syntactic resolution. Furthermore, hybridizing adaptive span attention with selective state-space models (SSMs), such as Mamba architectures, yields a hierarchical context engine: continuous state recurrences efficiently capture unbounded global background representations, while dynamically gated attention heads resolve sharp, token-level associative queries under strictly bounded memory overhead.

docs.title: Adaptive Sparse Attention: Dynamic Top-K & Threshold-Based Sparsification
docs.text: Family: Block-Sparse, Dilated & Sliding-Window Attentions · NeuralOps Registry ID: adaptive_sparse_attention

docs.title: Executive Abstract
docs.text:
Adaptive Sparse Attention dynamically selects a data-dependent subset of keys for each query, eliminating quadratic computation for tokens with negligible attention weights. Dynamically routes dense versus sparse paths.

In NeuralOps, adaptive_sparse_attention is integrated into the universal attention dispatch table, featuring full support for the 3-level fallback hierarchy, automatic shape validation, and end-to-end autograd backwards passes.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
The core operator computation is defined as:

\[ M_{ij} = \mathbb{I}\left( \frac{Q_i K_j^T}{\sqrt{d}} > \tau_i \right) \quad \text{or} \quad j \in \text{top-k}\left( Q_i K^T \right) \]

During execution, inputs \(Q, K, V\) are projected to dimension \(d\). In the causal configuration, lower-triangular masking ensures that tokens only attend to past and current time-steps, preserving autoregressive invariants.

docs.title: Adaptive SVD Attention: Low-Rank SVD Projections with Parallel Residual Adapters
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Adaptive SVD Attention (AdaptiveSVDAttention) provides a hybrid parameter-efficient adaptation architecture for Transformer attention modules. Standard model compression factorizes dense projection matrices (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\)) via truncated Singular Value Decomposition (\(W_{\text{svd}} \approx U V\)). However, freezing low-rank SVD components without fine-tuning limits domain adaptation performance.

AdaptiveSVDAttention augments the frozen/pretrained SVD base projections (\(U \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r_{\text{svd}}}, V \in \mathbb{R}^{r_{\text{svd}} \times D}\)) with parallel learnable low-rank residual adapters (\(A \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r_{\text{res}}}, B \in \mathbb{R}^{r_{\text{res}} \times D}\)) inside AdaptiveSVDLinear. The forward pass computes \(y = x V^\top U^\top + x B^\top A^\top + b\). This hybrid parameterization retains pretrained spectral knowledge in \(U, V\) while allowing dynamic task adaptation through lightweight residual parameters \(A, B\), achieving strong task transfer with minimal trainable parameters.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote input activations. Let \(H\) be query heads, \(d_k = D / H\) head dimension, \(r_{\text{svd}}\) fixed SVD rank, and \(r_{\text{res}}\) learnable residual rank.

docs.title: Low-Rank SVD Base + Learnable Residual Adapter (AdaptiveSVDLinear):
docs.text:
Dense weight matrix \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) with bias \(b \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}\) is parameterized as the sum of a low-rank SVD base and a low-rank residual adapter:

\[ W_{\text{adaptive}} = W_{\text{svd}} + W_{\text{res}} = U V + A B \]

where: \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r_{\text{svd}}}, V \in \mathbb{R}^{r_{\text{svd}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) hold pretrained truncated SVD factors. Furthermore, \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r_{\text{res}}}, B \in \mathbb{R}^{r_{\text{res}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) hold learnable residual adapter parameters.

Forward transformation for input \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{in}}}\):

[ Z_{\text{svd}} = (X V^\top) U^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{out}}} ] [ Z_{\text{res}} = (X B^\top) A^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{out}}} ] [ Y = Z_{\text{svd}} + Z_{\text{res}} + b \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{out}}} ]

docs.title: Multi-Head Adaptive Scaled Attention:
docs.text:
Adaptive SVD projections transform hidden states into Query, Key, Value, and Output multi-head states:

[ Q = \text{AdaptiveSVDLinear}_Q(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ K = \text{AdaptiveSVDLinear}_K(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ V = \text{AdaptiveSVDLinear}_V(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ]

Scaled dot-product attention scoring and context output projection proceed as:

[ S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} \sum_{m=1}^{d_k} Q_{b, h, i, m} \cdot K_{b, h, j, m} ] [ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (\text{apply_attention_mask}(S, M){b, h, i, j}) ] [ C_{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^N \text{Dropout}(A){b, h, i, j} \cdot V{b, h, j, m} \implies C \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ] [ Y = \text{AdaptiveSVDLinear}_O(C) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ]

docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D/H\), \(r_{\text{svd}}\) base rank, and \(r_{\text{res}}\) residual rank.

  1. Adaptive SVD Linear Projections: SVD Base Projections (\(X V^\top U^\top\)): \(4 \times (4 B N D r_{\text{svd}}) = 16 B N D r_{\text{svd}}\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Residual Adapter Projections (\(X B^\top A^\top\)): \(4 \times (4 B N D r_{\text{res}}) = 16 B N D r_{\text{res}}\) FLOPs. Concurrently, Total Projection Workload: \(16 B N D (r_{\text{svd}} + r_{\text{res}})\) FLOPs (\(8 B N D (r_{\text{svd}} + r_{\text{res}})\) MACs).

  2. Core Scaled Dot-Product Attention: \(Q K^\top\) & \(A V\): \(4 B N^2 D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Softmax & Masking: \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs.

  3. Total Workload Summary: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(8 B N D (r_{\text{svd}} + r_{\text{res}}) + 2 B N^2 D\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(16 B N D (r_{\text{svd}} + r_{\text{res}}) + 4 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2\)

docs.title: Parameter Footprint & Trainable Parameter Reduction
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Frozen Parameters}, \(4 \cdot r_{\text{svd}}(D + D) = 8 D r_{\text{svd}}\) floats. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Trainable Parameters}, \(4 \cdot r_{\text{res}}(D + D) + 4 D = 8 D r_{\text{res}} + 4 D\) floats.

For \(D = 4096, r_{\text{svd}} = 32, r_{\text{res}} = 8\): Standard Trainable MHA Parameters: \(4 \times 4096^2 \approx 67.1 \text{ million}\). Furthermore, Adaptive SVD Trainable Parameters: \(8 \times 4096 \times 8 + 4(4096) \approx 278,528 \text{ parameters}\) (\(99.6\%\) reduction in trainable parameters during fine-tuning).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Dual Projection Stream Memory Footprint
docs.text: Executing two parallel linear matrix passes (\(X V^\top U^\top\) and \(X B^\top A^\top\)) per projection increases transient activation memory allocation in PyTorch compared to single low-rank passes.

docs.title: Residual Adapter Gradient Domination
docs.text: If initial weights for adapter matrix \(A\) are un-scaled, initial gradients can over-write pretrained SVD representations. Initializing \(A\) or \(B\) with zero matrices guarantees identity mapping at step 0 (\(\Delta W = 0\)).

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for Adaptive SVD Attention fuses the frozen SVD base GEMM tile and trainable residual adapter GEMM tile in SRAM.

   │ Input: X [B, N, D]                                          │
   │ SVD Base: V [r_svd, D], U [D, r_svd]                        │
   │ Residual Adapter: B [r_res, D], A [D, r_res], bias [D]       │
   └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Vectorized Block Load
                                  ▼

 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Load Activation Tile X_i [BLOCK_M, D]                       │
 │ 2. Compute SVD Base Pass: Y_svd = (X_i @ V.T) @ U.T           │
 │ 3. Compute Residual Pass: Y_res = (X_i @ B.T) @ A.T            │
 │ 4. Fuse Add: Out_i = Y_svd + Y_res + bias                      │

 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Output
                                  ▼

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
1. Pre-Inference Weight Consolidation: After task fine-tuning, collapse residual adapter weights into SVD factors (\(W_{\text{final}} = U V + A B\)) to zero out residual branch FLOPs during deployment.
  2. Gated Adaptive SVD (G-ASVD): Introduce a learnable scalar gating parameter \(\gamma \in (0, 1)\) to dynamically modulate residual adapter influence: \(W = U V + \gamma (A B)\).
  3. Quantized Base + FP16 Adapter: Quantize fixed SVD factors \(U, V\) to INT4 while keeping residual adapter matrices \(A, B\) in FP16 for ultra-low memory fine-tuning.

docs.title: AdaSplash Attention: Adaptive Sparse-Splash Top-k Dynamic Context Routing
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Standard Softmax attention assigns non-zero probability mass to every sequence position, causing attention leakage across irrelevant context tokens and inducing computational inefficiency. AdaSplash Attention addresses this limitation by replacing the standard Softmax operator with Tsallis 1.5-entmax sparse activation mapping (Peters et al., 2019; Correia et al., 2019).

The 1.5-entmax activation function explicitly project attention score distributions onto the simplex boundary, yielding exact zero probabilities for low-scoring tokens. By integrating an iterative fixed-point algorithm to dynamically solve the entmax thresholding multiplier \(\tau\), AdaSplash creates sparse, highly interpretable context routing maps. This eliminates redundant key-value memory access overhead and sharpens attention focus on high-relevance tokens.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text:
Given input activation sequence \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}\), queries, keys, and values are projected as:

\[ Q = X W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}, \quad K = X W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}, \quad V = X W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D} \]

Multi-head formatting yields \(Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times d_k}\) with \(d_k = D / H\).

Unnormalized scaled dot-product logits with optional attention mask \(M\) are computed as:

\[ S = \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M_{\text{mask}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times L} \]

docs.title: Tsallis 1.5-Entmax Activation Mapping:
docs.text:
For score logit vector \(z \in \mathbb{R}^L\), the 1.5-entmax transformation is defined as:

\[ \text{entmax}_{1.5}(z) = \left[ \frac{1}{2} (z - \tau \mathbf{1}) \right]_+^2 \]

where \([a]_+ = \max(a, 0)\) enforces exact non-negativity and sparsity, and \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\) is the unique Lagrange multiplier satisfying the normalization constraint \(\sum_{j=1}^L p_j = 1\).

docs.title: Fixed-Point Iterative Normalization:
docs.text:
Because \(\tau\) cannot be solved in closed form, AdaSplash employs fixed-point iterations starting from \(p^{(0)} = \text{Softmax}(z)\):

[ q^{(t)} = \sqrt{p^{(t)}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times L} ] [ \tau^{(t)} = \sum_{j=1}^L q_{i, j}^{(t)} p_{i, j}^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times 1} ] [ p^{(t+1)} = \frac{q^{(t)}}{\tau^{(t)} + \epsilon} ]

Upon convergence (\(|p^{(t+1)} - p^{(t)}|_\infty < \epsilon\)), sparse probability matrix \(A = p^{(T)}\) is obtained.

docs.title: Context Aggregation & Output Projection:
docs.text:
Sparse attention probabilities aggregate value representations:

\[ O = A V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times d_k}, \quad Y = \text{Concat}(O_1, \dots, O_H) W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D} \]

docs.title: 3. Step-by-Step Tensor Execution Trace
docs.text:
Input: hidden_states [B, L, D]
  │
  ├──> Q = Linear(D, D)(hidden_states) ──> [B, H, L, d_k]
  ├──> K = Linear(D, D)(hidden_states) ──> [B, H, L, d_k]
  └──> V = Linear(D, D)(hidden_states) ──> [B, H, L, d_k]
         │
         ├──> MatMul: Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k) ──> Logits S: [B, H, L, L]
         ├──> Additive Masking (S + M_mask) ──> [B, H, L, L]
         │
         ├──> Fixed-Point 1.5-Entmax Loop (t = 0 ... T-1):
         │      ├──> p_0 = Softmax(S, dim=-1)
         │      ├──> q_t = sqrt(p_t)
         │      ├──> tau_t = sum(q_t * p_t, dim=-1)
         │      └──> p_{t+1} = q_t / tau_t
         │
         ├──> Sparse Attention Matrix A = p_T ──> [B, H, L, L] (Exact Zeros)
         ├──> Dropout(A) ──> [B, H, L, L]
         ├──> MatMul: A @ V ──> Context: [B, H, L, d_k]
         │
         └──> transpose(1, 2) ──> contiguous() ──> [B, L, D]
         └──> Linear(D, D)(Context) ──> Output: [B, L, D]

docs.title: Detailed Tensor Transformations:
docs.text: Step Operation Tensor Shape Description 1 Input \([B, L, D]\) Input hidden state sequence 2 \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\) Projections \([B, H, L, d_k]\) Query, Key, Value states 3 Scaled Logits Computation \([B, H, L, L]\) Dense pairwise dot-product score matrix \(S\) 4 Softmax Initialization \([B, H, L, L]\) Initial dense probabilities \(p^{(0)}\) 5 Fixed-Point Entmax Iterations \([B, H, L, L]\) Fixed-point update \(p^{(t+1)} = \sqrt{p^{(t)}} / \tau\) 6 Sparse Thresholding \([B, H, L, L]\) Probability matrix with exact zeros 7 Value Context Aggregation \([B, H, L, d_k]\) Sparse matrix multiplication \(A V\) 8 Output Projection \([B, L, D]\) Projection \(W_O\) to model dimension \(D\)

docs.title: FLOP and MAC Breakdown (\(B\): Batch, \(L\): Length, \(D\): Dim, \(H\): Heads, \(T_{\text{iter}}\): Entmax Iterations)
docs.text: The computational complexity of AdaSplash Attention is governed by the projection operators, pairwise logit formulations, and the iterative entmax fixed-point refinement loop. Specifically, the input query, key, and value linear projections require \(6 B L D^2\) FLOPs. Computing the unnormalized pairwise dot-product score matrix \(S = Q K^\top / \sqrt{d_k}\) demands \(2 B H L^2 d_k = 2 B L^2 D\) FLOPs. The iterative fixed-point entmax normalization entails \(6 T_{\text{iter}} B H L^2\) FLOPs across \(T_{\text{iter}}\) solver steps to converge upon the optimal thresholding Lagrange multiplier. Subsequently, context aggregation through the sparse probability matrix product \(A V\) accounts for \(2 B H L^2 d_k = 2 B L^2 D\) FLOPs, followed by the final linear projection \(W_O\) which incurs \(2 B L D^2\) FLOPs. In aggregate, the layer demands \(8 B L D^2 + 4 B L^2 D + 6 T_{\text{iter}} B H L^2\) total FLOPs, corresponding to an operational complexity of \(4 B L D^2 + 2 B L^2 D + 3 T_{\text{iter}} B H L^2\) Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operations.

docs.title: Memory Footprint & Tensor Buffering
docs.text: The static parameter memory footprint is bounded by \(4 D^2\) learned weights spanning the four linear transformations. During training and evaluation, transient activation memory scales as \(\mathcal{O}(B \cdot H \cdot L^2)\), driven primarily by the intermediate dot-product score logit buffers and the iterative fixed-point state tensors retained prior to simplex-boundary sparse truncation.

docs.title: 5. Failure Modes, Optimization Stability & Structural Tradeoffs
docs.text:
The mathematical formulation of exact simplex projection via Tsallis 1.5-entmax introduces distinct optimization pathologies and structural stability constraints that require rigorous mitigation. A primary failure mode is complete sparsity collapse, which occurs when pre-activation score logits exhibit excessive negative variance or extreme dispersion upon initialization. Under such regimes, the dynamic thresholding Lagrange multiplier \(\tau\) can strictly dominate all unnormalized logits for a given query position, truncating the entire attention distribution support to exact zeros. This induces immediate gradient detachment (\(\nabla_S \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\)), isolating the corresponding query representations from error propagation and trapping optimization parameters within uninformative plateaus on the loss landscape.

Furthermore, the numerical stability and runtime determinism of the architecture are inherently bounded by the asymptotic convergence rate of the iterative fixed-point solver. In context windows where attention weights approach quasi-uniform distributions, the recurrent update mapping \(p^{(t+1)} = \sqrt{p^{(t)}} / (\tau^{(t)} + \epsilon)\) exhibits sub-linear convergence, failing to satisfy strict boundary tolerances within fixed iteration limits (e.g., \(T_{\text{iter}} = 10\)). This incomplete convergence induces drift in the normalized probability mass, introducing non-negligible gradient bias during backpropagation. Concurrently, mixed-precision numerical formats (such as IEEE FP16) introduce subnormal floating-point vulnerabilities; specifically, evaluating the square-root transformation \(\sqrt{p}\) over small non-zero probability values (\(p < 10^{-7}\)) triggers catastrophic underflow to zero, which prematurely shifts active sparsity boundaries and degrades optimization smoothness across deep transformer stacks.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
Standard PyTorch entmax materializes intermediate matrices during each fixed-point iteration in HBM. A Triton implementation fuses the iterative loop into SRAM, loading score logits once and storing only active sparse entries.

# Triton Fused 1.5-Entmax Kernel Blueprint
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def _entmax15_fused_kernel(
    Logits_ptr, Out_ptr,
    stride_b, stride_h, stride_l,
    L, N_ITER: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_L: tl.constexpr
):
    pid_m = tl.program_id(0)
    pid_bh = tl.program_id(1)

    offs_l = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_L)
    logits = tl.load(Logits_ptr + pid_bh * stride_h + pid_m * stride_l + offs_l)

    # Initialize p = softmax(logits)
    max_logit = tl.max(logits, axis=0)
    p = tl.exp(logits - max_logit)
    p = p / tl.sum(p, axis=0)

    # Fixed-Point Iterative Loop in SRAM
    for _ in range(N_ITER):
        q = tl.sqrt(p)
        tau = tl.sum(q * p, axis=0)
        p = q / (tau + 1e-12)

    tl.store(Out_ptr + pid_bh * stride_h + pid_m * stride_l + offs_l, p)

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
To mitigate asymptotic memory bottlenecks and extend the expressive capacity of adaptive sparse routing, several architectural extensions present significant promise. Foremost among these is the integration of hardware-accelerated block-sparse entmax kernels, combining 1.5-entmax thresholding with FlashAttention-style SRAM block-tiling. By evaluating conservative upper bounds on block logit maxima, computation and memory traffic for entire inactive key-value tiles can be skipped dynamically, yielding empirical \(\mathcal{O}(L \log L)\) execution complexity without compromising numerical fidelity.

Concurrently, a compelling design evolution involves formulating an adaptive token-conditioned \(\alpha\)-entmax mechanism, wherein a continuous scalar \(\alpha(x) \in [1.0, 2.0]\) is dynamically predicted from localized token representations. This formulation enables the model to smoothly interpolate between standard entropy-maximizing dense softmax (\(\alpha = 1.0\)) and ultra-sparse bounded projections (\(\alpha = 1.5\) to \(2.0\)), dynamically adapting the dispersion budget according to semantic entropy requirements across different sequence modalities. Furthermore, integrating sparse entmax routing mechanisms into hybrid state-space models—such as AdaSplash-Mamba architectures—provides structured selective gating for recurrent state transitions. By leveraging exact zero simplex projections to filter low-relevance tokens prior to state updates, the recurrent backbone prevents state pollution, stabilizes long-range associative memory, and preserves gradient fidelity over extended sequence horizons.

docs.title: Aegis-Hybrid Attention: Low-Rank Factorized Multi-Scale Hybrid Attention with Adaptive Gated Pruning
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Standard multi-head self-attention (MHSA) in Transformer architectures presents quadratic computational complexity \(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\) with respect to sequence length \(N\), restricting long-context deployment. While localized sliding-window attention restricts receptive fields to achieve linear complexity \(\mathcal{O}(N \cdot W)\), it loses global contextual dependencies. Conversely, linearized kernel attention achieves global scope in \(\mathcal{O}(N \cdot d_h^2)\) complexity but degrades local representation fidelity due to unconstrained feature projection smoothing.

Aegis-Hybrid Attention presents a unified multi-scale hybrid paradigm designed to bridge this efficiency-expressivity divide: 1. Low-Rank Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) Projections: Linear projection operators \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\) are factorized into rank-\(r\) bottleneck matrices (\(W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D}\)) initialized via truncated SVD of pre-trained parameters, drastically reducing parameter count while retaining spectral energy. 2. Multi-Scale Hybrid Execution: Sequences undergo parallel evaluation through a local sliding-window dense attention branch (preserving high-frequency syntactic interactions) and a global kernelized linear attention branch utilizing non-negative feature activations \(\phi(x) = \text{ELU}(x) + 1\). 3. Adaptive Gated Soft-Pruning: Prior to global kernel aggregation, sequence tokens pass through a token-importance sigmoid gate \(g \in [0, 1]^{B \times N \times H}\), softly masking non-informative tokens to mitigate noise accumulation in the linear memory accumulator. 4. Dynamic Fusion: A learned per-token, per-head gating parameter \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\) dynamically balances local high-resolution details against global summary representations.

docs.title: 2.1 Low-Rank Factorized Projections
docs.text:
Given an input activation tensor \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\), the low-rank projection for query, key, value, and output representations is defined as:

\[\begin{aligned} Q &= (X W_{Q1}) W_{Q2} + b_{Q2}, \quad W_{Q1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, \, W_{Q2} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D} \\ K &= (X W_{K1}) W_{K2} + b_{K2}, \quad W_{K1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, \, W_{K2} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D} \\ V &= (X W_{V1}) W_{V2} + b_{V2}, \quad W_{V1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, \, W_{V2} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D} \end{aligned}\]

The weight matrices are initialized via truncated SVD of pre-trained weight \(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\):

\[W_0 = U \Sigma V^T \implies W_{1} = V_{:, :r}^T, \quad W_{2} = U_{:, :r} \Sigma_{:r, :r}\]

Reshaping into \(H\) heads with head dimension \(d_h = D / H\):

\[Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times d_h}\]

docs.title: 2.2 Local Sliding Window Attention Branch
docs.text:
For context window radius \(W_{\text{local}}\), the band-masked score matrix \(S^{\text{local}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times N}\) is formulated as:

\[S^{\text{local}}_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{Q_{b, i, h} \cdot K_{b, j, h}^T}{\sqrt{d_h}} + M^{\text{band}}_{i, j} + M^{\text{pad}}_{b, j}\]

where the spatial sliding-window mask \(M^{\text{band}}\) and padding mask \(M^{\text{pad}}\) are defined by:

\[M^{\text{band}}_{i, j} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |i - j| \le W_{\text{local}} \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad M^{\text{pad}}_{b, j} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \text{valid}(b, j) \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The local output is computed via row-wise softmax normalization:

\[A^{\text{local}} = \text{Softmax}\left( S^{\text{local}} \right), \quad O^{\text{local}}_{b, i, h} = \sum_{j=1}^N A^{\text{local}}_{b, h, i, j} V_{b, j, h}\]

docs.title: 2.3 Global Kernel Linear Attention with Adaptive Pruning
docs.text:
The global branch projects tokens into a non-negative feature space using \(\phi(x) = \text{ELU}(x) + 1.0\). The token pruning mask \(g \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H}\) computes token importance via a multi-layer perceptron:

\[g = \sigma\left( \text{ReLU}\left( X W_{g1} + b_{g1} \right) W_{g2} + b_{g2} \right)\]

Key and Value representations are modulated by \(g\):

\[\tilde{K} = g \odot K, \quad \tilde{V} = g \odot V\]

The global memory accumulation matrix \(M \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_h \times d_h}\) and normalization vector \(Z \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_h}\) aggregate token information across the sequence in linear time:

\[M_{b, h} = \sum_{j=1}^N \phi\left(\tilde{K}_{b, j, h}\right)^T \otimes \tilde{V}_{b, j, h}, \quad Z_{b, h} = \sum_{j=1}^N \phi\left(\tilde{K}_{b, j, h}\right)^T\]

The unnormalized and normalized global outputs are:

\[O^{\text{global}}_{b, i, h} = \frac{\phi\left(Q_{b, i, h}\right) M_{b, h}}{\phi\left(Q_{b, i, h}\right) Z_{b, h} + \epsilon}\]

docs.title: 2.4 Gated Fusion & Final Projection
docs.text:
Per-token and per-head blending coefficient \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times 1}\) is computed via linear transformation:

\[\alpha = \sigma\left( X W_{\text{fusion}} + b_{\text{fusion}} \right)\]

The local and global representations are fused and projected back to the hidden dimension \(D\):

\[O^{\text{fused}} = \alpha \odot O^{\text{local}} + (1 - \alpha) \odot O^{\text{global}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times d_h}\] \[Y = \left( \text{Reshape}(O^{\text{fused}}) W_{O1} \right) W_{O2} + b_{O2}\]

docs.title: 4.1 FLOPs Computation Breakdown
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) head count, \(d_h = D/H\) head dimension, \(r\) bottleneck rank, and \(W\) local window radius (\(W = W_{\text{local}}\)).

  1. Low-Rank Projections (\(Q, K, V, O\)): $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{proj}} = 4 \times 2 \cdot B \cdot N \cdot D \cdot r = 8 B N D r\)$

  2. Local Sliding-Window Branch: Query-Key product within window (\(W\) elements per token): \(2 \cdot B \cdot H \cdot N \cdot W \cdot d_h = 2 B N D W\) Furthermore, Softmax & Value contraction: \(2 \cdot B \cdot H \cdot N \cdot W \cdot d_h = 2 B N D W\) $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{local}} = 4 B N D W\)$

  3. Global Linear Branch: Pruning Gate MLP: \(2 B N D (D/4) + 2 B N (D/4) H \approx \frac{1}{2} B N D^2\) Furthermore, Memory State outer product \(\phi(\tilde{K})^T \tilde{V}\): \(2 B H N d_h^2 = 2 B N D d_h\) Concurrently, Global Context Matmul \(\phi(Q) M\): \(2 B H N d_h^2 = 2 B N D d_h\) $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{global}} = \frac{1}{2} B N D^2 + 4 B N D d_h\)$

  4. Fusion Gate & Combination: $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{fusion}} = 2 B N D H + 3 B N D\)$

\[\text{Total FLOPs} \approx 8 B N D r + 4 B N D W + \frac{1}{2} B N D^2 + 4 B N D d_h\]

docs.title: 4.2 MACs & Memory Footprint Analysis
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Multiply-Accumulate Operations (MACs)},

$\(\text{Total MACs} \approx 4 B N D r + 2 B N D W + \frac{1}{4} B N D^2 + 2 B N D d_h\)$ Specifically, regarding \textbf{Parameters},

$\(\Theta = 8 D r + \frac{D^2}{4} + \frac{D H}{4} + D H\)$ Specifically, regarding \textbf{Activation Memory}, Furthermore, Un-fused Local Logits Matrix: \(\mathcal{O}(B \cdot H \cdot N \cdot W)\) Concurrently, Global Memory States: \(\mathcal{O}(B \cdot H \cdot d_h^2)\) In this setting, Total Memory: \(\mathcal{O}(B N D + B H N W + B H d_h^2)\)

docs.title: 4.3 Asymptotic Scalability Comparison
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Standard Dense Attention}, \(\mathcal{O}(N^2 D)\) compute, \(\mathcal{O}(N^2 H)\) memory. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Aegis-Hybrid Attention}, \(\mathcal{O}\left(N D (r + W + d_h + D/N)\right)\) compute, \(\mathcal{O}(N D + H d_h^2)\) memory footprint.

docs.title: 5. Failure Modes, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
5.1 Low-Rank Projection Collapse
docs.text:
At the architectural level, the underlying operational mechanism reveals that restricting intermediate projections to rank \(r \ll D\) forces \(Q, K, V\) into an \(r\)-dimensional subspace. If the singular value spectrum of the pre-trained weight matrix exhibits high entropy (slow decay), truncation to rank \(r\) discards significant information, leading to representation capacity loss.

Specifically, regarding \textbf{Detection}, calculate nuclear norm ratio \(\frac{\|W_{:r}\|_*}{\|W\|_*}\). A ratio \(< 0.85\) indicates severe energy truncation.

docs.title: 5.2 Global Accumulator Saturation & Vanishing Gradients
docs.text: At the architectural level, the underlying operational mechanism reveals that in the global branch, denominator \(Z = \sum_{j=1}^N \phi(\tilde{K}_j)^T\) grows linearly with sequence length \(N\). As \(N \to \infty\), the magnitude of \(Z\) scales up to \(\mathcal{O}(N)\), causing \(\frac{\phi(Q) M}{\phi(Q) Z + \epsilon}\) gradients with respect to early key representations to decay as \(\mathcal{O}(1/N^2)\). To systematically mitigate this constraint, the framework enforces an optimization protocol such that introduce zero-sum key centering or length-normalized scaling factors \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\) within the kernel feature map.

docs.title: 5.3 Local-Global Gating Dominance Degeneracy
docs.text: At the architectural level, the underlying operational mechanism reveals that the fusion parameter \(\alpha = \sigma(X W_{\text{fusion}})\) can experience saturated logit distributions (\(\alpha \to 1.0\) or \(\alpha \to 0.0\)). If \(\alpha \to 1.0\), the global kernel branch receives zero backpropagation gradient, rendering the long-range sub-network un-trainable.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                            Triton Kernel Pipeline                                 |
|                                                                                   |
|  Input X [B, N, D] ---> [Low-Rank GEMM Fused Kernel] ---> Q, K, V [B, N, H, d_h] |
|                                                                                   |
|        +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+  |
|        |                                   |                                   |  |
|        v                                   v                                   v  |
| [Block-Sparse Local Attn]       [Gated Kernel Global Attn]     [Fusion Gate Kernel]|
|  Tile-based SRAM Loading         Fused ELU+1 & Outer Prod       Fused Sigmoid     |
|  Receptive Band Masking          SRAM Grid Reduction (d_h, d_h) Interpolation      |
|                                                                                   |
|        +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+  |
|        |                                                                          |
|        +---> Fused Combination & Low-Rank Out GEMM ---> Output Y [B, N, D]       |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 6.1 Triton Kernel Design: Fused Low-Rank GEMM
docs.text:
Standard PyTorch low-rank execution invokes two distinct GPU kernel launches per projection (x @ W1 followed by @ W2), incurring DRAM round-trips for the intermediate rank-\(r\) tensor.

Triton Strategy: Fuse W1 and W2 into a single custom C++/Triton kernel using persistent SRAM registers for intermediate rank outputs: Block Size Configuration: BLOCK_M = 64, BLOCK_N = 64, BLOCK_K = 32. Furthermore, Load input block \(X_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times D}\) into SRAM. Compute tile \(X_{i} W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times r}\) in registers, then immediately multiply by \(W_2\) before writing back to global memory.

docs.title: 6.2 Triton Kernel Design: Fused Local Sliding-Window Attention
docs.text: Instead of instantiating the dense \([B, H, N, N]\) tensor and applying masked fill: Use a block-sparse Triton kernel with BLOCK_SIZE_M = 64 and BLOCK_SIZE_N = 64. Furthermore, Skip block pairs \((i, j)\) where \(|i \cdot 64 - j \cdot 64| > W_{\text{local}} + 64\). Concurrently, Keep online Softmax accumulators (FlashAttention-style \(m_i, l_i\)) directly in SRAM registers to execute local windowed attention in \(\mathcal{O}(N \cdot W)\) IO complexity.

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
1. Orthogonal Low-Rank Projection Regularization: Add an explicit orthogonality penalty loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{ortho}} = \|W_1^T W_1 - I\|_F^2\) during fine-tuning to prevent rank collapse in \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\).
  2. State-Space Model (SSM) Integration for Global Branch: Replace linearized kernel feature maps \(\phi(K)^T V\) with Mamba-2 style selective state-space scan recurrence to achieve linear time sequence processing with dynamic state decay.
  3. Decoupled Local/Global Head Specialization: Assign \(75\%\) of attention heads strictly to local sliding-window FlashAttention and \(25\%\) of heads strictly to global linear kernel attention, eliminating gating projection overhead.
  4. FP8 Quantized Low-Rank Tensor Cores: Perform low-rank bottleneck GEMMs \(X W_1 W_2\) using FP8 (E4M3) precision to achieve \(4\times\) matrix math throughput on Hopper architecture GPUs.

docs.title: 1. Abstract & Executive Summary
docs.text: The Aegis-Spectron-FP8 module represents a state-of-the-art hybrid sequence modeling paradigm that integrates Aegis multi-branch local/global feature fusion with Spectron Lagrangian spectral entropy routing. By dynamically measuring the singular value entropy of incoming token streams, the module assigns computation across sliding-window, global low-rank, and linear state paths. Matrix operations are optimized using FP8 WGMMA instructions on NVIDIA Hopper architecture. This formulation solves the long-context memory limitations inherent in traditional Multi-Head Attention while maximizing tensor core utilization.

docs.title: 2. Architectural Concept & Rationale
docs.text:
Traditional Transformer layers apply homogenous attention mechanisms across all context windows, resulting in quadratic memory complexity and redundant computation for low-entropy sequences. The Aegis-Spectron-FP8 module mitigates this by decomposing attention into three specialized subnetworks: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Local Branch}, extracts high-frequency syntax and token-adjacent context via a sliding window. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Global Branch}, captures long-range document coherence through SVD-based low-rank projections. Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Linear Branch}, maintains infinite-context state through recursive scans (similar to State-Space Models).

A dynamic Spectron routing gate continuously evaluates the information entropy of the sequence, ensuring that computationally expensive paths are only engaged when sequence complexity demands it.

docs.title: 3. Mathematical Formulation & Derivations
docs.text:
Given an input activation sequence \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}\), the module first evaluates spectral entropy \(\mathcal{S}(X)\) to determine routing dynamics. The input is passed through three parallel transformation paths.

The unified output \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}\) is defined as a convex combination of branch outputs: $\(Y = \alpha_{loc} Y_{loc} + \alpha_{glob} Y_{glob} + \alpha_{lin} Y_{lin}\)$ where \(\alpha_b\) are the normalized soft-max branch allocations derived from Lagrangian optimization constraints on compute budgets.

docs.title: 4. Spectron Spectral Entropy Routing
docs.text:
To measure the structural entropy of an incoming token block \(X\), we compute the normalized singular values \(\sigma_i\) derived via randomized SVD: $\(p_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sum_{j=1}^R \sigma_j^2}, \quad \mathcal{S}(X) = -\sum_{i=1}^R p_i \ln p_i\)$

The dynamic branch routing vector \(\boldsymbol{\alpha} = [\alpha_{loc}, \alpha_{glob}, \alpha_{lin}]^T\) is solved subject to a compute budget constraint \(\mathcal{C}_{target}\). Using Lagrangian multipliers: $\(\alpha_b^* = \frac{\exp\left( \left( \mathcal{H}_b(X) - \lambda c_b \right) / \tau \right)}{\sum_{k} \exp\left( \left( \mathcal{H}_k(X) - \lambda c_k \right) / \tau \right)}\)$

docs.title: 5.1 Local Sliding-Window Path
docs.text: Operates strictly over a bounded neighborhood of tokens \(W\). Computation scales linearly with sequence length: $\(Y_{loc} = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d}} \odot M_{band}\right) V\)$

docs.title: 5.2 Global Low-Rank SVD Path
docs.text: Reduces the activation dimensionality by projecting Queries and Keys into an orthogonal rank-\(r\) subspace governed by a learned projection \(U_{svd}\): $\(Y_{glob} = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{(Q_{flat} U) (K_{flat} U)^T}{\sqrt{r}}\right) V_{flat}\)$

docs.title: 5.3 Linear Recurrence Path
docs.text: A hardware-efficient SSM-like associative scan that avoids explicit pair-wise dot products: $\(h_t = A \odot h_{t-1} + B \odot x_t, \quad y_t = C \odot h_t\)$

docs.title: 6. Hardware-Aware FP8 WGMMA Execution
docs.text: The underlying operations run on NVIDIA Hopper (H100) Tensor Cores leveraging FP8 E4M3 and E5M2 formats. Matrix multiplications are executed via asynchronous Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instructions: $\(D_{fp32} = A_{fp8, E4M3} \cdot B_{fp8, E4M3} + C_{fp32}\)$ By casting hidden states dynamically based on numerical stability constraints, the module doubles the theoretical peak TFLOPS compared to 16-bit primitives, avoiding bottleneck latency typical in high-branching architectures.

docs.title: 7. Integration & Complexity Profile
docs.text: Integrating Aegis-Spectron-FP8 requires a simple drop-in replacement via the @ATTENTION_REGISTRY decorator. Time Complexity: \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot D \cdot (W + r + 1))\) Furthermore, Memory Complexity: \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot D)\) eliminating quadratic sequence caching entirely. Concurrently, Hardware Mapping: Ideal for deep layers where high contextual entropy intersects with severe KV-cache limits, allowing continuous generative decoding without OOM regressions.

docs.title: Aegis V1: First-Generation Hardware-Fused Spectral Attention Kernel
docs.text: Family: Hardware-Fused, Low-Precision & Spectral-Transform Attentions · NeuralOps Registry ID: aegis_v1

docs.title: Executive Abstract
docs.text:
Aegis V1 is the founding architecture of the Aegis series in NeuralOps, executing hardware-fused spectral linear attention with low-rank singular projection and fused RMSNorm in a single CUDA execution pass.

In NeuralOps, aegis_v1 is integrated into the universal attention dispatch table, featuring full support for the 3-level fallback hierarchy, automatic shape validation, and end-to-end autograd backwards passes.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
The core operator computation is defined as:

\[ \text{Aegis}_1(Q, K, V) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\left( \mathcal{F}(Q K^T) \odot \Sigma_{\text{spectral}} \right) V \]

During execution, inputs \(Q, K, V\) are projected to dimension \(d\). In the causal configuration, lower-triangular masking ensures that tokens only attend to past and current time-steps, preserving autoregressive invariants.

     │         │

docs.title: Aegis-Attention V2: Low-Rank Factorized Hybrid Attention with Adaptive Soft-Pruning Gating & Multi-Head Dynamic Fusion
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Transformer models equipped with Standard Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) encounter severe quadratic scaling bottlenecks \(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\) when operating on long-sequence modalities. Existing mitigation strategies either enforce local receptive fields—sacrificing long-range semantic contextualization—or deploy linearized kernel approximations—which frequently degrade local syntactic precision due to kernel smoothing over localized token interactions.

Aegis-Attention V2 addresses this trade-off through a high-performance hybrid architecture that combines: 1. Truncated SVD Low-Rank Projections: All linear parameter matrices (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\)) are factorized into dual low-rank bottleneck projections (\(W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D}\)) initialized via singular value decomposition of pre-trained parameters. 2. Local Sliding-Window Dense Branch: Preserves spatial and local syntactic dependency modeling via localized band-masked softmax attention restricted to window radius \(W_{\text{local}}\). 3. Global Kernelized Linear Branch with Soft-Pruning: Computes unbounded sequence dependencies in \(\mathcal{O}(N \cdot d_h^2)\) time using the positive kernel map \(\phi(x) = \text{ELU}(x) + 1.0\). Crucially, a parameter-efficient MLP token-gating module \(g \in [0, 1]^{B \times N \times H}\) soft-prunes redundant or noisy tokens before global accumulator integration. 4. Dynamic Per-Token Multi-Head Fusion: Blends local high-resolution contexts and global summary states via a learned per-token, per-head gating function \(\alpha \in [0, 1]^{B \times N \times H \times 1}\).

docs.title: 2.1 Low-Rank Factorized Linear Transformations
docs.text:
For input hidden tensor \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\), query, key, value, and output linear projections are factorized via rank-\(r\) bottleneck matrices:

\[\begin{aligned} Q &= (X W_{Q1}) W_{Q2} + b_{Q2}, \quad W_{Q1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, \, W_{Q2} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D} \\ K &= (X W_{K1}) W_{K2} + b_{K2}, \quad W_{K1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, \, W_{K2} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D} \\ V &= (X W_{V1}) W_{V2} + b_{V2}, \quad W_{V1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, \, W_{V2} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D} \end{aligned}\]

Weight initialization uses truncated SVD of pre-trained weight matrix \(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\):

\[W_0 = U \Sigma V^T \implies W_1 = V_{:, :r}^T, \quad W_2 = U_{:, :r} \Sigma_{:r, :r}\]

Reshaping yields head-partitioned tensors \(Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times d_h}\), where \(d_h = D / H\).

docs.title: 2.2 Local Band Attention Branch
docs.text:
The local attention branch computes scaled dot-product attention scores within local window radius \(W_{\text{local}}\):

\[S^{\text{local}}_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{Q_{b, i, h} K_{b, j, h}^T}{\sqrt{d_h}} + M^{\text{band}}_{i, j} + M^{\text{pad}}_{b, j}\]

where masks are defined as:

\[M^{\text{band}}_{i, j} = \begin{cases} 0 & |i - j| \le W_{\text{local}} \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad M^{\text{pad}}_{b, j} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{valid}(b, j) \\ -\infty & \text{padded}(b, j) \end{cases}\]

The localized context output \(O^{\text{local}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times d_h}\) is given by:

\[A^{\text{local}} = \text{Softmax}\left( S^{\text{local}} \right), \quad O^{\text{local}}_{b, i, h} = \sum_{j=1}^N A^{\text{local}}_{b, h, i, j} V_{b, j, h}\]

docs.title: 2.3 Global Kernel Attention with Soft Token-Pruning
docs.text:
Global attention employs the positive feature kernel \(\phi(u) = \text{ELU}(u) + 1.0\). Token relevance is computed via a light gating network:

\[g = \sigma\left( \text{ReLU}\left( X W_{g1} + b_{g1} \right) W_{g2} + b_{g2} \right) \in [0, 1]^{B \times N \times H}\]

Key and value tensors are modulated prior to linear kernel aggregation:

\[K_g = g \odot K, \quad V_g = g \odot V\]

The global memory accumulation matrix \(M^{\text{global}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_h \times d_h}\) and normalization vector \(Z^{\text{global}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_h}\) aggregate masked representations:

\[M^{\text{global}}_{b, h} = \sum_{j=1}^N \phi\left(K_{g, b, j, h}\right)^T \otimes V_{g, b, j, h}, \quad Z^{\text{global}}_{b, h} = \sum_{j=1}^N \phi\left(K_{g, b, j, h}\right)^T\]

The global output context vector \(O^{\text{global}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times d_h}\) is formulated as:

\[O^{\text{global}}_{b, i, h} = \frac{\phi\left(Q_{b, i, h}\right) M^{\text{global}}_{b, h}}{\phi\left(Q_{b, i, h}\right) Z^{\text{global}}_{b, h} + \epsilon}\]

docs.title: 2.4 Multi-Head Gated Fusion & Layer Output
docs.text:
A per-token, per-head adaptive gate \(\alpha \in [0, 1]^{B \times N \times H \times 1}\) linearly interpolates between local and global contexts:

\[\alpha = \sigma\left( X W_{\text{fusion}} + b_{\text{fusion}} \right)\] \[O_{b, i, h}^{\text{fused}} = \alpha_{b, i, h} \odot O_{b, i, h}^{\text{local}} + (1 - \alpha_{b, i, h}) \odot O_{b, i, h}^{\text{global}}\]

The fused tensor is flattened across heads and passed through low-rank output projection \(W_O\):

\[Y = \left( \text{Reshape}(O^{\text{fused}}) W_{O1} \right) W_{O2} + b_{O2} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\]

docs.title: 4.1 FLOPs Computation Breakdown
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) head count, \(d_h = D/H\) head dimension, \(r\) bottleneck rank, and \(W = W_{\text{local}}\) local window width.

  1. Low-Rank Projections (\(Q, K, V, O\)): $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{proj}} = 4 \times \left( 2 B N D r + 2 B N r D \right) = 16 B N D r\)$

  2. Local Sliding-Window Branch: Scores: \(2 B H N W d_h = 2 B N D W\) Furthermore, Softmax & Value product: \(2 B H N W d_h = 2 B N D W\) $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{local}} = 4 B N D W\)$

  3. Global Soft-Pruned Kernel Branch: Pruning MLP: \(2 B N D (D/4) + 2 B N (D/4) H = \frac{1}{2} B N D^2 + \frac{1}{2} B N D H\) Furthermore, Key/Value soft-pruning modulation: \(2 B N H d_h = 2 B N D\) Concurrently, Memory State accumulation \(\phi(K_g)^T V_g\): \(2 B H N d_h^2 = 2 B N D d_h\) In this setting, Query projection \(\phi(Q) M^{\text{global}}\): \(2 B H N d_h^2 = 2 B N D d_h\) $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{global}} = \frac{1}{2} B N D^2 + \frac{1}{2} B N D H + 4 B N D d_h + 2 B N D\)$

  4. Fusion Gating & Output Assembly: $\(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{fusion}} = 2 B N D H + 3 B N D\)$

\[\text{FLOPs}_{\text{total}} \approx 16 B N D r + 4 B N D W + \frac{1}{2} B N D^2 + 4 B N D d_h\]

docs.title: 4.2 MACs & Memory Footprint Analysis
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Multiply-Accumulate Operations (MACs)},

$\(\text{Total MACs} \approx 8 B N D r + 2 B N D W + \frac{1}{4} B N D^2 + 2 B N D d_h\)$ Specifically, regarding \textbf{Parameter Memory},

$\(\Theta = 8 D r + \frac{D^2}{4} + \frac{5 D H}{4}\)$ Specifically, regarding \textbf{Activation Footprint}, Furthermore, Un-fused local logits: \(\mathcal{O}(B H N W)\) Concurrently, Global memory state: \(\mathcal{O}(B H d_h^2)\) In this setting, Total Memory: \(\mathcal{O}(B N D + B H N W + B H d_h^2)\)

docs.title: 4.3 Asymptotic Scalability Comparison
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Standard Dense Attention}, \(\mathcal{O}(N^2 D)\) compute, \(\mathcal{O}(N^2 H)\) memory. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Aegis-Attention V2}, \(\mathcal{O}\left(N D (r + W + d_h + D/N)\right)\) compute, \(\mathcal{O}(N D + H d_h^2)\) memory footprint.

docs.title: 5. Failure Modes, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
5.1 Low-Rank Approximation Error & Rank Collapse
docs.text:
At the architectural level, the underlying operational mechanism reveals that approximating \(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\) via rank \(r \ll D\) truncates the singular value tail. If pre-trained Transformer layers possess isotropic weight spectra (singular values decay slowly), rank truncation causes severe reconstruction loss \(\|W_0 - W_1 W_2\|_F^2 \gg 0\).

Specifically, regarding \textbf{Failure Mode}, network fails to converge during zero-shot initialization if \(r < 32\) on deep layers.

docs.title: 5.2 Soft-Pruning Gating Collapse
docs.text: At the architectural level, the underlying operational mechanism reveals that the sigmoid pruning gate \(g = \sigma(\text{MLP}(X))\) can suffer from vanishing gradients if initialized poorly, leading to \(g \to 0\) across all sequence tokens. Consequently, this dynamic induces structural implications wherein key and value representations in the global branch become zeroed (\(K_g = 0, V_g = 0\)), causing the global matrix \(M^{\text{global}}\) to collapse to zero and triggering division by zero (\(\epsilon = 1e-8\) instability).

docs.title: 5.3 Softmax Underflow in Local Window Branch
docs.text: At the architectural level, the underlying operational mechanism reveals that when tokens inside the sliding window are heavily masked due to padding \(M^{\text{pad}}\), rows containing all \(-\infty\) entries produce \(\text{NaN}\) outputs during PyTorch F.softmax(S, dim=-1). To systematically mitigate this constraint, the framework enforces an optimization protocol such that execute torch.nan_to_num(attn_local, nan=0.0) or apply explicit guard conditions prior to value multiplication.
