docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D/H\), and \(r_q, r_k, r_v, r_o\) the energy-derived SVD ranks per projection.

The computational workload decomposes into two primary operational phases: the factorized subspace linear projections and the core scaled dot-product attention mechanics. Under the factorized projection formulation, the Query transformation incurs \(2 B N D r_q + 2 B N r_q D = 4 B N D r_q\) FLOPs, while the Key and Value transformations concurrently demand \(4 B N D r_k\) and \(4 B N D r_v\) FLOPs, respectively. Furthermore, the context output linear mapping requires \(4 B N D r_o\) FLOPs, establishing an aggregate projection cost of \(4 B N D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o)\) FLOPs. In contrast to conventional dense linear layers whose complexity scales strictly as \(\mathcal{O}(B N D^2)\), this factorized scheme substantially curtails arithmetic complexity whenever the cumulative energy rank satisfies \(r \ll D\).

Subsequently, the core scaled dot-product attention operations execute pairwise similarity score calculation \(Q K^\top\) requiring \(2 B N^2 D\) FLOPs, followed by spatial softmax normalization and attention masking requiring \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs. Context aggregation via the matrix product \(A V\) contributes an additional \(2 B N^2 D\) FLOPs. Consequently, the cumulative computational requirements across the entire attention block aggregate to a total Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) workload of:

\[ \text{Total MACs} = 2 B N D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o) + 2 B N^2 D \]

and a comprehensive floating-point operation total of:

\[ \text{Total FLOPs} = 4 B N D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o) + 4 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2 \]

thereby preserving standard sequence scaling characteristics while fundamentally mitigating projection memory bandwidth overhead.

docs.title: Parameter Reduction Profile
docs.text: To evaluate the structural parameter economy, consider a canonical Transformer configuration with hidden dimension \(D = 768\). Standard uncompressed Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mandates \(4 D^2 + 4 D \approx 2,362,368\) parameters across the four dense weight matrices. Assuming a 95% spectral energy retention threshold yields an empirical average truncation rank of \(r = 32\), the parameter consumption under MinimalSVD contracts to \(4 \times (2 \times 768 \times 32) + 4(768) \approx 199,680\) parameters. This constitutes an immediate \(11.8\times\) parameter reduction, demonstrating that the vast majority of projection parameters reside in negligible singular subspaces whose elimination induces minimal spectral distortion.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Flat Energy Spectra & High-Rank Degradation
docs.text: When weight matrices exhibit an isotropic or heavy-tailed singular value distribution (a flat spectral decay profile), capturing a high cumulative energy threshold (\(E = 0.95\)) necessitates retaining a rank comparable to the uncompressed dimension (\(r \approx D\)). Under this condition, the factorized representation introduces two sequential matrix multiplications that cumulatively exceed the FLOP cost and memory footprint of the original dense operator without yielding parameter compression. To mitigate this structural degradation and safeguard against asymptotic overhead, an explicit rank cap (\(r \le 64\)) is enforced, establishing a strict upper bound on latent bottleneck dimensionality at the expense of controlled spectral truncation error.

docs.title: Zero-Rank Degeneracy & Subspace Collapse
docs.text: Conversely, in scenarios where the energy retention threshold is parameterized excessively low (\(E < 0.1\)) or singular values decay exponentially within initial indices, the cumulative energy criterion may yield a degenerate rank of \(r = 0\). This degenerates the intermediate activation space into a null manifold, obstructing forward signal propagation and inducing complete gradient vanishing during backpropagation. To guarantee structural integrity across extreme parameter regimes, an explicit lower bound \(r = \max(1, r)\) is strictly enforced, preserving non-trivial subspace projections and numerical stability.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for MinimalSVD fuses the down-projection (\(B\)) and up-projection (\(A\)) steps into a single SRAM GEMM block without writing intermediate rank-\(r\) activations back to DRAM.

                    Global Memory (HBM)
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Input: X [B, N, D]                                          │
   │ Projection Weights: B [r, D], A [D, r], bias [D]            │
   └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Direct Tile Load into SRAM
                                  ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Load Activation Tile X_i [BLOCK_M, D]                       │
 │ 2. Compute Fused Subspace Bottleneck: Z_i = X_i @ B.T          │
 │ 3. Reconstruct Output Tile: Y_i = Z_i @ A.T + bias             │
 │ 4. Execute Online Scaled Softmax Attention                     │
 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Context Output
                                  ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Context Output: Y [B, N, D]                                 │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
The architectural paradigm introduced by MinimalSVD unlocks several fertile trajectories for advanced compression and hybrid acceleration:

Adaptive Per-Layer Energy Budgeting: Rather than enforcing a static global energy retention threshold, a depth-aware scheduling policy dynamically modulates \(E\) across Transformer layers. Empirical spectral profiling reveals that early representational layers require stringent retention thresholds (\(E = 0.98\)) to preserve foundational geometric features, whereas deeper semantic layers exhibit substantial over-parameterization and tolerate aggressive compression (\(E = 0.90\)) without degrading downstream task performance.

Mixed-Precision Quantized Low-Rank SVD (Q-MinimalSVD): Synergizing low-rank factorization with sub-byte quantization enables further hardware acceleration. By quantizing down-projection matrices \(B\) to INT4 representations while maintaining up-projection matrices \(A\) in half-precision (FP16/BF16), memory bandwidth consumption during memory-bound decoding phases is halved while preserving high-rank reconstruction fidelity in the final activation space.

Sparse-SVD Hybrid Residual Adapters: To bridge the residual perplexity gap induced by aggressive rank truncation, low-rank factorized projections can be augmented with localized, magnitude-pruned sparse residual matrices. This hybrid structural parameterization captures both global low-rank subspace manifolds and high-frequency coordinate-aligned outlier weights, fully recovering uncompressed baseline accuracy while maintaining superior computational efficiency.

docs.title: MinimalSVD v2: Refined SVD Low-Rank Attention with Flexible Attention Mask Handling
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
MinimalSVD v2 (MinimalSVDAttentionV2) provides a refined, zero-shot SVD-factorized attention module for Transformer architectures. While standard Multi-Head Attention employs dense linear projections (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\)) that demand significant memory bandwidth, MinimalSVD v2 decomposes each linear parameter matrix into low-rank factor pairs (\(A \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, B \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D}\)) using truncated Singular Value Decomposition (SVD).

Version 2 introduces enhanced attention mask normalization and robust shape-checking for 2D ([B, N]), 3D ([B, 1, N]), and 4D ([B, 1, N, N]) mask tensors. It dynamically validates valid token positions to eliminate padding artifacts in low-rank projection spaces while retaining full scaled dot-product attention precision.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote input activations. Let \(H\) be the number of attention heads, \(d_k = D / H\) head dimension, \(E \in (0, 1]\) energy retention threshold, and \(r \in [1, 64]\) the rank for each projection.

docs.title: Low-Rank SVD Weight Decomposition:
docs.text:
Pre-trained projection weights \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\) undergo singular value decomposition:

\[ W = U \Sigma V^\top, \quad U \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}, \, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}, \, V \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D} \]

Truncated to rank \(r\) derived from cumulative spectral energy threshold \(E\):

\[ A = U[:, :r] \cdot \text{diag}(\Sigma[:r]) \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}, \quad B = V[:r, :]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times D} \]

docs.title: Factorised Forward Projection (FactorisedLinear):
docs.text:
For input \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\):

\[ \text{FactorisedLinear}(X) = (X B^\top) A^\top + b = X (A B)^\top + b \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} \]

Applying factorized linear transformations to compute Query, Key, and Value representations:

[ Q = \text{FactorisedLinear}_Q(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ K = \text{FactorisedLinear}_K(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ V = \text{FactorisedLinear}_V(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ]

docs.title: Robust Mask Validation & Scaled Attention:
docs.text:
Raw score matrices \(S = \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times N}\) are evaluated. Token valid boolean masks \(M_{\text{valid}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N}\) are parsed from inputs:

\[ \widehat{S}_{b, h, i, j} = \begin{cases} S_{b, h, i, j} & \text{if } M_{\text{valid}, b, j} = \text{True} \\ -10^5 & \text{if } M_{\text{valid}, b, j} = \text{False} \end{cases} \]

Softmax attention and output projections proceed as:

[ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (\widehat{S}{b, h, i, j}) ] [ C_{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^N \text{Dropout}(A){b, h, i, j} \cdot V{b, h, j, m} \implies C \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ] [ Y = \text{FactorisedLinear}_O(C) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ]

docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D/H\), and \(r_q, r_k, r_v, r_o\) SVD ranks.

  1. Factorised Linear Projections: Total projection workload: \(4 B N D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o)\) FLOPs.

  2. Core Attention Computation: \(Q K^\top\) & \(A V\): \(4 B N^2 D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Softmax & Masking: \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs.

  3. Total Workload Summary: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(2 B N D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o) + 2 B N^2 D\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(4 B N D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o) + 4 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2\)

docs.title: Parameter & Memory Footprint Comparison
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Uncompressed Projection Parameters}, \(4 D^2 + 4 D\) floats. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{MinimalSVD v2 Parameter Count}, \(2 D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o) + 4 D\) floats.

For \(D = 768\) and average rank \(r = 32\), parameter requirements drop by \(91.6\%\) (\(2.36\text{M} \to 199\text{k}\)).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Rank Saturation at High Spectral Thresholds
docs.text: If energy parameter \(E \ge 0.99\), rank \(r\) approaches \(\min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})\), which adds linear factor overhead (\(2 D r \approx 2 D^2 > D^2\)), increasing parameter storage beyond uncompressed linear layers.

docs.title: Dynamic Range Underflow in Reduced Precision
docs.text: Using large negative values (\(-10^5\)) in FP16 precision avoids NaN gradients while preventing underflow errors during Softmax exponentiation.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel fuses low-rank projections (\(B, A\)) and token mask validation directly inside SRAM memory.

   │ Input: X [B, N, D]                                          │
   │ Projection Matrices: B [r, D], A [D, r]                     │
   │ Token Valid Mask: token_valid [B, N]                        │

                                  │ Direct SIMD Register Load
                                  ▼

 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Load Activation Tile X_i [BLOCK_M, D]                       │
 │ 2. Compute Fused Down-Up Output: Y_i = (X_i @ B.T) @ A.T       │
 │ 3. Mask Invalid Tokens: S_ij = S_ij if valid else -1e5         │
 │ 4. Execute Online Scaled Softmax Attention                     │

                                  │ Write Output
                                  ▼

docs.text:
1. Per-Head Independent Rank Selection: Decompose \(W_Q, W_K\) per attention head into distinct head ranks \(r_h\) rather than shared layer-level ranks.
  2. Spectral Rank Distillation: Train student models using MinimalSVD v2 factorized layers distilled from full uncompressed teacher models.
  3. Low-Rank + Sparse Residual Injection: Combine MinimalSVD v2 factorized buffers with sparse residual adapters to recover full uncompressed model accuracy.

docs.title: 1. Abstract & Theoretical Motivation
docs.text:
Standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) computes full pairwise similarity scores across all \(L\) key-value sequence tokens \(\mathcal{O}(L^2)\), even though many sequence tokens contain redundant or low-information feature states. MixAttention-MoSKA implements Frequency and Variance-Aware Sparse Attention (FASA), a data-dependent token pruning paradigm that dynamically filters key-value representations based on information-theoretic variance metrics.

FASA computes channel feature variance across Key representations \(\text{Var}_{d_k}(K)\) as a real-time proxy for information entropy. Keys and Values are dynamically gathered down to a target retention ratio \(\rho = \text{fasa\_keep\_ratio}\) (\(\rho \ll 1\)), compressing Key-Value sequence length from \(L\) to \(\lfloor \rho L \rfloor\). By confining scaled dot-product attention queries to high-variance key-value subsets, MixAttention-MoSKA achieves linear sequence compute scaling \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot \rho L)\) while maintaining model contextual expressiveness.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Derivations & Formulations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}\) be the input hidden state tensor, where \(B\) is batch size, \(L\) is sequence length, and \(D\) is model hidden dimension. Let \(H\) be the number of attention heads, \(d_k = D / H\) the head dimension, and \(\rho \in (0, 1]\) the FASA token retention ratio.

docs.title: Subspace Projections:
docs.text:
Linear transformations project hidden states into query, key, and value tensors:

\[ Q = X W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}, \quad K = X W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}, \quad V = X W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D} \]

Reshaping into multi-head layouts: \(Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times d_k}\).

docs.title: FASA Information-Theoretic Importance Scoring:
docs.text:
For each key token \(t \in \{1, \dots, L\}\) in batch \(b\), variance across feature channels \(d \in \{1, \dots, d_k\}\) is computed per head:

\[ \text{Var}_{d_k}(K_{b, h, t, :}) = \frac{1}{d_k} \sum_{d=1}^{d_k} \left( K_{b, h, t, d} - \bar{K}_{b, h, t} \right)^2 \]

where \(\bar{K}_{b, h, t} = \frac{1}{d_k} \sum_{d=1}^{d_k} K_{b, h, t, d}\).

Token importance \(I_{b, t} \in \mathbb{R}\) is calculated by averaging variance across all \(H\) heads:

\[ I_{b, t} = \frac{1}{H} \sum_{h=1}^H \text{Var}_{d_k}(K_{b, h, t, :}) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L} \]

docs.title: Top-K Key-Value Pruning & Index Gathering:
docs.text:
Let \(K_{\text{keep}} = \max(1, \lfloor \rho \cdot L \rfloor)\) be the number of retained tokens. The index set \(\mathcal{I}_{b} \subset \{1, \dots, L\}\) of top key-value positions is derived via Top-K selection:

\[ \mathcal{I}_{b} = \text{TopK}_{t}\left(I_{b, t}, \, k=K_{\text{keep}}\right) \in \mathbb{Z}^{B \times K_{\text{keep}}} \]

Using index set \(\mathcal{I}\), compressed key and value tensors are gathered along the sequence length dimension:

[ K_{\text{pruned}} = \text{Gather}L(K, \mathcal{I}) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times K{\text{keep}} \times d_k} ] [ V_{\text{pruned}} = \text{Gather}L(V, \mathcal{I}) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times K{\text{keep}} \times d_k} ]

docs.title: Sparse Scaled Dot-Product Attention:
docs.text:
Query vectors \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times d_k}\) attend exclusively to pruned key states \(K_{\text{pruned}}\):

\[ S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} \sum_{m=1}^{d_k} Q_{b, h, i, m} \cdot (K_{\text{pruned}})_{b, h, j, m} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times K_{\text{keep}}} \]

If pruned attention mask \(M_{\text{pruned}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times K_{\text{keep}}}\) is present:

[ \widetilde{S}{b, h, i, j} = S{b, h, i, j} + (1.0 - M_{\text{pruned}, b, j}) \cdot (-10^9) ] [ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (\widetilde{S}{b, h, i, j}) = \frac{\exp(\widetilde{S}{b, h, i, j})}{\sum{l=1}^{K_{\text{keep}}} \exp(\widetilde{S}{b, h, i, l})} ] [ O{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^{K_{\text{keep}}} A_{b, h, i, j} \cdot (V_{\text{pruned}})_{b, h, j, m} \implies O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times d_k} ] [ Y = \text{Concat}(O_1, \dots, O_H) \cdot W_O + b_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}, \quad W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D} ]

docs.title: 3. Tensor Execution Flow & Dimensional Shape Tracing
docs.text:
Input: hidden_states [B, L, D]
  │
  ├──> Linear(D, D, bias=False) [W_q] ──> Q: [B, L, D] ──> view & permute ──> Q: [B, H, L, d_k]
  ├──> Linear(D, D, bias=False) [W_k] ──> K: [B, L, D] ──> view & permute ──> K: [B, H, L, d_k]
  └──> Linear(D, D, bias=False) [W_v] ──> V: [B, L, D] ──> view & permute ──> V: [B, H, L, d_k]
                                │
                                ├──> _fasa_prune(K, V, attention_mask):
                                │      K.var(dim=-1).mean(dim=1) ──> importance: [B, L]
                                │      TopK(importance, keep=ρ*L) ──> idx: [B, K_keep]
                                │      Gather K, V along sequence dim ──> K_p, V_p: [B, H, K_keep, d_k]
                                │      Gather attention_mask ──> p_mask: [B, K_keep]
                                │
                                ├──> MatMul: Q @ K_p.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(d_k) ──> scores: [B, H, L, K_keep]
                                ├──> Add p_mask (-1e9 for padding) ──> [B, H, L, K_keep]
                                ├──> Softmax(dim=-1) ──> attn_weights: [B, H, L, K_keep]
                                │
                                └──> MatMul: attn_weights @ V_p ──> context: [B, H, L, d_k]
                                        │
                                        └──> permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous().view([B, L, D])
                                        └──> Linear(D, D) [out_proj] ──> Output: [B, L, D]

docs.title: Operational & Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(L\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D / H\), and \(\rho\) retention ratio (\(K_{\text{keep}} = \rho L\)).

  1. Linear Projections: \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\): \(4 \times 2 B L D^2 = 8 B L D^2\) FLOPs (\(4 B L D^2\) MACs).

  2. FASA Importance Calculation & Top-K Gathering: Mean & Variance over head dimension: \(2 B H L d_k = 2 B L D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Head mean reduction: \(B H L\) FLOPs. Concurrently, Top-K Sort (\(B \times L\) array): \(\mathcal{O}(B \cdot L \log K_{\text{keep}})\) operations. In this setting, Tensor Gather: Index lookup & memory copying.

  3. Pruned Core Attention FLOPs (\(Q K_{\text{pruned}}^\top\) & \(A V_{\text{pruned}}\)): \(Q K_{\text{pruned}}^\top\): \([B, H, L, d_k] \times [B, H, d_k, \rho L] \implies 2 B H L (\rho L) d_k = 2 \rho B L^2 D\) FLOPs ($ \rho B L^2 D$ MACs). Furthermore, Softmax overhead: \(\approx 5 B H L (\rho L) = 5 \rho B H L^2\) FLOPs. Concurrently, \(A V_{\text{pruned}}\): \([B, H, L, \rho L] \times [B, H, \rho L, d_k] \implies 2 \rho B L^2 D\) FLOPs ($ \rho B L^2 D$ MACs).

docs.title: Complexity Summary:
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(4 B L D^2 + 2 \rho B L^2 D\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(8 B L D^2 + 4 \rho B L^2 D + 2 B L D + 5 \rho B H L^2\) Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Theoretical Flop Reduction}, for \(\rho = 0.189\), core attention FLOPs drop by \(\approx 81.1\%\) (\(5.29\times\) speedup on matrix multiplication).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Failure Modes
Non-Differentiable Top-K Selection Discontinuity
docs.text: The torch.topk operator is non-differentiable with respect to importance scores \(I_{b, t}\). Gradient propagation \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial I_{b, t}} = 0\) vanishes, preventing the key projection matrix \(W_K\) from explicitly learning to optimize FASA token selection.

docs.title: Non-Contiguous Memory Gathering Latency
docs.text: Gathering key and value vectors via K.gather(2, idx_exp) performs un-coalesced non-contiguous DRAM reads across the sequence length dimension. On GPUs, un-coalesced memory reads create bus serialization stalls, negating FLOP savings for small sequence lengths (\(L < 1024\)).

docs.title: Variance Entropy Blindness
docs.text: Low-variance key tokens (e.g., stationary positional indicators or BOS tokens) are aggressively pruned by FASA despite holding critical global contextual routing information. This causes performance collapse on tasks dependent on static anchor tokens.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Optimization Strategies
Fused FASA Filter & Sparse Matrix Triton Architecture
docs.text:
To overcome memory gathering latencies, Triton fused kernels execute variance filtering and sparse matrix multiplication directly in GPU L1 cache registers.

       Global Memory (HBM)
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ Q [B, H, L, d_k], K [B, H, L, d_k], V [B, H, L, d_k]   │
      └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Direct Block Load
                                  ▼
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                   Triton SRAM Scratchpad                         │
 │ 1. Load K Tile: Compute In-Register Variance Var(K_tile)         │
 │ 2. Mask Low-Variance Key Tokens (In-Register Bitmask)            │
 │ 3. Load Q Tile & Compute Sparse Multiplication:                   │
 │    S_tile = Q_tile @ K_pruned.T / sqrt(d_k)                      │
 │ 4. Execute Online Softmax & Accumulate Output Tile               │
 └────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Stream Output
                                  ▼
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ Context Output O [B, L, D]                             │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Key Triton Implementation Guidelines:
docs.text:
1. Gumbel-Softmax Continuous Relaxation: For training passes, replace hard torch.topk with Gumbel-Softmax soft-masking to provide continuous gradient flow back to \(W_K\): [ M_{b, t} = \text{Sigmoid}\left( \frac{I_{b, t} + g}{\tau} \right) ]
  2. Dynamic SRAM Bitmask Filtering: Avoid physical gather tensor copies in HBM. Generate a 1-bit presence mask in SRAM registers and skip Key-Value tile loads for unselected token indices.
  3. Anchor Token Retention Safeguard: Always force retention of the first \(K_{\text{anchor}}\) tokens (e.g., \(t \in \{0, 1\}\)) regardless of variance score, protecting global anchor context.

docs.title: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA): Low-Rank Latent Bottleneck Compression (DeepSeek-V2)
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024), represents a major architectural advance in compressing the Key-Value (KV) cache for large-scale autoregressive Transformer inference. Traditional approaches like Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) reduce KV cache overhead by sharing key-value heads across query groups. However, GQA still caches full head-dimensional Key and Value tensors for each shared head, creating substantial memory bandwidth bottlenecks during long-context generation.

MLA re-formulates attention parameterization by compressing Key and Value states into a low-rank latent vector \(\mathbf{c}_{KV} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c}\), where rank \(d_c \ll 2 H d_k\). Instead of caching high-dimensional key and value matrices (\(2 H d_k\) floats per token position), MLA caches only the low-rank vector \(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\). Key and Value representations are projected upward on-the-fly during decoding (k_up, v_up). During inference, the up-projection matrices can be mathematically absorbed directly into the Query and Output projections, reducing inference-time memory caching to a fraction of traditional MHA.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote the input activation tensor. Let \(H\) be the number of query heads, \(d_k = D / H\) the dimension per head, and \(d_c\) the low-rank latent compression dimension (typically \(d_c = 128\) or \(512\)).

docs.title: Query Projection & Low-Rank KV Latent Compression:
docs.text:
Query states are projected via un-biased linear transformation \(W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\):

\[ Q = X W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} \]

Key-Value hidden states are down-projected into the compressed latent subspace \(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\) via matrix \(W_{DKV} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d_c}\):

\[ \mathbf{c}_{KV} = X W_{DKV} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_c} \]

docs.title: Up-Projection to Key and Value Multi-Head States:
docs.text:
From low-rank latent representation \(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\), Multi-Head Key and Value states are restored on-the-fly using up-projection parameters \(W_{UK} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c \times D}\) and \(W_{UV} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c \times D}\):

\[ K = \mathbf{c}_{KV} W_{UK} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}, \quad V = \mathbf{c}_{KV} W_{UV} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} \]

Reshaping into head-partitioned multi-head layouts yields:

\[ Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k}, \quad K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k}, \quad V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} \]

docs.title: Scaled Dot-Product & Softmax Attention:
docs.text:
With reconstructed Key and Value states, standard scaled dot-product attention computes pairwise routing:

[ S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} \sum_{m=1}^{d_k} Q_{b, h, i, m} \cdot K_{b, h, j, m} ] [ \widehat{S}{b, h, i, j} = S{b, h, i, j} + M_{b, 1, i, j} ] [ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (\widehat{S}{b, h, i, j}) = \frac{\exp(\widehat{S}{b, h, i, j})}{\sum{l=1}^N \exp(\widehat{S}_{b, h, i, l})} ]

docs.title: Context Value Aggregation & Output Projection:
docs.text:
Context vectors are computed by aggregating multi-head values, followed by output projection \(W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\):

[ O_{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^N \text{Dropout}(A){b, h, i, j} \cdot V{b, h, j, m} ] [ Y = \text{Concat}(O_1, \dots, O_H) W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ]

docs.title: Mathematical Equivalence for Matrix Absorptive Inference:
docs.text:
During autoregressive decoding, explicit reconstruction of Key matrix \(K\) can be bypassed by absorbing \(W_{UK}\) directly into Query projection matrix \(W_Q\):

\[ Q K^\top = (X W_Q) (\mathbf{c}_{KV} W_{UK})^\top = X (W_Q W_{UK}^\top) \mathbf{c}_{KV}^\top \]

Thus, computing affinity scores reduces to an inner product between transformed Query states and low-rank latent vector \(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\).

docs.title: Tensor Shape Transformation Table
docs.text: Execution Stage Input Tensor Shape Transformation / Operation Output Tensor Shape Input [B, N, D] Received hidden activations [B, N, D] Query Projection [B, N, D] self.q_proj(X).view(B, N, H, d_k) [B, N, H, d_k] Latent KV Compression [B, N, D] self.kv_down(X) c_KV: [B, N, d_c] Key Up-Projection c_KV: [B, N, d_c] self.k_up(c_KV).view(B, N, H, d_k) [B, N, H, d_k] Value Up-Projection c_KV: [B, N, d_c] self.v_up(c_KV).view(B, N, H, d_k) [B, N, H, d_k] Multi-Head Transpose Q, K, V: [B, N, H, d_k] .transpose(1, 2) [B, H, N, d_k] each Score Matrix MatMul Q: [B, H, N, d_k], K: [B, H, N, d_k] torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / sqrt(d_k) [B, H, N, N] Mask & Softmax scores scores + attention_mask + F.softmax [B, H, N, N] Value Aggregation attn, V torch.matmul(attn, v) [B, H, N, d_k] Concat & Output Proj context .transpose(1, 2).view(B, N, D) + self.out_proj [B, N, D]

docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
The computational workload decomposes into distinct projection and pairwise routing phases governed by batch size \(B\), sequence length \(N\), hidden dimension \(D\), head count \(H\), head dimension \(d_k = D/H\), and compression rank \(d_c\). The primary linear projections encompass the un-biased query transformation \(W_Q\) consuming \(2 B N D^2\) FLOPs, the down-projection operator \(W_{DKV}\) requiring \(2 B N D d_c\) FLOPs, the dual multi-head up-projections \(W_{UK}\) and \(W_{UV}\) jointly contributing \(4 B N d_c D\) FLOPs, and the final linear projection \(W_O\) incurring \(2 B N D^2\) FLOPs. Consequently, the cumulative projection workload evaluates to \(4 B N D^2 + 6 B N d_c D\) FLOPs.

Within the core attention mechanism, computing the pairwise similarity tensor via the \(Q K^\top\) matrix multiplication requires \(2 B N^2 D\) FLOPs, while row-wise normalization and causal masking consume approximately \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs. Context aggregation via the attention-value contraction \(A V\) demands an additional \(2 B N^2 D\) FLOPs. In aggregate, the computational complexity yields a total multiply-accumulate count of \(2 B N D^2 + 3 B N d_c D + 2 B N^2 D\) MACs, translating to an arithmetic density of \(4 B N D^2 + 6 B N d_c D + 4 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2\) FLOPs.

docs.title: Memory Footprint & KV Cache Analysis
docs.text:
From a parameterization perspective, the static weight footprint comprises \(2 D^2 + 3 D d_c + D\) floating-point scalars. Crucially, during autoregressive decoding, the memory bandwidth bottleneck is substantially mitigated because the Key-Value cache stores solely the low-rank latent representation \(\mathbf{c}_{KV} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_c}\) rather than full multi-head key and value activations across all heads. The decoding cache allocation is formally defined by:

\[ \text{KV Cache Size}_{\text{MLA}} = B \cdot N \cdot d_c \cdot b \text{ bytes} \]

where \(b\) denotes the precision byte width. In contrast to standard Multi-Head Attention requiring \(2 B N D \cdot b\) bytes, setting \(d_c = 128\) for a representative model dimension of \(D = 4096\) yields:

\[ \text{Compression Ratio} = \frac{2 \cdot 4096}{128} = \mathbf{64\times \text{ Reduction in KV Cache Memory}} \]

This structural reduction alleviates High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) bandwidth saturation during long-sequence autoregressive generation, shifting execution characteristics from memory-bound memory-stall regimes toward compute-bound Tensor Core saturation.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Rank Collapse in Latent Bottleneck
docs.text: The low-rank compression architecture introduces intricate optimization trade-offs and structural failure modes that warrant rigorous analysis. A primary failure mode manifests as rank collapse within the latent bottleneck when the compression dimension \(d_c\) is aggressively constrained (e.g., \(d_c < 64\)). In this regime, the intermediate latent subspace \(\mathbf{c}_{KV}\) lacks sufficient representational capacity to span the diverse subspace trajectories required by disparate query heads. This induced rank deficiency restricts the effective rank of the reconstructed Key and Value matrices, thereby flattening the singular value spectrum and degrading the model's capacity to resolve multi-topic associations across extended sequence horizons.

docs.title: Up-Projection Compute Overhead and Gradient Dynamics
docs.text: Furthermore, propagating gradient signals through the consecutive down- and up-projection matrices (\(W_{DKV}\), \(W_{UK}\), and \(W_{UV}\)) alters the conditioning of the optimization loss landscape. During backward propagation, backpropagating through the latent bottleneck requires computing matrix products with shape \([B, N, d_c] \times [d_c, D]\), creating non-negligible training-time arithmetic overhead compared to standard dense attention. Concurrently, the composition of low-rank linear maps can amplify spectral radius discrepancies during early training phases, rendering parameter updates sensitive to learning rate scheduling and requiring precise weight initialization to prevent vanishing or exploding gradient norms across deep transformer layers.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
For inference, a fused Triton MLA decoding kernel absorbs up-projection weights into query registers, computing scores directly against cached latent vectors \(\mathbf{c}_{KV} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_c}\).

                     Global Memory (HBM)
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Query Activations: Q [B, H, N, d_k]                        │
    │ Cached Latent KV Vectors: c_KV [B, N, d_c]  (64x smaller!) │
    │ Transposed Up-Projection Weights: W_UK [H, d_k, d_c]       │
    └─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Pre-transform Queries: Q_trans = Q @ W_UK
                                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    Triton SRAM Scratchpad                    │
  │ 1. Load Transformed Query Tile Q_trans_i [BLOCK_M, d_c]      │
  │ 2. Load Latent KV Tile c_KV_j [BLOCK_N, d_c]                │
  │ 3. Compute Direct Score: S_ij = Q_trans_i @ c_KV_j.T        │
  │ 4. Online Softmax & Accumulate Output with W_UV              │
  └───────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Context Output
                                  ▼
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Context Output: O [B, N, D]                                │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
Future architectural trajectories for low-rank attention compression span several promising research directions. A prominent synthesis opportunity lies in Decoupled Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) Latent MLA, which augments compressed latent states with an uncompressed, decoupled positional query-key subspace. This structural formulation preserves exact relative geometric encoding while maintaining the full \(64\times\) KV cache reduction ratio during generation.

Concurrently, dynamic rank adapters (AdaMLA) offer a mechanism to dynamically modulate the compression rank \(d_c\) on a per-layer or per-token basis via input-dependent gating networks. By allocating higher rank capacity to semantically dense layers and lower capacity to diffuse routing layers, the architecture achieves optimal Pareto efficiency across heterogeneous sequence lengths. Furthermore, combining low-rank latent caching with low-bit post-training quantization or quantization-aware training (such as FP8 or INT4 latent representations) enables an order-of-magnitude reduction in state memory, compressing the effective cache footprint to less than 1% of dense Multi-Head Attention and unlocking extreme-scale context windows on memory-constrained accelerator clusters.

docs.title: MoBA Attention: Mixture-of-Block Attention via Centroid Cosine Routing
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Standard Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) computes dense pairwise token interactions across sequence length \(L\), incurring quadratic computational time complexity \(\mathcal{O}(L^2 d)\) and memory footprint \(\mathcal{O}(L^2 + L d)\). For long-context language modeling, this quadratic bottleneck severely restricts context length. MoBA (Mixture-of-Block Attention) addresses this limitation by reformulating fine-grained token-to-token attention as a two-stage hierarchical sparse routing process.

The sequence of length \(L\) is partitioned into uniform contiguous blocks of size \(B_{\text{sz}}\). Rather than calculating dense interactions between all tokens, MoBA abstracts each block into a single spatial centroid vector via uniform arithmetic mean pooling. Inter-block affinity scores are derived by computing scaled dot-product similarities between query block centroids and key block centroids. For each query block, MoBA dynamically selects the top-\(k\) most relevant key-value blocks based on these centroid affinities. Fine-grained dense attention is subsequently executed strictly between the query tokens within the block and the tokens belonging to the \(k\) routed key-value blocks.

This hierarchical routing scheme reduces the memory footprint and computational complexity of attention matrix generation from \(\mathcal{O}(L^2)\) to \(\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{L^2}{B_{\text{sz}}^2} d + L k B_{\text{sz}} d\right)\). When the condition \(k B_{\text{sz}} \ll L\) holds, MoBA achieves linear scaling behavior relative to sequence length for token-level attention while incurring only a minimal quadratic overhead at the coarse block-centroid level.

docs.title: 2.1 Multi-Head Projection and Block Partitioning
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}\) denote the input hidden states sequence. The linear projections for Query (\(\mathbf{Q}\)), Key (\(\mathbf{K}\)), and Value (\(\mathbf{V}\)) are defined as: $\(\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{W}_Q, \quad \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{W}_K, \quad \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{W}_V\)$ where \(\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K, \mathbf{W}_V \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\). Reshaping into \(H\) heads with head dimension \(d_k = D / H\) yields tensors \(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L \times d_k}\).

To handle arbitrary sequence lengths \(L\), zero-padding is applied along the spatial dimension to ensure \(L_p = \lceil L / B_{\text{sz}} \rceil \cdot B_{\text{sz}}\). The number of blocks is \(n_b = L_p / B_{\text{sz}}\). The padded tensors are partitioned into contiguous blocks: $\(\mathbf{Q}_b, \mathbf{K}_b, \mathbf{V}_b \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times n_b \times B_{\text{sz}} \times d_k}\)$

docs.title: 2.2 Centroid Reduction and Inter-Block Routing Matrix
docs.text:
For each block \(i \in \{1, \dots, n_b\}\), representative centroid vectors \(\bar{\mathbf{Q}}_i\) and \(\bar{\mathbf{K}}_j\) are derived via spatial arithmetic averaging: $\(\bar{\mathbf{Q}}_i = \frac{1}{B_{\text{sz}}} \sum_{t=1}^{B_{\text{sz}}} \mathbf{Q}_b[:, :, i, t, :] \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_k}\)$ $\(\bar{\mathbf{K}}_j = \frac{1}{B_{\text{sz}}} \sum_{t=1}^{B_{\text{sz}}} \mathbf{K}_b[:, :, j, t, :] \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times d_k}\)$

The coarse inter-block affinity routing matrix \(\mathbf{S}^{\text{block}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times n_b \times n_b}\) is evaluated by computing scaled inner products between query block centroids and key block centroids: $\(\mathbf{S}^{\text{block}}_{i, j} = \frac{\bar{\mathbf{Q}}_i \bar{\mathbf{K}}_j^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\)$

docs.title: 2.3 Sparse Top-k Gating and Index Selection
docs.text: For each query block \(i\), a discrete top-\(k\) routing operation identifies the indices \(\mathcal{I}_i\) of the \(k\) key-value blocks with the highest affinity scores: $\(\mathcal{I}_i = \operatorname{TopK}\left(\mathbf{S}^{\text{block}}_{i, :}, k\right) \in \{1, \dots, n_b\}^k\)$ where \(k = \min(\text{top\_k}, n_b)\). The selected key and value block tensors are gathered and flattened along the token dimension: $\(\mathbf{K}_{\text{sel}, i} = \operatorname{Gather}\left(\mathbf{K}_b, \mathcal{I}_i\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times (k \cdot B_{\text{sz}}) \times d_k}\)$ $\(\mathbf{V}_{\text{sel}, i} = \operatorname{Gather}\left(\mathbf{V}_b, \mathcal{I}_i\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times (k \cdot B_{\text{sz}}) \times d_k}\)$

docs.title: 2.4 Block-Sparse Attention Computation & Reassembly
docs.text:
For query block \(i\), local dense attention is computed between \(\mathbf{Q}_{b, i} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times B_{\text{sz}} \times d_k}\) and the routed key matrix \(\mathbf{K}_{\text{sel}, i}\): $\(\mathbf{A}_i = \operatorname{Softmax}\left( \frac{\mathbf{Q}_{b, i} \mathbf{K}_{\text{sel}, i}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times B_{\text{sz}} \times (k \cdot B_{\text{sz}})}\)$ $\(\mathbf{O}_{b, i} = \mathbf{A}_i \mathbf{V}_{\text{sel}, i} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times B_{\text{sz}} \times d_k}\)$

The individual output blocks \(\mathbf{O}_{b, i}\) are concatenated along the block dimension to reconstruct the padded sequence output \(\mathbf{O}_p \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times L_p \times d_k}\). The padding tokens beyond original length \(L\) are un-padded (sliced), reshaped to \(\mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}\), and mapped through the output projection linear layer: $\(\mathbf{Y} = \operatorname{Slice}\left(\mathbf{O}_p, :L\right) \mathbf{W}_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times D}\)$

docs.title: 4.1 FLOPs Computation Breakdown
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(H\) number of heads, \(d_k\) head dimension (\(D = H d_k\)), \(L\) sequence length, \(n_b = L / B_{\text{sz}}\) number of blocks, \(B_{\text{sz}}\) block size, and \(k\) number of routed blocks.

  1. Linear Projections (\(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}\)): $\(\operatorname{FLOPs}_{\text{proj}} = 3 \times 2 \cdot B \cdot L \cdot D^2 = 6 B L D^2\)$
  2. Block Centroid Mean Pooling: $\(\operatorname{FLOPs}_{\text{centroid}} = 2 \times B \cdot H \cdot n_b \cdot B_{\text{sz}} \cdot d_k = 2 B L D\)$
  3. Inter-Block Score Matrix Computation: $\(\operatorname{FLOPs}_{\text{block\_score}} = 2 \cdot B \cdot H \cdot n_b^2 \cdot d_k = 2 B H d_k \left(\frac{L}{B_{\text{sz}}}\right)^2 = \frac{2 B D L^2}{B_{\text{sz}}^2}\)$
  4. Top-\(k\) Sorting: $\(\operatorname{FLOPs}_{\text{topk}} \approx B \cdot H \cdot n_b \cdot (n_b \log k)\)$
  5. Per-Block Sparse Attention: For each of the \(n_b\) query blocks, attention matmul \(\mathbf{Q}_i \mathbf{K}_{\text{sel}, i}^\top\) requires \(2 \cdot B_{\text{sz}} \cdot (k B_{\text{sz}}) \cdot d_k\) FLOPs, and context matmul \(\mathbf{A}_i \mathbf{V}_{\text{sel}, i}\) requires \(2 \cdot B_{\text{sz}} \cdot (k B_{\text{sz}}) \cdot d_k\) FLOPs. Across all \(n_b\) blocks: $\(\operatorname{FLOPs}_{\text{attn}} = n_b \times \left( 4 \cdot B \cdot H \cdot B_{\text{sz}} \cdot k B_{\text{sz}} \cdot d_k \right) = 4 B H d_k L k B_{\text{sz}} = 4 B D L k B_{\text{sz}}\)$
  6. Output Projection (\(\mathbf{W}_O\)): $\(\operatorname{FLOPs}_{\text{out}} = 2 B L D^2\)$
\[\text{Total FLOPs} = 8 B L D^2 + \frac{2 B D L^2}{B_{\text{sz}}^2} + 4 B D L k B_{\text{sz}} + 2 B L D\]

docs.title: 4.2 MACs & Memory Footprint Analysis
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Multiply-Accumulate Operations (MACs)},

$\(\text{Total MACs} \approx 4 B L D^2 + \frac{B D L^2}{B_{\text{sz}}^2} + 2 B D L k B_{\text{sz}}\)$ Specifically, regarding \textbf{Peak Activation Memory}, Furthermore, Unpadded/Padded Q, K, V tensors: \(3 \times B \cdot L_p \cdot D \times 2 \text{ bytes}\) (FP16/BF16) Concurrently, Centroid matrices: \(2 \times B \cdot H \cdot n_b \cdot d_k \times 2 \text{ bytes}\) In this setting, Block Affinity Score matrix: \(B \cdot H \cdot n_b \cdot n_b \times 2 \text{ bytes}\) Additionally, Gathered \(K_{\text{sel}}, V_{\text{sel}}\) (in sequential block loop): \(2 \times B \cdot H \cdot k B_{\text{sz}} \cdot d_k \times 2 \text{ bytes}\) per iteration. Moreover, Per-block attention matrix: \(B \cdot H \cdot B_{\text{sz}} \cdot (k B_{\text{sz}}) \times 2 \text{ bytes}\).

docs.title: 4.3 Asymptotic Scalability Comparison
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Standard Dense Attention}, \(\mathcal{O}(L^2 d + L D^2)\) compute, \(\mathcal{O}(L^2 H)\) memory. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{MoBA Attention}, \(\mathcal{O}\left(L D^2 + \frac{L^2 D}{B_{\text{sz}}^2} + L k B_{\text{sz}} D\right)\) compute, \(\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{L^2 H}{B_{\text{sz}}^2} + L k B_{\text{sz}} H\right)\) memory. Concurrently, When \(B_{\text{sz}} = 64, k = 4\), block scaling reduces quadratic matrix elements by a factor of \(B_{\text{sz}}^2 = 4096 \times\).

docs.title: 5. Failure Modes, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
5.1 Centroid Arithmetic Mean Information Loss
docs.text: The coarse routing phase compresses an entire block of \(B_{\text{sz}}\) tokens into a single mean vector \(\bar{\mathbf{Q}}_i = \frac{1}{B_{\text{sz}}} \sum \mathbf{Q}_{i, t}\). This spatial mean pooling acts as an isotropic low-pass filter: 1. High-Frequency Token Erasure: Outlier tokens with high magnitude (e.g., sink tokens, initial punctuation, or salient keywords) become heavily diluted by non-informative background tokens. 2. False Negative Routing: If a critical key token is located in a key block whose remaining tokens have opposite directionality, the centroid vector \(\bar{\mathbf{K}}_j\) suffers destructive cancellation, producing an artificially low block affinity score \(S^{\text{block}}_{i, j}\). Consequently, the routing step drops the block containing the crucial token.

docs.title: 5.2 Discrete Routing Non-Differentiability & Gradient Starvation
docs.text: The discrete selection \(\operatorname{TopK}(\mathbf{S}^{\text{block}}_{i, :}, k)\) is a hard thresholding operation. Because \(\frac{\partial \operatorname{TopK}}{\partial \mathbf{S}^{\text{block}}} = 0\) almost everywhere: Gradients cannot backpropagate directly through the discrete routing decisions to adjust the projection matrices \(\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K\) specifically for block routing. Furthermore, Blocks not selected in the top-\(k\) receive zero gradient updates during the backward pass (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{K}_{\text{unselected}}} \mathcal{L} = 0\)), leading to cold-start routing collapse where early-selected blocks dominate future routing indefinitely.

docs.title: 5.3 Rank Collapse in Block Subspaces
docs.text: When sequence length \(L\) grows extremely large, key block centroids \(\bar{\mathbf{K}}_j\) tend to converge toward the global mean of the token distribution due to the Law of Large Numbers. This reduces the variance across block centroids, causing \(\operatorname{Rank}(\mathbf{S}^{\text{block}}) \ll n_b\). The resulting routing matrix becomes isotropic, leading to random or uniform block selection that degrades task performance to that of random block sampling.

docs.title: 5.4 Python Loop Overhead and Unmasked Zero-Padding Artifacts
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Sequential Execution Trap}, executing an explicit Python for i in range(nb): loop incurs substantial host-to-device kernel launch overhead, stalling GPU SM execution pipelines when \(n_b\) is large. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Padding Pollution}, zero-padding to length \(L_p\) introduces zero vectors into the final block. Without explicit boolean attention masking, zero vectors alter the block mean magnitude \(\frac{1}{B_{\text{sz}}} \sum \mathbf{Q}\), distorting cosine affinity and participating in softmax exponentiation (\(\exp(0) = 1\)), causing non-zero probability leakage to dummy tokens.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text: To overcome the performance bottlenecks of sequential Python loops and unfused gather/scatter operations, MoBA requires a specialized GPU custom kernel written in Triton.

docs.title: 6.1 Triton Kernel Architecture Blueprint
docs.text:
The hardware pipeline unifies block centroid computation, top-\(k\) routing, dynamic index gathering, and FlashAttention-style online softmax into a fused grid operator.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                            TRITON FUSED MOBA KERNEL                               |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  1. BLOCK CENTROID KERNEL (Grid: [B, H, n_b])                                     |
|     - Loads Q, K block [B_sz, d_k] into SRAM.                                     |
|     - Executes warp reduction sum along B_sz dimension.                           |
|     - Stores Q_mean, K_mean into global device memory [B, H, n_b, d_k].           |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  2. BLOCK AFFINITY & TOP-K KERNEL (Grid: [B, H, n_b])                             |
|     - Loads Q_mean_i and all K_mean [n_b, d_k].                                   |
|     - Computes dot product S[n_b] in register file.                               |
|     - Performs bitonic top-k sort across n_b elements in register/shared memory.  |
|     - Writes top-k block indices [B, H, n_b, k] directly to SRAM/Global Buffer.   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  3. FUSED BLOCK-SPARSE ATTENTION KERNEL (Grid: [B, H, n_b])                       |
|     - Loads Q_i block [B_sz, d_k].                                                |
|     - Loop over k (1..k):                                                         |
|         * Fetch target block id = idx[k_idx].                                     |
|         * Indirect memory load K_block, V_block [B_sz, d_k] via hardware pointer. |
|         * Compute S_block = Q_i @ K_block.T * scale.                              |
|         * Online Softmax update (m_new, d_new, O_acc).                            |
|     - Store final O_i [B_sz, d_k] back to global memory.                         |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 6.2 Implementation Code Blueprint (Triton JIT Pattern)
docs.text:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def _moba_fused_block_attn_kernel(
    Q_ptr, K_ptr, V_ptr, TopK_Idx_ptr, Out_ptr,
    stride_qb, stride_qh, stride_qn, stride_qd,
    stride_kb, stride_kh, stride_kn, stride_kd,
    stride_vb, stride_vh, stride_vn, stride_vd,
    stride_ob, stride_oh, stride_on, stride_od,
    stride_idx_b, stride_idx_h, stride_idx_q, stride_idx_k,
    scale,
    B_sz: tl.constexpr,
    D_K: tl.constexpr,
    K_TOP: tl.constexpr
):
    # Program Identifiers
    pid_q_block = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    pid_head = tl.program_id(axis=1)
    pid_batch = tl.program_id(axis=2)

    # Offset pointers for current batch & head
    q_block_ptr = Q_ptr + pid_batch * stride_qb + pid_head * stride_qh + pid_q_block * stride_qn
    out_block_ptr = Out_ptr + pid_batch * stride_ob + pid_head * stride_oh + pid_q_block * stride_on

    # Load Query block [B_sz, D_K] into SRAM
    offs_m = tl.arange(0, B_sz)
    offs_d = tl.arange(0, D_K)
    q_ptrs = q_block_ptr + (offs_m[:, None] * stride_qd + offs_d[None, :])
    q = tl.load(q_ptrs) # [B_sz, D_K]

    # Initialize Online Softmax Accumulators
    m_i = tl.full([B_sz], float("-inf"), dtype=tl.float32)
    l_i = tl.zeros([B_sz], dtype=tl.float32)
    acc = tl.zeros([B_sz, D_K], dtype=tl.float32)

    # Pointer to top-k block indices for current query block
    idx_base_ptr = TopK_Idx_ptr + pid_batch * stride_idx_b + pid_head * stride_idx_h + pid_q_block * stride_idx_q

    # Iterate over routed key blocks
    for k_idx in range(K_TOP):
        # Read target key block index from indices tensor
        target_k_block = tl.load(idx_base_ptr + k_idx * stride_idx_k)

        # Indirect Load Key block [B_sz, D_K]
        k_ptrs = K_ptr + pid_batch * stride_kb + pid_head * stride_kh + target_k_block * stride_kn + (offs_m[None, :] * stride_kd + offs_d[:, None])
        k = tl.load(k_ptrs) # [D_K, B_sz]

        # Compute inner product S = Q @ K.T * scale -> [B_sz, B_sz]
        s = tl.dot(q, k) * scale

        # Online Softmax updates
        m_ij = tl.max(s, axis=1)
        m_new = tl.maximum(m_i, m_ij)
        p = tl.exp(s - m_new[:, None])
        l_new = tl.exp(m_i - m_new) * l_i + tl.sum(p, axis=1)

        # Rescale prior accumulator
        acc_scale = tl.exp(m_i - m_new)
        acc = acc * acc_scale[:, None]

        # Indirect Load Value block [B_sz, D_K]
        v_ptrs = V_ptr + pid_batch * stride_vb + pid_head * stride_vh + target_k_block * stride_vn + (offs_m[:, None] * stride_vd + offs_d[None, :])
        v = tl.load(v_ptrs)

        # Accumulate context: acc += P @ V
        p_cast = p.to(v.dtype)
        acc = tl.dot(p_cast, v, acc)

        # Update stats
        l_i = l_new
        m_i = m_new

    # Final Softmax Normalization
    acc = acc / l_i[:, None]

    # Store computed block back to Global Memory
    o_ptrs = out_block_ptr + (offs_m[:, None] * stride_od + offs_d[None, :])
    tl.store(o_ptrs, acc.to(Out_ptr.dtype.element_ty))

docs.title: 6.3 Memory Access and SRAM Cache Optimization
docs.text:
1. Coalesced Memory Access: By storing \(\mathbf{K}\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) tensors in block-contiguous memory layouts [B, H, n_b, B_sz, d_k], indirect pointer calculations load continuous 128-byte DRAM segments, maximizing memory bus bandwidth.
  2. SRAM Accumulation: Queries \(\mathbf{Q}_i\) remain pinned in high-speed SRAM registers across all \(k\) iterations, eliminating repetitive DRAM re-reads.
  3. Register-Level Bitonic Top-k: For typical routing configurations (\(n_b \le 512, k \le 16\)), top-\(k\) block indexing is computed strictly within warp registers, avoiding costly global memory round trips.

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
1. Hierarchical Multi-Level Centroid Trees: Extend single-level block routing to 2-level or octree centroid hierarchies (\(B_{\text{macro}} = 256, B_{\text{micro}} = 32\)) to achieve logarithmic \(\mathcal{O}(\log(L/B_{\text{sz}}))\) routing complexity for million-token contexts.
  2. Soft Continuous Gating & Gumbel-Softmax Top-k: Replace non-differentiable hard top-\(k\) selection with straight-through Gumbel-Softmax routing or temperature-annealed soft block weighting to enable end-to-end gradient flow into key/query block projections.
  3. Hybrid MoBA-State Space Model (MoBA-Mamba): Combine coarse MoBA block selection for long-range associative memory retrieval with linear time-invariant state space models (SSMs) like Mamba-2 for localized high-frequency sequence processing.
  4. FP8 Block-Quantized Centroid Routing: Perform coarse centroid dot products using FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) tensor cores to quadruple matrix multiplication throughput during block affinity scoring.

docs.title: MoE-DeltaKV-Paged: Mixture-of-Block-Attention with Paged Delta-KV Compression
1. Abstract
docs.text: As Transformer models scale toward infinite context lengths, the memory footprint and bandwidth requirements of the Key-Value (KV) cache become the primary inference bottleneck. We introduce MoE-DeltaKV-Paged, a hybrid attention architecture that solves this by coupling a top-\(k\) Mixture-of-Block-Attention (MoBA) router with Paged Delta-KV temporal compression. By partitioning sequences into fixed physical pages and storing only low-rank quantized frame differences (\(\Delta K\), \(\Delta V\)), the module reduces KV cache memory consumption by up to 8x while preserving exact cross-token dependencies for high-entropy tokens.

docs.title: 2. Introduction & Motivation
docs.text:
Standard Multi-Head Attention scales as \(\mathcal{O}(L^2)\) in time and \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot d)\) in KV cache storage. While sparse routing mechanisms like Mixture-of-Block-Attention (MoBA) lower the time complexity to \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot B)\), they typically still necessitate caching the full history of token states.

MoE-DeltaKV-Paged directly addresses the cache capacity ceiling by acknowledging that token representations exhibit high temporal correlation. Instead of caching dense vectors per token, this architecture borrows from virtual memory systems and video compression: it manages context in discrete physical pages and stores temporal differences (deltas) compressed via low-rank SVD and 4-bit non-uniform quantization.

docs.title: 3. Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
Let physical KV memory be partitioned into blocks of size \(S_{page}\). For an incoming query block \(\bar{Q}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\), the router computes gating scores across historical key block centroids \(\bar{K}_j\): $$ g_j = \text{Softmax}\left( \text{TopK}\left( \frac{\bar{Q}i W{rg} \bar{K}j^T}{\sqrt{d}}, k{experts} \right) \right) $$

For active pages \(j \in \mathcal{P}_{active}\), the Key and Value matrices are dynamically reconstructed. The temporal delta is: $$ \Delta K_t = K_t - \hat{K}{t-1}, \quad \Delta V_t = V_t - \hat{V}{t-1} $$ These deltas are aggressively compressed via low-rank decomposition and 4-bit quantization: $$ \hat{\Delta K}t = \mathbf{U}{k, r} \mathbf{\Sigma}{k, r} \mathbf{V}{k, r}^T \cdot \text{Quantize}_4\left( \Delta K_t \right) $$ The final uncompressed states used for the attention computation are updated recursively: $$ \hat{K}t = \hat{K}{t-1} + \hat{\Delta K}t, \quad \hat{V}t = \hat{V}{t-1} + \hat{\Delta V}t $$ The block-sparse paged attention over routed pages evaluates as: $$ O_i = \sum{j \in \mathcal{P}{active}} g_j \cdot \text{Softmax}\left( \frac{\bar{Q}_i \hat{K}_j^T}{\sqrt{d}} \right) \hat{V}_j $$

docs.title: 4. Architecture & Implementation
docs.text: The architecture is structured in three cascading stages: 1. Delta-KV Temporal Compression Engine: Intercepts the \(K\) and \(V\) projections, computes differences against the previous sequence step, performs randomized SVD truncation, and executes min-max uniform quantization. 2. MoE-Block Router: Pools query and reconstructed key sequences into blocks of page_size. A dense linear mapping \(W_{rg}\) generates a correlation matrix. Causal masking ensures query blocks only select from past or current pages. 3. Paged Block-Sparse Attention: Gathers the top-\(k\) active key/value pages based on the routing indices. It evaluates the exact dot-product attention, applying intra-block causal masks dynamically to avoid future-token leakage within the currently active block.

docs.title: 5. Complexity & Hardware Efficiency
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{KV Cache Memory Footprint}, reduces per-token cache storage from \(2 \cdot d_{model}\) bytes (in 16-bit) to approximately \(0.25 \cdot d_{model}\) bytes (8x compression). Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Time Complexity}, \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot k \cdot S_{page} \cdot d)\) compared to \(\mathcal{O}(L^2 \cdot d)\) of dense attention. Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Hardware Profile}, supports structured memory fetching. The low-rank delta reconstruction operates inside GPU shared memory (SRAM), allowing uncompressed states to exist only ephemerally in fast registers before block-attention evaluation.

docs.title: 6. Hyperparameter & Routing Dynamics
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{page_size (\(S_{page}\))}, dictates the granularity of routing and compression. Larger pages (e.g., 64 or 128) maximize Tensor Core efficiency but increase the coarseness of routing. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{k_experts}, the number of pages selected per query block. Empirically, selecting 4 to 8 pages is sufficient to preserve perplexity on context lengths up to 128k. Concurrently, regarding \textbf{svd_rank}, the rank of the delta compression (default: 16). Higher ranks improve state reconstruction fidelity at the cost of larger compressed cache footprints.

docs.title: 7. Conclusion & Future Work
docs.text: MoE-DeltaKV-Paged represents a fundamental shift from dense, monolithic sequence memory to a dynamic, paged, and temporally compressed hierarchical cache. Future optimizations will integrate dynamic rank adaptation based on the spectral entropy of the temporal deltas (allocating larger SVD ranks to tokens with high information density) and deploying customized Triton kernels to perform the W4A16 register unpacking in a fused pass.

docs.title: Multi-Query Attention (MQA): Memory-Bandwidth Optimized Multi-Head Attention
docs.text: Family: Exact Softmax & IO-Aware Dense Attention · NeuralOps Registry ID: mqa

docs.title: Executive Abstract
docs.text:
Multi-Query Attention (MQA), introduced by Noam Shazeer (2019), drastically reduces memory bandwidth bottlenecks during autoregressive generation by sharing a single key-value head across all query heads. While standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) loads separate K and V tensors for each head from GPU HBM, MQA broadcasts a single shared KV head across all \(H\) query heads, achieving an \(H\times\) reduction in memory bandwidth consumption during generation.

In NeuralOps, mqa is integrated into the universal attention dispatch table, featuring full support for the 3-level fallback hierarchy, automatic shape validation, and end-to-end autograd backwards passes.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
The core operator computation is defined as:

\[ \text{MQA}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V \quad \text{where} \quad Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times T \times d}, \; K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 1 \times S \times d} \]

During execution, inputs \(Q, K, V\) are projected to dimension \(d\). In the causal configuration, lower-triangular masking ensures that tokens only attend to past and current time-steps, preserving autoregressive invariants.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: NASC (NEXUS-AEGIS Spectral Cascade) is a complexity-adaptive hybrid attention architecture that unifies the strengths of localized causal sliding windows, block-sparse Mixture-of-Experts routing, and global Random Fourier Feature (RFF) linear kernel approximations into a single gated layer.

docs.title: Architectural Taxonomy & Gated Routing
docs.text:
Input Sequence X ∈ ℝ^{B × L × D}
                                         │
                         ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
                         ▼               ▼               ▼
                   Local Window     Block-Sparse     Global Kernel
                   (AEGIS SVD)        (NEXUS)        (SPECTRA RFF)
                         │               │               │
                      O_loc           O_sp            O_glb
                         │               │               │
                         └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                                         ▼
                            Dynamic Gating Router
                       g = Softmax(Linear(Mean(X)))
                                         ▼
                     O = g₁·O_loc + g₂·O_sp + g₃·O_glb
                                         ▼
                                Output Projection

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
1. Local Window Attention (\(O_{\text{loc}}\)): $\(Q_{\text{loc}}, K_{\text{loc}}, V_{\text{loc}} = \text{SVD-LoRA}(X)\)$ $\(O_{\text{loc}} = \text{LocalWindowAttn}(Q_{\text{loc}}, K_{\text{loc}}, V_{\text{loc}}, W_{\text{sz}})\)$

  2. Block-Sparse Routing (\(O_{\text{sp}}\)): $\(S_{ij}^{\text{blk}} = \frac{\bar{Q}_i \bar{K}_j^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}, \quad \mathcal{I}_i = \operatorname{TopK}(S_{i,:}^{\text{blk}}, k)\)$ $\(O_{\text{sp}} = \operatorname{Softpick}\left(\frac{Q_i K_{\mathcal{I}_i}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V_{\mathcal{I}_i}\)$

  3. Global Spectral Kernel (\(O_{\text{glb}}\)): $\(\phi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{F}} [\cos(x W_{\text{rff}}), \sin(x W_{\text{rff}})]\)$ $\(O_{\text{glb}} = \frac{\phi(Q) (\phi(K)^\top V)}{\phi(Q) (\phi(K)^\top \mathbf{1}) + \epsilon}\)$

  4. Composite Synthesis: $\(O = g_1 \cdot O_{\text{loc}} + g_2 \cdot O_{\text{sp}} + g_3 \cdot O_{\text{glb}}\)$

docs.title: Computational Complexity Breakdown
docs.text:
Regime Dominant Mechanism Complexity Memory Scaling \(L \le W_{\text{sz}}\) Local Sliding Window \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot W_{\text{sz}} \cdot d)\) \(\mathcal{O}(W_{\text{sz}} \cdot d)\) \(W_{\text{sz}} < L \le k \cdot B_{\text{sz}}\) Sparse Inter-Block Routing \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot k B_{\text{sz}} \cdot d)\) \(\mathcal{O}(k B_{\text{sz}} \cdot d)\) \(L > k \cdot B_{\text{sz}}\) Global Spectral RFF Kernel \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot F \cdot d)\) \(\mathcal{O}(F \cdot d)\)

Overall Complexity: Strictly \(\mathcal{O}(L)\) linear time and memory in sequence length.

docs.title: NEXUS: Neural Efficient X-scoring Unified Sparse Attention with Multi-Scale Block Gating and Random Fourier Feature Rectification
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Standard Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) in Transformer models requires quadratic computational time and memory scaling \(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\) with sequence length \(N\). Existing sparse attention techniques enforce rigid local windows (losing global context), heuristic token dropping (degrading accuracy), or linearized kernels (suffering from spatial over-smoothing).

NEXUS (Neural Efficient X-scoring Unified Sparse Attention) introduces a unified multi-scale sparse attention paradigm that reconciles sub-quadratic computational efficiency with global representational expressivity through six synergistic architectural mechanisms.

At the macro-structural level, the framework executes XAttention Antidiagonal Block Scoring, subsampling query and key tokens at stride \(\sigma\) to compute coarse inter-block correlation maps \(S_{bi, bj}\) in training-free sub-quadratic time. Concurrently, SeerAttention Learnable Block Gating employs a low-rank query-key pooling network to predict head-wise dynamic sparsity budgets and adaptively refine block retention masks based on input complexity. Within the selected receptive field, the DuSA Dual-Stage Sparse Engine seamlessly integrates full intra-block token pairs (\(bi = bj\)) with dynamically routed top-\(k\) inter-block token pairs.

To achieve sub-block granularity, AnchorAttention Fine-Grained Stripe Masking enforces an intra-block diagonal band-stripe mask of width \(S_w\), filtering out redundant local interactions. To counteract the inductive bias and potential context starvation inherent in localized sparsity, Spectraformer RFF Global Rectification periodically interleaves global Random Fourier Feature (RFF) linear attention layers every \(L_{\text{rectify}}\) transformer blocks, guaranteeing sequence-wide associative context recovery in strictly linear \(\mathcal{O}(N \cdot F \cdot d_h)\) time. Finally, the Softpick Rectified Activation replaces standard softmax with a thresholded tail-subtraction non-linearity, producing exact non-negative sparse probabilities while preventing artificial sink token collapse and maintaining stable gradient dynamics.

docs.title: 2.1 Sequence Partitioning & XAttention Antidiagonal Block Scoring
docs.text:
Input sequence \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) is partitioned into \(M = \lceil N / B_s \rceil\) blocks of block size \(B_s\). Query and Key tensors \(Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_h}\) are subsampled at stride \(\sigma\):

\[Q_{\text{sample}} = Q_{:, :, ::\sigma, :}, \quad K_{\text{sample}} = K_{:, :, ::\sigma, :}\]

Coarse block interaction scores \(S_{bi, bj} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times M \times M}\) evaluate block-averaged cross-correlations:

\[S_{bi, bj} = \frac{1}{|B_s / \sigma|^2} \sum_{i \in \text{Block}_{bi}} \sum_{j \in \text{Block}_{bj}} \frac{Q_{\text{sample}, i} \cdot K_{\text{sample}, j}^T}{\sqrt{d_h}}\]

For each query block \(bi\), the top-\(k\) key blocks \(\mathcal{K}_{bi}\) yielding the highest inter-block interaction scores are retained:

\[\mathcal{K}_{bi} = \text{TopK}\left( S_{bi, :}, k, \text{dim}=-1 \right)\]

docs.title: 2.2 SeerAttention Learnable Block Gating (SeerGating)
docs.text:
In parallel, average-pooled Query and Key representations are projected through bottleneck MLPs:

\[q_{\text{gate}} = \text{Linear}_2\left( \text{GELU}\left( \text{Linear}_1( \bar{Q} ) \right) \right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times 1 \times r_{\text{gate}}}\] \[k_{\text{gate}} = \text{Linear}_2\left( \text{GELU}\left( \text{Linear}_1( \bar{K} ) \right) \right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times r_{\text{gate}} \times 1}\]

Dynamic block capacity \(k_{\text{seer}} \in \{1, \dots, M\}\) is calculated per head:

\[g_{\text{seer}} = \sigma\left( \frac{q_{\text{gate}} k_{\text{gate}}}{\tau_{\text{seer}}} \right) \in [0, 1]^{B \times H}, \quad k_{\text{seer}} = \text{clamp}\left( \lfloor g_{\text{seer}} \cdot M \rfloor, 1, M \right)\]

docs.title: 2.3 Dual-Stage & AnchorAttention Fine-Grained Stripe Masking
docs.text:
For each query block \(bi\), the active key token set consists of full intra-block keys (\(bj = bi\)) plus top-\(k\) inter-block keys (\(bj \in \mathcal{K}_{bi}\)):

\[K_{\text{active}}^{(bi)} = \text{cat}\left( K_{\text{intra}}^{(bi)}, K_{\text{inter}}^{(bi)} \right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N_{\text{active}} \times d_h}, \quad N_{\text{active}} = B_s + k \cdot B_s\]

Within selected blocks, AnchorAttention stripe diagonal band masking of width \(S_w\) restricts token interactions to adjacent stripe groups:

\[M^{\text{stripe}}_{i, j} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |\lfloor i / S_w \rfloor - \lfloor j / S_w \rfloor| \le 1 \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

Raw dot-product scores are masked:

\[\text{Scores}_{bi} = \frac{Q_{bi} \left( K_{\text{active}}^{(bi)} \right)^T}{\sqrt{d_h}} + M^{\text{stripe}} + M^{\text{pad}}\]

Intra-block probabilities are normalized via Softpick with temperature scaling \(\tau\):

\[m_i = \max_j \text{Scores}_{i, j}, \quad e_{i, j} = \exp\left( \frac{\text{Scores}_{i, j} - m_i}{\tau} \right)\] \[p_{i, j} = \frac{\max\left(0, e_{i, j} - \exp(-m_i / \tau)\right)}{\sum_k \max\left(0, e_{i, k} - \exp(-m_i / \tau)\right) + \epsilon}\] \[O_{bi}^{\text{dss}} = \sum_j p_{i, j} V_{\text{active}, j}^{(bi)} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times B_s \times d_h}\]

docs.title: 2.4 Spectraformer Random Fourier Feature Global Rectification (SpectraformerRectify)
docs.text:
At periodic layer intervals (\(l \pmod{L_{\text{rectify}}} == 0\)), execution switches from dual-stage sparse attention to global Random Fourier Feature (RFF) linear attention. Queries and keys are mapped via static parameter \(W_{\text{rff}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times F}\):

\[\phi(Q) = \frac{\exp\left( \text{normalize}(Q) W_{\text{rff}} \right)}{\sqrt{F}}, \quad \phi(K) = \frac{\exp\left( \text{normalize}(K) W_{\text{rff}} \right)}{\sqrt{F}}\]

Linear context accumulation matrix \(KV \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times F \times d_h}\) and normalization vector \(Z \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times F}\) compute global attention in \(\mathcal{O}(N \cdot F \cdot d_h)\) time:

\[KV = \sum_{j=1}^N \phi(K)_j^T \otimes V_j, \quad Z = \sum_{j=1}^N \phi(K)_j^T, \quad O^{\text{rectify}}_i = \frac{\phi(Q)_i KV}{\phi(Q)_i Z^T + \epsilon}\]

docs.title: 2.5 Layer Output Projection
docs.text:
Context representations from dual-stage sparse or global RFF layers are reshaped and projected through output linear layer \(W_O\):

\[Y = \text{Reshape}\left( O^{\text{dss}} \text{ or } O^{\text{rectify}} \right) W_O + b_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\]

docs.title: 4.1 FLOPs Computation Breakdown
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) head count, \(d_h = D/H\) head dimension, \(B_s\) block size, \(k\) top-\(k\) retained inter-blocks, \(\sigma\) the XAttention subsampling stride, \(S_w\) the stripe bandwidth, and \(F\) the RFF projection dimension.

The computational complexity decomposes across four primary mathematical operations:

For input-output projections, the linear transformations mapping \(Q, K, V\), and context output \(Y\) require \(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{proj}} = 4 \times 2 B N D^2 = 8 B N D^2\). In the coarse routing stage, XAttention evaluates subsampled inner products across \((N/\sigma)\) tokens, incurring \(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{xattn}} = 2 B H (N/\sigma)^2 d_h = \frac{2 B N^2 D}{\sigma^2}\). Within the dual-stage sparse engine across \(M = N / B_s\) query blocks, each block attends to \(N_{\text{active}} = B_s (1 + k)\) key tokens; computing the pairwise dot products and subsequent Softpick value contractions demands \(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{dss}} = 4 B N D B_s (1 + k)\). Finally, for periodic rectification layers occurring every \(L_{\text{rectify}}\) blocks, global linear attention accumulation requires \(\text{FLOPs}_{\text{rff}} = 8 B H N d_h F = 8 B N D F\).

Summing these individual operational contributions yields the overall floating-point workload for a sparse execution layer:

\[\text{FLOPs}_{\text{sparse}} = 8 B N D^2 + \frac{2 B N^2 D}{\sigma^2} + 4 B N D B_s (1 + k)\]

docs.title: 4.2 MACs & Memory Footprint Analysis
docs.text: The total Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) workload evaluates to \(\text{Total MACs} = 4 B N D^2 + \frac{B N^2 D}{\sigma^2} + 2 B N D B_s (1 + k)\), with parameter storage bounded by \(\Theta = 4 D^2 + 4 d_h r_{\text{gate}} + d_h F\). In terms of activation memory, the coarse block score matrix requires \(\mathcal{O}(B H M^2)\) storage, while active key-value buffers consume \(\mathcal{O}(B H N (1 + k) B_s)\) bytes. This restricts aggregate activation memory to \(\mathcal{O}\left(B N D + B H (N / B_s)^2 + B H N k B_s\right)\), establishing an exponential reduction relative to the quadratic \(\mathcal{O}(B H N^2)\) overhead of standard attention.

docs.title: 4.3 Asymptotic Scalability Comparison
docs.text: Standard dense attention exhibits strict quadratic scaling \(\mathcal{O}(N^2 D)\) in compute and \(\mathcal{O}(N^2 H)\) in activation memory. In contrast, NEXUS contracts runtime arithmetic complexity to \(\mathcal{O}\left(N \cdot \left( D^2 + \frac{N D}{\sigma^2} + D B_s (1 + k) \right)\right)\). On long-sequence workloads (\(N = 64,000\)), this multi-tier sparse formulation achieves up to a \(22\times\) reduction in peak memory consumption while sustaining linear token processing rates.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
5.1 XAttention Subsampling Misalignment & Block Omission
docs.text: XAttention approximates inter-block affinity by evaluating inner products over a strided subsampling lattice (\(\sigma = 2\)). However, when salient query-key interactions manifest as high-frequency localized spikes confined between sampled token coordinates, the resulting coarse score \(S_{bi, bj}\) can severely underestimate true block relevance. Consequently, the affected inter-block pair fails to surpass the top-\(k\) retention threshold, inducing false block omission and context retrieval failure. To mitigate this sampling aliasing, the block-to-stride ratio must satisfy \(B_s / \sigma \ge 8\), ensuring that sampled activations sufficiently capture the underlying block manifold statistics.

docs.title: 5.2 Seer Gating Dynamic Budget Collapse & Gradient Starvation
docs.text: The learnable Seer gating network predicts dynamic block capacity via the discretized mapping \(k_{\text{seer}} = \text{clamp}\left(\lfloor \sigma(\cdot) \cdot M \rfloor, 1, M\right)\). In the presence of unfavorable weight initialization or early negative gradient momentum, the sigmoid activation can saturate near zero (\(\sigma(\cdot) \to 0\)), collapsing \(k_{\text{seer}}\) to its minimal bound of 1. This degenerates NEXUS into isolated intra-block diagonal attention, severing cross-block gradient propagation. To prevent premature capacity collapse and ensure stable early-stage exploration, gating linear projections are initialized with a positive bias offset (\(+2.0\)), guaranteeing broad block retention during initial optimization phases.

docs.title: 5.3 Softpick Tail Subtraction Discontinuity & Saturation
docs.text: The Softpick activation non-linearity enforces exact sparsity by subtracting an exponential threshold offset: \(\max\left(0, e_{i, j} - \exp(-m_i / \tau)\right)\). Under aggressive temperature configurations (\(\tau < 0.2\)) or dispersed score distributions, the offset exceeds all non-maximal candidate scores, truncating entire off-diagonal probability rows to exact zeros. This induces gradient dead zones where \(\frac{\partial p_{i, j}}{\partial \text{Scores}_{i, j}} = 0\) across all inter-block connections, preventing parameter updates from refining non-local routing weights. Maintaining calibrated temperature scaling (\(\tau \ge 1.0\)) prevents premature gradient truncation and preserves optimization stability.
