docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D/H\), and \(r\) sequence SVD rank.

  1. Linear Projections: \(Q, K, V, O\): \(8 B N D^2\) FLOPs (\(4 B N D^2\) MACs).

  2. Randomized QR Basis Extraction: Random projection \(Y = X \Omega\): \(2 B N D r\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Householder QR decomposition: \(2 B N r^2\) FLOPs.

  3. Sequence Subspace Compression: \(K_{\text{proj}} = U_r^\top K\): \(2 B H (r N d_k) = 2 B N r D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, \(V_{\text{proj}} = U_r^\top V\): \(2 B N r D\) FLOPs.

  4. Compressed Attention Core: \(Q K_{\text{proj}}^\top\) MatMul: \(2 B H N r d_k = 2 B N r D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Softmax & Dropout: \(7 B H N r\) FLOPs. Concurrently, \(A V_{\text{proj}}\) MatMul: \(2 B H N r d_k = 2 B N r D\) FLOPs.

  5. Total Workload Summary: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(4 B N D^2 + 4 B N r D + B N D r + B N r^2\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(8 B N D^2 + 8 B N r D + 2 B N D r + 2 B N r^2 + 7 B H N r\) Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Linear Scaling in Sequence Length}, as \(N \to \infty\), core attention scaling is \(\mathcal{O}(N \cdot r)\) rather than \(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\).

docs.title: Memory Footprint & Activation Reduction
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Standard MHA Attention Matrix Memory}, \(B \cdot H \cdot N^2 \cdot b\) bytes. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{SVD Attention Matrix Memory}, \(B \cdot H \cdot N \cdot r \cdot b\) bytes.

For \(N = 16,384, r = 64\): Standard MHA: \(16384^2 = 268,435,456\) elements per head. Furthermore, SVD Attention: \(16384 \times 64 = 1,048,576\) elements per head (256\(\times\) reduction in intermediate score memory).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Subspace Truncation Loss in High-Variance Sequences
docs.text: If sequence length \(N\) is long and contains high-entropy diverse topics, restricting \(U_r\) to rank \(r = 64\) can discard fine-grained local dependencies, degrading retrieval performance on needle-in-a-haystack tasks.

docs.title: CPU Fallback Overhead in Randomized QR
docs.text: When single-precision GPU QR decomposition fails due to numerical underflow on padded rows, fallback to double-precision CPU execution (h_b_cpu.double()) causes GPU-CPU synchronization latency spikes.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for SVD Sequence Attention computes randomized projection \(Y = X \Omega\), Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization, and sequence key-value compression in SRAM registers.

                    Global Memory (HBM)
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Q, K, V: [B, H, N, d_k], X: [B, N, D]                       │
   │ Random Projection Matrix: Omega [D, r]                      │
   └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Direct Stream Load
                                  ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Compute Range Projection: Y_tile = X_tile @ Omega           │
 │ 2. In-Register Gram-Schmidt: U_r_tile = Orthonormalize(Y_tile) │
 │ 3. Down-Project Key/Value: K_proj = U_r_tile.T @ K_tile        │
 │ 4. Compute Compressed Score: S_ij = Q_tile @ K_proj.T          │
 │ 5. Online Softmax & Accumulate V_proj Tile                     │
 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Context Output

docs.title: SVD-Compressed Attention: Importance-Aware Lagrangian Rank Allocation Architecture
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
SVD-Compressed Attention (SVDCompressedAttention in svd_compressed.py) introduces a global parameter optimization framework that compresses Transformer attention layers using Truncated Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) guided by Lagrangian spectral-entropy budget allocation. Standard model compression approaches apply static, uniform truncation ranks across all layers, ignoring the reality that different layers and projection matrices (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\)) display vastly different singular value decay profiles and information capacities.

SVDCompressedAttention solves this mismatch by formulating rank selection as a constrained global optimization problem. Given a target global parameter budget \(B_{\text{target}}\) (e.g. 20% of original parameters), a Lagrangian multiplier optimization process evaluates cumulative spectral energy loss \(E_i(r) = \sum_{j=1}^r \sigma_{i, j}^2 / \sum \sigma_{i, j}^2\) across all \(M\) attention projection matrices in the network. The framework allocates optimal individual ranks \(\{r_i\}_{i=1}^M\) to each matrix. Additionally, an optional low-rank plus sparse residual decomposition (\(W \approx A B + S\)) captures high-magnitude outlier weights for maximum zero-shot fidelity.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(\{W_i\}_{i=1}^M\) denote the set of all linear projection matrices across \(L\) transformer attention layers, where \(W_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{i, \text{out}} \times d_{i, \text{in}}}\).

docs.title: Spectral Information Loss & Parameter Cost Modeling:
docs.text:
For matrix \(W_i\), Singular Value Decomposition yields singular values \(\sigma_{i, 1} \ge \sigma_{i, 2} \ge \dots \ge \sigma_{i, \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})} \ge 0\). The retained spectral energy fraction \(E_i(r)\) for rank \(r\) is:

\[ E_i(r) = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^r \sigma_{i, j}^2}{\sum_{j=1}^{\min(d_{i, \text{in}}, d_{i, \text{out}})} \sigma_{i, j}^2} \in (0, 1] \]

The spectral information loss cost function \(\text{Cost}_i(r)\) and parameter count function \(\text{Params}_i(r)\) are defined as:

[ \text{Cost}i(r) = 1.0 - E_i(r) ] [ \text{Params}i(r) = r \cdot (d{i, \text{in}} + d{i, \text{out}}) ]

docs.title: Global Lagrangian Rank Allocation Optimization:
docs.text:
Given global parameter budget target \(B_{\text{target}}\), the optimal rank allocation \(\{r_i^*\}_{i=1}^M\) solves the constrained minimization problem:

\[ \min_{\{r_i\}} \sum_{i=1}^M \text{Cost}_i(r_i) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{i=1}^M \text{Params}_i(r_i) \le B_{\text{target}} \]

Formulating unconstrained Lagrangian objective with multiplier \(\lambda > 0\):

\[ \mathcal{L}(\{r_i\}, \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^M \left[ \text{Cost}_i(r_i) + \lambda \cdot \text{Params}_i(r_i) \right] \]

Binary search over \(\lambda \in [\lambda_{\text{min}}, \lambda_{\text{max}}]\) determines the optimal per-projection ranks:

\[ r_i^*(\lambda) = \arg\min_{r \in [1, r_{\max}]} \left[ (1 - E_i(r)) + \lambda \cdot r (d_{i, \text{in}} + d_{i, \text{out}}) \right] \]

docs.title: Low-Rank Plus Sparse Residual Factorization (_create_pruned_residual):
docs.text:
Each projection matrix \(W_i\) is decomposed into low-rank factor matrices \(W_i^{\text{down}} \in \mathbb{R}^{r_i \times d_{\text{in}}}\) and \(W_i^{\text{up}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r_i}\), plus an optional sparse residual matrix \(S_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\):

\[ W_i \approx W_i^{\text{up}} W_i^{\text{down}} + S_i \]

Where sparse residual entries are thresholded at percentile \(\rho\) (sparsity level):

\[ S_{i, j, k} = \begin{cases} (W_i - W_i^{\text{up}} W_i^{\text{down}})_{j, k} & \text{if } |(W_i - W_i^{\text{up}} W_i^{\text{down}})_{j, k}| \ge \tau_{\rho} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

Forward pass transformation for input activation \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{in}}}\):

\[ Y = X (W_i^{\text{down}})^\top (W_i^{\text{up}})^\top + b_i + X S_i^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{out}}} \]

docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D/H\), \(\{r_q, r_k, r_v, r_o\}\) Lagrangian-assigned ranks, and \(\rho\) sparse residual density.

  2. Core Scaled Dot-Product Attention: \(Q K^\top\) & \(A V\): \(4 B N^2 D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Softmax & Masking: \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs.

  3. Total Workload Summary: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(2 B N D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o) + 2 B N D^2 (1 - \rho) + 2 B N^2 D\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(4 B N D (r_q + r_k + r_v + r_o) + 4 B N D^2 (1 - \rho) + 4 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2\)

docs.title: Parameter Budget Compression Verification
docs.text: For DistilBERT (\(L = 6\) layers, \(D = 768\), 24 attention projection matrices, original total parameters \(24 \times 768^2 = 14.15 \text{ million}\)): Target budget ratio \(\text{budget\_ratio} = 0.20\) (\(B_{\text{target}} \approx 2.83 \text{ million parameters}\)). Furthermore, Lagrangian optimization allocates high rank (\(r \approx 48\)) to critical query/key matrices in layers 0 and 1, and low rank (\(r \approx 16\)) to value/output matrices in layers 4 and 5. Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Exact Budget Enforced}, total parameters \(\le 2,831,155\) (\(80\%\) parameter reduction overall).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Binary Search Lambda Convergence Failure
docs.text: If target_budget is set below \(M \times (d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\) (i.e. below rank 1 per matrix), binary search fails to converge within bracket limits. The framework catches this case and safely falls back to \(r_i = 1\) across all projections.

docs.title: Sparse Residual Memory Overhead
docs.text: While low-rank projections \(A, B\) reduce parameter counts, adding un-structured sparse residual matrices \(S\) of size \([D, D]\) retains full parameter memory allocation unless stored in CUDA CSR sparse formats.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for Lagrangian SVD-Compressed Attention streams layer-specific rank buffers \(r_i\) into shared memory SRAM scratchpads.

                                  ▼

 │ 1. Load Activation Tile X_i [BLOCK_M, D]                       │
 │ 2. Compute Low-Rank Tile: Z_i = (X_i @ W_down.T) @ W_up.T     │
 │ 3. Accumulate Sparse Residual Tile: Z_i += X_i @ S_i.T         │
 │ 4. Execute Online Scaled Attention                             │
 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Context Output
                                  ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Context Output: Y [B, N, D]                                 │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.text:
1. Second-Order Hessian-Weighted Lagrangian Optimization: Weight spectral entropy loss \(E_i(r)\) by Fisher Information or Hessian curvature \(\mathbf{H}_i\) to prioritize ranks for high-gradient projections.
  2. End-to-End Joint Rank Fine-Tuning: Make ranks \(r_i\) continuous learnable parameters using Gumbel-Softmax rank gating masks.
  3. Quantized SVD + Block-Sparse Execution (Q-SVD-Sparse): Quantize low-rank matrices to INT4 and store sparse residuals in block-compressed FP8 formats for deployment on edge accelerators.

docs.title: SVD Linear: Low-Rank Factorized Linear Layer Replacement
docs.text: Family: SVD Spectral & Low-Rank Decomposed Attentions · NeuralOps Registry ID: svd_linear

docs.title: Executive Abstract
docs.text:
Core low-rank linear decomposition module in NeuralOps. Replaces dense \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times d_{in}}\) with two sequential projection layers with inner rank \(r\). Provides seamless backward pass, weight fusion, and optional activation scaling.

In NeuralOps, svd_linear is integrated into the universal attention dispatch table, featuring full support for the 3-level fallback hierarchy, automatic shape validation, and end-to-end autograd backwards passes.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
The core operator computation is defined as:

\[ W \approx U \Sigma V^T = A B, \quad A = U \sqrt{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times r}, \; B = \sqrt{\Sigma} V^T \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{in}} \]

During execution, inputs \(Q, K, V\) are projected to dimension \(d\). In the causal configuration, lower-triangular masking ensures that tokens only attend to past and current time-steps, preserving autoregressive invariants.

docs.title: SVD Linear Attention: Semi-Orthogonal Low-Rank Projection Factorization
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
SVD Linear Attention (SVDLinearAttention) introduces a zero-shot model compression framework for Multi-Head Attention by replacing standard dense linear projection layers (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\)) with low-rank factorized modules (SVDLinear). Standard dense projections consume \(4 D^2\) parameter storage per layer, creating significant memory bandwidth constraints during inference.

SVDLinearAttention factorizes each projection matrix into two lower-rank matrices \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}\) and \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}\), where \(r \ll D\) is a configurable bottleneck rank. The parameters are initialized zero-shot from pre-trained model checkpoints via truncated Singular Value Decomposition (\(W \approx U \Sigma V^\top\)). Semi-orthogonal initialization (reset_parameters) maintains gradient stability and representation capacity during fine-tuning while reducing projection parameter counts and FLOPs.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote input activations. Let \(H\) be the number of query heads, \(d_k = D / H\) head dimension, and \(r\) the factor rank per projection layer.

docs.title: Low-Rank Matrix Factorization & Semi-Orthogonal Initialization (SVDLinear):
docs.text:
A dense parameter matrix \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) with bias \(b \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}\) is factorized via truncated SVD:

\[ W = U_{\text{full}} \Sigma_{\text{full}} V_{\text{full}}^\top \implies U = U_{\text{full}}[:, :r] \cdot \text{diag}(\Sigma_{\text{full}}[:r]) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}, \quad V = V_{\text{full}}[:r, :]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}} \]

The forward pass computes down-projection followed by up-projection:

\[ Z = X V^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times r}, \quad Y = Z U^\top + b = X (U V)^\top + b \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{out}}} \]

docs.title: SVD-Factorized Multi-Head Projections:
docs.text:
Query, Key, Value, and Output linear transformations execute via factorized modules:

[ Q = \text{SVDLinear}_Q(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot d_k)} \implies Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ K = \text{SVDLinear}_K(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot d_k)} \implies K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ V = \text{SVDLinear}_V(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot d_k)} \implies V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ]

docs.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention & Output Projection:
docs.text:
Affinity score calculation and value aggregation proceed as:

[ S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} \sum_{m=1}^{d_k} Q_{b, h, i, m} \cdot K_{b, h, j, m} ] [ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (\text{apply_attention_mask}(S, M){b, h, i, j}) ] [ C_{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^N \text{Dropout}(A){b, h, i, j} \cdot V{b, h, j, m} \implies C \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ] [ Y = \text{SVDLinear}_O(C) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ]

docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D/H\), and \(r\) factor rank.

  1. SVD Linear Projections: Down-projections (\(X V^\top\)): \(4 \times (2 B N D r) = 8 B N D r\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Up-projections (\(Z U^\top\)): \(4 \times (2 B N r D) = 8 B N D r\) FLOPs. Concurrently, Total Projection Workload: \(16 B N D r\) FLOPs (\(8 B N D r\) MACs).

  2. Core Scaled Attention: \(Q K^\top\) & \(A V\): \(4 B N^2 D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Softmax & Masking: \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs.

  3. Total Workload Summary: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(8 B N D r + 2 B N^2 D\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(16 B N D r + 4 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2\)

docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Dense MHA Projection Parameters}, \(4 D^2 + 4 D\) floats. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{SVD Linear MHA Parameter Count},

[ \text{Params}_{\text{SVDLinear}} = 4 \cdot r(D + D) + 4 D = 8 D r + 4 D \text{ floats} ] For \(D = 4096, r = 64\): Dense MHA: \(4 \times 4096^2 \approx 67.1 \text{ million parameters}\). Furthermore, SVD Linear MHA: \(8 \times 4096 \times 64 \approx 2.09 \text{ million parameters}\) (\(96.8\%\) parameter compression).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Rank Deficiency in Deep Transformer Layers
docs.text: In deep layers where singular value spectra decay slowly, low rank \(r \le 16\) can truncate critical feature directions, leading to perplexity degradation unless fine-tuned with small learning rates.

docs.title: Semi-Orthogonal Gradient Drift
docs.text: During long fine-tuning runs, unconstrained backpropagation can cause matrices \(U\) and \(V\) to lose their initial semi-orthogonality. Periodic orthogonal re-projection or Gram-Schmidt regularization preserves gradient flow.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for SVD Linear Attention computes the low-rank product \(V^\top U^\top\) directly inside register tiles, bypassing intermediate memory writes.

                    Global Memory (HBM)
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Input: X [B, N, D]                                          │
   │ Low-Rank Buffers: V [r, D], U [D, r], bias [D]               │
   └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Vectorized Memory Streaming
                                  ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Load Activation Tile X_i [BLOCK_M, D]                       │
 │ 2. Compute Intermediate Tile: Vx_i = X_i @ V.T [BLOCK_M, r]   │
 │ 3. Reconstruct Head Projection: Out_i = Vx_i @ U.T + bias      │
 │ 4. Execute Online Scaled Attention                             │
 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Output
                                  ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

docs.title: SVD-LLM V2 Attention: Truncation-Aware Explicit Factor Buffer Architecture
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
SVD-LLM V2 (SVDLLMV2Attention) provides a truncation-aware SVD compression framework designed for Large Language Models (LLMs). Traditional post-training quantization and pruning methods often degrade generative accuracy when applied to LLMs due to outlier activation dimensions. Truncated SVD parameterization preserves global matrix energy while reducing parameter memory footprint.

SVD-LLM V2 parameterizes projection operators (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\)) using explicit, trainable factor buffers: left-singular vectors \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}\), singular values \(S \in \mathbb{R}^r\), and right-singular vectors \(V^H \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}\). Initialized zero-shot from pre-trained model weights via energy-based spectral thresholding (\(E \ge 95\%\)), the module includes an automatic padding mechanism (_pad_factors) to ensure consistent tensor shapes across variable-rank layers.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote input activations. Let \(H\) be the number of attention heads, \(d_k = D / H\) head dimension, \(r\) target compression rank, and \(\tau \in (0, 1]\) singular value energy threshold.

docs.title: Explicit \(U, \Sigma, V^H\) Factorization & Weight Matrix Synthesis:
docs.text:
For each projection matrix \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\), full SVD is performed during initialization:

\[ W = U_{\text{full}} \text{diag}(S_{\text{full}}) V_{\text{full}}^\top \]

Truncated to rank \(r = \min(\text{user\_rank}, \text{energy\_rank})\):

\[ U = U_{\text{full}}[:, :r] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}, \quad S = S_{\text{full}}[:r] \in \mathbb{R}^r, \quad V^H = V_{\text{full}}[:r, :]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}} \]

When \(r < r_{\text{target}}\), _pad_factors appends small random Gaussian entries to maintain tensor shape consistency across layers:

\[ U \leftarrow [U \,\|\, \delta_U] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r_{\text{target}}}, \quad S \leftarrow [S \,\|\, \mathbf{1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{r_{\text{target}}}, \quad V^H \leftarrow [V^H \,\|\, \delta_V] \in \mathbb{R}^{r_{\text{target}} \times d_{\text{in}}} \]

Reconstructing the effective weight matrix during forward propagation:

\[ W_{\text{synth}} = (U \odot S) V^H = \sum_{k=1}^r S_k \cdot U_{:, k} (V^H)_{k, :} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}} \]

Forward linear transformation for input \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{in}}}\):

\[ Y = F.linear(X, W_{\text{synth}}) = X W_{\text{synth}}^\top = \left((X (V^H)^\top) \odot S\right) U^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{out}}} \]

docs.title: Scaled Dot-Product Multi-Head Attention:
docs.text:
Synthesized projection weights \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\) compute multi-head states:

[ Q = F.linear(X, W_Q).view(B, N, H, d_k).permute(0, 2, 1, 3) ] [ K = F.linear(X, W_K).view(B, N, H, d_k).permute(0, 2, 1, 3) ] [ V = F.linear(X, W_V).view(B, N, H, d_k).permute(0, 2, 1, 3) ]

Affinity matrix evaluation and context output projection proceed as:

[ S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} \sum_{m=1}^{d_k} Q_{b, h, i, m} \cdot K_{b, h, j, m} ] [ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (S{b, h, i, j} + M_{b, 1, i, j}) ] [ C_{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^N \text{Dropout}(A){b, h, i, j} \cdot V{b, h, j, m} \implies C \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ] [ Y = F.linear(C, W_O) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ]

docs.title: Tensor Shape Transformation Table
docs.text: Execution Stage Input Shape Transformation / Operation Output Shape Input [B, N, D] Input activation batch [B, N, D] Synthesize W_q U: [D, r], S: [r], VH: [r, D] (query_u * query_s) @ query_vh W_q: [D, D] Q Linear Projection [B, N, D] F.linear(hidden_states, W_q) [B, N, H*d_k] Multi-Head Permute [B, N, H*d_k] .view(B, N, H, d_k).permute(0, 2, 1, 3) [B, H, N, d_k] each Score Matrix MatMul Q, K torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / sqrt(d_k) [B, H, N, N] Mask & Softmax scores scores + attention_mask + F.softmax [B, H, N, N] Value Aggregation attn, V torch.matmul(attn, V) [B, H, N, d_k] Synthesize W_o U_o: [D, r], S_o: [r], VH_o: [r, D] (out_proj_u * out_proj_s) @ out_proj_vh W_o: [D, D] Out Linear Projection context: [B, N, D] F.linear(context, W_o) Output: [B, N, D]

docs.title: Computational Workload & Asymptotic Complexity
docs.text:
The computational workload of SVD-LLM V2 encompasses explicit factor synthesis alongside standard scaled dot-product attention operations. Parameterized by batch size \(B\), sequence length \(N\), hidden dimension \(D\), attention head count \(H\) (with per-head dimension \(d_k = D/H\)), and truncated compression rank \(r\):

During forward propagation, synthesizing the effective projection weight matrices \(W_{\text{synth}} = (U \odot S) V^H\) across the four attention projections (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\)) requires \(4 \times 2 D^2 r = 8 D^2 r\) FLOPs. Once synthesized, the dense linear transformations mapping input activations into multi-head query, key, value, and output representations consume \(8 B N D^2\) FLOPs (\(4 B N D^2\) MACs). Concurrently, evaluating the scaled dot-product affinity matrix \(Q K^\top\) and aggregating context values \(A V\) demands \(4 B N^2 D\) FLOPs, supplemented by \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs for causal masking and Softmax normalization.

Summing these individual operational stages yields the total computational budget: [ \text{Total FLOPs} = 8 B N D^2 + 8 D^2 r + 4 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2 ] which corresponds to \(4 B N D^2 + 4 D^2 r + 2 B N^2 D\) Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operations. When factors are fused ahead of time or executed via two-stage low-rank matrix multiplications, the \(8 D^2 r\) synthesis overhead is entirely avoided.

docs.title: Parameter Footprint & Memory Reduction
docs.text: The primary architectural advantage of SVD-LLM V2 lies in its aggressive parameter compression. While standard dense multi-head attention blocks demand \(4 D^2 + 4 D\) parameters, the factorized representation stores only the explicit singular triplets: [ \text{Params}_{\text{SVDLLMV2}} = 4 \cdot [D \cdot r + r + r \cdot D] = 4 \cdot r (2D + 1) \text{ floats} ] For a typical model dimension of \(D = 4096\) with compression rank \(r = 64\), dense attention requires approximately \(67.1\) million parameters, whereas SVD-LLM V2 requires merely \(2.10\) million parameters—achieving an extraordinary \(96.9\%\) reduction in projection weight memory while capturing the vast majority of spectral energy.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Runtime Matrix Materialization and Memory Bandwidth Overhead
docs.text: A substantial computational bottleneck arises when projection weights are synthesized dynamically on every forward pass via \(W_{\text{synth}} = (U \odot S) V^H\). In eager execution, allocating temporary memory for the dense \(D \times D\) reconstructed matrices incurs an auxiliary cost of \(8 D^2 r\) FLOPs per layer along with elevated GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) traffic. During auto-regressive token generation, repeatedly reconstructing identical weight matrices introduces redundant arithmetic overhead. To mitigate this latency penalty, production deployment requires either static pre-synthesis caching or fused factor decomposition that maps activations directly through \(X V^H \text{diag}(S) U^\top\) without materializing full weight matrices.

docs.title: Spectral Underflow, Gradient Vanishing, and Rank Collapse
docs.text: During fine-tuning or post-training adaptation, the explicit parameterization of singular values \(S \in \mathbb{R}^r\) exposes the model to severe optimization instability. If small singular values decay toward zero under gradient descent, the gradient updates flowing back into the corresponding left-singular columns \(U_{:, k}\) and right-singular rows \(V^H_{k, :}\) vanish proportionally, as \(\nabla_U \mathcal{L} \propto S_k\) and \(\nabla_V \mathcal{L} \propto S_k\). This induces an unrecoverable rank collapse where dead spectral channels become frozen in optimization saddle points. To preserve the effective dimensionality of the factorized subspace, the training objective must incorporate spectral lower bounds (\(S_k \ge \epsilon\)) or spectral entropy penalties to stabilize gradient dynamics across the loss landscape.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for SVD-LLM V2 bypasses full \(D \times D\) matrix synthesis by streaming factor buffers directly into SRAM register blocks.

                    Global Memory (HBM)
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Input: X [B, N, D]                                          │
   │ Factor Buffers: U [D, r], S [r], VH [r, D]                  │
   └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Direct SIMD Register Load
                                  ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Load Activation Tile X_i [BLOCK_M, D]                       │
 │ 2. Compute Down-Projection: Z_i = X_i @ VH.T                   │
 │ 3. Scale by Singular Values: Z_i = Z_i * S                    │
 │ 4. Up-Project Output: Y_i = Z_i @ U.T                           │
 │ 5. Execute Online Scaled Attention                             │
 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Output
                                  ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Output Tensor: Y [B, N, D]                                  │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Zero-Cost Static Weight Consolidation for Inference
docs.text: Prior to deployment in auto-regressive generation engines, the explicit factor buffers can be deterministically fused into static dense projection weights \(W = (U \odot S) V^H\). This pre-computation completely eliminates runtime synthesis FLOPs and intermediate activation buffers, allowing compressed checkpoints to execute with the standard high-throughput execution profile of native GEMM kernels while maintaining extreme storage efficiency during distribution.

docs.title: Spectral Entropy Loss for Optimal Energy Compaction
docs.text: To maximize representation density across the factorized rank budget, model fine-tuning can incorporate a spectral entropy regularization term \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{entropy}} = -\sum_{k=1}^r p_k \log p_k\), where \(p_k = S_k / \sum_{j} S_j\). This objective penalizes diffuse singular value spectra and drives the dominant matrix energy into the top principal components, facilitating dynamic post-training pruning to even lower ranks without performance degradation.

docs.title: Mixed-Precision Quantized Factor Parameterization
docs.text: A powerful architectural synergy combines low-rank spectral decomposition with extreme quantization. By quantizing the high-dimensional singular vector matrices \(U\) and \(V^H\) into ultra-low bitwidths (e.g., INT4 or FP4) while preserving full FP32 precision for the compact vector of singular values \(S \in \mathbb{R}^r\), the architecture achieves up to \(32\times\) parameter compression. The explicit singular value scaling acts as a natural channel-wise scale factor, counteracting quantization noise and stabilizing the representational capacity of the quantized manifold.

docs.title: SVD Projection Attention: Explicit Low-Rank Matrix Reconstruction Paradigm
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
SVD Projection Attention (SVDProjectionAttention) provides a zero-shot model compression framework for Multi-Head Attention by factorizing linear projection operators into explicit low-rank matrix pairs (\(U \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}, V \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}\)) via SVDProjectionLinear. Standard dense linear projections (\(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\)) require \(4 D^2\) parameter storage per layer.

SVDProjectionAttention initializes \(U\) and \(V\) zero-shot from pre-trained checkpoint matrices using truncated Singular Value Decomposition (\(W \approx U V\)). During forward propagation, the module reconstructs full-dimensional projection weights on-the-fly via matrix multiplication \(W = U V\) prior to linear transformation (F.linear(x, U @ V, bias)). This allows fine-tuning in compressed rank-\(r\) subspaces while preserving compatibility with standard multi-head attention score calculation.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote input activations. Let \(H\) be query heads, \(d_k = D / H\) head dimension, and \(r\) rank per projection.

docs.title: Low-Rank Subspace Factorization & Matrix Reconstruction (SVDProjectionLinear):
docs.text:
Pre-trained projection matrix \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) with bias \(b \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}\) undergoes full SVD:

\[ W = U_{\text{full}} \Sigma_{\text{full}} V_{\text{full}}^\top, \quad U_{\text{full}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{out}}}, \, \Sigma_{\text{full}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}, \, V_{\text{full}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{in}}} \]

Truncating to rank \(r \ll \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})\):

\[ U = U_{\text{full}}[:, :r] \cdot \text{diag}(\Sigma_{\text{full}}[:r]) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}, \quad V = V_{\text{full}}[:r, :]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}} \]

On-the-fly weight matrix reconstruction:

\[ W_{\text{recon}} = U V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}} \]

Forward pass transformation for input activation tensor \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{in}}}\):

\[ Y = F.linear(X, W_{\text{recon}}, b) = X (U V)^\top + b \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times d_{\text{out}}} \]

docs.title: Multi-Head Scaled Dot-Product Attention:
docs.text:
Projections for Query, Key, Value, and Output proceed using reconstructed low-rank operators:

[ Q = \text{SVDProjectionLinear}_Q(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ K = \text{SVDProjectionLinear}_K(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ V = \text{SVDProjectionLinear}_V(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ]

Scaled score matrix calculation and context aggregation:

[ S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} \sum_{m=1}^{d_k} Q_{b, h, i, m} \cdot K_{b, h, j, m} ] [ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (S{b, h, i, j} + M_{b, 1, i, j}) ] [ C_{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^N \text{Dropout}(A){b, h, i, j} \cdot V{b, h, j, m} \implies C \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ] [ Y = \text{SVDProjectionLinear}_O(C) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ]

docs.title: Tensor Shape Transformation Table
docs.text: Execution Stage Input Shape Transformation / Operation Output Shape Input [B, N, D] Input activation batch [B, N, D] Weight Reconstruction U: [D, r], V: [r, D] W_q = U_q @ V_q W_q: [D, D] Q Projection [B, N, D] F.linear(X, W_q, b_q) [B, N, H*d_k] Multi-Head Transpose [B, N, H*d_k] .view(B, N, H, d_k).transpose(1, 2) [B, H, N, d_k] each Score Matrix MatMul Q, K torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / sqrt(d_k) [B, H, N, N] Mask & Softmax scores scores + attention_mask + F.softmax [B, H, N, N] Value Aggregation attn, V torch.matmul(attn, V) [B, H, N, d_k] Out Weight Reconstruction U_o: [D, r], V_o: [r, D] W_o = U_o @ V_o W_o: [D, D] Out Projection context: [B, N, D] F.linear(context, W_o, b_o) Output: [B, N, D]

docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D/H\), and \(r\) rank.

  1. Reconstruction FLOPs (\(W = U V\)): \(4 \times (2 D r D) = 8 D^2 r\) FLOPs per forward pass (independent of batch size \(B\) or sequence length \(N\)).

  2. Linear Projections: \(Q, K, V, O\): \(8 B N D^2\) FLOPs (\(4 B N D^2\) MACs).

  3. Core Scaled Dot-Product Attention: \(Q K^\top\) & \(A V\): \(4 B N^2 D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Softmax & Masking: \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs.

  4. Total Workload Summary: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(4 B N D^2 + 4 D^2 r + 2 B N^2 D\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(8 B N D^2 + 8 D^2 r + 4 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2\)

docs.title: Parameter Footprint Comparison
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Uncompressed Dense MHA}, \(4 D^2 + 4 D\) floats. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{SVD Projection Parameter Count},

[ \text{Params}_{\text{SVDProj}} = 4 \cdot r (D + D) + 4 D = 8 D r + 4 D \text{ floats} ] For \(D = 4096, r = 32\): Uncompressed: \(4 \times 4096^2 \approx 67.1 \text{ million parameters}\). Furthermore, SVD Projection: \(8 \times 4096 \times 32 \approx 1.05 \text{ million parameters}\) (\(98.4\%\) parameter compression).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Reconstruction Overhead in Small Batch Inference
docs.text: Because \(W = U V\) requires \(8 D^2 r\) FLOPs per forward pass regardless of sequence length, executing single-token decoding (\(N = 1, B = 1\)) incurs extra matrix multiplication overhead unless weights are cached prior to inference loops.

docs.title: Numerical Stability in Kaiming Uniform Initialization
docs.text: When initializing from scratch without pretrained weights (reset_parameters), using Kaiming uniform scaling on both \(U\) and \(V\) can magnify product variance (\(\text{Var}(U V) \propto r\)). Proper variance scaling prevents exploding activations.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for SVD Projection Attention caches reconstructed weights \(W = U V\) directly in SRAM or bypasses explicit \(D \times D\) materialization by executing split GEMM tiles (\(X \to r \to D\)).

                    Global Memory (HBM)
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Input: X [B, N, D]                                          │
   │ Singular Vectors: U [D, r], V [r, D], bias [D]               │
   └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Vectorized Block Load
                                  ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Load Activation Tile X_i [BLOCK_M, D]                       │
 │ 2. Compute Fused Bottleneck: Z_i = X_i @ V.T [BLOCK_M, r]      │
 │ 3. Reconstruct Projection Output: Y_i = Z_i @ U.T + bias       │
 │ 4. Execute Online Scaled Attention                             │
 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Stream Context Output
                                  ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Context Output: Y [B, N, D]                                 │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
1. Pre-Computed Inference Weight Caching: Fuse \(U V \to W\) prior to model evaluation loops to eliminate runtime reconstruction FLOPs during generation.
  2. SVD Projection + LoRA Fine-Tuning: Freeze low-rank SVD factors \(U, V\) and attach dynamic LoRA adapters \(\Delta W = A_{\text{lora}} B_{\text{lora}}\) for parameter-efficient adaptation.
  3. Spectral Rank Pruning: Dynamically prune columns of \(U\) and rows of \(V\) whose singular values fall below threshold \(\epsilon\) during training.

docs.title: SVD Seq: Temporal-Dimension Sequential SVD Factorization
docs.text: Family: SVD Spectral & Low-Rank Decomposed Attentions · NeuralOps Registry ID: svd_seq

docs.title: Executive Abstract
docs.text:
Performs singular value decomposition across the sequence dimension for long context sequences, projecting token sequences into an optimal orthogonal temporal subspace before calculating attention scores.

In NeuralOps, svd_seq is integrated into the universal attention dispatch table, featuring full support for the 3-level fallback hierarchy, automatic shape validation, and end-to-end autograd backwards passes.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
The core operator computation is defined as:

\[ X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \implies X \approx (X U_r) \Sigma_r V_r^T \]

During execution, inputs \(Q, K, V\) are projected to dimension \(d\). In the causal configuration, lower-triangular masking ensures that tokens only attend to past and current time-steps, preserving autoregressive invariants.

docs.text:
Input Tokens (B, T, D)

     │         │

docs.title: Template Attention: Extensible Base Architecture with Global Latent Modulation
1. Abstract & Theoretical Motivation
docs.text:
Extensible Transformer attention frameworks require modular software primitives that decouple subspace projection, sequence routing, and global contextual modulation. Template Attention (YourCustomAttention) provides an extensible blueprint that inherits from BaseAttention and integrates with the registry system.

The module demonstrates standard Multi-Head Scaled Dot-Product Attention combined with an optional global low-rank modulation mechanism. By pooling input representations over sequence length \(N\) into a global state vector \(h_{\text{pool}} \in \mathbb{R}^D\) and projecting through a rank-\(r\) bottleneck, the architecture synthesizes a dynamic gating factor \(\gamma \in (0, 1)\) per batch item. This scalar modulates attention score magnitudes, serving as a clean reference implementation for custom spatial, structural, or parametric attention extensions.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Derivations & Formulations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote the input activation tensor, where \(B\) is batch size, \(N\) is sequence length, and \(D\) is model hidden dimension. Let \(H\) be the number of attention heads, \(d_k = D / H\) the head dimension, and \(r\) the rank of the optional bottleneck projection.

docs.title: Linear Subspace Projections:
docs.text:
Input activations are transformed into query, key, and value states:

\[ Q = X W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}, \quad K = X W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}, \quad V = X W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} \]

where \(W_Q, W_K, W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\). Weights are initialized using Xavier uniform initialization (\(\mathcal{U}\left(-\sqrt{\frac{6}{2D}}, \sqrt{\frac{6}{2D}}\right)\)) with zero biases. Reshaping yields \(Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k}\).

docs.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention:
docs.text:
The unnormalized similarity score tensor \(S \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times N}\) is computed as:

\[ S_{b, h, i, j} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} \sum_{m=1}^{d_k} Q_{b, h, i, m} \cdot K_{b, h, j, m} \]

docs.title: Optional Global Low-Rank Pooling Modulation:
docs.text:
When low-rank parameter \(r > 0\) is specified, a global representation vector \(h_{\text{pool}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times D}\) is computed via mean-pooling across sequence length \(N\):

\[ h_{\text{pool}, b, d} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_{b, i, d} \]

The pooled vector is projected through bottleneck matrix \(W_{\text{rank}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times r}\):

\[ z_b = h_{\text{pool}, b, :} \cdot W_{\text{rank}} \in \mathbb{R}^r \]

A scalar modulation factor \(\gamma_b \in (0, 1)\) is derived by averaging Sigmoid activations over rank \(r\):

\[ \gamma_b = \frac{1}{r} \sum_{j=1}^r \sigma\left( z_{b, j} \right) \in (0, 1) \]

The modulation scalar scales score matrices elementwise:

\[ \widetilde{S}_{b, h, i, j} = S_{b, h, i, j} \cdot \gamma_b \]

docs.title: Masking, Softmax & Output Projection:
docs.text:
Incorporating additive mask \(M \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 1 \times N \times N}\):

[ \widehat{S}{b, h, i, j} = \widetilde{S}{b, h, i, j} + M_{b, 1, i, j} ] [ A_{b, h, i, j} = \text{Softmax}j (\widehat{S}{b, h, i, j}) = \frac{\exp(\widehat{S}{b, h, i, j})}{\sum{l=1}^N \exp(\widehat{S}_{b, h, i, l})} ]

Applying dropout \(p_{\text{drop}}\) and head mask \(H_{\text{mask}}\):

[ \overline{A} = \text{Dropout}(A, p_{\text{drop}}) \odot H_{\text{mask}} ] [ O_{b, h, i, m} = \sum_{j=1}^N \overline{A}{b, h, i, j} \cdot V{b, h, j, m} \implies O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k} ] [ Y = \text{Concat}(O_1, \dots, O_H) \cdot W_O + b_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}, \quad W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D} ]

docs.title: 3. Tensor Execution Flow & Dimensional Shape Tracing
docs.text:
Input: hidden_states [B, N, D]
  │
  ├──> Linear(D, D) [query]   ──> Q: [B, N, D] ──> view & permute ──> Q: [B, H, N, d_k]
  ├──> Linear(D, D) [key]     ──> K: [B, N, D] ──> view & permute ──> K: [B, H, N, d_k]
  └──> Linear(D, D) [value]   ──> V: [B, N, D] ──> view & permute ──> V: [B, H, N, d_k]
                                │
                                ├──> MatMul: Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(d_k) ──> scores: [B, H, N, N]
                                │
                                ├──> IF rank_proj IS NOT NONE:
                                │      mean(dim=1) ──> H_pool: [B, D]
                                │      Linear(D, r) ──> H_rank: [B, r]
                                │      Sigmoid & mean(dim=-1) ──> modulation: [B, 1, 1, 1]
                                │      scores = scores * modulation
                                │
                                ├──> Add attention_mask ──> [B, H, N, N]
                                ├──> Softmax(dim=-1) & Dropout & Head Mask ──> attn_probs: [B, H, N, N]
                                │
                                └──> MatMul: attn_probs @ V ──> context: [B, H, N, d_k]
                                        │
                                        └──> permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous().view([B, N, D])
                                        └──> Linear(D, D) [out_proj] ──> Output: [B, N, D]

docs.title: Computational Workload & Resource Requirements
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_k = D / H\), and \(r\) rank bottleneck.

  1. Linear Projection FLOPs: \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\): \(4 \times 2 B N D^2 = 8 B N D^2\) FLOPs (\(4 B N D^2\) MACs).

  2. Rank Modulation FLOPs (if \(r > 0\)): Sequence Mean-Pooling: \(B \cdot N \cdot D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Bottleneck Projection (\(W_{\text{rank}}\)): \(2 B D r\) FLOPs (\(B D r\) MACs). Concurrently, Sigmoid & Mean Reduction: \(2 B r\) FLOPs. In this setting, Score Modulation Scaling: \(B H N^2\) FLOPs.

  3. Core Attention Computation (\(Q K^\top\) & \(A V\)): \(Q K^\top\): \([B, H, N, d_k] \times [B, H, d_k, N] \implies 2 B N^2 D\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Softmax: \(\approx 5 B H N^2\) FLOPs. Concurrently, \(A V\): \([B, H, N, N] \times [B, H, N, d_k] \implies 2 B N^2 D\) FLOPs.

docs.title: Total Complexity:
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(4 B N D^2 + 2 B N^2 D + B D r\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(8 B N D^2 + 4 B N^2 D + B N D + 2 B D r + B H N^2 (1 + 5/H)\) Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Parameter Count}, \(4 D^2 + D r\) floats.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Failure Modes
Sequence Mean-Pooling Feature Dilution
docs.text: Mean-pooling across long sequences (\(N > 4096\)) dilutes local position signal into a homogeneous global vector \(h_{\text{pool}}\). Consequently, modulation scalar \(\gamma_b\) reflects coarse average sequence magnitude, failing to capture token-specific contextual dynamics.

docs.title: Global Score Gating Saturation
docs.text:
Because \(\gamma_b = \frac{1}{r} \sum \sigma(z_{b, j}) \in (0, 1)\), scalar multiplication \(\widetilde{S} = S \cdot \gamma_b\) uniformly shrinks all raw scores before Softmax. While this attenuates score magnitudes, Softmax is shift-invariant to additions but scale-sensitive to multiplication, altering the temperature \(\tau_{\text{eff}} = \frac{\sqrt{d_k}}{\gamma_b}\) and broadening the attention probability distribution.

Softmax Score Scale Sensitivity:
Softmax(S * γ)  ==>  Increases Distribution Entropy as γ -> 0

docs.title: High Memory Bandwidth Allocation Overhead
docs.text: The standard PyTorch implementation creates intermediate tensors for \(Q, K, V\), unnormalized scores \(S\), and modulated scores \(\widetilde{S}\), triggering multiple HBM round trips.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Optimization Strategies
Fused Template Kernel Architecture
docs.text:
Custom attention variants derived from this template should eliminate intermediate score materialization by fusing score scaling, pooling modulation, and online Softmax in a single Triton kernel.

       Global Memory (HBM)
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ Input x [B, N, D]                                      │
      │ Weight Projections W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O                  │
      │ Optional Modulation Weight W_rank [D, r]                │
      └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Precompute Global Modulation γ_b
                                  ▼
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                   Triton SRAM Scratchpad                         │
 │ 1. Load Tile Blocks: Q_tile [BLOCK_M, d_k], K_tile [BLOCK_N, d_k]│
 │ 2. Compute Raw Scores: S_tile = Q_tile @ K_tile.T / sqrt(d_k)    │
 │ 3. Apply In-Register Modulation: S_mod = S_tile * γ_b            │
 │ 4. Execute Online Softmax & Accumulate Output Tile O_tile        │
 └────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Stream Context Output Block
                                  ▼
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ Context Output O [B, N, D]                             │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Triton Implementation Guidelines:
docs.text:
1. Pre-Pass Global Pooling Kernel: Compute \(h_{\text{pool}}\) and modulation vector \(\gamma_b\) in a lightweight, pre-pass reduction kernel, passing scalar values to grid blocks via small SRAM constants.
  2. Fused Multi-Head Layout Transformations: Execute projection linear transformations \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\) and multi-head transposition inside shared memory scratchpads, bypassing PyTorch view and permute copy operations.
  3. Template Subspace Hooks: Provide modular inline Triton macro hooks (APPLY_SCORE_MODIFIER(S_tile)) allowing researchers to inject custom mathematical transformations into SRAM registers without re-writing tiling or reduction logic.

docs.title: YourCustomCompressor: A Modular Compressor Template for Flexible Transformer Compression
docs.text:
Abstract

We present a template compressor module that serves as a starting point for developing custom compression methods within the DistilBERT compression framework. The template, named YourCustomCompressor, provides a unified interface for applying structured compression to the weights of a Transformer model. It supports four common compression paradigms out‑of‑the‑box: low‑rank factorisation (via truncated SVD), magnitude‑based pruning, uniform quantisation, and a hybrid combination of pruning and low‑rank approximation. The compressor operates by traversing the model’s modules, identifying linear layers in attention, feed‑forward, and embedding sub‑layers, and replacing them with compressed counterparts. A lightweight SVDLinearLayer implements the low‑rank decomposition using a down‑/up‑projection pair initialised from the singular value decomposition of the original weight matrix. The compressor collects compression statistics and provides visualisation tools for analysis. The entire module is designed to be easily customised: users copy the template, rename the class and registry key, and adapt the compress flow or add new compression methods to suit their specific needs. This paper describes the architecture of the template, the mathematical underpinnings of each compression technique, the implementation details, and guidelines for extending the template to novel compression algorithms.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Model compression techniques are essential for deploying large Transformer models in resource‑constrained environments. The compression framework provides a rich set of pre‑built attention modules, but researchers frequently need to experiment with new weight compression strategies that go beyond attention replacement—such as pruning entire layers, quantising weights, or applying low‑rank approximations to feed‑forward networks. The YourCustomCompressor template offers a flexible, extensible foundation for building such custom compressors.

The template encapsulates the common workflow of a compressor: traversing the model architecture, identifying compressible linear layers, applying a chosen compression algorithm, and collecting statistics. It comes with four ready‑to‑use compression methods: low‑rank, pruning, quantisation, and hybrid, all implemented via a simple method string parameter. Additionally, it includes a reusable SVDLinearLayer that performs low‑rank factorisation of a pretrained weight matrix with zero‑shot initialisation. The compressor inherits from BaseCompressor, integrating seamlessly with the framework’s registry and evaluation pipeline.

In this paper, we detail the internal structure of the template, the mathematics of the provided compression algorithms, the execution flow of the compress method, and the statistics and visualisation utilities. We also provide a guide for customising the template to implement entirely new compression strategies, highlighting the key methods to override and the interface contracts to follow.

docs.title: 2.1 Low‑Rank Linear Layer (SVDLinearLayer)
docs.text:
The foundation of the low‑rank compression path is the SVDLinearLayer class. Given a pretrained linear layer with weight \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}\) and optional bias \(\mathbf{b}\), this module replaces it with a two‑layer bottleneck:

\[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{U}_r (\mathbf{V}_r \mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{b}, \]

where \(\mathbf{V}_r \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}\) is a down‑projection to a rank \(r\), and \(\mathbf{U}_r \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}\) is the up‑projection. The rank \(r\) is a hyperparameter. The matrices are initialised from the truncated singular value decomposition of \(\mathbf{W}\):

\[ \mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U}_{\text{full}} \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{V}_{\text{full}}^\top, \qquad \mathbf{V}_r = \mathbf{V}_{\text{full}[:r,:]}, \qquad \mathbf{U}_r = \mathbf{U}_{\text{full}[:,:r]} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{[:r]}. \]

The bias is copied directly. This initialisation ensures that the compressed layer’s output initially approximates the original transformation to high fidelity (the optimal rank‑\(r\) Frobenius approximation). The forward pass computes self.U(self.V(x)) + bias. This layer is used both directly for low‑rank compression and as the final step in the hybrid method.

docs.title: 2.2 Compressor Core (YourCustomCompressor)
docs.text:
The YourCustomCompressor class inherits from BaseCompressor and is registered under the placeholder key "your_compressor_name". The constructor accepts:

model: the pretrained Transformer model (e.g., DistilBERT). Furthermore, target_sparsity: fraction of weights to prune (for pruning/hybrid). Concurrently, target_rank: rank \(r\) for low‑rank factorisation. In this setting, method: one of "standard", "low_rank", "pruning", "quantization", or "hybrid". (Note: "standard" actually invokes the hybrid method in the current code—a small inconsistency.) Additionally, **kwargs: additional parameters like custom_param (used for quantisation bits).

The core entry point is the compress method, which orchestrates the compression in five steps:

  1. _compress_embeddings(): Locates the word embedding layer and applies compression to its linear layer (typically a lookup table, but here treated as a linear layer; a full implementation would handle embedding layers appropriately).
  2. _compress_attention_layers(): Iterates over modules whose name contains “attention”, compressing all internal linear layers.
  3. _compress_ffn_layers(): Targets modules with “ffn”, “intermediate”, or “output” in their name, compressing the feed‑forward network’s linear layers.
  4. _compress_classifier(): Compresses the final classification head (if present).
  5. Computes compressed parameter count and statistics via _compute_stats.

Each of these methods relies on _compress_linear_layers, which iterates over a module’s direct children, and for each nn.Linear found, creates a compressed replacement based on the selected method:

Specifically, regarding \textbf{Low‑rank}, instantiates an SVDLinearLayer with the given target rank. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Pruning}, calls _create_pruned_layer, which removes rows (and corresponding input features) with the smallest row norms. The new size is determined by target_sparsity: out_features → max(1, int(out_features * (1 - target_sparsity))), and similarly for in_features. This is a structured pruning that reduces both dimensions proportionally. The top‑\(k\) rows by L2 norm are kept, and the weight matrix is sliced accordingly. Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Quantization}, calls _create_quantized_layer, which uniformly quantises the weights to a fixed number of bits (given by custom_param, default 8). The weights are scaled to the range \([-scale, scale]\), rounded, and rescaled, simulating a simple uniform quantisation. In this setting, regarding \textbf{Hybrid}, first applies pruning to the original layer (using _create_pruned_layer), then applies low‑rank factorisation to the pruned layer via SVDLinearLayer, with the rank set to target_rank // 2. This demonstrates a pipeline combination.

After creating the new layer, _replace_layer uses setattr to swap the original layer in the parent module. Information about each replacement is stored in self.compressed_layers for later reporting.

docs.title: 2.3 Compression Statistics and Visualisation
docs.text:
The compressor tracks various metrics: _original_params: total parameters of the model before compression. Furthermore, _compressed_params: total parameters after compression. Concurrently, compression_stats: a dictionary with fields like compression_ratio, parameters_saved, reduction_percentage, and compressed_layers (a list of per‑layer details). In this setting, get_layer_wise_report(): returns a pandas DataFrame summarising all compressed layers. Additionally, visualize_compression(): uses matplotlib to plot a side‑by‑side bar chart of original vs. compressed parameters per layer and a pie chart of compression types (attention, FFN, etc.). The plots can be saved to disk.

These utilities aid in evaluating the compression’s impact and diagnosing potential bottlenecks.

docs.title: 2.4 Customisation Workflow
docs.text:
The template is designed to be copied and adapted. The typical steps for creating a new compressor are:

  1. Rename the class and update the registry decorator key to a unique name.
  2. Modify the constructor to accept new hyperparameters relevant to the desired compression algorithm.
  3. Implement new compression logic by overriding or adding new _create_*_layer methods and adjusting _compress_linear_layers to dispatch to them based on self.method or other conditions.
  4. Adjust the traversal logic if compression should target specific layer types differently (e.g., separate handling for attention vs. FFN).
  5. Optionally, enhance the statistics methods to report new metrics.

The template’s modular structure makes it straightforward to experiment with novel techniques, such as dynamic pruning schedules, non‑uniform quantisation, or activation‑aware low‑rank decomposition.

docs.title: 3. Implementation Details
docs.text: Specifically, regarding \textbf{SVDLinearLayer}, inherits from nn.Module. Uses torch.linalg.svd to factorise the original weight. The U and V layers are nn.Linear with biases set to False; the original bias (if any) is stored separately as self.bias (a nn.Parameter). The forward pass applies V then U then adds the bias. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{YourCustomCompressor}, inherits from BaseCompressor. The compress method must be called to perform compression; it returns a tuple (compressed_model, stats_dict). The class is registered with @COMPRESSOR_REGISTRY.register("your_compressor_name"). Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Layer traversal}, the _compress_linear_layers method uses module.named_modules() to recurse through sub‑modules. It replaces only direct nn.Linear instances. The replacement is done in‑place via setattr. In this setting, regarding \textbf{Pruning details}, the pruning method is aggressive: it reduces both input and output dimensions, effectively creating a smaller linear layer. This may break the model if not handled carefully (e.g., subsequent layers must also be adjusted). In practice, a compressor would need to ensure dimension consistency across the network; this template provides a simplified demonstration. Additionally, regarding \textbf{Quantisation}, the quantised weights are stored in floating point but with values restricted to a discrete set. This is a simulation of quantisation; a real deployment would convert to an integer representation. The number of bits defaults to 8. Moreover, regarding \textbf{Hybrid method}, the hybrid method first prunes and then low‑rank factorises. The rank is halved to maintain a similar parameter budget. The pruned layer’s dimensions are already reduced, so the SVD is performed on a smaller matrix, which can be beneficial.

docs.title: 4. Usage and Configuration
docs.text:
After customising the template (renaming and adjusting), the compressor can be invoked as follows:

from framework.compressors import YourCustomCompressor
compressor = YourCustomCompressor(
    model=pretrained_model,
    target_sparsity=0.5,
    target_rank=32,
    method="hybrid",
    custom_param=8   # used for quantization bits if method is "quantization"
)
compressed_model, stats = compressor.compress()
print(stats)
compressor.visualize_compression(save_path="compression_report.png")

The method parameter controls the compression strategy. The custom_param can be repurposed for additional algorithm‑specific settings. The target_sparsity and target_rank are the primary controls over the compression ratio.

After compression, the model can be fine‑tuned or evaluated directly, though the aggressive pruning may require some training to recover accuracy. The template also supports saving the compressed model via the framework’s utilities.

docs.title: 5. Discussion
docs.text:
The YourCustomCompressor template is a versatile starting point for implementing weight‑oriented compression techniques. It offers immediate access to four common methods, but its greatest value lies in the ease with which new methods can be added. The code is structured to separate the traversal logic, the layer creation logic, and the statistics, enabling developers to focus on the core algorithm.

However, there are several limitations that a developer should address when building a production‑ready compressor:

Specifically, regarding \textbf{Dimension consistency}, the pruning method naively reduces both input and output dimensions, which will break the connectivity between layers unless all affected layers are adjusted simultaneously. A practical compressor must ensure that the output dimension of one layer matches the input dimension of the next. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Embedding compression}, the embedding layer is treated as a linear layer; a more sophisticated approach might involve sharing weights with the output projection or applying a specialised factorisation (e.g., ALBERT‑style factorisation). Concurrently, regarding \textbf{Quantisation simulation}, the quantisation is stored in floating point but not truly quantised to integer arithmetic; this does not yield inference speed‑up. A real quantisation compressor would insert quantisation/dequantisation nodes or convert weights to integer tensors. In this setting, regarding \textbf{Lack of fine‑tuning support}, the template does not include a training loop; after compression, fine‑tuning is typically required to recover lost accuracy. The compressor returns the model, which can then be passed to a trainer. Additionally, regarding \textbf{Rigid method dispatch}, the method string defines the algorithm; a more flexible design might use a registry of compression methods that can be combined or applied per layer differently.

Despite these simplifications, the template achieves its goal of providing a clear, extensible base for rapid prototyping. The included visualisation tools and statistics reporting are valuable for quickly assessing the impact of different compression settings.

docs.title: 6. Conclusion
docs.text: We have presented a modular compressor template that encapsulates the common operations of Transformer weight compression: layer traversal, replacement with compressed variants, and statistics collection. The template ships with low‑rank, pruning, quantisation, and hybrid methods, all implemented in a transparent manner. By following the documented customisation steps, researchers can quickly implement novel compression algorithms and integrate them into the DistilBERT compression framework. The template reduces the boilerplate code required to build a new compressor, allowing the community to focus on innovation in model efficiency. Future improvements could include more sophisticated pruning with dimension matching, support for structured sparsity, and integration with the framework’s fine‑tuning pipelines. The code is freely available and encourages contributions from the broader open‑source community.

docs.title: Token-Compressed Attention Wrapper: Structural Abstraction & Pass-Through Layer-Wise Delegator
1. Abstract & Theoretical Motivation
docs.text:
In progressive network distillation, dynamic token pruning, and structural model compression benchmarks, maintaining a unified API interface across heterogeneous attention layers is critical. The Token-Compressed Attention Wrapper (TokenCompressedAttention) serves as a zero-overhead structural pass-through abstraction layer within the attention registry.

By wrapping pre-existing attention modules (old_attn) and enforcing a normalized output contract \(\mathcal{Y} = (\text{Output}, \text{AttentionWeights})\), TokenCompressedAttention enables seamless layer-wise injection, progressive sequence pruning experiments, and modular distillation harnesses. Mathematically, it acts as an identity operator over attention functions while providing hook boundaries for sequence length reduction and token aggregation.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Derivations & Formulations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote the input activation sequence, where \(B\) is batch size, \(N\) is sequence length, and \(D\) is model hidden dimension. Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{attn}}\) represent the underlying wrapped attention operator (old_attn).

docs.title: Identity Structural Mapping:
docs.text:
The forward pass delegates computation directly to \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{attn}}\):

\[ (Y, A) = \mathcal{F}_{\text{attn}}\left(X, M_{\text{attn}}, H_{\text{mask}}, \text{output\_attentions}\right) \]

where \(M_{\text{attn}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 1 \times N \times N}\) is the attention mask and \(H_{\text{mask}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H}\) is the optional head pruning mask.

docs.title: Interface Output Standardization:
docs.text:
If \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{attn}}(X)\) returns a single tensor \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\), the wrapper normalizes the return signature to a two-element tuple:

\[ \mathcal{T}(X) = \begin{cases} (Y, A) & \text{if } \text{isinstance}(Y, \text{tuple}) \\ (Y, \text{None}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Mathematical Equivalence to Sub-Module:
docs.text:
For any input state \(X\) and loss function \(\mathcal{L}\):

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X}_{\text{wrapper}} \equiv \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X}_{\mathcal{F}_{\text{attn}}} \] \[ \text{Params}(\text{TokenCompressedAttention}) = \text{Params}(\mathcal{F}_{\text{attn}}) \]

The wrapper introduces no additional parameters, mathematical transformations, or activation state alterations.

docs.title: 3. Tensor Execution Flow & Dimensional Shape Tracing
docs.text:
Input: hidden_states [B, N, D]
  │
  ├──> Delegate Forward Call to wrapped self.attn:
  │      self.attn(hidden_states, attention_mask, head_mask, output_attentions, **kwargs)
  │
  ├──> Receive Output from self.attn:
  │      IF Return is Tuple: (output [B, N, D], weights [B, H, N, N])
  │      ELSE: output [B, N, D] ──> Wrap as (output, None)
  │
  └──> Return Signature: Tuple[torch.Tensor, Optional[torch.Tensor]]

docs.title: Operational & Computational Workload
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, and \(d_k = D / H\).

  1. Wrapper Computational Overhead: FLOPs: \(0\) (Zero FLOP addition). Furthermore, MACs: \(0\) (Zero MAC addition). Concurrently, Parameters: \(0\) (Non-parametric pass-through wrapper).

  2. Inherited Base Attention Complexity: Full Attention (FullAttention wrapped): \(\mathcal{O}(8 B N D^2 + 4 B N^2 D)\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Linear Attention (LinformerAttention wrapped): \(\mathcal{O}(8 B N D^2 + 4 B N k D)\) FLOPs. Concurrently, Memory Footprint: Directly inherits activation retention buffers of wrapped module \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{attn}}\).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Failure Modes
Function Dispatch & Python Frame Overhead
docs.text: In high-throughput micro-batching inference pipelines (\(B=1, N \le 32\)), inserting Python wrapper classes introduces extra function call stack depth and frame resolution overhead. This induces minor execution latency spikes on CPU-bound control loops.

docs.title: Passthrough Degeneracy (Absence of Token Reduction)
docs.text: Although named TokenCompressedAttention, the module in its base form does not reduce sequence length \(N\). If downstream pipelines assume token sequence reduction (\(N \to N_{\text{compressed}}\)), downstream layers receive standard un-pruned sequence length \(N\), leading to misaligned sequence assumptions.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Optimization Strategies
Zero-Overhead Compiler Graph Inlining
docs.text:
To eliminate Python wrapper overhead in C++ / CUDA runtimes, PyTorch TorchScript, TorchDynamo, and Triton compiler backends automatically inline TokenCompressedAttention directly into the wrapped kernel graph.

       PyTorch Module Graph
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ TokenCompressedAttention Layer                         │
      │   └── self.attn (Wrapped Sub-Module)                  │
      └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ TorchDynamo Graph Inlining
                                  ▼
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ Direct Kernel Execution Graph (No Wrapper Latency)    │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Key Compilation Strategies:
docs.text:
1. TorchDynamo Pass-Through Extraction: Ensure forward contains no Python side-effects or mutable state modifications, allowing torch.compile(backend="inductor") to remove the wrapper node entirely during graph tracing.
  2. Zero-Copy Tuple Unpacking: Guarantee that tuple normalization constructs non-allocating view references, eliminating Python reference counting overhead on GPU device pointers.

docs.title: TPAttention: Tensor Product Attention with Factorised Query-Key Projections
1. Executive Abstract & Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Tensor Product Attention (TPAttention) introduces a polynomial kernel projection paradigm that factorizes traditional dense Query and Key projections into outer tensor products of low-rank vectors. In standard Multi-Head Attention, computing Query and Key projections \(Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_k}\) requires full rank matrix parameters \(W_Q, W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\).

TPAttention replaces standard \(D \to D\) linear maps with pair-factorised projections: \(q_1, q_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times r}\) and \(k_1, k_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times r}\), where factor rank \(r \ll d_k\) (typically \(r = 8\)). By constructing full head states via the Kronecker/outer tensor product \(Q = q_1 \otimes q_2\) and \(K = k_1 \otimes k_2\), the effective Query and Key head dimension expands to \(r^2\). This parameterization creates high-order polynomial similarity kernels (\(\langle q_1 \otimes q_2, k_1 \otimes k_2 \rangle = \langle q_1, k_1 \rangle \cdot \langle q_2, k_2 \rangle\)) while significantly reducing per-token linear projection parameter counts and FLOPs.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations & Derivations
docs.text: Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D}\) denote input activations. Let \(H\) be the number of attention heads, \(d_h = D / H\) value head dimension, and \(r\) the factor rank per head.

docs.title: Factorised Subspace Projections:
docs.text:
Input activations are projected into two low-rank factor vectors for Query and Key, and standard projections for Value:

[ q_1 = X W_{Q1} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot r)}, \quad q_2 = X W_{Q2} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot r)} ] [ k_1 = X W_{K1} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot r)}, \quad k_2 = X W_{K2} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot r)} ] [ V = X W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times (H \cdot d_h)}, \quad W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times (H \cdot d_h)} ]

Reshaping into multi-head layouts: \(q_1, q_2, k_1, k_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times r}\).

docs.title: Tensor Outer Product Expansion via Einstein Summation:
docs.text:
The composite Query and Key tensors \(Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times H \times r^2}\) are derived via head-wise outer products using torch.einsum:

[ Q_{b, n, h, i, j} = q_{1, b, n, h, i} \cdot q_{2, b, n, h, j} \implies Q = \text{reshape}(Q, [B, N, H, r^2]) ] [ K_{b, n, h, i, j} = k_{1, b, n, h, i} \cdot k_{2, b, n, h, j} \implies K = \text{reshape}(K, [B, N, H, r^2]) ]

Transposing layouts to multi-head shape \([B, H, N, r^2]\).

docs.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention & Tensor Kernel Identity:
docs.text:
Affinity scores are scaled by factor \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}\) (or \(1/r\)):

\[ S_{b, h, m, n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} \sum_{p=1}^{r^2} Q_{b, h, m, p} \cdot K_{b, h, n, p} \]

By the algebraic tensor product inner product identity:

\[ \sum_{p=1}^{r^2} (q_1 \otimes q_2)_p (k_1 \otimes k_2)_p = \left(\sum_{i=1}^r q_{1, i} k_{1, i}\right) \cdot \left(\sum_{j=1}^r q_{2, j} k_{2, j}\right) = (q_1^\top k_1) \cdot (q_2^\top k_2) \]

Softmax normalization, dropout, and context output aggregation proceed as:

[ A_{b, h, m, n} = \text{Softmax}n (S{b, h, m, n} + M_{b, 1, m, n}) ] [ O_{b, h, m, l} = \sum_{n=1}^N \text{Dropout}(A){b, h, m, n} \cdot V{b, h, n, l} \implies O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times N \times d_h} ] [ Y = \text{Concat}(O_1, \dots, O_H) W_O + b_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times D} ]

docs.title: Computational Workload (FLOPs & MACs)
docs.text:
Let \(B\) be batch size, \(N\) sequence length, \(D\) model dimension, \(H\) heads, \(d_h = D/H\), and \(r\) factor rank.

  1. Linear Projections: \(W_{Q1}, W_{Q2}, W_{K1}, W_{K2}\): \(4 \times (2 B N D (H r)) = 8 B N D H r\) FLOPs. Furthermore, \(W_V, W_O\): \(4 B N D^2\) FLOPs. Concurrently, Total Projection Cost: \(4 B N D^2 + 8 B N D H r\) FLOPs.

  2. Tensor Product Expansion (einsum): \(Q = q_1 \otimes q_2\): \(2 B N H r^2\) FLOPs. Furthermore, \(K = k_1 \otimes k_2\): \(2 B N H r^2\) FLOPs.

  3. Core Attention Workload: MatMul score \(Q K^\top\): \(2 B H N^2 r^2\) FLOPs. Furthermore, Softmax & Masking: \(7 B H N^2\) FLOPs. Concurrently, MatMul context \(A V\): \(2 B H N^2 d_h = 2 B N^2 D\) FLOPs.

  4. Total Workload Summary: Specifically, regarding \textbf{Total MACs}, \(2 B N D^2 + 4 B N D H r + B N H r^2 + B H N^2 (r^2 + d_h)\) Furthermore, regarding \textbf{Total FLOPs}, \(4 B N D^2 + 8 B N D H r + 4 B N H r^2 + 2 B H N^2 r^2 + 2 B N^2 D + 7 B H N^2\)

docs.title: Parameter Footprint Analysis
docs.text:
Specifically, regarding \textbf{Standard MHA Parameter Count}, \(4 D^2 + 4 D\) floats. Furthermore, regarding \textbf{TPAttention Parameter Count},

[ \text{Params}_{\text{TPA}} = 2 D^2 + 4 D H r + 2 D \text{ floats} ] For \(D = 4096, H = 32, r = 8\): Standard MHA QKV+O projections: \(4 \times 4096^2 = 67,108,864\) parameters. Furthermore, TPA QKV+O projections: \(2(4096)^2 + 4(4096)(32)(8) \approx 37,748,736\) parameters (43.7% parameter reduction on QKV projections).

docs.title: 5. Architectural Bottlenecks, Rank Collapse & Edge Cases
Rank Saturation in Outer Products
docs.text: If factor rank \(r\) is too small (\(r \le 4\)), outer product tensors \(Q = q_1 \otimes q_2\) become constrained to low numerical rank spaces in \(\mathbb{R}^{r^2}\), limiting expressive power compared to unconstrained dense matrices.

docs.title: Materialization of Intermediate Tensor Product Buffers
docs.text: Evaluating torch.einsum("blhi,blhj->blhij", q1, q2) creates intermediate 5D tensors of shape \([B, N, H, r, r]\) before flattening to \([B, H, N, r^2]\), increasing peak activation memory if executed in un-fused PyTorch.

docs.title: 6. Hardware Acceleration Blueprint & Triton Kernel Design
docs.text:
A Triton kernel for TPAttention eliminates intermediate \(r^2\) tensor materialization by computing the tensor product similarity on-the-fly inside SRAM using the factor inner product identity \((q_1^\top k_1) \cdot (q_2^\top k_2)\).

                    Global Memory (HBM)
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ q1, q2, k1, k2: [B, N, H, r]                                │
   │ V: [B, H, N, d_h]                                           │
   └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Direct Factor Tile Loading
                                  ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     Triton SRAM Scratchpad                     │
 │ 1. Load Factor Tiles q1_i, q2_i [BLOCK_M, r]                   │
 │ 2. Load Factor Tiles k1_j, k2_j [BLOCK_N, r]                   │
 │ 3. Compute Dual Scores: S1_ij = q1_i @ k1_j.T, S2_ij = q2_i @ k2_j.T│
 │ 4. Compute Fused Score: S_ij = (S1_ij * S2_ij) / sqrt(r)       │
 │ 5. Online Softmax & Accumulate V_j Tile                        │
 └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ Write Context Output
                                  ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Context Output: O [B, H, N, d_h]                            │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 7. Next-Generation Innovations & Synthesis Opportunities
docs.text:
1. Higher-Order Tensor Products: Extend to 3-factor tensor products \(Q = q_1 \otimes q_2 \otimes q_3 \in \mathbb{R}^{r^3}\) for cubic polynomial attention kernels.
  2. Spectral Rank Factorization: Initialize \(q_1, q_2\) via SVD rank decomposition of pretrained MHA query weights for zero-shot compression.
  3. TPAttention + GQA Fusion: Combine Tensor Product factorized queries with Grouped-Query shared values for sub-quadratic memory footprint during inference.

docs.text:
Tri-Branch Hybrid Attention fuses three complementary mechanisms: (1) local sliding-window attention for high-frequency token syntax, (2) linear recurrent attention for global sequence memory, and (3) low-rank SVD attention for semantic concepts.

In NeuralOps, tri_branch_hybrid is integrated into the universal attention dispatch table, featuring full support for the 3-level fallback hierarchy, automatic shape validation, and end-to-end autograd backwards passes.
