docs.title: 🧠 20 Novel & Game‑Like Features for the Ultimate Attention Visualization Dashboard
docs.text: Based on my comprehensive research across 25+ cutting‑edge academic papers, open‑source projects, and visualization systems from 2024‑2026, here are 20 truly novel features that transform attention visualization from a static analysis tool into an immersive, game‑like learning environment — where users don't just see attention, they play with it.

docs.title: 1. NeuroGame Attention Arena: Token Coalition Simulator
docs.text:
Inspiration: NeuroGame Transformer (NGT) — treats tokens as players in a cooperative game and computes attention via Shapley values and Gibbs distributions.

What it is: An interactive game arena where each token is a "player" with a health bar, resources, and coalition power. The user watches tokens form coalitions in real‑time — the attention weights are visualized as alliance strengths between players. The user can: - Click a token to see its Shapley value (marginal contribution to the coalition) - Disrupt coalitions by removing tokens and watching how the remaining tokens re‑form alliances - Compare standard pairwise attention vs. coalition‑based attention side‑by‑side - See tokens "compete" for attention via an animated scoreboard

The visualization uses a force‑directed graph where tokens are nodes, attention weights are springs, and the Gibbs distribution controls the "temperature" of the system — higher temperature = more diffuse attention (like entropy).

docs.title: 2. "Planet Neuron" Starmap Explorer
docs.text:
Inspiration: The Reddit project where each neuron in a transformer layer becomes a "planet" in a navigable game world, discovered in real time from your text input.

What it is: A WebGL/Three.js star system where: - Each attention head is a star system - Each neuron is a planet orbiting that star - The planet's size = its activation magnitude - The planet's color = its attention pattern type (positional heads are blue, semantic heads are red, delimiter heads are green) - Typing text generates new planets in real‑time - The user flies through the galaxy using arrow keys / WASD, zooming into layers and heads

The gamification: users collect "discovery badges" for finding rare attention patterns (e.g., "You discovered an Induction Head in Layer 5!").

docs.title: 3. Attention Flow Runner (Endless Runner Game)
docs.text:
Inspiration: Transformer Explainer's Sankey diagram dynamic system view + NeuroGame Transformer's "token competition" concept.

What it is: An endless runner game (like Temple Run but for attention). The user controls a "token" running through a landscape that represents the transformer layers: - Obstacles = attention decisions (split into multiple heads, information routing) - Power‑ups = high‑attention tokens that boost the runner's speed - The path = the attention flow through the model (Sankey‑style) - Score = based on how "faithful" the run is to real attention patterns

Users can slow down, pause, and inspect each "decision point" to see the math behind it. The game teaches attention flow intuitively — you feel how information propagates through layers.

docs.title: 4. VR/AR Attention Immersion Room
docs.text:
Inspiration: HeedVision (collaborative attention‑aware visualizations in WebXR), WarpVision (spatial curvature guiding attention in VR), and Semantic Pathway's cross‑layer trajectories.

What it is: A WebXR‑based VR experience (accessible via browser with a VR headset or even just mouse/keyboard in "explore mode") where: - The user stands inside a 360° attention matrix - Tokens float around them in a sphere - Attention connections are laser beams between tokens, colored by head, with thickness = weight - The user can reach out and "grab" a token to see its Q/K/V vectors - Layer transitions are visualized as the user "ascends" or "descends" through the model - Collaborative mode: multiple users in the same VR room, each represented as an avatar, exploring together (like HeedVision's CAAV concept)

docs.title: 5. Transformer Defense Tower Game
docs.text:
Inspiration: Othello‑GPT where attention heads are categorized into "my‑turn" vs "your‑turn" heads + game theory approaches to attention.

What it is: A tower defense game where: - Incoming tokens are "enemies" that must be processed - Attention heads are defense towers — each head specializes in a different type of token - The user places/removes heads and sees how the model's "defense" changes - Positional heads = long‑range artillery (they see far tokens) - Semantic heads = close‑range defenders (they focus on nearby related words) - The game visualizes how different head architectures affect model performance — it's a playful introduction to attention head pruning and architecture design

docs.title: 6. 3Blue1Brown‑Style Animated Math Engine (Powered by ManimML)
docs.text:
Inspiration: 3Blue1Brown's "Attention in transformers, visually explained" (built with Manim), ManimML for ML‑specific animations, and the Self Attention Flow interactive tool.

What it is: A fully integrated ManimML rendering pipeline in the browser (via Pyodide/WebAssembly or server‑side rendering). The user clicks any part of the attention formula and sees a stunning mathematical animation:

  • Q × K^T: Matrices slide together, numbers flow from one to another
  • ÷ √d_k: A scaling factor visually shrinks the matrix
  • softmax(): Each row "lights up" as values are exponentiated and normalized
  • × V: The weighted sum appears as colored bars

All animations are scrubbable (pause, rewind, slow‑motion). The user can resize matrices interactively to understand why dimensions must match.

docs.title: 7. TransforLearn‑Style Architecture‑Driven Tutorial
docs.text:
Inspiration: TransforLearn — the first interactive visual tutorial for Transformers, supporting architecture‑driven and task‑driven exploration.

What it is: A guided, step‑by‑step learning path that walks users from "What is attention?" to "Here's how multi‑head attention works" with: - Progressive disclosure: start with a single head, then add more - Architecture‑driven mode: click any component to see its internals - Task‑driven mode: "Show me how this model translates French to English" — attention patterns update as the user types - Knowledge checkpoints: interactive quizzes (drag‑and‑drop attention weights, match heads to their patterns) - Personalized learning: the system tracks what you've explored and suggests next steps

docs.title: 8. Inside the Matrix: 3D Matrix Multiplication Explorer
docs.text:
Inspiration: PyTorch's "Inside the Matrix" which uses 3D to visualize matrix multiplication and attention heads with real weights.

What it is: A dedicated 3D matrix visualization space where: - Q, K, V matrices are rendered as 3D blocks (like Minecraft blocks for each value) - The attention computation is shown as physical operations: blocks slide, multiply, and combine - Color gradient shows magnitude (blue = negative, white = zero, red = positive) - Users can "fly through" the matrix, inspecting individual values - Real model weights are loaded from any HuggingFace model - Diff mode: compare the attention matrices of two different models side‑by‑side

docs.title: 9. HeadVis‑Style Attention Head Diagnostic Center
docs.text:
Inspiration: HeadVis (May 2026) — an interactive tool for investigating attention heads using attention patterns, quantitative distribution metrics, low‑rank component projections, and SAE feature attributions through QK and OV circuits.

What it is: A comprehensive head diagnostic panel showing for each head: - Attention pattern (heatmap) with zoom - QK circuit visualization (what this head "looks for" in keys) - OV circuit visualization (what this head "writes" to the output) - Distribution metrics: entropy, concentration, sparsity - Low‑rank projection: how much of the head's behavior is captured by its top singular vectors - SAE (Sparse Autoencoder) feature attribution: which interpretable features does this head activate?

One‑click hypothesis testing: "I think this head is copying the previous token" → click to verify against known induction head patterns.

docs.title: 10. Logit Lens Time Machine
docs.text:
Inspiration: LogitLens4LLMs — extends Logit Lens to modern LLMs like Claude, GPT‑4, Llama. Also, the interactive logit lens webapp from 2025.

What it is: A timeline scrubber that shows how the model's prediction evolves across layers: - Layer 0: "The capital of France is …" → model predicts random words - Layer 4: starts considering "Paris", "Lyon", "Marseille" - Layer 8: converges to "Paris" - Layer 12: confident in "Paris"

Each layer shows a word cloud of top‑k predictions, sized by probability. The user can: - Click any layer to see which attention heads contributed to that prediction - Compare two inputs: "The capital of France is _" vs "The capital of Germany is _" — where do they diverge? - Intervene: modify a hidden state at layer X and see how predictions change downstream

docs.title: 11. Semantic Pathway Cross‑Layer Trajectory Visualizer
docs.text:
Inspiration: Semantic Pathway (IEEE VIS 2025) — reveals how token representations evolve across layers in autoregressive Transformers, with attention‑based influence filtering, nearest‑token projections, and Compare Mode.

What it is: An interactive "Google Maps for token meaning" where: - Each token is plotted in a 2D semantic space (via t‑SNE/UMAP) - Trajectories connect the same token across layers (like flight paths) - Attention influence: which tokens "pulled" this token's meaning in a particular direction? - Compare Mode: two different inputs, see how their trajectories diverge - Nearest‑token projections: at any layer, see which vocabulary words are closest to the hidden state (like "what is the model thinking right now?")

docs.title: 12. Dodrio‑Style Linguistic Annotation Overlay
docs.text:
Inspiration: Dodrio (ACL 2021) — integrates attention visualization with linguistic knowledge like syntactic dependencies, semantic roles, and coreference chains.

What it is: An overlay mode where linguistic annotations are superimposed on the attention heatmap: - Syntactic parse tree edges drawn on top of attention connections - Semantic role labels (AGENT, PATIENT, etc.) next to tokens - Coreference chains highlighted — does the attention head track entity mentions? - Part‑of‑speech coloring on token labels

Users can toggle between "raw attention view" and "linguistic overlay view" to see how well attention aligns with human‑annotated linguistic structure. Heads that strongly correlate with syntax get a "syntactic head" badge.

docs.title: 13. Arrakis‑Style Head Ablation Laboratory
docs.text:
Inspiration: Arrakis — provides ablate_head(layer_idx, head_idx) to temporarily disable attention heads for mechanistic interpretability experiments. Also, the push towards interactive transformer decoding with activation visualization, ablation, and freezing.

What it is: A "surgical" interface where users can: - Toggle individual heads on/off with a switch - See before/after predictions in real time - Measure impact: how much does ablating head X change the output probability? - Chain ablations: disable multiple heads and observe compound effects - Export ablation config as a pruning recipe → directly connected to your compression pipeline (one click: "Compress model with these heads pruned") - Auto‑ablation mode: the system automatically finds the minimal set of heads that preserves 95% of performance (like BHPVAS head pruning)

docs.title: 14. Causal Tracing: Knockout Experiment Playground
docs.text:
Inspiration: The logit lens approach of layer‑wise analysis combined with causal mediation analysis from mechanistic interpretability.

What it is: An interactive "knockout experiment" where users: - Select a source token (e.g., "The") - Select a target token (e.g., "dog") - Knock out attention from the source to the target at specific layers - See how the model's prediction changes - The system visualizes a causal graph showing which paths are critical for the prediction - "Path importance" scores computed via integrated gradients or activation patching

This is presented as a puzzle game: "Find the critical path that makes the model predict 'Paris' — knock out the wrong path and you lose points!"

docs.title: 15. Attention Pattern Evolution Time‑Lapse
docs.text:
Inspiration: Semantic Pathway's cross‑layer trajectories + BHPVAS head importance tracking over training.

What it is: For any training run, users can watch a time‑lapse animation of how attention patterns evolve: - Frame 1 (epoch 0): random attention, no clear patterns - Frame 30 (epoch 10): positional patterns emerging - Frame 60 (epoch 30): semantic patterns forming - Frame 100 (final): clean, specialized heads

Users can scrub through training time with a slider. The system highlights: - When each head "crystallizes" into its final pattern - Head importance curves (which heads become important early vs. late) - Pattern stability metrics (when do heads stop changing?)

Connected to your experiment monitor — this is the natural "post‑training analysis" view.

docs.title: 16. Attention‑to‑Everything Knowledge Graph
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your existing platform integration (notes, experiments, leaderboards, model versions).

What it is: Every attention visualization is a node in a knowledge graph: - Click any attention pattern → see all experiments that used this attention type - Click any head → see all notes that discuss this head - Click any token pair → see all analyses of that relationship - Bidirectional links: "This head was pruned in experiment #42 → click to see the compressed model's performance" - "Similar patterns" search: find other heads/layers/models with similar attention behavior

The knowledge graph is visualized as an interactive D3 force‑directed graph where users can explore connections freely.

docs.title: 17. Collaborative Attention Workshop (Multi‑User)
docs.text:
Inspiration: HeedVision's collaborative attention‑aware visualizations (CAAVs) + your existing WebSocket infrastructure.

What it is: Multiple researchers explore attention together in real time: - Shared view state: layer, head, zoom synchronized - Cursor presence: see where others are hovering - Annotation pins: drop comments on specific attention connections - Threaded discussion per head/layer - "Follow me" mode: one user leads, others follow their navigation - Session recording: replay an exploration session for teaching

This transforms the dashboard into a virtual lab meeting — perfect for research teams and classroom settings.

docs.title: 18. Particle Flow Attention Visualizer
docs.text:
Inspiration: Transformer Explainer's Sankey diagram with animated SVG paths and gradients + Particle system effects from modern game engines.

What it is: Attention connections are rendered as flowing particles (like the particle effects in games like Control or Destiny): - Each attention connection is a stream of glowing particles flowing from query token to key token - Particle density = attention weight - Particle speed = attention "confidence" - Color = attention head identity - Particles leave glow trails that fade over time - The user can "freeze" the flow at any moment to inspect the static pattern

docs.title: 19. Attention Sonification: Hear the Attention
docs.text:
Inspiration: Novel approaches to multimodal visualization.

What it is: Each attention head has a unique sound signature: - High attention = high pitch, fast tempo - Low attention = low pitch, slow tempo - Diffuse attention = white noise - Focused attention = pure tone - Positional head = rhythmic pattern - Semantic head = melodic pattern

Users can "listen" to the model thinking — hear how attention shifts as you change the input text. This is particularly powerful for accessibility and for detecting anomalies (a sudden change in sound indicates unusual attention behavior).

docs.title: 20. Attention Style Transfer Gallery
docs.text:
Inspiration: The variety of visualization styles across BertViz, Dodrio, SANVis, and Transformer Explainer.

What it is: A gallery mode where the same attention data is rendered in multiple artistic styles: - Heatmap (classic) - Sankey flow (dynamic) - Arc diagram (elegant) - Chord diagram (circular) - Hive plot (structural) - 3D particle flow (immersive) - Minimalist (for papers/publications) - Cyberpunk neon (for presentations)

Users can export any style as SVG/PNG/MP4 with one click. The "style transfer" metaphor makes attention visualization feel like an art form — and researchers can choose the style that best communicates their finding.

docs.title: 🧠 20 Social‑Network‑Style Interaction Features for the Attention Dashboard
docs.text: Here are 20 novel features that transform the attention visualization into a social experience, each deeply connected to every other part of the platform—experiments, notes, papers, profiles, leaderboards, marketplace, messaging, and more.

docs.title: Category 1: Reactions & Expression — "Like, Dislike, and Beyond"
1. Multi‑Dimensional Reaction System (Not Just 👍/👎)
docs.text:
Inspiration: HuggingFace model likes/downloads metadata, Higgsfield Chat's reaction system.

Researchers can react to attention heads/patterns with context‑rich signals: - 🔬 "Interesting" — this pattern warrants deeper investigation - ⚡ "Efficient" — this head does a lot with little - 🎯 "Specialized" — a clearly specialized head - 🔄 "Redundant" — likely prunable - 🧩 "Novel" — an unusual, undocumented pattern

These reactions create a "pattern quality score" displayed on every attention head. The score feeds into the head recommendation engine (which heads should users explore next?). Every reaction is also logged to the activity feed and the user's portfolio (showing their expertise in identifying attention patterns).

docs.title: 2. Attention Pattern Bookmarking & Collections
docs.text:
Inspiration: GitHub Stars/Forks, HuggingFace model likes, Kaggle kernel upvotes, Pinterest curation.

Users can star (bookmark) attention patterns into named collections: "Positional Heads Gallery," "Induction Head Candidates," "Anomalous Patterns." Collections can be public (shared with the community), team (shared with organization), or private. Each collection has its own discussion thread linked to the community Q&A app. Collections can be forked (GitHub‑style), with the fork lineage tracked. Top collections appear on a "Trending Collections" leaderboard.

This connects to: community (discussion threads), organizations (team‑level sharing), leaderboards (trending rankings), and portfolios (showcases curated work).

docs.title: 3. Attention Pattern "Battle" / A‑B Voting
docs.text:
Inspiration: Image Brawl voting platform, community curation voting tools.

A gamified side‑by‑side comparison where users vote on which of two attention patterns is "better" for a specific task (e.g., "Which head better captures syntactic dependencies?"). The system tracks Elo ratings for attention heads across dimensions (efficiency, specialization, interpretability). Users earn reputation points for voting consistently with the community consensus (similar to Kleros jury rewards in your gpu_reputation app). Results feed into the benchmark leaderboard and head recommendation system.

docs.title: 4. "Attention Spotlight" — Curated Daily Featured Pattern
docs.text:
Inspiration: PapersWithCode "Social" recommendation tab, Discourse Discover, community curation systems.

Every day, an algorithm (or community vote) selects one attention pattern as the "Spotlight Pattern". It appears on the homepage feed, with an explanation of why it's interesting (written by the curator or generated by an LLM). Users can discuss the spotlight in a dedicated thread (linked to community Q&A), try the pattern with their own text (one‑click from the spotlight), and nominate patterns for future spotlights. Past spotlights form a "Hall of Fame" gallery with permanent links.

docs.title: Category 2: Social Feed & Timeline — "The Attention News Feed"
5. Unified Activity Feed with ML‑Specific Event Types
docs.text:
Inspiration: MoltSocial unified feed (humans + AI agents), Kaggle activity tracking, GitHub contribution feed.

A scrollable "Attention Feed" showing platform‑wide activity: - "Dr. Smith ⭐ starred Head 7 in Layer 3 of BERT‑base (Induction Head)" - "Team Alpha 🧩 discovered a novel delimiter pattern in GPT‑2 Layer 5" - "Jane 🔄 pruned 3 redundant heads and improved accuracy by 2%" - "Benchmark 'GLUE‑Compression' 📊 updated — 12 new submissions"

Each feed item links directly to the relevant attention view, experiment, or note. Users can filter the feed by: following, team, global trending, or specific attention types. This is the same ActivityFeed infrastructure you already built—extended with attention‑specific event types.

docs.title: 6. "For You" Personalized Attention Recommendation Feed
docs.text:
Inspiration: Stream's ML‑powered feed personalization, Social-RAG for content recommendation.

A personalized feed that recommends attention patterns based on: the user's research interests (from their Profile), past interactions (which patterns they starred, discussed, or trained with), and collaborative filtering (users similar to you also explored…). The feed uses your existing community recommendation infrastructure. Each recommendation includes a "Why this?" explanation (e.g., "Because you studied positional heads in BERT").

docs.title: 7. "Following" Feed — Track Researchers & Their Discoveries
docs.text:
Inspiration: GitHub following feed, ResearchGate follow system, ProfBook social network.

Users can follow other researchers (already supported in your social_graph design). The "Following" feed shows: - New attention patterns they've published - Experiments they've launched - Notes they've written about attention - Comments they've made on community discussions - Leaderboard submissions

This turns the dashboard into a research social network where discoveries propagate through the community. Following a researcher also subscribes you to their collections and spotlight nominations.

docs.title: 8. Inline Pattern Discussion Threads (Per‑Head / Per‑Token‑Pair)
docs.text:
Inspiration: Discourse threaded discussions, Kaggle kernel comments, GitHub issue discussions.

Every attention pattern view has inline discussion threads anchored to specific elements: - Per‑head discussion: below each head view, a threaded comment section - Per‑token‑pair annotation: click any cell in the heatmap → add a note ("this token pair matters for coreference") - Per‑layer discussion: discuss layer‑level phenomena

Discussions are powered by your existing community Q&A infrastructure. Each thread supports @mentions, LaTeX equations, and embedded attention visualizations (SVG snippets). Threads can be marked as "resolved" (like GitHub issues). Resolved discussions become part of the pattern's knowledge graph.

docs.title: 9. Collaborative Annotation Overlay (Google Docs‑Style for Attention)
docs.text:
Inspiration: HeedVision collaborative attention‑aware visualizations, AnchorNote AR annotations, Bureau for Rapid Annotation Tool.

Multiple researchers can annotate the same attention visualization simultaneously. Annotations appear as colored pins on the heatmap, each with a comment. Users see cursor presence (who else is viewing this pattern right now). The annotation layer can be toggled on/off. All annotations are persisted and linked to the notes system—each annotation becomes a micro‑note with bidirectional links to the attention pattern. This uses your existing WebSocket/Channels infrastructure and collaborative editing patterns.

docs.title: 10. "Attention Review" — Structured Peer Review for Patterns
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your existing reviews peer review system, OpenReview structured reviews.

Researchers can submit an attention pattern for formal community review. Reviewers evaluate it on: novelty, interpretability, potential impact, reproducibility. The review form is structured (like your existing Review model) with scores and comments. Reviewed patterns get a "Peer Reviewed" badge displayed prominently. Highly‑rated reviews earn the reviewer reputation points (integrated with your gpu_reputation scoring system).

docs.title: 11. One‑Click Share Cards (Social Media‑Optimized)
docs.text:
Inspiration: PapersWithCode "copy image" leaderboard screenshots, HuggingFace shareable model cards.

Every attention visualization can be exported as a beautiful share card with one click. The card includes: - The attention pattern heatmap (as SVG/PNG) - Model name, layer, head info - Key statistics (entropy, concentration, head importance) - A QR code linking back to the interactive dashboard - The user's name/avatar (attribution)

Share cards are optimized for Twitter/X, LinkedIn, and Reddit. When someone scans the QR code, they land on the interactive dashboard—driving organic growth. Share metrics (impressions, clicks) are tracked and displayed on the user's portfolio.

docs.title: 12. "Clone & Remix" — Fork an Attention Analysis
docs.text:
Inspiration: GitHub fork model, Kaggle kernel copying, Higgsfield shared projects.

Every attention analysis can be cloned (forked) by another researcher. The fork creates a new analysis with the same configuration (model, text, layer/head selection). The forked analysis links back to the original (lineage tracking, like your ModelLineage). Users can modify the forked analysis (change the input text, try different heads) and publish their own version. The lineage graph is visualized as a tree/directed graph (like GitHub's network graph).

docs.title: 13. Attention Pattern "Stories" — Ephemeral Sharing
docs.text:
Inspiration: Instagram/Snapchat Stories, Twitter Fleets.

Researchers can create "Attention Stories" — short, ephemeral sequences of attention visualizations with commentary. For example: "Watch how attention shifts as we add more layers →" with 3-5 frames. Stories expire after 24 hours (or can be saved as permanent). Stories appear at the top of the feed. This encourages casual, frequent sharing of small discoveries without the overhead of writing a full note or paper.

docs.title: 14. Embed Anywhere — iFrame Widget for External Sites
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your existing WidgetEmbed system, WandB embedded reports.

Every attention pattern has an embeddable widget (like YouTube embeds). Researchers can paste a snippet into their personal website, blog, or paper supplementary material. The widget is interactive (users can hover, click, zoom) even when embedded. Widget analytics (views, interactions) flow back to the platform and appear on the pattern owner's portfolio and analytics dashboard.

docs.title: Category 5: Gamification & Reputation — "Level Up Your Attention Skills"
15. Attention Pattern Achievement Badges
docs.text:
Inspiration: Kaggle progression (Novice → Contributor → Expert → Master → Grandmaster), Stack Overflow reputation badges.

A tiered badge system for attention exploration: - 🥉 "First Look" — viewed your first attention pattern - 🥉 "Pattern Spotter" — identified 10 distinct head types - 🥈 "Head Hunter" — discovered a novel attention pattern that received 50+ stars - 🥈 "Curator" — created a collection with 100+ followers - 🥇 "Attention Master" — 1000+ reputation points from reviews, discussions, and discoveries - 💎 "Grandmaster" — top 10 on the attention leaderboard

Badges appear on the user's profile, portfolio, and dashboard. They integrate with your existing reputation_badge system.

docs.title: 16. Attention Leaderboard — "Top Pattern Discoverers"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Kaggle rankings, PapersWithCode leaderboard, Stack Overflow reputation leaderboard.

A global leaderboard ranking researchers by their attention‑related contributions: - Patterns discovered and published - Collections curated - Peer reviews completed - Discussions contributed - Stars/reactions received - Patterns that became "Spotlight"

The leaderboard has weekly, monthly, and all‑time views. Top‑ranked researchers get "Verified Expert" status and priority access to new features. This integrates with your leaderboards and gpu_reputation infrastructure.

docs.title: 17. Attention Challenges — "Weekly Pattern Hunt"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Kaggle competitions, CTF (Capture The Flag) challenges, gamification in AI education platforms.

Weekly community challenges: - "Find the Induction Head": given a model, locate the induction head(s) - "Explain This Pattern": write the best explanation for a mysterious attention pattern - "Prune to 90%": remove heads while maintaining >95% performance - "Attention Art": create the most visually striking attention visualization

Winners are determined by community voting + expert judging. Prizes include platform credits (GPU hours), exclusive badges, and featured spotlights. Challenges connect to your experiment launcher (one‑click to try the challenge) and leaderboards (challenge rankings).

docs.title: Category 6: Deep Platform Integration — "Everything Is Connected"
18. Attention‑to‑Experiment Pipeline (One‑Click Training)
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your existing experiment launcher, WandB experiment tracking.

Every attention pattern has a "Train with This" button. Clicking it opens the experiment launcher pre‑filled with: - The model, attention type, and sample text - A suggested experiment name: "Reproduce attention pattern L3‑H7 on BERT‑base" - The pattern's metadata as experiment notes - Links to related patterns and discussions

After the experiment runs, the results (actual attention patterns, metrics) are linked back to the original pattern. Users can compare expected vs. actual attention. This creates a closed loop: explore → experiment → verify.

docs.title: 19. Attention Pattern Knowledge Graph Navigator
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your NoteLink bidirectional links, knowledge graph visualization.

Every attention pattern is a node in a platform‑wide knowledge graph connected to: - The model it came from (linked to model_versioning) - The experiment that produced it (linked to experiment) - The notes that discuss it (linked to notes) - The papers that cite it (linked to agents paper library) - The community discussions about it (linked to community) - The collections that include it - The researchers who discovered, annotated, or reviewed it

The knowledge graph is visualized as an interactive D3 force‑directed graph. Users can traverse connections freely, discovering related work organically.

docs.title: 20. Attention‑Based Research Paper Generator
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your paper LaTeX app, model card generation, WandB reports.

With one click, generate a research paper section describing the attention analysis: - Methods: which model, text, and visualization techniques were used - Results: embedded attention visualizations with captions - Discussion: auto‑generated from community discussions and annotations - References: papers linked to the attention pattern (from the agents library)

Based on my research across ComparIA (French government LLM arena), Neuronpedia (open interpretability platform), Yupp ($33M crowdsourced AI evaluation), SciArena (20K+ researcher votes), Polis (ML-powered consensus), Anthropic Circuit Tracer (open-source attribution graphs), and many more, here are 20+ novel features that transform your platform into a community-driven attention generation and comparison ecosystem — where researchers don't just consume attention visualizations, they create, share, compete, and build reputation around them.

docs.title: 1. "Build Your Own Attention" — Drag-and-Drop Attention Constructor
docs.text:
Inspiration: CortexNodus (Flask + LiteGraph.js visual AI workbench — "not writing a single line of code to train AI models"), GitHub Interactive Neural Network visual builder, HuggingFace ZeroGPU Spaces.

A visual workbench where users can construct attention visualizations from scratch without code: - Model Picker: select any HuggingFace model (or upload their own) - Text Input: type or paste any text to analyze - Layer/Head Selector: choose which layers and heads to visualize - Visualization Type: choose from heatmap, Sankey, 3D, chord diagram, etc. - Style Editor: customize colors, fonts, annotations, and export format

Each created visualization is saved as a "Post" — a published artifact with a title, description, tags, and the full interactive visualization embedded. Other users can explore it interactively (not just a static image), change parameters, and fork it. This directly parallels CortexNodus's approach of "drag-and-drop neural network construction" applied to attention visualization generation, and Neuronpedia's model where users upload their own graphs regardless of the library used.

docs.title: 2. "Fork & Remix" — Attention Pattern Lineage Tracking
docs.text:
Inspiration: GitHub fork model, ComparIA open-source self-hostable arena, Neuronpedia upload-your-own-graphs.

Every published attention visualization can be forked by another researcher. The fork: - Copies all parameters (model, text, layer/head selection) - Allows modification (change the text, try different layers) - Maintains lineage tracking — showing the chain: "Alice created → Bob forked and added Layer 5 → Carol forked and changed to Galerkin attention" - The lineage is visualized as a tree/graph on every post

The original creator gets a notification and the fork count appears on their post. This is exactly how ComparIA is "fully open source, self-hostable, and customizable: choose your models, translate the interface, adapt prompt suggestions, add your logo" applied to attention visualization.

docs.title: 3. "Attention Challenge" — Community Contest Creator
docs.text:
Inspiration: Kaggle competitions, SciArena community-driven evaluation, Yupp crowdsourced model evaluation.

Any user can create an Attention Challenge: - "Find the most interesting attention pattern in BERT-base Layer 3" - "Best visualization of how Galerkin attention differs from standard MHA" - "Most creative attention visualization (any model, any style)"

Challenges have: - A submission deadline - Community voting period - Prizes (platform credits, GPU hours, exclusive badges) - A leaderboard of submissions ranked by votes

The SciArena platform has "collected over 20,000 votes from human researchers across diverse scientific domains" using exactly this community-driven evaluation approach for foundation models.

docs.title: 4. "Attention Studio" — Live Collaborative Creation Room
docs.text:
Inspiration: HeedVision collaborative attention-aware visualizations (CAAVs), Anthropic Circuit Tracer's "share graphs" feature.

A real-time collaborative workspace where multiple researchers can build attention visualizations together: - Shared canvas with cursor presence (like Figma/Google Docs) - Voice/video chat integrated (using your WebSocket infrastructure) - Live parameter changes: one person changes the layer → everyone sees it update - Annotation tools: draw on the heatmap, add comments, highlight token pairs - Session recording: export the entire collaboration session as a video for teaching

The Anthropic Circuit Tracer already supports "annotating, sharing graphs, and adjusting parameters to verify hypotheses". Your platform extends this to collaborative, real-time creation.

docs.title: 5. "Attention Arena" — Blind Pairwise Comparison (ComparIA-Style)
docs.text:
Inspiration: ComparIA blind pairwise comparison arena, SciArena community voting on model comparisons, Chatbot Arena approach.

A dedicated Arena mode where two attention visualizations are shown side-by-side, anonymized (hiding which model/head produced them). Users vote on: - "Which attention pattern is more interpretable?" - "Which head better captures syntactic dependencies?" - "Which visualization is more informative?"

Votes generate Elo ratings for attention patterns (like Chess rankings). The ComparIA platform uses exactly this approach: "users interact with two anonymous models simultaneously, vote on the better response, and subsequently reveal the models' identities" — generating "high-quality preference datasets". Your platform extends this from model outputs to attention visualizations.

docs.title: 6. Polis-Style Opinion Mapping for Attention Debates
docs.text:
Inspiration: Polis — ML-powered consensus visualization using PCA and k-means, which "visualizes the distribution of opinions and automatically generates groups."

For controversial topics (e.g., "Should attention heads be pruned or kept?"), users submit short statements. Other users vote "agree," "disagree," or "pass." The system: - Uses PCA and k-means to cluster participants into opinion groups - Visualizes bridging statements — opinions that both groups agree on - Shows consensus maps — where does the community agree vs. diverge?

Polis "uses machine learning and statistical algorithms to analyze participants' voting behavior" and "visualizes the distribution of opinions using principal component analysis (PCA) and k-means" — directly applicable to attention research debates.

docs.title: 7. "Attention Reputation" — Token-Weighted Voting (Like Yupp)
docs.text:
Inspiration: Yupp's blockchain-based crowdsourced evaluation with token incentives ($33M seed from a16z), SciArena's trusted researcher voting system.

Users earn Attention Reputation Tokens (ART) for: - Publishing high-quality attention visualizations (starred by many) - Providing insightful comments and annotations - Participating in blind pairwise voting (and voting consistently with consensus) - Winning challenges

When voting, a user's vote weight is proportional to their reputation score. Yupp "leverages blockchain and cryptocurrency economic incentives" so "diverse user feedback flows freely" — your platform applies this to attention quality assessment.

docs.title: 8. "Consensus Head" — Community-Verified Attention Pattern Certification
docs.text:
Inspiration: SciArena's peer-reviewed model evaluations, Neuronpedia's crowdsourced neuron explanations.

When enough expert votes confirm that an attention pattern represents a specific phenomenon (e.g., "This head in BERT-base Layer 5 is an Induction Head"), it receives a "Community Verified" badge. The verification requires: - At least 5 expert votes agreeing on the classification - At least one detailed annotation explaining the evidence - Reproducibility: at least 2 other researchers have reproduced the finding

Verified patterns appear in a "Verified Attention Library" — a curated, trusted reference for the community.

docs.title: 9. "Architecture Comparator" — Side-by-Side Cross-Architecture Attention View
docs.text:
Inspiration: ComparIA multi-model comparison, ScienceArena 47-model evaluation platform.

Users can load attention patterns from any deep learning architecture component — not just attention heads: - Attention mechanisms: standard MHA, Galerkin, LinFormer, PADRe, etc. - FFN layers: neuron activations as "attention to features" - Convolutional layers: filter response maps - RNN/LSTM: gate activations over time - Embedding layers: token similarity matrices

All are compared in the same interface, with normalized visualization and shared metrics (entropy, concentration, specialization score).

docs.title: 10. "Model Diff" — Attention Pattern Divergence Visualizer
docs.text:
Inspiration: ComparIA's blind comparison revealing model differences, Semantic Pathway's Compare Mode.

Select any two models (or two versions of the same model — before/after fine-tuning or compression) and see a divergence heatmap: where do their attention patterns differ most? The system: - Computes Jensen-Shannon divergence between attention distributions - Highlights heads that changed most after fine-tuning/compression - Shows "before/after" animations of attention shifts - Generates a diff report summarizing which architectural components changed

This connects directly to your compression pipeline — users can see exactly how compression affects attention patterns.

docs.title: 11. "Universal Attention Metric" — Cross-Architecture Scoring System
docs.text:
Inspiration: Yupp's VIBE scoring system, SciArena's meta-evaluation benchmark.

Every attention pattern (regardless of architecture) is scored on standardized dimensions: - Interpretability Score (0-100): how clearly does this pattern reveal model behavior? - Specialization Score (0-100): how distinct is this head from others? - Efficiency Score (0-100): how much information per parameter? - Stability Score (0-100): how consistent across different inputs?

These scores enable cross-architecture comparison — you can compare a BERT attention head with a GPT attention head on the same scale.

docs.title: 12. "Attention Feed" — Algorithmic Discovery Timeline
docs.text:
Inspiration: Nebils AI social network for humans, agents & models, MoltSocial unified feed, Folio intentional social sharing.

A personalized discovery feed showing: - "Trending": most starred/discussed attention patterns this week - "For You": ML-recommended patterns based on your interests - "Following": new posts from researchers you follow - "Challenges": active community challenges to participate in - "New Models": attention patterns from newly supported architectures

Each feed item is interactive — hover to preview the attention pattern, click to explore fully. The feed uses the same personalization approach as Imagen Network's "Grok-driven personalization engines for precise peer discovery in decentralized social ecosystems".

docs.title: 13. "Attention Stories" — Ephemeral Research Narratives
docs.text:
Inspiration: Instagram Stories, Kaggle notebook sharing, Folio intentional sharing.

Researchers create short, ephemeral narratives (3-10 frames) showing: - "Watch how attention shifts across layers →" - "Here's what happens when we ablate Head 7 →" - "Before vs. after compression →"

Each frame is an interactive attention visualization with text overlay. Stories appear at the top of the feed and expire after 7 days (or can be saved permanently as a "Research Highlight"). This encourages frequent, casual sharing of small discoveries.

docs.title: 14. "Attention Circles" — Interest-Based Research Groups
docs.text:
Inspiration: Nebils community building, Polis group consensus formation.

Users create or join Circles around specific topics: - "Induction Head Hunters" - "Vision Transformer Attention" - "Galerkin Attention Enthusiasts" - "Attention Pruning Research Group"

Circles have: - A shared feed of relevant attention patterns - Group challenges and discussions - Shared model access (members can pool GPU credits) - Circle reputation — top circles get featured on the platform

docs.title: 15. "Cite & Reference" — Academic Attribution System
docs.text:
Inspiration: Neuronpedia's research acceleration platform, PapersWithCode.

Every attention visualization can be cited: - A unique DOI-like identifier is generated - BibTeX citation is auto-generated - Citations are tracked and displayed (like Google Scholar) - "Cited by" links show which papers reference this pattern

This transforms attention exploration from casual browsing into citable research output — exactly as Neuronpedia aims to "accelerate interpretability researchers" by providing "a comprehensive reference and fast-feedback analysis platform".

docs.title: 16. "Attention Hunter" — Gamified Pattern Discovery Game
docs.text:
Inspiration: Kaggle progression tiers, Stack Overflow reputation, game-like visualization interactions.

A role-playing game where users earn XP for attention exploration: - Novice Explorer (0-100 XP): view 5 patterns, make 1 comment - Pattern Scout (100-500 XP): discover 10 distinct head types, create 3 posts - Head Hunter (500-2000 XP): find a novel pattern verified by community, win 1 challenge - Attention Sage (2000-5000 XP): curate a collection with 100+ followers, publish 50+ posts - Grandmaster (5000+ XP): top 10 on leaderboard, serve as challenge judge

The approach of "personifying visualization elements into dynamic game-like characters, adding narrative elements to the visualization and transforming it into a gamified experience" is already being explored in research.

docs.title: 17. "Daily Attention Puzzle" — Habit-Forming Mini-Challenge
docs.text:
Inspiration: Wordle/Heardle habit loops, Duolingo streaks.

Every day, a new mini-challenge: - Monday: "Guess the Head Type" — identify whether a head is positional, semantic, or delimiter - Tuesday: "Spot the Difference" — find what changed after ablation - Wednesday: "Match the Model" — match attention patterns to their architecture - Thursday: "Token Detective" — given attention weights, predict the input text - Friday: "Free Play" — most creative attention visualization wins

Users build streaks (consecutive days played). Streaks and scores are visible on their profile, encouraging daily return.

docs.title: 18. "Bounty Board" — Paid Attention Analysis Requests
docs.text:
Inspiration: Yupp's token-incentivized feedback marketplace, Bugcrowd/YesWeHack bounty models.

Researchers or companies post bounties for specific attention analysis tasks: - "Analyze the attention patterns of our fine-tuned model and identify redundant heads — $50" - "Compare attention across 3 model versions and write a report — $100" - "Create an interactive visualization dashboard for our model — $200"

Bounties are funded with platform credits or crypto. This creates a marketplace for interpretability expertise — like Yupp's "trustless AI feedback marketplace" where "diverse user feedback flows freely under blockchain and cryptocurrency economic incentives".

docs.title: 19. "Publish to Paper" — One-Click Research Output
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your existing paper LaTeX app, model card generation.

Any attention visualization can be exported as a paper-ready figure with one click: - Vector SVG for LaTeX papers - Interactive HTML for supplementary materials - Auto-generated figure caption describing the pattern - Methods section draft explaining how the visualization was created - Link to the live interactive version (QR code on the figure)

This connects directly to your paper app — the exported content opens in the LaTeX editor ready for submission.

docs.title: 20. "Train What You See" — Attention-to-Experiment Bridge
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your experiment launcher, Neuronpedia's fast-feedback analysis platform.

On any attention visualization, a "Train with This" button opens your experiment launcher pre-filled with: - The exact model and attention type shown - The sample text as calibration data - Suggested experiment name: "Reproduce attention pattern [ID] on [Model]" - The pattern's metadata as experiment notes

After training, the actual attention patterns from the trained model are automatically compared with the original visualization, showing how well the experiment reproduced the pattern. This creates a closed loop: explore → experiment → verify.

docs.title: 21. "Attention Portfolio" — Researcher Showcase
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your existing portfolios app, GitHub profile page, Kaggle profile.

Every researcher has a public Attention Portfolio showing: - Published patterns (with star counts and view counts) - Collections curated (thematic groupings of patterns) - Challenges won and badges earned - Reputation score and progression tier - Activity graph (GitHub-style contribution chart) - Expertise tags (e.g., "Induction Head Expert," "Vision Attention Specialist")

The portfolio is embeddable on personal websites and serves as a professional credential for interpretability researchers.

docs.title: 22. "Attention API" — Programmatic Access for Agents
docs.text:
Inspiration: Neuronpedia's free APIs/tools, Anthropic Circuit Tracer's open-source library, AI agent integration.

A public REST API (and Python SDK) allowing: - AI agents to query attention patterns programmatically - Automated analysis pipelines to run attention diagnostics on models - Third-party tools to embed attention visualizations - Bulk export for meta-analysis research

This follows Neuronpedia's model of providing "a suite of free APIs/tools that accelerate white-box understanding and experimentation of neural networks" — extended to your full attention visualization platform.

docs.title: 🧭 Zone 1: Global Navigation & Context Bar — Complete Implementation Specification
Overview
docs.text:
Zone 1 is the persistent header that spans the full width of the dashboard at the very top of the viewport (typically 56–64px height on desktop, 48–56px on mobile). It serves three critical functions simultaneously: (1) it informs the researcher exactly what they are looking at at all times, (2) it enables rapid switching between models, attention types, layers, heads, and input texts without losing context, and (3) it provides spatial orientation through breadcrumb navigation plus a temporal trail of past explorations. The bar must remain visible at all times (position: sticky, top: 0, z-index: 50) regardless of how far the user scrolls into the visualization canvas or analytics panels below.

The header follows an inverted‑L navigation pattern widely used in complex dashboards and research platforms: global navigation links on the left, contextual controls in the center, and user/account actions on the right. This is the same pattern employed by the New York Times, SAP Analytics Cloud, and enterprise observability platforms like Grafana.

docs.title: 1.1 Purpose & UX Philosophy
docs.text: When a researcher is deep in layer 7, head 3 of a Galerkin‑attention variant of BERT‑base, analyzing a specific input sentence, they must never wonder "Which model am I looking at?" or "What text is this?" This information must be immediately visible, glanceable, and always accurate. Research shows that dashboards lacking context "merely present data; they do not provide meaningful insights" — context bars improve "context observability by making the currently active dataset/model state explicit in the UI".

docs.title: 1.2 Visual Layout & Anatomy
docs.text:
The context header occupies the center section of the global navigation bar, between the breadcrumb trail (left) and the user menu (right). It displays as a horizontal chain of labeled chips/badges separated by subtle dividers (vertical pipe or chevron). Each chip is independently clickable and hoverable.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🏠 Home  >  Attention Lab  >  BERT-base  │  Attention: Galerkin (r=64) │ │
│                                         │  Text: "The quick brown..."  │ │
│                                         │  Layer 5  │  Head 7          │ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chip design specifications: - Background: bg-white/5 (glass effect), with a border border-white/10 for definition. - Padding: px-3 py-1.5 for comfortable click targets (minimum 32px height for accessibility). - Typography: The label portion (e.g., "Model:") uses text-[10px] font-bold text-slate-500 uppercase tracking-widest. The value portion (e.g., "BERT-base-uncased") uses text-sm font-semibold text-white. - Dividers: A subtle │ character or a 1px vertical line in border-white/10. - Hover state: hover:bg-white/10 transition-colors duration-150. - Active/Click state: A brief scale animation (active:scale-95) provides tactile feedback.

docs.title: Model Chip
docs.text:
• Display format: Model: BERT-base-uncased or Model: GPT-2 (fine-tuned).
  • Click behavior: Opens a compact dropdown listing the user's recently used models (last 5), models from their model_versioning registry, and a search input that queries HuggingFace Hub. This is the same model selector described in Feature 2, but embedded inline for quick access.
  • Tooltip: Hovering shows the full model name, parameter count, and last used date.
  • Truncation: If the model name exceeds 25 characters, it is truncated with an ellipsis (…), and the full name appears in the tooltip.

docs.title: Attention Type Chip
docs.text:
• Display format: Attention: Galerkin (rank=64) or Attention: Standard MHA (12 heads).
  • Click behavior: Opens a dropdown of all registered attention types from the ATTENTION_REGISTRY (Galerkin, TLinFormer, PADRe, Spectraformer, RPC, FUSIONATTN, etc.). Each option shows a one‑line description (e.g., "Galerkin: Petrov‑Galerkin projection with random sketching, O(N·r·D)").
  • Visual indicator: The attention type chip has a colored left border (3px) that matches the attention type's designated color in the system. For example, Galerkin = blue, TLinFormer = green, PADRe = purple. This color persists throughout the dashboard, creating a consistent visual language.

docs.title: Text Input Chip
docs.text:
• Display format: Text: "The quick brown fox jumps over..." (truncated to 30 characters).
  • Click behavior: Expands into an inline text input (replacing the chip with an <input> field) where the user can type or paste any text. Pressing Enter triggers re‑analysis. The input supports up to 512 tokens, with a character counter.
  • Recent texts: A small dropdown arrow reveals the last 10 analyzed texts, stored in localStorage per user.

docs.title: Layer & Head Chips
docs.text:
• Display format: Layer 5 and Head 7 as two separate chips, visually grouped together with a lighter background.
  • Interaction: Each chip is a stepper control — clicking reveals tiny ‑ and + buttons that appear on hover, allowing quick increment/decrement without opening the full control panel. For power users, the arrow keys (← →) change the layer, and (↑ ↓) change the head when the visualization canvas is focused.
  • Visual feedback: When the user changes the layer via the Zone 4 slider, the Layer chip updates instantly with a subtle pulse animation (scale 1.05 for 200ms) to draw attention to the change.

docs.title: 1.4 Responsive Behavior
docs.text: Viewport Width Behavior ≥ 1280px (Desktop) All chips displayed inline with full labels 1024–1279px (Tablet Landscape) Labels shortened: "Model:" → icon only, values preserved 768–1023px (Tablet Portrait) Chips collapse into a single dropdown: "BERT-base · Galerkin · Layer 5 · Head 7" with a dropdown arrow. Click expands all chips vertically. < 768px (Mobile) Only the most critical info shown: model name + layer/head. Full context accessible via a "Details" button that opens a bottom sheet.

docs.title: 1.5 Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• State management: The context state (model, attention type, text, layer, head) is stored in a Zustand store (useAttentionContext). All visualization components subscribe to this store. When any value changes, only the affected components re‑render.
  • URL synchronization: Every context change updates the URL query parameters (?model=bert-base&attn=galerkin&layer=5&head=7&text=...). This makes every exploration shareable via URL. On page load, the URL is parsed to restore the previous state.
  • Debouncing: Text input changes are debounced at 500ms to avoid excessive re‑computation while the user is typing.

docs.title: 1.6 Accessibility
docs.text:
• All chips are <button> elements with aria-label attributes (e.g., aria-label="Current model: BERT-base-uncased. Click to change.").
  • The context bar is reachable via the Tab key as the first focusable element on the page (after a "Skip to content" link).
  • Screen readers announce context changes via aria-live="polite" regions.

docs.title: 2.1 Purpose & Design Philosophy
docs.text: Researchers need to rapidly compare attention patterns across different models and attention mechanisms. The Quick‑Switch Model Selector enables changing the model without leaving the dashboard — the entire visualization updates reactively. This is inspired by Neuronpedia's approach where "you can now host Neuronpedia yourself, with your own model and data" and HuggingFace's model discovery interface, adapted for the specific needs of attention visualization comparison.

docs.title: 2.2 Architecture & Component Tree
docs.text:
ModelSelector (parent container)
├── AttentionTypeSelector (dropdown)
├── ModelSourceTabs (3 tabs: "Your Models" | "HuggingFace Hub" | "Upload")
├── SearchInput (text input with autocomplete)
├── ModelList (scrollable list of model cards)
│   └── ModelCard (individual model entry)
│       ├── ModelIcon (architecture indicator)
│       ├── ModelName + Version
│       ├── ModelMeta (parameter count, last used, attention types supported)
│       └── QuickActions (⭐ Favorite, 📊 Compare, ℹ️ Info)
└── SelectedModelPreview (confirmation footer)

docs.title: 2.3 The Dropdown Trigger
docs.text:
The dropdown trigger is integrated into the Model Chip in the context bar (see Feature 1). Additionally, a dedicated "Change Model" button sits in Zone 4 (Control Panel). Both open the same dropdown.

Trigger appearance: - Default state: The model chip (described above). - When dropdown is open: The chip gains a ring-2 ring-neon-blue/50 border and a subtle chevron rotation animation.

docs.title: 2.4 Dropdown Panel Anatomy
docs.text:
The dropdown is a floating panel (not a native <select>) rendered via a portal to avoid z‑index issues. It appears directly below the trigger with a smooth scale+fade animation (200ms, transform-origin: top).

Dimensions: 480px wide × 520px max‑height on desktop. On mobile, it becomes a full‑screen bottom sheet.

Internal structure (top to bottom):

docs.title: Tab Bar: "Your Models" | "HuggingFace Hub" | "Upload"
docs.text:
• Three tabs that filter the model source.
  • Active tab has a border-b-2 border-neon-blue indicator.
  • "Your Models" shows models from the user's model_versioning registry and recent experiments.
  • "HuggingFace Hub" queries the HF Hub API in real time.
  • "Upload" opens a file picker for local model weights.

docs.title: Search Bar
docs.text:
• A text input with a magnifying glass icon on the left.
  • Autocomplete suggestions appear after 3 characters typed.
  • Debounced at 300ms for HF Hub queries.
  • Supports filtering by: model name, architecture type, parameter count range, task type (classification, generation, etc.).

docs.title: Model List
docs.text:
• Virtualized list (using react-window or @tanstack/react-virtual) to handle hundreds of models smoothly.
  • Each row is a ModelCard component (described below).
  • Infinite scroll for HuggingFace results (loads 20 at a time).
  • Loading state shows skeleton cards (shimmer effect).

docs.title: ModelCard Design
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [🧠]  BERT-base-uncased                   ⭐  📊  ℹ️    │
│       110M params · Used 3 days ago                      │
│       Supported: MHA, Galerkin, PADRe, TLinFormer        │
│       Tasks: Classification, NER, QA                      │
│       ───────────────────────────────────────────────     │
│       [Select]  [Compare with current]                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Card anatomy: - Left icon: Indicates model architecture (🧠 = Transformer, 👁️ = Vision, etc.). - Model name: Bold, white text. Truncated with ellipsis if needed. - Meta line: Gray text showing parameter count, last used date. - Supported attention types: Small colored badges for each supported attention mechanism. - Tasks: Small tags for task compatibility. - Action buttons: "Select" (primary, blue) and "Compare with current" (secondary, outline). The "Compare" option opens a side‑by‑side view with the currently loaded model.

docs.title: Selected Model Preview Footer
docs.text:
When a model is selected but not yet confirmed, a sticky footer appears at the bottom of the dropdown: 

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Selected: Galerkin (rank=64) · BERT-base-uncased         │
│ This will re‑compute attention for the current text.     │
│ [Cancel]                              [Apply & Visualize]│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 2.5 Attention Type Quick‑Switch
docs.text:
Next to the model selector, a separate dropdown (or integrated tab) lists all registered attention types. Each option shows:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● Galerkin Attention                                 │
│   Petrov‑Galerkin projection with random sketching   │
│   Complexity: O(N·r·D) · Rank: 64                    │
│   Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14906            │
│   ───────────────────────────────────────────────     │
│ ● TLinFormer                                         │
│   Low‑rank projections for K and V                   │
│   Complexity: O(N·r·D) · Rank: 64                    │
│   ───────────────────────────────────────────────     │
│ ● PADRe (Polynomial Attention)                       │
│   Polynomial kernel: (1 + S/p)^p                     │
│   Order: 2 · Temperature: 1.0                        │
│   ───────────────────────────────────────────────     │
│ ...                                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Each attention type entry includes: - A colored dot matching the attention type's system color. - Name (bold). - One‑line description of the mechanism. - Complexity notation. - Configurable parameters (rank, order, temperature) that can be adjusted inline. - Link to paper/arXiv (external link icon).

docs.title: 2.6 Loading States & Transitions
docs.text: When a new model is selected: 1. The dropdown closes with a fade animation. 2. The Model Chip in the context bar shows a pulsing skeleton (shimmer effect) for 200–500ms while the model loads. 3. All visualization panels (Zone 2) show a loading overlay with a progress indicator: "Loading BERT‑base weights… (34MB / 440MB)". 4. If the model is already cached (in IndexedDB or browser cache), loading is near‑instantaneous with a success toast: "Model loaded in 0.3s". 5. If loading fails, an error toast appears: "Failed to load model. Check your connection or try a different model." with a retry button.

docs.title: 2.7 Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
• Model caching: Loaded models are cached in IndexedDB (via transformers.js or a custom caching layer). Subsequent loads of the same model are instant.
  • Lazy loading: Attention types are lazy‑loaded. Only the currently selected attention type's computation runs.
  • Web Worker: Heavy attention computation (matrix multiplication, softmax) runs in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread.
  • Optimistic UI: The context bar updates immediately (optimistic), then the visualization catches up. If the computation fails, the context bar reverts.

docs.title: 2.8 Accessibility
docs.text:
• The dropdown is fully keyboard‑navigable: Arrow keys move between options, Enter selects, Escape closes.
  • aria-expanded on the trigger button, aria-selected on the active option, role="listbox" on the dropdown.
  • Focus is trapped within the dropdown while it's open.

docs.title: 3.1 Purpose & UX Philosophy
docs.text:
Researchers exploring attention patterns often follow a non‑linear path: they might start with BERT‑base, switch to a fine‑tuned variant, compare two layers, jump to a different attention type, and then want to return to a previous view. The breadcrumb trail provides spatial orientation (where am I in the exploration?), while the history panel provides temporal navigation (how did I get here?).

This dual‑navigation system follows the pattern established by data analysis tools where "each 'crumb' in the breadcrumb path UI control may indicate a summary of a respective data query and/or filter submitted over the course of the current data analysis path" — enabling users to "jump from any first" step to any later step instantly.

docs.title: Visual Layout
docs.text:
The breadcrumb trail occupies the leftmost section of the navigation bar. It displays as a horizontal chain of clickable segments separated by chevron arrows (› or /).

🏠 Home  ›  Attention Lab  ›  BERT-base  ›  Layer 5  ›  Head 7

docs.title: Crumb Anatomy
docs.text: Each crumb is composed of: - An optional icon (home icon for the first crumb). - A text label (truncated to 20 characters max). - A separator (chevron › or forward slash /).

docs.title: Crumb States
docs.text: State Appearance Behavior Default text-slate-400 hover:text-white Click navigates to that level Current (last crumb) text-white font-semibold Not clickable (already here) Truncated (middle) text-slate-400 with … Click expands to show hidden crumbs Hover text-neon-blue underline Shows tooltip with full path

docs.title: Responsive Truncation
docs.text: When the breadcrumb trail exceeds the available width: 1. Middle crumbs are replaced with a … button. 2. Clicking … expands a dropdown showing the hidden crumbs. 3. On mobile (< 768px), only the current crumb is shown, with a back arrow (←) that navigates up one level.

docs.title: Breadcrumb Levels
docs.text:
The breadcrumb hierarchy follows the natural attention exploration path:

Level 1: Home (dashboard)
Level 2: Attention Lab (the attention dashboard itself)
Level 3: Model name (e.g., "BERT-base-uncased")
Level 4: Layer number (e.g., "Layer 5")
Level 5: Head number (e.g., "Head 7")

Additional optional levels: - Attention Type: Inserted between Level 2 and Level 3 if the user explicitly selects a non‑default attention type. - Comparison Mode: A special crumb "Compare: BERT vs GPT‑2" appears when in comparison view. - Text Preview: The first 15 characters of the input text can appear as a crumb if the text was explicitly set.

docs.title: Trigger
docs.text: A clock icon (🕐) with a badge showing the number of history entries sits at the right edge of the breadcrumb area. Clicking it opens the history panel.

docs.title: Panel Anatomy
docs.text:
The history panel is a dropdown/floating panel (320px wide, 480px max‑height) that appears below the breadcrumb.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 📜 Exploration History           [Clear] │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ● BERT-base / Layer 5 / Head 7          │
│   Galerkin (r=64) · 2 min ago           │
│   ───────────────────────────────────    │
│ ○ GPT-2 / Layer 3 / Head 2              │
│   Standard MHA · 8 min ago              │
│   ───────────────────────────────────    │
│ ○ BERT-base / Layer 5 / Head 3          │
│   PADRe (order=2) · 15 min ago          │
│   ───────────────────────────────────    │
│ ○ BERT-base / All Layers (Model View)   │
│   TLinFormer (r=32) · 22 min ago        │
│   ───────────────────────────────────    │
│ ...                                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: History Entry Anatomy
docs.text: Each history entry shows: - A colored dot indicating the attention type. - The model name, layer, and head (or view type). - The attention type and its configuration parameters. - A relative timestamp ("2 min ago", "1 hour ago"). - A preview thumbnail (tiny heatmap preview, 48×48px) generated at the time of the exploration. This thumbnail is stored in localStorage as a base64 data URL.

docs.title: Interactions
docs.text:
• Click an entry: Restores that exact exploration state (model, attention type, layer, head, text, view mode, zoom level). The entire dashboard updates to match.
  • Star (⭐) an entry: Saves it to "Saved Explorations" (persisted to the backend via the notes system). Saved explorations appear at the top of the history panel with a gold border.
  • Compare (📊) : Opens the selected entry in a side‑by‑side comparison view with the current exploration.
  • Delete (✕) : Removes the entry from history.
  • Clear All: Removes all history entries (with confirmation dialog).

docs.title: History Persistence
docs.text:
• localStorage: The last 50 explorations are stored in localStorage per browser. This survives page refreshes and tab closes.
  • Backend (optional) : If the user is authenticated, history entries are synced to the backend via the activity feed, enabling cross‑device history.
  • Export: Users can export their history as JSON or CSV for external analysis.

docs.title: 3.4 Back/Forward Navigation
docs.text:
In addition to the breadcrumb and history panel, the browser's native Back and Forward buttons are fully supported. Each context change pushes a new entry to the browser history stack via history.pushState(). This means:

  • Pressing the browser Back button returns to the previous attention exploration.
  • Pressing Forward returns to the later exploration.
  • The URL is always shareable and bookmarkable.

docs.title: 3.5 Related Explorations Panel
docs.text:
At the bottom of the history panel, a "Related Explorations" section appears. This uses collaborative filtering to suggest:

  • "Other researchers who viewed this pattern also explored…"
  • "Similar patterns" (based on attention pattern similarity metrics).
  • "Top‑starred patterns with this model".

Each suggestion is a clickable card that loads that exploration directly.

docs.title: 3.6 Edge Cases & Error States
docs.text: Scenario Behavior Empty history (first‑time user) Shows a friendly illustration: "Your exploration history will appear here. Start by selecting a model and text!" with a CTA button. History entry references a deleted model The entry is grayed out with a "Model no longer available" badge. The preview thumbnail remains visible. localStorage full Oldest entries are automatically evicted. A notification appears: "Your oldest exploration history has been cleared to save space." Browser in incognito mode History is session‑only. A banner at the top of the panel notes: "History is temporary in this session." Corrupted history entry Skipped gracefully. The entry shows "⚠️ Could not restore this exploration" and can be deleted.

docs.title: 3.7 Accessibility for History
docs.text:
• The history panel is opened via a button with aria-label="Exploration history" and aria-expanded.
  • Each history entry is a <button> with aria-label="Restore exploration: BERT-base Layer 5 Head 7, Galerkin attention, 2 minutes ago".
  • The clear history button requires confirmation via a modal dialog to prevent accidental data loss.

docs.title: 4.1 How Zone 1 Communicates with Other Zones
docs.text:
Zone 1 acts as the single source of truth for the current exploration context. All other zones subscribe to this state:

Zone 1 (Context Bar)
    │
    ├── Updates ──→ Zone 2 (Visualization Canvas) — re‑renders attention view
    │               Zone 3 (Math Panel) — re‑renders equations with new values
    │               Zone 4 (Control Panel) — syncs sliders and selectors
    │               Zone 5 (Analytics) — re‑computes statistics
    │               Zone 6 (Interpretability) — re‑runs ablation analysis
    │               Zone 7 (Social) — updates share links and metadata
    │               Zone 8 (Gamification) — triggers XP events

The communication is handled through: 1. Zustand store (useAttentionContext) for synchronous state. 2. URL query parameters for shareability and browser history. 3. WebSocket (optional) for collaborative sessions — when one user changes the context, it syncs to others.

docs.title: 4.2 State Contract
docs.text:
The context state object follows this TypeScript interface:

interface AttentionContext {
  // Model
  modelId: string;               // e.g., "bert-base-uncased"
  modelSource: 'registry' | 'huggingface' | 'upload';
  modelVersion?: string;         // from model_versioning

  // Attention
  attentionType: string;         // e.g., "galerkin", "padre"
  attentionConfig: Record<string, any>;  // e.g., { rank: 64, order: 2 }

  // Text
  inputText: string;
  tokens: string[];

  // Navigation
  selectedLayer: number;
  selectedHead: number;
  activeView: 'head' | 'model' | 'heatmap' | '3d' | 'sankey' | 'qk';

  // Comparison (optional)
  compareModelId?: string;
  compareAttentionType?: string;

  // Metadata
  lastModified: number;          // timestamp
  explorationId: string;         // unique ID for this exploration
}

docs.title: 4.3 Performance Budget
docs.text: Metric Target Context bar initial render < 16ms (one frame) Model switch response time (cached) < 100ms to update context bar Model switch response time (uncached) < 3s with progress indicator URL update after context change < 50ms History panel open < 100ms Breadcrumb update < 16ms

docs.title: 4.4 Testing Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Context bar remains sticky when scrolling to bottom of analytics panel
  • [ ] All chips are keyboard‑accessible (Tab, Enter, Escape)
  • [ ] Screen reader announces context changes
  • [ ] URL updates correctly on every context change
  • [ ] Browser Back/Forward correctly restores previous states
  • [ ] Model switching works when offline (cached models)
  • [ ] History persists across page refreshes
  • [ ] Mobile responsive: chips collapse correctly
  • [ ] Color contrast ratios meet WCAG AA standards (4.5:1 for text)
  • [ ] No layout shift when chips update (stable dimensions)
  • [ ] History panel handles 500+ entries without performance degradation
  • [ ] Breadcrumb correctly truncates on narrow viewports
  • [ ] Compare mode breadcrumb appears correctly
  • [ ] Attention type colors are consistent across all zones
  • [ ] "Clear history" confirmation dialog works
  • [ ] Starred explorations sync to backend
  • [ ] Related explorations load without blocking the UI
  • [ ] Error states (model load failure) are handled gracefully
  • [ ] First‑time user sees appropriate empty states

docs.title: 5. Summary
docs.text:
Zone 1 is the orchestrator of the entire attention dashboard. It provides three essential navigation functions:

Feature Core Value Key Innovation Persistent Context Header Never lose track of what you're looking at Live‑editable chips that serve as both display and control Quick‑Switch Model Selector Change models without leaving the dashboard Integrated attention type selector with complexity annotations and paper links Breadcrumb + History Navigate spatially and temporally Dual navigation with starred explorations, comparison mode, and cross‑device sync

Together, these three features ensure that researchers can explore attention patterns across dozens of models and attention mechanisms without ever feeling lost — while maintaining the ability to backtrack, compare, and share their discoveries at any moment.

docs.title: 🎨 Zone 2: Attention Canvas — Complete Advanced Implementation Specification
Overview
docs.text:
Zone 2 is the central visual real estate of the entire attention dashboard — occupying approximately 65–75% of the viewport width on desktop (the remaining space divided between Zone 4 Control Panel at left and Zone 5/6 analytics at right). It is the primary space where researchers see, touch, and manipulate attention data through six integrated visualization modalities plus two supplementary overlay modes. The canvas operates on a unified rendering pipeline that shares attention tensor data, color scales, and interaction state across all views, ensuring that switching between views is instantaneous (under 100ms) and maintains the user's exploration context.

The rendering architecture follows a layered compositing model inspired by modern game engines and professional visualization tools like ParaView and Helios-Web. Each visualization view is a self-contained React component that receives a shared AttentionData prop from the Zustand store, but internally manages its own WebGL/Canvas/SVG rendering context, camera state, and interaction handlers. A ViewSynchronizer middleware ensures that selections (highlighted tokens, focused heads, brushed regions) propagate bidirectionally across all active views.

docs.title: 1.1 Multi-Backend Rendering Pipeline
docs.text:
Before detailing individual views, Zone 2 is built on a tiered rendering architecture that selects the optimal graphics backend based on data complexity, viewport size, and device capability:

Rendering Tier Backend Use Case Max Data Points Tier 1: SVG D3.js + React Head View (small matrices ≤ 128 tokens), Sankey, Model View ~16,000 elements Tier 2: Canvas 2D HTML5 Canvas + custom render loop Head View (medium matrices ≤ 512 tokens), Heatmap, Scatter ~250,000 elements Tier 3: WebGL 2.0 Three.js via React Three Fiber 3D Topology Map, large scatter plots, particle systems ~5,000,000 vertices Tier 4: WebGPU Custom WGSL shaders (fallback to WebGL) Ultra-large attention matrices (>2048 tokens), real-time 3D with compute shaders ~50,000,000+ vertices

The pipeline auto-selects the tier based on a capability detection routine that runs once on dashboard mount: it probes navigator.gpu for WebGPU support, checks WEBGL_debug_renderer_info for GPU model, and measures frame timing with a calibration render. The tier can be manually overridden in Zone 4 controls.

Inspired by the GPT2-WebGL project that demonstrated "GPU-accelerated transformer model inference directly in the browser" via WebGL shader programs implementing matrix multiplication, layer normalization, and attention computation, and Helios-Web's approach to "GPU-based rendering for real-time visualization and interactive analysis of massive-scale networks and high-dimensional embeddings".

docs.title: 1.2 Shared Color Infrastructure
docs.text:
All views share a unified color system with multiple palettes selectable from Zone 4:

  • Heat (Default): A perceptually uniform diverging scale from dark navy (#1e293b) through orange (#ffa94d) to bright red (#ff6b6b), designed using the CIELAB color space for equal perceptual steps.
  • Viridis: The matplotlib default — perceptually uniform, colorblind-friendly, works in grayscale printing.
  • Blues: Single-hue sequential for minimalist displays.
  • Spectral: Full rainbow for detecting fine-grained differences (not recommended for accessibility).
  • Custom: User-defined via a color ramp editor (drag color stops, save presets).

All color scales are computed as 1D lookup textures uploaded to the GPU, enabling O(1) color mapping for millions of data points at 60fps.

docs.title: 1.3 View Synchronizer — Bidirectional Linked Highlighting
docs.text:
The ViewSynchronizer is the connective tissue between all six views. It maintains a shared selection state:

SelectionState {
  highlightedTokens: Set<number>       // token indices
  focusedHead: { layer: number, head: number } | null
  brushedRegion: { queryStart, queryEnd, keyStart, keyEnd } | null
  hoveredCell: { query: number, key: number } | null
  activeView: 'head' | 'model' | 'heatmap' | '3d' | 'sankey' | 'qk'
}

When a user hovers over token pair (3,7) in the Head View heatmap, the Synchronizer dispatches this event. The 3D View simultaneously highlights the connection between token sphere 3 and token sphere 7 with a glowing pulse. The Sankey View thickens the corresponding flow. The Q/K Joint View enlarges the dots for tokens 3 and 7 and draws a line between them. All views respond within one frame (16ms), creating the illusion of a single, cohesive visualization system.

docs.title: 2. Feature 4: Head View — BertViz‑Style Interactive Heatmap
2.1 Purpose & Core Design
docs.text: The Head View is the microscope of attention analysis — it shows exactly which tokens attend to which other tokens for a specific attention head in a specific layer. It is the most frequently used view (research from BertViz usage patterns shows ~60% of analysis sessions spend most time here). The design follows BertViz's core principle: "an interactive tool for visualizing attention in Transformer language models such as BERT, GPT2, or T5" that "focuses on one or more attention heads within a layer, exposing token-to-token attention weights".

docs.title: 2.2 Visual Layout
