docs.text:
The heatmap is rendered as an N×N matrix where N = number of tokens. The horizontal axis represents key tokens (what is being attended to), and the vertical axis represents query tokens (what is doing the attending). Each cell at position (i, j) represents "How much does query token i attend to key token j?"

Cell rendering: Each cell is a rectangle (size dynamically computed as min(48px, max(20px, canvasWidth / N))). The fill color is computed via the active color scale. Cells also have a subtle border radius (2px) for visual softness and a 1px gap between cells to prevent moiré patterns at high densities. Above 128×128 tokens, cells become 1px with no gap, and the visualization transitions to a pixel-perfect heatmap where individual cells are not distinguishable but patterns emerge at the macro level — like viewing a high-resolution thermal image.

Token labels: Token text appears along both axes. On the vertical (query) axis, labels are right-aligned. On the horizontal (key) axis, labels are rotated -45° and anchored at the top. Labels are truncated to 8 characters with ellipsis. Hovering a label shows the full token text in a tooltip. Labels use font-size: 9px, font-family: monospace, fill: #94a3b8.

Diagonal indicator: The diagonal (where query_index = key_index, representing self-attention) is highlighted with a subtle dashed line at 15% opacity. A toggle in Zone 4 can mask the diagonal to reveal off-diagonal patterns more clearly — a common analytical need since self-attention often dominates.

Color legend: A horizontal gradient bar at the bottom-right of the heatmap shows the mapping from 0.0 (color-scale minimum) to 1.0 (color-scale maximum). Tick marks at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 with numerical labels.

docs.title: 2.3 Interaction Model
docs.text:
The interaction model follows Ben Shneiderman's visual information seeking mantra: "Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand."

Overview: The initial render shows the full N×N matrix scaled to fit the viewport. The researcher can immediately see macro patterns — diagonal dominance, block structures, columnar attention (certain key tokens receiving attention from many queries), and row patterns (certain query tokens distributing attention broadly).

Zoom and Pan: Scroll wheel zooms in/out centered on the cursor position. The zoom range is 0.25× to 10×. At high zoom levels, individual cells become large enough to display numerical values inside them (values appear at cell size ≥ 32px). Pinch-to-zoom on touch devices. Click-drag pans the viewport. A minimap in the corner (like VS Code's minimap) shows the full matrix with the current viewport rectangle indicated, enabling rapid navigation of large matrices.

Details-on-demand — Hover: When the cursor hovers over a cell, three things happen simultaneously: (1) the cell gains a white 1.5px stroke and slight scale-up (1.05× for 150ms), (2) a tooltip appears showing: query_token → key_token : weight = 0.0423, and (3) the corresponding row and column headers highlight in bold white. The row and column are also semi-highlighted with a 10% white overlay, making it easy to see the full attention pattern for both the query and key tokens.

Details-on-demand — Click Selection: Clicking a cell selects the query token (the row). The entire row is outlined in white (2px stroke). All other rows dim to 30% opacity. This isolates the attention pattern for one query token, answering "Where is this token looking?" The selected row also triggers a cross-view highlight via the ViewSynchronizer — the selected token is highlighted in the 3D View, Sankey, and Q/K Joint View.

Double-click Selection: Double-clicking a cell selects both the query AND key tokens, showing the intersection: all query tokens that attend to the selected key token AND all key tokens that the selected query token attends to. This creates a crosshair highlight pattern on the heatmap.

Range Selection (Brush): Click-drag across multiple cells creates a rectangular selection. The selected region is highlighted, and the Synchronizer broadcasts the brushed range to other views. This enables "What's happening in this cluster of attention?" analysis.

Right-click Context Menu: Right-clicking any cell opens a context menu with options: "Pin this cell," "Add annotation," "Copy attention value," "Show in Q/K Joint View," "Trace causal path," and "Compare with head X."

docs.title: 2.4 Multi-Head Overlay Mode
docs.text:
A toggle in Zone 4 enables multi-head overlay mode. Instead of showing a single head, the heatmap shows an aggregate of multiple heads. Users select heads via checkboxes in the Control Panel. The overlay uses:

  • Average mode: Each cell shows the mean attention weight across selected heads. Tooltip shows individual head values: H3: 0.04, H5: 0.12, H7: 0.08 → avg: 0.08.
  • Maximum mode: Each cell shows the maximum attention weight across selected heads, colored by which head contributed the max (a small colored dot in the corner of each cell indicates the winning head).
  • Variance mode: Each cell shows the variance (or standard deviation) across heads, colored by a separate "agreement" scale — blue for high agreement (low variance), red for disagreement (high variance). This reveals which token pairs different heads agree or disagree on.

docs.title: 2.5 Diff Mode
docs.text: A comparison mode that shows the difference between two attention heads (or the same head across two models). Cells are colored by a diverging scale: blue for "Head A attends more," red for "Head B attends more," white for no difference. A summary statistic panel shows: Jensen-Shannon divergence, correlation coefficient, and "top-10 most different token pairs."

docs.title: 2.6 Performance Optimization
docs.text:
For large matrices (>256×256), the heatmap uses level-of-detail (LOD) rendering:

  • Zoomed out (viewing the full matrix): Cells are rendered as a single WebGL texture quad with the attention matrix uploaded as a float texture. The GPU interpolates between texels. This renders in a single draw call regardless of matrix size.
  • Zoomed in (viewing a small region): Only the visible cells are rendered as individual SVG rects or canvas draw calls. The number of rendered elements is bounded by viewport size, not matrix size.
  • Transition: The transition between LOD levels is seamless — at zoom level 2×, the system cross-fades between the texture-based overview and the geometry-based detail view over 200ms.

This approach, inspired by the GPU-accelerated heatmap generation that "allows for real-time generation of attention maps for 3D models" and GPT2-WebGL's shader-based approach, enables smooth 60fps interaction even with 2048×2048 attention matrices.

docs.title: 2.7 Export Capabilities
docs.text:
The Head View supports multiple export formats:

  • SVG: Vector export for inclusion in LaTeX papers. Includes embedded CSS for consistent rendering. The exported SVG preserves the interactive tooltip data as <title> elements.
  • PNG: High-resolution raster export (up to 4K) for presentations and social media.
  • CSV: Raw attention matrix data for external analysis in Python/R.
  • JSON: Full attention data with metadata (model, layer, head, tokens, timestamps) for reproducibility.

docs.title: 3. Feature 5: Model View — Bird's‑Eye Across All Layers × Heads
3.1 Purpose & Core Design
docs.text:
The Model View provides a macroscopic perspective — it simultaneously shows every attention head across every layer, enabling researchers to quickly identify patterns, outliers, and structural properties of the attention mechanism as a whole. It follows Dodrio's design principle of "tightly integrating an overview that summarizes the roles of different attention heads".

This view answers questions like: "Which layers have the most specialized heads?", "Are there layers where all heads behave similarly?", "How does head diversity change across layers?", and "Where are the induction heads located?"

docs.title: 3.2 Visual Encoding
docs.text:
The Model View is a compact grid where:

  • X-axis: Head index (0 to H-1, where H = number of heads, typically 12)
  • Y-axis: Layer index (0 to L-1, where L = number of layers, typically 6 or 12)

Each cell in this grid represents one attention head. The cell encodes four dimensions of information simultaneously:

  1. Size (area) = Head Importance Score. More important heads (those whose ablation causes larger output change) are represented by larger squares. Size ranges from 50% (least important) to 100% (most important) of the cell's available space.

  2. Color (hue) = Head Specialization Type. A classification algorithm (based on attention pattern clustering) assigns each head to a category: Positional Heads (blue), Semantic Heads (red), Delimiter/Punctuation Heads (green), Induction Heads (gold), Broad-Context Heads (purple), and Unclassified (gray).

  3. Brightness (value) = Head Diversity Score. How different is this head's pattern from other heads in the same layer? Brighter = more unique/distinctive. Darker = more similar to others (potentially redundant).

  4. Border thickness = Confidence in the classification. Thicker border = higher confidence (the system is sure this is an induction head). Thin or no border = low confidence (the head's pattern is ambiguous).

docs.title: 3.3 Interaction Model
docs.text:
Hover: Hovering over a cell shows a tooltip with: Layer X, Head Y, Type: Induction Head (confidence: 87%), Importance: 0.78, Diversity: 0.63, Top attended token pair: "the → cat" (weight: 0.34).

Hover preview: A miniature heatmap (64×64px thumbnail) appears as a floating tooltip next to the cursor, showing the actual attention pattern for that head. This allows rapid scanning without clicking — the researcher can move their mouse across the grid and see each head's pattern in quick succession.

Click: Clicking a cell zooms into the Head View (Feature 4) for that specific head. The transition is animated: the clicked cell expands from its grid position to fill the canvas, while the grid fades out. This creates a smooth "zoom into detail" experience.

Shift+Click: Adds the head to a multi-select set (up to 8 heads). Selected heads are highlighted with a glowing border. The user can then choose "Compare Selected" (shows side-by-side heatmaps) or "Overlay Selected" (aggregates them in the Head View).

Layer-level interactions: Clicking a layer label on the Y-axis selects all heads in that layer, enabling layer-level analysis. A right-click on a layer label shows layer statistics: mean importance, mean diversity, entropy distribution, and head type composition.

Brush selection: Click-drag across multiple cells selects a rectangular region of heads. The analytics panel (Zone 5) updates to show aggregated statistics for the selected region.

docs.title: 3.4 Supplementary Views
docs.text:
Head Similarity Matrix: A toggle switches the Model View to show an H×H matrix (where H = total heads across all layers = L × H_per_layer). Each cell shows the similarity (1 - Jensen-Shannon divergence) between two heads' attention patterns. This reveals clusters of similar heads and identifies truly unique heads. The similarity matrix is reorderable via hierarchical clustering — drag a dendrogram to reorder rows/columns.

Head Evolution Over Layers: A second toggle shows how individual head "positions" change across layers. Heads are tracked by their pattern fingerprint — e.g., "Head 3 in Layer 0 has a 0.87 similarity to Head 7 in Layer 1, suggesting it may have shifted position." This is visualized as connecting lines between corresponding heads across layers, like a parallel coordinates plot.

Attention Type Comparison Overlay: When comparing two models (e.g., standard MHA vs. Galerkin), the Model View splits into two grids side-by-side. Differences are highlighted: heads that exist in one model but not the other, heads whose importance changed significantly, and heads whose specialization type changed. The Diff Mode (from Feature 4) can be triggered by clicking any head pair.

docs.title: 3.5 Performance Considerations
docs.text: The Model View grid for a 12-layer, 12-head model contains only 144 cells — rendering is trivial even with SVG. The complexity comes from the hover preview thumbnails, which require generating miniature heatmaps on-the-fly. These are pre-computed when the Model View is opened and cached as 64×64px PNG data URLs (stored in a Map keyed by layer+head). With 144 heads, this consumes approximately 144 × 4KB = 576KB of memory, well within budget.

docs.title: 4. Feature 6: 3D Attention Topology Map — React Three Fiber
4.1 Purpose & Core Design
docs.text:
The 3D Attention Topology Map transforms the flat, abstract attention matrix into an immersive spatial experience where tokens become tangible objects and attention connections become visible forces. This view is designed to leverage human spatial reasoning — our brains are wired to understand 3D relationships, making complex attention patterns more intuitive.

The design is inspired by TensorSpace, which "provides Keras-like APIs to build deep learning layers, load pre-trained models, and generate a 3D visualization in the browser" using Three.js, and by the Reddit "Planet Neuron" project where each neuron becomes a planet in a navigable game world. The Helios-Web project further demonstrates that "GPU-based rendering for real-time visualization and interactive analysis of massive-scale networks and high-dimensional embeddings" is feasible in browser environments.

docs.title: 4.2 Scene Architecture
docs.text:
The 3D scene is organized as a multi-layered cylindrical space:

Layer Rings: Each transformer layer is represented as a horizontal ring (torus) in 3D space. Layers are stacked vertically with equal spacing (2.0 world units apart). The first layer (Layer 0) is at the bottom, and the last layer is at the top. Rings are semi-transparent (opacity 0.15) with a subtle glow.

Token Spheres: Within each layer ring, tokens are positioned as spheres distributed around the ring's circumference. The angular position of each token on the ring is determined by a dimensionality reduction of its hidden state at that layer (t-SNE or UMAP, computed once when the view loads and cached). This means tokens with similar meanings cluster together on the ring.

Token sphere properties: - Size: Proportional to the token's L2 norm (activation magnitude) at that layer. Important tokens are larger. - Color: By token position in the sequence (rainbow gradient from blue for early tokens to red for late tokens) OR by part-of-speech (noun=blue, verb=red, adjective=green, etc.) OR by semantic cluster (auto-assigned via k-means on hidden states). The coloring mode is selectable from Zone 4. - Emissive glow: Tokens that are currently "attending strongly" to other tokens glow brighter.

Attention Connections: Between token spheres, attention weights are visualized as curved tubes/arcs (using Three.js TubeGeometry along a quadratic Bezier curve). The arc rises above the ring plane, creating a visible "web" of connections: - Thickness: Proportional to attention weight (logarithmic scale, range 0.02 to 0.3 world units). - Color: Matches the source (query) token's color, with opacity proportional to attention weight. - Animation: Active connections have particles flowing along the tube from query to key, at a speed proportional to the attention weight. High-attention connections "flow" faster, creating a dynamic, living visualization.

docs.title: 4.3 Multi-Layer 3D Visualization
docs.text:
Unlike the Head View which shows one layer at a time, the 3D View can show all layers simultaneously. This is the killer feature: the researcher can physically see how attention patterns evolve across layers. A token that receives diffuse attention in Layer 0 might become sharply focused on a specific other token by Layer 6 — this journey is visible as the tube thickness and direction changes across the vertical stack.

Cross-layer connections: When a token in Layer 3 strongly attends to a token in Layer 3 (same-layer attention), the tube is horizontal. When showing cross-layer connections (e.g., residual stream flow), tubes angle upward from lower to higher layers.

docs.title: 4.4 Camera & Navigation
docs.text:
The camera system supports multiple navigation modes:

Orbit Mode (Default): The camera orbits around the center of the layer stack. Left-drag rotates, scroll zooms, right-drag pans. The orbit target can be set by double-clicking any token sphere — the camera smoothly animates to center on that token.

Fly-Through Mode: WASD keys move the camera freely through the 3D space. Q and E roll. This enables "flying through" the attention web — the researcher can navigate inside the model, seeing attention connections from the perspective of individual tokens.

Layer-Focus Mode: Pressing a number key (0-9) instantly animates the camera to focus on that layer, with all other layers dimmed to 20% opacity. This enables rapid layer comparison without losing spatial context.

Preset Views: Six preset camera angles accessible via buttons: "Top Down," "Side View," "Front View," "Isometric," "Token's Eye" (camera positioned at a selected token, looking outward at what it attends to), and "Global Overview" (camera far back, showing all layers).

docs.title: 4.5 Interactive Token Selection
docs.text:
Clicking a token sphere triggers a system-wide event via the ViewSynchronizer: 1. The selected token sphere pulses (scale animation: 1.0 → 1.3 → 1.0 over 600ms) and glows brighter. 2. All attention connections FROM this token are highlighted (other connections dim to 10%). 3. The Head View (if visible) highlights the corresponding row. 4. The Q/K Joint View centers on this token's vectors. 5. A floating info panel appears near the token showing: token text, position, layer, top-3 attended tokens, and attention entropy.

Double-click a token to "lock" the selection. Shift+click to add to multi-select (up to 5 tokens). Multi-selected tokens show all connections between them — useful for analyzing "How does the subject, verb, and object interact through attention?"

docs.title: 4.6 Animation & Time-Based Features
docs.text:
Attention Flow Animation: Connections are not static — particles continuously flow from query tokens to key tokens along the attention tubes. This gives the visualization a living, breathing quality. The flow speed for each connection is proportional to its attention weight. Users can pause the flow with Spacebar to inspect a static snapshot.

Layer Propagation Animation: A special animation mode (triggered by the "Propagate" button) shows how a single input token's influence spreads through the network. Starting from the selected token at Layer 0, the animation "lights up" tokens at Layer 1 that receive attention from it, then Layer 2 tokens that receive attention from those Layer 1 tokens, and so on — like watching ripples spread across a pond. Each step takes 500ms, with the full propagation through 12 layers taking 6 seconds.

Timeline Scrubber: For autoregressive models, a timeline at the bottom shows generation steps (Token 1, Token 2, ..., Token N). Scrubbing the timeline shows the 3D scene at that generation step — new tokens appear, connections re-form, and the spatial arrangement updates.

docs.title: 4.7 Visual Effects & Atmosphere
docs.text:
The 3D scene incorporates several atmospheric effects to enhance immersion:

Particle System Background: A subtle starfield of 500-1000 slowly drifting particles fills the background, giving depth cues and a sense of vastness. Particle density increases near highly active attention connections.

Bloom Post-Processing: An Unreal Bloom pass (via @react-three/postprocessing) adds a soft glow to bright attention connections. The bloom threshold is set so only connections with weight > 0.3 glow, creating a natural visual hierarchy.

Ambient Occlusion: A subtle SSAO pass adds depth to the token spheres and helps distinguish overlapping connections.

Fog: Exponential fog with density 0.002 provides depth perception — distant layers fade slightly into the background.

docs.title: 4.8 Performance & LOD
docs.text:
The 3D view implements aggressive LOD:

  • Distance-based: Token spheres beyond a certain camera distance are rendered as simpler geometries (icosahedron with 2 subdivisions instead of 4). Attention tubes beyond medium distance become simple lines.
  • Frustum culling: Only objects within the camera's view frustum are rendered.
  • Instanced rendering: Token spheres across all layers are rendered via InstancedMesh — a single draw call for all spheres, with per-instance transforms and colors passed via buffer attributes.
  • Web Workers: The t-SNE/UMAP computation for token positioning runs in a Web Worker, avoiding main thread blocking. The initial positioning for 128 tokens across 12 layers takes approximately 2-3 seconds and is cached.

docs.title: 5.1 Purpose & Core Design
docs.text: The Sankey Attention Flow Diagram visualizes the Transformer as a dynamical system — showing how information flows from input tokens, through attention heads at each layer, and ultimately to output predictions. The Transformer Explainer pioneered this approach: it "adopts the Sankey diagram visual design, inspired by recent work viewing Transformers as dynamical systems, emphasizing how input data flows through model components" and "the Sankey component visualizes data flow between model components using SVG paths and gradients".

docs.title: 5.2 Visual Structure
docs.text:
The Sankey diagram is organized as a left-to-right flow:

Input Tokens ──→ Layer 0 Heads ──→ Layer 1 Heads ──→ ... ──→ Layer L-1 Heads ──→ Output
   (N nodes)     (H nodes)        (H nodes)                 (H nodes)          (N nodes)

Each column represents a stage in the processing pipeline. Between adjacent columns, flow paths connect nodes with thickness proportional to attention weight (or information flow magnitude).

docs.title: 5.3 Node Design
docs.text:
Input Token Nodes (leftmost column): Each input token is a rounded rectangle showing the token text (truncated to 8 characters). Node height is proportional to the token's total "outgoing attention" (sum of its attention to all keys). Nodes are colored by token position (same rainbow as the 3D view).

Head Nodes (middle columns): Each attention head is a rounded rectangle labeled "H3" (for Head 3). Node height is proportional to the head's importance score. Nodes are colored by head specialization type (blue=positional, red=semantic, etc.).

Output Nodes (rightmost column): For encoder models, the output nodes mirror the input tokens. For autoregressive models, the output shows the predicted next token(s), with node height proportional to prediction probability.

docs.title: 5.4 Flow Path Design
docs.text:
Flow paths between columns are rendered as curved SVG paths using custom path generators. Each path represents the aggregate attention flow from one source node to one target node.

Path thickness: Proportional to the attention weight, logarithmically scaled. The minimum visible thickness is 1px (for weights below 0.01), and the maximum is 20px (for weights above 0.5).

Path color: Gradient from source node color (at the left) to target node color (at the right), creating a smooth visual transition that helps the eye track flow direction.

Path opacity: By default, all paths are rendered at 60% opacity. Hovering a path increases its opacity to 100% and brings it to the front (z-index), while dimming all other paths to 15%.

Path curvature: Paths use a custom cubic Bezier curve generator that produces smooth, aesthetically pleasing curves. The curvature parameter is adjustable from Zone 4 (straight lines → gentle curves → dramatic swoops).

docs.title: 5.5 Interaction Model
docs.text:
Hover on node: Highlights all incoming and outgoing flows for that node. Other flows dim. A tooltip shows: "Layer 3, Head 7 | Receives from: token 'the' (0.12), token 'cat' (0.08) | Sends to: token 'sat' (0.15), token 'mat' (0.11)."

Hover on flow: The flow path brightens and thickens slightly. A tooltip shows: "token 'the' → Head 3 → token 'cat' | Weight: 0.23 | Rank: #4 of 144 flows from 'the'."

Click on node: Selects that node (highlighted with a glowing border). The ViewSynchronizer propagates this selection — the Head View jumps to that layer/head, the 3D View centers on that token.

Click on flow: "Pins" that flow (rendered in gold, always on top). Multiple flows can be pinned for comparison. A pinned flow remains highlighted even when hovering elsewhere.

Drag to reorder nodes: Nodes within a column can be vertically reordered by drag-and-drop. The default ordering is by token position (left column) or head index (middle columns), but reordering by "total flow magnitude" or "entropy" can reveal structural patterns.

docs.title: 5.6 Animation
docs.text:
Flow animation: Animated particles (small circles) travel along the flow paths at constant speed, creating a sense of movement and direction. The animation can be toggled on/off and the speed adjusted.

Layout transition animation: When switching between models or attention types, nodes smoothly transition to their new positions (using FLIP animation — First, Last, Invert, Play) over 600ms with easing.

docs.title: 5.7 Scalability
docs.text:
For models with many heads (e.g., 32-head architectures) or many layers, the Sankey diagram can become cluttered. Mitigation strategies:

  • Collapse layers: A range slider lets the user select which layers to show (e.g., "Show layers 0-5 only").
  • Filter by head type: Show only positional heads, or only semantic heads.
  • Aggregate heads: Multiple heads in the same layer can be aggregated into a single "meta-node" showing total flow.
  • Minimum flow threshold: Flows below a certain weight (adjustable slider, default 0.02) are hidden.

docs.title: 6. Feature 8: Query/Key Joint Embedding Explorer — AttentionViz‑Style
6.1 Purpose & Core Design
docs.text:
The Q/K Joint Embedding Explorer visualizes the geometric relationship between queries and keys. The key insight from AttentionViz (VIS 2023) is that "the main idea behind our method is to visualize a joint embedding of the query and key vectors used by transformer models to compute attention" — and that "unlike previous attention visualization techniques, our approach enables the analysis of global patterns across multiple input sequences".

Instead of showing the attention result (weights), this view shows the attention computation — the raw Q and K vectors that are multiplied to produce attention scores. This reveals why certain tokens attend to others: because their Q and K vectors point in similar directions (high dot product).

docs.title: 6.2 Dimensionality Reduction
docs.text:
Q and K vectors live in a high-dimensional space (typically 64 dimensions for each head). To visualize them in 2D, the system applies dimensionality reduction:

PCA (Principal Component Analysis): Fast (O(d²n)), deterministic, preserves global structure. Best for initial exploration.

t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding): Slower (O(n²)), non-deterministic, preserves local structure. Best for revealing clusters.

UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection): Medium speed, preserves both local and some global structure. Best for detailed analysis.

The reduction method is selectable from Zone 4. The computation runs in a Web Worker and results are cached. For 128 tokens with d=64, all three methods complete in under 2 seconds.

docs.title: 6.3 Visual Encoding
docs.text:
The main view is a 2D scatter plot where each point represents either a query vector or a key vector for a specific token:

  • Query vectors (Q): Rendered as circles (●). Color-coded by token position (same rainbow scale).
  • Key vectors (K): Rendered as triangles (▲). Color-coded by token position.

Token labels appear next to points (showing the first 6 characters of the token text). Labels can be toggled on/off.

Background color: Each point has a "halo" — a subtle radial gradient showing its attention magnitude (sum of attention weights involving this token).

Connections: When a query token is selected (clicked), lines are drawn from its Q point to all K points, with line opacity proportional to the attention weight. This reveals the geometric interpretation of attention: a query attends strongly to keys whose vectors are nearby in the embedding space.

docs.title: 6.4 Brushing and Linking
docs.text:
The core interaction pattern is brushing and linking — a fundamental technique in visual analytics where selection in one view propagates to all linked views.

Brush: Click-drag to draw a lasso or rectangular selection on the scatter plot. All Q and K points within the selection are highlighted.

Link: The ViewSynchronizer propagates the selection: - The Head View highlights the corresponding rows (for selected Q) and columns (for selected K). - The 3D View highlights the corresponding token spheres and attention connections between selected tokens. - The Sankey View highlights flows involving selected tokens. - The Analytics panel (Zone 5) computes statistics for the selected subset.

Zoom: Scroll to zoom, centered on the scatter plot. Double-click to reset zoom.

Hover: Hovering a point shows a tooltip with the full token text, its vector norm, and its "attention footprint" (how broadly it distributes or receives attention).

docs.title: 6.5 Multi-Head Mode
docs.text:
A selector in Zone 4 enables showing Q/K vectors for multiple heads simultaneously. Each head's Q and K vectors are projected into the same 2D space using a joint dimensionality reduction (computed on the concatenated Q and K matrices across all selected heads). Different heads use different point shapes: Head 0 = ●/▲, Head 1 = ■/▼, Head 2 = ◆/◀, etc.

This reveals how different heads partition the embedding space — e.g., Head 0 might separate tokens by position (early tokens cluster together), while Head 3 separates tokens by semantic role (subjects cluster together).

docs.title: 6.6 Trajectory Mode
docs.text: A unique feature: for a selected token, draw its trajectory across layers. The Q vector for token "cat" at Layer 0, Layer 1, ..., Layer L-1 are connected by a path with arrows showing the direction of change. This reveals how a token's "query intent" evolves as it passes through the transformer — does it become more focused? Does it shift from attending to nearby tokens to attending to semantically related tokens?

docs.title: 7.1 Purpose & Core Design
docs.text: For autoregressive models (GPT-style), this view animates the step-by-step generation process, showing how attention patterns evolve as each new token is generated. Semantic Pathway (IEEE VIS 2025) is the primary inspiration: it "integrates layerwise semantic trajectories, attention overlays, and output probability views into a unified interface, enabling users to trace how meaning accumulates and decisions emerge during generation".

docs.title: 7.2 Timeline & Playback Controls
docs.text:
The primary control is a horizontal timeline at the bottom of the view, showing generation steps as tick marks:

[Step 1]──[Step 2]──[Step 3]──...──[Step 20]──[Step 21 (current)]

Playback controls: Play/Pause, Step Forward (→), Step Backward (←), Speed (0.25×, 0.5×, 1×, 2×, 4×), Jump to Start, Jump to End.

Scrubber: Drag the playhead to any position to instantly jump to that generation step. The visualization updates reactively.

Step indicator: Shows "Generating token 15 of 50 | Current token: 'cat' | Top-5 predictions: cat (0.34), dog (0.12), bird (0.08), ..."

docs.title: 7.3 Visualization Modes During Animation
docs.text:
The generation animation can be viewed through any of the other five visualization modes, creating a powerful multi-perspective analysis:

Heatmap mode: The attention matrix grows as new tokens are added. At step 5, the matrix is 5×5. At step 20, it's 20×20. The new row (for the latest token) is highlighted with a brief pulse animation (300ms). The researcher can see how the latest token distributes its attention.

Sankey mode: New nodes appear at each column as tokens are generated. Flow paths thicken/thin as attention patterns shift. This is particularly effective for seeing how earlier tokens' attention to later tokens evolves.

3D mode: New token spheres materialize at each layer ring with a "spawn" animation (scale from 0 to 1 over 400ms). New attention connections form as curved tubes growing from the new token to existing tokens.

Q/K Joint mode: New Q and K points appear in the scatter plot. The trajectory of a specific token's Q vector across generation steps can be traced — does its "query intent" change as more context becomes available?

docs.title: 7.4 Semantic Pathway Overlay
docs.text: A unique overlay inspired by Semantic Pathway: for each token, draw its cross-layer trajectory — how its hidden state evolves across layers during a single generation step. The trajectory is a colored path (rainbow from Layer 0 = blue to Layer L = red) in a 2D t-SNE projection. Hovering a trajectory point shows the token's nearest vocabulary words at that layer ("At Layer 4, this token's hidden state is closest to the word embedding of 'feline'").

docs.title: 7.5 Output Probability View
docs.text: Below the main visualization, a bar chart shows the model's output probabilities for the next token. As generation progresses, the bar chart updates to show predictions for the current position. The bar for the token that was actually generated (in the real model's output) is highlighted in gold, while other top predictions are shown in gray. This enables comparison: "The model predicted 'cat' with 34% probability, but the next most likely token was 'dog' at 12%."

docs.title: 7.6 Intervention Mode
docs.text:
A powerful feature for causal analysis: at any generation step, the user can intervene:

  • Force a different token: Instead of the model's top prediction, the user selects a different token from the probability chart. The animation continues with this forced token, showing how the "alternate reality" unfolds.
  • Ablate a head mid-generation: Toggle off a head and see how the remaining generation differs. The "alternate path" is shown as a ghost overlay (semi-transparent) alongside the original path.
  • Modify attention: Click a cell in the heatmap and manually set its attention weight to 0 or 1. The generation continues with this modified attention, revealing the causal impact.

docs.title: 8.1 Chord Diagram View (Supplementary Module A)
docs.text:
The Chord Diagram represents attention as a circular layout where tokens are arranged around a circle and attention connections are drawn as chords (arcs) connecting them. This is particularly effective for small numbers of tokens (≤20) where individual connections are distinguishable.

Visual encoding: Token nodes are evenly spaced around the circle. Each token's "total attention received" is shown as an arc along the circumference (thicker arc = receives more attention). Attention connections are chords colored by the source token's color, with opacity proportional to weight.

Interaction: Hovering a chord highlights both connected tokens and shows the attention weight. Clicking a token filters to show only connections involving that token.

docs.title: 8.2 Particle Flow View (Supplementary Module B)
docs.text:
An advanced, visually stunning alternative to the static heatmap. Attention is rendered as flowing particles — thousands of tiny, glowing dots that stream from query tokens to key tokens along curved paths. This is inspired by particle system effects in modern games and the dynamic visualization approach of the Transformer Explainer's animated Sankey paths.

Particle properties: Each particle has a lifetime of 2-3 seconds (configurable). Density of particles along a path is proportional to attention weight. Particle color matches the query token. Particles leave a subtle glow trail that fades over time.

Interaction: The particle flow can be "frozen" (all particles stop in place) to inspect the static pattern. A "wind" slider adjusts the flow speed. Individual paths can be "seeded" (boost particle density) by clicking a token pair.

docs.title: 9. Cross-View Synchronization Protocol
docs.text:
The ViewSynchronizer operates on a pub/sub event bus implemented via a Zustand store slice. Each view subscribes to selection events and publishes its own. The protocol avoids circular updates through event source tracking:

Event { type, sourceView, payload, timestamp }

When View A publishes a selection event, Views B through F receive it and update their own highlighting. Views B through F do NOT re-publish the event (detected by matching timestamp and sourceView), preventing infinite loops.

The synchronization latency target is < 16ms (one frame), achieved by using direct store mutations rather than React state updates for cross-view highlighting data.

docs.title: 10. Accessibility Across All Views
docs.text:
All views implement:

  • Keyboard navigation: Tab between interactive elements, arrow keys for fine-grained control (move selection one token at a time), +/- for zoom.
  • Screen reader support: aria-label attributes on all interactive elements. The heatmap cells include aria-label="Attention from token 'The' to token 'cat': 0.0423".
  • High-contrast mode: A toggle in Zone 4 switches all color scales to high-contrast alternatives optimized for visual impairments.
  • Reduced motion: Respects the prefers-reduced-motion media query — animations are disabled or simplified when this is set.
  • Focus indicators: All interactive elements have visible focus rings (2px solid white outline with 2px offset).

docs.title: 11. Summary
docs.text: Zone 2 provides six primary visualization modalities (Head View, Model View, 3D Topology Map, Sankey Flow, Q/K Joint Explorer, Token-by-Token Animation) plus two supplementary modes (Chord Diagram, Particle Flow), all synchronized through a unified rendering pipeline and shared selection state. The tiered rendering architecture (SVG → Canvas → WebGL → WebGPU) ensures smooth performance from small matrices to massive 2048×2048 attention grids. Every view supports multi-head overlay, diff mode, and bidirectional linked highlighting. The zone is fully accessible, responsive, and optimized for both rapid exploration and deep analysis.

docs.title: 📐 Zone 3: Live Math Panel — 3Blue1Brown‑Style Complete Implementation Specification
Overview
docs.text:
Zone 3 is the mathematical nerve center of the attention dashboard. Occupying a dedicated panel (collapsible, default width 400–480px on desktop, full‑width bottom sheet on mobile), it renders the actual LaTeX equations for attention computation, highlights variables in sync with the visualization canvas, animates step‑by‑step computations, exposes raw numerical values, and supports architectural comparison. Its design is directly inspired by 3Blue1Brown’s “Attention in transformers, visually explained” video (built with Manim) and the Self Attention Flow interactive tool, but taken further into a fully interactive, explorable, and deeply integrated component.

The panel operates on a bidirectional binding with all other zones: hovering a token pair in Zone 2’s Head View highlights the corresponding variables in the equation and shows the exact numerical computation path in Zone 3’s Inspector; changing a parameter (e.g., rank in Galerkin attention) in Zone 4 updates the equation and the numerical tables in Zone 3 instantly.

docs.title: 1. Feature 10: Live LaTeX Equation Renderer with Animated Steps
1.1 Purpose & UX Philosophy
docs.text: Researchers (especially those new to attention mechanisms) often struggle to map the abstract formula to the actual computations happening inside the model. The Live LaTeX Renderer bridges this gap by rendering the attention formula in a beautiful, annotated LaTeX display where each variable is color‑coded and linked to the corresponding visualization element. Furthermore, the user can click any part of the formula to trigger an animated step‑by‑step walkthrough of the computation, using the currently loaded data (model, layer, head, tokens). The goal is to make the math alive—a dynamic, explorable artifact rather than a static image.

docs.title: 1.2 Primary Equation Display
docs.text:
For standard scaled dot‑product attention, the main formula displayed is:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( QK^T / √d_k ) V

Each component is rendered as an interactive LaTeX sub‑expression:

Component Color Code Description Q Blue (#3b82f6) Query matrix K Red (#ef4444) Key matrix V Green (#22c55e) Value matrix dₖ Gray (#94a3b8) Head dimension softmax(…) Purple (#a855f7) Softmax function √dₖ Orange (#f59e0b) Scaling factor QK^T Teal (#14b8a6) Dot‑product scores

These colors are consistent across all views: the Q/K Joint View uses the same blue/red for its scatter points, the Sankey view uses them for node borders, etc.

docs.title: 1.3 Variable Highlighting via Hover
docs.text:
When the user hovers over a token pair (i, j) in Zone 2’s Head View, the Live Math Panel responds within 16ms:

  • The Q and K sub‑expressions gently pulse (scale 1.05 with a 300ms easing).
  • A small tooltip appears near the equation, showing the numeric indices: “Q[3] · K[7]”.
  • The QK^T part is underlined with a subtle animated wavy line to indicate that this product is being computed for that specific pair.
  • The softmax part briefly highlights when the hovered cell’s weight has been computed.

This reactive highlighting transforms the static formula into a dynamic legend of the attention process.

docs.title: 1.4 Step‑by‑Step Animated Computation
docs.text: Clicking on any part of the equation opens the Computation Stepper—a modal or inline panel (depending on viewport size) that breaks the attention calculation into discrete, animated steps:

docs.title: Step 1: Matrix Multiplication (Q × K^T)
docs.text:
• The LaTeX equation shows: Scores = Q K^T
  • The actual Q and K matrices for the selected layer/head are displayed as mini heatmaps (using the same color scale as Zone 2) side‑by‑side.
  • An animation shows the two matrices sliding together, with the dot‑product values appearing cell‑by‑cell in the resulting Scores matrix.
  • The user can scrub a timeline slider to rewind/fast‑forward the animation.
  • The Q, K, and Scores matrices are rendered as small, labeled heatmaps (size proportional to the number of tokens, max 200×200px).

docs.title: Step 2: Scaling by √dₖ
docs.text:
• Equation: ScaledScores = Scores / √dₖ
  • The numeric value of √dₖ (e.g., √64 = 8) is displayed.
  • An animation shows the Scores matrix being uniformly scaled down—the heatmap colors shift, and the numerical values update.
  • A comparison view (toggleable) shows the Scores matrix before and after scaling, with a difference heatmap.

docs.title: Step 3: Softmax (Row‑by‑Row)
docs.text:
• Equation: AttentionWeights = softmax(ScaledScores)
  • The softmax is animated row by row: the user can select which row (query token) to watch, or let the animation cycle through all rows.
  • For the selected row:
  • The raw scaled scores are shown as a bar chart.
  • One by one, the bars transform: exponentiate (eˣ) → sum → normalize.
  • The resulting attention weights are displayed as a final bar chart and also as percentages.
  • The animation uses a glow‑and‑fade effect on each step, with a speed control (0.25× to 4×).

docs.title: Step 4: Weighted Sum (× V)
docs.text:
• Equation: Output = AttentionWeights × V
  • The attention weights (row vector) and the Value matrix (columns) are displayed.
  • The animation shows each Value vector being multiplied by its corresponding attention weight, then summed to produce the output vector for that query token.
  • The final output vector is displayed, and optionally compared to the actual hidden state (from the model) to show the impact of the residual connection (though that’s beyond the attention formula, it’s a nice educational touch).

docs.title: 1.5 Scrubber & Playback Controls
docs.text: The Computation Stepper includes: - Play/Pause button - Step Forward/Backward (skip to next/previous major step) - Micro‑step Forward/Backward (advance within a step, e.g., exponentiate just one more score) - Timeline Slider (scrub through the entire computation) - Speed Selector (0.25×, 0.5×, 1×, 2×, 4×) - Loop Toggle (loop the entire animation) - Auto‑Advance Toggle (automatically proceed to next step after a configurable delay)

docs.title: 1.6 Multi‑Head and Multi‑Layer Support
docs.text: When the user has selected multiple heads (via Zone 4 checkboxes or the Model View shift‑click), the Live Math Panel adapts: - The Q, K, V matrices shown are the concatenated or averaged versions (user‑selectable). - The computation steps show the per‑head contributions before aggregation. - A small head‑indicator tab appears above the matrices, allowing the user to see individual head computations.

docs.title: 1.7 Variant Equations for Different Attention Types
docs.text:
The dashboard supports many attention types (Galerkin, TLinFormer, PADRe, Spectraformer, RPC, FUSIONATTN, etc.), each with its own mathematical formulation. The Live Math Panel automatically switches the displayed formula based on the selected attention type. For example:

  • Galerkin Attention: 

    K_sketch = K·S,   V_sketch = V·S
Scores = Q·K_sketch^T / √d
Attention = softmax(Scores)
Output = Attention · V_sketch
    The formula shows the random sketching matrix S (with its dimensions N × r indicated) and highlights how the complexity reduces from O(N²) to O(N·r).

  • PADRe (Polynomial Attention): 

    Scores = QK^T / √d
Base = 1 + Scores / p
AttentionWeights = (Base)^p  (clamped and normalized)
Output = AttentionWeights · V
    The polynomial order p is highlighted, and the animation step shows the polynomial evaluation instead of softmax.

  • TLinFormer: 

    K_proj = E·K,   V_proj = F·V
Scores = Q·K_proj^T / √d
Attention = softmax(Scores)
Output = Attention · V_proj
    The low‑rank projection matrices E and F are displayed with their dimensions.

Each variant is accompanied by a short textual description and a link to the original paper (pulled from the attention registry). The equation rendering uses a unified expression tree, allowing shared components (like Scores, softmax) to be rendered consistently while swapping out the outer structure.

docs.title: 1.8 Architecture Comparison Math Diff (Link with Feature 12)
docs.text: When the user is in comparison mode (two attention types selected), the math panel splits vertically (or stacks on narrow screens). Both formulas are displayed side‑by‑side, with diff highlighting: - Components that are identical between the two formulas are rendered in normal opacity. - Components that differ (e.g., softmax vs. polynomial, or presence/absence of a projection matrix) are highlighted with a glow and a subtle “changed” badge. - A unified step‑by‑step animation can run both formulas simultaneously, allowing the user to see how the computation diverges at each step.

docs.title: 2.1 Purpose & Design
docs.text: The Numerical Value Inspector is a live, scrollable data table that shows the exact floating‑point values at each stage of the attention computation for the currently selected token pair. It’s the “debugger” of the attention mechanism—researchers can trace exactly which numbers led to a particular attention weight. This feature is inspired by the “watch” panels in scientific computing environments like MATLAB, Mathematica, and the PyTorch debugger.

docs.title: 2.2 Table Structure
docs.text:
The Inspector table has a hierarchical row layout, organized by computation step:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ COMPUTATION INSPECTOR — Token: 'The' (i=3) → 'cat' (j=7) │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ① Q·K Dot Product                                   │
│   Q[3] vector norm: 3.42                             │
│   K[7] vector norm: 2.89                             │
│   Q[3] · K[7] = 0.847 (raw score)                   │
│                                                      │
│ ② Scale by √dₖ (√64 = 8.000)                        │
│   0.847 / 8.000 = 0.106 (scaled score)               │
│                                                      │
│ ③ Softmax                                            │
│   Row 3 scaled scores: [0.106, 0.034, 0.215, ...]    │
│   e^(0.106) = 1.112                                  │
│   Σ e^(row) = 48.731                                 │
│   1.112 / 48.731 = 0.023 (attention weight)          │
│                                                      │
│ ④ Weighted Value                                     │
│   V[7] vector (first 5 dims): [0.12, -0.34, ...]     │
│   0.023 × V[7] = [0.003, -0.008, ...]                │
│                                                      │
│ FINAL: attention weight = 0.0228                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Each row group is collapsible. The currently active row (based on the animation step) is highlighted with a blue left border. The table uses monospace font (JetBrains Mono or Fira Code) for numerical values, with right alignment for readability.

docs.title: 2.3 Live Updates
docs.text: The Inspector updates instantly when: - The user hovers over a different cell in the Head View (new token pair → new computation path). - The user scrubs through the Computation Stepper (values update to reflect the current step). - The user changes the layer, head, or attention type (entire table recomputes). - The user modifies attention parameters (temperature, rank, etc.) — the values re‑compute with the new parameters.

docs.title: 2.4 Color Coding of Values
docs.text:
To make the table scannable, values are color‑coded: - Positive large (≥ 0.5): green (#22c55e) - Positive small (0 to 0.5): gray (#94a3b8) - Zero: faint (#64748b) - Negative: red (#ef4444) - Extreme (≥ 10 or ≤ ‑10): bold with orange highlight (#f59e0b)

The attention weight (the final value) is displayed in a slightly larger font size and in bold.

docs.title: 2.5 Token Pair Selection Methods
docs.text: The Inspector can display values for: - A single token pair (hovered or clicked in Head View) — default mode. - All token pairs for a selected query row (user clicks a query token → table shows the entire softmax row with all key values). - Top‑N pairs (sorted by attention weight) for a selected head. - Custom pair (user types token indices manually).

docs.title: 2.6 Export Capabilities
docs.text:
• Copy row: A copy icon next to each row copies that row’s values to clipboard.
  • Export CSV: A button exports the entire Inspector data for the current selection as a CSV file.
  • Export LaTeX table: For inclusion in papers, a button generates a LaTeX tabular environment with the values.
  • Pin values: The user can “pin” a specific computation (e.g., the softmax row for token 3) so it remains visible even when hovering elsewhere. Pinned rows appear in a separate “Pinned” section at the top of the Inspector.

docs.title: 2.7 Performance Considerations
docs.text: For large matrices (e.g., 512 tokens), computing and displaying values for all pairs would be overwhelming. The Inspector uses lazy evaluation: only the values needed for the currently selected token pair (or top‑N pairs) are computed. The underlying attention data is stored in a Float32Array for fast random access.

docs.title: 3.1 Purpose & Core Design
docs.text: This feature allows researchers to compare the mathematical formulations of two attention mechanisms side‑by‑side. It is an extension of the Live LaTeX Renderer that renders two formula panels and visually highlights the differences. This is critical for understanding the trade‑offs between attention types (e.g., standard MHA vs. Galerkin) and for educational purposes (showing how approximations modify the original formula).

docs.title: 3.2 Side‑by‑Side Layout
docs.text:
When comparison mode is activated (via a toggle in Zone 4 or by selecting “Compare” in the Model Selector), the math panel splits into two columns:

┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ STANDARD MHA                 │ GALERKIN (r=64)              │
│                              │                              │
│ S = QK^T / √d               │ K' = K·S  (sketch)          │
│ A = softmax(S)               │ V' = V·S                    │
│ O = A·V                      │ S' = Q·K'^T / √d            │
│                              │ A' = softmax(S')             │
│                              │ O' = A'·V'                   │
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 3.3 Visual Diff Mechanism
docs.text:
Differences between the two formulas are highlighted using a unified diff model (like git diff but for math):

  • Lines present in Left but not Right: shaded red on the left, with a - marker.
  • Lines present in Right but not Left: shaded green on the right, with a + marker.
  • Lines that are identical: displayed normally (gray text on both sides).
  • Lines that are similar but with different parameters: highlighted in yellow, with the differing parameter emphasized (e.g., √d vs. √d_new).

docs.title: 3.4 Interactive Parameter Linking
docs.text: When a parameter differs between the two formulas (e.g., the rank r in Galerkin, or the polynomial order p in PADRe), the user can adjust that parameter via a slider in the comparison panel. As the slider moves, the right‑hand formula updates in real time, and the corresponding numerical values in the Inspector recompute. This enables interactive “what‑if” analysis: “What happens to the attention weights if I increase the Galerkin rank from 32 to 128?”

docs.title: 3.5 Synchronized Step‑by‑Step Animation
docs.text:
The Computation Stepper can run both formulas simultaneously, with the animation steps synchronized. For example:

  • Step 1 (Left): S = QK^T | Step 1 (Right): K' = K·S (these are fundamentally different, so the animation diverges).
  • Step 2 (Left): A = softmax(S) | Step 2 (Right): S' = Q·K'^T.
  • Step 3 (Left): O = A·V | Step 3 (Right): A' = softmax(S').
  • Step 4 (Right): O' = A'·V'.

The animation timeline shows markers where the two computations diverge and re‑converge (e.g., both produce an output matrix of the same shape).

docs.title: 3.6 Complexity & Performance Annotations
docs.text:
Below each formula, a compact table shows the computational complexity (Big‑O notation) and estimated FLOPs for the current sequence length and dimensions. For example:

Metric Standard MHA Galerkin (r=64) Time Complexity O(N²·D) O(N·r·D) Memory O(N²) O(N·r) Est. FLOPs (N=128) 2.1M 0.3M Speedup 1× 7×

This table updates dynamically when the user changes the sequence length (via a test‑sentence input) or the attention parameters. It directly links to the benchmark leaderboard (Zone 5) where actual measured performance data is available.

docs.title: 3.7 “Learn More” Deep Links
docs.text: Each attention type in the comparison view has a “Learn More” button that opens a side panel with: - The original paper abstract (fetched from the agents paper library or Semantic Scholar). - Key equations from the paper. - Links to implementations (GitHub, HuggingFace). - Community discussions (from the community Q&A app). - Example usage in experiments (from the experiment app).

docs.title: Module A: Interactive Matrix Visualization (Mini‑Heatmaps)
docs.text:
Alongside the LaTeX formula, small heatmap thumbnails of the Q, K, V, and attention matrices are displayed. These are not just static images—they are live and interactive:

  • Hovering over a cell in a mini‑heatmap shows the value in a tooltip.
  • Clicking a mini‑heatmap expands it to fill the panel (like a picture‑in‑picture).
  • The mini‑heatmaps are synchronized with the Head View: selecting a region in the Head View highlights the corresponding rows/columns in the Q/K/V mini‑heatmaps.

This gives the researcher a direct visual mapping from the abstract matrices in the formula to the concrete attention weights they see in Zone 2.

docs.title: Module B: Animated Proof/Explanation of the Attention Mechanism
docs.text:
A dedicated “Explain” mode that walks the user through why attention works, not just how. This uses a combination of: - Animated illustrations (e.g., tokens talking to each other). - Textual explanations at each step (e.g., “The dot product measures how ‘compatible’ a query is with a key. If Q and K are similar, their dot product is large, meaning this token pair should have high attention.”) - Interactive quizzes at the end of each section.

This transforms Zone 3 into a built‑in mini‑course on attention mechanisms, reducing the barrier to entry for new researchers.

docs.title: Module C: Computational Graph View
docs.text:
Instead of (or in addition to) the linear step‑by‑step view, the user can switch to a computational graph representation. The attention computation is shown as a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) where nodes are operations (MatMul, Scale, Softmax) and edges are data tensors. Each node shows: - Operation name - Input/output shapes - FLOP count - Live status (completed, in‑progress, error)

Clicking a node highlights the corresponding sub‑expression in the LaTeX formula. This is inspired by TensorBoard’s graph visualization and is especially useful for understanding complex attention variants like FUSIONATTN, which combine multiple operations.

docs.title: Module D: Parameter Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text:
A panel where the user can adjust key parameters (e.g., temperature, rank, polynomial order, number of heads) via sliders and see real‑time effects on: - The LaTeX formula (parameters update inline). - The numerical values in the Inspector. - The attention heatmap in Zone 2 (via the ViewSynchronizer). - The FLOPs estimate and complexity table.

A sensitivity plot (generated by running multiple forward passes with varying parameters) can be displayed, showing how attention entropy, concentration, or output similarity changes as a function of the parameter. This enables researchers to tune attention mechanisms for their specific needs.

docs.title: Module E: Citation & Reference Panel
docs.text:
A collapsible panel that pulls in relevant literature for the currently displayed attention type. It shows: - The paper title, authors, and year. - The abstract (truncated to 3 lines with “Read more”). - Key mathematical definitions from the paper. - BibTeX citation that can be copied with one click. - Links to the paper on arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and the user’s own library (if saved via the agents paper library). - “Related papers” section based on citation graph or semantic similarity.

This is integrated with the agents paper search and library, so researchers can immediately save a paper to their collection or annotate it.

docs.title: Module F: Export to Notebook / LaTeX
docs.text: The entire math panel content—including the LaTeX formula, computation steps, numerical values, and mini‑heatmaps—can be exported as: - Jupyter Notebook (.ipynb): A Python notebook that reproduces the attention computation using PyTorch/TensorFlow code, with the current parameters and data. This allows researchers to take their exploration directly into code. - LaTeX Document: A compilable LaTeX file with the equations, tables, and embedded figures (SVG heatmaps), suitable for inclusion in a paper. This connects to the paper app for further editing and compilation.

docs.title: Module G: Voice‑Over Narration
docs.text: An accessibility and educational feature: the step‑by‑step animation can be accompanied by auto‑generated audio narration (using Web Speech API or a TTS service). The narration reads out the explanation for each step. The user can select the narration language (English, Chinese, Spanish, etc.) and speed. This makes the math panel accessible to visually impaired users and auditory learners.

docs.title: Module H: Gamified Challenge Mode
docs.text:
To make learning attention mechanisms more engaging, a Challenge Mode can be activated. The system presents the user with a partially completed computation (e.g., a softmax row with one value missing) and asks them to predict the missing value. Points are awarded for accuracy. Challenges can be: - Timed: Complete as many predictions as possible in 60 seconds. - Precision‑based: Score based on how close the prediction is to the actual value. - Head‑type identification: Given an attention heatmap, identify whether the head is positional, semantic, etc.

High scores are saved to the user’s profile and contribute to the gamification system (Zone 8).

docs.title: 5. Integration with Other Zones
docs.text:
Zone 3 is tightly coupled with the rest of the dashboard:

Zone Integration Zone 1 (Navigation) The context bar’s model/attention type selection updates the formula displayed in Zone 3. Zone 2 (Visualization) Hover/select events in the Head View highlight variables and update the Numerical Inspector. The Computation Stepper can be triggered from Zone 2’s context menu (“Explain this cell”). Zone 4 (Control Panel) Parameter sliders (temperature, rank, etc.) update the equation and numerical values in real time. Zone 5 (Analytics) The FLOPs table and complexity annotations are linked to the analytics panel for more detailed profiling. Zone 7 (Social) The “Share” button generates a shareable link that includes the current math panel state (selected attention type, parameters, computation step).

docs.title: 6. Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• LaTeX rendering: Use KaTeX (faster than MathJax) for initial render. Pre‑compile the equation templates for each attention type and cache the DOM.
  • Animation performance: The computation animations use CSS transforms and requestAnimationFrame for smooth 60fps. Heavy computations (e.g., recomputing attention for parameter sweeps) are offloaded to a Web Worker.
  • Numerical values: Store attention tensors as Float32Array for fast random access without re‑computing the entire matrix for each hover.
  • Memory: Mini‑heatmaps are rendered as small canvas elements (< 50KB each). Only the currently visible matrices are kept in memory.

docs.title: 7. Accessibility
docs.text:
• Keyboard navigation: The Computation Stepper can be controlled entirely via keyboard (Space to play/pause, Left/Right arrows to step, numbers to jump to step).
  • Screen reader: All LaTeX formulas have aria-label attributes with plain‑text descriptions (e.g., “Attention equals softmax of Q times K transpose over square root of d_k, times V”). The Numerical Inspector table uses proper <table> semantics with <caption> and <th> elements.
  • Color contrast: The formula colors meet WCAG AA contrast ratios against the dark background. The diff highlighting uses both color and symbols (‑/+) for colorblind users.
  • Reduced motion: The prefers-reduced-motion media query disables all animations and shows static computation steps instead.

docs.title: 8. Internationalization
docs.text: All textual explanations (step descriptions, tooltips, labels) are externalized into locale files and can be translated. The LaTeX formulas themselves are language‑independent, but the surrounding explanatory text adapts to the user’s locale. Initial supported languages: English, Chinese, Spanish, Japanese, Arabic (right‑to‑left layout for the math panel is supported).

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text: Zone 3 is not just a math display—it is a fully interactive, animated, and deeply integrated computational environment that makes the abstract mathematics of attention tangible and explorable. With features like live LaTeX highlighting, step‑by‑step computation animations, numerical inspection, architecture comparison diffs, and additional modules (mini‑heatmaps, computational graphs, sensitivity analysis, export, narration, gamification), it serves both novice learners and expert researchers. It is the bridge between the visual (Zone 2) and the analytical (Zone 5), and it turns the dashboard into a comprehensive platform for attention mechanism research.

docs.title: 🎛️ Zone 4: Control Panel — Complete Implementation Specification
Overview
docs.text:
Zone 4 is the orchestration hub of the entire Attention Dashboard. It sits as a vertical panel (typically 320–380px wide) on the left side of the main content area, between the global navigation bar (Zone 1) and the visualization canvas (Zone 2). This zone is the primary interaction surface where researchers configure what they see, launch experiments, and export their findings. Unlike Zone 1 which is "read‑oriented" (showing what's currently active), Zone 4 is "write‑oriented" — every interaction here changes the state of the entire dashboard.

The panel follows the "Control Room" metaphor: just as a mission control center has sliders, buttons, and panels that affect the main display, Zone 4 provides the tactile controls that shape the attention visualization. Research on complex dashboard design emphasizes that "providing value" requires "different logics, such as investigation, inquiry, finding, discovery, and persuasion" — Zone 4 enables all of these modes through its three core features.

docs.title: 2.1 Core Technology Decisions
docs.text:
The Control Panel is built on a carefully selected stack of modern frameworks chosen for performance, developer experience, and the unique demands of real‑time ML visualization:

Layer Technology Rationale UI Framework React 18 with Concurrent Features useTransition for non‑blocking state updates when changing layers/heads; useDeferredValue for debouncing text input without blocking the UI thread; Suspense boundaries for progressive loading of heavy visualization components State Management Zustand 5 + Immer middleware Zustand's minimal API avoids the boilerplate of Redux while providing "speed and production reliability" for dashboards with "dozens of interactive components". Immer enables mutable‑style updates to deeply nested state (the attention context has 15+ nested fields) without spreading nightmares Animation Framer Motion 11 60fps animations for slider transitions, button feedback, and panel expand/collapse; layoutId for shared layout animations when the layer/head changes; AnimatePresence for exit animations on thumbnail previews Computation Offload Comlink + Web Workers Attention matrix computation (Q×K^T, softmax, ×V) runs in a Web Worker via Comlink's transparent RPC — "offloading heavy computations to background threads while keeping your UI silky smooth" Model Inference Transformers.js (WASM/WebGPU backend) Runs HuggingFace models directly in the browser via WebAssembly or WebGPU, with "zero dependency" and "low latency inference". Models cached in IndexedDB for instant reload Model Caching IndexedDB via Transformers.js cache API "IndexedDB is a real attempt to give the browser a database" — model weights (up to 2GB+) are persisted locally so subsequent loads are near‑instantaneous Virtual Scrolling @tanstack/react-virtual The model selector dropdown may contain hundreds of HuggingFace models — virtual rendering ensures smooth scrolling at 60fps Search Orama (hybrid full‑text + vector search) For the model selector's search functionality, Orama provides "full-text, vector, and hybrid search with a unique API" in less than 2KB — runs entirely in the browser Data Persistence PGlite (PostgreSQL in WASM) for local‑first sync Enables SQL queries on the client for exploration history, saved configurations, and offline support — "run Postgres in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno, with no need to install any other dependencies"

docs.title: 2.2 State Architecture
docs.text:
The entire Zone 4 shares a single Zustand store (useAttentionContext) with the rest of the dashboard. The store is organized into slices for modularity:

useAttentionContext
├── modelSlice: { modelId, modelSource, modelVersion, modelCache }
├── attentionSlice: { attentionType, attentionConfig, supportedTypes }
├── textSlice: { inputText, tokens, tokenizer }
├── navigationSlice: { selectedLayer, selectedHead, activeView }
├── comparisonSlice: { compareModelId, compareAttentionType }
├── historySlice: { pastEntries, futureEntries, starredEntries }
└── uiSlice: { sliderPreviewVisible, panelCollapsed, activeTab }

Each slice uses Immer for immutable updates. Changes to any slice automatically synchronize to the URL via a custom middleware, and to the backend (for authenticated users) via a debounced sync hook.

docs.title: 3.1 Purpose & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
The Unified Selector is the most frequently used control in the dashboard. Researchers rapidly iterate through layers and heads to find interesting patterns, then type custom text to test hypotheses. The design follows three principles: speed (changes should feel instantaneous), preview (users should see what they're selecting before committing), and precision (both coarse and fine‑grained control should be available).

Traditional range sliders are insufficient for this use case because they provide no preview of the selection and require trial‑and‑error clicking. The Unified Selector innovates with live thumbnail previews that render miniature attention heatmaps as the user drags — inspired by video editing timeline thumbnails and the "PreviewSlider" pattern used in design tools.

docs.title: 3.2 Component Tree
docs.text:
UnifiedSelector (container)
├── TabBar: [Layer Selector | Head Selector | Text Input]
├── LayerSelectorPanel
│   ├── LayerThumbnailStrip (horizontal scroll of mini heatmaps)
│   ├── LayerSlider (range input with custom thumb)
│   ├── LayerStepper (‑ / + buttons for fine control)
│   └── LayerQuickJump (numeric input for direct entry)
├── HeadSelectorPanel
│   ├── HeadGrid (grid of colored dots, size = importance)
│   ├── HeadSlider (range input)
│   ├── HeadStepper (‑ / + buttons)
│   └── HeadQuickJump (numeric input)
└── TextInputPanel
    ├── TextArea (expandable input)
    ├── TokenCounter (live character/token count)
    ├── RecentTexts (dropdown of last 10 inputs)
    └── PresetTexts (curated examples: "Simple sentence", "Long document", "Code snippet")

docs.title: 3.3 Layer Selector — Live Preview Thumbnail Strip
docs.text: This is the most innovative UI element in Zone 4 and deserves detailed specification.

docs.title: Visual Layout
docs.text:
The Layer Selector displays a horizontal strip of miniature attention heatmaps — one thumbnail per layer. The strip is scrollable (via mouse wheel, drag, or touch swipe) and the currently selected layer's thumbnail is highlighted with a glowing border.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER SELECTOR                              │
│                                             │
│ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌═════┐ ┌─────┐   │
│ │ L0  │ │ L1  │ │ L2  │ ║ L3  ║ │ L4  │ → │
│ │ ░░  │ │ ▓▓  │ │ ░▓  │ ║ ▓░  ║ │ ░░  │   │
│ └─────┘ └─────┘ └─────┘ └═════┘ └─────┘   │
│ ◄───────────────────●─────────────────────► │
│ Layer: [ 3 ]  [ ‹ ] [ › ]                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Thumbnail Generation Pipeline
docs.text:
Each thumbnail is a 48×48px SVG rendered on‑the‑fly. The generation pipeline uses a dedicated Web Worker (via Comlink) to avoid blocking the main thread:

  1. Worker receives: layer index, attention matrix data (from the current model's forward pass), token count
  2. Worker computes: a downsampled 48×48 matrix using bilinear interpolation
  3. Worker returns: a Float32Array of 2304 values (48×48) representing normalized attention weights
  4. Main thread renders: a <canvas> element colored with the selected color scale (heat/blues/viridis)

For models with many layers (e.g., 24‑layer GPT‑2), thumbnails are rendered lazily — only the visible portion of the strip (plus 2 thumbnails on each side for scroll buffer) is computed. As the user scrolls, new thumbnails stream in via a requestIdleCallback scheduler.

docs.title: Performance Budget
docs.text:
• Thumbnail generation: < 16ms per thumbnail (Web Worker time)
  • Canvas rendering: < 4ms per thumbnail (main thread)
  • Strip scroll: 60fps maintained via CSS will-change: transform and GPU‑accelerated scrolling
  • Memory: at most 10 thumbnails in memory at once (visible + buffer), ~22KB each = ~220KB total

docs.title: Interaction Design
docs.text:
• Hover: thumbnail enlarges to 72×72px via a smooth scale(1.5) transform with a 150ms spring animation. A tooltip appears: "Layer 3 · 12 heads · Entropy: 2.34"
  • Click: selects the layer. The thumbnail gains a ring-2 ring-neon-blue shadow-lg shadow-neon-blue/30 border. The main visualization (Zone 2) updates via a crossfade transition (200ms).
  • Drag: the slider thumb can be dragged. As it moves, the corresponding thumbnail pulses briefly to indicate the current position.
  • Keyboard: Arrow keys (← →) change the layer by 1. Shift+Arrow changes by 5. The slider thumb animates smoothly to the new position.

docs.title: Fallback States
docs.text:
• Model not yet loaded: thumbnails show a shimmer skeleton (pulsing gray gradient) — identical to the loading state used in YouTube and Netflix thumbnails
  • Computation in progress: thumbnails show a progress ring (SVG circle with animated dashoffset) indicating "Computing attention..."
  • Computation failed: thumbnail shows a warning icon (⚠️) with a "Retry" button on hover

docs.title: 3.4 Head Selector — Interactive Head Grid
docs.text: Rather than a second slider, heads are selected through a visual grid of colored dots arranged in a 4×3 grid (for 12‑head models) or a 4×4 grid (for 16‑head models). This design was chosen because researchers often want to compare specific heads (e.g., "Heads 3 and 7 look similar") — a grid enables rapid visual scanning.

docs.title: Visual Design
docs.text:
Each head is represented as a circle (24px diameter) with: - Fill color: the head's "specialization type" color (positional = blue, semantic = red, delimiter = green, induction = purple, unknown = gray) - Size: proportional to the head's importance score (ranges from 16px to 32px) - Border: the currently selected head has a 2px white border with a neon‑blue glow - Opacity: heads with very low importance (< 0.1) are rendered at 30% opacity

┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HEAD SELECTOR                        │
│                                      │
│   ●  ●  ●  ●     H0  H1  H2  H3     │
│   ○  ●  ○  ●     H4  H5  H6  H7     │
│   ○  ○  ●  ○     H8  H9  H10 H11    │
│                                      │
│ Head: [ 7 ]  [ ‹ ] [ › ]            │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Interaction Design
docs.text:
• Hover: the circle enlarges to 32px, and a tooltip appears: "Head 7 · Induction Head · Importance: 0.87 · Entropy: 1.23"
  • Click: selects the head. The circle animates with a "pop" effect (scale 1.0 → 1.3 → 1.0 over 200ms).
  • Keyboard: Up/Down arrows navigate through heads in column order; Left/Right in row order.
  • Multi‑select (Shift+Click): selects multiple heads for comparison mode. Selected heads appear in the comparison panel (Zone 5).

docs.title: Dynamic Head Count
docs.text: For models with variable numbers of heads (e.g., ALBERT with 64 heads), the grid dynamically adjusts: 8×8 for 64 heads, with the ability to zoom in/out via pinch gesture or scroll wheel.

docs.title: 3.5 Text Input Panel
docs.text: The text input is where researchers test hypotheses: "What happens to attention if I change 'The cat sat on the mat' to 'The dog sat on the mat'?" The panel supports both quick edits and batch processing.

docs.title: Component Design
docs.text:
• TextArea: an auto‑resizing <textarea> that grows from 2 lines to 12 lines. Styled with the glass aesthetic (bg-white/5 border border-white/10). Placeholder text: "Enter text to analyze attention patterns..."
  • Token Counter: a live counter showing "Characters: 47 | Tokens: 12 | Max: 512". Changes color from green → yellow → red as the limit approaches.
  • Preset Library: a dropdown of curated texts: "Simple sentence", "Paragraph with coreference", "Code snippet", "Multi‑lingual", "Mathematical notation". Each preset includes a brief description of what attention phenomena it demonstrates.
  • Recent Texts: the last 10 analyzed texts, stored in localStorage. Displayed as a dropdown with preview snippets. Click any to reload.

docs.title: Debouncing Strategy
docs.text: Text input is debounced at 500ms using React 18's useDeferredValue hook. This means: - The text in the input updates immediately (responsive typing) - The attention computation is deferred until the user pauses typing - The UI never blocks — the user can continue interacting with other controls while computation runs

docs.title: Batch Mode
docs.text: A "Batch" toggle enables pasting multiple texts (one per line). The system processes each text through the current model and generates a comparison view showing how attention patterns differ across inputs. This is invaluable for linguistic analysis (e.g., comparing active vs. passive voice, or different languages).

docs.title: 4.1 Purpose & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
This button is the bridge between exploration and experimentation. It transforms the attention dashboard from a passive analysis tool into an active research platform. The philosophy is: "Every insight should be immediately testable." When a researcher discovers an interesting attention pattern, they should be able to launch a training experiment with one click, pre‑configured to reproduce or extend that pattern.

This feature is what connects Zone 4 to the rest of the NeuralOps platform — it's the implementation of the "closed loop" that makes the dashboard not just a visualization tool, but a research accelerator.

docs.title: 4.2 Visual Design
docs.text:
The button is the most visually prominent element in Zone 4. It uses a gradient background (from neon‑blue to purple‑500), a subtle glow animation (animate-glow-pulse), and an icon of a rocket (🚀) or lightning bolt (⚡).

┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                          │
│   ⚡  TRAIN WITH THIS ATTENTION           │
│   ───────────────────────────────────     │
│   Model: BERT‑base‑uncased               │
│   Attention: Galerkin (rank=64)          │
│   Text: "The quick brown fox..."         │
│   Layer: 5 · Head: 7                     │
│                                          │
│   [Configure & Launch]  [Quick Launch]   │
│                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

When expanded (by clicking the main button or the expand arrow), it reveals a compact configuration panel:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   ⚡  TRAIN WITH THIS ATTENTION    [−]   │
│   ───────────────────────────────────     │
│   Experiment Name:                       │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ Reproduce L5-H7 on BERT-base     │   │
│   └──────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                          │
│   Task: [GLUE-MRPC ▾]                   │
│   Epochs: [3]  Batch: [16]  LR: [2e-5] │
│   ───────────────────────────────────     │
│   ☐ Compare with standard MHA           │
│   ☐ Track attention during training     │
│   ☐ Auto‑generate report                │
│   ───────────────────────────────────     │
│   [Save as Draft]    [Launch Experiment] │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 4.3 Pre‑Filled Configuration Pipeline
docs.text: When the user clicks "Configure & Launch", the system assembles a configuration object by reading from multiple sources:
