docs.title: Source 1: Current Attention Context (Zone 1 + Zone 4)
docs.text:
• model_name: from the Model chip in Zone 1
  • attention_type: from the Attention chip in Zone 1
  • attention_config: rank, order, temperature, etc. from Zone 4 controls
  • sample_text: from the Text Input in Zone 4
  • selected_layer: from the Layer Selector
  • selected_head: from the Head Selector

docs.title: Source 2: User Profile & Preferences
docs.text:
• default_task: from the user's profile preferences (stored in PGlite local‑first database)
  • default_epochs, default_batch_size, default_learning_rate: from user's training history (most frequently used values)
  • preferred_hardware: GPU preference from the gpu_marketplace usage history

docs.title: Source 3: Platform Intelligence
docs.text:
• suggested_experiment_name: auto‑generated from the context (e.g., "Reproduce_L5‑H7_BERT‑base_Galerkin_r64")
  • related_experiments: fetched from the experiment app — other experiments with similar configurations
  • estimated_cost: computed from the gpu_marketplace current pricing and the selected configuration
  • estimated_duration: computed from historical run data for similar experiments

docs.title: 4.4 Integration Architecture
docs.text:
The button integrates with the NeuralOps platform through a tRPC‑based API layer that provides end‑to‑end type safety between the React frontend and the Django backend:

Frontend (Zone 4)                    Backend (Django)
─────────────────                    ────────────────
TrainButton.click()
    │
    ├─→ tRPC mutation: createExperiment(config)
    │       │
    │       ├─→ Experiment.objects.create(...)
    │       ├─→ TrainingRun.objects.create(...)
    │       ├─→ scheduler.enqueue(run_id)
    │       └─→ return { experimentId, runId, estimatedStart }
    │
    ├─→ Zustand store: setPendingExperiment(runId)
    │
    ├─→ Toast notification: "Experiment launched!"
    │
    └─→ Router.push(`/experiments/${runId}/monitor`)

The tRPC layer is implemented using Next.js App Router Route Handlers with Server‑Sent Events (SSE) for real‑time progress updates. As the experiment runs, the dashboard can optionally display a live progress bar showing training progress without leaving the attention view.

docs.title: 4.5 Quick Launch vs. Configure & Launch
docs.text:
Two launch modes cater to different user intents:

Mode Behavior Target User Quick Launch Takes all defaults, launches immediately with a single click. Shows a 3‑second countdown with "Undo" option. Power users who know exactly what they want Configure & Launch Expands the configuration panel with all options editable. Includes cost estimate and duration prediction. Researchers who want fine‑grained control

docs.title: 4.6 Post‑Launch Experience
docs.text:
After launching an experiment, the dashboard does not navigate away. Instead:

  1. A non‑blocking toast appears: "Experiment launched! [View Live] [Dismiss]"
  2. The "Train with This Attention" button transforms into a progress indicator: a circular progress ring showing the experiment's status (queued → running → completed)
  3. A side drawer (accessible via a tab on the right edge of Zone 4) shows a mini‑dashboard with live training metrics (loss curve, accuracy, current epoch)
  4. When training completes, a notification prompts the user to compare the trained model's attention patterns with the original visualization

docs.title: 4.7 Edge Cases & Error Handling
docs.text: Scenario Behavior No GPU available The button shows "No GPU Available" in a warning state. Clicking opens the gpu_marketplace to rent GPU time. Insufficient credits A modal appears: "You need $2.50 in credits. Current balance: $1.20. [Add Credits] [Cancel]" Model too large for browser For models >2GB, the button redirects to the server‑side launcher (the existing /launcher page) with all parameters pre‑filled in the URL User not authenticated The button shows "Sign in to train". Clicking opens the login modal with a return URL back to the current dashboard state. Network offline The configuration is saved to PGlite local database. When connectivity returns, the experiment is automatically submitted. Experiment fails A notification appears with the error message and a "Retry with different config" button that opens the configuration panel with the previous settings preserved.

docs.title: 📝 Feature 15: Create Note / Generate Report / Export to Paper
5.1 Purpose & Design Philosophy
docs.text:
These three buttons transform attention exploration into persistent, shareable, and citable research output. They represent the final stage of the research workflow: Discover → Analyze → Document → Publish. Each button serves a different audience and use case:

  • Create Note: Quick capture for personal reference or team sharing (informal)
  • Generate Report: Comprehensive documentation for presentations, meetings, or supplementary materials (semi‑formal)
  • Export to Paper: Publication‑ready output for conferences and journals (formal)

docs.title: 5.2 Visual Design
docs.text:
The three buttons are displayed as a segmented control (like iOS segmented buttons) — a single row with three segments, where only one can be active at a time:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [ 📝 Note ]  [ 📊 Report ]  [ 📄 Paper ] │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

When a segment is clicked, it expands downward to reveal its specific options, while the other segments collapse. The animation uses Framer Motion's layoutId for a smooth shared‑element transition between segments.

docs.title: What It Does

docs.title: What It Does

The report is suitable for: - Lab meetings and internal presentations - Supplementary materials for paper submissions - Grant proposals and progress reports - Educational materials for teaching

docs.title: Report Structure
docs.text:
The generated report contains six sections, each populated from a different zone or app:

Section Source Content 1. Executive Summary Auto‑generated by LLM 2‑3 paragraph summary of findings, written in natural language 2. Model & Configuration Zone 1 + Zone 4 Model details, attention type, hyperparameters, input text 3. Attention Visualization Zone 2 Embedded interactive SVG heatmaps (head view + model view) 4. Quantitative Analysis Zone 5 Entropy, concentration, importance scores, clustering dendrogram, Logit Lens timeline 5. docs.title: LLM‑Powered Summary Generation
docs.text:
The Executive Summary is generated by calling an LLM (via the Vercel AI SDK's streamText) with a carefully constructed prompt:

You are an expert in transformer interpretability. Given the following data about an attention head, write a 2-3 paragraph executive summary suitable for a research report. Include:
- What type of head this is (positional, semantic, induction, etc.)
- What linguistic phenomena it captures
- How it compares to other heads in the same model
- Practical implications (e.g., "This head could be pruned with minimal impact")

Model: BERT-base-uncased
Layer: 5, Head: 7
Attention Type: Galerkin (rank=64)
Input Text: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
Entropy: 2.34
Head Importance: 0.87
Head Type: Induction Head (confidence: 0.92)
...

The LLM response streams token‑by‑token into the report preview, using the Vercel AI SDK's useChat hook for real‑time streaming.

docs.title: Export Formats
docs.text: The report can be exported in multiple formats: - Interactive HTML: A self‑contained HTML file with embedded interactive visualizations (using the same React components, compiled to static JS/CSS) - PDF: Rendered server‑side via Puppeteer or browser‑side via window.print() with optimized print styles - Markdown: For version control (Git) or import into other tools (Notion, Obsidian) - LaTeX: For direct inclusion in papers (connects to Feature 15c)

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Opens the platform's paper LaTeX editor with a pre‑written "Methods" and "Results" section containing the attention visualization as a publication‑ready figure. This is the final stage of the research pipeline: from exploration to publication.

docs.title: Pre‑Generated Content
docs.text:
Methods Section (auto‑generated): 

\subsection{Attention Analysis}

We analyzed the attention patterns of \texttt{BERT-base-uncased} using the
NeuralOps Attention Visualization Lab. The model was loaded via the
\texttt{transformers} library and the attention weights were extracted for
all 12 layers and 12 heads. The input text ``The quick brown fox jumps over
the lazy dog'' was tokenized using the BERT WordPiece tokenizer, resulting in
10 tokens. Attention patterns were visualized using the BertViz-style head
view, with colors scaled by attention weight magnitude (0.0--1.0).

For the Galerkin attention variant (rank=64), the Petrov-Galerkin projection
was applied to the key and value matrices using a random sketching matrix
$S \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times r}$ drawn from $\mathcal{N}(0, 1/\sqrt{N})$.

Results Section (auto‑generated): 

\subsection{Results}

Figure~\ref{fig:attention-l5-h7} shows the attention pattern for Layer 5,
Head 7. This head exhibits a strong diagonal pattern characteristic of an
induction head, attending primarily to the immediately preceding token.
The head's entropy of 2.34 bits indicates moderately focused attention,
with 67.3\% of the attention mass concentrated on the top-3 tokens.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/attention_l5_h7.pdf}
  \caption{Attention pattern for BERT-base-uncased, Layer 5, Head 7,
           with Galerkin attention (rank=64).}
  \label{fig:attention-l5-h7}
\end{figure}

When compared to standard multi-head attention, the Galerkin variant
preserves 94.2\% of the attention pattern structure (measured by Jensen-Shannon
divergence), while reducing computational complexity from $O(N^2 \cdot D)$
to $O(N \cdot r \cdot D)$.

docs.title: Figure Export Pipeline
docs.text:
The attention visualization is exported as a publication‑ready PDF figure through a pipeline:

  1. SVG Capture: The current Zone 2 SVG is captured at 2× resolution (for print quality)
  2. LaTeX Font Rendering: Token labels and annotations are re‑rendered using LaTeX fonts (Computer Modern) via a WebAssembly build of MathJax, ensuring the figure matches the paper's typography
  3. PDF Conversion: The SVG is converted to PDF via svg2pdf (a client‑side library) or server‑side via rsvg-convert
  4. Figure Caption: Auto‑generated using the LLM, following academic writing conventions
  5. BibTeX Entry: The attention type's paper is auto‑cited, with the BibTeX entry fetched from the agents paper library

docs.title: Integration with Paper App

docs.title: Performance Considerations

• SVG capture uses XMLSerializer which runs synchronously but takes <5ms for typical heatmaps
  • For very large matrices (512×512 tokens), SVG capture is deferred to a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread
  • The capture engine includes a size estimator that warns users if the exported SVG exceeds 10MB (common for large models with many tokens)

  • Generated content includes alt text for figures
  • Reports include proper heading hierarchy (H1 → H2 → H3) for screen reader navigation

docs.title: 6.1 Real‑Time Synchronization
docs.text:
All changes made in Zone 4 are synchronized in real‑time to: 1. Zone 1 (Context Bar): updates the model/attention/layer/head chips 2. Zone 2 (Visualization Canvas): re‑renders the attention view 3. Zone 3 (Math Panel): updates the formula highlighting 4. Zone 5 (Analytics): re‑computes statistics 5. Zone 6 (Interpretability): re‑runs ablation analysis 6. Zone 7 (Social): updates share links and metadata 7. URL: updates query parameters for shareability

Synchronization uses Zustand's subscribe API with selective subscriptions — each zone only re‑renders when its relevant slice changes, avoiding unnecessary re‑renders.

docs.title: 6.2 Offline Support

docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
Zone 4 is the mission control of the Attention Dashboard. Its three core features — the Unified Selector, the "Train with This Attention" button, and the Create Note/Report/Paper trio — provide a complete workflow from exploration to publication:

Feature Core Innovation Key Technology Unified Selector Live thumbnail previews on layer slider; visual head grid with size‑encoded importance Comlink Web Workers for thumbnail generation; Framer Motion for animations; @tanstack/react-virtual for performance Train with This Attention One‑click bridge from visualization to experiment; pre‑filled launcher with cost estimation tRPC for type‑safe API calls; SSE for real‑time progress; PGlite for offline queuing Create Note / Report / Paper Three‑tier output: informal note → semi‑formal report → formal paper; LLM‑powered summarization Vercel AI SDK for streaming LLM generation; MathJax WASM for LaTeX font rendering; svg2pdf for figure export

Together, these features transform the attention dashboard from a passive visualization tool into an active research platform where every insight can be immediately tested, documented, and published — all without leaving the browser.

docs.title: 📈 Zone 5: Analytics & Diagnostics Dashboard — Complete Implementation Specification
Overview
docs.text:
Zone 5 is the quantitative intelligence center of the attention dashboard. While Zone 2 shows what attention looks like and Zone 3 explains how it works mathematically, Zone 5 answers why certain heads matter, which heads are similar, when patterns emerge during training, and where token meaning travels across layers. It transforms raw attention tensors into actionable diagnostic metrics that directly inform model compression, architecture selection, and training monitoring.

The five features in this zone are arranged as a tabbed panel occupying the right half of the dashboard (or the full width below the canvas on smaller screens). Each tab is a self‑contained analytical view, but all share a common data pipeline and state management architecture.

docs.title: Shared Infrastructure for All Zone 5 Features
A. Data Pipeline Architecture
docs.text:
All five features consume the same underlying data but transform it differently. The pipeline follows a three‑stage ETL pattern optimized for browser execution:

┌──────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
│  RAW DATA    │────▶│  COMPUTE LAYER  │────▶│  RENDER LAYER    │
│  (Zone 2)    │     │  (Web Worker)   │     │  (Main Thread)   │
│              │     │                 │     │                  │
│ • Attention  │     │ • Head scoring  │     │ • 3D Scatter     │
│   matrices   │     │ • Clustering    │     │ • Dendrogram     │
│ • Hidden     │     │ • Logit lens    │     │ • Timeline       │
│   states     │     │ • UMAP/t‑SNE    │     │ • Trajectories   │
│ • Gradients  │     │ • Time‑lapse    │     │ • Word cloud     │
└──────────────┘     └─────────────────┘     └──────────────────┘
        │                     │                       │
        ▼                     ▼                       ▼
   IndexedDB             Pyodide +              React + Three.js
   (cache)              NumPy/SciPy            + Deck.gl + D3.js
                         in Web Worker

Stage 1 — Raw Data Extraction: Attention matrices and hidden states are extracted from the model via transformers.js (running ONNX Runtime in the browser) or fetched from the Django backend API. For models too large for client‑side inference, the backend computes attention and streams results via the existing WebSocket infrastructure or REST endpoints. Raw data is cached in IndexedDB using idb-keyval for instant recall on repeated explorations.

Stage 2 — Compute Layer (Web Worker with Pyodide): Heavy numerical computation—singular value decomposition, hierarchical clustering, t‑SNE/UMAP projection, head importance scoring—runs in a dedicated Web Worker using Pyodide (CPython compiled to WebAssembly). Pyodide provides NumPy, SciPy, and scikit‑learn directly in the browser, avoiding the need to re‑implement these algorithms in JavaScript. The worker receives raw tensors as JSON/ArrayBuffer, executes Python scripts, and returns computed results via postMessage. This keeps the main thread free for rendering and interaction, maintaining 60fps even during heavy computation.

Stage 3 — Render Layer (Main Thread): Computed results arrive as typed arrays or JSON and are passed to the visualization components. Each feature uses a specialized rendering library chosen for its performance characteristics with the expected data size:

Feature Data Size Rendering Library Rationale 3D Scatter 144–1200 points (heads) Deck.gl (ScatterplotLayer) GPU‑accelerated via WebGL2; handles millions of points; built‑in picking, brushing, viewport Dendrogram 144–1200 leaves D3.js (d3-hierarchy) + React‑wrapper SVG rendering for crisp vector output; interactive zoom/pan via d3-zoom Logit Lens Timeline 10–50 layers × top‑k words Custom Canvas + Framer Motion Canvas for word cloud rendering; Framer Motion for smooth timeline scrubbing Evolution Time‑Lapse 144 heads × N epochs Deck.gl + requestAnimationFrame GPU‑accelerated point updates; smooth animation loop Semantic Pathway 10–50 tokens × 10–50 layers Deck.gl + Three.js lines GPU scatter for points; Three.js for curved trajectory tubes

docs.title: B. State Management
docs.text:
All Zone 5 features share a single Zustand store (useAnalyticsStore) that holds computed metrics, derived from the raw attention data. This store is separate from the main useAttentionContext store (Zone 1) to avoid unnecessary re‑renders of the visualization canvas when only analytics data changes.

interface AnalyticsState {
  // Head metrics (Feature 16)
  headScores: HeadScore[];           // importance, stability, similarity per head
  headClusters: ClusterResult | null; // dendrogram data (Feature 17)

  // Logit lens (Feature 18)
  layerPredictions: LayerPrediction[]; // top‑k tokens per layer

  // Evolution (Feature 19)
  evolutionData: EvolutionSnapshot[];  // head scores per epoch
  currentEpoch: number;

  // Semantic pathway (Feature 20)
  tokenEmbeddings: TokenEmbedding[];   // 2D coordinates per token per layer
  tokenTrajectories: Trajectory[];

  // Computation state
  isComputing: boolean;
  computeProgress: number;            // 0–100
  computeError: string | null;
}

Components subscribe to granular selectors (e.g., useAnalyticsStore(s => s.headScores)) to prevent re‑renders when unrelated state changes.

docs.title: C. Computation Trigger & Loading States
docs.text: All five features are computed lazily—only when the user opens the corresponding tab for the first time, or when the underlying model/text/layer changes. A progress indicator (skeleton shimmer with percentage) appears during computation. If the computation takes longer than 2 seconds, a "Running in background" toast appears, allowing the user to continue exploring other zones while analytics compute.

docs.title: Feature 16: Head Importance × Stability × Similarity 3D Scatter
16.1 Scientific Foundation
docs.text: This feature directly implements the three pruning criteria proposed by BHPVAS (Liu et al., Journal of Visualization, 2024): importance score, stability score, and similarity score for evaluating self‑attention heads. These three metrics form a comprehensive diagnostic framework where each head can be assessed simultaneously for its contribution (importance), consistency (stability), and redundancy (similarity).

docs.title: 16.2 Metric Definitions
docs.text:
Importance Score: For head h in layer l, the importance measures how much the model output changes when this head is ablated (zeroed out). It is computed as:

I(l,h) = ‖L(x) − L_{¬(l,h)}(x)‖₂

where L(x) is the original loss (or output logits) and L_{¬(l,h)}(x) is the loss after masking head (l,h). In practice, this is approximated using the first‑order Taylor expansion:

I(l,h) ≈ ‖∂L/∂A_{l,h} ⊙ A_{l,h}‖₂

where A_{l,h} is the attention weight matrix for head (l,h). This avoids the computational cost of full ablation. The gradient ∂L/∂A_{l,h} is obtained during a single backward pass on the calibration text.

Stability Score: Stability quantifies how consistent a head's attention pattern is across different inputs. Given a set of K calibration texts, the attention matrix A_{l,h}^{(k)} is computed for each. The stability is:

S(l,h) = 1 − σ( { ‖A_{l,h}^{(i)} − A_{l,h}^{(j)}‖_F } ) / μ

where σ is the standard deviation of pairwise Frobenius distances between attention matrices, and μ is their mean. A low stability score indicates a head whose behavior varies wildly with input, while high stability suggests a specialized, consistent function.

Similarity Score: Similarity measures how redundant a head is with respect to other heads in the same layer. For head (l,h), the similarity is the average Jensen‑Shannon divergence between its attention distribution and every other head in layer l:

Sim(l,h) = (1/N) Σ_{j≠h} JSD( A_{l,h} ‖ A_{l,j} )

where JSD is the Jensen‑Shannon divergence between the row‑wise attention distributions. High similarity indicates a head that could potentially be pruned without significant loss.

docs.title: 16.3 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Rationale Computation Pyodide (NumPy/SciPy) in Web Worker SVD, JSD, pairwise distances—native Python scientific stack compiled to WASM 3D Rendering Deck.gl (ScatterplotLayer) GPU‑accelerated via WebGL2; handles millions of points at 60fps; built‑in picking, brushing, tooltip, viewport controls React Integration @deck.gl/react Declarative React component for Deck.gl layers Axes & Labels Deck.gl TextLayer + GridLayer GPU‑rendered text for axis labels Orbit Controls Custom OrbitController class wrapping Deck.gl view state Provides rotate, pan, zoom with inertia Color Mapping d3-scale-chromatic Continuous color scales (Viridis, Plasma, Turbo) for head type encoding Brushing Deck.gl BrushingExtension Rectangle selection to filter heads by metric range

docs.title: 16.4 Why Deck.gl Over Plotly or Three.js
docs.text: Plotly.js 3D scatter plots struggle with more than a few thousand points and lack GPU acceleration for true 3D. React Three Fiber, while powerful, requires manual shader programming for optimal performance with large point clouds. Deck.gl provides the ideal middle ground: a pre‑built, GPU‑accelerated ScatterplotLayer designed explicitly for large‑scale data visualization, with built‑in interactivity (hover, click, brush) and seamless React integration via @deck.gl/react.

docs.title: 16.5 Component Architecture
docs.text:
HeadScatter3D (container)
├── DeckGL (canvas)
│   ├── ScatterplotLayer (head points)
│   │   └── Each point: position=[importance, stability, similarity]
│   │                  radius=10, color=by head type, opacity=0.8
│   ├── TextLayer (axis labels)
│   │   └── "Importance →", "Stability →", "Similarity →"
│   ├── GridLayer (reference grid on floor plane)
│   └── BrushingExtension (rectangle selection)
├── ScatterTooltip (floating div, positioned by Deck.gl picking)
│   └── Shows: Layer, Head, Scores, Head Type, "Click to zoom"
├── ScatterLegend (fixed position, bottom‑left)
│   └── Color → Head Type mapping
├── ScatterControls (top‑right overlay)
│   ├── Metric selector: which metric on which axis (swappable)
│   ├── Color by: [Head Type | Layer | Importance | Stability | Similarity]
│   ├── Size by: [Uniform | Importance | Stability]
│   ├── Reset view button
│   └── Export PNG/SVG button
└── SelectedHeadPanel (slides up from bottom when a head is clicked)
    ├── Miniature attention heatmap preview
    ├── Numerical scores
    ├── "Zoom to Head View" button (switches Zone 2 to this head)
    └── "Compare with…" button (opens side‑by‑side comparison)

docs.title: 16.6 Rendering Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Data arrives from Web Worker as Float32Array of shape (N_heads, 3) for positions plus (N_heads,) for colors and sizes.
  2. Deck.gl layer receives data as an array of plain objects: [{importance, stability, similarity, layer, head, type, color, size}, …].
  3. Vertex shader (GPU) transforms each point from data space to clip space using the current view matrix.
  4. Fragment shader (GPU) applies Gaussian blur for depth‑of‑field effect (distant points appear softer).
  5. Picking engine (GPU) renders an off‑screen framebuffer with unique color IDs per point. On mouse move, the color under the cursor is read back to identify the hovered point with zero CPU overhead.
  6. Brushing uses the BrushingExtension to render a selection rectangle; selected points are highlighted and an onBrushEnd callback filters the dendrogram and other linked views.

docs.title: 16.7 Interactive Behaviors
docs.text: Interaction Behavior Orbit (left‑drag) Rotate the camera around the data center Pan (right‑drag or shift+left‑drag) Translate the camera Zoom (scroll) Zoom in/out; Deck.gl handles this natively Hover Tooltip appears showing head ID, layer, exact scores, head type Click Selects the head; opens the SelectedHeadPanel; highlights the head in the dendrogram and Model View Double‑click Zooms the camera to frame the selected head; resets on second double‑click Brush (shift+drag) Rectangle selection; selects all heads within the rectangle; updates dendrogram to highlight selected cluster Axis drag Swap which metric is on which axis (drag "Importance" label to the Y‑axis, etc.) Color legend click Filter by head type (e.g., show only "Positional" heads)

docs.title: 16.8 Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
• Instanced rendering: Deck.gl uses GPU instancing to render all points in a single draw call, avoiding per‑point CPU overhead.
  • Level‑of‑detail (LOD): Points beyond a certain distance threshold are rendered as smaller dots or skipped entirely, controlled by Deck.gl's pointRadiusMinPixels and radiusMaxPixels.
  • Data update: When only colors or sizes change (not positions), Deck.gl updates only the affected GPU buffers without re‑uploading geometry.
  • Memoization: The ScatterplotLayer data array is wrapped in useMemo with dependencies on [headScores, colorBy, sizeBy].
  • Web Worker offload: All scoring computation runs in the worker; the main thread only receives the final array of numbers.

docs.title: 16.9 Edge Cases & Error States
docs.text: Scenario Behavior No data (model not yet loaded) Shows placeholder: "Run a forward pass to compute head scores." with a CTA button Single layer model Z‑axis (Similarity) is disabled; scatter becomes 2D; a note explains "Similarity requires ≥2 heads per layer" Computation timeout (>30s) Worker is terminated; error state shows "Computation timed out. Try a smaller model or fewer calibration texts." with retry All heads identical All points cluster at a single location; a warning banner: "All heads exhibit identical behavior—this model may be untrained or collapsed." GPU not available Falls back to SVG rendering via D3.js (slower but functional); a banner indicates "Software rendering mode"

docs.title: 16.10 Accessibility
docs.text:
• Keyboard navigation: Tab to focus the scatter plot; arrow keys rotate the view; +/- zoom; Enter selects the hovered point.
  • aria-label on the Deck.gl canvas: "3D scatter plot of attention head scores. X‑axis: Importance. Y‑axis: Stability. Z‑axis: Similarity. {N} heads displayed."
  • The SelectedHeadPanel announces via aria-live="polite" when a head is selected.
  • Color‑blind safe mode: toggle in the controls switches from Viridis to a CVD‑friendly palette (Cividis).

docs.title: 17.1 Scientific Foundation
docs.text:
Hierarchical clustering groups attention heads based on the similarity of their attention patterns. Heads that consistently produce similar attention distributions across multiple inputs are grouped into the same cluster. The resulting dendrogram reveals the functional organization of the attention mechanism—for example, BERT models typically exhibit distinct clusters for positional heads (attending to adjacent tokens), semantic heads (attending to related content words), delimiter heads (attending to punctuation/separators), and induction heads (copying previous token patterns).

The clustering uses agglomerative hierarchical clustering with Ward's linkage criterion, which minimizes the within‑cluster variance. The input is the pairwise Jensen‑Shannon divergence matrix between all heads, computed across a set of calibration texts.

docs.title: 17.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Rationale Computation Pyodide (scipy.cluster.hierarchy) in Web Worker SciPy's linkage and dendrogram functions are the gold standard for hierarchical clustering; running in Pyodide avoids re‑implementation Dendrogram Rendering D3.js (d3-hierarchy + custom d3-cluster) D3's cluster layout produces publication‑quality dendrograms with precise control over node positioning React Integration Custom DendrogramView component using useRef + useEffect D3 manipulates the DOM directly within a React‑managed container; React owns the container, D3 owns the internals Zoom/Pan d3-zoom Built‑in zoom behavior with smooth transitions and touch support Color Coding d3-scale-chromatic Consistent color scheme with the scatter plot Export svg-crowbar or manual XMLSerializer Extracts the SVG for download as PNG/SVG

docs.title: 17.3 Component Architecture
docs.text:
DendrogramPanel (container)
├── DendrogramControls (top bar)
│   ├── Linkage method selector: [Ward | Average | Complete | Single]
│   ├── Distance metric selector: [JSD | Cosine | Euclidean]
│   ├── Color by: [Auto‑label | Layer | Head Type]
│   ├── Expand/Collapse all button
│   ├── Export SVG button
│   └── Search head input (highlights matching leaf)
├── DendrogramSVG (scrollable SVG container)
│   ├── <g class="links"> (the tree branches, as curved paths)
│   ├── <g class="nodes"> (internal nodes, as circles)
│   ├── <g class="leaves"> (leaf nodes = individual heads)
│   │   └── Each leaf: colored rectangle + head label
│   ├── <g class="heatmap-strip"> (optional: mini heatmap next to each leaf)
│   └── <g class="cluster-labels"> (auto‑generated cluster names)
├── ClusterDetailPanel (right sidebar, shown when a cluster is selected)
│   ├── Prototypical attention pattern (the cluster centroid)
│   ├── Head count in cluster
│   ├── Average importance/stability/similarity for the cluster
│   ├── "Prune this cluster" button (exports pruning recipe)
│   └── "Explore cluster in 3D" button (highlights cluster in Feature 16)
└── DendrogramTooltip (follows cursor on hover)
    └── Shows: Head ID, Layer, Head Type, Cluster assignment

docs.title: 17.4 Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Raw attention matrices for all heads across K calibration texts are fetched from the cache or computed.
  2. Web Worker receives the matrices as a flat Float32Array.
  3. Python (Pyodide) computes the pairwise JSD matrix using scipy.spatial.distance.jensenshannon, then runs scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage with Ward's method.
  4. The linkage matrix (a (N-1)×4 array) and the leaf order are returned to the main thread.
  5. D3.js receives the linkage data and renders the dendrogram using d3.cluster(). The d3-hierarchy module implements "several popular techniques for visualizing hierarchical data" including node‑link diagrams.
  6. Auto‑labeling: The system traverses the dendrogram and assigns cluster labels based on the prototypical attention pattern of each cluster. The labeling uses a rule‑based classifier: if the centroid attention pattern shows a strong diagonal (token attending to itself), it's a "Positional" cluster; if attention is concentrated on semantically related tokens (detected via word embeddings), it's a "Semantic" cluster; if attention is on punctuation/CLS/SEP tokens, it's a "Delimiter" cluster.

docs.title: 17.5 Interactive Behaviors
docs.text: Interaction Behavior Hover leaf Tooltip with head details; highlights the corresponding point in the 3D scatter Click leaf Selects the head; switches Zone 2 to that head; opens the SelectedHeadPanel Click internal node Selects the cluster; opens ClusterDetailPanel; highlights all leaves in that cluster Double‑click internal node Collapses/expands the subtree below that node Brush (drag on heatmap strip) Selects a range of heads; filters the scatter plot to show only those heads Scroll Zooms the dendrogram in/out (using d3-zoom) Drag Pans the dendrogram Search Highlights the leaf matching the typed head ID; scrolls it into view Linkage change Recomputes clustering (triggers Web Worker) with the new method; dendrogram animates to the new layout

docs.title: 17.6 Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
• Lazy leaf rendering: Only leaves visible in the viewport (plus a buffer of 50) are rendered as full elements; off‑screen leaves are placeholder rectangles with the same dimensions to maintain scroll height.
  • Virtualized heatmap strip: The optional mini‑heatmap next to each leaf uses Canvas rendering for hundreds of leaves, avoiding SVG DOM bloat.
  • Memoized linkage: If the user switches between linkage methods and then back, the previous result is cached (in the Zustand store) to avoid recomputation.
  • Web Worker reuse: The Pyodide worker is kept alive between computations; subsequent clustering runs use the already‑initialized Python environment, reducing startup latency from ~3s to ~100ms.

docs.title: 17.7 Edge Cases & Error States
docs.text: Scenario Behavior Single head in a layer That layer's heads are excluded from clustering (or shown as isolated leaves); a note explains All heads identical The dendrogram shows a single deep branch with all leaves clustered at zero distance; warning displayed Computation failure Error state with "Clustering failed. Try a different distance metric or fewer heads." Very large model (1000+ heads) Dendrogram becomes too dense; auto‑switch to "circular dendrogram" layout (using d3.cluster().size([360, radius]) for radial display)

docs.title: 17.8 Auto‑Labeling Algorithm
docs.text:
The auto‑labeling works as follows:

  1. For each cluster, compute the centroid attention pattern by averaging the attention matrices of all heads in the cluster (after aligning them via the leaf order).
  2. Extract diagnostic features from the centroid:
  3. diagonal_strength: mean of the diagonal entries (token self‑attention)
  4. adjacent_strength: mean of the first off‑diagonal (attention to immediate neighbors)
  5. delimiter_strength: attention weight on [CLS], [SEP], punctuation tokens
  6. semantic_strength: correlation between attention weights and word embedding similarity
  7. Classify using a decision tree: 
    if diagonal_strength > 0.3: → "Positional"
elif delimiter_strength > 0.2: → "Delimiter"
elif semantic_strength > 0.15: → "Semantic"
elif adjacent_strength > 0.3: → "Local Context"
else: → "Mixed / Diffuse"

docs.title: 17.9 Accessibility
docs.text:
• The dendrogram SVG includes aria-label on each leaf: "Head L{layer}H{head}, cluster {name}, similarity score {score}."
  • Keyboard: Arrow keys navigate between leaves; Enter selects; +/- expand/collapse.
  • Screen reader announces "Dendrogram updated. {N} clusters identified: {cluster names}."

docs.title: 18.1 Scientific Foundation
docs.text:
The Logit Lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) is a training‑free interpretability method that reveals how a transformer model's prediction evolves layer by layer. At each layer, the hidden state h_l is projected into vocabulary space using the model's unembedding matrix W_U:

p_l = softmax(W_U · h_l)

This "directly reads out the model's implicit prediction at each layer" without any extra machinery. The logit lens shows that early layers produce confused, diffuse predictions, mid layers gradually converge toward the correct token, and final layers refine the probability distribution.

docs.title: 18.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Rationale Hidden state extraction transformers.js (ONNX Runtime) or backend API Extracts hidden states from each transformer layer in the browser or via API Vocabulary projection Custom WebAssembly module or Pyodide (NumPy) Matrix multiplication W_U @ h_l for all layers; NumPy is sufficient Top‑k extraction Pyodide (NumPy argsort) Finds top‑k token indices and probabilities Timeline Scrubber Framer Motion + custom slider Smooth animation between layers; spring physics for scrubber Word Cloud Custom Canvas component Renders variable‑sized text with collision detection Token Highlighting React state + CSS transitions Highlights the predicted token in the original input text

docs.title: 18.3 Component Architecture
docs.text:
LogitLensPanel (container)
├── TimelineScrubber (top)
│   ├── Layer indicator: "Layer 5 / 12"
│   ├── Slider input (range 0 to N_layers-1)
│   ├── Play/Pause button (auto‑advances through layers)
│   ├── Speed control (0.5×, 1×, 2×)
│   └── Current prediction display: "Model predicts: 'Paris' (87.3%)"
├── PredictionWordCloud (center, main visualization)
│   └── Canvas element rendering top‑k tokens as sized text
├── TokenContributionBar (bottom)
│   ├── Horizontal stacked bar showing which tokens contributed to the top prediction
│   └── Each segment colored by attention head, width proportional to contribution
├── LayerTimeline (vertical bar on the left)
│   ├── 12–48 dots representing layers
│   ├── Current layer dot is highlighted and pulsing
│   ├── Click any dot to jump to that layer
│   └── Color gradient: early layers (cold/blue) → late layers (hot/red)
└── InputTextHighlight (overlaid on the original text display)
    └── Each token colored by its attention to the predicted token

docs.title: 18.4 Data Flow
docs.text:
1. The model runs a forward pass on the input text. Hidden states h_0, h_1, …, h_L are captured at each layer's output (after the attention sub‑layer and FFN, before layer norm).
  2. The unembedding matrix W_U (also called the LM head) is extracted from the model. For BERT, this is the cls.predictions.decoder.weight; for GPT, it's lm_head.weight.
  3. For each layer l, the logit lens projection is computed: logits_l = W_U @ h_l (matrix multiplication of shape [vocab_size, d_model] × [d_model]).
  4. Softmax is applied to get probabilities: p_l = softmax(logits_l).
  5. The top‑k (k=20) tokens and their probabilities are extracted.
  6. The Canvas word cloud renders each token as text sized proportionally to its probability, positioned using a force‑directed layout to avoid overlaps.

docs.title: 18.5 Interactive Behaviors
docs.text: Interaction Behavior Scrub timeline Real‑time update of the word cloud and token contribution bar Click a word in the cloud Highlights that token's probability across all layers (shows a sparkline) Click a layer dot Jumps the timeline to that layer Play Auto‑advances through layers at the selected speed; word cloud animates smoothly Hover a token in the input text Shows which layers attend to that token most strongly Double‑click a layer Switches Zone 2 (Attention Canvas) to show the attention pattern at that layer

docs.title: 18.6 Canvas Word Cloud Rendering
docs.text:
The word cloud uses a custom Canvas implementation for performance:

  1. Layout: A simple force‑directed algorithm places tokens. Each token is a circle (radius ∝ log(probability)). Tokens repel each other; the canvas center attracts all tokens. The simulation runs for 50 iterations (sufficient for 20 tokens).
  2. Rendering: ctx.font is set proportionally to probability (min 12px, max 48px). ctx.fillStyle uses a gradient from the current layer's color. ctx.fillText() renders each token at its computed position.
  3. Animation: When the layer changes, tokens smoothly transition to their new positions and sizes using requestAnimationFrame with linear interpolation over 300ms.

docs.title: 18.7 Edge Cases & Error States
docs.text: Scenario Behavior Model without LM head (e.g., encoder‑only without pretraining head) Shows "This model does not have a language modeling head. Logit lens requires an unembedding matrix." Vocabulary too large (100K+ tokens) Top‑k is increased to 50; word cloud switches to "dense pack" layout All layers predict the same token Timeline shows a flat line; info banner: "This model converges early—all layers agree on the prediction." Early layers produce uniform distribution Word cloud shows many tiny, equally‑sized words; a note explains "Early layers have not yet focused on a specific token"

docs.title: 19.1 Scientific Foundation
docs.text:
During training, attention heads do not immediately specialize. Research shows that positional patterns emerge first (often within the first few hundred steps), followed by semantic patterns, and finally delimiter/induction patterns. This feature visualizes that developmental trajectory, allowing researchers to identify the "critical period" when each head crystallizes into its final function.

The time‑lapse is generated from training checkpoints saved during the experiment. For each checkpoint, the attention patterns for all heads are extracted, and the head scores (importance, stability, similarity) are computed. The animation shows how heads move through the 3D metric space over training time.

docs.title: 19.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Rationale Checkpoint loading Backend API (/api/experiments/{id}/checkpoints/) Checkpoints are stored on the server; loaded on‑demand Head score computation Pyodide (NumPy) in Web Worker Same scoring pipeline as Feature 16, applied per checkpoint Animation requestAnimationFrame + Deck.gl data updates Smooth 60fps animation; Deck.gl efficiently updates point positions without full re‑render Timeline Custom React slider + Framer Motion Scrubbable timeline with keyframe markers Sparklines D3.js (d3-shape) rendered to SVG Small inline charts showing individual head trajectories

docs.title: 19.3 Component Architecture
docs.text:
EvolutionPanel (container)
├── EvolutionTimeline (top)
│   ├── Slider: epoch 0 → epoch N
│   ├── Keyframe markers (vertical lines at significant events: "Head 7 crystallizes", "Loss drops")
│   ├── Play/Pause/Step controls
│   └── Speed selector
├── EvolutionScatter3D (center, reuses Feature 16's Deck.gl component)
│   └── Points animate along trajectories as the timeline scrubs
├── HeadTrajectoryPanel (right sidebar)
│   ├── Selected head's trajectory sparkline (importance over time)
│   ├── "Crystallization epoch": when the head's pattern stabilized
│   ├── "Pruning recommendation": based on final scores
│   └── "Compare with another head" selector
├── CrystallizationTimeline (bottom)
│   ├── Horizontal Gantt‑style chart
│   ├── Each row = one head; each bar = from first emergence to crystallization
│   └── Color‑coded by final head type
└── EventLog (bottom‑right)
    └── Auto‑generated timeline of significant events during training

docs.title: 19.4 Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Checkpoint list is fetched from the backend: [{epoch: 0, checkpoint_path: …}, {epoch: 10, …}, …].
  2. For each checkpoint, the Web Worker loads the attention data (from cache or backend), computes head scores, and stores the result.
  3. The animation interpolates between consecutive checkpoints. For epochs between saved checkpoints, linear interpolation is used (with a note indicating "interpolated").
  4. Crystallization detection: A head is considered "crystallized" when its attention pattern's JSD to the final pattern drops below a threshold (default 0.1) and remains below for at least 3 consecutive checkpoints.

docs.title: 19.5 Animation Pipeline
docs.text:
The animation loop uses requestAnimationFrame:

  1. On each frame, the current epoch (float) is computed from the timeline position.
  2. For each head, its position (importance, stability, similarity) is interpolated between the two nearest checkpoints.
  3. The Deck.gl ScatterplotLayer data array is updated in place (mutating the positions) and layer.setChangeFlags({dataChanged: true}) is called to trigger a GPU buffer update.
  4. The frame rate is capped at 60fps; if computation takes longer than 16ms, frames are skipped to maintain smooth animation.
