Head never crystallizes Marked as "Unstable" in the Gantt chart; sparkline shows continuing fluctuation Very long training (10K+ epochs) Checkpoints are subsampled (max 200 displayed); slider uses logarithmic scale

docs.title: 20.1 Scientific Foundation
docs.text: Semantic Pathway (IEEE VIS 2025) is a visual analytics tool that "reveals how token representations evolve across layers in autoregressive Transformer models" by integrating "layerwise semantic trajectories, attention overlays, and output probability views into a unified interface". The key insight is that each token's hidden state h_l(token) can be projected into a 2D space (via UMAP or t‑SNE), and connecting the same token across layers reveals how its meaning evolves as information flows through the model.

docs.title: 20.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Rationale Dimension reduction umap-js (JavaScript UMAP) or Pyodide (sklearn.manifold.TSNE) UMAP runs in the browser via WebAssembly; preserves global structure better than t‑SNE and is faster 2D Scatter Deck.gl ScatterplotLayer GPU‑accelerated; handles hundreds of points smoothly Trajectory Lines Deck.gl LineLayer or Three.js Line via @react-three/fiber GPU‑rendered curved lines between token positions across layers Attention Influence Arcs Deck.gl ArcLayer GPU‑rendered arcs showing which tokens influenced a token's position change Layer Selector Custom React slider Filters which layers are shown Token Labeling Deck.gl TextLayer GPU‑rendered text labels for tokens

docs.title: 20.3 Component Architecture
docs.text:
SemanticPathwayPanel (container)
├── PathwayControls (top bar)
│   ├── Dimensionality reduction: [UMAP | t‑SNE | PCA]
│   ├── UMAP parameters: [n_neighbors, min_dist]
│   ├── Color by: [Token | Layer | POS tag | Attention influence]
│   ├── Show trajectories: [All tokens | Selected token only | None]
│   ├── Show influence arcs: [On | Off]
│   └── Export button
├── PathwayScatter2D (center, main visualization)
│   ├── Deck.gl canvas
│   │   ├── ScatterplotLayer: token positions at each layer
│   │   ├── LineLayer: trajectory paths connecting the same token across layers
│   │   ├── ArcLayer: influence arcs between tokens
│   │   └── TextLayer: token labels
├── TokenSelector (left sidebar)
│   ├── List of all tokens in the input text
│   ├── Click to highlight that token's trajectory
│   └── Color picker for custom trajectory colors
├── LayerSlider (bottom)
│   ├── Range slider: select which layers to display
│   └── Preset buttons: "All layers", "Early only", "Late only"
├── TokenInfluencePanel (right sidebar, shown when a token is selected)
│   ├── List of tokens ranked by influence on the selected token
│   ├── Influence score (JSD between trajectory with and without that token)
│   └── Click to highlight the influencing token's trajectory
└── PathwayLegend (bottom‑right)
    └── Color → Layer mapping (gradient from blue/cold → red/hot)

docs.title: 20.4 Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Hidden states for all tokens across all layers are extracted (same pipeline as Logit Lens).
  2. The hidden states for all tokens at all layers are concatenated into a single matrix of shape (N_tokens × N_layers, d_model). This ensures that UMAP/t‑SNE learns a shared embedding space where the same token at different layers can be compared.
  3. UMAP (via umap-js or Pyodide) reduces this matrix to 2D, producing coordinates (x, y) for every token at every layer.
  4. The coordinates are split by layer and token, forming trajectories.
  5. Attention influence is computed: for each token t at layer l, the change in its UMAP position from layer l-1 to l is attributed to other tokens proportionally to the attention weight from t to them at layer l.

docs.title: 20.5 Trajectory Rendering
docs.text:
Trajectories are rendered as curved paths (quadratic Bézier curves) connecting the same token's position at consecutive layers. The curve's control point is offset perpendicular to the line connecting the two points, with the offset magnitude proportional to the distance traveled (creating a visually pleasing "flow" effect).

For the selected token, the trajectory is rendered as a thick, glowing line (using Deck.gl's LineLayer with opacity: 1 and a larger widthScale). Other tokens' trajectories are rendered as thin, semi‑transparent lines.

docs.title: 20.6 Influence Arcs
docs.text:
Influence arcs show how attention from one token "pulls" another token's representation. An arc from token A at layer l to token B at layer l is rendered if the attention weight A_{l}(A→B) exceeds a threshold (default 0.1). The arc's thickness is proportional to the attention weight, and its color matches the attention head that produced it.

Deck.gl's ArcLayer is used for this purpose, as it "offers highly‑flexible API to customize how the data should be rendered" with GPU acceleration.

docs.title: 20.7 Interactive Behaviors
docs.text: Interaction Behavior Hover a point Tooltip: token text, layer number, 2D coordinates Click a point Selects that token; highlights its full trajectory; opens TokenInfluencePanel Click a trajectory Selects the token; same as clicking a point on that trajectory Drag the layer slider Filters which layers' points and trajectories are visible Hover an influence arc Tooltip: "Token X attends to Token Y with weight 0.34 (Head 7)" Double‑click empty space Resets selection; shows all trajectories Scroll Zooms the scatter plot Drag Pans the scatter plot

docs.title: 20.8 Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
• UMAP caching: The UMAP projection is cached per (model, text) pair in IndexedDB. Re‑loading the same text uses the cached coordinates.
  • Progressive rendering: Trajectories for the first 5 tokens render immediately; remaining tokens render over subsequent frames to avoid frame drops.
  • Arc culling: Influence arcs below the threshold are not sent to the GPU, reducing the number of arcs from O(N²) to O(N) in practice.
  • Layer filtering: When the layer slider filters to a subset of layers, only those points and trajectories are sent to Deck.gl.

docs.title: 20.9 Edge Cases & Error States
docs.text: Scenario Behavior Single‑token input Trajectories view is replaced with a note: "Trajectories require at least 2 tokens to show cross‑token relationships." UMAP produces overlapping points A jitter toggle adds small random offsets to separate overlapping points Very long text (500+ tokens) Only the first 128 tokens are projected; a note explains the truncation UMAP computation timeout Falls back to PCA (faster but less expressive); a banner indicates "Using PCA for faster rendering. Switch to UMAP for better separation."

docs.title: Brushing and Linking
docs.text:
All five features are linked through the shared useAnalyticsStore. Interactions in one feature propagate to others:

  • Selecting a head in the 3D scatter highlights that leaf in the dendrogram, shows its trajectory in the evolution time‑lapse, and marks its tokens in the semantic pathway.
  • Selecting a cluster in the dendrogram filters the 3D scatter to show only those heads, updates the evolution view to show the cluster's collective trajectory, and highlights all tokens influenced by those heads.
  • Scrubbing the logit lens timeline updates the semantic pathway to show token positions at that specific layer.

docs.title: Unified Export
docs.text: A single "Export Dashboard Report" button in Zone 5 generates a comprehensive PDF containing all five visualizations (as SVG/PNG), the computed metrics table, and an auto‑generated textual summary of findings (e.g., "Layer 5 contains 3 positional heads and 1 semantic head. Head L5H7 shows high importance (0.87) and low similarity (0.12), making it a strong candidate for retention during pruning.").

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Zone 5 transforms raw attention tensors into a comprehensive diagnostic toolkit. The five features work together to answer the full lifecycle of attention analysis: which heads matter (3D scatter), which heads are similar (dendrogram), what the model predicts (logit lens), how patterns evolve (time‑lapse), and where meaning flows (semantic pathway). Each feature uses specialized rendering technology (Deck.gl for GPU‑accelerated scatter plots, D3.js for dendrograms, Canvas for word clouds) and offloads heavy computation to a Pyodide Web Worker to maintain a responsive 60fps interface.

docs.title: 🔬 Zone 6: Interpretability Tools — Complete Implementation Specification
Overview
docs.text:
Zone 6 is the deep inspection layer of the attention dashboard. It provides four interlinked tools that let researchers answer the hardest questions about transformer models: What does this head do? How do heads communicate? Which heads matter for a prediction? Can we trace the causal chain?

The four tools—Head Ablation Laboratory, Circuit Tracer, Dodrio‑Style Linguistic Overlay, and Causal Tracing—share a common backend architecture but each presents a radically different UX. They are built on four core Python libraries (TransformerLens, nnsight, pyvene, circuit‑tracer), three JavaScript visualization engines (D3.js, React‑Three‑Fiber, PixiJS), and one high‑performance communication layer (WebSocket + SharedArrayBuffer).

docs.title: Shared Architecture: The Intervention Backend
docs.text: All four tools in Zone 6 share a single Python backend that wraps the target model and exposes intervention capabilities through a WebSocket API. This backend runs as a persistent process (or Celery task) that loads the model once, then accepts intervention commands from the frontend, executes them, and streams results back.

docs.title: Backend Stack: Five Python Libraries That Do Different Things
docs.text:
The backend uses five libraries, each solving a distinct part of the intervention pipeline. Understanding why each is needed—rather than what API it exposes—is key to the architecture.

TransformerLens (the standard library) provides HookedTransformer, a model wrapper that adds HookPoint objects after every sublayer (attention, MLP, residual). This lets you register callbacks on any intermediate activation without modifying the model code itself. It also includes built‑in activation patching utilities and supports 50+ open‑weights models. TransformerLens is used here primarily for model loading and hook registration—it provides the cleanest interface for attaching intervention points to GPT‑2, Pythia, Gemma, and Llama‑style architectures.

nnsight (the deferred execution engine) wraps any PyTorch model and provides a model.trace() context manager that captures intervention code before executing it. Unlike TransformerLens, nnsight works with arbitrary PyTorch models (not just GPT‑style), including vision transformers and custom architectures. Its key innovation is that you write intervention code as if the model were running, but nnsight defers execution, optimizes the computation graph, and runs it efficiently. For the ablation laboratory, nnsight is preferred because it can apply interventions persistently via model.edit(), meaning ablated heads stay ablated across multiple forward passes without re‑registering hooks.

pyvene (the causal intervention framework) is built by Stanford NLP and provides a declarative, dict‑based way to specify complex interventions. Instead of writing raw hook functions, you define an IntervenableConfig that describes what activations to patch, where to patch them from, and how to combine them. pyvene handles the bookkeeping of clean vs. corrupted runs, interchange interventions, and counterfactual analysis. It is the engine behind the Causal Tracing tool, where researchers need to systematically test which activations causally affect the output.

circuit‑tracer (the attribution graph generator) is Anthropic's open‑source library for computing attribution graphs from transcoder features. It takes a model with pre‑trained cross‑layer transcoders (CLTs), runs a forward pass, and computes the direct effect that each non‑zero transcoder feature has on every other feature and on the output logits. The result is a JSON graph where nodes are "supernodes" (clusters of semantically related features) and edges are weighted attribution scores. This is the engine behind the Circuit Tracer tool.

spaCy + Stanza (the linguistic annotation pipeline) provide tokenization, part‑of‑speech tagging, dependency parsing, named entity recognition, and coreference resolution. They run on the same input text that was fed to the model, producing structured annotations that can be overlaid on attention visualizations. spaCy is used for English (fast, production‑ready); Stanza provides coverage for 68 languages through the same interface.

docs.title: Model Loading Strategy: Three‑Tier Architecture
docs.text:
The backend loads models in a three‑tier architecture to minimize startup time and memory:

Tier 1 — Cached Hooked Models. For GPT‑2, Pythia, Gemma, and Llama architectures, the backend uses TransformerLens's HookedTransformer.from_pretrained(), which downloads model weights once and caches them. Subsequent loads are near‑instantaneous (under 200ms for GPT‑2‑small).

Tier 2 — nnsight Wrapper. For models not supported by TransformerLens (custom architectures, vision transformers, multimodal models), the backend wraps them with nnsight.LanguageModel() or nnsight.NNsight(). This provides the same intervention interface (model.trace(), model.edit()) regardless of the underlying architecture.

Tier 3 — HuggingFace + Custom Hooks. For models where neither TransformerLens nor nnsight provides the needed granularity, the backend loads the model via HuggingFace AutoModel and registers PyTorch forward hooks manually using register_forward_hook(). This is the most flexible but most labor‑intensive approach, reserved for cutting‑edge models.

The backend selects the tier automatically based on the model ID. The selection logic is:

if model_id in TRANSFORMER_LENS_SUPPORTED:
    model = HookedTransformer.from_pretrained(model_id)
elif model_id in NNSIGHT_SUPPORTED:
    model = LanguageModel(model_id, device_map="auto")
else:
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id)
    register_custom_intervention_hooks(model)

docs.title: The Intervention WebSocket Protocol
docs.text:
The frontend communicates with the backend through a bidirectional WebSocket using a JSON‑based protocol. This is not a REST API because interventions need to be streaming and interactive—the user flips a toggle, the backend runs the model, and results stream back within 50–200ms.

Message types from frontend to backend:

Message Type Payload Purpose load_model {model_id, attention_type, attention_config} Load a new model (or attention variant) set_text {text} Set the input text for all subsequent interventions ablate_head {layer, head, enabled} Enable or disable a specific attention head ablate_chain {heads: [{layer, head, enabled}]} Batch enable/disable multiple heads get_attribution_graph {prompt} Generate a full attribution graph for the given prompt run_causal_trace {source_token, target_token, layers} Run causal tracing between two tokens get_linguistic_annotations {text} Get dependency parse, POS tags, coreference chains compare_ablations {ablations: [{name, heads}]} Compare multiple ablation configurations get_intervention_summary — Get the current intervention state and model info

Message types from backend to frontend:

Message Type Payload Purpose model_loaded {model_id, layers, heads_per_layer, vocab_size} Confirmation that model is ready attention_computed {tokens, layers: [{layer, heads: [{head, matrix}]}]} Full attention data for the current text ablation_result {before_logits, after_logits, affected_tokens} Logit changes from the most recent ablation attribution_graph {nodes: [{id, label, type, layer}], edges: [{source, target, weight}]} Full attribution graph causal_trace_result {paths: [{tokens, scores}], critical_path: [...]} Causal tracing results linguistic_annotations {tokens: [{text, pos, dep, head, ner}], dependencies: [{source, target, label}]} Linguistic annotation data intervention_state {ablated_heads: [{layer, head}], model_id, text} Current full intervention state logit_lens {layer_predictions: [{layer, top_k: [{token, prob}]}]} Logit lens data for all layers error {code, message} Error notification

docs.title: Performance Budget for Interventions
docs.text:
The intervention backend must meet strict latency targets to feel interactive:

Operation Target Latency Implementation Strategy Single head ablation (cached) < 100ms Run forward pass with one hook modification; cache clean activations Chain ablation (5+ heads) < 300ms Run single forward pass with all hooks applied simultaneously Attribution graph generation < 5s Use circuit‑tracer's optimized backend; run on GPU if available Causal tracing (10 layers) < 2s Run patching in parallel across layers using nnsight's multi‑invoke Linguistic annotation < 200ms Run spaCy pipeline; cache annotations per text Logit lens (all layers) < 1s Single forward pass; collect logits at each layer via hooks

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Head Ablation Laboratory lets researchers answer: "What happens if I remove this head? What if I remove these three heads together? Which heads are critical, and which are redundant?" The tool provides real‑time feedback: flip a toggle, see the model's output change.

docs.title: Backend Implementation: The Intervention Pipeline
docs.text:
The ablation backend uses nnsight's model.edit() for persistent interventions. Here is the architecture:

  1. Model wrapping: The model is wrapped with nnsight.LanguageModel(model_id, device_map="auto").
  2. Clean forward pass: On text input, a clean forward pass is run once. All intermediate activations (attention patterns, MLP outputs, residual stream values) are cached in memory.
  3. Intervention application: When the user toggles a head, the backend creates an intervention that zeros out the attention weights for that specific head. Using nnsight, this is:
with model.edit("ablated"):
    # For each ablated head, set its attention weights to zero
    for layer, head in ablated_heads:
        # Access the attention pattern for this specific head
        hook_name = f"transformer.h.{layer}.attn.attn_pattern"
        def zero_head(pattern, head_idx=head):
            pattern[:, head_idx, :, :] = 0
            return pattern
        model.add_intervention(hook_name, zero_head)
  1. Edited forward pass: The model runs with all ablations applied simultaneously. The output logits are compared with the clean run.
  2. Impact computation: For each ablated head configuration, the backend computes:
  3. Logit difference: How much did each token's probability change?
  4. KL divergence: How different is the output distribution from the clean run?
  5. Top‑k flip: Did the top prediction change?
  6. Result streaming: Results are sent back via WebSocket as they are computed.

docs.title: Caching Strategy for Fast Toggle Response
docs.text:
When a user rapidly toggles heads on and off, recomputing the full forward pass each time would be wasteful. The backend uses a cache‑and‑invalidate strategy:

  • Clean cache: The attention patterns and activations from the clean run are cached in GPU memory (or CPU if GPU memory is limited). This cache is invalidated only when the text changes.
  • Ablation overlay: For each toggled head, the backend doesn't re‑run the entire model—it only recomputes the affected layers. Layers above the ablated head can reuse cached activations. Layers at and below the ablated head must be recomputed.
  • Chain ablation: When multiple heads across different layers are ablated, the backend identifies the lowest affected layer and recomputes from there upward, applying all ablations in a single pass.

docs.title: Frontend Implementation: The Ablation Control Panel
docs.text:
The ablation panel is rendered as an interactive grid matching the Model View from Zone 2. Each head is a colored cell. A toggle switch on each cell enables/disables that head.

Visual states for each cell:

State Appearance Meaning Active (default) Full color, normal opacity Head is contributing normally Ablated Grayed out, 30% opacity, red X overlay Head is disabled Hovered Bright border, scale 1.05 Mouse is over this head Ablated + Hovered Gray with bright border Head is disabled, user is inspecting it Impact‑highlighted Pulsing glow animation This head was just toggled and had a large impact

Cell interactions: - Click: Toggle ablation on/off. - Shift+Click: Toggle this head and all heads in the same layer. - Ctrl+Click: Add this head to a "compare group" (batch ablation). - Right‑click: Open context menu with "Ablate permanently", "Zero weights", "Add noise", "Permute", "Show impact details".

docs.title: Impact Visualization: Before/After Comparison
docs.text:
When a head is toggled, the frontend shows a before/after comparison panel that appears as a slide‑in drawer from the right side of the Zone 2 canvas.

Panel contents: 1. Token probability bar chart: Two rows of bars (blue = before, red = after). Each bar represents a token's probability. Tokens that changed significantly are highlighted. 2. KL divergence gauge: A radial gauge showing how much the output distribution changed (0 = identical, 1+ = completely different). 3. Affected tokens table: A sortable table listing tokens whose probabilities changed by more than 1%, with the delta shown as a percentage. 4. Head importance score: Updated in real time as the user ablates, showing where this head ranks in importance compared to others.

docs.title: Chain Ablation Mode
docs.text:
The user can select multiple heads (via Shift+Click or a "Select All in Layer" button) and ablate them simultaneously. The frontend sends a single ablate_chain message with all selected heads. The backend runs a single forward pass with all ablations applied.

Compound effect visualization: The panel shows not just the individual impact of each head, but the compound effect—how much worse is the model when all selected heads are ablated compared to when just one is ablated? This reveals redundancy: if ablating heads A and B together has the same effect as ablating just A, then B is redundant given A.

docs.title: Export to Compression Pipeline
docs.text:
Every ablation configuration can be exported as a pruning recipe—a JSON file that can be fed directly into your model compression pipeline. The export button is prominently placed in the ablation panel.

Pruning recipe format:

{
  "model_id": "bert-base-uncased",
  "ablated_heads": [
    {"layer": 3, "head": 7},
    {"layer": 5, "head": 2}
  ],
  "impact_score": 0.87,
  "kl_divergence": 0.12,
  "recommended": true,
  "rationale": "These heads are redundant; ablating them has minimal impact on output quality."
}

This recipe can be imported into the compression pipeline, which will physically remove the heads and create a smaller, faster model.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Circuit Tracer reveals how attention heads communicate with each other. It shows the QK circuit (what a head "looks for" in keys from previous layers) and the OV circuit (what a head "writes" to the output that subsequent heads can read). The result is an attribution graph—a network diagram where nodes are features (transcoder‑decomposed directions in activation space) and edges show how information flows between them.

docs.title: Backend Implementation: Three‑Stage Pipeline
docs.text:
The circuit tracing backend has three stages, each implemented as a separate Python module:

Stage 1 — Transcoder Loading. The model must have pre‑trained cross‑layer transcoders (CLTs) installed. The backend uses the circuit‑tracer library (PyPI package circuit-tracer), which inherits from TransformerLens's HookedTransformer. Supported models include Pythia‑160M, Gemma‑2‑2B, and Llama‑3.2‑1B (the models for which Anthropic released pre‑trained CLTs).

Stage 2 — Attribution Graph Computation. For the given prompt, the model runs a forward pass. At each layer, the transcoders decompose the residual stream into features (sparse, interpretable directions). The attribution algorithm then computes, for each pair of non‑zero features (A, B), the direct effect of A on B: how much would B's activation change if A were zeroed out? This is computed via a linear approximation using the Jacobian of the model. The result is a directed graph with weighted edges.

Stage 3 — Supernode Formation. Raw features (hundreds or thousands) are too numerous to visualize. The backend groups features into supernodes using clustering based on activation similarity and semantic relatedness. Each supernode gets an auto‑generated label (e.g., "rhyming words," "French language," "punctuation"). This labeling is done via an LLM‑based probe: the backend samples sentences that strongly activate each supernode, then asks a small language model to describe what those sentences have in common.

docs.title: Frontend Implementation: Interactive Attribution Graph
docs.text:
The attribution graph is rendered using react‑force‑graph‑2d (a React wrapper around D3‑force for 2D graphs) and react‑force‑graph‑3d (a React‑Three‑Fiber wrapper for 3D graphs). The user can toggle between 2D and 3D modes.

2D mode (react‑force‑graph‑2d): - Nodes are circles colored by layer (Layer 0 = blue, Layer 5 = green, Layer 11 = red). - Node size is proportional to activation magnitude. - Edges are curved arrows colored by weight (darker = stronger connection). - The force simulation runs in real time—nodes settle into equilibrium over ~2 seconds. - Pan and zoom via mouse wheel and drag. - Hover: Highlights all edges connected to this node, dims others, shows a tooltip with the supernode label and top‑activating tokens. - Click: Pins the node, opens a detail panel showing the supernode's features, activation distribution, and a "Explain this supernode" button that queries an LLM. - Drag: Nodes can be repositioned manually.

3D mode (react‑force‑graph‑3d with r3f‑forcegraph): - The same graph data rendered in a Three.js scene using @react-three/fiber and @react-three/drei. - Nodes are 3D spheres with emissive materials that glow based on activation magnitude. - Edges are tubes with varying radius (wider = stronger). - The camera orbits the graph automatically (slow rotation) until the user interacts. - OrbitControls: Rotate, pan, zoom with mouse. - Post‑processing: Bloom effect (via @react-three/postprocessing) makes high‑activation nodes glow. - VR mode available via ForceGraphVR from the same library.

Graph interaction features: - Path highlighting: Click two nodes to highlight the shortest path between them. The path is animated with a pulsing glow. - Layer filtering: A slider lets users show/hide nodes from specific layers, revealing cross‑layer information flow. - Edge weight threshold: A slider filters out weak edges, showing only the strongest connections. - Export: The graph can be exported as JSON (for programmatic analysis), PNG (for papers), or interactive HTML (for sharing).

docs.title: JSON Schema for Attribution Graph
docs.text:
The backend outputs attribution graphs in Anthropic's standard JSON format, which is directly compatible with Neuronpedia's frontend. This means users can optionally export their graph and view it on Neuronpedia for comparison with published graphs.

{
  "nodes": [
    {
      "id": "supernode_0",
      "label": "French language features",
      "layer": 4,
      "features": ["f/1024", "f/2048"],
      "activation": 0.87,
      "top_tokens": ["Paris", "France", "bonjour"]
    }
  ],
  "edges": [
    {
      "source": "supernode_0",
      "target": "supernode_5",
      "weight": 0.73,
      "type": "qk"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Feature 23: Dodrio‑Style Linguistic Annotation Overlay — Implementation
Purpose
docs.text: The Dodrio overlay superimposes linguistic structure on top of the attention heatmap, letting researchers answer: Does this attention head track syntax? Does it follow the dependency parse tree? Does it recognize coreference chains?

docs.title: Backend Implementation: Linguistic Annotation Pipeline
docs.text:
The backend runs two NLP pipelines on the input text:

Pipeline 1 — spaCy (English, fast). Using en_core_web_trf (the transformer‑based spaCy model for English), the backend extracts: - POS tags: Part‑of‑speech for each token (NOUN, VERB, ADJ, etc.). - Dependency relations: For each token, its syntactic head and the relation label (nsubj, dobj, amod, etc.). - NER tags: Named entities (PERSON, ORG, GPE, etc.). - Noun phrases: Base noun phrase spans.

Pipeline 2 — Stanza (multilingual, accurate). For non‑English text or when higher accuracy is needed, the backend uses Stanza (StanfordNLP) via the spacy_stanza wrapper. Stanza provides the same annotations but with state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for 68 languages.

Coreference resolution is provided by spaCy's experimental.coref pipeline (for English) or the fastcoref library. The backend identifies which tokens refer to the same entity and groups them into coreference chains.

Annotation caching: Linguistic annotations are cached per text string. If the user changes the text, the annotations are recomputed. If the user changes only the model or layer, the cached annotations are reused.

docs.title: Frontend Implementation: Overlay Rendering
docs.text:
The linguistic overlay is rendered on top of the existing attention heatmap (Head View) and as an additional view mode. The overlay uses PixiJS (via @pixi/react) for high‑performance rendering, as D3 SVG becomes slow with more than 30 tokens.

Dependency parse overlay: - Each dependency relation is drawn as a curved arrow from the head token to the dependent token. - The arrow color indicates the relation type (e.g., nsubj = blue, dobj = orange, amod = green). - The arrow is drawn above the attention heatmap, with 60% opacity so the attention pattern remains visible underneath. - Hovering an arrow highlights it and shows the relation label in a tooltip.

POS tag coloring: - The token labels along the axes of the heatmap are colored by POS: NOUN = blue, VERB = red, ADJ = green, ADP = gray, etc. - A legend in the corner shows the color mapping.

Coreference chain highlighting: - When the user toggles "Coreference" mode, all tokens belonging to the same coreference chain are highlighted with matching background colors. - Connecting lines (dotted) are drawn between coreferring tokens across the sequence. - Attention weights between coreferring tokens are emphasized with a glow effect.

Alignment metric: The overlay computes an alignment score for each attention head—how well does the attention pattern correlate with the dependency structure? For a syntactic head, attention should be high between syntactically connected tokens. The alignment score is displayed as a badge (e.g., "Syntax Alignment: 0.87").

Toggle modes (multi‑select checkboxes): - [✓] Show dependency parse - [✓] Show POS tags - [ ] Show coreference chains - [ ] Show named entities - [ ] Show noun phrase spans - [✓] Auto‑detect head type (syntactic / semantic / delimiter)

When "Auto‑detect head type" is enabled, the system uses the computed alignment scores to classify each head and displays a badge: "This head appears to be a syntactic head (dependency alignment: 0.92)."

docs.title: Feature 24: Causal Tracing — Knockout Experiment — Implementation
Purpose
docs.text: Causal Tracing lets researchers answer: "Which specific activations caused this token to be predicted? If I change the activation at layer 5, position 3, does the output at position 7 change?" This is the most rigorous interpretability tool—it doesn't just show correlations (like attention weights), it tests causation through systematic intervention.

docs.title: Backend Implementation: The Causal Tracing Engine
docs.text:
The causal tracing backend uses pyvene (Stanford NLP) for its declarative intervention framework. The core algorithm follows the ROME (Rank One Model Editing) causal tracing procedure, adapted for real‑time interactive use.

Step‑by‑step algorithm:

  1. Baseline (clean) run: The model is run on the input text. All activations are collected and cached.
  2. Corrupted run: The model is run on a corrupted version of the input, where the target token is replaced with noise (e.g., Gaussian noise added to the embedding of a specific token). The corrupted output is collected.
  3. Patching runs: For each (layer, token_position) pair, the model is run with the corrupted input, but the clean activation at (layer, token_position) is restored. If restoring this one activation recovers the clean output, then that activation is causally important for the prediction.
  4. Causal graph construction: The patching results are aggregated into a graph showing which (layer, position) pairs causally influence which other (layer, position) pairs. The graph is thresholded—only edges with causal influence above a significance threshold are shown.

pyvene implementation:

The backend uses pyvene's IntervenableConfig to declaratively specify the patching experiment:

config = IntervenableConfig(
    intervenable_type="ActivationPatching",
    source_representation="block_output",
    intervention_type="SwapIntervention",
    intervention_locations=[
        {"layer": L, "component": "attention_output"} for L in range(num_layers)
    ]
)

Then, pyvene's intervene() function runs all patching configurations efficiently, parallelizing across layers where possible.

Optimization for interactive use: Running patching for every (layer, token) pair is computationally expensive (O(L × N²) for N tokens). The backend uses two optimizations:

  1. User‑directed search: The user selects a source token and target token. The backend only traces causal paths between these two, reducing the search space from O(L × N²) to O(L).
  2. Gradient‑based approximation: For a first‑pass estimate (shown immediately), the backend uses integrated gradients to compute an attribution score for each (layer, position) pair in a single backward pass. This is approximate but fast (< 1s). The full patching results are computed in the background and replace the approximation when ready.

docs.title: Frontend Implementation: The Causal Graph Explorer
docs.text:
The causal tracing results are displayed as an interactive causal graph overlaid on a simplified model diagram.

Causal graph visualization (D3‑force): - The X‑axis represents token positions (0 to N‑1). - The Y‑axis represents model layers (0 to L‑1). - Each (layer, token_position) that had a significant causal effect is shown as a node (colored circle). - Edges are drawn from cause to effect with thickness proportional to causal strength. - The user's selected source and target tokens are highlighted with gold borders.

Critical path highlighting: The backend identifies the critical path—the sequence of (layer, token) pairs that carries the most causal influence from source to target. This path is highlighted with a glowing animation (like a neural pulse traveling along the path). The user can scrub through the path with a slider, seeing how information propagates through the model step by step.

Node inspection: - Hover a node: Shows the exact causal influence score and the patching result (e.g., "Restoring this activation recovers 87% of the clean output"). - Click a node: Pins it and shows a detail panel with the activation vector visualized as a bar chart. - Double‑click a node: Opens the attention pattern for that layer, filtered to show only the tokens that causally influence this position.

Knockout experiment mode (game‑like): For educational and exploratory use, the tool includes a "Knockout Challenge" mode. The system presents a prediction task (e.g., "The model predicts 'Paris' at position 7. Find the activation that, when knocked out, changes this prediction."). The user clicks on nodes to "knock them out" (set activation to zero) and sees if the prediction changes. Points are awarded for finding the minimal set of knockouts that change the output. This gamifies causal tracing and teaches researchers how to think causally about model internals.

Export to compression: The causal graph can be exported as a pruning guide: edges with low causal influence indicate redundant connections that can be pruned. Nodes (heads) with no outgoing causal edges are candidates for ablation. This export feeds directly into the compression pipeline.

docs.title: Technology Stack Summary
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Model loading TransformerLens, nnsight Load and hook GPT‑2/Pythia/Gemma/Llama models Intervention engine pyvene, nnsight edit() Declarative intervention specification Attribution graph circuit‑tracer (Anthropic) Compute transcoder‑based attribution graphs Linguistic pipeline spaCy + Stanza POS, dependency parse, NER, coreference 2D graph visualization react‑force‑graph‑2d, PixiJS Attribution graph, causal graph 3D graph visualization react‑force‑graph‑3d, r3f‑forcegraph 3D circuit view Attention heatmap D3.js, Canvas API High‑performance attention matrix rendering Communication WebSocket (JSON protocol) Real‑time intervention streaming State management Zustand Frontend intervention state GPU computation PyTorch CUDA Fast forward passes and patching Caching IndexedDB (frontend), Redis (backend) Model weights, annotations, attention patterns

docs.title: Implementation Roadmap for Zone 6
docs.text: Phase Duration Deliverables Phase 1: Backend Core Weeks 1‑3 Model loading (TransformerLens + nnsight), hook system, ablation engine, WebSocket server Phase 2: Ablation UI Weeks 4‑5 Ablation grid, toggle interaction, before/after comparison panel, export to compression Phase 3: Circuit Tracer Weeks 6‑8 circuit‑tracer integration, attribution graph computation, 2D/3D force‑graph visualization Phase 4: Linguistic Overlay Weeks 9‑10 spaCy/Stanza integration, PixiJS overlay rendering, auto‑detect head type Phase 5: Causal Tracing Weeks 11‑13 pyvene integration, causal graph visualization, knockout challenge mode Phase 6: Polish Weeks 14‑16 Performance optimization, caching, accessibility, documentation

docs.title: 🧠 Zone 7: Social & Community Layer — Complete Implementation Specification
docs.text: After extensive research across 15+ production systems—including ComparIA (FastAPI + SvelteKit arena architecture), Neuronpedia (microservices with open‑source circuit‑tracer integration), Yupp ($33M a16z blockchain‑incentivized evaluation), Polis (PCA + k‑means consensus visualization), Anthropic Circuit Tracer (open‑source attribution graphs), HeedVision (WebXR collaborative attention‑aware visualizations), Yorkie (CRDT‑based real‑time collaboration), and Liveblocks (sync engine architecture)—here is the complete, production‑ready implementation specification for all nine Zone 7 features.

docs.title: 📐 Overall Architecture for Zone 7
docs.text: Zone 7 follows a decoupled micro‑frontend architecture where each social feature is an independent module that communicates through a shared event bus and centralized state management. The architecture is inspired by ComparIA's "decoupled web application featuring a SvelteKit frontend and a FastAPI backend" and Neuronpedia's "microservices architecture, separating the webapp, database, inference, and auto‑interpretation services."

docs.title: Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Rationale Frontend Framework React 19 with Concurrent Mode Enables 60FPS rendering during real‑time updates, even with large reaction counts. As noted in research: "利用其最新的 use 钩子和增强的并发模式（Concurrent Mode），显著降低了重绘频率，确保在万人大群消息滚动时依然保持 60FPS 的流畅度。" State Management Zustand + Immer Lightweight, performant stores for reaction state, voting sessions, and discussion threads. Zustand's immutable update pattern via Immer prevents unnecessary re‑renders. Real‑time Communication WebSocket (Django Channels) + Server‑Sent Events (SSE) Dual protocol: WebSocket for bidirectional communication (discussions, collaboration), SSE for unidirectional streaming (vote count updates, reaction notifications). ComparIA uses "a hybrid approach combining FastAPI for the web server and REST endpoints with a custom SSE (Server‑Sent Events)" for real‑time streaming. Collaborative Editing Yjs + y‑websocket provider CRDT‑based conflict‑free synchronization for simultaneous annotation and discussion editing. "True CRDTs underpin frameworks like Yjs and Automerge, powering many collaborative text editors and document tools." Data Fetching TanStack Query (React Query) v5 Automatic cache invalidation, optimistic updates for reactions/votes, and background refetching. The research confirms: "With React Query, you'll master efficient data fetching." Backend API Django REST Framework + FastAPI microservice DRF for core CRUD; FastAPI for high‑throughput endpoints (Elo rating computation, feed aggregation). ComparIA's architecture validates this hybrid: "ComparIA uses a hybrid approach combining FastAPI for the web server and REST endpoints." Graph Visualization D3.js 7.9.0 + react-force-graph-2d For knowledge graph and lineage visualization. The research confirms: "核心采用D3.js 7.9.0实现力导向图布局、节点拖拽和缩放交互，结合React 19.2.3进行组件化开发，使用TypeScript确保类型安全。" Widget Embedding iframe + postMessage API Isolated sandbox for embedded attention visualizations. "The inter‑frame communication system uses the browser's postMessage API to enable secure, cross‑origin communication between the parent page and the iframe." Caching Redis + IndexedDB (via idb‑keyval) Redis for server‑side caching of aggregated reaction counts and Elo ratings; IndexedDB for client‑side persistence of draft comments and vote history.

docs.title: Event Bus Architecture
docs.text:
All Zone 7 features communicate through a centralized AttentionEventBus (implemented as a Zustand store with middleware):

// Conceptual architecture (not implementation code)
interface AttentionEvent {
  type: 'reaction' | 'vote' | 'comment' | 'fork' | 'challenge_submission' | 'collection_update';
  payload: Record<string, unknown>;
  patternId: string;
  userId: string;
  timestamp: number;
}

// Features subscribe to relevant event types
eventBus.subscribe('reaction', updateReactionCounts);
eventBus.subscribe('vote', updateEloRatings);
eventBus.subscribe('comment', notifyDiscussionParticipants);

This pattern follows the "decoupled web application" approach validated by ComparIA, where "the backend handles complex logic for LLM orchestration via LiteLLM, session management, and persistent logging."

docs.title: 25.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Researchers react to attention patterns with context‑rich signals beyond binary like/dislike: 🔬 Interesting, ⚡ Efficient, 🎯 Specialized, 🔄 Redundant, 🧩 Novel. Each reaction is a distinct data point that contributes to a multi‑faceted "pattern quality score" displayed on every attention visualization and feeding into the recommendation engine.

docs.title: 25.2 Backend Implementation
docs.text:
Database Model (Django ORM, extends existing reaction system):

The model uses a composite unique constraint to prevent duplicate reactions per user per pattern, with a JSON field for extensible metadata.

API Endpoint: POST /api/attention/{pattern_id}/react/

The endpoint handles both creation and toggling (if user already reacted with the same type, remove it; otherwise, add it). This follows the toggle pattern used by HuggingFace model likes and GitHub star/unstar interactions.

Aggregation Service (Celery task):

A periodic Celery task (every 60 seconds) recalculates the aggregate reaction counts and quality scores for patterns that have received new reactions. This avoids expensive real‑time aggregation on every reaction. The task: 1. Queries all patterns with reactions_updated_at > last_run 2. Groups reactions by pattern and type 3. Computes weighted quality score: score = Σ (reaction_count × reaction_weight) / total_reactions 4. Updates the pattern's cached score in Redis and the database

Reaction Weights (configurable per community norms): | Reaction | Weight | Rationale | |----------|--------|-----------| | 🔬 Interesting | +2 | Indicates research value | | ⚡ Efficient | +3 | Strong signal for compression | | 🎯 Specialized | +3 | Indicates clear head function | | 🔄 Redundant | -1 | Negative signal, useful for pruning | | 🧩 Novel | +4 | Highest value, rare discovery |

docs.title: 25.3 Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
Component: ReactionBar (rendered below every attention pattern in Zone 2)

The component uses React 19's useOptimistic hook for instant UI feedback. When a user clicks a reaction, the UI updates immediately (optimistic), the API call is dispatched in the background, and if the API fails, the optimistic update is rolled back. This approach is validated by React 19's "use 钩子和增强的并发模式（Concurrent Mode），显著降低了重绘频率。"

State Management: A Zustand store useReactionStore holds reaction state per pattern. The store subscribes to the AttentionEventBus for real‑time reaction updates from other users (received via WebSocket).

Real‑time Updates: When User A reacts to a pattern, the backend broadcasts the event via Django Channels to all other users currently viewing that pattern. The WebSocket message contains { pattern_id, reaction_type, user_id, action: 'add' | 'remove' }. Other clients update their local state immediately.

docs.title: 25.4 Integration Points
docs.text:
• Recommendation Engine (Zone 7, Feature "For You" Feed): The quality score computed from reactions is one of the primary signals for the personalized recommendation algorithm.
  • Leaderboards (existing leaderboards app): Patterns with the most reactions per type appear on dedicated leaderboards ("Most Interesting Patterns", "Most Novel Discoveries").
  • Portfolio (existing portfolios app): The reactions a user has given and received are displayed on their Attention Portfolio, contributing to their reputation score.
  • Activity Feed (existing activity system): Each reaction generates an activity event visible to the user's followers.

docs.title: 25.5 Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Debounced aggregation: Reaction counts are not recomputed on every click. The Celery task runs every 60 seconds, and interim counts are cached in Redis with a 60‑second TTL.
  • Optimistic UI: The frontend updates immediately; the user never waits for a server response.
  • Batch WebSocket messages: If a pattern receives many reactions in a short time (e.g., during a live demo), the backend batches WebSocket messages every 500ms to avoid flooding clients.

docs.title: Feature 26: Attention Arena — Blind Pairwise Voting (ComparIA‑Style)
26.1 Core Concept
docs.text:
Two attention visualizations are shown side‑by‑side, anonymized (hiding which model/head produced them). Users vote on specific criteria: "Which pattern is more interpretable?" or "Which better captures syntax?" Votes generate Elo ratings for attention patterns, enabling a community‑driven ranking system.

The implementation is directly inspired by ComparIA's architecture: "users interact with two anonymous models simultaneously, vote on the better response, and subsequently reveal the models' identities" — generating "high‑quality preference datasets." The Bradley‑Terry model, which "is a statistical basis for ELO‑like ratings," is used with "bootstrap resampling to provide robust confidence intervals."

docs.title: 26.2 Backend Implementation
docs.text:
Database Models:

  1. ArenaMatch — Records each pairwise comparison session.
  2. ArenaVote — Records each individual vote with criterion and winner.
  3. AttentionPatternElo — Stores current Elo rating and match history for each pattern.

Elo Rating Algorithm:

The Elo computation uses the standard formula: 

E_A = 1 / (1 + 10^((R_B - R_A) / 400))
R_A_new = R_A + K × (S_A - E_A)

Where: - R_A, R_B are current ratings (starting at 1500) - E_A is the expected probability of A winning - S_A is the actual outcome (1 for win, 0 for loss, 0.5 for tie) - K is the development factor (32 for new patterns, 16 for established ones)

The implementation follows the elote Python library approach: "a powerful Python library for implementing and comparing rating systems ... sports teams, or prioritizing features in your product backlog." The K‑factor decays as the pattern accumulates matches: K = max(16, 32 / sqrt(1 + matches_played)).

Arena Session Management:

The arena uses a session‑based approach where each user is assigned a unique arena session. The backend selects two patterns for comparison using a smart pairing algorithm:

  1. First, select patterns within ±200 Elo of each other (balanced matches provide more information)
  2. Prioritize patterns that have fewer total matches (exploration vs. exploitation trade‑off)
  3. Ensure the user hasn't already voted on this exact pair
  4. Randomly assign which pattern appears on the left vs. right (to avoid position bias)

API Endpoints:

  • GET /api/attention/arena/next-pair/ — Returns the next pair of patterns for the user to compare. The response includes anonymized visualization data (SVG/JSON) with model/head metadata stripped.
  • POST /api/attention/arena/vote/ — Submits a vote. Body: { match_id, winner_id, criterion }. The backend updates Elo ratings synchronously within the transaction.
  • GET /api/attention/arena/leaderboard/ — Returns the current Elo rankings, filterable by criterion and model architecture.
  • GET /api/attention/arena/my-stats/ — Returns the user's voting history, accuracy (how often they agree with consensus), and contribution to the dataset.

Bootstrap Resampling for Confidence Intervals:

Following ComparIA's approach, the backend periodically (daily) runs bootstrap resampling to compute confidence intervals for Elo ratings. This "provides robust confidence intervals for model positions." The process: 1. Sample the vote history with replacement 1000 times 2. Recompute Elo ratings for each bootstrap sample 3. Report the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the 95% confidence interval

docs.title: 26.3 Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
Arena Page Layout:

The arena page displays two attention visualizations side‑by‑side in a split‑screen layout. Each visualization is rendered in a sandboxed component that strips identifying information (model name, layer/head numbers replaced with "Pattern A" and "Pattern B").

Reactive State Management:

ComparIA's approach is replicated: "The arena interface is powered by a reactive state object arena defined in chatService.svelte.ts." In React, this translates to a Zustand store useArenaStore that manages: - Current match pair - User's vote history for this session - Loading states for next pair fetching - Anonymized visualization data

Vote Flow:

  1. User arrives at the arena → automatically fetches the first pair
  2. Both visualizations render simultaneously with a loading skeleton
  3. User examines both patterns (hover, zoom, pan — all standard interactions work)
  4. User clicks a vote button below either pattern
  5. Optimistic update: The UI immediately shows a checkmark on the winner and a subtle animation
  6. The API call is dispatched in the background
  7. After a brief transition (500ms), the next pair slides in
  8. After 5 votes, the user can optionally reveal the identities of the patterns they just voted on

Reveal Mechanism: After voting, a "Reveal Identities" button becomes available. Clicking it replaces the "Pattern A/B" labels with the actual model names, attention types, layer/head numbers, and the current Elo ratings. This delayed reveal prevents bias during voting.

docs.title: 26.4 Integration Points
docs.text:
• Leaderboards (existing leaderboards app): Elo ratings are displayed on the Attention Pattern Leaderboard, with weekly/monthly/all‑time rankings.
  • Recommendation Engine: High‑Elo patterns are prioritized in the "For You" feed.
  • Reputation System (existing gpu_reputation app): Users earn reputation points for voting consistently with consensus. Inversely, users who consistently vote against consensus have their vote weight reduced.
  • Dataset Generation: Arena votes are exported as a preference dataset (JSONL format) for research use, following ComparIA's model of "collecting real‑world interaction data."

docs.title: 26.5 Anti‑Gaming Measures
docs.text:
• Minimum account age: Users must have been registered for at least 24 hours and have completed at least 5 attention explorations before voting.
  • Vote consistency scoring: Users who always vote for the left option (position bias) are flagged and their votes are weighted lower.
  • Time‑based filtering: Votes cast in under 2 seconds are discarded (insufficient time to evaluate).
  • CAPTCHA on rapid voting: If a user submits more than 10 votes per minute, a CAPTCHA challenge is triggered.

docs.title: 27.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Every published attention visualization can be forked by another researcher, maintaining full lineage tracking. The implementation follows Neuronpedia's model where the platform "fully supports uploading your own graphs, regardless of whether or not you use the circuit‑tracer library, your own library, or different models." GitHub's fork model is adapted for attention visualization: each fork creates a new exploration with the original's configuration, maintains a parent pointer, and visualizes the lineage as a directed acyclic graph.

docs.title: 27.2 Backend Implementation
docs.text:
Database Models:

  1. AttentionFork — Links a forked exploration to its parent.
  2. ForkChain — Denormalized table storing the full lineage path for efficient querying: { exploration_id, ancestor_id, depth }.

Lineage Chain Query:

Using Django's recursive CTE (Common Table Expression) support, the full lineage is retrieved in a single query:

WITH RECURSIVE lineage AS (
    SELECT id, parent_id, creator_id, 0 AS depth
    FROM attention_fork
    WHERE id = {fork_id}
    UNION ALL
    SELECT af.id, af.parent_id, af.creator_id, l.depth + 1
    FROM attention_fork af
    JOIN lineage l ON af.id = l.parent_id
)
SELECT * FROM lineage ORDER BY depth;

This returns the complete ancestor chain, enabling the lineage tree/graph visualization.

Fork Operation:

When a user clicks "Fork," the backend: 1. Creates a new AttentionExploration record with the same configuration (model, attention type, text, layer/head) 2. Creates an AttentionFork record linking the new exploration to the original 3. Copies any annotations/discussions from the original (optional, user‑selectable) 4. Generates a fork notification for the original creator

docs.title: 27.3 Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
Fork Button: A prominent "Fork" button (⑂ icon, like GitHub) appears in the pattern toolbar. Clicking it opens a modal with options: - Fork name (auto‑generated: "fork of [original_name]") - What to copy: configuration only, or configuration + annotations - Visibility: public / team / private

Lineage Graph Visualization:

The lineage is visualized using react-force-graph-2d (a React wrapper around D3.js force simulation). The research confirms this approach: "核心采用D3.js 7.9.0实现力导向图布局、节点拖拽和缩放交互，结合React 19.2.3进行组件化开发，使用TypeScript确保类型安全。"

The graph shows: - Nodes: Each exploration as a colored circle (color = attention type, size = number of reactions) - Edges: Fork relationships as directed arrows - Current node: Highlighted with a glowing border - Root node: The original exploration marked with a star icon - Interactions: Click a node to navigate to that exploration, hover to see metadata (creator, date, fork count), drag to rearrange

Graph Component Implementation:

The component uses react-force-graph-2d with the following configuration: - Physics simulation: d3‑force with centering, collision detection, and link distance proportional to time between forks - Zoom: mouse wheel with limits (0.5x to 3x) - Pan: drag on empty space - Node color: mapped from attention type color palette - Node size: 5 + (reaction_count * 0.5) pixels - Link width: 1 + (depth * 0.5) pixels (thicker for deeper lineages)

docs.title: 27.4 Integration Points
docs.text:
• Attention Portfolio (Feature 33): Forked explorations appear on the creator's portfolio with "Forked by X users" count.
  • Activity Feed (existing activity system): Fork events are broadcast to followers of both the original creator and the forker.
  • Knowledge Graph (future Zone 7 feature): The lineage graph is integrated into the larger platform knowledge graph, connecting explorations, models, and researchers.

docs.title: 28.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Users create challenges for the community, the community submits attention patterns as entries, votes determine winners, and badges/platform credits are awarded. This feature combines elements of Kaggle competitions, SciArena's community‑driven evaluation ("collected over 20,000 votes from human researchers across diverse scientific domains"), and ComparIA's preference dataset generation.

docs.title: 28.2 Backend Implementation
docs.text:
Database Models:

  1. AttentionChallenge — Challenge definition with title, description, criteria, deadline, prize pool.
  2. ChallengeSubmission — Links an attention exploration to a challenge.
  3. ChallengeVote — Community votes on submissions.
  4. ChallengeBadge — Badges awarded to winners and participants.

Challenge Lifecycle:

  1. Draft: Creator defines the challenge, criteria, and rules
  2. Open: Community can submit attention patterns
  3. Voting: Community votes on submissions (blind pairwise voting or ranked choice)
  4. Finalized: Winners are calculated, prizes distributed
  5. Archived: Challenge is preserved for reference

Winner Determination:

Two modes are supported: - Community Vote: Winner is the submission with the highest vote score (upvotes − downvotes) - Expert Panel: A designated panel of expert judges scores each submission on defined criteria

For community vote mode, the system uses a Bayesian ranking approach (similar to Reddit's "best" sorting) to avoid the "first‑mover advantage": 

score = (upvotes / (upvotes + downvotes)) × log(upvotes + downvotes + 1)

docs.title: 28.3 Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
Challenge Creation Wizard:

A multi‑step form (like your existing experiment launcher) guides the creator through: 1. Basic Info: Title, description, category 2. Criteria: What makes a winning submission? (e.g., "Most interpretable attention pattern in BERT‑base Layer 5") 3. Rules: Submission limits, voting period, eligibility 4. Prize Pool: Platform credits, exclusive badges, featured spotlight 5. Preview & Publish: Review before making the challenge public

Challenge Dashboard:

Each challenge has a dedicated dashboard showing: - Leaderboard: Ranked submissions with scores - Submit Button: Opens a modal to select an existing attention exploration or create a new one - Voting Interface: For active challenges, a voting panel for community members - Timeline: Key dates (submission deadline, voting start, results announcement)

docs.title: 28.4 Integration Points
docs.text:
• Leaderboards (existing): Challenge rankings integrate with the global leaderboard system. The "Ladder" framework's approach is adopted: "a robust adaptive mechanism that updates leaderboards only when statistically significant improvements are detected."
  • Badge System (Zone 8): Winners receive exclusive badges ("🏆 Challenge Champion").
  • Reputation (existing gpu_reputation): Challenge participation and wins contribute to reputation score.
  • Portfolio: Challenge achievements are prominently displayed.

docs.title: 29.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Every attention pattern has threaded discussions anchored to specific elements: per‑head, per‑token‑pair, per‑layer. Supports @mentions, LaTeX equations, and embedded attention SVGs. Powered by the existing community Q&A infrastructure.

docs.title: 29.2 Backend Implementation
docs.text:
The implementation leverages the existing community app's Question, Answer, and Comment models, extended with polymorphic association to attention pattern elements.

Database Extensions:

A DiscussionAnchor model links a discussion thread to a specific element within an attention visualization:

The element_type field supports: 'head', 'token_pair', 'layer', 'entire_pattern'. The element_identifier is a JSON field storing context‑specific data (e.g., { "layer": 5, "head": 7 } for a head discussion, or { "query_index": 3, "key_index": 7 } for a token‑pair discussion).

WebSocket Integration for Real‑time Discussions:

Discussions use Django Channels for real‑time updates. When a user posts a comment: 1. The comment is saved to the database via REST API 2. The backend broadcasts the comment to all users currently viewing the same pattern via WebSocket 3. Other users see the comment appear in real‑time without page refresh 4. The comment count badge updates instantly

docs.title: 29.3 Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
Threaded Comment Component:

The discussion panel renders below each attention pattern in Zone 2. The component uses a tree‑structured rendering for threaded replies (like Reddit or GitHub Issues).

LaTeX Rendering:

Mathematical expressions within comments are rendered using KaTeX (faster than MathJax, server‑side rendering compatible). Users wrap LaTeX in $...$ for inline and $$...$$ for block equations. The frontend uses react‑katex for client‑side rendering.

Embedded Attention SVGs:

Users can embed a snapshot of the current attention visualization in their comment by clicking a "Capture View" button. This generates a base64‑encoded SVG of the current canvas state and inserts it into the comment as an image. The SVG is stored as a NoteImage (using your existing notes infrastructure) and referenced by URL in the comment.

@Mentions:

The mention system is implemented using tiptap (a headless rich‑text editor) with the @mentions extension. As the user types @, a dropdown appears with suggested users (filtered from the platform user base). Selecting a user inserts a mention tag that triggers a notification.

docs.title: 29.4 Integration Points
docs.text:
• Notifications (existing): @mentions generate notifications via the existing notification pipeline.
  • Notes (existing notes app): A "Save Discussion as Note" button exports the entire thread to a ResearcherNote for permanent reference.
  • Search (existing search infrastructure): Discussion content is indexed for global search, enabling queries like "discussions about induction heads in BERT."

docs.title: 30.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Export any attention visualization as a beautiful, social‑media‑optimized share card with one click. The card includes the heatmap, key statistics, model info, a QR code linking back to the interactive dashboard, and researcher attribution.

docs.title: 30.2 Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
Server‑Side Rendering with Puppeteer:

The share card is generated server‑side using Puppeteer (headless Chrome) to render a dedicated HTML template. This ensures: - Consistent rendering across all devices (no CSS differences) - High‑resolution output (2x for Retina displays) - Inclusion of WebGL/Canvas content (which can't be captured by simple DOM serialization)

Generation Pipeline:

  1. User clicks "Share" → Frontend sends POST /api/attention/share-card/ with the current exploration state (model, layer, head, view type, zoom level)
  2. Backend launches a Puppeteer instance (from a pool to avoid cold starts)
  3. Puppeteer loads a dedicated share‑card HTML page with the same React components used in the dashboard
  4. The page renders the attention visualization at the specified state
  5. Puppeteer captures a screenshot of the card region
  6. The image is saved to cloud storage (S3 or similar)
  7. A unique short URL is generated
  8. Response: { image_url, share_url, twitter_text, linkedin_text }

QR Code Generation:

The QR code is generated server‑side using the qrcode Python library, encoding the full URL to the interactive dashboard with all parameters (model, layer, head, text). This ensures anyone scanning the code lands on the exact same visualization state.

docs.title: 30.3 Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
Share Modal:

Clicking the "Share" button opens a modal with multiple sharing options: - Copy Link: Copies the short URL to clipboard - Download Image: Downloads the PNG image - Twitter/X: Pre‑filled tweet with image and text - LinkedIn: Pre‑filled post - Reddit: Pre‑filled post to r/MachineLearning - Embed Code: Copy‑paste HTML snippet for embedding (see Feature 32)

Preview: The modal shows a live preview of the share card before sharing, with options to customize: - Card title (default: pattern description) - Subtitle (default: model + attention type) - Show/hide specific statistics - Color theme (dark/light)

docs.title: 31.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Users create themed collections of attention patterns. Collections can be public, team‑scoped, or private. Each collection has its own discussion thread and can be forked.

docs.title: 31.2 Backend Implementation
docs.text:
Database Models:

  1. AttentionCollection — Collection metadata (name, description, creator, visibility, fork_of).
  2. CollectionItem — Ordered membership of patterns in a collection, with optional notes.

Visibility Model:

Following Notion's teamspace model: public (visible to all, appears in gallery), team (visible to members of a specific organization), private (visible only to creator).

Forking Collections:

When a collection is forked, all items are copied into a new collection with a forked_from pointer. The forked collection can be independently modified. The lineage is tracked similarly to Feature 27.

docs.title: 31.3 Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
Collection Grid View:

The collections gallery page displays collections as cards in a responsive grid (1 column on mobile, 2 on tablet, 3 on desktop). Each card shows: - Collection name and description - Creator avatar and username - Number of patterns in the collection - Number of stars and forks - Preview thumbnails of the first 4 patterns (mosaic layout) - Visibility badge (public/team/private)

Collection Detail Page:

Opening a collection shows: - Header with metadata and action buttons (Star, Fork, Share, Edit) - Discussion thread below the header (powered by the same infrastructure as Feature 29) - Pattern grid/list toggle with sorting options (date added, reaction count, pattern type) - Each pattern card links to the full interactive visualization

Curated Collections Leaderboard:

The homepage and attention dashboard feature a "Trending Collections" section showing the most starred and forked collections this week. The ranking algorithm uses a time‑decay weighted score: score = stars × 2 + forks × 3 / (hours_since_creation + 2) ^ 1.5.

docs.title: 32.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Every attention pattern has an embeddable interactive widget (like YouTube embeds) that researchers can paste into personal websites, blogs, or paper supplementary materials.

docs.title: 32.2 Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
iframe‑Based Embedding with postMessage Communication:

The widget is implemented as a standalone React application that runs inside a sandboxed iframe. Communication between the host page and the widget uses the browser's postMessage API, validated by research: "The inter‑frame communication system uses the browser's postMessage API to enable secure, cross‑origin communication between the parent page (where the giscus script is embedded) and the iframe (where the widget renders). The protocol is bidirectional."

Widget Application Architecture:

Following the Chatwoot widget model: "The widget application is a standalone Vue.js 3 single‑page application that runs inside an iframe created by the SDK." In our implementation: 1. The widget is a React application built with Vite, outputting a single JavaScript bundle and HTML file 2. The iframe loads https://neuralops.com/embed/{pattern_id} 3. The host page includes a lightweight SDK script (neuralops‑embed.js) that creates the iframe and manages postMessage communication 4. The SDK supports responsive sizing: the iframe automatically resizes based on content height

postMessage Protocol:

The host page and widget communicate via a JSON‑RPC‑style protocol:

Host → Widget: - { type: 'init', patternId: '...', theme: 'dark' | 'light', token: '...' } — Initialize the widget - { type: 'resize', width: 800, height: 600 } — Resize the widget - { type: 'setLayer', layer: 5 } — Change the displayed layer - { type: 'setHead', head: 7 } — Change the displayed head

Widget → Host: - { type: 'ready' } — Widget is loaded and ready - { type: 'resize', width: 800, height: 600 } — Widget requests resize (for responsive content) - { type: 'interaction', action: 'hover', data: {...} } — User interacted with the visualization

Security:

The iframe is sandboxed with sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin". "The MCP App widget already runs inside a host‑sandboxed iframe, but HTML outputs need a nested iframe with sandbox='allow‑scripts' (no allow‑same‑origin) to prevent kernel‑generated scripts from accessing the parent's PostMessageTransport." The widget validates the origin of postMessage events to prevent cross‑origin attacks.

docs.title: 32.3 Analytics
docs.text:
The widget SDK includes analytics tracking (using the existing platform analytics infrastructure): - Impressions: How many times the widget was loaded - Interactions: Hover, click, zoom events within the widget - Session duration: How long users interact with the embedded visualization - Referrer: Which websites are embedding the widget

These analytics are displayed on the pattern owner's portfolio dashboard.

docs.title: 33.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Every researcher has a public portfolio showing: published patterns, collections curated, challenges won, reputation score, activity graph, expertise tags. The portfolio is embeddable on personal websites and serves as a professional credential.

docs.title: 33.2 Backend Implementation
docs.text:
Data Aggregation Service:

The portfolio is powered by an aggregation service that collects data from across the platform: - Patterns Published: From AttentionExploration model - Collections Curated: From AttentionCollection model - Challenges Won: From ChallengeSubmission + AttentionChallenge models - Reactions Received: Sum across all published patterns - Reputation Score: From gpu_reputation app - Badges Earned: From UserBadge model (Zone 8) - Activity History: From ActivityLog model (existing)

API Endpoint: GET /api/attention/portfolio/{username}/

Returns a comprehensive JSON object with all portfolio data. The endpoint is optimized with Redis caching (5‑minute TTL for public portfolios, real‑time for the owner's view).

docs.title: 33.3 Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
Portfolio Layout:

The portfolio page follows a layout inspired by GitHub profile pages and Kaggle profiles:

Header Section: - Avatar, display name, username - Headline/bio from user profile - Reputation score with tier badge - Social links (GitHub, Twitter, LinkedIn, Google Scholar) - "Edit Profile" button (for the owner)

Stats Bar: - Total patterns published - Total collections curated - Total challenges won - Total reactions received - Total forks of their patterns - Followers count

Activity Graph (GitHub‑Style Contribution Chart):

A heatmap showing attention‑related activity over the past year. Each cell represents a day, colored by activity level (number of patterns published, reactions given, discussions participated in). The implementation uses D3.js with a calendar heatmap layout.

Tabs Section:

  1. Patterns: Grid of published attention patterns with thumbnail previews, reaction counts, and fork counts
  2. Collections: Grid of curated collections
  3. Challenges: List of challenges created and participated in
  4. Badges: Grid of earned badges with tooltips
  5. Activity: Chronological feed of recent actions

Expertise Tags:

Auto‑generated tags based on the researcher's activity patterns: - "Induction Head Expert" (if they've published 5+ patterns classified as induction heads) - "Vision Attention Specialist" (if they've analyzed 10+ vision transformer patterns) - "Compression Researcher" (if they've used the compression pipeline on attention heads) - "Community Mentor" (if they've answered 20+ discussion questions)

docs.title: 33.4 Integration Points
docs.text:
• Embed Widget (Feature 32): The entire portfolio can be embedded on external websites using the same widget infrastructure.
  • Profile (existing profiles app): The Attention Portfolio extends the existing user profile with attention‑specific sections.
  • Social Graph (existing social_graph): Follow/unfollow buttons on the portfolio, follower/following counts.
  • Messaging (existing messaging app): A "Message" button on the portfolio opens a direct message with the researcher.

docs.title: Security & Access Control
docs.text:
• Row‑Level Security: All social features respect the existing platform permission model. Patterns marked as private are only visible to their creator and explicitly shared users.
  • Rate Limiting: Reaction and vote endpoints are rate‑limited to 60 requests per minute per user (via Django REST Framework throttling).
  • Content Moderation: Discussion comments are filtered through a profanity filter and optional AI‑based toxicity detection before publication.
  • GDPR Compliance: Users can export all their social data (reactions, comments, votes) via a "Download My Data" button, and request deletion of their social footprint.

docs.title: Performance Optimization
docs.text:
• CDN Caching: Share card images and widget assets are served via CDN with long cache TTLs (1 year for versioned assets).
  • Lazy Loading: The discussion thread component is lazy‑loaded only when the user scrolls to the discussion section.
  • Virtual Scrolling: Collections with hundreds of patterns use virtual scrolling (via @tanstack/react‑virtual) to maintain performance.
  • WebSocket Connection Pooling: Multiple Zone 7 features share a single WebSocket connection, multiplexed by message type.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text: Test Type Scope Tools Unit Tests Individual reaction/vote/discussion components Vitest + React Testing Library Integration Tests End‑to‑end vote flow, fork lineage chain Playwright Load Tests Arena voting under 1000 concurrent users Locust Accessibility WCAG 2.1 AA compliance for all interactive elements axe‑core + pa11y Visual Regression Share card rendering consistency Percy (for server‑side rendered cards)
