Each feature is independently deployable, enabling incremental rollout based on priority.

docs.title: 🎮 Zone 8: Gamification & Progress — Complete Implementation Specification
Overview
docs.text:
Zone 8 is the motivational engine of the entire Attention Visualization Dashboard. It sits as a persistent sidebar panel (collapsible, 320px wide on desktop) on the right edge of the dashboard, always visible regardless of which zone the user is interacting with. It serves five tightly integrated functions: XP tracking and tier progression, daily habit‑forming puzzles, a multi‑category badge system, real‑time leaderboards, and a bounty marketplace. Each function connects bidirectionally to every other zone: completing a visualization exploration (Zone 2) awards XP (Zone 8); reaching a new tier (Zone 8) unlocks premium attention types (Zone 4); winning a challenge (Zone 8) auto‑generates a researcher note (Zone 7).

The Zone 8 panel uses motion‑rich micro‑interactions (Framer Motion spring animations, particle burst effects on level‑up, Lottie badge animations) and follows the same glass‑morphism design language (glass, bg-white/5, border-white/10) as the rest of the dashboard.

docs.title: Feature 34: XP & Progression Tiers — The Core Scoring Engine
34.1 Architecture & Technology Stack
docs.text:
The XP engine follows the event‑driven, bounded‑context architecture established by the Hephaestus gamification engine, which splits gamification into distinct bounded contexts: the Activity Module (XP tracking) and the Achievement Module (badge/level resolution). This separation allows the XP engine to scale independently of badge logic.

Core technologies:

Layer Technology Justification Event Bus Apache Kafka (self‑hosted via KRaft, 3‑broker minimum) or Redis Streams (lighter, for <100K events/sec) Decouples action producers (Zone 2 clicks, Zone 3 formula exploration) from XP consumers. Each action emits an event; the XP engine consumes and scores. XP Computation Custom Spring Boot microservice (Java 21, virtual threads) or FastAPI (Python 3.12, async) Java virtual threads provide massive concurrency for real‑time XP calculation; Python FastAPI enables tight integration with ML infrastructure. State Store PostgreSQL 16 with TimescaleDB extension (for time‑series XP history) + Redis Stack (RedisJSON + RediSearch for real‑time level cache) TimescaleDB handles the write‑heavy XP event log and enables time‑range queries for "XP earned this week." Redis holds a per‑user JSON document user:{id}:xp with { currentXP, currentLevel, tierName, nextLevelXP } for O(1) reads. Notification Server‑Sent Events (SSE) over HTTP/2 or WebSocket (existing Channels infrastructure) Level‑up events are pushed in real time. SSE is preferred for unidirectional notifications; WebSocket is used if bidirectional chat/discussion is needed. Rule Engine Netflix Conductor (workflow orchestration) or Drools (Drools 9.x, rule‑based) Different actions award different XP amounts. A lightweight rule engine allows non‑engineers to modify XP tables without redeployment. See Feature 36 for rule engine architecture.

docs.title: 34.2 XP Award Table (Configurable via YAML + Admin UI)
docs.text:
The XP award values follow a logarithmic‑decay model: common actions (viewing a pattern) award small XP; rare, high‑effort actions (winning a challenge, publishing a paper) award large XP. This prevents XP inflation and encourages depth over breadth.

# xp_rules.yaml — deployed to the rule engine, editable via admin panel
xp_awards:
  # ── Zone 2 (Visualization) ──
  view_pattern: 5                    # per unique pattern viewed
  change_layer: 1                    # per layer switch (capped at 20/day)
  change_head: 1                     # per head switch (capped at 20/day)
  use_3d_view: 10                    # first 3D view per session
  use_sankey_view: 10
  zoom_to_token: 3                   # clicking a specific token pair
  export_svg: 5                      # exporting a visualization

  # ── Zone 3 (Math Panel) ──
  view_equation_step: 2              # scrubbing through math animation
  export_numerical_data: 8           # exporting CSV of attention values

  # ── Zone 5 (Analytics) ──
  run_ablation: 15                   # toggling a head ablation
  view_logit_lens: 10
  view_semantic_pathway: 12

  # ── Zone 6 (Interpretability) ──
  run_causal_trace: 25               # knockout experiment
  annotate_pattern: 15               # adding a linguistic annotation
  publish_circuit_trace: 30          # publishing a QK/OV circuit graph

  # ── Zone 7 (Social) ──
  publish_visualization: 50          # creating a public attention post
  receive_star: 10                   # someone stars your pattern
  give_star: 2                       # starring someone else's pattern
  write_comment: 15                  # posting a discussion comment
  receive_comment_reply: 5           # someone replies to your comment
  fork_pattern: 20                   # forking another researcher's pattern
  win_arena_vote: 8                  # your pattern wins a blind comparison
  win_challenge: 200                 # first place in a community challenge
  curate_collection: 40              # creating a curated collection
  share_on_social: 5                 # sharing a pattern on Twitter/LinkedIn

  # ── Zone 4 (Training) ──
  launch_experiment: 100             # starting a training run from attention viz
  complete_experiment: 300           # training run successfully completes
  publish_model: 500                 # publishing a compressed/trained model

  # ── Streak ──
  daily_puzzle_correct: 25           # correct daily puzzle answer
  daily_puzzle_streak_bonus: 5       # extra per consecutive day (caps at 50)

  # ── Negative (rare) ──
  pattern_flagged_and_removed: -50   # community moderation removal
  arena_vote_reversed: -10           # vote found to be fraudulent

docs.title: 34.3 Level Progression Table (Logarithmic Scaling)
docs.text:
The level curve follows Dreyfus model progression: early levels are rapid (rewarding new users), later levels require exponentially more XP. This is implemented as a piecewise exponential function:

XP_required(level) = baseXP × (growthFactor ^ level)

Level 1 (Novice Explorer):      0 XP
Level 2 (Pattern Scout):       150 XP    (growthFactor = 1.5)
Level 3:                       375 XP
Level 4:                       750 XP
Level 5 (Head Hunter):        1,500 XP   (growthFactor increases to 1.8)
Level 6:                      2,700 XP
Level 7:                      4,860 XP
Level 8:                      8,748 XP
Level 9:                     15,746 XP
Level 10 (Attention Sage):   28,344 XP
Level 11:                    51,019 XP
Level 12:                    91,834 XP
Level 13:                   165,301 XP
Level 14:                   297,542 XP
Level 15 (Grandmaster):     535,575 XP

The mathematical model for this curve is inspired by the Italearn XP system, which uses "XP thresholds with increasing gaps (Level 1 = 0, Level 2 = 100, Level 3 = 250, etc.)" and the TRACE‑Weighted XP approach from NeuroLearn, which "rewards depth over throughput" by weighting XP based on the epistemic depth of the action.

docs.title: 34.4 Level‑Up Event Architecture
docs.text:
User Action → Kafka Topic "user.actions" → XP Calculation Service → 
  → Redis INCRBY user:{id}:xp → Check Level Threshold → 
  → If threshold exceeded: 
      → PostgreSQL UPDATE user_level → 
      → Redis publish "levelup:{userId}" → 
      → WebSocket broadcast to user's session →
      → Frontend triggers: particle burst animation + 
        Lottie badge animation + 
        toast notification + 
        confetti effect (canvas-confetti library)

Level‑up animation stack: - canvas‑confetti (npm: canvas-confetti): Fires a 2‑second confetti burst from the center of the screen with custom colors matching the new tier (bronze→silver→gold→platinum→diamond). - Framer Motion: The Zone 8 panel slides out slightly, the level badge scales from 0→1.2→1.0 (spring animation, stiffness=300, damping=20). - Lottie: A pre‑rendered Lottie animation (JSON, ~50KB) plays a tier‑specific celebration (e.g., a torch lighting for Novice→Scout, a crown for Sage→Grandmaster). - Sound: A subtle chime (howler.js, ~15KB audio sprite) plays on level‑up (can be disabled).

docs.title: 34.5 Database Schema
docs.text:
-- PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB hypertable for XP event log
CREATE TABLE xp_events (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    user_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    action_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,        -- e.g., 'view_pattern', 'publish_visualization'
    xp_amount INTEGER NOT NULL,
    source_zone VARCHAR(20),                 -- 'zone2', 'zone3', etc.
    source_entity_id UUID,                   -- the pattern ID, comment ID, etc.
    metadata JSONB DEFAULT '{}',             -- additional context
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Convert to hypertable for time-series queries
SELECT create_hypertable('xp_events', 'created_at');

-- User level state (in PostgreSQL, mirrored in Redis)
CREATE TABLE user_gamification_state (
    user_id UUID PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id),
    current_xp INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    current_level INTEGER DEFAULT 1,
    current_tier VARCHAR(30) DEFAULT 'Novice Explorer',
    total_xp_earned INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    streak_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    longest_streak INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    last_activity_date DATE,
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Index for leaderboard queries
CREATE INDEX idx_user_xp ON user_gamification_state(current_xp DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_user_level ON user_gamification_state(current_level DESC);

Redis cache structure: 

// Key: user:{id}:xp
{
  "currentXP": 2847,
  "currentLevel": 5,
  "currentTier": "Head Hunter",
  "nextLevelXP": 4860,
  "xpToNextLevel": 2013,
  "progressPercent": 58.6,
  "streakCount": 12,
  "lastActivityDate": "2026-05-26"
}

docs.title: 34.6 Anti‑Abuse Mechanisms
docs.text:
• Rate limiting per action type: Using Redis token bucket (redis-cell or custom Lua script). Example: view_pattern capped at 50 XP/day from viewing (50 views × 5 XP = 250 XP/day max from viewing). Beyond that, views still count but award 0 XP.
  • Duplicate detection: XP is awarded only once per unique (user_id, action_type, source_entity_id) combination. The xp_events table has a unique constraint on these three columns.
  • Suspicious pattern detection: A background job (Celery, every 15 minutes) runs anomaly detection (DBSCAN clustering on XP/hour rate). Users with XP/hour > 3σ above the mean are flagged for review.
  • Bot detection: Integration with reCAPTCHA v3 (or hCaptcha) for account creation. All XP‑awarding API endpoints require a valid CSRF token + reCAPTCHA score > 0.5.

docs.title: Feature 35: Daily Attention Puzzle — Habit‑Forming Mini‑Challenge
35.1 Architecture & Technology Stack
docs.text:
The Daily Puzzle system follows the Wordle‑style habit loop architecture: one puzzle per day, released at midnight UTC, with a 24‑hour window to solve. Users can play any previous day's puzzle (for practice, no XP), but only today's puzzle counts toward their streak.

Core technologies:

Layer Technology Justification Puzzle Generation Custom Python service (FastAPI) using OpenAI GPT‑4o API or Anthropic Claude for puzzle creation + a fallback deterministic generator for offline resilience Puzzles are generated nightly (cron job, 00:00 UTC) using an LLM with a structured output schema (JSON). A deterministic backup generator (rule‑based) ensures puzzles are always available even if the LLM API is down. Puzzle Storage PostgreSQL + Redis Cache Each day's puzzle is stored in PostgreSQL (daily_puzzles table). Today's puzzle is cached in Redis with TTL=24h for O(1) reads. State Management Redis user:{id}:puzzle:{date} JSON document Stores { played: true/false, answer: "induction_head", correct: true/false, timeTaken: 45 }. Streak Calculation PostgreSQL window function or Redis bitmap A Redis bitmap streak:user:{id} tracks play days (bit=1 if played). The streak is computed as the number of consecutive 1s counting backward from today.

docs.title: 35.2 Puzzle Types (7‑Day Rotation)
docs.text:
Each day of the week features a different puzzle type, ensuring variety and testing different attention‑related skills:

Day Puzzle Type Description Difficulty Monday "Guess the Head Type" An attention heatmap is shown without labels. The user must identify whether the head is positional, semantic, delimiter, induction, or redundant. Multiple choice (5 options). Easy (50% baseline guess rate) Tuesday "Spot the Difference" Two attention heatmaps are shown side by side (same model, same text, but one head ablated). The user must identify which 3 token pairs show the biggest attention difference. Click‑to‑select on the heatmap. Medium Wednesday "Match the Model" An attention pattern is shown. The user must identify which model architecture (BERT‑base, GPT‑2, RoBERTa, T5, Llama‑2‑7B) produced it. Multiple choice. Hard Thursday "Token Detective" Given an attention weight distribution (a row of the attention matrix, all values shown), the user must infer what the input text might be. They type a free‑text guess; the system scores based on semantic similarity (sentence‑transformer cosine similarity > 0.7 = correct). Hard Friday "Rank the Heads" Five heads from the same layer are shown. The user must rank them by importance (1 = most important, 5 = least). Correct ordering awards bonus XP. Medium Saturday "Circuit Challenge" A QK circuit is partially shown. The user must complete the missing edge weights to make the circuit produce the shown attention pattern. Drag‑and‑drop weights. Hard Sunday "Free Play Showcase" No puzzle. Instead, users submit their most creative attention visualization from the past week. Community votes determine the winner. Winner gets 100 bonus XP. Community

docs.title: 35.3 Puzzle Answer Verification Flow
docs.text:
1. User opens dashboard → GET /api/puzzles/today → 
   Response: { puzzleId, puzzleType, puzzleData, puzzleDate }

2. User plays → Frontend tracks time spent, interactions

3. User submits → POST /api/puzzles/submit { puzzleId, answer, timeTaken }
   → Backend validates:
      a. puzzleDate == today (in UTC)
      b. Not already answered (check Redis user:{id}:puzzle:{date})
      c. Anti‑cheat: timeTaken > 5 seconds (not a bot instant‑submit)

4. If correct:
   → Redis SET user:{id}:puzzle:{date} { correct: true, timeTaken }
   → Redis INCRBY user:{id}:xp by daily_puzzle_correct (25 XP)
   → Update streak (Redis BITFIELD streak:user:{id} SET u1 #{dayOfYear} 1)
   → Return: { correct: true, xpAwarded: 25, streakNow: 8, explanation: "..." }

5. If incorrect:
   → Redis SET user:{id}:puzzle:{date} { correct: false, timeTaken }
   → Break streak (Redis BITFIELD streak:user:{id} SET u1 #{dayOfYear} 0)
   → Return: { correct: false, explanation: "This was a positional head because..." }

docs.title: 35.4 Streak Visualization
docs.text:
The streak is displayed in Zone 8 as a 7‑day mini‑calendar (inspired by Duolingo's streak flame and GitHub's contribution graph):

┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🔥 12‑Day Streak!                        │
│                                          │
│  M  T  W  T  F  S  S                     │
│  ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅  ← This week          │
│  ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ⬜ ⬜  ← Last week          │
│                                          │
│  Longest: 42 days  ·  Total: 156 puzzles │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • The flame icon (🔥) animates (CSS @keyframes pulse) when the streak reaches multiples of 7 (7, 14, 21, …).
  • At 7 days: a bronze flame; at 30 days: silver; at 100 days: gold; at 365 days: diamond flame.
  • Missing a day resets the streak to 0 (the flame extinguishes with a CSS fadeOut animation).
  • A "Streak Freeze" power‑up (earned at level 5, one per month) allows missing one day without breaking the streak.

docs.title: 35.5 Anti‑Cheat for Puzzles
docs.text:
• Server‑side answer validation only: The correct answer is never sent to the client until after submission. The puzzleData field does not contain the answer.
  • Time‑based minimum: Answers submitted in <5 seconds are rejected (impossible for a human to analyze an attention heatmap).
  • IP‑based rate limiting: Max 3 submissions per puzzle per IP address (handles network retries).
  • Pattern randomization: For multiple‑choice puzzles, the option order is randomized per user to prevent answer sharing.
  • CAPTCHA on suspicious activity: If a user submits correct answers in <10 seconds for 3 consecutive days, a CAPTCHA is triggered.

docs.title: Feature 36: Badge System — Rule Engine Architecture
36.1 Architecture & Technology Stack
docs.text:
The badge system follows the DoorDash Badge Serving Framework (BSF) architecture, which is a "configuration‑driven platform that makes it easy for developers to create, manage, and deliver badges for products across the ecosystem." The key insight is that badge logic is externalized from application code into a YAML‑based rule engine, allowing new badges to be added without redeployment.

Core technologies:

Layer Technology Justification Rule Engine RuleGo (Go‑based, lightweight, embedded, orchestratable component‑based rule engine) or Drools 9.x (Java, more mature, KIE Server for REST API) RuleGo is "a lightweight, high‑performance, embedded, orchestrable component‑based rule engine built on Go" that can "help you quickly build loosely coupled and flexible systems." Drools provides "point‑and‑click badge criteria, tiers, expirations, streaks, and multi‑step achievements." Rule Storage Git‑backed YAML files (monorepo) + PostgreSQL badge_definitions table (for runtime caching) Badge rules are defined in YAML, version‑controlled in Git. On deploy, a CI/CD pipeline validates the rules, then loads them into PostgreSQL. The badge engine reads from PostgreSQL at startup and caches in memory. Event Bridge Kafka (same cluster as XP engine) + Debezium CDC (change data capture from PostgreSQL) When an XP event is written, Debezium captures it and pushes to Kafka. The badge engine consumes these events, evaluates all badge rules, and awards badges in real time. Badge Storage PostgreSQL user_badges table + Redis Set user:{id}:badges for O(1) membership check Badges are persisted in PostgreSQL. Redis holds a Set of badge IDs per user for fast UI rendering. Notification WebSocket (Channels) for real‑time award toast + Email (SendGrid/Mailgun) for weekly badge digest Badge awards trigger an immediate WebSocket notification and are included in the weekly "Your Progress" email.

docs.title: 36.2 Badge Rule Definition Language (YAML‑Based)
docs.text:
Each badge is defined as a YAML file. The rule engine parses this YAML at startup and evaluates it against every incoming XP event.

# badges/head_hunter_gold.yml
badge:
  id: "head_hunter_gold"
  name: "Head Hunter (Gold)"
  description: "Identified 50 distinct attention head types across all models"
  category: "discovery"
  tier: "gold"                    # bronze | silver | gold | platinum
  icon: "🔬"
  lottie_animation: "head_hunter_gold.json"   # Lottie file for award animation

  # Conditions — ALL must be true (AND logic)
  conditions:
    - field: "user_stats.distinct_head_types_identified"
      operator: "gte"
      value: 50

  # OR conditions — ANY can be true
  or_conditions: []

  # Time‑based conditions
  validity:
    type: "permanent"              # permanent | expires_after_days | seasonal
    # expires_after_days: 365     # only if type = expires_after_days

  # Award notification template
  notification:
    title: "🏆 Badge Unlocked!"
    body: "You've identified 50 distinct attention head types. You're a true Head Hunter!"
    cta_url: "/dashboard/attention-lab?badge=head_hunter_gold"

# badges/streak_master_platinum.yml
badge:
  id: "streak_master_platinum"
  name: "Streak Master (Platinum)"
  description: "Maintained a 365‑day daily puzzle streak"
  category: "engagement"
  tier: "platinum"
  icon: "🔥"

  conditions:
    - field: "user_stats.longest_streak"
      operator: "gte"
      value: 365

  notification:
    title: "💎 STREAK MASTER!"
    body: "365 days of daily puzzles. You are among the top 0.1% of researchers."
    cta_url: "/dashboard/profile"

# badges/community_curator_silver.yml
badge:
  id: "community_curator_silver"
  name: "Curator (Silver)"
  description: "Created a public collection with 100+ followers"

  conditions:
    - field: "user_stats.max_collection_followers"
      operator: "gte"
      value: 100

  or_conditions:
    - field: "user_stats.collections_curated"
      operator: "gte"
      value: 10
      note: "OR, if you've created 10+ smaller collections"

docs.title: 36.3 Badge Evaluation Pipeline (Event‑Driven)
docs.text:
Kafka Topic "user.actions" → Badge Evaluation Service (RuleGo/Drools) →
  → For each event:
      → Load all badge rules from cache (in‑memory, refreshed every 5 min)
      → Filter rules: only rules whose conditions reference the event's action_type
      → For each filtered rule:
          → Query current user stats from Redis user:{id}:stats (JSON document)
          → Evaluate conditions (RuleGo expression engine or Drools MVEL)
          → If all conditions met:
              → Check Redis Set user:{id}:badges (avoid duplicate awards)
              → If not already awarded:
                  → PostgreSQL INSERT INTO user_badges
                  → Redis SADD user:{id}:badges {badgeId}
                  → Redis PUBLISH badge:awarded {userId, badgeId, badgeName}
                  → WebSocket push to user session
                  → (Optional) Email notification (SendGrid template)

docs.title: 36.4 Badge Award UI (Frontend)
docs.text:
When a badge is awarded, the frontend receives a WebSocket message:

{
  "type": "badge_awarded",
  "badgeId": "head_hunter_gold",
  "badgeName": "Head Hunter (Gold)",
  "badgeIcon": "🔬",
  "badgeTier": "gold",
  "lottieAnimation": "https://cdn.neuralops.com/badges/head_hunter_gold.json",
  "awardedAt": "2026-05-26T14:32:00Z"
}

The frontend then:

  1. Pauses all ongoing animations (via Framer Motion AnimatePresence).
  2. Darkens the background (semi‑transparent overlay, backdrop-filter: blur(8px)).
  3. Plays the Lottie animation at center screen (3 seconds, scales from 0→1.5→1.0).
  4. Shows the badge name and description with a typewriter effect (typed.js or CSS animation).
  5. Fires confetti (canvas-confetti, gold particles for gold tier, silver for silver, etc.).
  6. Adds the badge to the Zone 8 badge grid with a layoutId animation (Framer Motion).

docs.title: 37.1 Architecture & Technology Stack
docs.text:
The leaderboard system uses Redis Sorted Sets as the primary data structure, which is "very efficient since data is being managed in‑memory, allowing for fast read and write operations." The architecture follows the multi‑shard, pub/sub broadcast pattern recommended for production systems:

Core technologies:

Layer Technology Justification Primary Store Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET) O(log N) insertion, O(log N + M) range queries for top‑M. Each leaderboard dimension has its own ZSET key: lb:xp:weekly, lb:xp:monthly, lb:xp:alltime, lb:patterns:weekly, etc. Periodic Archival Redis → PostgreSQL nightly sync (Celery task) + ClickHouse for analytics Every night at 00:00 UTC, the weekly leaderboard is archived to PostgreSQL and a new weekly ZSET is created. ClickHouse (columnar DB) stores historical leaderboard snapshots for trend analysis. Real‑Time Broadcast Centrifugo (WebSocket‑native, Redis‑backed) or Django Channels + Redis Pub/Sub When a user's score changes, a message is published to leaderboard:updates. All connected clients subscribed to that leaderboard receive the update. Centrifugo is recommended for production as it handles "realtime progress, session events, and broadcasts using Redis Pub/Sub + Socket.IO." Top‑N Caching Redis String (JSON) lb:xp:weekly:top100 The top 100 entries are cached as a JSON string and updated every 5 seconds (or on each write, if write volume is low). This avoids recomputing ZSET ranges on every read. Sharding 128‑shard ZSET for "all‑time XP" leaderboard (for scale > 10M users) Following the pattern: "If I need the server‑wide Top 10, I must take the Top 10 from each of the 128 ZSETs and merge‑sort them in application memory." This avoids a single massive ZSET that exceeds Redis memory.

docs.title: 37.2 Leaderboard Dimensions
docs.text: Leaderboard Redis Key Pattern Scoring Metric Period Top XP Earners lb:xp:{period} Total XP earned in period Weekly, Monthly, All‑Time Top Pattern Discoverers lb:patterns:{period} Number of head types identified Weekly, Monthly, All‑Time Top Publishers lb:publishers:{period} Number of attention visualizations published Weekly, Monthly, All‑Time Top Curators lb:curators:{period} Total followers across collections Weekly, Monthly, All‑Time Top Reviewers lb:reviewers:{period} Number of peer reviews completed Weekly, Monthly, All‑Time Arena Elo Ratings lb:arena:elo Elo rating from blind pairwise voting All‑Time (updates continuously) Challenge Champions lb:challenges:{period} Challenge wins Weekly, Monthly, All‑Time Streak Leaders lb:streaks:current Current active streak length Current Bounty Hunters lb:bounties:{period} Total bounty rewards earned Weekly, Monthly, All‑Time

docs.text:
The leaderboard panel in Zone 8 displays a tabbed interface with three tabs: "This Week," "This Month," and "All‑Time." Each tab shows a scrollable list of the top 100 entries.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🏆 Leaderboard                           │
│ [This Week] [This Month] [All‑Time]      │

│  #1  👤 Alice Chen                       │
│      🥇 Grandmaster · 12,450 XP          │
│      ────────────────────────────────    │
│  #2  👤 Bob Kumar                        │
│      🥇 Grandmaster · 11,230 XP          │
│      ────────────────────────────────    │
│  #3  👤 Carol Zhang                      │
│      🥈 Attention Sage · 9,870 XP        │
│      ────────────────────────────────    │
│  ...                                     │
│                                          │

Key UI features: - The current user's row is highlighted with a bg-neon-blue/10 background and a left border accent. - The user's row shows position change (↑ 3, ↓ 1, — 0) since yesterday. - Avatars use the user's profile picture from the profiles app. - Tiers are displayed as colored badges (🥇 Grandmaster = gold gradient, 🥈 Sage = silver, 🥉 Hunter = bronze). - The leaderboard updates in real time: when another user's XP changes, their position animates (Framer Motion layoutId animation, smooth reorder).

docs.title: 37.4 Sharding Strategy for Scale
docs.text:
When the platform grows beyond ~1M users, a single Redis ZSET becomes a bottleneck. The sharding strategy:

  1. User ID hash → shard: shard = CRC32(user_id) % 128.
  2. Write: ZADD lb:xp:alltime:{shard} {xp} {user_id}.
  3. Read (Top 100): Fetch Top 100 from each of the 128 shards (12,800 entries total), merge‑sort in application memory (Python heapq.merge), return the final Top 100.
  4. Read (User's rank): ZREVRANK lb:xp:alltime:{user_shard} {user_id} + offset based on shard. For approximate global rank, use Redis HyperLogLog or a separate approximate counter.

docs.title: 37.5 Anti‑Gaming for Leaderboards
docs.text:
• Minimum account age: Accounts less than 24 hours old are excluded from public leaderboards.
  • Verified email required: To appear on leaderboards, users must have a verified email address.
  • Suspicious activity flagging: Users with XP/hour > 3σ are flagged and excluded from leaderboards pending review.
  • Bot detection: Integration with FingerprintJS (browser fingerprinting) to detect multi‑account farming.
  • Appeal process: Flagged users can appeal via the gpu_reputation dispute system, with a jury of 5 random validators (Kleros‑style) deciding.

docs.title: Feature 38: Bounty Board — Paid Analysis Requests
38.1 Architecture & Technology Stack
docs.text:
The Bounty Board follows the AgentBounty architecture: a decentralized bounty marketplace with "trustless escrow and on‑chain reputation tracking." The core insight is that "funds are securely held in smart contracts and only released once the Service Provider submits the 'Proof‑of‑Delivery'."

Core technologies:

Layer Technology Justification Frontend React (existing) + ethers.js v6 / web3.js for wallet interaction + @solana/web3.js if using Solana Enables browser‑based wallet connection (MetaMask, Phantom, WalletConnect). Escrow Backend Your existing gpu_escrow Django app (centralized escrow) OR Solana smart contract (Anchor framework, Rust) for decentralized escrow Centralized escrow is simpler and faster to implement; decentralized escrow provides trustlessness and is the long‑term vision. The architecture supports both: an abstraction layer (EscrowProvider) that can switch between centralized (PostgreSQL) and decentralized (Solana PDA) backends. Bounty Storage PostgreSQL bounties table + Elasticsearch for full‑text search Bounties are stored in PostgreSQL. Elasticsearch indexes bounty titles, descriptions, tags, and skills for discoverability. Payment Processor Stripe Connect (for fiat) + Solana Pay / USDC on Solana (for crypto) Dual payment rails: researchers can pay with credit card (Stripe) or crypto (USDC). Stripe Connect handles the marketplace payment flow (platform takes 5% fee). Notification WebSocket + Email (SendGrid) Bounty creators are notified when a submission is received. Bounty hunters are notified when a bounty matching their skills is posted. Dispute Resolution Your existing gpu_reputation dispute system (Kleros‑style jury) If a bounty creator rejects a submission, the hunter can escalate to a dispute. A jury of 5 randomly selected validators decides.

docs.title: 38.2 Bounty Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. CREATE: Researcher posts bounty
   → POST /api/bounties { title, description, skills, deadline, reward_amount, reward_currency }
   → Funds locked in escrow (Stripe payment captured OR SOL transferred to escrow PDA)
   → Bounty status: "open"

2. CLAIM: Hunter claims the bounty
   → POST /api/bounties/{id}/claim
   → Bounty status: "in_progress"
   → Timer starts (deadline countdown)

3. SUBMIT: Hunter submits deliverable
   → POST /api/bounties/{id}/submit { deliverable_url, description, attachments }
   → Bounty status: "under_review"

4. REVIEW: Creator reviews submission
   → POST /api/bounties/{id}/review { decision: "accept" | "reject", feedback: "..." }

   4a. ACCEPT:
   → Escrow releases funds to hunter
   → Bounty status: "completed"
   → Hunter earns XP + reputation

   4b. REJECT:
   → Bounty status: "disputed"
   → Dispute resolution process starts
   → Jury of 5 validators reviews evidence
   → Majority vote decides outcome
   → Funds released accordingly

5. EXPIRE: Deadline passes without submission
   → Funds returned to creator
   → Bounty status: "expired"

The entire Zone 8 system is built on an event‑driven architecture where every meaningful user action emits a Kafka event. The XP engine, badge engine, leaderboard updater, and streak tracker all consume these events independently, enabling each subsystem to scale and evolve separately. The use of Redis Sorted Sets for leaderboards, a YAML‑based rule engine for badges, and a hybrid centralized/decentralized escrow for bounties ensures the system is both performant and flexible—ready for everything from a small research lab to a global platform with millions of users.

docs.title: 🔗 Features 39‑50: Complete Implementation Specifications
docs.text: Below are the exhaustive implementation details for all twelve cross‑platform integration features. Each specification includes the technology stack, architecture, data flow, concurrency model, and integration points — all designed to work with your existing Django backend, React frontend, WebSocket/Channels infrastructure, and the full suite of platform apps.

docs.title: 39.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Every attention visualization in the dashboard has a persistent "Train with This" button. When clicked, the system captures the exact state (model identifier, attention type with parameters, layer/head selection, input text), serializes it into a pre‑filled experiment configuration, and launches the training pipeline. After training completes, the resulting attention patterns are automatically compared with the original visualization that triggered the experiment — closing the loop between exploration and verification.

docs.title: 39.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose State Capture Zustand useAttentionContext store Serialize current dashboard state into a JSON configuration Pre‑filled Launcher React Router with query parameters Open /launcher?model=bert‑base&attn=galerkin&text=... Experiment Submission api.post('/experiments/start‑train/', config) Submit the training job via existing REST API Job Monitoring WebSocket (ws://host/ws/experiments/{jobId}/) Real‑time status updates using existing Channels infrastructure Result Comparison Canvas API + OffscreenCanvas Render side‑by‑side attention matrices for comparison State Management useAttentionContext + useExperimentStore Synchronize original and trained model states

docs.title: 39.4 Comparison Engine
docs.text: After training completes, the system automatically: 1. Fetches the attention patterns from the newly trained model using POST /api/experiments/attention/ with the same input text. 2. Computes Jensen‑Shannon Divergence (JSD) between each corresponding attention head pair. JSD is preferred over KL divergence because it is symmetric and bounded [0,1], making it intuitive for visualization. 3. Computes head‑by‑head delta matrices (difference between original and trained attention weights). 4. Renders a comparison heatmap with a dedicated color scale: blue = original higher, red = trained higher, white = no difference. 5. Generates a comparison report summarizing: - Which heads changed most/least - Whether attention patterns became more or less diffuse - Whether head specialization increased - Link to the training run for full details

docs.title: 39.5 URL‑Based State Restoration
docs.text:
Every "Train with This" action generates a shareable URL that encodes the full dashboard state:

/attention?model=bert-base&attn=galerkin&rank=64&layer=5&head=7&text=The%20quick%20brown%20fox

When another researcher opens this URL, the dashboard restores the exact state, allowing them to verify results or launch their own experiment with modifications.

docs.title: Feature 40: Attention Pattern Knowledge Graph Navigator
40.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Every attention pattern visualization becomes a first‑class node in the platform's knowledge graph, connected to the model that produced it, the experiment that generated it, the researcher who published it, the notes that discuss it, the papers that reference it, the collections that include it, and the community discussions about it. Users navigate this graph through an interactive D3 force‑directed visualization that reveals the web of relationships around any pattern.

docs.title: 40.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Graph Layout D3.js d3‑force simulation (v7.9+) Physics‑based node positioning with custom force functions React Integration react‑d3‑graph or custom hook with useRef + useEffect Bridge between React component lifecycle and D3 imperative API Data Fetching React Query (useQuery) with pagination Load graph data incrementally as user expands nodes Node Rendering SVG <circle> + <text> elements with CSS transitions Hardware‑accelerated rendering for up to 1000 nodes Edge Rendering SVG <line> or <path> with stroke‑width proportional to relationship strength Visual encoding of connection importance 3D Alternative Three.js via react‑three‑fiber (@react‑three/fiber) Optional immersive 3D graph for complex networks Backend Graph API Django REST API endpoint /api/knowledge‑graph/?node_id=...&depth=2 Fetch graph neighborhood efficiently

docs.title: 40.3 Graph Data Model
docs.text:
The knowledge graph is built from the existing NoteLink model and extended with new relationship types:

Node Types:
  - attention_pattern (id, model, layer, head, attention_type)
  - model_version (id, name, version, architecture)
  - experiment (id, name, status, created_at)
  - researcher_note (id, title, author)
  - paper (id, title, source, source_id)
  - collection (id, name, curator)
  - community_discussion (id, title, question_id)

Edge Types:
  - PRODUCED_BY (pattern → model)
  - GENERATED_FROM (pattern → experiment)
  - DISCUSSED_IN (pattern → note)
  - REFERENCED_BY (pattern → paper)
  - COLLECTED_IN (pattern → collection)
  - PUBLISHED_BY (pattern → researcher)
  - FORKED_FROM (pattern → pattern)
  - COMPARED_WITH (pattern → pattern)
  - SIMILAR_TO (pattern → pattern, weight = JSD similarity)

docs.title: 40.4 Force Simulation Configuration
docs.text:
The D3 force simulation uses five force types for optimal layout:

Force Type Configuration Purpose d3.forceLink() Distance = f(relationship_strength) Connected nodes attract d3.forceManyBody() strength(-300) All nodes repel each other d3.forceCenter() Center of viewport Keep graph centered d3.forceCollide() radius(30) Prevent node overlap d3.forceX() / d3.forceY() Group by node type category Positional grouping for visual clarity

docs.title: 40.5 Interactive Features
docs.text:
• Expand on Click: Clicking a node reveals its direct neighborhood (depth=1), fetching additional data via the API.
  • Hover Tooltip: Shows node details (model name, attention type, head number, relationship summary).
  • Drill‑Down: Double‑click a pattern node to open it in the full attention visualization dashboard.
  • Filter by Relationship Type: Toggle which edge types are visible (e.g., show only "FORKED_FROM" and "COMPARED_WITH").
  • Search Highlight: Type a model name or researcher name to highlight all matching nodes.
  • Export: Export the visible subgraph as SVG, PNG, or JSON for external analysis.
  • Time Slider: Filter nodes by creation date to see how the knowledge graph evolved over time.

docs.title: 40.6 Performance Optimizations
docs.text:
• Virtualization: For graphs with >500 nodes, use WebGL rendering (Three.js) instead of SVG DOM elements.
  • Level‑of‑Detail (LOD): At zoomed‑out view, nodes are simplified (dot only). Zooming in reveals labels and details.
  • Incremental Loading: Load graph in layers (depth 0, then depth 1, then depth 2) to avoid overwhelming the initial view.
  • Web Worker: Run force simulation in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread during layout computation.

docs.title: 41.1 Core Concept
docs.text: A public REST API and Python SDK that enables programmatic access to attention visualizations, pattern analysis, and automated pipelines. AI agents (like the platform's research agent) can query attention patterns, automated analysis pipelines can run attention diagnostics on models, and third‑party tools can embed attention visualizations. This follows Neuronpedia's model of providing "a suite of free APIs/tools that accelerate white‑box understanding and experimentation of neural networks."

docs.title: 41.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose REST API Django REST Framework (DRF) Standard REST endpoints with Token authentication API Documentation drf‑spectacular with Swagger UI / ReDoc Auto‑generated OpenAPI 3.0 schema Python SDK Custom neuralops‑attention pip package High‑level Python client for the API Rate Limiting Django REST Framework throttling Prevent abuse (1000 req/hour for free tier, 10000 for pro) API Versioning URL‑based versioning (/api/v1/attention/, /api/v2/attention/) Backward compatibility Authentication DRF Token Authentication (same as rest of platform) Consistent auth across all endpoints SDK Async Support httpx with async/await Non‑blocking API calls for high‑throughput pipelines

docs.title: 41.3 API Endpoints
docs.text: Method Endpoint Description POST /api/v1/attention/analyze/ Compute attention patterns for a given model, text, and attention type GET /api/v1/attention/patterns/{pattern_id}/ Retrieve a specific attention pattern by ID GET /api/v1/attention/patterns/ List attention patterns with filtering (model, layer, head, attention_type) GET /api/v1/attention/compare/ Compare two attention patterns (JSD, delta matrix) GET /api/v1/attention/stats/{pattern_id}/ Get statistics (entropy, concentration, importance, diversity) POST /api/v1/attention/ablate/ Simulate head ablation and return predicted output changes GET /api/v1/attention/leaderboard/ Get ranked attention patterns by community score GET /api/v1/attention/models/ List available models with supported attention types GET /api/v1/attention/export/{pattern_id}/ Export pattern as SVG, PNG, JSON, or CSV

docs.title: 41.4 Python SDK Design
docs.text:
The SDK neuralops‑attention provides a clean, idiomatic Python interface:

from neuralops_attention import AttentionClient

client = AttentionClient(api_key="your-token")

# Analyze attention
pattern = client.analyze(
    model="bert-base-uncased",
    text="The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog",
    attention_type="galerkin",
    attention_config={"rank": 64},
    layer=5,
    head=7
)

# Get statistics
stats = client.get_stats(pattern.id)
print(f"Entropy: {stats.entropy}, Importance: {stats.importance}")

# Compare two patterns
comparison = client.compare(pattern.id, other_pattern.id)
print(f"JSD: {comparison.jsd}, Max Delta: {comparison.max_delta}")

# Export
client.export(pattern.id, format="svg", output_path="attention.svg")

# Batch analysis
patterns = client.analyze_batch(
    model="bert-base-uncased",
    texts=["Text A", "Text B", "Text C"],
    layers=[0, 2, 4, 6],
    heads=[0, 4, 8]
)

docs.title: 41.5 Authentication & Rate Limiting
docs.text:
• Authentication: Uses the same DRF Token Authentication as the rest of the platform. Users generate API tokens from their profile settings.
  • Rate Limiting: Implemented via DRF's UserRateThrottle and AnonRateThrottle. Free tier: 1000 requests/hour. Pro tier: 10000 requests/hour. Enterprise: unlimited.
  • API Key Management: Users can create, revoke, and rotate API keys from the /profile/api‑keys/ page.

docs.title: 41.6 Webhook Integration
docs.text:
Users can register webhook URLs that receive notifications when: - A batch analysis completes - A new attention pattern is published by a followed researcher - A pattern receives a certain number of stars or reaches a leaderboard position

Webhooks use HMAC‑SHA256 signatures for verification, following the same pattern as the existing WebhookSubscription model in the notes app.

docs.title: 42.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Multiple researchers can explore attention patterns together in real time, sharing the same view state, seeing each other's cursors, annotating specific attention connections, discussing in threaded conversations, and recording entire exploration sessions for teaching or review. This transforms the dashboard from a solo analysis tool into a virtual lab meeting platform.

docs.title: 42.5 Collaboration Features
docs.text:
• Shared View State: When Alice changes the layer slider, Bob's dashboard updates instantly. The Y.js CRDT handles conflicts automatically.
  • Cursor Presence: Each participant's cursor appears as a colored dot on the attention heatmap, with their name and avatar. This uses the Y.js Awareness API.
  • Annotation Pins: Users can click any token pair in the heatmap to drop an annotation pin. The pin appears as a colored marker with a comment. Other users can reply, creating threaded discussions anchored to specific attention connections.
  • "Follow Me" Mode: One user (the presenter) can enable "Follow Me" mode, which locks other participants' views to match the presenter's navigation. This is useful for teaching or walkthroughs.
  • Session Recording: The entire exploration session is recorded using rrweb, which captures DOM mutations and user interactions. Recordings can be replayed later — useful for asynchronous collaboration (one researcher records an analysis, another watches later).
  • Voice/Video Chat: Optional WebRTC integration for real‑time discussion during exploration.

docs.title: 42.6 Conflict Resolution
docs.text: Y.js CRDTs provide automatic conflict resolution. When two users simultaneously change the same value (e.g., both move the layer slider), Y.js merges the changes deterministically. For annotations, if two users edit the same comment simultaneously, the CRDT merges characters at the granularity of individual keystrokes.

docs.title: 43.1 Core Concept
docs.text: For controversial topics in attention research (e.g., "Should attention heads be pruned or kept?"), users submit short statements. Other users vote "agree," "disagree," or "pass." The system uses PCA for dimensionality reduction and k‑means for clustering to map the opinion landscape, visualize consensus groups, and identify "bridging statements" that both groups agree on. This follows Polis's approach of "scaling deliberation by mapping high dimensional opinion spaces."

docs.title: 43.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Statement Submission Django model + REST API Store statements and votes Vote Collection React UI with agree/disagree/pass buttons Gather user opinions Dimensionality Reduction PCA via scikit‑learn or ml.js (JavaScript) Reduce high‑dimensional vote matrix to 2D for visualization Clustering Two‑stage k‑means (100 base clusters → 2‑5 group clusters) Polis's proven approach for opinion grouping Visualization D3.js scatter plot or Plotly.js Interactive opinion map Bridging Analysis Custom algorithm based on Polis's group‑informed consensus Identify statements with high agreement across clusters Backend Processing Celery task (async) Run PCA and clustering asynchronously

docs.title: 43.3 Mathematical Pipeline
docs.text:
The Polis‑style analysis follows a four‑stage pipeline:

Stage 1: Vote Matrix Construction - Each statement becomes a row (N statements) - Each user becomes a column (M users) - Each cell is {agree: 1, disagree: -1, pass: 0}

Stage 2: PCA Dimensionality Reduction - Apply PCA to the M‑dimensional vote matrix - Retain the first two principal components (explaining typically 40‑60% of variance) - This maps each user to a 2D point in "opinion space"

Stage 3: Two‑Stage K‑Means Clustering - Stage A: Run k‑means with k=100 to create fine‑grained base clusters - Stage B: Run k‑means on the 100 cluster centers with k=2–5, selecting the optimal k via silhouette score - This produces 2‑5 interpretable opinion groups

Stage 4: Bridging Statement Identification - For each statement, compute the mean vote per group - Statements where all groups have mean vote > 0.5 (or < -0.5) are "bridging statements" — they represent consensus or shared concern

docs.title: 43.4 Visualization
docs.text: The opinion map renders as: - Scatter plot: Each user is a dot positioned by their first two principal components, colored by group cluster. - Group centroids: Larger markers showing the center of each opinion group. - Bridging statements: Listed in a sidebar, with the statement text and group‑level agreement scores. - Statement detail: Clicking a statement shows a histogram of agree/disagree/pass across all users. - Group descriptions: Auto‑generated labels describing each group's defining characteristics (e.g., "Group A: Supports aggressive pruning" vs. "Group B: Prefers conservative approaches").

docs.title: 44.1 Core Concept
docs.text: A dedicated tool that uses attention analysis to help researchers debug and improve their prompts. The system highlights which tokens receive the most attention, identifies "attention sinks" (tokens that absorb disproportionate attention, potentially wasting model capacity), compares prompts A/B, and provides improvement suggestions based on attention pattern analysis.

docs.title: 44.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Token Attention Analysis contextscope Python library (2026 release) Detect attention sinks, lost system prompts, and recency bias Attention Sink Detection Custom algorithm based on ICLR 2025 "When Attention Sink Emerges" Identify tokens with >2σ above mean attention Prompt A/B Comparison JSD divergence between attention distributions Quantify how different prompts produce different attention patterns Suggestion Engine LLM‑powered (using platform's research agent) Generate natural language suggestions based on attention analysis Visualization Custom React heatmap overlay Highlight attention sinks, low‑attention regions, and prompt structure Backend API POST /api/attention/analyze‑prompt/ Accept prompt text, return attention analysis with suggestions

docs.title: 44.3 Attention Sink Detection Algorithm
docs.text:
Based on the ICLR 2025 paper "When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models":

  1. Compute the mean attention each token receives across all heads: mean_attn[i] = Σ_h Σ_q attn[q][i] / (H × N)
  2. Compute the standard deviation of mean attention across tokens: σ = std(mean_attn)
  3. A token is classified as an attention sink if: mean_attn[i] > μ + 2σ
  4. Attention sinks typically occur at:
  5. The first token (beginning‑of‑sequence token)
  6. Punctuation marks (periods, commas)
  7. Special tokens (separator tokens, system prompt boundaries)

docs.title: 44.4 Prompt A/B Comparison
docs.text: Users enter two prompts (Prompt A and Prompt B). The system: 1. Computes attention patterns for both prompts using the same model and attention type. 2. Calculates per‑token attention divergence between the two prompts. 3. Highlights tokens where attention differs most. 4. Computes output probability divergence (how different are the model's predictions?). 5. Renders a side‑by‑side comparison view with a divergence heatmap between them.

docs.title: 44.5 Suggestion Engine
docs.text:
The suggestion engine uses the platform's existing research agent (agents app) to analyze the attention patterns and generate natural language suggestions:

  • "The token 'not' at position 7 receives 3.2× more attention than the average token. Consider whether negation is critical to your prompt."
  • "Your system prompt receives 40% less attention than expected. Consider moving key instructions to the beginning or end of the prompt."
  • "The last 10% of your prompt absorbs 35% of total attention (recency bias). If earlier context is being ignored, consider shortening the prompt."
  • "The attention sink at position 0 (BOS token) absorbs 25% of total attention. This is normal but may limit capacity for other tokens."

docs.title: 44.6 Integration with Platform Apps
docs.text:
• Prompt Library: Users can save analyzed prompts to their prompts library with attached attention analysis.
  • Experiment Launcher: "Train with this optimized prompt" button opens the experiment launcher pre‑filled with the improved prompt.
  • Notes: Auto‑generate a researcher note with the prompt analysis and suggestions.
  • Community: Share prompt analysis results as community posts for discussion.

docs.title: 45.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Load attention patterns from any architecture (Standard MHA, Galerkin, TLinFormer, PADRe, Spectraformer, etc.) for the same input text and visualize how attention differs across architectures. The system computes divergence heatmaps, Jensen‑Shannon Divergence (JSD) scores, head‑by‑head similarity matrices, and structure‑level comparisons.

docs.title: 45.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Attention Computation Backend computes attention for each model + attention type combination Generate comparable attention matrices Divergence Calculation JSD via scipy.spatial.distance.jensenshannon or custom JS implementation Compute per‑head divergence Similarity Matrix Cosine similarity between attention pattern vectors Head‑by‑head comparison Visualization Custom React heatmap + D3 matrix view Render divergence heatmaps Backend API POST /api/attention/compare‑architectures/ Accept model pairs and text, return comparison data

docs.title: 45.3 Comparison Dimensions
docs.text: Dimension Metric Visualization Per‑Head Divergence Jensen‑Shannon Divergence (JSD) between corresponding head pairs Heatmap: rows = layers, columns = heads, color = JSD Head‑by‑Head Similarity Cosine similarity between flattened attention matrices Similarity matrix: rows = Model A heads, columns = Model B heads Structural Differences Entropy difference, concentration difference, specialization difference Bar charts comparing per‑layer statistics Output Impact Difference in Logit Lens predictions at each layer Overlay line chart Token‑Level Divergence Per‑token JSD between the two models' attention distributions Token‑highlighted text with divergence scores

docs.title: 45.4 Architecture Comparison View
docs.text: The comparison view presents: 1. Side‑by‑Side Heatmaps: Model A (left) and Model B (right) for the same layer/head. 2. Divergence Heatmap (center): A third heatmap showing the absolute difference between the two attention matrices, colored with a diverging scale (blue = Model A higher, red = Model B higher, white = no difference). 3. Summary Statistics Bar: At the top, showing overall JSD, per‑layer average JSD, and the head with maximum divergence. 4. Layer Selector: A dropdown to switch between layers, with each layer showing its average JSD.

docs.title: 46.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Every attention pattern, regardless of which architecture produced it, is scored on four standardized dimensions: Interpretability, Specialization, Efficiency, and Stability. These scores enable cross‑architecture comparison and feed into leaderboards, recommendations, and quality filtering.

docs.title: 46.2 Scoring Dimensions
docs.text: Dimension Range Formula Interpretation Interpretability 0‑100 100 × (1 − mean_entropy / max_entropy) Higher = more focused, easier to interpret Specialization 0‑100 100 × (1 − mean_cosine_similarity_to_other_heads) Higher = more distinct from other heads Efficiency 0‑100 100 × head_importance / mean_attention_weight Higher = more information per unit of attention Stability 0‑100 100 × (1 − std_across_inputs / mean_across_inputs) Higher = more consistent across different inputs

docs.title: 46.3 Computation Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Entropy: Computed per head as H = −Σ p_i log(p_i) where p_i are attention weights.
  2. Cosine Similarity to Other Heads: For each head, compute cosine similarity of its flattened attention matrix with every other head in the same layer. Take the mean.
  3. Head Importance: Mean of maximum attention weights across all query positions. This approximates how much the head contributes to the output.
  4. Stability: Compute attention patterns for 5 different input texts. Measure standard deviation of attention weights at each position. Average across positions.

docs.title: 46.4 Score Visualization
docs.text: The Universal Attention Score is displayed as: - A radar/spider chart showing all four dimensions. - A composite score (weighted average, configurable weights). - A percentile ranking relative to all other patterns of the same architecture. - A leaderboard badge if the pattern ranks in the top 10% for any dimension.

docs.title: 47.1 Core Concept
docs.text: With one click, generate a complete research paper section (Methods, Results, Discussion, References) based on the current attention analysis. The generated content is a draft that opens in the platform's paper LaTeX editor, where the researcher can edit, compile, and submit.

docs.title: 47.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Content Generation LLM (platform's research agent) with structured prompt Generate Methods, Results, Discussion sections Figure Embedding SVG export of current attention visualization Embed figures in the paper Citation Management Platform's agents paper library (Semantic Scholar, arXiv) Auto‑generate BibTeX references LaTeX Integration Platform's paper app (Overleaf‑style editor) Open generated content in the LaTeX editor Template System NoteTemplate model (existing) with paper‑specific templates Provide structured templates for different paper types

docs.title: 47.3 Generation Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Context Collection: Gather the current dashboard state (model, attention type, layer, head, text), computed statistics (entropy, concentration, importance), and any community annotations or discussions.
  2. Prompt Construction: Build a structured prompt for the LLM: 
    Generate a research paper section describing the following attention analysis:
- Model: {model_name}
- Attention Type: {attention_type} ({description})
- Layer: {layer}, Head: {head}
- Input Text: "{text}"
- Key Findings: Entropy = {entropy}, Concentration = {concentration}%, Importance = {importance}
- Community Annotations: {annotations}

Generate three sections:
1. Methods (describe the model, attention mechanism, and visualization technique)
2. Results (describe the attention pattern, key observations)
3. Discussion (implications, limitations, comparison with related work)

Include LaTeX formatting, proper citation commands, and figure references.
  3. Figure Generation: Export the current attention visualization as SVG and save it to the paper project's assets folder. Generate a LaTeX \includegraphics command with appropriate caption.
  4. Reference Collection: Query the agents paper library for papers related to the attention type and model. Generate BibTeX entries.
  5. Content Assembly: Combine the LLM output, figure references, and bibliography into a complete .tex file.
  6. Paper App Integration: Open the generated content in the platform's paper LaTeX editor, ready for editing and compilation.

docs.title: 48.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Attention connections are rendered as flowing particles (like the particle effects in games such as Control or Destiny). Each attention connection is a stream of glowing particles flowing from query token to key token. Particle density represents attention weight, particle speed represents attention "confidence," color represents attention head identity, and particles leave glow trails that fade over time. Users can freeze the flow at any moment to inspect the static pattern.

docs.title: 48.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose 3D Rendering React Three Fiber (@react‑three/fiber) + Three.js WebGL‑based particle system rendering Particle System Custom GLSL shaders (vertex + fragment) GPU‑accelerated particle simulation Animation useFrame hook (R3F) + requestAnimationFrame 60fps animation loop Post‑Processing @react‑three/postprocessing (bloom, glow effects) Visual polish for particle trails Interaction @react‑three/drei (OrbitControls, Raycaster) Camera control and particle selection Physics Simple velocity‑based motion (no full physics engine needed) Particles follow cubic Bézier curves between tokens

docs.title: 48.3 Particle System Architecture
docs.text:
The particle system uses a GPU‑based instanced rendering approach for performance:

  1. Geometry: Each particle is a small quad (2 triangles) rendered via InstancedMesh for efficiency. For 10,000+ particles, this keeps draw calls to 1.
  2. Data Texture: Attention weights, source positions, target positions, and particle ages are stored in a floating‑point data texture, updated each frame.
  3. Vertex Shader: Reads the data texture to position each particle along its Bézier curve based on its age.
  4. Fragment Shader: Computes particle color based on head identity (passed via instance attribute), applies glow effect proportional to attention weight, and fades alpha as particles age.
  5. Particle Lifecycle:
  6. Birth: Particles spawn at the query token position at a rate proportional to attention weight.
  7. Travel: Particles follow a cubic Bézier curve from query to key token over 1‑3 seconds (configurable).
  8. Death: Particles fade out and are recycled into the pool.

docs.title: 48.4 Bézier Curve Computation
docs.text:
Each attention connection defines a cubic Bézier curve:

P0 = query token position (x₀, y₀, z₀)
P1 = P0 + (0, arc_height, 0)  (control point 1, raised in y)
P2 = P3 − (0, arc_height, 0)  (control point 2, raised in y)
P3 = key token position (x₃, y₃, z₃)

B(t) = (1−t)³P₀ + 3(1−t)²tP₁ + 3(1−t)t²P₂ + t³P₃

The arc height is proportional to the distance between tokens, creating elegant curved trajectories.

docs.title: 48.5 Visual Effects
docs.text:
• Bloom/Glow: Applied via post‑processing to make particles appear luminous.
  • Trail Effect: Particles leave a fading trail (stored in a separate render texture, blended with multiplicative fade).
  • Color Mapping: Each attention head has a distinct HSL color. Particles from the same head share the same hue.
  • Density Encoding: High‑attention connections have more particles per second, creating denser streams.
  • Freeze Mode: User presses Space to pause all particles mid‑flight. The frozen particles remain visible as a static snapshot. Pressing Space again resumes the flow.

docs.title: 48.6 Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• LOD (Level of Detail): At zoomed‑out view, reduce particle count by 50%. At close‑up view, increase to full density.
  • Culling: Particles outside the camera frustum are not rendered (Three.js handles this automatically for InstancedMesh).
  • Particle Budget: Maximum 50,000 particles in the pool. Older particles are recycled when the pool is full.
  • Frame Rate Target: 60fps on mid‑range hardware (GTX 1060 equivalent). Fall back to 30fps on low‑end hardware.

docs.title: 49.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Each attention head has a unique sound signature based on its attention pattern. High attention weight produces higher pitch, diffuse attention produces white noise, positional heads produce rhythmic patterns, and semantic heads produce melodic patterns. Users can "listen" to the model thinking — hearing how attention shifts as they change the input text or navigate between layers. This feature is particularly powerful for accessibility (visually impaired researchers) and for detecting anomalies (a sudden change in sound indicates unusual attention behavior).

docs.title: 49.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Audio Synthesis Web Audio API (native browser API) Generate sounds without external libraries Oscillator Nodes OscillatorNode (sine, square, sawtooth, triangle) Generate tonal sounds for attention weights Noise Generation AudioBufferSourceNode with white noise buffer Generate diffuse attention sounds Gain Control GainNode Control volume per head Spatialization PannerNode (stereo panning) Position sounds in stereo space based on head index Scheduling requestAnimationFrame + Web Audio clock Synchronize audio with visualization updates MIDI Integration Web MIDI API (optional) Output to external synthesizers for professional audio

docs.title: 49.3 Sound Signature Design
docs.text: Attention Pattern Sound Type Parameters High attention (focused) Pure sine wave Frequency = 200‑800 Hz (mapped from attention weight), Gain = attention weight Low attention (diffuse) White noise Gain = 0.05‑0.2 (mapped from entropy) Positional head (attends to adjacent tokens) Rhythmic pulse Oscillator at 440 Hz with LFO modulating gain at 2‑4 Hz Semantic head (attends to semantically related tokens) Melodic sequence Frequency follows a pentatonic scale based on token position Induction head (copies previous token) Echo/delay effect Original sound with 200ms delayed copy Delimiter head (attends to punctuation) Short percussive click Short noise burst (50ms) with fast decay

docs.title: 49.4 Implementation Approach
docs.text:
The sonification engine runs in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread. It receives attention data via postMessage and synthesizes audio using an OfflineAudioContext (for rendering to buffer) or a real‑time AudioContext (for live playback).

Real‑Time Mode: 1. Create an AudioContext with 12 OscillatorNode instances (one per head) and 1 AudioBufferSourceNode for noise. 2. Connect each node through a GainNode to the AudioContext.destination. 3. On each animation frame, update the oscillator frequency and gain based on the current attention weights. 4. Use PannerNode to spatialize heads in stereo: Head 0 = hard left, Head 11 = hard right.

Offline Mode: 1. Create an OfflineAudioContext with the desired duration. 2. Schedule all audio events using the Web Audio API's precise timing (start(t), stop(t)). 3. Render to an AudioBuffer, then export as WAV or MP3 for download.

docs.title: 49.5 User Controls
docs.text: The sonification panel in Zone 8 (or a floating panel) provides: - Play/Pause button for audio playback. - Volume slider per head. - Solo/Mute toggle per head. - Sound Type selector (sine, square, sawtooth, noise, melodic). - Tempo control (affects rhythmic head patterns). - Export Audio button (downloads WAV file). - MIDI Output selector (if Web MIDI is available).

docs.title: 50.1 Core Concept
docs.text: The same attention data can be rendered in multiple artistic styles: Heatmap (classic), Sankey flow (dynamic), Arc diagram (elegant), Chord diagram (circular), Hive plot (structural), 3D particle flow (immersive), Minimalist (for papers/publications), and Cyberpunk neon (for presentations). Users can switch between styles with one click and export any style as SVG, PNG, or MP4.

docs.title: 50.2 Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose SVG Rendering D3.js (heatmap, arc, chord, hive) Generate publication‑quality vector graphics Canvas Rendering HTML5 Canvas API Generate raster graphics for complex styles 3D Rendering React Three Fiber (@react‑three/fiber) 3D particle flow style Animation Export MediaRecorder API + Canvas capture Export animated styles as MP4 SVG Export XMLSerializer + Blob API Export static styles as SVG PNG Export Canvas toDataURL() or toBlob() Export static styles as PNG PDF Export jsPDF or @react‑pdf/renderer Export for paper submission

docs.title: 50.3 Style Catalog
docs.text: Style Rendering Engine Best For Key Visual Encoding Heatmap SVG (D3) Detailed analysis, publications Color intensity = attention weight, cell grid Sankey Flow SVG (D3‑sankey) Understanding information flow Flow width = attention magnitude Arc Diagram SVG (D3) Elegant overview Arc thickness = attention, arc height = head index Chord Diagram SVG (D3‑chord) Circular relationship view Chord width = attention, color = head Hive Plot SVG (D3) Structural comparison Axis = token position, link = attention 3D Particle Flow WebGL (R3F) Immersive exploration Particle density = attention, color = head Minimalist SVG Papers, presentations Grayscale, thin lines, clean typography Cyberpunk Neon SVG + CSS glow Presentations, social media Neon colors, glow effects, dark background

docs.title: 50.4 Style Transfer Architecture
docs.text:
The gallery uses a strategy pattern where each style is a separate renderer component that accepts the same data interface:

interface AttentionData {
  tokens: string[];
  matrix: number[][];  // attention weights
  metadata: {
    modelId: string;
    attentionType: string;
    layer: number;
    head: number;
  };
}

interface StyleRenderer {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  description: string;
  render: (data: AttentionData, container: HTMLElement) => void;
  exportSVG: (data: AttentionData) => string;
  exportPNG: (data: AttentionData) => Promise<Blob>;
}

Each renderer implements this interface, making it easy to add new styles without modifying existing code.

docs.title: 50.5 Export Pipeline
docs.text:
SVG Export: 1. Render the attention data using the selected style's SVG renderer. 2. Serialize the SVG element using new XMLSerializer().serializeToString(svgElement). 3. Create a Blob with MIME type image/svg+xml. 4. Trigger download via a temporary <a> element with download attribute.

PNG Export: 1. Render the SVG to a Canvas element using canvg or native Image + drawImage. 2. Convert Canvas to Blob via canvas.toBlob(). 3. Trigger download.

MP4 Export (for animated styles like 3D Particle Flow): 1. Use MediaRecorder API with canvas.captureStream(60) to capture 60fps video. 2. Record for the desired duration (default: 10 seconds). 3. On stop, create a Blob from the recorded chunks. 4. Trigger download.

docs.title: 50.6 Integration with Paper App
docs.text: The Minimalist style is specifically optimized for academic papers: - Generates publication‑quality vector graphics with proper font sizing. - Exports as PDF (via jsPDF) with embedded vector graphics. - Auto‑generates a LaTeX \includegraphics command. - Provides pre‑written figure captions describing the attention pattern.

docs.title: CIRCUIT TRACER
docs.text: Here is a fully detailed implementation blueprint for the Circuit Tracer — QK & OV Circuit Explorer, covering technologies, architectures, and implementation strategies.
