docs.title: 2.1 Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The circuit extraction pipeline follows the Transformer Circuits mathematical framework where every attention head is understood in terms of two matrices:

  • QK Circuit: Score(q,k) = (W_Q · x_i)^T · (W_K · x_j) / √d — determines where the head attends
  • OV Circuit: Output = Σ_j A_ij · (W_V · x_j) · W_O — determines what information the head reads and writes

The extraction runs in four phases:

docs.title: Phase 1: Hook Point Registration
docs.text: Using TransformerLens's HookPoint system, attach hooks to every attention head's Q, K, V, O projection outputs across all layers. This captures the full QK and OV matrices for any given input text. HookPoints provide standardized access: blocks.{layer}.attn.hook_q, blocks.{layer}.attn.hook_k, blocks.{layer}.attn.hook_v, blocks.{layer}.attn.hook_z.

docs.title: Phase 2: Attribution Graph Construction
docs.text: Following the Anthropic attribution graph methodology, compute the direct effect (edge weight) between every pair of non-zero features. This uses cross-layer transcoders (trained via sparse autoencoders) to decompose the residual stream into interpretable features. The edge weight from feature A to feature B equals the dot product of the gradient of B's activation with respect to A, multiplied by A's activation value.

docs.title: Phase 3: Circuit Pruning
docs.text: Apply a threshold pruning strategy: remove all edges below a configurable threshold (default 0.01). Then apply transitive reduction to remove redundant indirect edges—if A→B and B→C exist with high weight, and A→C exists with low weight, A→C may be pruned since it's already explained by the path A→B→C.

docs.title: Phase 4: Automatic Circuit Classification
docs.text: Run automated head type detection using detection patterns (positional, previous-token, induction, copy, etc.) as implemented in TransformerLens's head_detector module. Each head is classified by comparing its attention pattern against known templates.

docs.title: 2.2 Browser-Side Computation Architecture
docs.text:
For client-side circuit extraction (no server needed for small models):

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  MAIN THREAD (React)                 │
│  • UI rendering, user interactions, state management│
│  • Renders circuit graph using Cytoscape/R3F        │
└─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                  │ postMessage
┌─────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────┐
│           WEB WORKER 1: Model Inference              │
│  • Loads model via Pyodide + TransformerLens         │
│  • Runs forward pass with HookPoints                 │
│  • Extracts QK and OV matrices                       │
│  • Posts results back to main thread                 │
└─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                  │ SharedArrayBuffer
┌─────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────┐
│        WEBGPU COMPUTE SHADER (WGSL)                  │
│  • Performs QK^T matrix multiplication on GPU        │
│  • Computes attention weights via softmax             │
│  • Processes matrices up to 2048×2048 in real-time   │
│  • Handles OV projection computations                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Web Worker handles model inference via Pyodide, while matrix operations are offloaded to WebGPU compute shaders written in WGSL. A SharedArrayBuffer enables zero-copy data transfer between the worker and GPU.

docs.title: 3.1 Bipartite Circuit Graph Design
docs.text:
The core visualization is a bipartite directed graph with two node types: - Feature Nodes: Represent individual transcoder features (e.g., "detects capital cities," "detects Texas-related text") - Input/Output Nodes: Represent input tokens (left side) and output logits (right side)

Edges flow left-to-right: - QK edges (blue): Show attention routing—which query features attend to which key features - OV edges (orange): Show information writing—which features write to which output directions

docs.title: 2D View (Cytoscape.js)
docs.text:
• Layout: Dagre hierarchical layout for top-to-bottom or left-to-right circuit display
  • Edge bundling: Hierarchical edge bundling (TP-Bundle approach) to reduce visual clutter in large circuits
  • Interaction: Hover on edge → tooltip showing weight value; click on node → highlight all connected edges; drag nodes to reposition
  • Supernodes: User-defined groups of features (e.g., "capital-related features") can be collapsed into a "supernode" for high-level circuit views

docs.title: 3D View (React Three Fiber + r3f-forcegraph)
docs.text:
• Force-directed 3D layout: Nodes positioned in 3D space; edges rendered as directional particle flows with arrow indicators
  • Node encoding: Sphere size = feature activation magnitude; color = feature type (QK circuit = blue, OV circuit = orange, Input = green, Output = purple)
  • Edge encoding: Particle density = edge weight; particle speed = edge confidence; particle color = circuit type
  • Camera controls: Orbit, pan, zoom; double-click on node to "fly to" it

docs.title: 3.3 GPU-Accelerated Edge Rendering (Deck.gl GraphLayer)
docs.text: For large circuits (100+ nodes, 1000+ edges), Deck.gl's GraphLayer provides WebGL2/WebGPU-based rendering: - Renders nodes as instanced circles and edges as instanced line segments - GPU aggregation for collision detection and label placement - Handles real-time interaction at 60 FPS for graphs with thousands of nodes

docs.title: 4.1 Data Model
docs.text:
For each attention head in each layer:

QKCircuit {
  headId: "L5_H7",
  queryFeatures: [{ id, label, activationValue }],
  keyFeatures: [{ id, label, activationValue }],
  edges: [{ sourceId, targetId, weight, type: "qk" }],
  attentionPattern: number[][], // raw attention matrix
  headType: "induction" | "previous_token" | "copy" | "positional" | "semantic" | "unknown"
}

docs.title: 4.2 Computation Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Extract QK matrix: From blocks.{layer}.attn.hook_q and blocks.{layer}.attn.hook_k, compute QK^T / √d_head. Apply causal mask if the model is autoregressive.
  2. Feature decomposition: Using pre-trained transcoders (sparse autoencoders), decompose both Q and K vectors into interpretable feature coefficients. Each transcoder feature has a human-readable label (e.g., "feature 27: detects 'is' relationship").
  3. Edge weight computation: For feature pair (f_q, f_k), compute the dot product of their respective Q and K projection components, weighted by the feature activations.
  4. Pattern classification: Run the TransformerLens head_detector to classify the head type based on its attention pattern template.

docs.title: 4.3 Visualization Layout
docs.text: A bipartite graph rendered as two columns: - Left column: Query features (labeled with activation values) - Right column: Key features - Edges: Arrows from query to key, color-coded by weight magnitude - Side panel: Shows the raw attention matrix for this head as a heatmap

docs.title: 5.1 Data Model
docs.text:
OVCircuit {
  headId: "L5_H7",
  valueFeatures: [{ id, label, activationValue }],
  outputFeatures: [{ id, label, activationValue }],
  edges: [{ sourceId, targetId, weight, type: "ov" }],
  headFunction: "copy" | "move" | "delete" | "transform" | "unknown"
}

docs.title: 5.2 Computation Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Extract OV matrix: From blocks.{layer}.attn.hook_v and blocks.{layer}.attn.hook_z, compute W_V · x_j and W_O. The OV circuit is: Output = Σ_j A_ij · (W_V · x_j) · W_O.
  2. Feature mapping: Decompose V and O vectors into transcoder features.
  3. Functional classification: Based on the OV matrix's eigenvalue spectrum: positive eigenvalues → copying function (amplifying features); negative eigenvalues → deleting function (suppressing features); mixed eigenvalues → transformation.

docs.title: 5.3 Visualization Layout
docs.text: A layered flow diagram: - Bottom layer: Value features (input to the OV circuit) - Middle layer: The attention-weighted combination (visualized as a blend operation) - Top layer: Output features (what the head writes to the residual stream) - Connection lines show the strength of each feature's contribution

docs.title: 6.1 Detection Algorithm
docs.text:
The induction head detector follows the Transformer Circuits mathematical framework:

An induction head has: 1. OV circuit: Behaves like a copying head — maps features X to say(X) (outputs that would make the model predict X) 2. QK circuit: "If the query token is X, attend to a key token preceded by X"

Detection Steps: 1. Compute the attention pattern for every head 2. For each head, measure how much attention mass is on the "previous token" vs. "two tokens back" 3. Induction heads show a characteristic pattern: high attention to tokens that followed similar tokens 4. Validate by computing the OV circuit's eigenvalue spectrum — induction heads show positive eigenvalues in the copy-detection subspace

docs.title: 6.2 Implementation
docs.text:
Using TransformerLens's head_detector module with a custom detection pattern:

Detection Pattern (for autoregressive models):
- Expectation: attention[i, j] is highest when token_j == token_{i-1}
- This creates a "previous token matching" pattern
- Quantified by the "prefix matching score"

docs.title: 7.1 Causal Intervention Architecture
docs.text:
Following pyvene's intervention framework:

  1. Select source features (e.g., feature 27 at token position 5)
  2. Set intervention value (e.g., set activation to 0.0 to "knock out" the feature, or to 2.0 to amplify)
  3. Re-run forward pass with the intervention applied at the HookPoint
  4. Measure effect: Compare the output logits before and after intervention

docs.title: 7.2 Implementation
docs.text: Using pyvene's Intervention API: - Register HookPoint interventions at specific layers/heads - Support counterfactual interventions (set to zero, set to specific value, swap with another position's activation) - Visualize the effect as a "diff" in the circuit graph: edges that changed are highlighted in red (decreased) or green (increased)

docs.title: 8.1 Graph Serialization Format
docs.text:
Following the Anthropic Circuit Tracer's JSON format:

{
  "modelId": "gemma-2-2b",
  "prompt": "The capital of Texas is",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "27_22605_10", "layer": 27, "featureIdx": 22605, "activation": 10.2 },
    { "id": "input_0", "type": "input", "token": "The" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "source": "input_5", "target": "27_22605_10", "weight": 0.83, "type": "qk" }
  ],
  "annotations": [
    { "nodeId": "27_22605_10", "label": "Detects state names" }
  ],
  "supernodes": [
    { "name": "Texas detection", "nodes": ["27_22605_10", "20_15589_10"] }
  ]
}

docs.title: 8.2 Neuronpedia Integration
docs.text: Circuits can be uploaded to Neuronpedia for community exploration. The sharing workflow: 1. User clicks "Share Circuit" → generates a unique URL 2. The circuit is uploaded to the platform (or to Neuronpedia) 3. Other users can view, annotate, and fork the circuit 4. Annotations are collaborative (real-time via WebSockets)

docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  QUICK OPERATIONS (< 50 nodes)               │
│  → Main thread (JavaScript)                  │
│  → Instantaneous response                    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  MEDIUM OPERATIONS (50-500 nodes)            │
│  → Web Worker for circuit extraction         │
│  → WebGPU for matrix operations              │
│  → < 100ms total latency                     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LARGE OPERATIONS (500+ nodes)               │
│  → Server-side Python for circuit extraction │

│  → Progressive rendering as data arrives     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 10. INTEGRATION WITH EXISTING PLATFORM
docs.text:
The Circuit Tracer connects to your existing Django apps:

Connection Integration Point Models Load from model_versioning registry or HuggingFace Hub Experiments "Run Circuit Analysis" button on experiment detail page Notes Auto-generate note with circuit diagram + analysis Paper Export circuit graph as LaTeX figure Community Share circuits with threaded discussions Leaderboards "Most Interesting Circuit" challenge GPU Marketplace Use rented GPU for circuit extraction on large models

docs.title: 11. ADVANCED: WEBGPU COMPUTE SHADER FOR REAL-TIME ATTENTION
docs.text:
For the most performance-critical path—computing attention matrices in real-time—a WGSL compute shader:

Workgroup: 8×8 threads
Dispatch: ceil(N/8) × ceil(N/8)

Each thread computes one cell of the QK^T matrix, then a second dispatch applies softmax row-wise. This enables real-time attention pattern updates as the user changes input text, without requiring a server round-trip. The WebGPU pipeline handles QKV projections and attention score computation, while CPU threads manage non-matmul operations.

docs.title: "Interactive Model Surgery" for the Attention Visualization Dashboard
docs.text: This document provides an exhaustive, production‑grade implementation blueprint for the Compression Studio — a full‑featured interactive model compression environment integrated into the NeuralOps Attention Dashboard. Every section specifies the technologies, architectural patterns, component hierarchies, data flow designs, rendering strategies, and integration touchpoints needed to build this system from scratch.

1. Architectural Overview & Technology Stack

  4. Zone 2: Compression Impact Heatmap — The WebGL/WebGPU Layer

docs.title: 1. Architectural Overview & Technology Stack
docs.text: The Compression Studio is not a single component — it is a multi‑layer, multi‑runtime application composed of five tightly coupled zones that share state through a centralized state machine. The architecture draws from: OpenAI's circuit_sparsity Streamlit dashboard (parameterized pruning sweep exploration), DL‑Playground's drag‑and‑drop neural network editor with visual architecture construction, Penzai + Treescope's interactive tensor visualization from Google DeepMind, React Flow's node‑graph rendering substrate (used by AgentForge and FlowiseAI), deck.gl's GPU‑powered large‑scale data visualization framework, and GPT2‑WebGL's browser‑based transformer implementation with WebGL2 matrix visualization.

docs.title: 1.2 Browser‑Side Compute Architecture
docs.text:
The Compression Studio performs actual SVD computation in the browser using a dual‑approach strategy:

  1. Small matrices (< 1000×1000): Compute via Pyodide (NumPy/SciPy running in WebAssembly). Pyodide compiles CPython 3.12 to WebAssembly, enabling numpy.linalg.svd() directly in the browser without server round‑trips. This is ideal for per‑layer weight matrices and singular value spectrum visualization.

  2. Large matrices (≥ 1000×1000): Offload to a Web Worker using Comlink for RPC‑style communication, or delegate to the Django backend via REST API. The Web Worker runs the SVD using either Pyodide or a pure JavaScript implementation, keeping the main thread responsive.

  3. GPU‑accelerated visualization: The compression impact heatmap renders via deck.gl's WebGL2/WebGPU layer system, which can handle millions of data points (weight entries, activation differences) at 60fps. GPT2‑WebGL demonstrates that full transformer model matrices can be loaded as WebGL textures and visualized in‑browser.

docs.title: 3. Zone 1: Model Architecture Map — The Interactive Tree Canvas
3.1 Core Concept
docs.text: The Model Architecture Map is a React Flow‑based interactive tree that renders the complete model architecture as a navigable graph. Each node represents a component (attention head, FFN neuron, embedding dimension, normalization layer). The user clicks any component to inspect its parameters, importance scores, and available compression options. A split‑view mode shows the original architecture side‑by‑side with a live preview of the compressed architecture.

docs.title: 3.2 Technology & Framework Choices
docs.text:
Primary rendering substrate: React Flow 12.x (xyflow)

React Flow is chosen as the rendering engine because it provides: - Built‑in node dragging, zooming, panning, and minimap - Custom node rendering with React components - Edge (connection) rendering with labels and styling - Event handling for node click, hover, selection - Programmatic layout control

Multiple production AI workflow editors use React Flow as their foundation, including the Workflow Designer UI for Giselle (which uses Zustand for state management alongside React Flow), AgentForge's pipeline editor, and FlowiseAI's agent flow editor.

Layout engine: Dagre

Dagre is used to compute a hierarchical (top‑to‑bottom or left‑to‑right) layout for the model architecture tree. The layout is computed once when the model loads and recalculated when layers are pruned or compressed. React Flow provides a useNodesInitialized hook that integrates with Dagre's positioning.

3D complement: React Three Fiber (r3f)

For an alternative "immersive" view, the same architecture data can be rendered in 3D using React Three Fiber. The r3f-nn-visualizer project demonstrates interactive neural network visualization with tf.js and react‑three‑fiber, including live demos with layer‑by‑layer inspection. The Vercel AI SDK's json‑render project further shows how structured JSON specifications (model architecture) can be rendered as 3D scenes with React Three Fiber components.

docs.title: 3.5 Key Implementation Details
docs.text:
Custom React Flow Node (ArchitectureNode)

The custom node uses React Flow's Handle components for connection points and renders a styled card with: - Background color gradient based on importance score (green=important, red=prunable) - A circular gauge (SVG arc) showing the importance percentage - An icon badge indicating the compression method applied (scissors for pruning, sigma for SVD, etc.) - The node is resizable — larger nodes have more parameters

Node selection behavior: - Single click → opens NodeInspector with per‑component details - Double click → zooms into that node (expands to show sub‑components like individual heads) - Shift+click → adds to multi‑selection for batch compression operations - Right click → context menu with "Compress this component," "Exclude from compression," "Set as compression anchor"

Before/After Split View

The split view uses two synchronized React Flow instances (locked viewport). The left shows the original architecture; the right shows a live preview of the compressed architecture. Differences are highlighted: - Green outline: component unchanged - Orange outline: component compressed - Red outline with strikethrough: component pruned

The split view is draggable (the divider can be moved). When the user hovers over a compressed component, a tooltip shows the delta: "Parameters: 589K → 98K (83% reduction), FLOPs: 2.3M → 0.4M."

Model Architecture JSON Schema

docs.title: 4. Zone 2: Compression Impact Heatmap — The WebGL/WebGPU Layer
4.1 Core Concept
docs.text: The Compression Impact Heatmap shows a layer‑by‑layer, parameter‑by‑parameter visualization of how a selected compression strategy will affect the model. Each "cell" in the heatmap represents a weight matrix entry; the color intensity encodes the relative change in that entry after compression (original value minus compressed value, normalized). Users can zoom into individual weight matrices, hover to see exact before/after values, and compare different compression strategies side‑by‑side.

docs.title: 4.2 Technology & Framework Choices
docs.text:
Primary rendering: deck.gl 9.x

deck.gl is chosen because it is "the definitive high‑performance, GPU‑powered framework for rendering massive datasets on the web, specifically addressing the challenge of visualizing millions of data points". The compression impact heatmap may need to render weight matrices with hundreds of thousands of entries — deck.gl's BitmapLayer, HeatmapLayer, and custom CompositeLayer can handle this at 60fps using WebGL2/WebGPU.

deck.gl also provides a React integration (@deck.gl/react) that wraps deck.gl into React's lifecycle, including a DeckGL React component and hooks for state management.

Alternative: GPT2‑WebGL approach

GPT2‑WebGL demonstrates that full transformer weight matrices can be loaded as WebGL2 textures and rendered in‑browser. For weight matrices up to 4096×4096, a WebGL2 fragment shader approach (treating weights as texture data) can provide real‑time updates as compression parameters change. The implementation uses "GPU‑accelerated matrix operations on the GPU" via WebGL2 shaders.

Color scale: d3‑scale‑chromatic

Scientific color scales from d3 (interpolateViridis, interpolatePlasma, interpolateRdYlBu) are used to encode the impact magnitude. The interpolateRdYlBu scale (red=high impact, blue=low impact) is particularly intuitive for compression visualization.

docs.title: 4.4 Data Flow
docs.text:
compressionStore (Zustand)
    │
    │ selectedCompressor, compressorParams, originalWeights, compressedWeights
    ▼
useBrowserSVD() hook OR backend API
    │
    │ Computes compressed weights based on selected strategy and params
    │ For SVD: runs numpy.linalg.svd in Pyodide or Web Worker
    │ For pruning: applies threshold mask
    │ For quantization: applies uniform quantization
    ▼

    │
    ▼

    │
    │ Renders via WebGL2 texture (BitmapLayer) with color mapping
    ▼
User hovers over cell → deck.gl picking → ImpactTooltip displays exact values

docs.title: 4.5 Key Implementation Details
docs.text:
Custom deck.gl CompositeLayer

The ImpactHeatmapLayer extends deck.gl.CompositeLayer and composites three sub‑layers:

  1. BitmapLayer: Renders the full weight matrix as a 2D image where each pixel's color encodes the impact magnitude. For a 768×768 matrix, this is a 768×768 pixel image rendered via WebGL texture. The bitmap is regenerated on the GPU whenever compression parameters change (via shouldUpdateState).

  2. ColumnLayer: Renders the singular value spectrum as vertical bars along the bottom edge. Each bar height represents a singular value; colored bars are retained, gray bars are pruned. This directly visualizes the SVD truncation.

  3. ScatterplotLayer: Highlights the top‑N most affected weight entries (largest delta) as glowing dots, making it easy to spot where compression has the greatest impact.

Web Worker SVD Computation

The svd.worker.ts file implements off‑main‑thread SVD computation:

// Conceptual architecture (not code)
// Main thread:
const svdWorker = wrap(new Worker('./svd.worker.ts'));
const { U, S, Vt } = await svdWorker.computeSVD(weightMatrix, targetRank);

// Worker thread:
// Option A: Pyodide
self.importScripts('pyodide.js');
const pyodide = await loadPyodide();
await pyodide.loadPackage(['numpy', 'scipy']);
const result = pyodide.runPython(`
    import numpy as np
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(weight_matrix, full_matrices=False)
    U_r = U[:, :rank]
    S_r = np.diag(S[:rank])
    Vt_r = Vt[:rank, :]
    (U_r.tolist(), S_r.tolist(), Vt_r.tolist())
`);

// Option B: Pure JS (for small matrices)
// Uses numeric.js or ml-matrix for SVD

Pyodide Integration

Pyodide is loaded lazily (only when the user first opens the Compression Studio) via dynamic import. The Pyodide runtime (~6.5MB compressed) is cached by the browser's service worker. For SVD computation, Pyodide loads numpy and scipy packages on‑demand.

Progressive rendering strategy: - Matrices < 256×256: render instantly via Pyodide in main thread (fast enough) - Matrices 256×256 to 1024×1024: compute in Web Worker, show skeleton loading state - Matrices > 1024×1024: fetch pre‑computed impact data from backend API, show progressive loading

docs.title: 5. Zone 3: Live Math Panel — The LaTeX Computation Engine
5.1 Core Concept
docs.text: The Live Math Panel renders the mathematical formula for the selected compression method in real‑time, showing the actual numerical values plugged into the equation. It also displays parameter count before/after and estimated FLOPs reduction. The panel is inspired by 3Blue1Brown's Manim animations and the SVD‑vis interactive tool.

docs.title: 5.2 Technology Choices
docs.text:
LaTeX rendering: KaTeX

KaTeX is chosen over MathJax for its speed (renders synchronously, no DOM scanning) and smaller bundle size. KaTeX renders LaTeX strings to HTML in under 5ms for typical formulas, which is critical for real‑time updates as the user drags sliders.

Numerical computation: Pyodide (NumPy) or pure JS

Parameter counts and FLOPs estimations are computed client‑side: - Parameter count: simple multiplication of matrix dimensions × (1 − compression_ratio) - FLOPs estimation: uses formulas from the compression library (e.g., for SVD: r(M+N) vs original MN) - Singular value energy: Σ σ²_kept / Σ σ²_total computed via NumPy in Pyodide

docs.title: 5.4 Key Implementation Details
docs.text:
Real‑time formula updates

The formula display uses a debounced (16ms) update loop: as the user drags a rank slider, the KaTeX string is regenerated with the new numerical values and re‑rendered. KaTeX's synchronous rendering ensures no flicker.

Supported compression formula templates:

Each compression method in the registry has an associated formula template:

const FORMULA_TEMPLATES: Record<string, FormulaTemplate> = {
  'a3': {
    latex: 'W \\approx U_{{$rank}} \\Sigma_{{$rank}} V_{{$rank}}^T',
    variables: ['rank'],
    paramCountFn: (m, n, rank) => rank * (m + n),
    flopsFn: (m, n, rank) => rank * (m + n),
  },
  'ast_pruner': {
    latex: 'W_{2:4} = \\text{TopK}_{k=2}(W_{ij}), \\; j \\in \\{0,4,8,...\\}',
    variables: [],
    paramCountFn: (m, n) => m * n * 0.5,  // 50% sparsity
    flopsFn: (m, n) => m * n * 0.5,        // 50% fewer multiplies
  },
  'kmeans': {
    latex: 'W \\approx \\text{KMeans}_{k={$clusters}}(W)',
    variables: ['clusters'],
    paramCountFn: (m, n, clusters) => clusters + m * n * Math.ceil(Math.log2(clusters)) / 32,
    flopsFn: (m, n) => m * n,  // No FLOP reduction
  },
  // ... templates for all 60+ compressors
};

Parameter count bar chart animation

The before/after parameter count comparison uses an animated bar chart (Framer Motion layout animation). When the user changes compression parameters, the "after" bar smoothly animates to its new width, with the percentage reduction displayed as a label that counts up/down.

docs.title: 6. Zone 4: Controls — The Compression Parameter Orchestrator
6.1 Core Concept
docs.text: The Controls Zone is the command center where users select compression strategies, adjust parameters via sliders, set budget constraints, and trigger compression. It is designed to be immediately understandable while exposing the full power of the 60+ compression library.

docs.title: 6.2 Technology Choices
docs.text:
Slider library: Custom React components + @radix‑ui/react‑slider

Custom slider components are built on top of Radix UI's accessible slider primitive. Each slider is annotated with: - Real‑time numerical value display - A mini sparkline showing the parameter's effect on model size - Color‑coded range indicators (green=recommended, yellow=aggressive, red=extreme)

Compressor selector: Combobox with search

A command palette‑style combobox (built with cmdk or @radix‑ui/react‑popover) allows users to search and filter through all 60+ compression methods. Each result shows: - Compressor name - Category badge (SVD, Pruning, Quantization, Hybrid) - Short description - Typical compression ratio range

Budget constraint solver: Custom algorithm

The budget constraint input accepts a target model size (in MB) and uses a greedy allocation algorithm to suggest per‑layer compression parameters that meet the budget. The solver runs in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the UI.

docs.title: 6.4 Key Implementation Details
docs.text:
Budget constraint solver algorithm

Input: target_size_mb, model_layers (with parameter counts and compressibility scores)
Output: per_layer_params (rank, sparsity, bits for each layer)

Algorithm:
1. Calculate current total size: Σ layer_params_count × 4 bytes / (1024²)
2. Calculate required reduction: current_total - target_size_mb
3. Sort layers by compressibility_score (high score = can be compressed more)
4. For each layer (in descending compressibility order):
   a. Apply maximum compression (lowest rank, highest sparsity)
   b. Recalculate total size
   c. If total ≤ target_size_mb, stop and return params
5. If still over budget, show warning: "Target size not achievable with this compressor"

This solver runs in a Web Worker and returns results in < 100ms for models with up to 100 layers.

Slider‑to‑visualization reactivity

All sliders are connected to the Zustand store via useStore selectors. When a slider value changes: 1. Zustand store updates immediately (synchronous) 2. The Live Math Panel re‑renders (KaTeX, sub‑millisecond) 3. The Compression Impact Heatmap schedules a re‑computation (debounced at 100ms) 4. The Model Architecture Tree re‑renders the compressed view (debounced at 100ms)

This architecture ensures smooth slider dragging (60fps) without expensive recomputation on every frame.

docs.title: 7. Zone 5: Cross‑Platform Integration — The Action Pipeline
7.1 Core Concept
docs.text: The Cross‑Platform Integration Zone connects the Compression Studio to the rest of the NeuralOps platform — the compression pipeline, the leaderboard, the experiment launcher, and the model versioning system. A single "Compress Now" button triggers the full workflow.

docs.title: 7.2 Technology Choices
docs.text:
API calls: TanStack Query mutations

TanStack Query's useMutation hook is used for the compression API call. It provides: - Optimistic updates (immediately show "compressing" state) - Automatic retry on failure (3 retries with exponential backoff) - Cache invalidation (refresh model version list after compression) - Progress tracking via onMutate, onSuccess, onError callbacks

Real‑time progress: WebSocket

During compression, the Django backend sends progress updates via WebSocket (e.g., "Compressing layer 5/12... 42%"). The useCompressionProgress hook subscribes to the WebSocket channel and updates the progress bar.

Before/After Leaderboard: Your existing leaderboard infrastructure

The compressed model can be submitted to the benchmark leaderboard via your existing gpu_benchmark app. The submission includes: - Original model name and version - Compression method and parameters - Before/after metrics (accuracy, FLOPs, model size) - The attention pattern visualization captured at the time of compression

docs.title: 7.3 Component Hierarchy
docs.text:
OneClickApply
├── ApplyButton ("Compress Now")
│   └── onClick → triggers compression pipeline
├── CompressionProgressBar
│   ├── ProgressBar (animated, shows current layer and percentage)
│   ├── CurrentOperationLabel ("Compressing Layer 5: Q projection...")

    ├── StatsComparison

    │   ├── FLOPsBefore ("2.3M → 0.4M (83% reduction)")
    │   └── AccuracyBefore (if benchmarked)

    │   ├── "Download Model"

├── SubmitButton (opens submission modal)

docs.title: 7.4 Key Implementation Details
docs.text:
Compression Pipeline Integration

The OneClickApply component sends a POST request to your existing compression API:

POST /api/runs/start-compress/
Body: {
  "model_name": "bert-base-uncased",
  "compressor": "a3",
  "compressor_config": { "rank": 32 },
  "attention_type": "galerkin",
  "sample_text": "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog",
  "save_to_registry": true,
  "submit_to_leaderboard": true
}

The backend processes the compression (using your existing 60+ compression library), saves the compressed model to the model versioning system, and returns a run ID. The frontend then subscribes to WebSocket updates for progress tracking.

Auto‑generated compression report

After compression completes, an auto‑generated note is created using your notes/report_generator.py. The note includes: - The compression method and parameters - Before/after parameter counts and FLOPs estimates - The singular value spectrum (embedded as SVG) - The compression impact heatmap (embedded as PNG) - Links to the compressed model version and leaderboard submission

Attention pattern capture

At the moment of compression, the attention pattern visualization is serialized (including layer/head selection, sample text, and the rendered SVG). This is stored as metadata on the compression run and linked to both the model version and the compression report.

docs.title: 8.1 Dual‑Store Architecture: Zustand + XState
docs.text:
The Compression Studio uses a dual‑store approach:

Zustand manages the application data state — the model being compressed, the selected compressor, the slider values, the compressed architecture preview, and the impact matrix. Zustand is chosen for its simplicity, performance (no provider wrapper needed), and excellent TypeScript support. The Workflow Designer UI for Giselle demonstrates this pattern: React Flow for graph visualization combined with Zustand for state management.

XState manages the compression workflow state machine — the sequence of states the compression process goes through. XState provides formal state machine semantics: each state has defined transitions, guards, and actions. This prevents "impossible states" (e.g., "comparing" before "compressing") and makes the workflow predictable and testable. XState is recommended for "complex orchestration with guards, timers, and hierarchies".

docs.title: 8.2 XState Machine Definition
docs.text:
States:
  idle
    → analyzing (on SELECT_COMPRESSOR)
  analyzing
    → ready (on ANALYSIS_COMPLETE)
    → error (on ANALYSIS_FAILED)
  ready
    → compressing (on APPLY_COMPRESSION)
    → idle (on CLEAR_SELECTION)
  compressing
    → completed (on COMPRESSION_SUCCESS)
    → failed (on COMPRESSION_FAILED)
    → idle (on CANCEL)
  completed
    → comparing (on COMPARE_WITH_ORIGINAL)
    → idle (on NEW_COMPRESSION)
    → submitted (on SUBMIT_TO_LEADERBOARD)
  comparing
    → completed (on CLOSE_COMPARISON)
    → submitted (on SUBMIT_TO_LEADERBOARD)
  submitted
    → completed (on CLOSE)
    → idle (on NEW_COMPRESSION)

Guards:
  canCompress: selectedCompressor !== null && selectedModel !== null
  canSubmit: compressionRunId !== null
  hasBudget: budgetConstraint !== null

Actions (side effects):
  onCompressing: start WebSocket subscription, show progress bar
  onCompleted: fetch compressed model architecture, update Zustand store
  onFailed: show error toast, log to activity feed

docs.title: 8.3 Zustand Store Design
docs.text:
The Zustand store is sliced into logical domains using the slice pattern:

// compressionStore.ts — conceptual structure
interface CompressionStore {
  // Model slice
  model: ModelArchitecture | null;
  setModel: (model: ModelArchitecture) => void;

  // Compressor slice
  selectedCompressor: string | null;
  compressorParams: Record<string, number>;
  setCompressor: (name: string) => void;
  setParam: (key: string, value: number) => void;

  // Preview slice
  compressedArchitecture: ModelArchitecture | null;
  impactMatrix: Float32Array | null;
  paramCountBefore: number;
  paramCountAfter: number;
  flopsBefore: number;
  flopsAfter: number;

  // Budget slice
  budgetConstraint: number | null; // in MB
  setBudget: (mb: number) => void;
  isBudgetFeasible: boolean;

  // UI slice
  selectedNode: string | null;
  splitViewEnabled: boolean;
  heatmapLayer: number | null;
  setSelectedNode: (nodeId: string | null) => void;
  toggleSplitView: () => void;

  // History slice
  compressionHistory: CompressionRun[];
  addToHistory: (run: CompressionRun) => void;
}

docs.title: 9.1 Rendering Tiers
docs.text:
The Compression Studio implements a three‑tier rendering strategy based on the complexity of the visualization:

Tier Data Size Rendering Approach Target FPS Tier 1: Small < 10K data points (single weight matrix < 100×100) Standard React rendering (SVG with React) 60fps Tier 2: Medium 10K–500K data points (weight matrix 100×100 to 700×700) deck.gl BitmapLayer via WebGL2 texture 60fps Tier 3: Large > 500K data points (weight matrix > 700×700) deck.gl with progressive loading + Web Worker computation 30fps (acceptable for static exploration)

docs.title: 9.2 Memory Management
docs.text:
Float32Array for impact matrices: The impact matrix is stored as a Float32Array (4 bytes per entry) rather than a regular JavaScript array (8+ bytes per entry), reducing memory usage by 50%+ for large matrices.

Web Worker offloading: SVD computation and compression simulation are offloaded to Web Workers. The main thread only receives the results (U, S, Vt matrices), keeping it responsive for UI interactions.

Lazy Pyodide loading: Pyodide is loaded only when the user first opens the Compression Studio. The 6.5MB download is cached by the browser's service worker. Subsequent visits load Pyodide from cache in < 1 second.

docs.title: 9.3 Debouncing Strategy
docs.text:
User drags slider
  │
  ├─→ Zustand store updates (immediate, synchronous)
  │
  ├─→ Live Math Panel re‑renders (immediate, KaTeX < 5ms)
  │
  ├─→ Parameter count / FLOPs recompute (immediate, simple arithmetic)
  │
  ├─→ Architecture Tree compressed preview (debounced 100ms)
  │
  └─→ Impact Heatmap recompute (debounced 200ms, Web Worker)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Compression Studio is a six‑layer, multi‑runtime application that combines:

  • React 18 + TypeScript for the UI framework
  • React Flow for the interactive model architecture tree
  • deck.gl + WebGL2 for GPU‑accelerated impact heatmaps
  • Pyodide (CPython 3.12 in WASM) for client‑side SVD computation
  • Web Workers for off‑main‑thread computation
  • KaTeX for real‑time LaTeX formula rendering
  • Zustand + XState for dual‑layer state management
  • TanStack Query for server state caching
  • Framer Motion for animation
  • WebSocket for real‑time compression progress
  • Your existing 60+ compression library for actual model compression
  • Your existing leaderboard, experiment launcher, notes, and model versioning apps for cross‑platform integration

Every component is designed to be independently testable, lazy‑loaded for code splitting, and accessible via keyboard navigation and screen readers. The entire system operates at 60fps for interactive exploration while supporting matrices with millions of entries via GPU‑accelerated rendering.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The Embedding Explorer is designed as a browser‑native, zero‑upload application following the architecture pioneered by Apple's Embedding Atlas — all computation (embedding generation, dimensionality reduction, clustering, similarity search) executes entirely on the client side via WebAssembly, eliminating the need for any backend server beyond your existing Django API. The rendering pipeline uses WebGPU as the primary backend with WebGL2 fallback, enabling smooth interaction with millions of data points while maintaining 60fps on consumer hardware.

The system is organized into six interconnected architectural layers that map to the dashboard zones the user specified:

docs.title: 🔧 Layer 0: Core Computation Engine — Rust → WebAssembly Pipeline
Framework: wasm-pack + rustc → .wasm binary
docs.text:
The heart of the embedding explorer is a Rust codebase compiled to WebAssembly that handles all heavy computation directly in the browser. This follows Apple's approach of combining "Rust‑based clustering modules with WebAssembly UMAP implementations to significantly optimize dimensionality reduction performance".

Modules compiled to WASM:

Module Rust Crate WASM Package Purpose Dimensionality Reduction umap-rs @neuralops/umap-wasm UMAP/t‑SNE/PCA projection of 768‑dim vectors to 2D/3D Vector Similarity simsimd @neuralops/simd-wasm SIMD‑accelerated cosine similarity, dot product, Euclidean distance on Float32 arrays Clustering Engine linfa-clustering @neuralops/cluster-wasm HDBSCAN, k‑means, mean‑shift for automatic cluster labeling Linear Classification liblinear-rs wrapper @wlearn/liblinear Logistic regression / linear SVM for probe training directly in browser KDE Renderer kde-rs @neuralops/kde-wasm Kernel density estimation for contour/density heatmap generation

Communication Pattern: The WASM modules receive Float64Array typed arrays via a shared ArrayBuffer to avoid JavaScript↔WASM copy overhead. The @wlearn/liblinear package demonstrates this pattern — it exposes an API accepting { data: Float64Array, rows, cols } for zero‑copy training.

Initialization Sequence (on page load): 1. Web Worker spawns and loads all WASM modules in parallel via WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming 2. Worker exposes a message‑passing API: { type: 'umap_project', vectors: Float64Array, params: {...} } 3. Main thread sends typed arrays via postMessage (transferred, not copied, via transferList) 4. Worker returns projected coordinates, cluster labels, or similarity scores 5. Results flow into the React state via a Zustand store slice

docs.title: Rendering Framework: @react-three/fiber (R3F) + Three.js + WebGPU backend
docs.text: The 3D canvas uses React Three Fiber as the declarative React wrapper around Three.js, with the WebGPURenderer (three@latest with WebGPURenderer from three/webgpu) as the primary renderer and WebGLRenderer as fallback. This approach mirrors Apple's strategy: "WebGPU is adopted as the default rendering backend (with WebGL 2 compatibility layer)". The Project Golem project validates this architecture — it "uses UMAP to project high‑dimensional embeddings into 3D and Three.js to render them interactively in the browser".

docs.title: Component Architecture:
docs.text:
<EmbeddingSpace3D>
  ├── <WebGPURenderer fallback={<WebGLRenderer />} />
  ├── <OrbitControls />                          ← camera rotation/zoom/pan
  ├── <TokenSphereCloud>                         ← primary rendering
  │   ├── <InstancedMesh args={[sphereGeometry, material, count]}>
  │   │   ← GPU‑instanced rendering for millions of spheres
  │   └── <HoverHighlight />                     ← raycasting on hover
  ├── <SemanticClusters>                         ← cluster envelopes
  │   └── <ConvexHullMesh />                     ← transparent hull per cluster
  ├── <TokenTrajectoryLines>                     ← semantic pathway
  │   └── <Line segments />                      ← line from layer N to N+1
  ├── <SearchTeleporter />                       ← "teleport to token"
  ├── <SemanticAxisIndicator />                  ← PCA/ICA axis arrows
  └── <DensityContour />                         ← KDE contour overlay

docs.title: GPU Instanced Rendering Strategy
docs.text:
For 1 million+ spheres, standard React rendering (one <mesh> per sphere) would crash. Instead, the TokenSphereCloud component uses GPU instancing via Three.js InstancedMesh:

  1. Geometry: A single SphereGeometry(radius=0.02, segments=8, rings=8) is created once
  2. Material: MeshStandardMaterial with per‑instance color via instanceColor buffer attribute
  3. Matrix Buffer: A Float32Array of size count × 16 holds the model matrix for each instance (position from UMAP coords, uniform scale)
  4. Color Buffer: A Float32Array of size count × 3 holds the color for each token (mapped from cluster label, token type, or attention weight)
  5. Update on hover: The raycasting system identifies the instance index; the matrix and color for that instance are updated to show a glow/highlight

This is the same technique used by DiVE: "an interactive 3D web viewer of up to million points on one screen ... based on graphosaurus.js and three.js". The Helios‑Web project further validates "GPU‑based rendering for real‑time visualization and interactive analysis of massive‑scale networks and high‑dimensional embeddings" using WebGL.

docs.title: Token Search & Teleport
docs.text:
The Search Teleporter component provides a text input where users type any word/token. Under the hood:

  1. Frontend: User types "Paris" → React state updates
  2. WASM Worker: The token's embedding vector is retrieved from the model's embedding matrix (loaded as a Float32Array at page initialization)
  3. Nearest‑neighbor search: The WASM similarity module finds the 50 nearest tokens in embedding space and returns their indices + distances
  4. Camera animation: useFrame in R3F animates the camera from its current position to the target sphere's position using THREE.Vector3.lerp with an easing function
  5. Highlight effect: The target sphere's emissive intensity is set to 1.0, and its scale is temporarily increased

docs.title: Semantic Cluster Rendering
docs.text:
After the WASM clustering module computes cluster assignments, each cluster is rendered as a transparent convex hull (or alpha shape). The implementation uses the quickhull3d algorithm compiled to WASM or a JavaScript port:

  1. Cluster centers and boundaries are computed by the WASM clustering module
  2. For each cluster with ≥ 5 points, a ConvexGeometry is generated from the outermost points
  3. The hull is rendered as a semi‑transparent mesh with cluster‑specific color
  4. A text label (the cluster's auto‑generated name like "food words" or "location terms") is positioned at the hull centroid using @react-three/drei's <Text> component

docs.title: Token Trajectory View
docs.text:
Inspired by Prompt Rover which "builds a minimum path graph between embeddings and projects it with t‑SNE to trace the semantic trajectory from input to output", and by InterpreT which provides "the ability to track and visualize token embeddings through each layer of a Transformer":

  1. When a user selects a specific token in a specific sentence, the system queries your Django API for that token's hidden state at every layer of the model
  2. Each layer's hidden state is projected into the same 3D space (using the same UMAP projection previously computed)
  3. The positions are connected by a curved tube (using CatmullRomCurve3 in Three.js) with a color gradient from blue (layer 0) to red (layer 12)
  4. The tube thickness varies to represent the change magnitude between consecutive layers (where the representation changes most)
  5. The tube animates on hover — a glowing particle travels along the path from input to output

docs.title: Rendering: HTML5 Canvas 2D with OffscreenCanvas + Web Worker
docs.text:
For the vocab_size × d_model matrix (typically 30,000+ × 768), a canvas‑based approach is required because SVG with that many elements would crash. The implementation:

  1. OffscreenCanvas in a Web Worker renders the full matrix at high resolution into an ImageBitmap
  2. The ImageBitmap is transferToImageBitmap() to the main thread and drawn onto a visible canvas
  3. Zoom/Pan: The visible canvas shows a viewport into the full matrix. Zooming in triggers re‑rendering at higher resolution for the visible region only
  4. Color scale: Blue for negative values, white for zero, red for positive (matching the 3Blue1Brown visualization convention)
  5. Search: Typing a token name scrolls the viewport to that row and highlights it with a yellow border
  6. Row comparison: Selecting two tokens renders both rows side‑by‑side with a difference row showing the delta

docs.title: Dimension Importance via PCA
docs.text: The WASM PCA module computes: 1. Explained variance ratio per principal component 2. The top‑10 dimensions are rendered as a bar chart 3. The "semantic axis discovery" feature (powered by ICA) is described in Zone 5 below

docs.title: 📐 Zone 3: Live Math Panel — Embedding Formulas
Rendering: react-latex / katex for LaTeX, framer-motion for animation
docs.text:
The math panel displays the embedding computation formula:

E[token] = W_e[token_id, :] + W_p[pos, :]

Where: - W_e: The token embedding matrix (learned during training) - W_p: The positional encoding matrix (sinusoidal or learned)

docs.title: Animated Computation Steps
docs.text:
Inspired by the Self Attention Flow tool and 3Blue1Brown's Manim animations:

  1. Step 1: The token embedding row is highlighted in the heatmap, values animate from gray to color
  2. Step 2: The positional encoding vector is rendered as a separate bar chart
  3. Step 3: The two vectors "merge" (element‑wise addition animation) to form the final embedding
  4. Step 4: The final embedding vector is shown, and the user can see which dimensions are dominated by token identity vs. position

docs.title: Cosine Similarity Calculator
docs.text:
1. User selects any two tokens from dropdowns
  2. The WASM similarity module computes cos(a,b) = (a·b) / (||a||·||b||)
  3. The result is displayed as a large number (0.0–1.0) with a color‑coded bar
  4. Dimension contribution breakdown: A bar chart shows which dimensions contribute most to the similarity (the element‑wise product a_i × b_i before summation)
  5. The computation uses the wasm-similarity library which "moves the hot loop into WebAssembly compiled from Rust" for "high-performance vector similarity and distance metrics"

docs.title: Vocabulary Coverage Histogram
docs.text: Rendered using recharts (already in your project). The histogram shows how often each token appears in a calibration corpus, revealing the long‑tail distribution typical of language.

docs.title: Embedding Norm Distribution
docs.text: A box‑plot or violin plot showing the distribution of L2 norms across all token embeddings. Tokens with unusually high norms (like [CLS] or [SEP]) are annotated. This reveals "anisotropy" — the tendency of embeddings to cluster in a narrow cone.

docs.title: Nearest‑Neighbor Graph
docs.text: The WASM similarity module computes the top‑5 nearest neighbors for every token in the vocabulary (or a user‑selected subset). The graph is rendered as a D3 force‑directed graph, where edge thickness = similarity. This is the same concept as the GPT‑2 Token Similarity Visualizer which "visualizes token similarity relationships across GPT‑2 layers ... providing an interactive 'microscope' into how language models process and understand text".

docs.title: Semantic Axis Discovery (ICA‑Based)
docs.text:
This is the most novel feature, inspired by the research "Discovering Universal Geometry in Embeddings with ICA" which demonstrates "that each embedding can be expressed as a composition of a few intrinsic interpretable axes and that these semantic axes remain consistent across different languages, algorithms, and modalities".

Implementation approach:

  1. WASM ICA module: An Independent Component Analysis implementation compiled to WebAssembly. ICA differs from PCA in that it finds statistically independent components rather than merely uncorrelated ones, which tend to align with interpretable semantic concepts.

  2. Axis discovery workflow:

  3. User selects a subset of the vocabulary (e.g., all nouns, or all emotion‑related words)
  4. The ICA module decomposes their embeddings into independent components
  5. Each component is tested for correlation with known semantic labels (e.g., sentiment scores from SentiWordNet, concreteness ratings)

  6. Components that strongly correlate with known labels are presented as "discovered semantic axes"

  7. Visualization: Each discovered axis is rendered as a labeled arrow in the 3D embedding space. For example, an axis pointing from "sad" tokens to "happy" tokens is labeled "Sentiment (+)". The axes are overlaid on the 3D scatter plot.

  8. User‑defined axes: Following Parallax's approach which "allows the user to explicitly define the axes of the projection through algebraic formulae", users can also define custom axes by providing word pairs (e.g., "king – man + woman = queen") and the system computes and visualizes the resulting direction.

docs.title: Framework: @wlearn/liblinear (WebAssembly LIBLINEAR)
docs.text:
The linear probe playground uses LIBLINEAR v2.50 compiled to WebAssembly. This enables browser‑side training of linear classifiers on embedding vectors — no server, no GPU, no Python required.

Workflow:

  1. Data preparation: The user selects a classification task from a dropdown (e.g., "POS tagging: Noun vs. Verb", "Sentiment: Positive vs. Negative", or a custom task defined by the user)
  2. Feature extraction: For the selected tokens, their embedding vectors are extracted from the loaded model's embedding matrix. The WASM module receives these as Float64Array typed arrays.
  3. Training: The LinearModel is instantiated with solver: 'L2R_LR' (L2‑regularized logistic regression) and fit on the training split. Training completes in milliseconds on a few thousand examples.
  4. Evaluation: Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 are displayed. The decision boundary is visualized as a plane in the 3D embedding space — tokens correctly classified appear in their true color; misclassified tokens appear in the predicted color with an X marker.
  5. Layer comparison: Users can train probes on embeddings from different layers of a transformer (layer 0, 3, 6, 9, 12) to see how semantic information becomes more linearly separable in deeper layers.

Why this works in the browser: LIBLINEAR uses a dual coordinate descent algorithm that is highly efficient for linear models. When compiled to WebAssembly, it runs at near‑native speed because the hot loop consists of simple arithmetic operations that WASM executes efficiently. The @wlearn/liblinear package demonstrates this by providing model.fit(), model.predict(), model.predictProba(), and model.score() APIs that all execute entirely client‑side.

docs.title: Token Activation Comparison
docs.text:
After fine‑tuning a model (tracked in your experiment app), users can compare embeddings before and after fine‑tuning:

  1. Load the original model's embeddings and the fine‑tuned model's embeddings
  2. For each token, compute the cosine similarity between its original and fine‑tuned embedding
  3. Render a scatter plot where X = original norm, Y = fine‑tuned norm, color = cosine similarity
  4. Tokens that moved most during fine‑tuning (low cosine similarity) are highlighted as "most affected by fine‑tuning"
  5. One‑click link to the training run that produced the fine‑tuned model

docs.title: "Embedding of the Day"
docs.text: A community‑curated daily feature where: 1. Users submit interesting embedding relationships they've discovered (e.g., "The embedding of 'dog' is closer to 'cat' in BERT than in GPT‑2") 2. The community votes on submissions 3. The winning submission is featured on the dashboard homepage 4. Submissions include the interactive 3D visualization embedded (not just a screenshot)

docs.title: Embedding Visualization Sharing
docs.text: Every embedding visualization state (camera position, selected tokens, cluster view, projection method) is serialized to a URL parameter. Sharing the URL recreates the exact same view for another researcher. This uses the same pattern as your attention dashboard's sharing system.

docs.title: Collections: "Interesting Embedding Clusters"
docs.text: Users create themed collections of embedding discoveries, similar to GitHub Stars or Pinterest boards. Example collections: "Multilingual Embedding Comparisons" (showing how the same concept clusters in English vs. French vs. Chinese models), "Fine‑tuning Effects" (before/after comparisons), "Semantic Axis Gallery" (showcasing discovered interpretable axes).

docs.title: 🎮 Zone 7: Gamification — "Embedding Detective"
docs.text:
A daily puzzle game where:

  1. The system selects a random token from the vocabulary
  2. Its embedding vector is displayed (as a bar chart or radar plot of the top‑20 PCA dimensions)
  3. The user must guess which token it represents
  4. After guessing, the correct token is revealed along with its nearest neighbors
  5. Scoring: Points awarded based on how close the guess was (measured by cosine similarity between the guessed token's embedding and the target)
  6. Streaks: Consecutive days played are tracked and displayed
  7. XP rewards: XP contributes to the user's overall platform level

docs.title: 🔗 Zone 8: Cross‑Platform Integration Points
docs.text:
The embedding explorer connects to every other part of your platform:

Platform App Integration experiment Load embeddings from any training run; compare before/after fine‑tuning model_versioning Load embeddings from any saved model version notes Save embedding analysis as a researcher note with embedded 3D scene paper Export embedding visualizations as LaTeX figures community Discuss embedding discoveries in linked Q&A threads portfolios Embedding discoveries appear in the researcher's portfolio leaderboards "Embedding Detective" scores on weekly leaderboards gpu_reputation XP from embedding exploration contributes to overall reputation profiles User's embedding expertise badges displayed on profile messaging Share embedding discoveries via private messages organizations Team‑level embedding collections for research groups

docs.title: 📊 Technology Stack Summary
docs.text:
Layer Technology Purpose 3D Rendering Three.js via R3F + WebGPU GPU‑accelerated sphere cloud, camera, effects 2D Rendering HTML5 Canvas + OffscreenCanvas Embedding matrix heatmap at scale WASM Compute Rust → wasm‑pack UMAP, PCA, ICA, clustering, similarity Linear Classification @wlearn/liblinear (WASM) Browser‑side linear probe training Data Analysis DuckDB‑WASM Client‑side SQL queries on embedding metadata State Management Zustand + immer Reactive embedding state, undo/redo Animation framer-motion + GSAP Math panel step animations, camera transitions Charts recharts + d3 Statistics dashboard charts Math Rendering katex / react-latex Live LaTeX formula display Backend Django REST API Model loading, embedding extraction, experiment data Real‑time WebSocket / Channels Collaborative exploration, live updates

The entire system operates with zero data upload — all computation happens client‑side through WebAssembly, following Apple's "privacy‑preserving, reproducible" design that "completes all computational tasks including embedding generation and projection locally within the browser". This architecture makes the Embedding Explorer both fast and privacy‑respecting, suitable for researchers working with proprietary models or sensitive text data.

docs.title: 📐 OVERALL ARCHITECTURE
docs.text:
The FFN/MLP Explorer follows a six-tier architecture identical to the approach used by OpenAI's Transformer Debugger: a React frontend, a FastAPI activation server, and a specialized model inference library with hooking capabilities. This architecture separates concerns into: Model & Inference System → Activation Data Management → Activation Server → Frontend Canvas.

The core data abstraction is the ActivationRecord (a @dataclass pairing activation values with token strings) and the NeuronRecord (organizing multiple activation records per neuron with statistical moments: mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis). The NeuronId uniquely identifies each neuron by (neuron_index, layer_index). This simple but powerful data model underpins every visualization zone.

docs.title: 📊 ZONE 1: CANVAS — Neuron Activation Heatmap (tokens × neurons)
Implementation Stack
docs.text: Component Technology Justification Activation Extraction TransformerLens 3.0+ via TransformerBridge Supports 50+ architectures, exposes all internal activations through hook points including mlp.post_act Backend Server FastAPI (Python 3.11+) with asyncio OpenAI's TDB uses FastAPI activation server; AXON uses the same pattern with WebSocket streaming Data Format Apache Arrow via pyarrow Zero-copy columnar transfer between Python and JavaScript; critical for matrices with up to 16384 neurons × 1024 tokens (16M values) Frontend Rendering @deck.gl/layers (BitmapLayer + ColumnLayer) GPU-powered via WebGL2/WebGPU; renders millions of rectangles at 60fps using instanced rendering Color Scale Custom GLSL fragment shader (Viridis/Inferno) Bypasses CPU color computation; all color mapping happens on GPU Zoom/Pan deck.gl built-in OrthographicView with viewState Handles coordinate transforms in WebGL without re-rendering data

docs.title: Implementation Details
docs.text:
Backend Pipeline (FastAPI):

POST /api/ffn/activations
Body: { model_id, text, layers: [0..N] }
→ TransformerLens runs forward pass with hooks on mlp.post_act for each layer
→ ActivationCache stores all values
→ For each layer, extract tensor [n_tokens, d_mlp] as float32
→ Convert to Arrow RecordBatch (columns: token_index, neuron_index, activation_value)
→ Return as Arrow IPC stream (binary)

The model system uses TransformerHooks to intercept activations at mlp.post_act for each transformer block. The activation server exposes API endpoints for accessing model activations and managing inference operations.

Frontend Rendering Pipeline:

1. Receive Arrow IPC stream → deserialize into TypedArray (Float32Array)
2. Upload to GPU as SSBO (Shader Storage Buffer Object) via WebGL2
3. Vertex shader: each instance = one (token, neuron) pair; position computed from indices
4. Fragment shader: sample Viridis colormap from 1D texture based on activation value
5. Instanced rendering: single draw call for entire heatmap (up to 16M quads)
6. Hover detection: render separate "picking layer" with encoded (token_idx, neuron_idx)

For real-time updates (e.g., changing input text), use deck.gl's data prop reactivity — only the SSBO buffer is updated, not the shader program.

docs.title: Top-Activating Examples Explorer
docs.text:
For each neuron, display the top-10 text snippets that maximally activate it. Implementation: NeuronRecord stores most_positive_activation_records — the highest-activating examples for each neuron. These are pre-computed during a calibration pass over a corpus.

Backend: 

GET /api/ffn/neuron/{layer}/{neuron}/examples?n=10
→ Query pre-computed NeuronRecord
→ Return list of {text, tokens, activations_per_token, max_activation_value}

Frontend: Render as a scrollable Masonry gallery using react-virtuoso for virtualized scrolling. Each card shows the text with tokens color-highlighted by activation intensity, plus the max activation value.

docs.title: Neuron "Planet" 3D Map
docs.text:
Implementation Stack:

Component Technology Dimensionality Reduction umap-learn 0.5+ (Python) with n_components=3; fitted once per model on activation matrix [n_neurons, n_tokens] 3D Rendering @react-three/fiber + @react-three/drei (Three.js React bindings) Point Cloud three.js InstancedMesh with SphereGeometry — single draw call for all neurons Labels drei Text component using troika-three-text for SDF (signed distance field) text rendering Post-Processing @react-three/postprocessing for bloom (glow effect on high-activation neurons)

Pipeline: 

1. Python: collect activation vectors for all neurons → matrix [N_neurons, D_tokens]
2. Python: fit UMAP(n_components=3) → 3D coordinates for each neuron
3. Store coordinates in SQLite/PostgreSQL (updated only when model changes)
4. Frontend: fetch coordinates + metadata (neuron_index, layer, specialty_label)
5. Three.js: InstancedMesh with 1 sphere per neuron, colored by cluster, sized by avg_activation
6. Interaction: Raycaster for hover/click → show neuron detail panel

The AXON project demonstrates this exact pattern: "3D force graph where nodes = SAE features, node size & brightness = activation magnitude".

docs.title: 📐 ZONE 2: MATH PANEL — Live Formula Rendering
Implementation Stack
docs.text: Component Technology Justification LaTeX Rendering KaTeX 0.16+ (client-side) 5-10× faster than MathJax; renders to DOM not SVG Animation Engine GSAP (GreenSock) + Framer Motion GSAP for math step animations; Framer Motion for layout transitions Numerical Computation Pyodide (Python in WebAssembly) Runs NumPy in browser for live attention computation on small matrices Formula Typesetting Custom React component wrapping KaTeX Renders formula from JSON-serializable AST (not raw LaTeX strings)

docs.title: Implementation Details
docs.text:
The FFN formula panel shows:

FFN(x) = W_2 · GELU(W_1 · x + b_1) + b_2

Each term is clickable/hoverable, triggering animations that expand the computation:

  1. W₁ · x: Shows W₁ as a matrix, x as a column vector, and the resulting intermediate vector
  2. b₁ addition: Shows bias being added
  3. GELU: Shows the GELU curve with a red dot tracking the current value
  4. W₂ · GELU(...): Shows the final projection

Architecture: 

FormulaAST (JSON)
  ├── term: "W_2"
  ├── term: "GELU"
  │   ├── term: "W_1"
  │   ├── term: "x"
  │   └── term: "b_1"
  └── term: "b_2"

Each AST node maps to a React component that renders KaTeX and accepts onHover, onClick, highlighted props. When a user hovers over "W₁" in the formula, the corresponding weight matrix lights up in the visualization canvas, and the numerical panel shows the actual values.

docs.title: SVD of W₁ — Feature Direction Explorer
docs.text:
Backend: 

# Compute once when model loads
U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(W1, full_matrices=False)
# Store top-K singular vectors (K=256)
# Each right singular vector Vh[i] is a "feature direction" in the input space

Frontend: Display the top singular vectors as interactive bar charts. Each bar represents a dimension's contribution. Click a singular vector to see which neurons are most aligned with it (via dot product). The LM Transparency Tool provides exactly this: decomposed_ffn_out(batch_i, layer, pos) showing "the decomposed contribution of each neuron in the feed-forward network".

docs.title: Neuron Importance Ranking
docs.text:
Computation (Python backend, pre-computed): 

# For each neuron i in layer l:
importance_score[i] = mean_activation[i]  # Average activation across corpus
selectivity[i] = 1 - entropy(normalized_activation_distribution[i])  # How selective
dead_score[i] = (max_activation[i] < epsilon)  # Binary: is this neuron dead?

NeuroX provides built-in methods for neuron importance extraction: "The toolkit can extract either a local ranking of neurons important to a particular target class, or a global ranking of neurons important to all the target classes".

Frontend: Render as a sortable table using @tanstack/react-table with virtualized rows. Columns: Rank, Layer, Neuron Index, Importance Score, Selectivity, Status (Active/Dead). Click a row → scroll to that neuron in the heatmap.

docs.title: Dead Neuron Detector
docs.text: Flag neurons where max_activation < 1e-6 across the entire calibration corpus. Display count per layer as a "health bar" (green → yellow → red). The Neuron Record stores statistical moments (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) that enable systematic detection of inactive neurons.

docs.title: Neuron Co-Activation Graph
docs.text:
Computation: 

# For each pair of neurons (i, j):
co_activation[i][j] = correlation(activation_i, activation_j)  # Pearson r
# Threshold at 0.7 → create edge list

Frontend: Render as an interactive force-directed graph using deck.gl GraphLayer with GPU-powered layout computation. Nodes = neurons, edges = co-activation relationships. Node color = layer, node size = importance score. Double-click a node to "expand" — show its top-10 activating examples and connected neurons.

docs.title: Neuron Ablation Laboratory
docs.text:
Implementation: Uses TransformerLens hook system to zero out specific neurons during forward pass. The hook system "enables the inspection and/or alteration of activations in individual components like attention heads and MLP layers".

Backend Pipeline: 

POST /api/ffn/ablate
Body: { model_id, text, ablated_neurons: [{layer, neuron_index}] }
→ TransformerLens runs forward pass with ablation hooks
→ Returns { original_logits, ablated_logits, logit_diff, affected_tokens }

Frontend: Toggle switches per neuron (rendered as a grid with react-window for performance). Each toggle triggers an API call; results stream back via WebSocket for real-time feedback. Show a "diff view" highlighting which output tokens changed probability.

docs.title: SAE (Sparse Autoencoder) Feature View
docs.text:
Implementation Stack: SAELens library (maintained and actively developed) for training and loading SAEs. SAELens "exists to help researchers train sparse autoencoders and analyse sparse autoencoders" and integrates with sae-vis for visualization.

Pipeline: 

1. Train SAE on MLP activations using SAELens (offline, GPU)
2. Store encoder/decoder weights + feature labels
3. Frontend: for each token, run SAE encode → sparse feature vector
4. Display top-K activated features per token as a "feature cloud"

The SAE visualizer provides two complementary views: "a feature-centric view (which sequences in a large dataset this feature fires strongest on) and a prompt-centric view (which features score highest on a custom prompt)".

docs.title: Neuron Labeling System
docs.text:
Community-contributed labels (e.g., "this neuron detects French text") stored in a dedicated model:

class NeuronLabel(models.Model):
    model_id = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    layer_index = models.IntegerField()
    neuron_index = models.IntegerField()
    label = models.CharField(max_length=500)
    confidence = models.FloatField()  # 0-1, from voting
    proposed_by = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    votes_up = models.IntegerField(default=0)
    votes_down = models.IntegerField(default=0)
    evidence = models.JSONField(default=dict)  # links to top-activating examples

This integrates with your existing community voting infrastructure and gpu_reputation scoring. Neuronpedia provides the model: "EXPLANATION TYPE np_max-act — Forces concise explanations and shows the model the top activating tokens and texts".

docs.title: "Neuron of the Week"
docs.text: A scheduled Celery task that selects the most interesting neuron based on: (a) community votes for "interesting" reactions, (b) uniqueness of activation pattern (low similarity to other neurons), (c) quality of community labels. The selected neuron appears on the homepage spotlight, in the weekly digest email, and gets a dedicated discussion thread in the community Q&A app.

docs.title: Neuron Labeling Game
docs.text:
A gamified interface where users are shown a neuron's top-10 activating examples and asked to propose a label. Labels are voted on by the community. Correct labels (those that survive community voting with high confidence) earn XP and badges. Incorrect labels lose XP. This follows the Yupp model of "token-incentivized feedback" where "diverse user feedback flows freely under blockchain and cryptocurrency economic incentives."

Architecture: 

Frontend: NeuronLabelingGame component
  → Shows neuron metadata + activating examples
  → Text input for label proposal
  → Submit → POST /api/ffn/neuron/{id}/label
Backend: Django view
  → Creates NeuronLabel with proposed_by and confidence=0
  → Emits WebSocket event for real-time leaderboard update
Community: Voting system (up/down) using existing Vote model

docs.title: Game Mechanics
docs.text:
A daily challenge where users are given a description (e.g., "Find the neuron that activates most strongly on question marks") and must navigate the Neuron Activation Universe to locate it. The game uses:

  1. Search mode: Users can filter neurons by activation statistics (top-activating tokens, activation distribution metrics)
  2. Hints: Progressively revealed clues (first hint: layer range, second hint: activation pattern description, third hint: specific example)
  3. Scoring: Points based on time-to-find and number of hints used
  4. Leaderboard: Daily/weekly/all-time rankings connected to your existing leaderboard infrastructure

Implementation: 

Backend:
  - DailyNeuronChallenge model (date, neuron_id, description, hints[])
  - Pre-compute challenge neuron each day (random selection from "interesting" neurons)
  - POST /api/ffn/challenge/check → verify if user found the correct neuron

Frontend:
  - NeuronHunterGame component with timer, hint system, search interface
  - Connects to Neuron Activation Heatmap (click neuron to "submit guess")
  - Score animation and XP reward on success

docs.title: 🧠 Full Pipeline Studio — Complete Implementation Architecture
"From Input Token to Final Prediction — Every Step Visible, Every Value Inspectable"
TABLE OF CONTENTS
docs.text:
1. Overall Architecture & Technology Stack
  2. Model Execution Engine
  3. Data Flow & State Management
