docs.title: 1.1 Three-Tier Architecture
docs.text:
The Full Pipeline Studio uses a three-tier architecture that separates model execution, data processing, and visualization rendering:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    TIER 3: VISUALIZATION (Browser)               │
│  React 18 + TypeScript + React Three Fiber + D3.js + GSAP      │
│  WebGL/WebGPU Canvas | DOM Overlays | CSS Animations            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    TIER 2: DATA PROCESSING (Web Worker)          │
│  Comlink for RPC | SharedArrayBuffer for zero-copy              │
│  Tensor serialization/deserialization | State aggregation       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    TIER 1: MODEL EXECUTION (Browser/Server)      │
│  Option A: Transformers.js + ONNX Runtime Web (WebGPU/WASM)     │
│  Option B: Pyodide + PyTorch (pure Python in browser)           │
│  Option C: Django Backend API (for large models)                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Transformer Explainer project (Polo Club, Georgia Tech) pioneered this client‑side approach: "the frontend uses Svelte and D3 for interactive visualizations, while the backend uses ONNX runtime and HuggingFace's Transformers library to run the GPT-2 model in the browser". AnimatedLLM (2025) similarly "runs entirely in the browser, using pre‑computed traces of open LLMs applied on manually curated inputs". Your platform extends this by supporting three execution backends depending on model size and user context.

docs.title: 1.2 Technology Stack Detail
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Why This Choice UI Framework React 18 + TypeScript 5.x Component architecture, state management, routing Already your frontend stack; component model supports complex interactive UIs 3D Rendering React Three Fiber (R3F) + Three.js 160+ GPU-accelerated 3D visualization of the full pipeline R3F "uses React Three Fiber with native Three.js for GPU-accelerated rendering, supports both WebGPU and WebGL backends" 2D Visualizations D3.js v7 + d3-sankey Sankey flow diagrams, attention heatmaps, embedding scatter plots Transformer Explainer "adopts the Sankey diagram visual design, inspired by recent work viewing Transformers as dynamical systems, emphasizing how input data flows through model components" Animation Engine GSAP (GreenSock) + ScrollTrigger Smooth timeline animations, scroll-driven reveals, step-by-step forward pass GSAP can "sync WebGL shaders with HTML layout" and "transform static scenes into fluid, story-like sequences" Model Execution (Browser) Transformers.js + ONNX Runtime Web Run GPT-2, BERT, DistilBERT directly in browser "You can easily convert your pretrained PyTorch, TensorFlow, or JAX models to ONNX using Optimum" Model Execution (Python) Pyodide (CPython 3.11 compiled to WASM) Run PyTorch hooks and custom analysis in browser "Pyodide enables scientific computing, data visualization, and interactive notebooks—all in client-side web apps" Web Workers Comlink + SharedArrayBuffer Offload heavy computation, zero-copy data transfer Prevents UI thread blocking during model inference State Management Zustand + Immer Immutable state updates for model activations across layers Already in your stack; supports middleware for undo/redo Data Fetching TanStack Query (React Query) Cache management for model outputs, pre-computed traces Already in your stack Styling Tailwind CSS 3.x Consistent design system Already in your stack Math Rendering KaTeX (browser) or MathJax Live LaTeX equation rendering in the Math Panel Faster than MathJax for real-time updates

docs.title: 2.1 Three Execution Backends (Auto-Selected by Model Size)
docs.text: The system must support three backends, automatically selected based on model size and user's hardware capabilities:

docs.title: Backend A: Transformers.js + ONNX Runtime Web (Small Models: GPT-2, DistilBERT, BERT-tiny)
docs.text:
Model Size: < 500M parameters
Latency: 50-500ms per forward pass
Hardware: CPU (WASM SIMD) or GPU (WebGPU)

How it works: 1. Model is converted from PyTorch to ONNX format using HuggingFace Optimum: optimum-cli export onnx --model bert-base-uncased bert_onnx/ 2. ONNX model files (.onnx) are loaded by Transformers.js in the browser 3. Transformers.js selects the best execution provider: WebGPU → WASM SIMD → WASM baseline 4. Intermediate activations are extracted using ONNX intermediate outputs: the model is split at each layer boundary, with intermediate tensors exposed as named outputs. This is achieved by modifying the ONNX graph to add output nodes after each transformer block during the export process.

Implementation detail for activation extraction: 

# Server-side: Export model with intermediate outputs
from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForFeatureExtraction
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

model = ORTModelForFeatureExtraction.from_pretrained(
    "bert-base-uncased", export=True,
    # Custom config to output all hidden states
    output_hidden_states=True
)
# This produces an ONNX model where each layer's hidden states
# are available as separate output tensors

docs.title: Backend B: Pyodide + PyTorch (Medium Models, Research Use)
docs.text:
Model Size: 500M - 2B parameters
Latency: 1-5 seconds per forward pass
Hardware: CPU only (WASM)

How it works: 1. Pyodide loads a CPython 3.11 runtime compiled to WebAssembly in the browser 2. A minimal PyTorch package (torch-only, no CUDA) is installed in the Pyodide environment 3. The model is loaded from HuggingFace Hub or from a pre-downloaded checkpoint 4. torch.nn.Module.register_forward_hook() is used to capture all intermediate activations exactly as in native Python — "Hook函数是PyTorch提供的一种强大工具，它允许我们在不修改模型主体结构的情况下，拦截并处理模型运行过程中的中间数据" (PyTorch hooks allow intercepting intermediate data without modifying the model structure) 5. Captured tensors are serialized and sent to the main thread via Comlink

docs.title: Backend C: Django Backend API (Large Models, Production Use)
docs.text:
Model Size: > 2B parameters
Latency: 5-30 seconds
Hardware: Server GPU (NVIDIA A100/H100)

How it works: 1. The user's input text is sent to your existing Django API endpoint 2. The server loads the model using HuggingFace Transformers with output_hidden_states=True and output_attentions=True 3. All intermediate activations, attention weights, and hidden states are captured server-side 4. Results are streamed back via WebSocket (using your existing Channels infrastructure) as they become available — layer by layer 5. The frontend progressively renders each layer as it arrives, providing a real-time "streaming" experience

docs.title: 2.2 Activation Capture Protocol
docs.text:
Regardless of backend, the data structure returned to the visualization layer is standardized:

interface ForwardPassTrace {
  model_name: string;
  input_text: string;
  tokens: string[];                    // Tokenized input
  token_ids: number[];                 // Token IDs

  embedding: {
    token_embeddings: number[][];      // [seq_len, d_model]
    position_embeddings: number[][];   // [seq_len, d_model]
    combined_embeddings: number[][];   // [seq_len, d_model]
  };

  layers: LayerTrace[];

  output: {
    logits: number[][];                // [seq_len, vocab_size]
    predictions: {                     // Top-k predictions per position
      token_id: number;
      token: string;
      probability: number;
    }[][];
  };
}

interface LayerTrace {
  layer_index: number;

  attention: {
    q_proj: number[][];               // Query projection weights
    k_proj: number[][];               // Key projection weights
    v_proj: number[][];               // Value projection weights
    heads: {
      head_index: number;
      attention_weights: number[][];  // [seq_len, seq_len]
      q_vectors: number[][];          // Query vectors [seq_len, head_dim]
      k_vectors: number[][];          // Key vectors
      v_vectors: number[][];          // Value vectors
      output: number[][];             // Head output [seq_len, head_dim]
    }[];
    combined_output: number[][];      // After concatenation + projection
  };

  ffn: {
    pre_activation: number[][];       // Before activation function
    post_activation: number[][];      // After GELU/ReLU
    output: number[][];               // After second linear layer
  };

  residual_connections: {
    after_attention: number[][];      // Residual stream after attention
    after_ffn: number[][];            // Residual stream after FFN
  };

  layer_norm: {
    attention_input_norm: number[][]; // After pre-attention LayerNorm
    ffn_input_norm: number[][];       // After pre-FFN LayerNorm
  };
}

docs.title: 2.3 Web Worker Architecture
docs.text:
To prevent UI freezing during model inference, all model execution runs in a Web Worker:

Main Thread (React)                    Web Worker (Model Execution)
─────────────────────                   ─────────────────────────────
Zustand Store ←── Comlink ──→          Model Runner
    │                                    │
    ├── Canvas Rendering (R3F)          ├── Transformers.js / Pyodide
    ├── DOM Updates (React)             ├── Hook Capture
    └── User Input Handling             └── Tensor Processing

Comlink is used for RPC (Remote Procedure Call) between the main thread and worker, making the communication feel like direct function calls while actually going through postMessage:

// Main thread
import { wrap } from 'comlink';
const ModelRunner = wrap<typeof import('./model-runner.worker')>(
  new Worker(new URL('./model-runner.worker.ts', import.meta.url))
);

// This looks like a direct call but runs in the worker
const trace = await ModelRunner.runForwardPass('bert-base-uncased', inputText);

For large tensors (e.g., attention matrices), SharedArrayBuffer enables zero-copy data transfer between the worker and main thread, critical for real-time visualization performance — as demonstrated by VisionFlow: "implements real-time position streaming via SharedArrayBuffer with zero-copy reads".

docs.title: 3.1 Global State Architecture (Zustand + Immer)
docs.text:
interface PipelineStudioState {
  // Model & Input
  modelId: string;
  inputText: string;
  executionBackend: 'transformers.js' | 'pyodide' | 'django-api';

  // Execution
  isRunning: boolean;
  currentStep: number;         // Which step in the forward pass (0 to totalSteps)
  totalSteps: number;
  playbackMode: 'manual' | 'auto';
  playbackSpeed: number;       // 0.25x to 4x

  // Data
  trace: ForwardPassTrace | null;

  // Visualization
  activeView: 'pipeline' | 'attention' | 'math' | 'analytics';
  selectedLayer: number;
  selectedHead: number;
  hoveredToken: number | null;
  hoveredComponent: string | null;  // e.g., 'layer_3.attention.head_7'

  // Math Panel
  showMathSteps: boolean;
  currentMathStep: number;

  // Pipeline Challenge
  challengeActive: boolean;
  challengeReconstruction: Record<string, number[][]>;  // User's reconstructed activations
  challengeScore: number | null;
}

docs.title: 3.2 Progressive Data Loading
docs.text:
For large models (Backend C), data arrives progressively via WebSocket, and the visualization updates layer by layer as data streams in. This is the same WebSocket infrastructure you already use for experiment monitoring:

WebSocket Message Flow:
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Server → { type: "layer_start", layer_index: 0, data: LayerTrace }
Server → { type: "layer_complete", layer_index: 0 }
Server → { type: "layer_start", layer_index: 1, data: LayerTrace }
...
Server → { type: "forward_pass_complete", output: OutputTrace }

Each incoming layer is immediately merged into the Zustand store and rendered. The GSAP timeline automatically adjusts to accommodate new data as it arrives.

docs.title: 3.3 Undo/Redo for Exploration
docs.text:
Since the user can modify input text, change models, or toggle components, the state supports undo/redo via Zustand's temporal middleware:

import { temporal } from 'zundo';

const usePipelineStore = create<SliceState>()(
  temporal(
    (set, get) => ({ /* ... state and actions ... */ }),
    { limit: 50 }  // Keep last 50 states
  )
);

This enables "go back and try a different input" or "undo that head ablation" workflows.

docs.title: 4.2 Key Design Decisions
docs.text:
Why separate the canvas into stages rather than a single monolithic SVG? Each stage (Tokenization, Embedding, Layer 1...N, Output) is a separate React component that can be independently mounted, animated, and optimized. This follows the Transformer Explainer's modular approach: "The architecture consists of five primary subsystems that work together to provide an interactive educational experience". When a stage is not visible (scrolled past), it can be unmounted or simplified to save memory.

Why React Three Fiber for the 3D view instead of raw Three.js? R3F provides a declarative React API for Three.js, allowing the 3D pipeline to share state (via Zustand) with the rest of the React application. When the user hovers over a token in the 2D attention heatmap, the corresponding 3D sphere can highlight simultaneously — because both components read from the same hoveredToken state. This bidirectional linking is significantly harder with imperative Three.js code.

docs.title: 5.1 Zone 1: Global Context Bar
docs.text:
Purpose: Persistent header showing what model, text, and backend are active.

Implementation: - Renders at the top of the viewport, position: sticky - Uses your existing ModelPicker, AttentionPicker, and text input components - The backend indicator is a small badge: 🟢 "Running in browser (WebGPU)" or 🔵 "Connected to server (A100)" - Breadcrumbs are clickable: Pipeline Studio > BERT-base > Layer 3 > Attention Head 7

docs.title: 5.2 Zone 2: Main Pipeline Canvas (The Core)
docs.text:
Purpose: A single, unified interactive canvas showing the entire forward pass as a flowing diagram.

Implementation strategy — Three rendering layers:

docs.title: Layer 1: DOM-based layout (CSS Grid/Flexbox)
docs.text: The pipeline structure itself — the boxes representing each component, their labels, and the flow arrows between them — is rendered as standard DOM elements. Each stage is a div positioned using CSS Grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) for horizontal layout. This approach was chosen because: - DOM elements are inherently accessible (screen readers can parse them) - CSS transitions and transforms are GPU-accelerated - Text rendering in DOM is sharper than canvas text

docs.title: Layer 2: SVG overlay (D3.js)
docs.text:
The flowing connections between components — curved arrows showing data flow — are rendered as an SVG overlay positioned absolutely on top of the DOM layout. D3.js generates the path data:

// Sankey-style flow between pipeline stages
const linkGenerator = d3.sankeyLinkHorizontal();
// For each connection between two stages:
svg.selectAll('path')
  .data(connections)
  .join('path')
  .attr('d', linkGenerator)
  .attr('stroke-width', d => Math.max(1, d.value * 20))
  .attr('fill', 'none')
  .attr('stroke', d => colorScale(d.layerIndex))
  .attr('opacity', 0.7);

The Sankey approach follows Transformer Explainer's design: it "adopts the Sankey diagram visual design, inspired by recent work viewing Transformers as dynamical systems, emphasizing how input data flows through model components".

docs.title: Layer 3: WebGL overlay (React Three Fiber, optional)
docs.text:
When the user toggles the 3D view, a full-screen R3F canvas replaces the DOM/SVG view. This canvas uses:

  • @react-three/drei for camera controls (OrbitControls)
  • Custom GLSL shaders for particle effects (attention flow visualization)
  • Instanced rendering for hundreds of identical neuron nodes
  • Post-processing effects (bloom, glow) via @react-three/postprocessing

The 3D view maps each token to a sphere in 3D space (via t-SNE/UMAP of hidden states), with attention connections as curved tubes between spheres. The entire pipeline is "flyable" — users can navigate through layers as if flying through a tunnel.

Interaction Model:

  • Click any component (e.g., "Attention Head 3") → zooms into that component's detailed dashboard (Zone 5 updates)
  • Hover over any component → highlights its connections, shows tooltip with key values
  • Hover over a token → highlights all connections from/to that token across all layers
  • Scroll (with GSAP ScrollTrigger) → advances through the forward pass step by step. As the user scrolls, the animation progresses from Tokenization → Embedding → Layer 1 → Layer 2 → ... → Prediction. This creates a "story-telling" experience where the user physically moves through the model.

Implementation of scroll-driven animation:

// Using GSAP ScrollTrigger for the scroll-driven forward pass
useEffect(() => {
  const tl = gsap.timeline({
    scrollTrigger: {
      trigger: '.pipeline-canvas',
      start: 'top top',
      end: 'bottom bottom',
      scrub: 1,        // Smooth scrubbing, 1 second lag
      pin: true,       // Pin the canvas while scrolling
    }
  });

  // Each stage appears and animates as user scrolls
  tl.from('.tokenization-stage', { opacity: 0, y: 50 })
    .from('.embedding-stage', { opacity: 0, y: 50 })
    .from('.layer-0', { opacity: 0, scale: 0.8 })
    .from('.layer-1', { opacity: 0, scale: 0.8 })
    // ... and so on
    .from('.prediction-stage', { opacity: 0, y: -50 });

  return () => tl.kill();
}, [trace]);

GSAP with ScrollTrigger is chosen because it can "transform static scenes into fluid, story-like sequences" and "sync WebGL shaders with HTML layout". For scroll-driven animation, GSAP + ScrollTrigger is the industry standard — used by Apple, Google, and most award-winning interactive websites.

docs.title: 5.3 Zone 3: Live Math Panel
docs.text:
Purpose: Display the mathematical equations underlying each component in the pipeline, with animated step-by-step computation.

Implementation:

The Math Panel uses KaTeX for rendering LaTeX equations in real-time. KaTeX is chosen over MathJax because it renders synchronously (no flicker) and is about 5x faster for repeated updates.

The panel has three sub-sections:

docs.title: 5.3.1 Live Equation Display
docs.text:
As the user hovers over different pipeline components, the equation updates to show the relevant formula:

Hover over "Attention" node:
─────────────────────────────────────────
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √d_k) · V

Where:
  Q = X · W_Q    (query projection)
  K = X · W_K    (key projection)
  V = X · W_V    (value projection)
  d_k = 64       (head dimension)

When the user clicks the equation, it expands to show numerical values:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √64) · V

With current values:
  Q[3] · K[7] = 0.847  →  ÷ 8  →  0.106  →  softmax  →  0.023

docs.title: 5.3.2 Step-by-Step Computation Animation
docs.text:
When the user clicks "Show Steps," a GSAP timeline animates through each computation step:

  1. Matrix Multiplication: Two rectangles (representing Q and K^T) slide together, and the resulting matrix appears
  2. Scaling: A "÷ √d_k" label appears over each cell, values shrink proportionally
  3. Softmax: Each row "lights up" as values are exponentiated (red glow for high values), then the row normalizes (all values sum to 1)
  4. Weighted Sum: The attention weights are shown multiplying the V matrix, with weighted lines flowing to the output

This animation style is directly inspired by 3Blue1Brown's videos, which "built his own open source Python animation library, manim, to enable his YouTube work". While we use GSAP for browser performance rather than Manim (which renders video), the visual language is the same: "cinematic animation inspired by 3Blue1Brown, made with ManimCE".

docs.title: 5.3.3 Numerical Inspector
docs.text:
A floating panel that follows the cursor, showing precise numerical values for whatever the user hovers over:

┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ Token: "fox"                │
│ Position: 3                 │
│                             │
│ Q · K (token "quick"):      │
│   Raw dot product: 0.847    │
│   Scaled (÷ √64):  0.106    │
│   After softmax:    0.023   │
│                             │
│ Contribution to output:     │
│   Weight: 0.023             │
│   Value vector norm: 1.24   │
│   Weighted norm: 0.029      │
└─────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 5.4 Zone 4: Control Panel
docs.text:
Purpose: Layer navigation, playback controls, and quick actions.

Implementation: - Layer Navigator: A vertical list of all layers, each with a miniature preview of its attention pattern (rendered as a tiny SVG heatmap, 30×30px). Click a layer to zoom into it. The active layer is highlighted with a glow effect. - Playback Controls: A transport bar (like a video player) with play/pause, step forward, step backward, speed selector (0.25×, 0.5×, 1×, 2×, 4×), and a scrubber showing progress through the forward pass. - Component Filter: Toggle checkboxes: ☑ Attention, ☑ FFN, ☑ LayerNorm, ☑ Residual. Unchecking a component fades it out in the pipeline visualization and removes it from the math panel. - Quick Actions: Four buttons that connect to other platform apps — "⚡ Train with This" → experiment launcher, "📝 Create Note" → notes app, "📄 Generate Report" → paper app, "🔗 Copy Citation" → clipboard.

docs.title: 5.5 Zone 5: Analytics & Diagnostics
docs.text:
Purpose: Quantitative breakdown of latency, memory, and activation patterns.

Implementation: - Latency Breakdown Chart: A horizontal stacked bar chart (using Recharts, already in your stack) showing: Embedding time | Layer 1 (Attention + FFN) | Layer 2 | ... | Output. Each segment is clickable to zoom into sub-components. - Memory Breakdown: A treemap visualization (using D3.js treemap) showing memory allocation per component. Larger rectangles = more memory. Color intensity = memory utilization percentage. - Component Latency Comparison: When comparing two attention types (e.g., Standard MHA vs. Galerkin), a side-by-side bar chart shows the latency difference for each component. - Activation Distribution Plot: A violin plot or histogram showing the distribution of activation values in a selected layer, revealing saturation patterns (are neurons dying?) or unusual distributions.

docs.title: 5.6 Zone 7: Social & Pipeline Challenge
docs.text: Purpose: Community interaction and a gamified challenge mode.

docs.title: 5.6.1 Pipeline Challenge Mode
docs.text:
This is the core gamified feature. The challenge works as follows:

  1. The system shows the user the input text and the final output prediction of a model
  2. The intermediate activations (attention weights, hidden states) are hidden — the pipeline appears as a "mystery" with grayed-out components
  3. The user must reconstruct the intermediate activations by dragging attention weights, adjusting hidden state values, or selecting from multiple-choice options
  4. After submitting, the system reveals the actual activations and computes a reconstruction score based on cosine similarity, KL divergence, or exact match percentage
  5. Scores are posted to a community leaderboard (integrated with your existing leaderboards app)

Implementation of the reconstruction interface:

Each grayed-out component becomes an interactive "puzzle piece": - Attention weights: The user sees a 2D grid and can drag sliders on individual cells or use a "paint" tool to distribute attention across tokens - Hidden states: The user sees a bar chart of activation magnitudes and can adjust them - FFN activations: The user sees a simplified view of neuron activations (top-10 neurons by magnitude) and can toggle them on/off

The challenge system uses Polis-style consensus voting to aggregate community results: "Polis uses machine learning and statistical algorithms to analyze participants' voting behavior" and "visualizes the distribution of opinions" using PCA and k-means. Similarly, the Pipeline Challenge clusters users by their reconstruction strategies, revealing common patterns and misconceptions.

docs.title: 5.6.2 Integration with Comparison Mode
docs.text:
The pipeline studio supports side-by-side comparison of two different models, inputs, or attention mechanisms. This is implemented as a split-screen view:

┌───────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────┐
│   Model A: BERT-base  │ │   Model B: Galerkin   │
│                       │ │                       │
│   [Pipeline Canvas]   │ │   [Pipeline Canvas]   │
│                       │ │                       │
│   Latency: 12.3ms     │ │   Latency: 4.7ms      │
│   Memory: 438MB       │ │   Memory: 112MB       │
└───────────────────────┘ └───────────────────────┘

Both canvases are linked — hovering over a component in one highlights the corresponding component in the other. The math panel shows a diff view of the equations.

docs.title: 6.1 The Three Animation Systems
docs.text:
The pipeline studio uses three complementary animation systems, each for a specific purpose:

Animation System Technology Use Case CSS Transitions Tailwind CSS + framer-motion Layout changes, component fade-in/out, hover effects, responsive resizing GSAP Timeline GSAP + ScrollTrigger Scroll-driven forward pass progression, step-by-step math animations, complex coordinated sequences WebGL Shaders React Three Fiber + GLSL Particle flow effects, 3D token movement, real-time data visualization in 3D space

docs.title: 6.2 Coordinated Animation Flow
docs.text:
The three animation systems are coordinated through the Zustand store:

// The store acts as a "conductor" synchronizing all animation systems
const usePipelineStore = create((set, get) => ({
  currentStep: 0,

  advanceStep: () => {
    const next = get().currentStep + 1;
    set({ currentStep: next });

    // GSAP timeline advances
    gsapTimeline.seek(next / totalSteps);

    // CSS classes update reactively via React state
    // R3F frame updates via useFrame hook reading currentStep
  }
}));

docs.title: 6.3 Particle Flow Effect (GLSL Shader)
docs.text:
For the "flowing attention" effect, a custom GLSL fragment shader runs on the GPU:

// Fragment shader pseudocode for attention flow particles
// Runs thousands of particles in parallel on the GPU
// Each particle represents an "attention quantum" flowing from query to key

uniform float uTime;
uniform vec2 uQueryPositions[128];  // Positions of query tokens
uniform vec2 uKeyPositions[128];    // Positions of key tokens
uniform float uAttentionWeights[128][128];  // Attention matrix

void main() {
  // Each particle is assigned a (query, key) pair based on attention weight
  // It flows along a bezier curve from query position to key position
  // Opacity and speed are proportional to attention weight
  // Glow effect via gaussian blur in a post-processing pass
}

This approach leverages the GPU for massive parallelism — rendering 10,000+ particles at 60fps — which would be impossible with DOM or SVG alone. VisionFlow demonstrates this pattern: "implements real-time position streaming via SharedArrayBuffer with zero-copy reads" for GPU-based rendering.

docs.title: 6.4 Color Palette for Pipeline Stages
docs.text:
Each stage in the pipeline has a distinct color, creating a visual "rainbow" that helps users understand the flow:

Tokenization:     🔵 Blue (#3B82F6)
Embedding:        🟣 Purple (#8B5CF6)
Positional Enc:   🟢 Green (#10B981)
Attention:        🔴 Red (#EF4444)
FFN:              🟡 Yellow (#F59E0B)
LayerNorm:        ⚪ Gray (#6B7280)
Residual:         🟠 Orange (#F97316)
Output/Prediction:🟦 Cyan (#06B6D4)

docs.title: 7.1 Data Transfer Optimization
docs.text:
For large models, the activation trace can be tens of megabytes. Transferring this from worker to main thread must be optimized:

  1. Float32 → Float16 conversion: Attention weights don't need 32-bit precision for visualization. Quantize to Float16 (via Float16Array) before transfer, halving the data size.
  2. Sparse representation for attention: Most attention weights are near zero. Only transmit values above a threshold (e.g., > 0.01), with a sparse matrix format (CSR/CSC).
  3. Progressive loading: Transmit layer by layer rather than the entire trace at once. The visualization can start rendering Layer 0 while Layer 11 is still being computed.

docs.title: 7.2 Rendering Optimization
docs.text:
1. Virtualization: For models with many layers (e.g., GPT-2 Large with 36 layers), only render layers currently visible in the viewport. Layers above and below are placeholder divs with fixed height.
  2. Canvas layering: Use multiple canvas elements stacked via z-index rather than redrawing the entire canvas when only one element changes.
  3. Web Worker for D3 layout: D3's Sankey layout computation can be CPU-intensive. Offload it to a Web Worker.
  4. Memoization: All derived values (computed attention statistics, normalized scores) are memoized with useMemo to avoid recalculation on every render.

docs.title: 7.3 Memory Management
docs.text:
1. LRU Cache for model traces: Keep the last 5 forward pass traces in memory. When the user runs a 6th input, evict the oldest.
  2. IndexedDB persistence: Optionally persist traces to IndexedDB for offline access and historical comparison.

docs.text:
These endpoints need to be added to your Django backend:

POST   /api/pipeline/run-forward-pass/       ← Run a forward pass and return trace
GET    /api/pipeline/traces/                  ← List saved traces

docs.title: Phase 1: Core Pipeline Canvas (Weeks 1-3)
docs.text:
Goal: A working, scrollable pipeline visualization showing the full forward pass.

Tasks: 1. Set up the data flow: Web Worker + Comlink + Zustand store 2. Implement Backend A (Transformers.js + ONNX Runtime Web) for GPT-2/DistilBERT 3. Build the DOM-based pipeline layout with CSS Grid 4. Implement SVG overlay for data flow arrows (D3.js Sankey) 5. Add GSAP ScrollTrigger for scroll-driven forward pass animation 6. Build the Layer Navigator and Playback Controls

Deliverable: User can select a small model, type text, and watch the full forward pass animate step by step as they scroll.

docs.title: Phase 2: Math Panel + Analytics (Weeks 4-5)
docs.text:
Goal: Live equations, step-by-step math animations, and latency/memory analytics.

Tasks: 1. Integrate KaTeX for live equation rendering 2. Build the Step-by-Step Computation Animation (GSAP timeline) 3. Implement the Numerical Inspector floating panel 4. Build Latency Breakdown Chart (Recharts) 5. Build Memory Breakdown Treemap (D3.js) 6. Add Component Filter toggles

Deliverable: User can hover over any component to see its math, click to expand step-by-step computation, and view latency/memory analytics.

docs.title: Phase 3: 3D View + Advanced Visualization (Weeks 6-8)
docs.text:
Goal: Immersive 3D pipeline view and particle flow effects.

Tasks: 1. Set up React Three Fiber canvas with camera controls 2. Build the 3D token-to-token attention visualization (spheres + tubes) 3. Implement GLSL particle flow shader 4. Add layer "tunnel" navigation (fly through layers) 5. Synchronize 2D and 3D views (hover in 2D highlights in 3D)

Deliverable: User can toggle between 2D and 3D views, with smooth transitions and real-time synchronization.

docs.title: Phase 4: Pipeline Challenge + Social Features (Weeks 9-10)
docs.text:
Goal: Gamified reconstruction challenge and community sharing.

Tasks: 1. Build the Challenge Mode (hide activations, user reconstructs) 2. Implement reconstruction scoring (cosine similarity, KL divergence) 3. Integrate with leaderboards for challenge rankings 4. Add share/discuss buttons connected to community 5. Build the side-by-side comparison mode (split screen)

Deliverable: Users can participate in challenges, compare models side-by-side, and share their explorations.

docs.title: Phase 5: Backend B + C Integration (Weeks 11-12)
docs.text:
Goal: Support for medium and large models via Pyodide and Django API.

Tasks: 1. Set up Pyodide + PyTorch in browser for medium models 2. Build the Django API endpoint for large model inference 3. Implement WebSocket streaming for progressive layer-by-layer data loading 4. Auto-select backend based on model size and hardware capabilities 5. Add GPU marketplace integration (dispatch inference jobs to provider GPUs)

Deliverable: Full pipeline works for any model size, from GPT-2 in the browser to Llama-70B on server GPUs.

docs.title: Phase 6: Polish & Performance (Weeks 13-14)
docs.text:
Goal: Smooth 60fps performance, accessibility, and cross-browser compatibility.

Tasks: 1. Performance profiling and optimization (Chrome DevTools, React Profiler) 2. Implement Float16 quantization for data transfer 3. Add progressive loading for large traces 4. Accessibility audit (screen readers, keyboard navigation, color contrast) 5. Cross-browser testing (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) 6. Mobile responsive design (simplified view for small screens)

Deliverable: Production-ready pipeline studio with 60fps performance and full accessibility.

docs.title: Key References (From Research)
docs.text:
1. Transformer Explainer (Polo Club, Georgia Tech, 2024): "The frontend uses Svelte and D3 for interactive visualizations, while the backend uses ONNX runtime and HuggingFace's Transformers library to run the GPT-2 model in the browser" — directly validates the browser-based execution approach.

  2. AnimatedLLM (2025): "AnimatedLLM runs entirely in the browser, using pre-computed traces of open LLMs applied on manually curated inputs" — validates the pre-computed trace approach for smooth visualization.

  3. GPT2-WebGL (2025): Real-time visualization components that "update in real-time as the model generates text, providing an interactive window into the model's reasoning process" — validates WebGL for real-time activation visualization.

  4. React Three Fiber + WebGPU (2025): "R3F with native Three.js for GPU-accelerated rendering, supports both WebGPU and WebGL backends, and implements real-time position streaming via SharedArrayBuffer with zero-copy reads" — validates the R3F + WebGPU approach.

  5. Pyodide (2025): "Python 3.11+ in the browser via WebAssembly" for "interactive environments such as JupyterLite" — validates the Pyodide backend for Python-based model analysis.

  6. Transformers.js + ONNX (2025): "You can easily convert your pretrained PyTorch, TensorFlow, or JAX models to ONNX using Optimum" and run them "in the browser using onnxruntime-web" — validates the ONNX export pipeline.

  7. GSAP + ScrollTrigger (2025): Can "transform static scenes into fluid, story-like sequences" with "shader-based depth" and "scroll-controlled showcases with moving cameras and animated typography" — validates GSAP for scroll-driven animation.

  8. Polis (consensus tool): "Uses machine learning and statistical algorithms to analyze participants' voting behavior" and "visualizes the distribution of opinions using PCA and k-means" — validates the Pipeline Challenge consensus mechanism.

docs.title: 🧠 KV Cache Monitor — Complete Implementation Specification
docs.text: Based on my research across nano‑vllm (paged KV cache visualization), nano‑kvllm (KV cache compression integration), StreamingLLM, H2O, KVSink, KV‑Tracker, WebGPU, React Three Fiber v10, D3.js force graphs, and WebSocket real‑time monitoring architectures, here is the complete, implementation‑level specification for the KV Cache Monitor feature of the NeuralOps Attention Dashboard.

docs.title: 1. KV Cache Block Grid (3D PagedAttention Visualizer)
docs.text:
Primary Framework: React Three Fiber v10 with WebGPU backend Secondary Libraries: @react-three/drei (OrbitControls, Text, Billboard), three-stdlib (RoundedBoxGeometry), zustand (state management for block data)

Architecture: - The Block Grid renders each KV cache block as a 3D cube within a grid layout, following the nano‑vllm paged memory model where block_size (default: 256) defines the fundamental unit. The grid is organized as a 2D array of blocks, where rows represent different sequences and columns represent block indices within each sequence's block table. - Each cube uses GPU instancing via THREE.InstancedMesh to render thousands of blocks efficiently. Color encoding uses a custom GLSL shader that maps memory utilization to a color gradient: green (block fully utilized), yellow (partially filled), red (empty/evicted), and blue (attention sink block). - Hover interactions use R3F's onPointerOver/onPointerOut events with raycasting. When a user hovers over a block, a @react-three/drei Html overlay appears showing: block ID, sequence ID, token range stored, memory utilization percentage, and whether this block is shared across sequences (prefix caching). - The BlockManager's reference counting system from nano-vllm is visualized via block opacity: blocks with multiple references (prefix-shared blocks) appear more opaque with a glow effect via a custom post-processing pass using @react-three/postprocessing.

Implementation Details: - Use R3F v10's WebGPU renderer for GPU‑accelerated rendering when available, falling back to WebGL. R3F v10 now supports both WebGLRenderer and WebGPURenderer, with state.gl becoming state.renderer. - Block position calculation: position = (sequenceIndex * spacingX, -blockIndex * spacingY, layerIndex * spacingZ) where each sequence is a column, each block is a row within that column, and layers stack in depth. - Real‑time updates come via WebSocket binary protocol (MessagePack) to minimize overhead. Only changed blocks are updated using React Three Fiber's useFrame scheduler. - The grid uses @react-three/drei Grid component as a floor reference, and OrbitControls with damping for smooth camera movement.

docs.title: 2. Memory Timeline (Real‑Time Streaming Chart)
docs.text:
Primary Framework: D3.js v7 + Canvas rendering Secondary Libraries: d3-scale, d3-shape, d3-axis, d3-array, d3-brush

Architecture: - The Memory Timeline shows KV cache memory usage over time as a stacked area chart. The X‑axis represents time (scrolling window of the last 300 seconds), and the Y‑axis represents memory in GB. - Three stacked layers: Active KV Cache (tokens currently in use, green), Freed/Evicted (tokens removed by compression, red), Reserved/Allocated (blocks reserved but not yet filled, gray). - The chart uses Canvas rendering (not SVG) for performance with real‑time data streams. A requestAnimationFrame loop drives updates at 60fps, batching incoming WebSocket events. - A brush control (d3-brush) at the bottom allows users to select a time range, which synchronizes the Block Grid to show the state at that specific moment. - Vertical dashed lines mark compression events (when a strategy like H2O or StreamingLLM was applied), with clickable labels showing the strategy name and tokens evicted.

Implementation Details: - The chart is wrapped in a React component using useRef for the Canvas element and useEffect for D3 lifecycle. The WebSocket data is pushed into a ring buffer (circular array) of size 600 (10 seconds at 60fps). - Data structure: [{timestamp, activeMB, freedMB, reservedMB, event: 'compress'|'evict'|'alloc'|'free', strategy: string|null}] - The animation uses d3.transition with duration(0) for instant updates (no interpolation, since data is already time‑stamped). - Tooltip on hover uses D3's bisect to find the nearest data point and displays exact values.

docs.title: 3. Attention Sink Detection Panel
docs.text:
Primary Framework: SVG + Recharts (for statistical charts) Secondary Libraries: recharts (BarChart, ScatterChart), d3-scale-chromatic (color scales)

Architecture: - The Sink Detector identifies which tokens are "attention sinks" — tokens that absorb disproportionate attention mass across all heads and layers. Research shows that 1–4 tokens typically absorb 45‑55% of total attention. - The detection algorithm runs in the backend (Python), computing per‑token attention mass: sink_score[token_i] = Σ_{layers} Σ_{heads} attention_weight[:, token_i]. Tokens with scores exceeding 2× the mean are flagged as potential sinks. - The KVSink method (published at COLM 2025) is used for prediction: it identifies sink tokens with negligible overhead by examining cross‑layer activation outliers rather than computing full attention matrices. This approach "effectively predicts sink tokens with negligible overhead, enabling more thorough preservation" and "outperforms the existing Preserve-First-N (PFN) strategy." - The visualization shows three panels: (a) Attention Mass Bar Chart — per‑token attention mass with sink threshold line; (b) Cross‑Layer Evolution — a heatmap showing how sink scores change across layers; (c) Sink Token Timeline — during generation, which tokens become sinks and when.

Implementation Details: - The frontend receives sink scores as a flat array [score_0, score_1, ..., score_N] via WebSocket. The Recharts BarChart component renders this with a red reference line at 2 × mean(score). - The cross‑layer heatmap is an SVG matrix (like the attention heatmap but smaller: num_layers × num_tokens) colored by sink score magnitude. - Hovering on any token in the bar chart highlights that token's cross‑layer trajectory and shows the exact sink score.

docs.title: 4. Compression Strategy Selector & Live Comparison
docs.text:
Primary Framework: React with @headlessui/react (Listbox, Combobox) Secondary Libraries: zustand (for strategy state), react-query (for REST fallback)

Architecture: - A dropdown selector lets users choose from multiple KV cache compression strategies: Full Cache (no compression), Sliding Window (keep last W tokens), H2O (Heavy‑Hitter Oracle) (keep high‑attention tokens), StreamingLLM (keep attention sinks + recent window), SnapKV (keep tokens with highest attention to last query), TOVA (Token Omission Via Attention), K‑Norm (keep tokens with highest key norm), and your DeltaKV compressor. - Each strategy is implemented as a pluggable Python class in the backend (CompressMethod pattern from nano‑kvllm). The frontend sends the selected strategy via REST: POST /api/kv-cache/set-strategy/ { "strategy": "h2o", "budget": 0.3 }. - A live comparison mode shows the memory usage and attention patterns for two strategies side‑by‑side. The SplitPane layout (using react-split-pane) divides the dashboard into two synchronized views, each running a different strategy on the same input.

Implementation Details: - The strategy state is stored in zustand with a strategy field and budget field. Changing strategy triggers a REST call that re‑initializes the compression on the backend. - The backend's CompressMethod.py (following the nano‑kvllm architecture) contains a class hierarchy: BaseCompressMethod with abstract compress(kv_cache, budget) method, and concrete implementations: H2OCompress, StreamingLLMCompress, SnapKVCompress, DeltaKVCompress. - The nano‑kvllm approach of "keeping the original source layout unchanged" is adopted: compression hooks are injected at the Attention.forward() level, between store_kvcache() and flash_attn_with_kvcache().

docs.title: 5. Memory Formula & Computation Panel
docs.text:
Primary Framework: React + KaTeX (for LaTeX rendering) Secondary Libraries: katex (fast LaTeX), react-katex

Architecture: - The math panel renders the KV cache memory formula using KaTeX for instant rendering (faster than MathJax for small formulas). - The formula: Memory = 2 × L × H × N × d_head × bytes_per_element - Each variable is rendered as an interactive slider or input that the user can modify. Changing any variable instantly updates the computed memory value and the Block Grid visualization adjusts (showing hypothetical states). - Below the formula, a breakdown table shows memory contributions: "Attention KV Cache: X GB", "Model Weights: Y GB", "Activations: Z GB", "Total: X+Y+Z GB".

Implementation Details: - The KaTeX string is built dynamically from the current state. Example: M = 2 \\times ${L} \\times ${H} \\times ${N} \\times ${d_head} \\times ${bytes} - Sliders for integer parameters (L: 1‑96, H: 1‑64, N: 1‑32768, d_head: 32‑256) and a dropdown for bytes_per_element (2 for fp16, 1 for int8, 0.5 for int4). - The computed memory is displayed as a gauge (using Recharts RadialBarChart) showing how much of the available GPU memory is used.

docs.title: 6. Cross‑Platform Integration: DeltaKV, HybridKV, ZeroKV‑Neo
docs.text:
Primary Framework: Django REST API + WebSocket + Celery Secondary Libraries: Your existing compression infrastructure

Architecture: - The KV Cache Monitor directly connects to your existing compressors (delta_kv, hybridkv, zerokv_neo) registered in COMPRESSOR_REGISTRY. Each compressor provides a method compress_kv_cache(k_cache, v_cache, config) that the KV Cache Service Layer calls. - When a user selects a compression strategy and budget, the frontend sends: POST /api/kv-cache/apply-compression/ { "strategy": "delta_kv", "config": { "rank": 16, "sparsity": 0.29 } } - The backend returns compression statistics: { "original_size_mb": 2048, "compressed_size_mb": 594, "compression_ratio": 0.29, "tokens_evicted": 3276, "sink_tokens_preserved": 4 }. - The Memory Timeline shows a vertical marker at the compression event, with a tooltip showing these statistics. - The Block Grid updates to show which blocks were evicted (red) and which were preserved (green/blue).

Implementation Details: - The backend's KVSnapshotCollector runs in a separate thread that polls the GPU worker agent every 100ms via WebSocket. The collected data includes: block table state, memory allocation, compression events, and attention sink scores. - The Django asgi.py is configured to use channels with Redis channel layer for broadcasting KV cache updates to all connected clients via a group kv_cache_{run_id}.

docs.title: 7. WebSocket Communication Protocol
docs.text:
Primary Framework: Django Channels (backend) + native WebSocket (frontend) Secondary Libraries: msgpack (binary serialization), zlib (compression)

Architecture: - The WebSocket connection uses a binary protocol with MessagePack serialization for performance (30‑40% smaller payloads than JSON, faster encode/decode). Payloads larger than 4KB are compressed with zlib. - Message types: block_update (partial block state changes), memory_snapshot (full memory state), compression_event (strategy applied), sink_update (attention sink scores), error (backend error). - The frontend uses a custom useKVWebSocket hook that manages connection lifecycle, reconnection with exponential backoff (starting at 1s, max 30s), and heartbeat messages (every 15s). - For debugging, a "protocol inspector" panel shows the raw WebSocket messages with timestamps and sizes.

Implementation Details: - Frontend: useKVWebSocket(runId) returns { blocks, memory, sinks, events, isConnected, sendCommand }. The hook maintains an internal ring buffer for each data type and exposes them as React state. - Backend: KVConsumer(AsyncWebsocketConsumer) in Django Channels. On connect, it joins the kv_cache_{run_id} group. On receive, it handles set_strategy, get_snapshot, pause commands. The consumer pushes updates to the group, which fans out to all connected clients.

docs.title: 8. Performance Considerations & Optimization
docs.text:
Rendering Performance: - Use THREE.InstancedMesh for the Block Grid to render up to 10,000 blocks at 60fps. - Use Canvas rendering (not SVG) for the Memory Timeline for smooth real‑time updates. - Use react-window for virtualizing any lists (e.g., event log). - Use R3F v10's new scheduler with useFrame priority system to ensure GPU visualization updates don't block UI interactions.

Data Transfer Performance: - Use MessagePack binary protocol instead of JSON for WebSocket messages. - Use delta encoding: only send changed blocks, not the entire block table. - Compress large payloads with zlib (threshold: 4KB). - Use a ring buffer on the client to limit stored data points (max 600 for timeline).

Backend Performance: - The KVSnapshotCollector runs in a separate thread, not blocking the main inference loop. - Attention sink computation uses the KVSink method (negligible overhead, ~0.1% of total computation). - Block state tracking uses a copy‑on‑write approach to avoid locking during reads.

docs.title: 📊 Technology Stack Summary
docs.text: Component Primary Framework Secondary Libraries Rendering Block Grid (3D) React Three Fiber v10 @react-three/drei, three-stdlib, @react-three/postprocessing WebGPU/WebGL Memory Timeline D3.js v7 + Canvas d3-scale, d3-shape, d3-brush, d3-array Canvas 2D Sink Detector SVG + Recharts recharts (BarChart, ScatterChart) SVG Strategy Selector React + Headless UI zustand, react-query HTML/CSS Math Panel React + KaTeX katex, react-katex HTML/CSS WebSocket Layer Native WebSocket msgpack, zlib N/A Backend Service Django Channels + Celery numpy (sink computation), Redis N/A GPU Telemetry Python (provider agent) pynvml, NVIDIA DCGM N/A

docs.title: 🎯 Integration Points with Existing Platform
docs.text: Feature Connects To How Compression Strategy Selector delta_kv, hybridkv, zerokv_neo compressors Compressors registered in COMPRESSOR_REGISTRY are auto‑discovered and listed in the selector Memory Timeline gpu_marketplace provider listings The memory usage data comes from the provider agent running on the GPU machine Block Grid gpu_benchmark scores GPU benchmark scores (DLPerf) are displayed as metadata on the block grid tooltip Sink Detection experiment monitoring When a training run is active, sink scores are tracked per‑epoch and compared Math Panel notes / paper apps The formula and computed values can be exported as LaTeX to notes or papers WebSocket Existing Channels infrastructure Uses the same Redis channel layer as your existing real‑time features Strategy Comparison leaderboards Compression strategy effectiveness (memory vs. accuracy) can be submitted to leaderboards

docs.title: 🚀 Implementation Phases
docs.text:
Phase Features Duration Key Deliverable Phase 1 Memory Timeline + Math Panel + Strategy Selector Week 1‑2 Basic monitoring with REST‑based strategy switching Phase 2 Block Grid (3D) + WebSocket binary protocol Week 3‑4 Real‑time 3D visualization with live updates Phase 3 Sink Detector + Cross‑Platform Integration Week 5‑6 Attention sink visualization + DeltaKV/HybridKV/ZeroKV integration Phase 4 Live Comparison Mode + Performance Optimization Week 7‑8 Split‑pane strategy comparison + production optimization

This implementation specification provides complete detail for every component: which frameworks to use (React Three Fiber v10 with WebGPU for 3D, D3.js with Canvas for timeline, KaTeX for math, Django Channels for WebSocket), the data flow architecture (provider agent → Django → WebSocket → React), the performance optimization strategies (instanced rendering, MessagePack binary protocol, delta encoding), and the integration points with every part of your existing platform (compressors, leaderboards, experiments, notes, paper). Every component is backed by real‑world systems that have proven the approach works: nano‑vllm for paged block visualization, KVSink for attention sink prediction, nano‑kvllm for compression integration, and the WebGPU standard for GPU‑accelerated browser rendering.

docs.title: Complete Implementation Blueprint (No Code — Full Architecture & Technology Stack)
📐 PART 0: ARCHITECTURE PHILOSOPHY — The Four-Tier Computation Stack
docs.text:
The Stabilizer Lab requires a hybrid computation architecture because it must simultaneously: (a) run real ML model inference to extract hidden states before/after normalization, (b) perform heavy mathematical computations (mean, variance, RMS, gradient norms), (c) render GPU-accelerated 3D vector field visualizations, and (d) keep the UI responsive with 60fps interactivity. No single technology can handle all four demands alone, so we use a four-tier stack:

Tier Technology Responsibility Why This Choice Tier 1 — Browser ML Inference Transformers.js (Xenova) + ONNX Runtime Web with WebGPU backend Run actual GPT-2/BERT models in-browser to extract hidden states before/after LayerNorm. No server needed. Transformers.js "uses ONNX Runtime to run models in the browser" and "WebGPU + JavaScript: How Browsers Became Real AI Runtimes" proves this is production-ready. Firefox's native ONNX Runtime integration demonstrates "accelerating inference by replacing the default onnxruntime-web with its native C++ counterpart." Tier 2 — Scientific Computation Pyodide (Python-in-Wasm) with NumPy + SciPy Compute per-layer statistics (mean, variance, RMS, gradient norms), run PCA/t-SNE for vector field projections, compute cosine similarity between pre/post normalization vectors. Runs in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the UI. Pyodide "includes NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, and SciPy out-of-the-box" enabling "powerful data analysis, math, and visualization right inside the browser." The Web Worker with SharedArrayBuffer approach enables "zero-copy data transfer" between the ML thread and the computation thread. Tier 3 — GPU-Accelerated Visualization React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber + @react-three/drei) + Deck.gl + ECharts-GL Render 3D vector field (how LayerNorm maps vectors onto unit sphere), 3D bar charts for γ/β parameters, real-time line charts for norm statistics, heatmaps for gradient flow. Helios-Web demonstrates "real-time visualization and interactive analysis of massive-scale networks and high-dimensional embeddings" using "GPU-based rendering, modern web technologies (WebGL and WebAssembly)." ECharts-GL provides "3D visualization capabilities through WebGL" with "hardware acceleration for large-scale datasets." Deck.gl is "GPU-driven" and handles "millions of data points." Tier 4 — Reactive UI & Dashboard React 18 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS + Framer Motion + Zustand Dashboard layout, zone management, user interactions, state synchronization across zones, animation orchestration. Standard modern stack; Framer Motion for layout animations; Zustand for lightweight global state without Redux boilerplate.

docs.title: ZONE A: NORM STATISTICS DASHBOARD — "The Vital Signs Monitor"
docs.text: What it shows: Per-layer, a comprehensive dashboard of what happens to hidden states before and after LayerNorm. Think of it as the "vital signs monitor" for each transformer layer — you can instantly see if a layer is healthy (stable activations) or sick (vanishing/exploding activations).

docs.title: Sub-Feature A1: Pre/Post Mean & Variance Line Charts
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Data Source: Pyodide Web Worker computes np.mean(hidden_states, axis=-1) and np.var(hidden_states, axis=-1) for each layer, both before and after LayerNorm, across all tokens in the input sequence.
  • Visualization Library: ECharts-GL (not D3 or Plotly). Why? Because with 12+ layers × 768+ dimensions × potentially hundreds of tokens, we need GPU-accelerated rendering for smooth pan/zoom. ECharts-GL "extends the core ECharts library to enable the creation of 3D charts... while maintaining a similar API to standard ECharts." The renderer: 'webgl' option activates hardware acceleration.
  • Rendering Strategy: Two overlaid line series per chart: (1) Pre-LayerNorm values in orange/red (indicating "before stabilization"), (2) Post-LayerNorm values in blue/green (indicating "after stabilization"). The Y-axis shows the statistic value; the X-axis shows layer index.
  • Interactivity: Hover over any point to see the exact numerical value. Click a layer to "zoom into" that layer and see per-dimension breakdown in Zone B. A toggle switches between "Mean View" and "Variance View."
  • Performance: For 12 layers × 768 dimensions, ECharts-GL with WebGL backend renders 60fps even with animated transitions. The "Performance Optimization" page documents "techniques and best practices for optimizing the performance of 3D visualizations in ECharts-GL."

docs.title: Sub-Feature A2: Distribution Histogram (Per-Layer Pre/Post)
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Data Source: Pyodide computes histograms of hidden state values for each layer, before and after LayerNorm.
  • Visualization: Deck.gl HexagonLayer or standard ECharts histogram. Deck.gl is chosen because it's "GPU-driven" and can handle millions of data points — important when we're binning 768 dimensions × 128 tokens = ~98K values per layer.
  • Rendering: Two overlapping semi-transparent histograms: pre-norm in red, post-norm in blue. The post-norm distribution should be visibly more "compact" (around mean 0, variance 1). The before-norm distribution reveals if the layer has activation drift or exploding values.
  • Animation: When the user changes the selected layer, the histogram smoothly transitions between layers using Deck.gl's built-in transition system.

docs.title: Sub-Feature A3: Gradient Flow Through Normalization
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Data Source: This requires running a backward pass through the model. Transformers.js supports this? Actually, for a production system, we use the ONNX Runtime Web with WebGPU to compute gradients via a custom training loop. Alternatively, we pre-compute gradients server-side and stream them via WebSocket (using your existing Channels infrastructure).
  • Visualization: A heatmap (Deck.gl ScreenGridLayer or ECharts heatmap) showing gradient magnitude per layer × per training step (or per input token). The Visual Sandbox paper "gains insights into training dynamics, circuit transferability, and the causes of loss spikes, including those induced by the high curvature of normalization layers" — this is exactly what we want to visualize.
  • Color Scale: Green = healthy gradient flow, Yellow = warning (gradient getting small), Red = critical (vanishing gradient). The Pre-LN vs Post-LN comparison from the literature "clearly visualizes the instability and spikes inherent in Post-LN, validating the modern preference for Pre-LN stability."
  • Key Insight Display: A prominent banner shows: "Layer 7 gradient norm: 0.003 (⚠️ Vanishing)" or "Layer 3 gradient norm: 1.2 (✅ Healthy)" based on configurable thresholds.

docs.title: ZONE B: VECTOR FIELD VISUALIZATION — "The Sphere Mapper"
docs.text: What it shows: A 3D interactive view of how LayerNorm transforms vectors. Before LayerNorm, vectors are scattered throughout space. After LayerNorm, they're projected onto (or near) a unit sphere. This is the most visually striking and educationally powerful feature.

docs.title: Sub-Feature B1: The Unit Sphere + Pre/Post Vectors
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Visualization Library: React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber + @react-three/drei) — this is the gold standard for 3D in React. TensorSpace.js "translates neural network data into interactive 3D objects using THREE.js" and "enables the 3D representation of neural network components, handling both the visual elements and the interaction with neural network data."
  • Scene Composition:
  • Unit Sphere: A semi-transparent wireframe sphere (radius=1) rendered with <Sphere> from @react-three/drei. The sphere represents the "target" — after LayerNorm, all vectors should lie on or near this sphere.
  • Pre-Norm Vectors: Each token's hidden state (before LayerNorm) is rendered as an arrow pointing from the origin to its vector position. Color-coded by token index (using a viridis colormap). These arrows will be scattered at various distances from the origin.
  • Post-Norm Vectors: Each token's hidden state (after LayerNorm) is rendered as a dot on (or near) the sphere surface. The same color coding shows which pre-norm vector mapped to which post-norm position.
  • Connection Lines: Dashed lines connect each token's pre-norm position to its post-norm position, showing the "journey" through LayerNorm.
  • Camera Controls: <OrbitControls> from @react-three/drei allows rotation, zoom, and pan. The initial camera position shows the sphere from a slight angle so the 3D nature is immediately apparent.
  • Animation: When the user changes the layer or input text, the vectors animate from their old positions to new positions using react-spring/three or Framer Motion 3D. This is crucial — without animation, users can't track which vector moved where.
  • Performance: For 128 tokens × 768 dimensions, we use PCA (computed in Pyodide) to reduce to 3 dimensions before rendering. The 3D scene handles 128 arrows + 128 dots + 128 lines = ~384 objects, which React Three Fiber renders effortlessly at 60fps.

docs.title: Sub-Feature B2: LayerNorm "Magnifying Glass" — Single Vector Detail
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • When the user clicks on a single vector (either pre-norm arrow or post-norm dot), a "magnifying glass" panel appears showing:
  • The raw 768-dimensional vector as a mini bar chart (too many bars to be readable, but gives a sense of distribution)
  • The mean and variance of that specific token
  • The cosine similarity between pre-norm and post-norm vectors (computed in Pyodide)
  • The LayerNorm formula applied to this specific vector, showing: x - μ = [...], σ = [...], (x - μ)/σ = [...], γ ⊙ (x-μ)/σ + β = [...]
  • This is the "3Blue1Brown moment" — the user sees the math applied to concrete numbers, making the abstract formula tangible.
  • Implementation Approach: The formula rendering uses KaTeX (fastest LaTeX renderer for web) with live-substituted numerical values. The Transformer Explainer similarly "visualizes different operations within the transformer block: Layer Normalization — visualized as a curved line and a circle with tooltips."

docs.title: ZONE C: γ/β PARAMETER VISUALIZATION — "The Scaling/Shifting Dashboard"
docs.text: What it shows: LayerNorm has two learnable parameter vectors: γ (scale) and β (shift), each of dimension d_model. This zone shows which dimensions the model has learned to amplify vs. suppress, revealing the model's "feature importance" per layer.

docs.title: Sub-Feature C1: 3D Bar Chart of γ and β
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Visualization Library: ECharts-GL Bar3D chart type. ECharts-GL "provides 3D visualization capabilities through WebGL" including "3D bar charts." The 3D nature is important because 768 dimensions cannot be shown in a 2D bar chart without scrolling.
  • Rendering: The X-axis represents dimension index (0 to 767), the Z-axis represents the parameter value, and the Y-axis can represent different layers (or vice versa). Bars for γ are colored warm (red/orange) for values > 1 (amplifying), cool (blue) for values < 1 (suppressing). Bars for β are colored green for positive shifts, purple for negative shifts.
  • Interactivity: The user can rotate the 3D view, zoom into specific dimension ranges, and hover over any bar to see exact values. A "Top 10" panel lists the most amplified and most suppressed dimensions.
  • Alternative View: A 2D heatmap (using Deck.gl or ECharts) where rows = layers, columns = dimension ranges (binned into groups of 32), and color = average γ or β value.

docs.title: Sub-Feature C2: γ/β Distribution Histogram
docs.text:
• A simple histogram showing the distribution of γ values and β values across all dimensions. Are they clustered around 1 and 0 (the initialization values)? Has the model learned to deviate significantly?
  • Library: ECharts with renderer: 'webgl' for smooth rendering.

docs.title: ZONE D: MATH PANEL — "The Formula Lab"
docs.text: What it shows: Interactive, step-by-step visualization of the LayerNorm and RMSNorm formulas, with live numerical values from the currently selected token/vector.

docs.title: Sub-Feature D1: LayerNorm Step-by-Step Animator
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Math Rendering: KaTeX (via react-katex) for LaTeX formula rendering. KaTeX is "the fastest math typesetting library for the web."
  • Animation Engine: Framer Motion for step-by-step reveal animations. The formula is displayed as a sequence of steps:
  • x = [0.847, -0.312, 1.203, ...] — show the raw vector
  • μ = 0.042 — compute and display the mean
  • σ² = 0.891 — compute and display the variance
  • (x - μ) / √(σ² + ε) = [...] — show the normalized vector
  • γ ⊙ norm + β = [...] — show the final output
  • Each step reveals with a Framer Motion animation (fade + slide). The numerical values update in real-time as the user changes the selected token (by clicking on a vector in the 3D view) or the selected layer.
  • Color coding: Raw values in gray, computed statistics in yellow, normalized values in green, final output in blue.

docs.title: Sub-Feature D2: RMSNorm Comparison Mode
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Side-by-side display of LayerNorm and RMSNorm formulas. The key difference (RMSNorm skips mean subtraction) is highlighted in red.
  • Numerical comparison table: For the same input vector, show:
  • LayerNorm output vs. RMSNorm output
  • Cosine similarity between the two outputs
  • Computational cost comparison (RMSNorm "少了求均值和减均值两个操作，在大模型里能明显提速")
  • Performance note: A small badge shows: "RMSNorm: 2 fewer operations per dimension → ~15% faster in large models."

docs.title: Sub-Feature D3: Interactive Parameter Tweaking
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Two sliders (using your existing Slider component) allow the user to manually adjust γ and β values for any dimension.
  • As the user drags the slider, the 3D vector field (Zone B) updates in real-time, showing how the vector moves.
  • This is the "what if" experimentation mode — researchers can test hypotheses like "What if γ was 2.0 for dimension 42?"

docs.title: ZONE E: INTERPRETABILITY & DIAGNOSTICS — "The Doctor's Toolkit"
Sub-Feature E1: Norm Ablation — What Happens If We Remove LayerNorm?
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Data Source: This requires running the model twice — once normally, once with LayerNorm bypassed (identity function). Pyodide can't do this efficiently; we use the Django backend to run the ablation and stream results via WebSocket (your existing Channels infrastructure).
  • Visualization: A side-by-side comparison:
  • Left: Attention patterns WITH LayerNorm
  • Right: Attention patterns WITHOUT LayerNorm
  • Bottom: A "difference heatmap" showing where attention changed most
  • Metrics display: "Without LayerNorm at Layer 5: attention entropy increased by 23%, output probability of correct token dropped from 0.87 to 0.12."

docs.title: Sub-Feature E2: Pre-LN vs. Post-LN Architecture Comparison
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Diagram Rendering: Use D3.js (not a charting library — raw D3 for custom SVG) to draw two architecture diagrams side-by-side:
  • Post-LN (original Transformer): x → Attention → Add → LayerNorm → FFN → Add → LayerNorm
  • Pre-LN (modern): x → LayerNorm → Attention → Add → LayerNorm → FFN → Add
  • Gradient Flow Comparison: Below each diagram, show a line chart of gradient norms per layer during training. Post-LN typically shows a U-shaped curve (large gradients at first and last layers, small in middle), while Pre-LN shows a flatter, more uniform distribution. The literature "clearly visualizes the instability and spikes inherent in Post-LN, validating the modern preference for Pre-LN stability."
  • Animation: The user can scrub through "training steps" to see how gradient flow evolves over time.

docs.title: Sub-Feature E3: RMSNorm vs. LayerNorm Side-by-Side Analyzer
docs.text:
Implementation:

  • Data Source: The Django backend runs the same model twice — once with LayerNorm, once with RMSNorm substituted — and streams the hidden states for comparison.
  • Visualization: Three panels:
  • Statistics comparison table: Per layer, show mean, variance, and RMS for both normalization methods.
  • Output cosine similarity: Per layer, how similar are the outputs of LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm? (Should be very high for most layers.)
  • Performance comparison: Bar chart showing FLOPs per layer for each method.
  • Key Insight: RMSNorm "保持非零均值分布，不执行均值对零的对齐操作" — the visualization should make this geometric difference visible.

docs.title: 2.1 Transformers.js (Browser ML Inference)
docs.text:
npm install @xenova/transformers

Key Configuration: - Use pipeline('feature-extraction', model_name) to get hidden states. - For attention-specific work, use the lower-level API to extract per-layer hidden states before/after LayerNorm. - Enable quantized: true for faster loading (the model runs in-browser, so quantization is essential). - The library "uses ONNX Runtime to run models in the browser" and supports WebGPU backend for hardware acceleration.

docs.title: 2.2 Pyodide (Scientific Computing in Browser)
docs.text:
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/v0.25.0/full/pyodide.js"></script>

Key Configuration: - Load in a Web Worker (not the main thread) to avoid blocking the UI. - Pre-load packages: await pyodide.loadPackage(['numpy', 'scipy']). - Use SharedArrayBuffer for zero-copy data transfer between the ML worker and the compute worker. - Pyodide "includes NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, and SciPy out-of-the-box" enabling "powerful data analysis, math, and visualization right inside the browser."

docs.title: 2.3 React Three Fiber (3D Visualization)
docs.text:
npm install @react-three/fiber @react-three/drei three

Key Configuration: - Use <Canvas> with gl={{ antialias: true, alpha: true }} for high-quality rendering. - Use <OrbitControls> for camera interaction. - Use react-spring/three for smooth animation transitions. - Reference implementation: TensorSpace.js "translates neural network data into interactive 3D objects using THREE.js."

docs.title: 2.4 Deck.gl (GPU-Accelerated 2D/3D Charts)
docs.text:
npm install deck.gl @deck.gl/react @deck.gl/layers

Key Configuration: - Use DeckGL component with WebGLRenderer. - Primary layers: ScatterplotLayer (vector field points), LineLayer (connections), HeatmapLayer (gradient flow). - Deck.gl is "GPU-driven" and handles "millions of data points."

docs.title: 2.5 ECharts-GL (3D Bar Charts, Line Charts)
docs.text:
npm install echarts echarts-gl

Key Configuration: - Register ECharts-GL: import 'echarts-gl'. - Set renderer: 'webgl' in chart options for GPU acceleration. - Primary chart types: bar3D, line3D, scatter3D, surface. - ECharts-GL "extends the core ECharts library to enable the creation of 3D charts, globe visualizations, and other WebGL-accelerated graphics."

docs.title: 2.6 KaTeX (Formula Rendering)
docs.text:
npm install katex react-katex

Key Configuration: - Use \\displaystyle for full-size formulas. - Use \\color{...} for color-coded formula elements. - Wrap in React.memo since formulas don't change often.

docs.title: 3.1 Initial Load Sequence
docs.text:
1. User enters text + selects model
2. Transformers.js loads model in Web Worker #1 (may take 5-15 seconds for first load)
3. Model runs forward pass → hidden states extracted at each layer (before/after LN)
4. Hidden states transferred to Web Worker #2 via SharedArrayBuffer
5. Pyodide computes statistics (mean, var, RMS, PCA)
6. Computed data posted back to main thread
7. All 5 zones render simultaneously with smooth entrance animations

docs.title: 3.2 Real-Time Update Sequence (User Changes Input)
docs.text:
1. User changes text or layer selection
2. If text changed: Steps 3-6 from above repeat
3. If only layer changed: Only Zone B (3D view) and Zone C (γ/β) need updates
4. Zone A (statistics) updates the highlighted layer marker
5. All transitions animated with Framer Motion (200ms duration)

docs.title: 3.3 WebSocket Stream (For Training Dynamics / Gradient Flow)
docs.text:
1. Django backend runs training loop
2. At each logging step, backend sends WebSocket message:
   { layer: 5, pre_mean: 0.04, post_mean: 0.00, gradient_norm: 0.023, ... }
3. Frontend Zustand store updates
4. Zone A (statistics line charts) appends new data point
5. Zone D (math panel) shows live-updating gradient values

docs.title: 4.1 What Runs Where
docs.text: Computation Location Justification Model inference (forward pass) Web Worker #1 (Transformers.js + ONNX Runtime Web) Avoids blocking main thread; uses WebGPU for GPU acceleration Statistical computation (NumPy) Web Worker #2 (Pyodide) Heavy computation offloaded; SharedArrayBuffer enables zero-copy data transfer 3D rendering (Three.js) Main thread (WebGL) Must be on main thread for DOM access; GPU-accelerated 2D charts (ECharts-GL, Deck.gl) Main thread (WebGL) GPU-accelerated; lightweight compared to 3D React UI updates Main thread Standard React rendering; Zustand for efficient state updates

docs.title: 4.2 Memory Budget
docs.text:
• Model weights (GPT-2 small): ~500MB in browser memory (quantized to 8-bit)
  • Hidden states cache (12 layers × 2 states × 768 dims × 128 tokens × 4 bytes): ~9.4MB
  • 3D scene geometry (vectors, sphere, lines): ~2MB GPU memory
  • Total browser memory: <600MB — feasible for modern browsers

docs.title: 4.3 Fallback Strategy
docs.text:
• If WebGPU is unavailable → fallback to WebAssembly (ONNX Runtime Web WASM backend)
  • If Pyodide fails to load → fallback to pure JavaScript computation (using math.js or manual implementation)
  • If WebGL is unavailable → degrade 3D view to 2D projection using ECharts with Canvas renderer
