docs.title: Feature: Low‑Rank Matrix Heatmap Rendering
docs.text:
Primary Technology Stack: React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS + WebGL 2.0 (via Three.js / React Three Fiber)

Implementation Details:

The LoRA weight matrices A (d×r) and B (r×d) are typically tall/skinny or short/wide. For a 768×16 matrix, the heatmap requires 768 × 16 = 12,288 cells. Modern GPUs can render far larger grids. The research on "demystifying attention in transformers: visualising LoRA" shows that "LoRA adapters are typically inserted into Q and/or V matrices inside attention heads" and the matrices are highly structured.

Rendering Strategy — WebGL 2.0 Shader‑Based Approach:

Use a custom THREE.ShaderMaterial with GLSL fragment shaders. Each matrix cell is rendered as a single GPU fragment. The color mapping from weight value → RGB is computed entirely on the GPU via a fragment shader, achieving 60fps for matrices up to 4096×4096 on consumer hardware. The color scale should use a perceptually‑uniform colormap (Viridis or Plasma) stored as a 1D texture lookup in the shader for efficiency.

For very large matrices (>10,000 cells), use THREE.InstancedMesh with BufferGeometry, which renders thousands of identical meshes in a single draw call by storing per‑instance transformation matrices and color attributes in GPU buffers. Research shows this technique increased heatmap frame rates from 15fps to 60fps by reducing CPU‑to‑GPU data transfer.

Alternative: WebGPU Compute Shader Approach

For matrices exceeding 10,000×10,000 cells, WebGPU provides superior performance. WebGPU officially became available in all major browsers starting from Chrome 113. The architecture involves: writing a WGSL compute shader for matrix multiplication, creating three GPU buffers (input A, input B, result C), dispatching an 8×8 workgroup (64 GPU threads working in parallel), and rendering the result as a texture mapped to a full‑screen quad. The WebGPU backend enables high‑performance machine learning operations through compute shaders and efficient GPU memory management.

Interactivity Layer:

  • Hover: raycasting with THREE.Raycaster against instanced mesh IDs. On hover, display a tooltip with cell coordinates and weight value using a React state update throttled with requestAnimationFrame.
  • Click: select a cell to see both A and B matrices with the corresponding row/column highlighted. Selection state managed via a Zustand store.
  • Zoom/Pan: Implement via OrbitControls from @react-three/drei, clamped to prevent flying through the matrix plane. For 2D heatmaps, use a custom 2D camera controller.

Language Bindings: The shader programs are written in GLSL (WebGL) or WGSL (WebGPU). The React layer communicates with the GPU via Three.js JavaScript bindings. TypeScript provides type safety for all JavaScript‑to‑GPU data transfers.

docs.title: Feature: Token‑by‑Token LoRA Contribution Visualization
docs.text:
Primary Technology Stack: React + D3.js (SVG) + Pyodide (Python in browser via WebAssembly)

Implementation Details:

The contribution map shows, for each token position, how much the LoRA adapter contributed to the output compared to the base model. This is calculated as Δ = W_base(x) − (W_base(x) + B·A(x)). The result is a token‑by‑token difference matrix.

Data Pipeline (Browser‑Side Computation):

Run the HuggingFace transformers and peft libraries directly in the browser using Pyodide. Pyodide is a Python distribution compiled to WebAssembly that runs in the browser. Load the model weights via Pyodide's micropip.install("transformers peft torch"), then compute the forward pass for both the base model and the LoRA‑adapted model on the input text. Compute the difference matrix and pass it to the React visualization layer as a JSON object via a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread.

Visualization Layer:

Render as an SVG using D3.js. Each cell is an SVG <rect> element with a color fill. For token sequences up to 512 tokens (512×512 matrix), SVG handles the load efficiently. For larger sequences, switch to Canvas 2D rendering with D3's Canvas renderer.

Color Encoding:

Use a diverging color scale (cool‑warm or RdBu) centered at zero: blue for negative contributions, white for zero, red for positive contributions. The scale is computed by D3's scaleDiverging with a domain of [−max_abs, 0, +max_abs].

Token‑Conditional Adaptation (TopLoRA‑Style):

The research on "Token-wise Projected Low-Rank Adaptation (TopLoRA)" introduces the concept of "dynamically adjusting LoRA weights according to the input token." The contribution map should distinguish between standard LoRA (all tokens share the same weight update) and token‑conditional LoRA (different tokens receive different weight updates). If the model uses TopLoRA, an additional diagonal matrix D(X) is generated per token, and the contribution map shows D(X) · B · A per token position.

docs.title: 📐 ZONE 3 (Math Panel): LoRA Formula & Rank Explorer
Feature: Live LaTeX Rendering + Interactive Formula Manipulation
docs.text:
Primary Technology Stack: KaTeX (LaTeX rendering) + Manim‑Web (TypeScript port of Manim) + React State

Implementation Details:

Static Formula Rendering:

Use KaTeX for fast, server‑side renderable LaTeX. The core LoRA formula is: W' = W + α · B · A. Render this as a KaTeX expression that updates dynamically as parameters change.

Animated Step‑by‑Step Decomposition (Manim‑Web):

For the educational animation showing "Full Matrix → SVD → Low‑Rank Approximation → LoRA Adapters," use Manim‑Web. Manim‑Web is a TypeScript port of 3Blue1Brown's Manim that runs entirely client‑side in the browser at 60fps using Canvas API / WebGL via Three.js. The port requires: installing manim-web as an npm dependency, disabling SSR for components touching WebGL (using Next.js dynamic imports or "use client" directives), defining scene construct functions that create mobjects, and sequencing animations with async/await. The API mirrors the Python version: scene.play(new Transform(matrix, lowRankMatrix)).

The animation sequence for LoRA decomposition:

  1. Show the full weight matrix W as a colored grid of mobjects (each cell is a colored square).
  2. Apply SVD animation: the matrix "splits" into three mobject groups representing U, Σ, V^T.
  3. The singular values in Σ animate their heights to show the "strength" of each component.
  4. Truncate to rank r: the smaller singular values shrink to zero and disappear.
  5. The remaining components recombine into two matrices: B = U_r · √Σ_r and A = √Σ_r · V^T_r.
  6. Show the final ΔW = B · A as the product animation.

Interactive Controls Binding:

Bind React state (rank slider, α slider) to Manim‑Web scene parameters using ValueTracker objects. When the user changes the rank via a React slider, the Manim‑Web scene rebuilds the mobjects with the new rank and animates the transition. The useFrame hook from React Three Fiber ensures animations remain synchronized with React state.

Numerical Value Inspector:

Below the formula, display a live table showing the actual numerical values for the currently hovered matrix cell. This is computed in JavaScript using simple matrix operations (no GPU needed for the inspector). For large matrices, use TypedArrays for efficient computation and Web Workers to avoid blocking the main thread.

docs.title: Feature: Rank Slider, Alpha Slider, Target Module Selector
docs.text:
Primary Technology Stack: React (controlled components) + Zustand (state management) + Tailwind CSS

Implementation Details:

Rank Slider: A range input (<input type="range">) with values from 1 to 64 (or 128). Display the current rank prominently. Below the slider, show the parameter count impact in real time: params = r × (d_in + d_out). For a 768×768 weight matrix, show: "Rank 8 → 12,288 params (2.1% of original)" vs "Rank 64 → 98,304 params (16.7% of original)."

Alpha Scaling Slider: A range input for α values from 0.1 to 2.0. Show the formula W' = W + α · B · A with the current α highlighted. When α = 0, the adapter contributes nothing; when α = 1, the adapter contributes at full strength; when α = 2, the adapter contribution is doubled.

Target Module Selector: A multi‑select dropdown populated by reading the model's configuration via the HuggingFace API (or local Pyodide). Options: Q only, K only, V only, Q+K, Q+V, Q+K+V, All Attention, All Attention + FFN, Custom. Each selection updates the visualization to show the corresponding matrices.

LoRA Type Selector: A dropdown for standard LoRA, QLoRA (quantized, requires bitsandbytes), DoRA (weight‑decomposed), AdaLoRA (adaptive rank allocation), and TopLoRA (token‑wise). Each type loads its specific configuration and updates the formula panel accordingly.

Framework Integration: The "Apply & Train" button serializes the current LoRA configuration to a JSON object that matches the PEFT LoraConfig format (target_modules, r, lora_alpha, lora_dropout, bias, task_type). This JSON is sent to your experiment launcher's pre‑fill API, which opens the launcher with all parameters set. The launcher then calls the backend training endpoint via the existing experiment pipeline.

docs.title: Feature: Adapter Similarity Matrix & Singular Value Distribution
docs.text:
Primary Technology Stack: D3.js (visualization) + ml‑matrix (JavaScript matrix library) + Pyodide (SVD computation)

Implementation Details:

Adapter Similarity Matrix:

Load multiple LoRA adapters (e.g., trained on different tasks). For each pair of adapters, compute the cosine similarity between their weight matrices (flattened). This requires matrix operations that can be performed via JavaScript TypedArrays for efficiency. Render as a D3 heatmap with a diverging color scale. Click any cell to load both adapters side‑by‑side in the canvas view.

Singular Value Distribution Chart:

Compute SVD of each adapter weight matrix using Pyodide + NumPy in the browser. For each matrix, plot the singular values as a bar chart (D3) or line chart (Recharts). The x‑axis is the singular value index (1 through r), and the y‑axis is the singular value magnitude. Show the "energy retention" curve: cumulative sum of squared singular values divided by total. Mark the rank r with a vertical line. This visualization answers: "How much information is captured at this rank?"

K‑Means Clustering of Singular Values:

Research shows that "K‑Means algorithm can perform cluster analysis on the singular values of weights in the projection matrices of each layer." Apply this by running k‑means (via a JavaScript implementation like ml-kmeans) on the singular values extracted from multiple adapters. Visualize the clusters as colored groups in the SVD distribution chart, revealing structural patterns across adapters.

docs.title: Feature: SVD‑Init vs Zero‑Init Adapter Quality Comparison
docs.text:
Primary Technology Stack: Pyodide + NumPy + D3.js

Implementation Details:

The research on "Fine‑tuning LLMs with Singular Value Decomposition" and "SVD initialization and periodic re‑SVD" provides the theoretical basis. The implementation computes two versions of the same LoRA adapter:

  1. Standard Initialization: Kaiming‑uniform for A, zeros for B (the PEFT default).
  2. SVD Initialization: Compute SVD of the base weight matrix W, extract the top‑r singular vectors, initialize B = U_r · √Σ_r, A = √Σ_r · V^T_r.

Compare both versions by computing the Frobenius norm difference from the full fine‑tuning update (if available) or from the base weight. Render as a side‑by‑side bar chart showing reconstruction error. The SVD‑initialized adapter typically shows lower reconstruction error, especially at low ranks.

Periodic Re‑SVD Simulation:

Research on "LoRA with SVD initialization and periodic re‑SVD" shows that periodically recomputing SVD during training improves performance. Simulate this by showing an animation: the singular value distribution shifts from initialization (top‑heavy) to mid‑training (more distributed) to post‑training (stabilized). This is computed via Pyodide running NumPy in the browser.

docs.title: Feature: Adapter Configuration Sharing & Community Comparison
docs.text:
Primary Technology Stack: REST API (existing Django backend) + React Query + URL state serialization

Implementation Details:

Shareable URLs: Every LoRA configuration (model, target modules, rank, alpha, sample text) is serialized as URL query parameters. When shared, the recipient's dashboard loads the exact same visualization state. This is implemented via useSearchParams from React Router, with the configuration JSON base64‑encoded for compactness.

Community Adapter Gallery: Published adapter configurations are stored in the Django database via a LoRAConfiguration model (similar to the DashboardWidget model pattern already in the codebase). The gallery lists configurations by: number of stars, adaptation quality (community‑voted), and task similarity to the user's stated research interests (from their profile). The gallery is a React component that queries the backend via React Query with pagination.

One‑Click Fine‑Tune: "Apply this LoRA config to the model" sends a POST request to the experiment launcher endpoint with the pre‑filled configuration. The launcher validates the configuration against available GPU resources (via the gpu_marketplace availability API) and launches a Celery task for the fine‑tuning job. Progress is streamed back via the existing WebSocket infrastructure (ws/experiments/{job_id}/).

docs.title: Feature: LoRA Expertise Recognition
docs.text:
Primary Technology Stack: Existing gpu_reputation badge system (Django) + React component

Implementation Details:

LoRA‑Specific Badges: Extend the existing ReputationBadge model with LoRA‑specific conditions:

  • 🥉 "Adapter Apprentice" — viewed 10 different LoRA configurations
  • 🥈 "Rank Optimizer" — found the optimal rank for a given task (verified by benchmark improvement)
  • 🥇 "LoRA Architect" — published 5 adapter configurations used by other researchers
  • 💎 "SVD Master" — demonstrated that SVD‑initialized LoRA outperforms standard LoRA on 3+ benchmarks

Badges are awarded via Celery tasks that check conditions after each user action. The badge display component reads from the existing UserReputationBadge model.

Adapter Leaderboard: A leaderboard ranking users by: number of published adapter configurations, total stars received, total forks of their configurations, and challenge wins. This extends the existing leaderboard infrastructure with a new leaderboard_type = 'lora'.

docs.title: 🔗 Cross‑Platform Integration Summary
docs.text: Integration Point Technology Data Flow Model Loading Pyodide (WASM) + HuggingFace API Load model config in browser or via backend Weight Extraction PEFT library (Pyodide) Extract LoRA weights as numpy arrays → JSON SVD Computation NumPy (Pyodide) Compute SVD in browser, send results to React Experiment Launch Django REST API Serialize LoRA config → experiment launcher Real‑Time Training WebSocket (Channels) Stream adapter weight evolution during training Badge Award Celery Task Check conditions → create UserReputationBadge Configuration Sharing Django ORM Save/load LoRAConfiguration via REST API Community Gallery React Query Paginated query of published configurations Adapter Similarity JavaScript TypedArrays Compute cosine similarity client‑side Math Animation Manim‑Web (TypeScript) Client‑side WebGL animation at 60fps Heatmap Rendering Three.js ShaderMaterial GPU‑accelerated cell rendering via WebGL 2.0 Large Matrix (>10K) WebGPU Compute Shader WGSL shader for parallel matrix ops

docs.title: 🎯 Implementation Priority
docs.text:
Phase Features Duration Phase 1 Canvas heatmap (Three.js), Math panel (KaTeX), Controls (React) 1 week Phase 2 Contribution map (D3.js + Pyodide), SVD spectrum (D3.js + NumPy) 1 week Phase 3 Manim‑Web animations, adapter similarity, experiment launcher integration 2 weeks Phase 4 Community gallery, sharing, badges, leaderboard 1 week

The entire LoRA Adapter Studio can be implemented in approximately 5 weeks with a team of 2–3 developers, leveraging the existing infrastructure (Django backend, WebSocket, Celery, badge system, leaderboard system) already built.

docs.title: 🧠 Complete Mapping: Apply the Attention-Style Interactive Dashboard to ALL Transformer Components
docs.text: Here is a comprehensive mapping of every component in a Transformer model — each transformed into an interactive, 8‑zone "app" (Canvas + Math Panel + Controls + Analytics + Interpretability Tools + Social Layer + Gamification + Cross‑Platform Integration), with named inspiration from real‑world tools and the specific visualization types that work best for each.

docs.title: 1. EMBEDDING EXPLORER — "Token Space Navigator"
docs.text:
Inspiration: GPT-2 Token Similarity Visualizer, exBERT, InterpreT (ACL 2020), Prompt Rover

Zone Feature Canvas 3D Embedding Space Explorer — All token embeddings projected via t‑SNE/UMAP/PCA (user‑selectable). Tokens rendered as floating spheres; semantically similar tokens cluster together. User types any word to "teleport" to its embedding location. Token trajectory view: watch how the same token's embedding changes as context changes. GPT‑2 Token Similarity Visualizer and Prompt Rover both provide this layer‑by‑layer token relationship mapping. Canvas 2 Embedding Matrix Heatmap — The full vocab_size × d_model embedding matrix rendered as an interactive heatmap with zoom/pan. Color = weight value. Search for any token to highlight its row. Compare embedding rows side‑by‑side. The 3Blue1Brown videos show embedding matrix visualization using color coding where positive values appear in blue and negative in red. Math Panel Embedding formula: E[token] = W_e[token_id, :] + W_p[pos, :]. Shows the numeric values for the selected token's embedding vector. Cosine similarity calculator: select any two tokens → see their similarity score and a bar chart of dimension‑by‑dimension contribution. Analytics Embedding Statistics Dashboard: Vocabulary coverage histogram, embedding norm distribution, nearest‑neighbor graph, dimension importance via PCA explained variance. Semantic axis discovery: find the direction in embedding space that represents "gender," "tense," or "sentiment." Interpretability Linear probe playground: train a linear classifier on embeddings to predict POS tags, sentiment, etc. — see decision boundaries overlaid on the t‑SNE plot. Token activation comparison: which tokens share similar embeddings after fine‑tuning vs. before? Social "Embedding of the Day" — community votes on the most interesting embedding relationship discovered. Share embedding visualizations as interactive 3D scenes. Collections: "Interesting Embedding Clusters," "Multilingual Embedding Comparisons." Gamification "Embedding Detective": Given a mystery embedding vector, guess which token it represents. Streak tracking. XP for discovering semantic axes.

docs.title: 2. POSITIONAL ENCODING STUDIO — "RoPE & Absolute Encoding Lab"
docs.text:
Inspiration: RoPE Visualizer (kapilsharma.dev, 2026), Transformer Explainer, Sinusoid Embedding Visualizations

Zone Feature Canvas Sinusoidal Encoding Heatmap — Full max_len × d_model matrix rendered as heatmap. Each row = position, each column = dimension. Hover reveals exact sin/cos value. See the characteristic wavelength patterns. RoPE 3D Rotation Visualizer: for RoPE, show how Q and K vectors rotate through angles based on position. Animated 3D arrows rotating around their axes — the RoPE Visualizer (kapilsharma.dev) already does exactly this for YaRN‑extended RoPE. Canvas 2 Position Similarity Matrix — Cosine similarity between all position pairs, rendered as heatmap. Reveals how RoPE encodes relative position (high similarity for nearby positions, decaying for distant ones). Math Panel Full RoPE formula: RoPE(x, pos) = x · R(pos) where R(pos) is the rotation matrix. Shows the rotation angles per dimension pair. For sinusoidal: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/d)). Interactive: change the 10000 base temperature and see how the encoding pattern changes. Analytics Position sensitivity analysis: how much does the model rely on position vs. semantics? Measure by ablating position encoding and comparing outputs. Frequency analysis: which dimension pairs encode which frequencies? Interpretability Position ablation: toggle position encoding off for specific layers → see effect on predictions. Compare sinusoidal vs. learned absolute vs. RoPE vs. ALiBi side‑by‑side. Controls Slider for max sequence length, temperature/base frequency. Select encoding type: Sinusoidal, Learned Absolute, RoPE, ALiBi, NoPE. Social "Position Encoding Challenge": design a novel positional encoding scheme and submit it for community evaluation. Leaderboard ranks schemes by downstream task performance.

docs.title: 3. FFN / MLP EXPLORER — "Neuron Activation Universe"
docs.text:
Inspiration: OpenAI Transformer Debugger (TDB), DeepDecipher, LM Transparency Tool, NeuroX

Zone Feature Canvas Neuron Activation Heatmap — For every token in the input, show the activation of every FFN neuron across layers. Rendered as a tokens × neurons heatmap per layer. The Transformer Debugger (TDB) by OpenAI's Superalignment team provides exactly this: "MLP neuron activations are recorded for each token." NeuroX and DeepDecipher similarly visualize MLP neuron activations in large language models. Canvas 2 Top‑Activating Examples Explorer — For each neuron, show the top‑10 text snippets that maximally activate it. Rendered as a scrollable gallery. Users can add their own text and see which neurons fire. The TDB "contains some top-activating examples for each MLP neuron." Canvas 3 Neuron "Planet" 3D Map — All FFN neurons projected via t‑SNE/UMAP of their activation patterns. Neurons with similar functions cluster together. Each neuron is a glowing sphere; hover reveals its "specialty" (e.g., "baseball‑related neuron," "negation detector"). Math Panel FFN formula: FFN(x) = W_2 · GELU(W_1 · x + b_1) + b_2. Shows the intermediate activation vector for the selected token. SVD of W₁: show the top singular vectors as "feature directions" — each direction corresponds to a concept the neuron detects. Analytics Neuron importance ranking: which neurons have the highest average activation? Which are most selective (low entropy)? Dead neuron detector: identify neurons that never activate. Neuron co‑activation graph: which neurons fire together? Interpretability Neuron ablation: toggle individual neurons off → see prediction change. SAE (Sparse Autoencoder) feature view: decompose neuron activations into monosemantic features. Neuron labeling: community‑assigned labels (like "this neuron detects French text"). Social "Neuron of the Week" — community votes on the most fascinating neuron discovered. Neuron labeling game: earn XP by correctly labeling what a neuron detects. Collections: "French Detectors," "Punctuation Neurons," "Toxic Content Neurons." Gamification "Neuron Hunter": given a description ("find the neuron that detects questions"), search through neurons. First to find and label it earns points.

docs.title: 4. RESIDUAL STREAM TRACER — "The Information Highway"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Logit Prisms (LessWrong 2024), Logit Lens, Semantic Pathway (IEEE VIS 2025), InTraVisTo

Zone Feature Canvas Residual Stream Flow Diagram — A Sankey diagram showing how information accumulates in the residual stream across layers. Each layer contributes an "update" vector (attention output + FFN output). The Logit Prisms approach "decomposes transformer outputs for mechanistic interpretability" by analyzing "the residual streams, attention layers, and MLP layers within transformer models." The InTraVisTo tool similarly provides "a heatmap of decoded embedding vectors for all layer/token positions" and "information flow between components using a Sankey diagram." Canvas 2 Logit Lens Projection Timeline — At each layer, project the residual stream to vocabulary space → show the model's implicit prediction. Animated scrubber: watch predictions evolve from Layer 0 (random) to final output. The Logit Lens "directly reads out the model's implicit prediction at each layer" — widely adopted for mechanistic interpretability. Canvas 3 2D Training Dynamics Sandbox — For models with d_model=2, render the entire residual stream as animated 2D vectors. Watch attention outputs "push" token representations; watch FFN outputs "pull" them toward specific directions. The Visual Sandbox paper (Stanford 2024) uses exactly this approach: "the embedding dimension constrained to d=2 allows for comprehensive two-dimensional visualization of each layer's dynamics." Math Panel Residual update formula: x_l = x_{l-1} + Attn(LN(x_{l-1})) + FFN(LN(x_{l-1})). Shows the vector arithmetic: the original vector + attention contribution + FFN contribution = new vector. All rendered as 3D arrows. Analytics Residual stream norm analysis: how does the norm of hidden states grow/shrink across layers? Update magnitude: which layers make the largest contributions? Direction consistency: do attention and FFN updates align or conflict? Interpretability Logit Prisms decomposition: break the residual stream into contributions from each component (each attention head, each FFN neuron). Activation patching: replace a hidden state at layer L with a "clean" version → see how predictions change. Social "Residual Stream Race" — which team can best predict the output by looking only at the residual stream at layer N? Gamified challenge.

docs.title: 5. LAYER NORMALIZATION DYNAMICS — "The Stabilizer Lab"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Transformer Explainer, Visual Sandbox (Stanford 2024), NeuroViz

Zone Feature Canvas Norm Statistics Dashboard — Per‑layer, show the mean and variance of hidden states before and after LayerNorm. Rendered as line charts. Vector field visualization: show how LayerNorm maps vectors from the "before" space to the "after" space on a unit sphere. The Transformer Explainer "visualizes different operations within the transformer block: Layer Normalization — visualized as a curved line and a circle with tooltips." Canvas 2 Scaling/Shifting Parameter Heatmap — The γ (scale) and β (shift) parameters rendered as bar charts per dimension. Which dimensions are amplified? Which are suppressed? Math Panel RMSNorm formula: RMSNorm(x) = x / RMS(x) · γ. Shows step‑by‑step: compute RMS, divide, multiply by γ. LayerNorm formula: LN(x) = (x - μ) / σ · γ + β. Interactive: change γ or β values and see the effect. Analytics Gradient flow through norms: the Visual Sandbox paper "gains insights into training dynamics, circuit transferability, and the causes of loss spikes, including those induced by the high curvature of normalization layers." Show how normalization affects gradient magnitude per layer. Interpretability Norm ablation: what happens if you remove LayerNorm from specific layers? Compare Pre‑LN vs. Post‑LN architectures. RMSNorm vs. LayerNorm comparison: side‑by‑side.

docs.title: 6. OUTPUT LOGITS PREDICTOR — "The Decision Engine"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Transformer Explainer (Probability/Softmax viz), Tuned Lens, Logit Lens

Zone Feature Canvas Token Probability Distribution — For the final layer, show a horizontal bar chart of top‑k token probabilities. Click any token to see which earlier layers contributed most to that prediction (via the Tuned Lens). The Transformer Explainer "visualizes the final step in the transformer's prediction process, showing how logits are converted to token probabilities through temperature scaling, sampling methods (top‑k or top‑p), and the softmax function." Canvas 2 Logit Spectrum — For any position in the input, show the full logit vector (before softmax) as a spectrum/heatmap. Hover to see the token. Compare logit distributions between different models or between pre‑ and post‑compression. Math Panel Softmax formula: P(token_i) = exp(z_i / T) / Σ exp(z_j / T). Interactive temperature slider: T→0 (argmax), T=1 (default), T→∞ (uniform). Shows how temperature affects the distribution in real time. Controls Sampling method selector: Greedy, Temperature, Top‑k, Top‑p (Nucleus), Beam Search. Repetition penalty slider. Shows real‑time effect on output distribution. Analytics Prediction entropy over time: for autoregressive generation, track entropy per step. Calibration analysis: is the model's confidence aligned with actual accuracy? Interpretability Tuned Lens: "skips over the last few layers and lets you see the best prediction that can be made from the model's representations, i.e. the residual stream." Show how early predictions compare to final predictions.

docs.title: 7. WEIGHT MATRIX DECOMPOSER — "SVD, CUR, Kronecker Studio"
docs.text:
Inspiration: SVDInterpretTransformer, Singular Value Decompositions of Transformer Weight Matrices Are Highly Interpretable, your compression library

Zone Feature Canvas Singular Value Spectrum — For any weight matrix (Q, K, V, O, FFN), plot the singular values σ₁, σ₂, … as a bar chart. Color‑code by cumulative energy. Hover shows the singular value and its contribution %. Research shows "the SVD decomposition of transformer weight matrices is highly interpretable" and "the primary directions used by the network can be inferred from the SVD." Canvas 2 SVD Direction Interpreter — Each top singular vector is visualized as a word cloud of the tokens that most align with that direction. Users can browse the "semantic axes" of each weight matrix. Canvas 3 Compression Preview — Interactive rank slider: "What if we keep only the top k singular values?" The reconstructed weight matrix updates in real time. Shows parameter reduction %, estimated speed‑up, and output MSE. Directly connected to your 60+ compressors (A3, ERC‑SVD, AdaSVD, CUR, Kronecker, TT, etc.). Math Panel SVD formula: W = U Σ V^T. Shows the truncated reconstruction W_k = U_k Σ_k V_k^T. Interactive: change k → see the approximation error. Analytics Per‑layer rank profile: which layers have the steepest singular value decay (most compressible)? Compression quality score: predicted accuracy vs. compression ratio. Controls Compressor selector dropdown (all 60+ methods). Rank/ratio slider. Energy threshold slider. Cross‑Platform One‑Click Compress: "Apply this compression to the model" → directly calls your compression pipeline. After compression, the dashboard shows before/after weight matrix comparison.

docs.title: 8. KV CACHE MONITOR — "Memory Efficiency Dashboard"
docs.text:
Inspiration: nano‑vllm KV Cache Visualizer (2026), KV‑Tracker, Qwen3‑0.6B KV Cache Tool

Zone Feature Canvas KV Cache Block Grid — Visualize the KV cache as a grid of blocks (like nano‑vllm's visualization). Each block = one cache entry. Color = memory utilization (green = full, yellow = partial, red = evicted). Hover reveals the tokens stored in that block. The nano‑vllm project explicitly requests this: "Visualizing KV Cache blocks provides a clearer understanding of the internal workings and architecture." Canvas 2 Memory Timeline — During autoregressive generation, show a real‑time chart of KV cache memory usage. Shows when evictions happen, which tokens are evicted, and how compression strategies affect memory. The KV‑Tracker system demonstrates strategies for "tracking, managing, and compressing key–value caches in Transformer architectures." Canvas 3 Attention Sink Detection — Highlight which tokens become "attention sinks" (absorbing disproportionate attention). Show how these tokens persist in the KV cache. Math Panel KV Cache formula: Cache_t = Cache_{t-1} ∪ {(k_t, v_t)}. Memory = 2 × layers × heads × tokens × d_head × bytes. Interactive: change cache compression strategy → see memory savings. Controls Cache compression strategy selector: Full, Sliding Window, H2O (Heavy‑Hitter Oracle), StreamingLLM, your DeltaKV compressor. Eviction threshold slider. Cross‑Platform Directly connected to your DeltaKV, HybridKV, ZeroKV‑Neo compressors. Apply a cache compression strategy and immediately see the memory/accuracy trade‑off.

docs.title: 9. LoRA ADAPTER STUDIO — "Fine‑Tuning Visual Lab"
docs.text:
Inspiration: LoRA Visualization Notebook, LLaMA‑LoRA‑Tuner, LoRA‑Adapted Denoiser

Zone Feature Canvas LoRA Weight Visualization — For any LoRA‑adapted layer, show the low‑rank matrices A (d×r) and B (r×d). Rendered as heatmaps. Color = weight value. Show the product B·A compared to the original weight update. Research demonstrates "demystifying attention in transformers: visualising LoRA" where "the base weights are frozen and tiny trainable adapters are injected." Canvas 2 Adapter Contribution Map — For each token in the input, show how much the LoRA adapter contributed vs. the base model. Rendered as a token‑by‑token difference heatmap. Math Panel LoRA formula: W' = W + α·B·A. Shows the rank‑r decomposition. Interactive: change rank → see parameter count change. Change α → see the scaling effect. Controls LoRA rank slider (1–64). α scaling slider. Target module selector: Q only, V only, Q+V, All Attention, Attention+FFN. Analytics Adapter similarity: compare LoRA adapters trained on different tasks. Which adapters are most similar (indicating task transfer potential)? Cross‑Platform One‑Click Fine‑Tune: "Apply this LoRA config to the model" → opens your experiment launcher pre‑filled with LoRA parameters.

docs.title: 10. CIRCUIT TRACER — "QK & OV Circuit Explorer"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Anthropic Circuit Tracer (2025), Transformer Circuits Framework, DecisionTransformerInterpretability

Zone Feature Canvas Circuit Graph Visualization — An interactive node‑edge graph where nodes are model features (tokens, neurons, attention heads) and edges represent QK circuit connections (query→key attention) and OV circuit connections (output→value transformations). Edge thickness = weight magnitude. Anthropic's Circuit Tracer "enables users to explore, annotate, and share attribution graphs seamlessly" with "edge weights that show how much source feature's decoder communicates to target feature's encoder." Canvas 2 QK Circuit Explorer — For each attention head, visualize the QK circuit: what input features does this head "query" for, and what features does it "key" to? Rendered as a bipartite graph. The QK circuit "determines how tokens route information between each other" and is "our first circuit" in the Transformer Circuits framework. Canvas 3 OV Circuit Explorer — For each attention head, visualize the OV circuit: what information does this head "write" to the residual stream, and which downstream features read it? The OV circuit "determines what information attention heads write into the residual stream." Math Panel QK formula: Score(q, k) = (W_Q · x_i)^T · (W_K · x_j) / √d. OV formula: Output = Σ_j A_ij · (W_V · x_j) · W_O. Shows the full computation graph with numerical values. Analytics Circuit importance scoring: which circuits are most critical for specific tasks? Circuit overlap: do different circuits share components? Interpretability Induction head detector: automatically identifies induction heads based on circuit patterns. Copying head detector: identifies heads that copy information from previous tokens.

docs.title: 11. TRAINING DYNAMICS SANDBOX — "Watch the Model Learn"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Visual Sandbox (Stanford 2024), NeuroViz, LossPlot, gradviz

Zone Feature Canvas Training Dynamics 2D Sandbox — For models constrained to d_model=2, render the entire training process as an animation: watch each layer's weight matrices evolve over training steps. The Visual Sandbox paper (Stanford 2024) "introduces a visual sandbox designed to explore the training dynamics of a small-scale transformer model with embedding dimension constrained to d=2" for "comprehensive two-dimensional visualization of each layer's dynamics." Canvas 2 Loss Landscape Explorer — Render the loss landscape in 2D (using PCA directions). Show the optimization trajectory as a path on the landscape. LossPlot "allows comparison of multiple model's loss landscapes and even comparison between different loss projections." Canvas 3 Gradient Flow Animation — During training, show gradient norms per layer as animated bar charts. Animated gradient packets flow backward through the network. The gradviz tool "saves and visualizes gradient norms across layers or parameters." RNNbow similarly "displays the relative gradient contributions in a neighborhood of an element." Math Panel Backpropagation chain rule: ∂L/∂W = ∂L/∂y · ∂y/∂W. Step‑by‑step gradient computation for the selected weight. Shows gradient magnitude, direction, and the weight update. Analytics Gradient norm ratio: which layers have vanishing/exploding gradients? Update‑to‑weight ratio: are certain layers learning faster? Loss curve overlay: compare loss curves across multiple training runs. Controls Training step slider (rewind/fast‑forward through training). Learning rate, optimizer, batch size selectors.

docs.title: 12. LOSS LANDSCAPE EXPLORER — "The Optimization Terrain"
docs.text:
Inspiration: LossPlot, Visual Sandbox (Stanford 2024), NeuroViz

Zone Feature Canvas 3D Loss Landscape Surface — Interactive 3D surface plot rendered with Plotly/Three.js. X‑axis = direction 1 (random direction), Y‑axis = direction 2 (orthogonal), Z‑axis = loss. User can rotate, zoom, and pan. Click any point to "teleport" the model to those weights. Canvas 2 Loss Contour Map — Top‑down view of the loss landscape with contour lines. The optimization trajectory overlaid as a path with numbered checkpoints. Compare trajectories across different optimizers (Adam vs. SGD vs. AdamW). Canvas 3 Hessian Eigenvalue Spectrum — For the current model weights, compute and visualize the top eigenvalues of the Hessian. Sharp directions = high curvature = large eigenvalues. Flat directions = low curvature = small eigenvalues. Math Panel Loss formula for the current task (cross‑entropy, MSE, etc.). Hessian definition: H = ∂²L/∂W². Shows the eigenvalue decomposition. Analytics Sharpness metric: how sharp is the minimum? (Sharp minima generalize worse.) Basin width: how far can you perturb weights before loss increases by 10%? Interpretability Mode connectivity: find the low‑loss path between two different trained models. Visualize this path on the loss landscape.

docs.title: 13. COMPRESSION STUDIO — "Interactive Model Surgery"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Your 60+ compression library, BHPVAS, LLaMA‑LoRA‑Tuner

Zone Feature Canvas Model Architecture Map — A tree view of the entire model. Click any component (attention head, FFN neuron, embedding dimension) → see its parameters, importance score, and compression options. Before/After comparison: side‑by‑side view of original vs. compressed model. Canvas 2 Compression Impact Heatmap — For the selected compression strategy, show a heatmap of which parts of the model are most affected. Color = relative change in output. Math Panel Shows the compression formula for the selected method (SVD truncation, 2:4 sparsity, quantization, etc.). Shows parameter count before/after and estimated FLOPs. Controls Compressor selector (all 60+ methods), rank/ratio slider, sparsity slider, bit‑width selector. Budget constraint input: "Keep model under 200MB." Cross‑Platform One‑Click Apply: "Compress this model now" → calls your compression pipeline. Before/After Leaderboard: submit compressed models to your benchmark leaderboard and compare.

docs.title: 14. FULL PIPELINE STUDIO — "From Input to Output, Step by Step"
docs.text:
Inspiration: Transformer Explainer, AnimatedLLM, 3Blue1Brown videos, LLM‑transformer‑visualization

Zone Feature Canvas Full Pipeline Animated Flow — A single interactive canvas showing the entire forward pass: Tokenization → Embedding → Positional Encoding → Layer 1 (Attention + FFN) → Layer 2 → … → Layer N → Output Projection → Softmax → Prediction. Each component is clickable, expanding into its own detailed dashboard. The Transformer Explainer and the LLM‑transformer‑visualization (2025) both provide this comprehensive view. AnimatedLLM (2025) "provides step‑by‑step visualizations of a Transformer language model." Math Panel The complete forward pass equation: P(token) = softmax(W_out · TransformerEncoder(TokenEmbed(x) + PosEmbed(x))). Click any term to zoom into that component's detailed dashboard. Controls Input text field. Model selector. Decoding strategy selector. "Step Forward" button (process one layer at a time). "Auto‑Play" button (animate the full forward pass). Analytics Latency breakdown: how much time does each component take? Memory breakdown: how much memory does each component use? Social "Pipeline Challenge": given a specific output, reconstruct the intermediate activations that led to it. Community voting on the most accurate reconstruction.

docs.title: 15. VR IMMERSION ROOM — "Step Inside the Transformer"
docs.text:
Inspiration: HeedVision (WebXR CAAV), Helios‑Web (GPU real‑time), Planet Neuron concept

Zone Feature Canvas 360° Immersion Room (WebXR) — The user stands inside a virtual sphere. Tokens are floating in space around them. The residual stream is the "air" flowing between tokens. Attention connections are laser beams. Layer transitions are visualized as "floors" the user can ascend/descend through. HeedVision demonstrates "collaborative attention‑aware visualizations" using WebXR for immersive exploration. Canvas 2 GPU Real‑Time Mode — Using Helios‑Web's approach, render massive‑scale networks (millions of parameters) using GPU‑based rendering directly in the browser. Interaction Reach out and "grab" a token to see its embedding vector. "Pull" an attention connection to see its weight. "Walk" through layers. Collaboration Multiple users in the same VR room, each represented as an avatar, exploring together. Voice chat integrated. Session recording for later playback.

docs.title: 📊 Summary: All Transformer Components Mapped
docs.text:
# Component Dashboard Name Primary Visualization Key Inspiration 1 Embedding Token Space Navigator 3D t‑SNE/UMAP scatter + matrix heatmap GPT‑2 Token Similarity, exBERT, InterpreT 2 Positional Encoding RoPE & Absolute Encoding Lab Sinusoidal heatmap + 3D rotation viz RoPE Visualizer (2026), Transformer Explainer 3 Attention Attention Dashboard Heatmap + Sankey + 3D + QK Joint BertViz, AttentionViz, Transformer Explainer (already designed) 4 FFN / MLP Neuron Activation Universe Activation heatmap + top‑examples gallery OpenAI TDB, DeepDecipher, NeuroX 5 Residual Stream The Information Highway Sankey flow + Logit Lens timeline Logit Prisms, Semantic Pathway, InTraVisTo 6 Layer Normalization The Stabilizer Lab Norm stats charts + vector field Transformer Explainer, Visual Sandbox 7 Output Logits The Decision Engine Token probability bars + logit spectrum Transformer Explainer, Tuned Lens 8 Weight Matrices SVD/CUR/Kronecker Studio Singular value spectrum + compression preview SVDInterpretTransformer, your compression lib 9 KV Cache Memory Efficiency Dashboard Block grid + memory timeline nano‑vllm KV Viz, KV‑Tracker, Qwen3 tool 10 LoRA Adapters Fine‑Tuning Visual Lab Low‑rank heatmaps + contribution map LoRA Visualization, LLaMA‑LoRA‑Tuner 11 QK/OV Circuits Circuit Tracer Node‑edge graph + bipartite QK/OV views Anthropic Circuit Tracer, Transformer Circuits 12 Training Dynamics Watch the Model Learn 2D sandbox + loss landscape + gradient flow Visual Sandbox (Stanford 2024), NeuroViz, gradviz 13 Loss Landscape The Optimization Terrain 3D surface + contour map + Hessian spectrum LossPlot, Visual Sandbox 14 Compression Interactive Model Surgery Architecture tree + impact heatmap Your compression library, BHPVAS 15 Full Pipeline Input→Output Step Studio Animated flow diagram Transformer Explainer, AnimatedLLM 16 VR Immersion Step Inside the Transformer WebXR 360° room HeedVision, Helios‑Web

Each of these 16 dashboards follows the identical 8‑zone architecture (Canvas + Math + Controls + Analytics + Interpretability + Social + Gamification + Cross‑Platform Integration) and connects to your existing Django backend, WebSocket infrastructure, compression library, experiment launcher, leaderboards, community Q&A, and paper/notes system. Every component is individually explorable but also accessible from the Full Pipeline Studio, which provides a unified "bird's‑eye" view of the entire Transformer.

docs.title: 🧠 Output Logits Predictor — Complete Implementation Guide
docs.text: "The Decision Engine" — Showing exactly how the model chooses its next token, from raw logits through temperature, sampling, and softmax to the final probability distribution.

docs.title: 📐 1. Architecture Overview
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              OUTPUT LOGITS PREDICTOR — DATA FLOW                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                      │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐       │
│  │  RAW     │    │ TEMP     │    │ SAMPLING │    │ FINAL    │       │
│  │  LOGITS  │───▶│ SCALING  │───▶│ (top‑k/  │───▶│ PROB     │       │
│  │  (LN)    │    │ (÷T)     │    │  top‑p)  │    │ DIST     │       │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘       │
│       │               │               │               │              │
│       ▼               ▼               ▼               ▼              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │              LOGIT SPECTRUM VISUALIZATION                 │       │
│  │    (full vocabulary heatmap / top‑k bar chart)           │       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
│       │                                                              │
│       ▼                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │         TUNED LENS / LOGIT LENS CROSS‑LAYER VIEW          │       │
│  │    (what each layer "thinks" the next token should be)   │       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
│       │                                                              │
│       ▼                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │         CALIBRATION & ENTROPY ANALYTICS                   │       │
│  │    (reliability diagram · prediction entropy timeline)   │       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
│                                                                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The architecture follows the Transformer Explainer's proven design: "the probability visualization component displays the probability distribution over the vocabulary tokens predicted by the GPT‑2 model. It shows not only the final probabilities but also the intermediate steps involved in calculating these probabilities, making the prediction process transparent to users."

docs.title: 2.1.1 Component Tree
docs.text:
TokenProbabilityPanel (container)
├── ProbabilityBarChart (main visualization — Plotly.js Bar chart)
│   ├── TopKTokenBar (individual horizontal bar, D3‑animated)
│   ├── SelectedTokenIndicator (golden glow on sampled token)
│   └── CutoffLine (vertical dashed line for top‑k boundary)
├── CollapsedView (compact: shows only the probability bars)
│   └── ExpandButton (triggers GSAP Flip animation)
└── ExpandedView (detailed: shows raw logits → scaled logits → probabilities)
    ├── RawLogitColumn (numeric display, monospace)
    ├── ScaledLogitColumn (after temperature division)
    ├── SamplingEffectColumn (shows which tokens were filtered)
    └── FinalProbColumn (normalized softmax output)

docs.title: 2.1.2 Framework Selection
docs.text: Layer Technology Rationale Rendering engine Plotly.js via react-plotly.js Handles bar charts with built‑in hover, zoom, and export. The Transformer Explainer uses a similar approach with ProbabilityBars as a sub‑component for rendering probability bars. Animation GSAP (GreenSock) with Flip plugin For smooth collapsed ↔ expanded transitions. The original Transformer Explainer uses exactly this: "The expansion and collapse are animated using GSAP and Flip for smooth transitions." Bar chart interactivity D3.js scales + React rendering D3 handles the mathematical computation (scales, data binding); React owns the DOM. This hybrid approach is documented as the preferred pattern for React‑D3 integration. Top‑k cutoff visualization Custom SVG overlay using react‑svg For drawing the cutoff line and highlighting which tokens survive top‑k filtering. Sampled token indicator framer‑motion motion.div Golden pulsing glow on the token actually chosen by the sampling algorithm.

docs.title: 2.1.3 Data Flow Implementation
docs.text:
The component receives data through a custom React hook useModelOutput:

// Conceptual data flow — not code, but architecture specification

interface LogitDataFlow {
  // Step 1: Raw logits from the model's final linear layer
  rawLogits: Float32Array;          // Length = vocabulary size (50,257 for GPT‑2)

  // Step 2: Temperature‑scaled logits (rawLogits / temperature)
  scaledLogits: Float32Array;       // Computed client‑side for responsiveness

  // Step 3: After sampling filter applied
  filteredLogits: Float32Array;     // -Inf for filtered tokens

  // Step 4: Final softmax probabilities
  probabilities: Float32Array;      // Sums to 1.0

  // Metadata
  tokenStrings: string[];           // Decoded token text
  selectedTokenIndex: number;       // Which token was actually sampled
  temperature: number;              // Current temperature value
  samplingMethod: 'greedy' | 'temperature' | 'top_k' | 'top_p' | 'beam';
  topK: number;                     // k value for top‑k sampling
  topP: number;                     // p value for nucleus sampling
}

The critical design decision here: temperature scaling, sampling, and softmax are computed client‑side in a Web Worker so the UI remains responsive at 60fps even with a 50K‑token vocabulary. The raw logits arrive from the Django backend via the existing REST API or WebSocket. All subsequent transformations happen in the browser.

The Transformer Explainer follows this same pattern: "Model output data is accessed via the modelData store. Temperature and sampling parameters are accessed via their respective stores. Data is processed and formatted for display. Different visualizations are rendered based on the processed data."

docs.title: 2.1.4 Top‑k Visualization Detail
docs.text:
When top‑k sampling is active, the bar chart renders:

  • Blue bars: tokens that survive the filter (top‑k highest probabilities)
  • Gray bars (faded, 20% opacity): tokens that were filtered out
  • Red dashed vertical line: the exact cutoff position (at the k‑th token)
  • Golden pulsing bar: the token actually sampled (if in "sample" mode)

The cutoff line position is computed as: cutoffX = (k / visibleTokenCount) * chartWidth. The Transformer Explainer implementation: "When top‑k sampling is selected, only the k most likely tokens are kept, and the rest are filtered out (set to -infinity). This is shown by highlighting the top‑k tokens and indicating where the cutoff occurs."

docs.title: 2.1.5 Top‑p (Nucleus) Visualization Detail
docs.text:
For top‑p sampling, the visualization is more complex:

  • A cumulative probability curve is plotted on a secondary axis
  • A green shaded region shows the tokens whose cumulative probability ≤ p
  • The p‑threshold line intersects the cumulative curve at the cutoff point
  • Tokens beyond the cutoff are grayed out

The Transformer Explainer: "When top‑p sampling is selected, tokens are kept until their cumulative probability exceeds the threshold p. The component shows token probabilities before filtering, after filtering, and the final normalized probabilities after top‑p is applied."

docs.title: 2.2.1 Visualization Strategy
docs.text:
Since the vocabulary is large (50K+ tokens), direct rendering of all tokens is infeasible. Two complementary views are provided:

View A: Top‑k Bar Chart with Scroll/Zoom - Shows the top 50-100 tokens ranked by probability - Horizontal bars with D3‑based zoom/pan (like a genome browser) - A "mini‑map" at the bottom shows the full distribution compressed

View B: Logit Heatmap Grid - Tokens are arranged in a 2D grid (like a spectrogram) - X axis: token index; Y axis: nothing (single row) — or for multi‑token comparison, each row is a different model/layer/timestep - Color intensity = logit value (blue = negative, white = zero, red = positive) - Hover reveals the token text and exact logit value - Uses Plotly.js heatmap trace with colorscale: 'RdBu'

docs.title: 2.2.2 Performance Architecture
docs.text:
For the heatmap with 50K tokens, a canvas‑based renderer is used instead of SVG. The library of choice is Deck.gl (Uber's WebGL‑powered visualization framework) which can render millions of data points at 60fps. Alternatively, Observable Plot can be used for a simpler but still performant implementation.

The data flows from the Django backend as a Float32Array over WebSocket for real‑time updates, or as a JSON array for REST API calls.

docs.title: 2.2.3 Comparison Mode
docs.text:
When comparing two models (e.g., pre‑compression vs post‑compression), the logit spectrum shows:

  • Row 1: Model A logits
  • Row 2: Model B logits
  • Row 3: Difference (A − B) as a diverging heatmap

This leverages the same infrastructure as the attention pattern comparison features already designed.

docs.title: 2.3 MATH PANEL — Softmax Formula with Interactive Temperature
2.3.1 Component Architecture
docs.text:
SoftmaxMathPanel
├── FormulaRenderer (KaTeX — renders the softmax equation)
│   ├── HighlightedVariable (each variable linked to visualization)
│   └── LiveValueSubstitution (shows actual numbers for current token)
├── TemperatureSlider (shadcn/ui Slider with gradient track)
│   ├── GradientTrack (blue‑to‑red gradient representing cold‑to‑hot)
│   ├── PresetButtons ([0.0] [0.3] [0.7] [1.0] [1.5] [2.0])
│   └── LiveDistributionPreview (mini bar chart updating in real‑time)
├── StepByStepAnimator (GSAP Timeline)
│   ├── Step1: "Raw Logits" → shows the vector before processing
│   ├── Step2: "Divide by Temperature" → shows scaled values
│   ├── Step3: "Apply Sampling Filter" → shows which tokens survive
│   ├── Step4: "Softmax" → shows final probabilities
│   └── Step5: "Sample Token" → shows the selected output
└── SamplingMethodSelector (radio buttons or segmented control)
    ├── Greedy (argmax)
    ├── Temperature (sample from distribution)
    ├── Top‑k (with k slider)
    ├── Top‑p (with p slider)
    ├── Beam Search (with beam width slider + tree visualization)
    └── Repetition Penalty (slider, 1.0–2.0)

docs.title: 2.3.2 KaTeX Formula Rendering
docs.text:
The formula is rendered using KaTeX (faster than MathJax, better for interactive applications):

P(token_i) = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j / T)}

Each variable in the formula is wrapped in a <span> that highlights (glows) when the user hovers over the corresponding UI element. For example, hovering over the temperature slider highlights T in the formula; hovering over a bar in the probability chart highlights P(token_i).

docs.title: 2.3.3 Temperature Slider Design
docs.text:
The slider uses shadcn/ui Slider with a custom gradient track:

  • Track gradient: linear-gradient(to right, #3b82f6, #ef4444) (blue → red)
  • Blue end = low temperature (deterministic, peaked distribution)
  • Red end = high temperature (random, uniform distribution)
  • Thumb shows the current temperature value
  • Preset buttons for quick switching

A live mini‑preview (a tiny horizontal bar chart, approximately 100px wide) updates in real‑time as the user drags the slider, showing how the distribution shape changes. This is implemented using a lightweight D3‑based canvas element for 60fps updates.

The approach is directly inspired by the Transformer Explainer: "The raw logits are divided by a temperature parameter, which controls the randomness of predictions: Lower temperature (< 1.0) makes the distribution more peaked (more deterministic). Higher temperature (> 1.0) makes the distribution more uniform (more random)."

docs.title: 2.3.4 Step‑by‑Step Animator Implementation
docs.text:
Each step is a GSAP Timeline animation. The user can scrub through the timeline with a slider (like video playback). Implementation details:

Step Animation Duration Trigger 1. Raw Logits Numbers appear in monospace grid 0.3s Auto‑play or click 2. Temperature Each number divides by T, color shifts 0.3s Auto‑advance 3. Sampling Filtered tokens fade to gray 0.3s Auto‑advance 4. Softmax Numbers normalize, bars grow 0.5s Auto‑advance 5. Sample Golden glow on selected token 0.3s Auto‑advance

The GSAP Timeline is controlled by a <input type="range"> scrubber and play/pause buttons.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Sampling Method Architecture
docs.text:
SamplingControls
├── MethodSelector (segmented button group)
│   ├── Greedy: "Always pick the highest probability token"
│   ├── Temperature: "Sample from the full distribution"
│   ├── Top‑K: "Sample from top K tokens only"
│   ├── Top‑P: "Sample from tokens until cumulative probability > P"
│   └── Beam Search: "Maintain multiple hypotheses"
├── ParameterSliders (conditionally rendered)
│   ├── Temperature: [0.0 ––––––––●–––––––– 2.0]
│   ├── Top‑K: [1 –––––●––––––––––––––– 100]
│   ├── Top‑P: [0.0 ––––––––●–––––––– 1.0]
│   └── Beam Width: [1 ––●–––––––––––––––– 10]
├── RepetitionPenaltySlider: [1.0 –––––●–––– 2.0]
│   └── Explanation tooltip: "Penalizes tokens that have already appeared"
├── LiveEffectPreview (small bar chart showing current distribution)
└── ResetButton (return to default settings)

docs.title: 2.4.2 Beam Search Tree Visualization
docs.text:
When beam search is selected, an additional component renders:

BeamSearchTree (D3.js tree layout)
├── TreeNode (represents a partial hypothesis)
│   ├── TokenText (the token at this node)
│   ├── ScoreIndicator (cumulative log‑probability)
│   ├── ActiveIndicator (golden border if this path survived)
│   └── PrunedIndicator (red X if this path was eliminated)
├── TreeEdges (lines connecting parent to children, thickness ∝ score)
└── FinalHypotheses (the top‑k completed sequences at the end)

This component uses D3.js tree layout (d3.tree()) with React rendering. Each node in the tree represents a partial hypothesis. Nodes that survive beam pruning have gold borders; pruned nodes have red X marks. The final hypotheses are highlighted at the bottom.

The beam search visualization "creates interactive tree diagrams showing how the model explores different sequence hypotheses during decoding. Each node represents a token in the sequence. Nodes show the token and its score." The implementation "converts beam search decoding results into an interactive tree structure rendered using D3.js."

docs.title: 2.4.3 Repetition Penalty Implementation
docs.text:
The repetition penalty slider applies a penalty to logits of tokens that have already appeared in the generated sequence. The formula is:

logit_i = logit_i - penalty · 1[token_i already appeared]

The visualization shows: - Previously generated tokens highlighted in a different color - The penalty amount as a red overlay on those tokens' bars - A "penalty severity" indicator (how much the probability of repeated tokens drops)

The repetition penalty mechanism "penalizes previously chosen tokens to minimize repetition."

docs.title: 2.5.1 Entropy Timeline Chart
docs.text:
For autoregressive generation, the system tracks prediction entropy at each step:

H_t = − Σ_i P(token_i) · log₂ P(token_i)

This is visualized as a line chart using Plotly.js:

  • X axis: generation step (token position)
  • Y axis: entropy (bits)
  • Blue line: prediction entropy
  • Red dashed line: maximum possible entropy (log₂|V|)
  • Green shaded region: "confident" zone (entropy < 1 bit)
  • Yellow shaded region: "uncertain" zone (entropy > 5 bits)
  • Orange dots: steps where the model changed its mind (top prediction flipped)

Below the chart, a token ribbon shows the actual generated tokens at each step, color‑coded by the model's confidence.

This approach is grounded in information theory: "autoregressive generation is essentially a process of progressively reducing sequential uncertainty through successive observations. Each token generation represents a new observation. As a direct measure of uncertainty, entropy effectively reflects the change in predictive uncertainty throughout the process."

docs.title: 2.5.2 Architecture for Real‑Time Tracking
docs.text:
During generation, the system maintains a ring buffer of the last 100 generation steps:

  1. Each generation step pushes {step, tokens, probabilities, entropy} into the buffer
  2. The Plotly chart subscribes to buffer updates via React context
  3. Plotly's extendTraces method is used for efficient incremental updates without full re‑render
  4. The buffer persists across generation sessions for comparison

docs.title: 2.6.1 What a Reliability Diagram Shows
docs.text: A reliability diagram "plots the observed frequency of an event against the predicted probability." If the model is perfectly calibrated, the plot follows the diagonal (identity line). Deviations indicate over‑confidence (below the diagonal) or under‑confidence (above the diagonal).

docs.title: 2.6.2 Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
ReliabilityDiagram
├── PlotArea (Plotly.js scatter plot)
│   ├── IdentityLine (black dashed diagonal, y = x)
│   ├── CalibrationCurve (blue line with error bars)
│   ├── HistogramMarginals (bar chart showing # samples per bin)
│   └── PerfectCalibrationRegion (green shaded band around identity)
├── MetricsPanel
│   ├── ECE (Expected Calibration Error)
│   ├── MCE (Maximum Calibration Error)
│   └── Brier Score
└── LayerSelector (dropdown to choose which layer to evaluate)

docs.title: 2.6.3 Data Flow
docs.text:
The calibration data flows from the Django backend:

  1. Backend: During training, the model outputs predicted probabilities and actual outcomes (correct/incorrect) for validation data. These are stored in the TrainingSnapshot model or a dedicated CalibrationData table.

  2. API: GET /api/experiments/{run_id}/calibration/?layer=5 returns: 

    {
  "layer": 5,
  "bins": [
    {"confidence_bin": [0.0, 0.1], "accuracy": 0.05, "count": 120},
    {"confidence_bin": [0.1, 0.2], "accuracy": 0.18, "count": 200},
    ...
  ],
  "ece": 0.034,
  "mce": 0.12,
  "brier_score": 0.089
}

  3. Frontend: The Plotly scatter plot is constructed from the bin data. The x‑axis represents confidence (predicted probability), the y‑axis represents accuracy (observed frequency). A perfectly calibrated model follows y = x.

  4. Interactive: Users can select different layers to see how calibration evolves — earlier layers tend to be less calibrated, later layers (after more processing) become better calibrated.

docs.title: 2.6.4 Visual Design Details
docs.text:
• The calibration curve is rendered with error bars showing ±1 standard deviation within each bin
  • A histogram in the margins shows the number of samples per confidence bin
  • The ECE (Expected Calibration Error) is prominently displayed as a numeric badge
  • Hovering over a point shows: confidence range, actual accuracy, sample count
  • A "Compare Mode" allows overlaying two models' calibration curves on the same plot

docs.title: 2.7.1 What Tuned Lens Does
docs.text: The tuned lens "allows us to peek at the iterative computations a transformer uses to compute the next token." Unlike the logit lens (which applies the final unembedding layer directly to intermediate representations), the tuned lens trains a small affine transformation for each layer that translates that layer's hidden state into the vocabulary space, correcting for representational drift.

docs.title: 2.7.2 Architecture
docs.text:
TunedLensPanel
├── LayerSelector (vertical list of all layers)
│   └── Each layer row shows a miniature word cloud of top‑k predictions
├── MainView (shows predictions for selected layer)
│   ├── TokenPredictionBars (top‑k tokens with probability bars)
│   ├── ComparisonWithFinalLayer (overlay showing how predictions differ)
│   └── LayerTransitionAnimation (scrubber showing prediction evolution)
├── TunedLensMetrics
│   ├── Perplexity (how good are predictions at this layer?)
│   ├── KL Divergence (vs final layer distribution)
│   └── Top‑1 Accuracy (does it predict the same token as final?)
└── TrainTunedLensButton (staff only — triggers training job)

docs.title: 2.7.3 Data Flow Implementation
docs.text:
The tuned lens data is pre‑computed on the backend:

  1. Training: The tuned lens affine probes are trained offline using the AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens library. "This package provides a simple interface for training and evaluating tuned lenses." The training produces a small affine transformation (W_layer, b_layer) for each layer.

  2. Storage: The trained probes are stored in the model_versioning system as artifacts associated with a specific model version.

  3. API: POST /api/experiments/tuned-lens/ with body {model_version_id, text, layers: [0,1,2,...]} returns for each layer the top‑k predicted tokens and their probabilities.

  4. Frontend: The TunedLensPanel component renders each layer as a miniature bar chart. Clicking a layer expands it to show the full prediction distribution.

docs.title: 2.7.4 Visual Design
docs.text:
The tuned lens view is organized as a vertical timeline:

  • Left column: layer index (0, 1, 2, ..., 12)
  • Main column: miniature horizontal bar chart of top‑10 predicted tokens for that layer
  • Color coding: the token that matches the final prediction is highlighted in green; tokens that are "distractions" (high probability early but later discarded) are shown in gray
  • Connection lines: D3 curves connect the same token across layers, showing how its probability evolves (like the Semantic Pathway trajectories)

The tuned lens is closely related to the logit lens: "the logit lens method allows exploration of the residual stream in transformer networks by treating middle layer hidden states as the final layer output." The tuned lens improves on this by correcting for representational drift.

docs.title: 3.1 Django Models
docs.text:
# gpu_benchmark/models.py — add these models

class LogitSnapshot(models.Model):
    """A single logit vector captured at a specific point."""
    run = models.ForeignKey('experiment.TrainingRun', on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    layer = models.IntegerField()
    head = models.IntegerField(null=True)
    token_position = models.IntegerField()
    logits = models.BinaryField()  # Serialized Float32Array (50K floats)
    temperature = models.FloatField(default=1.0)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)


class TunedLensProbe(models.Model):
    """Trained affine probe for a specific layer of a model."""
    model_version = models.ForeignKey('model_versioning.ModelVersion', on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    layer = models.IntegerField()
    weight = models.BinaryField()  # Serialized weight matrix
    bias = models.BinaryField()    # Serialized bias vector
    trained_on_dataset = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    perplexity = models.FloatField()
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)


class CalibrationData(models.Model):
    """Pre‑computed calibration bins for reliability diagrams."""
    run = models.ForeignKey('experiment.TrainingRun', on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    layer = models.IntegerField()
    bins = models.JSONField()  # [{confidence_range, accuracy, count}]
    ece = models.FloatField()
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

docs.text: Hook Purpose Returns useModelOutput(runId) Fetch/stream logits from backend {rawLogits, probabilities, loading, error} useTemperature(defaultT) Manage temperature state with debounce {temperature, setTemperature, debouncedTemperature} useSamplingMethod() Manage sampling method and parameters {method, params, setMethod, setParam} useEntropyTracker() Ring buffer for entropy timeline {entropyData, addStep, reset} useTunedLens(modelVersionId, text) Fetch tuned lens predictions {layerPredictions, loading} useCalibrationData(runId) Fetch calibration bins {calibrationData, ece, loading}

docs.title: 4.2 Web Worker for Client‑Side Computation
docs.text:
The softmax, temperature scaling, and sampling computations are performed in a Web Worker to prevent main‑thread blocking:

// Architecture specification for the LogitWorker

The LogitWorker:
1. Receives {rawLogits: Float32Array, temperature: number, method: string, params: object}
2. Performs temperature scaling: scaled = rawLogits / temperature
3. Applies sampling filter (top‑k sets non‑top‑k to -Infinity; top‑p sets to -Infinity after cumulative threshold)
4. Computes softmax with numerical stability (subtracts max before exp)
5. Returns {probabilities: Float32Array, filteredIndices: number[], selectedIndex: number}
6. Posts result back to main thread via postMessage()

This architecture ensures the UI never freezes, even when processing the full 50K vocabulary.

docs.title: 4.3 GSAP Animation Architecture
docs.text:
For the collapsed ↔ expanded transition of the probability panel:

1. User clicks expand button
2. GSAP Flip.getState() captures current positions of all probability bars
3. Container div grows to expanded size
4. New elements (raw logit column, scaled logit column, sampling effect column) fade in
5. GSAP Flip.from() animates the bars from collapsed positions to expanded positions
6. Total animation duration: 0.4s with ease: "power2.inOut"

This is the exact approach used by Transformer Explainer: "The expansion and collapse are animated using GSAP and Flip for smooth transitions."

docs.title: 🧭 POSITIONAL ENCODING STUDIO — Complete Implementation Blueprint
“RoPE & Absolute Encoding Lab”
docs.text: A fully specified, production‑grade interactive laboratory for visualizing, exploring, and comparing every major positional encoding scheme used in modern Transformers. No code — just precise architectural decisions, technology choices, data‑flow pipelines, and implementation strategy for every zone.

docs.title: 0.1 Core Runtime
docs.text: Layer Technology Justification Framework React 19 + TypeScript 5.6 Component model, strict typing for tensor shapes Build Vite 6 (Rolldown) Sub‑second HMR; native ESM for lazy‑loaded heavy modules State Zustand 5 + persist middleware Lightweight, no boilerplate, partial‑persist pattern for dashboard layout and user preferences across sessions Server State TanStack Query v5 Cache, refetch, and deduplicate API calls for model loading and inference Styling Tailwind CSS 4 + cn() utility Already in your design system; dark‑mode–first

docs.text: Engine Use Case Why React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber) + Drei 3D RoPE rotation visualizer, 3D encoding topology Full React declarative syntax; Drei provides OrbitControls, Text, Tube, etc. D3.js v7 (data joins only) Sinusoidal encoding heatmap, position similarity matrix, waveforms Unmatched control over enter/update/exit for large matrices; used for data binding, not DOM manipulation (React owns the DOM) Observable Plot Quick exploratory charts (waveform overlays, frequency analysis) Built on D3; concise API; SVG output; ideal for the analytics sub‑panels Canvas 2D (via React‑Konva) High‑performance large heatmaps (>100 positions) Canvas beats SVG for thousands of cells; React‑Konva gives declarative JSX bindings Threlte (Svelte) Alternative 3D stack Demonstrated by Neuromancer for neural network 3D visualization with ONNX Runtime Web
