docs.title: 1. Zone: Sinusoidal Encoding Heatmap — The Foundation View
1.1 What It Visualizes
docs.text:
The full max_len × d_model positional encoding matrix P where:

P(pos, 2i)   = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d))
P(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d))

Each row = one token position (0…max_len‑1), each column = one embedding dimension (0…d_model‑1). The characteristic "staircase" wavelength pattern reveals how low‑frequency dimensions encode coarse position and high‑frequency dimensions encode fine position.

docs.title: 1.2 Technology Decision: D3 Data‑Join + React‑Konva Canvas
docs.text:
For up to 512 positions × 768 dimensions (≈ 393k cells), SVG becomes unusably slow. The correct architecture is:

Layer Technology Responsibility Data computation Pyodide (NumPy) in Web Worker Generate the (max_len, d_model) float32 matrix Color mapping D3‑scale scaleSequential(interpolateTurbo) Map float value → RGBA Rendering React‑Konva <Rect> per cell, virtualized Only render cells in the viewport via react‑konva clipping + manual culling Interactivity React state for hover/select; Konva event handlers onMouseEnter, onClick per cell

docs.title: 1.3 Virtualization Strategy
docs.text:
For large matrices, implement a viewport‑culled grid:

  1. Compute which row/column range is visible based on stage.scale() and stage.position().
  2. Only instantiate <Rect> components for cells within ±50 rows/columns of the viewport.
  3. Use a useMemo that depends on scroll position to re‑compute the visible set.
  4. This reduces DOM nodes from ~400k to ~10k at any moment.

docs.title: 1.4 Waveform Sub‑Panel (Line Chart Overlay)
docs.text:
Below or beside the heatmap, show the actual sine/cosine curves for selected dimensions. Use Observable Plot for rapid rendering:

Plot.plot({
  marks: [
    Plot.line(data, {x: "position", y: "value", stroke: "dimension"}),
  ],
  color: {scheme: "tableau10"}
})

Hovering a cell in the heatmap highlights the corresponding waveform; clicking pins it for comparison.

docs.title: 2. Zone: RoPE 3D Rotation Visualizer — The Crown Jewel
2.1 What It Visualizes
docs.text:
Rotary Position Embedding applies a position‑dependent rotation to pairs of embedding dimensions. For a query/key vector x ∈ ℝ^d at position p, dimension pairs (2i, 2i+1) are rotated by angle θ_i = p · base^(-2i/d):

RoPE(x, p)_{(2i, 2i+1)} = R(θ_i) · [x_{2i}, x_{2i+1}]^T

where R(θ) is the 2D rotation matrix [[cos θ, -sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].

docs.title: 2.2 Technology: React Three Fiber + Custom TubeGeometry
docs.text: The visualization has three layers in a single <Canvas>:

docs.title: Layer 1 — Embedding Space Sphere (Background)
docs.text:
• Tokens as spheres positioned on the surface of a unit hypersphere projected to 3D via PCA (computed in Pyodide).
  • Dimension pair rings: For each (2i, 2i+1) pair, draw a transparent ring in 3D space representing the rotation plane. These rings are color‑coded by frequency (low‑frequency = blue, high‑frequency = red).

Implementation: Use <Ring> from Drei with rotation set so each ring is perpendicular to its rotation axis.

docs.title: Layer 2 — Rotation Arrows (Interactive)
docs.text:
• For the currently hovered token, draw arrows showing how each dimension pair rotates as position increases.
  • Use TubeGeometry along a parametric curve: for a rotation by angle θ, the path is (cos(t·θ), sin(t·θ), 0) for t ∈ [0, 1].
  • Color intensity encodes rotation magnitude (earlier dimension pairs rotate faster).

Implementation:

// Pseudocode for one dimension pair rotation tube
const curve = new THREE.CatmullRomCurve3([
  new THREE.Vector3(x1, y1, 0),           // original position
  new THREE.Vector3(cos(θ/3), sin(θ/3), 0),
  new THREE.Vector3(cos(2θ/3), sin(2θ/3), 0),
  new THREE.Vector3(cos(θ), sin(θ), 0),   // rotated position
]);
<TubeGeometry args={[curve, 64, 0.02, 8, false]} />

docs.title: Layer 3 — Position Slider (Temporal)
docs.text: A <Slider> (HTML, outside the canvas) controls p. As the user scrubs from position 0 to max_len: * All rotation arrows animate smoothly (GSAP timeline). * The angle labels update in real‑time. * The similarity matrix (Zone 3) updates reactively.

docs.title: 2.3 RoPE‑Specific Math Panel
docs.text:
The math panel for RoPE shows:

  • The full formula in LaTeX (using react‑latex or KaTeX): 
    RoPE(x, p)_{(2i, 2i+1)} = R(p · θ_i) · [x_{2i}, x_{2i+1}]^T
  • A live numerical table showing for each dimension pair i:
  • θ_i (base frequency)
  • p · θ_i (rotation angle at position p)
  • cos(p·θ_i) and sin(p·θ_i) (the actual rotation values)
  • A frequency spectrum chart (bar chart) showing θ_i vs. dimension index i, rendered with Observable Plot.

docs.title: 3. Zone: Position Similarity Matrix — "How RoPE Encodes Relative Position"
3.1 What It Visualizes
docs.text: For every pair of positions (i, j), compute cosine_similarity(PE_i, PE_j). With sinusoidal encoding, the similarity depends on |i - j| and the frequency spectrum. With RoPE, the similarity encodes relative position: the dot product q_i · k_j depends only on (i - j).

docs.title: 3.2 Technology: React‑Konva Canvas Heatmap
docs.text:
• Matrix size: max_len × max_len (e.g., 128×128 = 16k cells — canvas‑native).
  • Color: blue = low similarity, white = medium, red = high similarity.
  • Diagonal: always 1.0 (self‑similarity).
  • Anti‑diagonal bands reveal the relative‑position encoding property of RoPE.

docs.title: 3.3 Interactivity
docs.text:
• Hover: show (pos_i, pos_j, similarity_value, relative_distance).
  • Click: pin a reference position i. The heatmap re‑colors to show |similarity(i, j) - expected_similarity(|i-j|)| — a residual view highlighting where the encoding deviates from perfect relative encoding.
  • Encoding comparison: load two encodings (e.g., RoPE vs. Sinusoidal) and show a difference heatmap (Jensen‑Shannon divergence per cell).

docs.title: 4. Zone: Interactive Controls — The Parameter Dashboard
4.1 Sliders (Real‑Time Reactive)
docs.text: Parameter Range Effect max_len 16 … 2048 Regenerate all encodings; all views update d_model 64 … 4096 Regenerate; heatmap width changes base (RoPE θ) 500 … 1,000,000 Changes rotation frequency distribution position (current) 0 … max_len‑1 Animates rotation arrows; highlights row in heatmap encoding_type [sinusoidal, learned, RoPE, ALiBi, NoPE, YaRN, NTK] Switches the entire studio

docs.title: 4.2 Technology
docs.text:
All sliders use HTML <input type="range"> styled with Tailwind. State lives in a Zustand store (useEncodingStore) with the persist middleware so the user's last configuration is restored on reload.

The store shape:

interface EncodingStore {
  encodingType: 'sinusoidal' | 'rope' | 'alibi' | 'learned' | 'nope' | 'yarn' | 'ntk';
  maxLen: number;          // 128
  dModel: number;          // 768
  baseFrequency: number;   // 10000
  currentPosition: number; // 0
  selectedDimPair: number; // null | 0..dModel/2-1
  comparisonEncoding: EncodingType | null;
  viewMode: 'heatmap' | 'waveform' | '3d' | 'similarity' | 'compare';
  // ... persist this slice to localStorage
}

docs.title: 5. Zone: Position Sensitivity Analysis — "How Much Does Position Matter?"
5.1 Ablation Test Framework
docs.text:
The system can answer: "If I remove the positional encoding entirely from layer L, how much does the model's output change?"

This requires real model inference. The architecture is:

User clicks "Run Ablation" →
  1. Web Worker loads model via ONNX Runtime Web
  2. Runs inference twice:
     a. With full positional encoding (baseline)
     b. With positional encoding zeroed out for the selected layer (ablation)
  3. Returns output difference (KL divergence, top‑k change, attention pattern delta)
  4. UI renders an "impact heatmap" per layer

docs.title: 5.2 Technology
docs.text: ONNX Runtime Web with WebGPU backend for acceleration. The model must be exported from PyTorch to ONNX with a custom "inject zero encoding at layer L" node. This is done via the onnx Python package (model surgery), similar to Neuromancer's approach of modifying models to expose internal tensors.

docs.title: 5.3 Visualization Output
docs.text:
A bar chart (Observable Plot) with: * X‑axis: layer index * Y‑axis: output KL divergence when encoding is ablated * Color: green (low impact) → red (high impact)

This reveals which layers rely most heavily on positional information — early layers typically depend more.

docs.title: 6. Zone: Frequency Analysis — "Which Dimension Encodes Which Frequency?"
6.1 Fourier Analysis of the Encoding
docs.text:
For sinusoidal encoding, dimension pair i encodes a pure sinusoid with wavelength 2π · 10000^(2i/d). For RoPE, the frequency spectrum is similar but applied as rotations.

Visualize this as:

  1. Frequency vs. Dimension chart: a scatter plot where X = dimension index, Y = log(wavelength). The characteristic exponential curve appears.
  2. Waveform gallery: a grid of small line charts, each showing the encoding value across positions for one dimension pair. Color‑coded by frequency band.

docs.title: 6.2 Technology
docs.text: All computation in Pyodide (NumPy's fft module for frequency analysis). Rendering via Observable Plot's Plot.plot({ facet: { data, x: "position", y: "value", fx: "dimension" } }) for the waveform gallery.

docs.title: 7.1 Multi‑Encoding View
docs.text:
The user can load two (or more) encoding schemes simultaneously:

  • Split heatmap: left half = Encoding A, right half = Encoding B
  • Difference heatmap: |PE_A - PE_B| per cell, normalized
  • Similarity matrix comparison: two matrices side‑by‑side
  • Frequency spectrum overlay: both spectra on one chart

docs.title: 7.2 Technology
docs.text: The Zustand store holds encodingType (primary) and comparisonEncoding (secondary). The data computation runs twice in the Web Worker and returns both matrices. The visualization components receive both datasets and render them in split/diff mode.

docs.title: 8. Zone: Social & Community Features — "The Encoding Arena"
8.1 Blind Pairwise Comparison (ComparIA‑Style)
docs.text:
Two anonymous encodings are shown side‑by‑side. Users vote on: * "Which encoding better preserves relative position?" * "Which encoding produces more interpretable attention patterns?" * "Which encoding would you use for a new model?"

Votes generate Elo ratings for encoding schemes. The ComparIA approach is validated: "users interact with two anonymous models simultaneously, vote on the better response, and subsequently reveal the models' identities."

docs.title: 8.2 "Design an Encoding" Challenge
docs.text: Users can: 1. Define a custom encoding function f(pos, dim) → ℝ (via a code editor or parameter sliders). 2. The system generates the full matrix in Pyodide. 3. The encoding is scored on: relative‑position preservation, frequency coverage, smoothness, and novelty. 4. Submit to the community leaderboard. 5. Other users can fork, modify, and re‑submit.

docs.title: 8.3 Encoding Collections & Knowledge Graph
docs.text: Every encoding exploration can be: * Saved as a ResearcherNote (connects to your notes app). * Starred and added to collections ("Best RoPE Configurations for Long Context"). * Linked to experiments that used that encoding (connects to experiment app). * Discussed in threaded comments (connects to community app).

docs.title: 11.1 Pyodide‑in‑Worker Architecture
docs.text: Unlike most visualization tools that pre‑compute encodings server‑side, this studio runs full NumPy in the browser via Pyodide in a Web Worker. This means: * No server round‑trips for parameter changes. * The user can modify max_len, d_model, base and see results in <50ms. * Pyodide loads once (~10MB WASM), then all computation is local.

docs.title: 11.2 Hybrid SVG/Canvas/WebGL Rendering
docs.text:
Most tools pick one renderer. This studio uses all three strategically: * SVG (Observable Plot) for charts with <1k elements (waveforms, bar charts). * Canvas 2D (React‑Konva) for heatmaps with 10k–500k cells. * WebGL (React Three Fiber) for 3D rotation visualization.

The switching is seamless to the user because all three are wrapped in React components with identical props interfaces.

docs.title: 11.3 WebGPU Compute Shaders for RoPE Rotation
docs.text: The RoPE 3D visualizer can animate hundreds of dimension‑pair rotations at 60 FPS by using WebGPU compute shaders to compute the rotated positions on the GPU, then read the results directly into Three.js BufferGeometry (zero‑copy via GPUBuffer → WebGLBuffer interop where supported).

docs.title: 11.4 Model Surgery for Internal Tensor Access
docs.text: For ablation testing and real attention visualization, models are modified via the ONNX Python package to expose intermediate tensors at every layer — the same approach used by Neuromancer. This means the studio can show exactly how positional encoding affects attention patterns, not just the encoding matrix itself.

docs.title: 🧠 Residual Stream Tracer — Complete Implementation Specification
"The Information Highway" — Full Architecture & Implementation Guide
0. Technology Stack Summary
docs.text: Layer Technology Purpose Backend Computation Python 3.11+ with nnsight (0.4+) Primary library for model instrumentation, tracing, and activation capture. Wraps HuggingFace or custom PyTorch models. Provides remote execution via Modal for GPU-accelerated inference with snapshot-based cold-start reduction — exactly as demonstrated by the mechinterp webapp which uses FastAPI + Modal for GPU processing Backend Computation (Alternative) TransformerLens (2.0+) Alternative to nnsight for HookedTransformer models. Provides built-in logit_lens(), activation_patching(), residual_stack_plot(), and cache-based activation collection Logit Lens Computation nnsight tracing context + LM head projection The nnsight library provides first-class support for Logit Lens: "A classic application: decode each layer's hidden states through the final layer norm and language model head to see what the model 'thinks' at each layer" Activation Patching nnpatch library or pyvene nnpatch sits on top of nnsight and eliminates manual loop writing for activation patching workflows. pyvene provides counterfactual intervention primitives with a "worlds" axis for parallel model runs Logit Prisms Decomposition Custom PyTorch module using frozen activations The Logit Prisms paper treats non-linear activations as constants, enabling linear decomposition of logit output into per-component contributions via linear projections. Implemented as a post-hoc analysis pass over cached activations API Layer FastAPI (async) + Modal (serverless GPU) FastAPI serves as the bridge between the React frontend and GPU-accelerated model computation. Modal provides cold-start-optimized GPU inference with snapshot caching Data Transport WebSocket (Django Channels) for streaming + REST for one-shot requests Real-time residual stream data streams via WebSocket at configurable frame rates; static snapshots via REST. Both transported as compressed JSON with Float32Array optimization Frontend Rendering — SVG/DOM D3.js v7 + d3-sankey plugin + @visx/sankey + React 18 The Sankey diagram layout engine. d3-sankey computes the node positions and link paths; @visx/sankey provides React component wrappers. D3's d3-force module also used for force-directed token relationship graphs Frontend Rendering — 3D/WebGL react-three-fiber (@react-three/fiber v9) + three.js v0.170+ + @react-three/drei Renders the 3D vector arithmetic visualization (tokens as spheres, attention as curved tubes, residual updates as arrow vectors). R3F drives a render loop outside React without overhead, using GPU rendering via WebGL Frontend Rendering — Particle Systems @newkrok/three-particles (v0.4+) with WebGPU compute shaders + wawa-vfx For the flowing particle attention visualization. GPU compute shaders handle per-particle physics (gravity, velocity, force fields) enabling 50K-350K+ particles at interactive frame rates via Three.js WebGPU renderer and TSL (Three Shading Language) Large-Scale Network Rendering helios-web (optional integration) For datasets with hundreds of thousands of token nodes, Helios-Web provides GPU-based rendering, Web Workers for parallel computing, and customizable force-directed layouts that mitigate the "hairball" effect 2D Vector Arithmetic Rendering Canvas API via react-konva or raw HTML5 Canvas with Web Worker offloading For the Visual Sandbox-style 2D training dynamics view. Dimensionality reduction (UMAP/t-SNE) computed in a Web Worker; Canvas renders the 2D point cloud with animated arrows showing vector updates Dimensionality Reduction umap-js (in-browser) or sklearn.umap (backend via Modal) For projecting high-dimensional hidden states to 2D/3D for visualization. In-browser UMAP via WebAssembly for small datasets; server-side sklearn for large datasets State Management zustand + @tanstack/react-query Zustand stores the visualization state (selected layer, active views, animation parameters); React Query manages server state (fetched activations, cached model outputs) Animation Orchestration framer-motion (v11+) + GSAP (ScrollTrigger) Framer-motion for declarative React animations (view transitions, panel animations). GSAP for high-performance timeline-based animations (scrubbing through layers, animated vector arrows) Color & Typography d3-scale-chromatic + Tailwind CSS D3 provides perceptually uniform color scales (Viridis, Turbo, Cividis) for attention weight mapping. docs.title: Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
Backend Data Pipeline: 1. The model receives input text via a FastAPI endpoint. Using nnsight's tracing context, every intermediate residual stream hidden state is captured at each layer: model.trace(input_ids) → access model.transformer.h[layer].output[0] (the residual stream output after attention + FFN). 2. The Logit Prisms decomposition is applied: treating non-linear activations as constants, the residual stream at layer L is decomposed into the sum of contributions from every previous component (embedding + attention_0 + FFN_0 + attention_1 + FFN_1 + … + attention_L + FFN_L). Each contribution is computed via a linear projection through the unembedding matrix. 3. For each token position, a "flow bundle" is computed: the magnitude of the residual update from each component (attention head, FFN neuron group) is measured as the L2 norm of the update vector projected to vocabulary space. These magnitudes become the Sankey link widths. 4. The data is serialized as: { nodes: [{id, label, layer, componentType}], links: [{source, target, value, tokens}] } where value is the normalized flow magnitude.

Frontend Sankey Rendering: 1. The d3-sankey library computes the layout. Nodes are organized as vertical columns: Column 0 = Embedding, Columns 1-L = Layer 1 through Layer L (each with sub-nodes for Attention output and FFN output), Final Column = Output Logits. The @visx/sankey React wrapper renders the SVG with proper link gradients and node rectangles. 2. Each link is colored by its source component type (blue for attention, green for FFN, orange for embedding). Link opacity is proportional to flow magnitude. Hovering a link highlights all connected nodes and displays the exact flow value in a tooltip. 3. The Sankey diagram supports zoom/pan via D3's d3-zoom behavior integrated into the SVG. Clicking a node expands it into its sub-components (e.g., clicking "Attention Layer 3" expands into individual attention heads as separate thin links).

Performance Optimization: - For models with many layers (12+), the Sankey layout is computed asynchronously in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread. - Link rendering uses SVG <path> elements with stroke-dasharray animation to create a "flowing" effect (like liquid moving through pipes). The animation is driven by requestAnimationFrame with CSS stroke-dashoffset animation for GPU-accelerated rendering. - For very large models (100+ layers), links below a configurable threshold (e.g., 0.1% of max flow) are aggregated into an "Other" category to keep the visualization readable.

docs.title: Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
Backend Computation: 1. Using nnsight's tracing context, at each transformer layer, the hidden state (after the residual update) is captured. The nnsight library provides this natively: "decode each layer's hidden states through the final layer norm and language model head to see what the model 'thinks' at each layer". 2. For autoregressive models, at each layer the hidden state at the last token position is projected through the final LayerNorm and unembedding matrix (lm_head) to obtain a probability distribution over the vocabulary. This produces a [n_layers, vocab_size] tensor of log-probabilities. 3. The top-k predictions (k=10, configurable) at each layer are extracted with their probabilities. Additionally, the probability of the actual next token (if known) is tracked across layers. 4. Data format: { layers: [{ layer_index, top_k: [{ token, token_id, logit, probability }], actual_token_probability }] }.

Frontend Timeline Rendering: 1. The timeline is rendered as a horizontal scrubber bar (like a video timeline) representing layers 0 through N. A draggable "playhead" allows the user to select any layer. Below the scrubber, the current layer's top-k predictions are displayed as a horizontal bar chart, with bar width proportional to probability. 2. The "prediction convergence" animation is the key visual: as the user scrubs through layers, the bars animate smoothly between layer states. At early layers (0-2), the predictions are scattered and low-confidence (many small bars). At middle layers (3-8), the correct prediction starts dominating. At late layers (9-11), the probability distribution sharpens to a single clear answer. 3. A secondary "prediction convergence line chart" shows how the probability of the top-1 token evolves across all layers as a single line, with hover annotations at each data point showing the exact token and probability. 4. Color coding: correct prediction = green, plausible alternatives = yellow, clearly wrong = red. The color intensity scales with probability.

Performance: - The full vocabulary distribution is computed server-side and only the top-k results are transmitted to the frontend (reducing payload from ~50K floats to ~100 floats per layer). - Layer data is streamed progressively via WebSocket as computation completes, so the user sees results appear layer-by-layer rather than waiting for all layers to finish.

docs.title: Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
This feature uses the "Visual Sandbox" approach from the Stanford 2024 paper: "with the embedding dimension constrained to d=2, allows for comprehensive two-dimensional visualization of each layer's dynamics" through three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.

Backend: 1. A small transformer model (d_model=2, 2-4 layers, 2-4 attention heads) is either loaded from a pre-trained checkpoint or trained on-the-fly using a tiny synthetic dataset (e.g., XOR pattern, simple sequence copying). 2. During a forward pass, nnsight captures every hidden state vector (2D) at every token position and every layer. The attention outputs and FFN outputs are also captured as 2D vectors. 3. The residual update formula is visualized: x_{l} = x_{l-1} + attn_out + ffn_out. All three vectors (the original position, the attention contribution, and the FFN contribution) are returned for each token at each layer. 4. Data format: { tokens: [{ text, positions: [{ layer, x, y, attn_dx, attn_dy, ffn_dx, ffn_dy }] }] }.

Frontend Canvas Rendering: 1. The main canvas (HTML5 Canvas via react-konva for declarative React integration) renders the 2D embedding space. Each token is a colored circle positioned at its 2D coordinates at the currently selected layer. The token's text label is displayed above/below the circle. 2. Vector arrows: For the selected token, three arrows emanate from its position at the previous layer: - A blue arrow showing the attention output contribution (attn_dx, attn_dy) - A green arrow showing the FFN output contribution (ffn_dx, ffn_dy) - A white dashed arrow showing the net residual update (attn + ffn) - These arrows animate in using GSAP's fromTo with staggered delays to show the "addition" happening step-by-step. 3. Layer scrubber: A slider at the bottom changes the layer. As the slider moves, all token positions smoothly interpolate (using GSAP) from their positions at the old layer to their positions at the new layer, creating a fluid "morphing" animation. 4. Training time-lapse mode: For models trained on-the-fly, a separate slider controls "training epoch." The Canvas shows the same tokens but at a specific epoch. An animation loop can play through all epochs, showing how the embedding geometry evolves through the memorization → circuit formation → cleanup phases identified in the Visual Sandbox paper.

Performance: - The 2D vectors are tiny (2 floats per vector), so data transfer is minimal. All computation is done server-side with nnsight. - Canvas rendering of ~100 tokens with arrows at 60fps is trivial for HTML5 Canvas. The bottleneck is the GSAP animation of arrow appearances, which is GPU-accelerated via CSS transforms.

docs.title: Zone 4 — Math Panel: Residual Update Formula
Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
The math panel renders the residual stream update formula as an interactive LaTeX display:

Formula: x_l = x_{l-1} + \text{Attn}(\text{LN}_1(x_{l-1})) + \text{FFN}(\text{LN}_2(x_{l-1}))

Implementation: 1. The formula is rendered using KaTeX (faster than MathJax for real-time updates) in a dedicated panel. Each term in the formula is wrapped in a <span> with a unique CSS class for highlighting. 2. When the user hovers over a term (e.g., "Attn(LN₁(x))"), the corresponding visual element in the 2D Canvas (the blue attention arrow) and in the Sankey diagram (the attention flow links) simultaneously highlight with a glow effect. This cross-view brushing is implemented via a shared zustand store. 3. 3D Vector Arithmetic Mode: For users who want to see the vector math in 3D, the React Three Fiber scene renders the residual stream vectors as 3D arrows. A token's embedding at layer L-1 is a sphere, the attention output is a blue arrow extending from it, the FFN output is a green arrow, and the resulting position is a larger sphere. The camera orbits automatically to show the 3D relationship. All three vectors are labeled with 3D text sprites. 4. Numerical value overlay: Below the formula, a table shows the actual numerical values: ‖x_{l-1}‖ = 3.42, ‖attn‖ = 0.87, ‖ffn‖ = 1.23, cos(attn, ffn) = 0.34. These update in real-time as the user changes layers or tokens.

Technology: KaTeX for LaTeX rendering, react-three-fiber for the 3D vector scene, zustand for cross-component state synchronization.

docs.title: Zone 5 — Analytics: Residual Stream Norm Analysis
Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
Three analytics panels provide quantitative insight into the residual stream:

1. Residual Stream Norm Growth Chart: - A line chart (using recharts or visx) plotting the L2 norm of the residual stream at each layer, averaged across all token positions. Multiple lines can be shown for different input texts (overlay comparison mode). - Backend: nnsight captures the hidden states and computes per-layer norms. A single API call returns the full norm vector. - Frontend: recharts LineChart with ReferenceLine at y=0 and tooltips showing exact values at each layer.

2. Update Magnitude Distribution: - A stacked bar chart showing, for each layer, the relative contribution of attention output vs. FFN output to the total residual update. The ratio ‖attn‖/(‖attn‖+‖ffn‖) is plotted as a percentage. - This reveals which layers are "attention-dominated" vs. "FFN-dominated." - Backend: norms are computed from the captured attention and FFN output vectors.

3. Direction Consistency Matrix: - A heatmap (layer × layer) showing the cosine similarity between the residual update direction at layer i and layer j. High off-diagonal values indicate layers that "push" in similar directions, suggesting redundancy. - Backend: cosine similarities computed from the captured vectors. - Frontend: rendered as an SVG heatmap using D3, with a Viridis color scale. Hovering a cell shows the exact cosine value.

docs.title: Zone 6 — Interpretability: Logit Prisms Decomposition & Activation Patching
Logit Prisms Decomposition
docs.text:
Backend Implementation (using nnsight + custom PyTorch): 1. The Logit Prisms method is implemented as a post-hoc analysis. After capturing all intermediate activations via nnsight's tracing context, the key insight is applied: "by treating the model's non-linear activations as constants, we can decompose the output in a linear fashion, expressing it as a sum of contributions". 2. For the residual prism: the residual stream at layer L is expressed as resid_L = embed + Σ_{i=0}^{L} (attn_out_i + mlp_out_i). Each term's contribution to the final logit is computed by multiplying by the unembedding matrix: logit_contribution_i = unembed @ LN_final(component_i). This is a single matrix-vector multiplication per component. 3. For the attention prism: the attention output at layer L is further decomposed into per-head contributions: attn_out_L = Σ_{h=0}^{H-1} head_out_{L,h} · W_O[:, h*d_head:(h+1)*d_head]. Each head's logit contribution is computed similarly. 4. For the MLP prism: the MLP output is decomposed into per-neuron contributions using the activation values as constants.

Frontend: 1. The "Prism Decomposition View" shows a waterfall chart (horizontal stacked bar) for a selected target token. Each bar segment represents one component's contribution (positive = pushing toward the token, negative = pushing away). Segments are colored by component type (embedding = orange, attention heads = blue shades, MLP neurons = green shades). 2. Clicking a segment drills down: clicking an attention bar reveals per-head sub-contributions. Clicking an MLP bar reveals per-neuron sub-contributions. 3. The total bar length equals the final logit value for the target token.

docs.title: Activation Patching
docs.text:
Backend Implementation (using nnpatch + pyvene): 1. Two forward passes are performed: a "clean" run (original input) and a "corrupted" run (modified input, e.g., with a key token changed). The nnsight library supports this via its tracing context, and nnpatch eliminates the need for manual loop writing by providing a declarative API. 2. For each component (attention head, MLP neuron, layer), the activation from the clean run is "patched" into the corrupted run (replacing the corrupted activation). The effect on the output logit difference is measured. 3. The result is an "attribution matrix": [component_index, token_position] → Δlogit. Components with large positive Δlogit are causally important for the clean output.

Frontend: 1. The "Patching Results View" displays the attribution matrix as a heatmap (components × token positions), with color intensity proportional to causal effect size. 2. A ranked list shows the top-10 most causally important components for the selected prediction. 3. An interactive mode allows the user to click any component to see a "what-if" comparison: the model's output distribution with and without that component's contribution.

docs.title: Zone 7 — Social: "Residual Stream Race" Gamified Challenge
Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
This is a multiplayer competitive game where researchers race to predict the model's output by observing only the residual stream at progressively earlier layers.

Game Mechanics: 1. The game presents a model's input text and the residual stream logit lens projection at layer N (starting from the final layer). Players submit their prediction of the next token. Correct predictions earn points; points decrease as N decreases (earlier layers are harder). 2. A leaderboard tracks scores in real-time (using WebSocket for live updates). Players can see each other's predictions appear as they submit. 3. The game has rounds: each round, a new input text is processed by the model. Round 1: layer 11 (easy), Round 2: layer 8 (medium), Round 3: layer 5 (hard), Round 4: layer 2 (expert), Round 5: layer 0 (master — only the embedding!).

Backend: 1. The model processes the input once, and all layer projections are cached. Player predictions are compared against the actual top-1 token. 2. Scores are computed server-side and broadcast via WebSocket. The leaderboard is stored in PostgreSQL and updated transactionally.

Frontend: 1. The game interface shows the Logit Lens projection timeline (Zone 2) for the current layer. A text input allows players to type their prediction. A countdown timer adds urgency. 2. The leaderboard is displayed as an animated ranking list using framer-motion for position-change animations. 3. Player avatars and usernames are pulled from the existing profiles app. Badges earned from the game appear on the player's portfolio.

docs.title: Zone 11: Training Dynamics Sandbox — Complete Implementation Specifications
docs.text: This document provides a fully exhaustive implementation blueprint for adding a real‑time, interactive training dynamics sandbox to the NeuralOps Attention Dashboard. Every sub‑component is specified with its programming language, framework, library dependencies, data flow, rendering approach, and integration points.

docs.title: 11.1 Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The Training Dynamics Sandbox consists of five interconnected rendering surfaces that share a common training-state data source and are synchronized through a unified time‑slider controller. Data flows from the PyTorch training loop through a WebSocket bridge into the browser, where React state drives three.js/WebGL, SVG, and Canvas visualizations simultaneously.

docs.title: 11.2 Canvas 1: 2D Embedding Training Sandbox — EmbeddingSandbox.tsx
docs.text: Inspiration: Visual Sandbox (Stanford 2024) constrains transformer embeddings to d=2, allowing each layer's dynamics to be plotted as particles moving in a 2D plane.

docs.title: 11.2.1 Core Concept
docs.text: For a small‑scale transformer where d_model = 2, every token embedding is a 2D point. During training, the weight matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V, and W_O evolve, and the effect is visible as tokens physically moving in the 2D plane. The Visual Sandbox paper "reduces the problem to the study of a system of particles, which interact according to properties of the data distribution and correlations between embeddings, and shows that training dynamics can be understood through particle interactions".

docs.title: 11.2.2 Implementation Stack
docs.text: Component Technology Purpose Language TypeScript (strict mode) Type safety for complex geometry 3D Rendering Three.js (v0.170+) via @react-three/fiber WebGL‑accelerated 2D particle rendering disguised as 3D scene (orthographic camera) Particle System three.js InstancedMesh + custom ShaderMaterial GPU‑accelerated rendering of 1,000+ token particles with per‑particle color, size, and opacity Animation Loop useFrame from @react-three/fiber 60fps render loop synced with training step updates State Management Zustand store (useTrainingSandboxStore) Central store for training state: embeddings per layer per step, loss, gradients Data Serialization Protocol Buffers (protobuf) via protobufjs Efficient binary serialization of embedding tensors from Python to browser WebSocket Transport Django Channels (existing) + custom binary WebSocket sub‑protocol Streaming embedding snapshots at each training step

docs.title: 11.2.3 Data Flow
docs.text:
[PyTorch Training Loop]
    │
    ├── On each optimizer step:
    │   ├── Capture embeddings: layer.attention.q_proj(input) → 2D points
    │   ├── Serialize via protobuf: { step, layer, token_embeddings: [{x, y, token_id}] }
    │   └── Send via WebSocket binary frame
    │
    ▼
[Django Channels Consumer]
    │  (existing WebSocket infrastructure)
    ├── Deserialize protobuf → JSON
    └── Broadcast to channel group "training_sandbox_{run_id}"
    │
    ▼
[React WebSocket Hook: useTrainingStream]
    ├── Receives JSON snapshots
    ├── Updates Zustand store: trainingSnapshots[step] = { layer_embeddings, loss, gradients }
    └── Triggers re-render of Three.js scene

docs.title: 11.2.4 Rendering Approach
docs.text:
Scene Setup: - Orthographic camera (not perspective) → true 2D view with zoom/pan - Coordinate system: X axis = embedding dimension 0, Y axis = embedding dimension 1 - Background: dark grid (#0f172a with subtle grid lines at intervals)

Particle Representation: - Each token embedding rendered as a InstancedMesh sphere - Per‑instance attributes: color (by token position), size (by attention weight), opacity - Custom GLSL vertex shader applies Gaussian blur for soft glow - Custom GLSL fragment shader computes Fresnel‑like edge glow

Animation Between Steps: - Use requestAnimationFrame with linear interpolation (lerp) between current and target positions - Spring physics via @react-spring/three for smooth transitions when user scrubs the timeline - Motion trails: each particle leaves a fading trail (stored as a Line geometry with decaying opacity)

Token Connections (Attention): - For the currently selected layer/head, draw semi‑transparent lines between tokens with attention weight > 0.1 - Line opacity = attention weight; line color = head identity - Lines rendered as LineSegments with LineBasicMaterial

Layer Switching: - User clicks "Layer 0" → "Layer 5" → all particles smoothly animate to their new positions - Layer indicator shows: Layer {n}: Q/K/V/O transformations applied

docs.title: 11.2.5 Particle Interaction Model (Research Insight)
docs.text: The Visual Sandbox paper shows that embedding vectors "tend to organize into two types of structures: grids and circles" during training. The implementation should: - Auto‑detect and highlight these emergent structures (grid detection via Hough transform, circle detection via RANSAC) - Show "particle interaction forces" as vector arrows between tokens (computed from attention weights) - Display the "circuit formation" as tokens that consistently attend to each other form visible clusters

docs.title: 11.3 Canvas 2: Loss Landscape Explorer — LossLandscapeExplorer.tsx
docs.text: Inspiration: loss-landscapes library, Landscaper (2025, Vis4SciML), GradVis toolbox.

docs.title: 11.3.1 Core Concept
docs.text: The loss landscape is a 3D surface where X and Y axes represent random directions in parameter space (using filter normalization), and the Z axis (height/color) represents the loss value. The optimization trajectory is plotted as a path on this surface, showing how the optimizer navigates the loss terrain.

docs.title: 11.3.2 Implementation Stack
docs.text: Component Technology Purpose Loss Landscape Computation loss-landscapes PyTorch library (v0.5+) Computes loss values along random parameter directions with filter normalization Topological Analysis Landscaper (v1.0+) Hessian‑based subspace construction and topological data analysis for basin detection 3D Surface Rendering Plotly.js (react-plotly.js) with gl3d trace type High‑quality 3D surface plots with built‑in camera controls, lighting, and contour lines Trajectory Overlay Plotly scatter3d trace Optimization path as a colored 3D line (color gradient from blue=start to red=end) Real‑time Updates Plotly extendTraces / restyle Incremental surface updates without full re‑render Python Backend Celery task Offloads expensive loss landscape computation to worker nodes Caching Redis Caches computed landscape data for replay without recomputation

docs.title: 11.3.3 Computation Pipeline (Python Side)
docs.text:
# gpu_benchmark/loss_landscape_task.py (conceptual)
import loss_landscapes
import landscaper
from loss_landscapes.model_interface import ModelInterface

@celery_app.task(bind=True)
def compute_loss_landscape(self, model_state_dict, data_batch, resolution=50):
    # 1. Restore model
    model = build_model_from_state(model_state_dict)
    metric = loss_landscapes.metrics.Loss()

    # 2. Compute random plane with filter normalization
    landscape = loss_landscapes.random_plane(
        model, metric,
        distance=5, steps=resolution,
        normalization='filter',  # Li et al. 2018 normalization
    )

    # 3. (Optional) Advanced: Landscaper Hessian subspace
    # hessian_subspace = landscaper.HessianSubspace(model, data_batch)
    # landscape = landscaper.sample_landscape(hessian_subspace, resolution)

    # 4. Return as JSON for Plotly
    return {
        'x': landscape.coords[0].tolist(),  # alpha values
        'y': landscape.coords[1].tolist(),  # beta values
        'z': landscape.loss_values.tolist(),
    }

docs.title: 11.3.5 Filter Normalization Detail
docs.text:
The filter normalization technique (Li et al. 2018, "Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets") is critical for producing meaningful loss landscapes for large models. Without it, the landscape appears flat because parameter scales vary across layers. The implementation should:

  1. For each random direction vector d, normalize each filter (convolutional kernel or weight matrix row) to have the same Frobenius norm as the corresponding filter in the original parameters
  2. This ensures that all layers contribute proportionally to the perturbation, revealing the true curvature of the loss surface

docs.title: 11.4 Canvas 3: Gradient Flow Animation — GradientFlowAnimation.tsx
docs.text: Inspiration: gradviz PyPI package, RNNbow (IEEE CG&A 2018), TorchExplorer.

docs.title: 11.4.1 Core Concept
docs.text: Gradient flow visualization shows how gradient magnitudes propagate backward through the network during backpropagation. Each layer is represented as a vertical bar whose height/color corresponds to the L2 norm of its gradients. The visualization uses RNNbow's approach of "displaying the relative gradient contributions from cells in a neighborhood" but generalized to transformer layers.

docs.title: 11.4.2 Implementation Stack
docs.text: Component Technology Purpose Gradient Capture PyTorch hook: module.register_full_backward_hook() Captures gradient norms per layer during backpropagation Gradient Storage gradviz (PyPI, 2025) Saves gradient L2 norms to CSV during training Chart Rendering D3.js (v7) with React wrapper (react-d3) Custom animated bar chart with gradient flow particles Particle Animation Custom Canvas2D particle system Animated gradient "packets" flowing backward through layer bars Color Encoding d3-scale-chromatic with interpolateRdYlBu Color gradient from blue (small gradient) to red (large gradient / potential explosion)

docs.title: 11.4.3 Gradient Capture (Python Side)
docs.text:
# gpu_benchmark/gradient_capture.py (conceptual)
import torch

class GradientCaptureHook:
    """Captures gradient norms for all nn.Linear modules during training."""
    def __init__(self, model):
        self.gradient_norms = {}
        self.hooks = []
        for name, module in model.named_modules():
            if isinstance(module, torch.nn.Linear):
                hook = module.register_full_backward_hook(
                    lambda m, g_in, g_out, n=name: self._capture(n, g_in, g_out)
                )
                self.hooks.append(hook)

    def _capture(self, name, grad_input, grad_output):
        # grad_input[0] is gradient w.r.t. module input
        # grad_output[0] is gradient w.r.t. module output
        self.gradient_norms[name] = {
            'input_grad_norm': grad_input[0].norm().item(),
            'weight_grad_norm': module.weight.grad.norm().item() if module.weight.grad is not None else 0,
            'output_grad_norm': grad_output[0].norm().item(),
        }

    def snapshot(self):
        return self.gradient_norms.copy()

docs.text:
Layer Bar Chart: - Each layer rendered as a horizontal bar (D3 <rect>) - Bar height proportional to gradient L2 norm (log scale for visibility) - Bar color mapped via d3.interpolateRdYlBu: blue = small gradient, red = large gradient - Layer labels on the y‑axis: "Embedding", "Layer 0 Attn Q", "Layer 0 Attn K", ..., "Layer N FFN Out" - Threshold lines: horizontal dashed lines at gradient norm = 1.0 (healthy) and gradient norm = 100 (exploding)

Gradient Flow Particles: - Animated particles (Canvas2D overlay) flow from right (output) to left (input) - Particle speed = gradient magnitude (faster for larger gradients) - Particle density = number of parameters in that layer - Particles burst into red sparkles when gradient norm exceeds explosion threshold

Animation Control: - Play/Pause button for the gradient flow animation - Speed control slider (0.5× to 4×) - Step forward/backward one training iteration

Comparison Mode (RNNbow‑inspired): - Show gradient norms for two different training runs side‑by‑side - Highlight layers where gradient behavior diverges significantly - Useful for comparing optimizer configurations or learning rates

docs.title: 11.5.1 Core Concept
docs.text: When the user clicks any layer in the gradient flow visualization, the math panel shows the exact chain rule computation for that layer's weight gradient, with live numerical values substituted from the actual training data.

docs.title: 11.5.2 Implementation Stack
docs.text: Component Technology Purpose LaTeX Rendering KaTeX (v0.16+) via react-katex Fast, server‑side renderable LaTeX for mathematical expressions Step Animation CSS @keyframes + React state machine Animated highlighting of each computation step Numerical Values React state from WebSocket Live substitution of actual gradient values from training Diagram D3.js force‑directed graph Visual representation of the computation graph for the selected layer

docs.title: 11.5.3 Formula Display
docs.text:
For a linear layer y = xW^T + b, the chain rule is:

∂L/∂W = ∂L/∂y · ∂y/∂W = (∂L/∂y)^T · x

The panel shows: 1. Step 1: ∂L/∂y — the upstream gradient (displayed as a matrix of actual values) 2. Step 2: x — the layer input (displayed as a matrix) 3. Step 3: The multiplication (animated as matrices sliding together) 4. Result: ∂L/∂W — the weight gradient (displayed with color‑coded magnitude)

For the attention mechanism, the chain rule is more complex:

∂L/∂W_Q = ∂L/∂A · ∂A/∂S · ∂S/∂Q · ∂Q/∂W_Q

where: - ∂L/∂A = gradient of loss w.r.t. attention weights - ∂A/∂S = Jacobian of softmax - ∂S/∂Q = K^T / √d_k - ∂Q/∂W_Q = x^T (input)

Each sub‑step is expandable/collapsible, with numerical values populated in real time.

docs.title: 11.9.1 Rendering Performance
docs.text:
• Three.js InstancedMesh: renders all token particles in a single draw call (critical for 1000+ tokens)
  • Web Worker: offloads protobuf deserialization and data processing to a dedicated worker thread
  • RequestAnimationFrame throttling: limit embedding sandbox to 30fps when tab is not visible (via Page Visibility API)
  • Level‑of‑Detail (LOD): when zoomed out, tokens are rendered as simple points; when zoomed in, as detailed spheres with glow

docs.title: 11.9.2 Data Transfer Optimization
docs.text:
• Delta encoding: only transmit changed values between steps (most embeddings change incrementally)
  • Quantization: reduce float32 → float16 for embedding coordinates (2D, so precision loss is negligible)
  • Chunking: split large snapshots across multiple WebSocket frames to avoid blocking

docs.title: 1.2 Data Flow
docs.text:
The data flows through five distinct stages:

  1. Fetch Stage: Attention data is loaded from the Django REST API (/api/experiments/attention/) or streamed via WebSocket for live training visualization. The data includes tokens, attention matrices per layer/head, hidden states for embedding projection, and model metadata.

  2. Process Stage: Web Workers compute t-SNE/UMAP projections for 3D token positioning, PCA for dimensionality reduction of Q/K/V vectors, and layout algorithms for the spatial arrangement of layers. This prevents blocking the main thread.

  3. Render Stage: React Three Fiber constructs the scene graph. The <XR> provider from @react-three/xr wraps the entire scene for VR support. GPU compute shaders handle particle physics for attention flow visualization.

  4. Interact Stage: Hand tracking data from WebXR (via @react-three/xr's <Hands> component) enables grabbing, pointing, and gesturing. Eye tracking (where available via HeedVision's approach) records where users look.

  5. Sync Stage: For multi-user sessions, Yjs CRDT synchronizes shared state (which tokens are selected, which layer the group is viewing). WebRTC DataChannels stream avatar positions and hand poses peer-to-peer with minimal latency.

docs.title: 3.1 Canvas Setup
docs.text:
The root <Canvas> component from React Three Fiber must be configured with WebGPU support and VR-ready settings:

Key configuration parameters: - gl prop set to use WebGPU backend when available, falling back to WebGL2 - frameloop="demand" to only render when needed (saves battery on mobile/standalone headsets) - dpr={[1, 1.5]} for Quest 3 — lower pixel ratio for performance; dpr={[1, 2]} for desktop VR - shadows="soft" disabled in VR (too expensive) - camera={{ position: [0, 1.6, 0], fov: 90 }} — human height, wide FOV for VR

docs.title: 3.2 XR Provider Setup
docs.text:
The <XR> component from @react-three/xr wraps the entire scene:

XR features to enable: - referenceSpace="local-floor" — user stands on the floor, can walk around - handTracking — enables hand skeletal tracking - controllerTracking — enables motion controllers as fallback - eyeTracking (experimental) — where supported by headset (Apple Vision Pro, Quest Pro) - foveatedRendering — renders center of view at full resolution, periphery at lower resolution (Quest 2/3/Pro)

Non-VR fallback mode: When no headset is detected, the scene renders in "explore mode" with mouse/keyboard controls (OrbitControls for rotation, WASD for movement, scroll for zoom). This is critical — most users will first experience the immersion room on desktop before putting on a headset.

docs.title: 3.3 Rendering Order & Layer Composition
docs.text:
The scene uses Three.js render layers to compose the final image:

  1. Layer 0 — Environment: Skybox/sphere, ambient lighting, floor grid
  2. Layer 1 — Token Nodes: Spheres and text labels for each token
  3. Layer 2 — Attention Connections: Curved tubes, particle flows, laser beams
  4. Layer 3 — Layer Floors: Transparent rings representing each transformer layer
  5. Layer 4 — UI Overlay: Diegetic panels, tooltips, selection highlights
  6. Layer 5 — Avatar Representation: Other users' avatars and gaze indicators

For VR headsets that support WebXR Layers API (composition layers), static UI panels can be rendered at native resolution on a separate quad layer: "a static cylinder or quad layer can be drawn once at high resolution and is resampled only once by the compositor".

docs.title: 4.2 Spatial Layout Algorithm
docs.text:
The spatial layout is computed by a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread:

Token positioning uses t-SNE or UMAP projection of the hidden states (or, for a simpler initial approach, positions tokens on a circular ring within each layer). The ring radius is proportional to the number of tokens — larger for longer sequences.

Layer spacing is uniform (e.g., 3 meters between layers). The user starts at Layer 0 and can "ascend" or "descend" through the model. The current layer is highlighted with a brighter ring.

Connection routing uses quadratic Bezier curves: the control point is offset perpendicular to the ring, creating arcs that rise above/below the layer plane. Thicker connections (higher attention) arc higher, making them visually prominent.

docs.title: 4.3 Reference Space Configuration
docs.text: The WebXR reference space is "local-floor" — the user's physical floor is the origin. The virtual scene is positioned so that the user stands in the center of the token ring at the first layer. Teleportation targets are placed at each layer for quick navigation.

docs.title: 5.1 Token Node Design
docs.text:
Each token is represented as a sphere with a text label floating above it:

  • Sphere radius: Proportional to the token's "importance" (e.g., max attention received across all heads, or its norm in the hidden state)
  • Sphere material: MeshStandardMaterial with roughness=0.3, metalness=0.1
  • Sphere color: Mapped by token position (HSL gradient along the sequence) or by part-of-speech (noun=blue, verb=red, etc.) using the Dodrio-style linguistic annotation overlay
  • Text label: Rendered using @react-three/drei's <Text> component with fontSize scaled by distance. The text shows the token string (truncated to 8 characters for long tokens). The text always faces the camera (billboarding) for readability.

docs.title: 5.2 Token Interaction States
docs.text: State Visual Effect Trigger Idle Subtle glow, normal scale Default Hovered Brighten, scale 1.2x, show tooltip Gaze or controller ray hover Selected Pulsing ring, emit connections highlight Click / pinch gesture Grabbed Follow hand position, semi-transparent Grab gesture (pinch + hold) Attention Source Emitting particles Being queried (row of attention matrix) Attention Target Receiving particles, brightening Being keyed (column of attention matrix)

docs.title: 5.3 Embedding Vector Visualization
docs.text: When a token is "grabbed" (pinched), a small 3D arrow appears showing its embedding vector direction. For tokens in the same layer, the cosine similarity between their embeddings is visualized as the angle between their arrows — users can physically align tokens to compare their embeddings. This is a direct spatial analog of the dot product in attention computation.

docs.title: 6.1 Three Rendering Modes
docs.text:
The attention connections between tokens can be rendered in three modes, user-switchable via a diegetic panel:

Mode A: Tube Geometry (Default) - Uses Three.js TubeGeometry with a QuadraticBezierCurve3 - Tube radius proportional to attention weight - Material: MeshBasicMaterial with vertex colors (gradient from query color to key color) - Performance: ~5,000 connections at 60fps on Quest 3

Mode B: Particle Flow (GPU Compute) - Uses WebGPU compute shader to simulate particles flowing along Bezier paths - Each attention connection spawns N particles where N ∝ weight - Particles are rendered as point sprites with additive blending - Performance: ~100,000 particles at 60fps using WebGPU compute + draw indirect - Visual effect: "attention as flowing energy" — particles stream from query tokens to key tokens, creating a dynamic, alive visualization

Mode C: Laser Beam (Highest Attention Only) - For the top-10 strongest attention connections in the current view - Uses a CylinderGeometry (thin tube) with emissive material and bloom post-processing - Creates dramatic "laser" lines that are visually striking in VR - Performance: negligible (only 10 connections)

docs.title: 6.2 Particle Flow Physics (WebGPU Compute Shader)
docs.text:
The particle flow is the most visually impressive mode and deserves detailed specification:

Compute Shader Structure (WGSL):

The shader runs one workgroup per attention connection, with each workgroup processing 64 particles:

  1. Input Buffers: Particle positions (vec3), velocities (vec3), lifetimes (f32), Bezier control points per connection (vec3 × 4)
  2. Per-Frame Update: Each particle advances along its Bezier curve based on velocity. When a particle reaches the end of the curve (reaches the key token), it respawns at the start (query token) with a small random offset.
  3. Velocity Variation: Particles at the center of the beam (higher attention weight) move faster; edge particles move slower, creating a natural "core flow" appearance.
  4. Color Computation: Each particle's color is interpolated between the query token color and key token color based on its position along the curve.

Rendering Pipeline: 1. Compute shader dispatches particle updates (GPU → GPU, no CPU readback) 2. Vertex shader reads particle positions from the storage buffer 3. Fragment shader renders each particle as a soft circle (distance-based alpha) with additive blending 4. A post-processing bloom pass (using @react-three/postprocessing) makes the particles glow

Performance target: 100,000 particles at 300 FPS on desktop GPU (WebGPU), or 50,000 particles at 72 FPS on Quest 3 (WebGL2 compute fallback).

docs.title: 6.3 Connection Culling & LOD
docs.text:
For scenes with many tokens (e.g., 128+ token sequence), not all connections can be rendered. A level-of-detail system applies:

  • Distance-based culling: Connections further than a threshold distance from the user are not rendered
  • Weight-based filtering: Below a minimum attention weight (configurable via slider), connections are hidden
  • Head-based filtering: User selects which heads to visualize; only connections from selected heads appear
  • Token-pair filtering: When a user selects a specific query token, only connections from that token are shown (all others dim to 10% opacity)

docs.title: 7.1 Layer Ring Design
docs.text:
Each transformer layer is represented as a transparent ring (torus) at a specific Y-height in the scene. The ring serves as both a spatial reference and a navigation target:

  • Ring radius: Slightly larger than the token ring (e.g., 4.5m vs 4.0m for tokens)
  • Ring material: Semi-transparent (opacity: 0.3) with emissive glow
  • Ring color: Layer index mapped to HSL gradient (Layer 0 = blue, Layer N = red)
  • Layer label: Large floating text above each ring showing "Layer N"

docs.title: 7.2 Ascending/Descending Through Layers
docs.text:
The user navigates between layers using:

In VR: - Teleport beam: Point controller at a layer ring and press trigger to teleport - Thumbstick vertical: Push thumbstick up/down to smoothly "elevator" between layers - Hand gesture: Palm-up → ascend one layer; palm-down → descend one layer

In desktop explore mode: - Scroll wheel: Ascend/descend layers - Page Up/Page Down keys: Jump between layers - Layer selector panel: Click on a layer in the minimap

docs.title: 7.3 Cross-Layer Attention Visualization
docs.text: When the user stands at Layer N and looks at tokens in Layer N+1, cross-layer attention connections (residual stream flow) appear as vertical arcs connecting tokens across layers. This visualizes the "residual stream" concept — the information flowing through the model. The arcs use a different color (gold/amber) to distinguish them from intra-layer attention connections.

docs.title: 8.1 Hand Tracking Implementation
docs.text:
Hand tracking is implemented via @react-three/xr's <Hands> component, which uses the WebXR Hand Tracking API: "Controllers can be added with <Controllers /> for motion-controllers and/or <Hands /> for hand-tracking".

Joint data structure: The OpenXR hand tracking API provides 25 joint positions per hand (wrist, 4 joints per finger including metacarpal, proximal, intermediate, distal, and tip). The XR_EXT_hand_tracking_data_source extension (available in Monado 25.1.0+) "enables distinguishing between unobstructed and conforming hand-tracking modes" for more robust tracking.

Hand mesh rendering: Each joint is rendered as a small sphere. Joints are connected by cylinder segments to form a skeletal hand. The hand mesh uses a semi-transparent material with a subtle glow. When the hand is near an interactive object, the fingertip spheres brighten to provide visual feedback.

docs.title: 8.2 Gesture Recognition System
docs.text:
Gestures are recognized using a finite state machine that processes joint positions each frame:

Gesture Joint Configuration Action Point Index finger extended, others curled Raycast to select/highlight tokens Pinch (Grab) Thumb tip + index tip distance < 2cm Grab selected token, move it in space Pinch + Pull Grab + move hand apart "Stretch" an attention connection to see its weight Palm Up Palm normal facing upward Ascend one layer Palm Down Palm normal facing downward Descend one layer Fist All fingers curled Release grabbed object / cancel selection Pinch + Rotate Grab + twist wrist Rotate the token ring (change viewing angle) Two-Hand Spread Both hands, move apart Zoom in (scale the scene) Two-Hand Pinch Both hands, move together Zoom out

docs.title: 8.3 Raycasting for Selection
docs.text: The pointing gesture casts a ray from the index fingertip. The ray is visualized as a thin laser line. Objects within a small radius of the ray are highlighted. When the user pinches (thumb + index), the closest highlighted object is "grabbed" — it follows the hand position with physics-based smoothing.

docs.title: 8.4 Controller Fallback
docs.text: When hand tracking is unavailable (or for users who prefer controllers), the standard VR controller with trigger/grip/thumbstick is supported. The controller model is rendered with a laser pointer emanating from the front. All gestures have controller equivalents (e.g., trigger = pinch, grip = grab).

docs.title: 8.5 Desktop Mouse/Keyboard Fallback
docs.text: For non-VR users, standard FPS controls apply: - Mouse: Look around (pointer lock) - WASD: Move through the scene - Left click: Select token - Right click + drag: Rotate view - Scroll: Zoom in/out or ascend/descend layers - Shift + click: "Grab" and move a token

docs.title: 9.1 Why GPU Compute?
docs.text: The attention visualization requires rendering thousands of flowing particles representing attention weights. On CPU, updating 100,000 particles per frame would consume ~15ms (below 60fps). WebGPU compute shaders can process all particles in parallel on the GPU in <1ms: "WebGPU通过计算着色器（Compute Shader）直接调用GPU的并行计算能力，显著提升了科学数据的处理效率。例如，在流体动力学模拟中，WebGPU可将粒子系统的更新计算从CPU卸载到GPU，实现毫秒级渲染迭代".

docs.title: 9.2 Buffer Architecture
docs.text:
The particle system uses a triple-buffer approach to avoid synchronization stalls:

  1. Particle State Buffer (Storage Buffer): Contains position (vec3f32), velocity (vec3f32), lifetime (f32), connectionID (u32), seed (u32) for each particle. Size = numParticles × 32 bytes.
  2. Connection Metadata Buffer (Uniform Buffer): Contains the Bezier control points (vec3f32 × 4), query token color (vec3f32), key token color (vec3f32), and weight (f32) for each attention connection. Size = numConnections × 64 bytes.
  3. Indirect Draw Buffer: Contains vertexCount, instanceCount, firstVertex, firstInstance — written by the compute shader for GPU-driven rendering.

docs.title: 9.3 Compute Shader Dispatch
docs.text: The compute shader is dispatched with ceil(numParticles / 256) workgroups of 256 threads each. Each thread: 1. Reads its particle state from the Storage Buffer 2. Reads the connection metadata for its assigned connection 3. Updates position by advancing along the Bezier curve: P(t + Δt) = (1-t)³P₀ + 3(1-t)²tP₁ + 3(1-t)t²P₂ + t³P₃ 4. Checks if the particle has reached the end (t ≥ 1.0) — if so, resets to t = 0 with random jitter 5. Writes updated state back to the Storage Buffer

docs.title: 9.4 Rendering from Compute Output
docs.text: The vertex shader reads particle positions directly from the Storage Buffer (no CPU readback). Each particle is rendered as a camera-facing quad (billboard) using THREE.Points or a custom InstancedMesh. The fragment shader applies a soft circular alpha mask and blends additively. A post-processing bloom pass (via @react-three/postprocessing) creates the glow effect.

docs.title: 9.5 WebGPU Feature Detection & Fallback
docs.text: The system detects WebGPU support via navigator.gpu. If available, compute shaders are used. If not (e.g., on older devices or browsers without WebGPU), fallback strategies apply: - WebGL2 Transform Feedback: Emulates compute by using vertex shader to update positions - CPU fallback with WASM: Rust compiled to WebAssembly for particle physics, running in a Web Worker - Reduced particle count: Automatically reduces maxParticles to maintain 60fps

docs.title: 10.1 Architecture
docs.text:
The multi-user system enables multiple researchers to explore the same attention visualization together in VR. The architecture follows a hybrid client-server + peer-to-peer model:

  • Django Channels (Server): Room management, initial state sync, session recording
  • WebRTC DataChannel (P2P): Avatar pose streaming (head position, hand joints, gaze direction), low-latency interaction sync
  • Yjs CRDT (Shared State): Conflict-free replicated data type for shared selection state, annotation pins, and layer position. "Using Three.js for 3D graphics, Yjs for data synchronization, and WebSockets for real-time communication"

docs.title: 10.2 Avatar Representation
docs.text: Each remote user is represented as a simplified avatar: - Head: A small sphere at the user's headset position, colored uniquely per user - Hands: Skeletal hand meshes that mirror the user's real hand poses - Gaze beam: A thin laser from the head position showing where the user is looking (inspired by HeedVision: "CAAVs that track, record, and revisualize the collective attention of multiple users over time") - Name label: Floating text above the head showing the user's name

docs.title: 10.3 Collaborative Interaction
docs.text:
Shared interactions include:

Interaction Sync Method Latency Target Token selection Yjs shared state <100ms Layer navigation Yjs shared state <100ms Annotation pins Yjs shared state (persistent) <500ms Avatar pose WebRTC DataChannel <50ms Voice chat WebRTC audio track <200ms Hand gestures WebRTC DataChannel <50ms

docs.title: 10.4 Session Modes
docs.text: Mode Description Use Case Explore Together All users freely navigate; shared selection state Casual exploration Follow Mode One user is the "guide"; others automatically follow their viewpoint Teaching, presentations Presentation Mode Guide controls what everyone sees; audience can raise hands to ask questions Conference demos Annotation Mode Users place persistent annotation pins; threaded discussion per pin Research collaboration

docs.title: 11.1 Audio Sources
docs.text:
The spatial audio system uses Three.js PositionalAudio objects attached to 3D positions in the scene. The Web Audio API's PannerNode provides head-related transfer function (HRTF) processing for spatial perception.

Audio sources in the scene:

Source Position Sound Purpose Token nodes Each token's 3D position Soft chime when attention is high Auditory indication of important tokens Layer transitions Layer ring positions Whoosh sound when ascending/descending Spatial feedback for navigation Connection flow Midpoint of Bezier curves Variable-pitch hum (pitch ∝ attention weight) Auditory attention "weight map" Ambient Scene center Low drone, subtle Background atmosphere

docs.title: 11.2 Attention Sonification
docs.text:
Each attention connection produces a subtle sound whose characteristics encode the attention weight:

  • Pitch: Higher attention → higher pitch. Mapped logarithmically: pitch = 220Hz × (1 + weight × 4) (range: 220Hz–1100Hz)
  • Volume: Higher attention → louder. Mapped: volume = -40dB + weight × 30dB
  • Timbre: Positional heads → pure sine tone; semantic heads → rich harmonic series
  • Panning: Sound source positioned at the midpoint of the attention arc, so the user hears it spatially

docs.title: 11.3 Voice Chat (Multi-User)
docs.text: WebRTC audio tracks are captured from the user's microphone (with permission). Each remote user's audio is spatialized at their avatar's head position: "I added 3D positional audio using Three.js's PositionalAudio. Depending on your seat's location, the sound gets softer, louder, or shifts left/right". This means you hear other researchers' voices coming from where they're standing in the virtual room.

docs.title: 12.1 Diegetic vs. Non-Diegetic UI
docs.text:
The VR immersion room uses diegetic interfaces — UI elements that exist within the 3D world rather than being overlaid on the screen. This is more immersive and natural in VR.

Diegetic panels (floating in 3D space): - Control panel (attached to the user's off-hand, like a wristwatch) - Token information panel (appears next to selected/gazed token) - Layer selector (floating ring near the user) - Minimap (small 3D overview of all layers, like a tabletop model)

Non-diegetic (only in desktop fallback mode): - Settings menu overlay - Performance stats (FPS, particle count) - Session recording controls

docs.title: 12.2 Wrist-Mounted Control Panel
docs.text:
The user's non-dominant hand has a small panel "attached" to it (like a smartwatch). It shows: - Current layer number / total layers - Active head selection - Connection mode toggle (Tubes / Particles / Laser) - Particle density slider - Session recording button

The panel uses a PlaneGeometry rendered to a MeshStandardMaterial with a canvas texture (using Three.js CanvasTexture). The canvas is drawn using standard HTML Canvas 2D API, then updated as a texture each frame. This approach is compatible with React Three Fiber via useFrame.

docs.title: 12.3 Token Information Popup
docs.text: When a user gazes at (or points at) a token, a small information panel appears floating next to the token. It shows: - Token text - Token position in sequence - Top-3 attention targets (which tokens does this token attend to most?) - Top-3 attention sources (which tokens attend to this token most?) - Hidden state norm - If available: Dodrio-style linguistic annotations (POS tag, dependency role)

docs.title: 12.4 Minimap (Tabletop Model)
docs.text: A small 3D model of the entire transformer sits on a "table" at the center of the room (or floats at waist height). It shows all layers stacked vertically, with tokens as tiny dots. The user's current position and gaze direction are highlighted. Other users' positions are also shown. The minimap can be "grabbed" and resized, rotated, or moved.

docs.title: 13.1 Rendering Performance Targets
docs.text: Platform Target FPS Max Particles Max Connections Max Tokens Desktop (RTX 4090, WebGPU) 120 500,000 10,000 512 Desktop (GTX 1660, WebGL2) 60 50,000 2,000 256 Quest 3 (Standalone) 72 20,000 500 128 Quest 2 (Standalone) 72 10,000 200 64 Apple Vision Pro (WebXR) 90 50,000 1,000 256 Mobile (AR mode) 30 5,000 100 32

docs.title: 13.2 Optimization Techniques
docs.text:
Frustum Culling: Tokens and connections outside the user's field of view are not rendered. Three.js does this automatically for mesh objects.

Occlusion Culling: Tokens hidden behind other tokens or layer rings are not rendered. Implemented via a simple distance-based check (if token A is within 0.5m of token B and behind it, skip rendering A).

LOD (Level of Detail): - High detail (within 2m of user): Full text labels, sphere with 32 segments, emissive glow, particle flows - Medium detail (2m–10m): Smaller text labels, sphere with 16 segments, simplified connections - Low detail (10m+): Dots only, no labels, aggregate connections shown as a "cloud"

GPU Instancing: Tokens are rendered using THREE.InstancedMesh — a single draw call for all token spheres. Colors and transforms are stored in instance buffers updated each frame.

Texture Atlas for Labels: All token text labels are rendered to a single texture atlas using Canvas 2D. Each label is a quad mapped to its region of the atlas, reducing draw calls from N to 1.

Foveated Rendering (VR headsets that support it): The center 20° of the user's view is rendered at full resolution; the periphery at 1/4 resolution. This can yield 30-50% GPU savings on Quest Pro and Apple Vision Pro.

Web Worker Offloading: t-SNE/UMAP computation, matrix operations, and layout algorithms run in Web Workers, never on the main thread.

docs.title: 13.3 Memory Budget
docs.text:
Buffer Size (for 100K particles, 1K connections) Particle State Buffer 100,000 × 32B = 3.2 MB Connection Metadata Buffer 1,000 × 64B = 64 KB Token Position Buffer 256 × 12B = 3 KB Instance Matrix Buffer 256 × 64B = 16 KB Label Texture Atlas 2048×2048 RGBA = 16 MB Total GPU Memory ~20 MB

This is well within the memory budget of even standalone VR headsets (Quest 3 has 8GB shared RAM).

docs.title: 14.3 Feature Detection & Graceful Degradation
docs.text:
The system detects capabilities at startup and adjusts accordingly:

if (navigator.gpu) → Use WebGPU compute shaders for particles
else if (WEBGL2_compute) → Use WebGL2 transform feedback
else → Use CPU + WASM for particles, reduced count

if (navigator.xr) → Enable full VR mode with hand tracking
else → Desktop explore mode with mouse/keyboard

if (handTracking supported) → Enable gesture recognition
else → Use controllers or mouse/keyboard

if (eyeTracking supported) → Enable foveated rendering + gaze beams

docs.title: 15.1 Recording Data
docs.text:
Each VR session can be recorded for later playback, sharing, or teaching. The recording captures:

  • Headset pose (position, orientation) at 72Hz
  • Hand joint poses (25 joints × 2 hands) at 72Hz
  • Voice audio (if enabled) as a WebM/Opus stream
  • Interaction events: token selections, layer changes, annotation placements, gesture events
  • Scene state: which model, layer, head, and text are being visualized

The recording is compressed (poses use delta encoding, audio uses Opus codec) and uploaded to the Django backend for storage. A 10-minute session with 2 users produces approximately 15-30 MB of data.

docs.title: 15.2 Playback
docs.text: Playback runs entirely in the browser (desktop or VR). The recorded poses are replayed through the same React Three Fiber scene. The viewer can: - Watch from the recorder's perspective (first-person) - Watch from any angle (free camera) - Watch from a "god's eye" overview - Pause, rewind, fast-forward - Click on tokens during playback to see what the recorder was looking at

docs.title: 15.3 Integration with Platform
docs.text: Recorded sessions are stored as VRRecording models in Django, linked to the user's profile and the attention pattern being explored. Sessions can be: - Shared via link (like the existing share-link system) - Embedded in notes or papers (using the existing widget embed) - Used as teaching materials in courses - Reviewed collaboratively (multiple people watching the same recording with synced playback)
